--- Page 8 ---
<meta>This page contains the formal legal privilege (an early form of copyright) granted in 1670 by the provincial government to the publisher Jan Rieuwertsz. This legal protection was essential for a massive undertaking like Brandt’s history to prevent "pirated" editions by other printers. Note that while this privilege is dated 1670, it appears here in the 1677 edition, as the rights were typically granted for fifteen years.</meta>

# PRIVILEGE. <note>A "Privilege" was a legal grant of exclusive printing and selling rights, an early form of copyright protection issued by the government.</note>

The States of Holland and West Friesland make known: Whereas it has been shown to us by *Jan Rieuwertsz*, Citizen and Bookseller at *Amsterdam*, how *Gerard Brandt*, some years ago, had composed and published the *History of the Reformation* and other *Ecclesiastical Histories* occurring in and around the *Netherlands* since the year 712; which *History* the same *Author* had expanded with significant additions and continuations, divided into various volumes, and intended to have printed and published by the *Petitioner* <term>Petitioner: translated from 'Suppliant', the person making the formal request to the government</term>; but since he, the *Petitioner*, was fearful that some profit-seeking individuals might make the labor of the new printing fruitless, he, the *Petitioner*, turned to us, humbly requesting that it might please us to grant him, the *Petitioner*, letters of *Patent* <term>Patent: translated from 'Octroy', a formal document granting exclusive rights</term> in the usual form for a period of fifteen years, to the end that he, the *Petitioner*, might print and have printed, publish, and sell the same *History of the Reformation*, with its additions and continuations, during the aforementioned time, within the aforementioned lands; forbidding any and all persons to reprint the same in any manner, directly or indirectly, in whole or in part, in large or in small format, or to bring into the aforementioned lands, sell, or trade any copies reprinted elsewhere, without the consent of the *Petitioner*, on pain of forfeiture of the reprinted, imported, or sold copies, and such penalties as it should please us to find good and to decree: **SO IT IS**, that we, having considered the matter and the request aforementioned, and being inclined toward the prayer of the *Petitioner*, out of our certain knowledge, sovereign power, and authority, have authorized and granted patent to the *Petitioner*, and do authorize and grant patent to the same by these presents, to the end that he, during the period of fifteen years, shall alone be allowed to have printed, publish, and sell the aforementioned book within the aforementioned lands of *Holland* and *West Friesland*; forbidding any and all persons to reprint the same book in any manner, in whole or in part, in large or small format, or [to trade] copies reprinted elsewhere, imported, traded, or sold, under a fine of three hundred guilders, one-third of which is to be applied to the *Officer* of the place where the case occurs, one-third for the *Poor*, and the remaining third for the *Petitioner*. Providing it is understood that we, wishing to gratify the *Petitioner* with this our *Patent* to prevent his loss through the reprinting of the aforementioned book, do not thereby in any way intend to authorize or endorse the contents thereof, and much less to give the same any further credit, status, or reputation under our protection and defense, but rather that the *Petitioner*, in case anything improper should be included therein, shall be held responsible to answer for all of it at his own expense. <note>This disclaimer was standard; the government protected the publisher's commercial rights without necessarily agreeing with the religious or political views expressed in the book.</note> And to the end that the *Petitioner* may enjoy the effect of this our consent and patent as is proper, we charge any and all whom it may concern to let the *Petitioner* enjoy and use the contents of this peacefully, quietly, and fully, ceasing all hindrance to the contrary. Done in *The Hague* under our great Seal appended hereto, the *21st of April*, in the year of our Lord and Savior sixteen hundred and seventy.

->JOHAN de WITT. vt. <note>original: "vt." is an abbreviation for "vidit," Latin for "he has seen [it]," indicating official approval by the Grand Pensionary Johan de Witt.</note> 1670.<-

->By order of the States<-

->HERBERT van BEAUMONT. 1670.<-

<summary>This document is the official fifteen-year copyright "Privilege" granted by the States of Holland to publisher Jan Rieuwertsz for Gerard Brandt's history. It includes a stiff fine for counterfeiters and a government disclaimer regarding the book's content, signed by the famous statesman Johan de Witt.</summary>
<keywords>Privilege, Copyright, Jan Rieuwertsz, Gerard Brandt, Johan de Witt, 17th-century law, book trade, Amsterdam, The Hague, Holland</keywords>

<image-desc>A large ornamental woodcut initial letter 'D' decorated with intricate vine, leaf, and scrollwork patterns within a square border.</image-desc>Through the rise of the Reformation and the weapons of this state <note>A reference to the Dutch Republic’s military struggle for independence during the Eighty Years' War</note>, God has brought about a beneficial blessing for us and delivered us from an evil destructive to both soul and country. Holy Scripture, the only rule of faith and life, which the Papacy <term>Papacy: translated from 'Pausdom', referring here to the Roman Catholic Church hierarchy</term> withheld from the people, has been placed back into our hands. Also, the coercion of conscience has been driven away:

->*The strangling, burning, and carving*<-
->*Is over. —*<-
<note>This poetic fragment refers to the brutal methods of the Inquisition used against reformers.</note>

One may now read the Gospel, live according to one's conscience, and make known whatever one understands to be for the best of the church and Christendom with more safety, without having to fear unlawful violence. For this we must thank, after God, the freedom of the fatherland and the just rule of the high Authorities.

Thus the light is set upon the candlestick <note>A biblical allusion to Matthew 5:15, suggesting that truth is no longer hidden</note>, and its use is left free to everyone.

But what was the consequence? Have people been willing to see the truth that shone in our eyes? Have they given place to love—the soul of true faith—and put it into practice?

Let each person ask this of their own heart, which is conscious of itself: whether

Ask experience, and immediately one will notice that that true and simple godliness <term>Godliness: translated from 'godtvruchtigheit', referring to sincere, lived piety</term>, which flourished during the oppression of persecution, gradually declined again in times of prosperity, and fell into corruption, indeed from bad to worse. The tree of knowledge, just as happened in the beginning <note>A reference to the Fall of Man in the Garden of Eden</note>, has been chosen over the tree of life. Piety had to give way to subtle scholarship. Various virtues,

-> which at all times <-
-> *Observing is more unbearable than suffering,* <-
<note>This poetic line suggests that witnessing the moral decay of the reformed church is more painful than the physical persecution they once endured.</note>

innocence, patience, humility, and love find themselves pushed aside on our soil: wickedness, impatience, arrogance, hatred, and envy take the upper hand. Each bends the healing word <note>The Holy Scriptures</note> to his own liking. Each makes himself a personal Gospel.

Everyone wants the weeds—the evil of the Papacy—to be rejected, and rejects it in his own way. Many seek to root it out, yet by the very means that sustain it: they seek help from the arm of the flesh <note>The 'arm of the flesh' refers to secular power, such as the government or military, used to enforce religious will</note>; they wish to convert by force. The sword of the spirit, on the other hand—the word of God—ought to wear away harmful beliefs in a more fitting manner through proper teaching and upright living.

Many have departed from the Roman church in such a way that, because of the evil that existed there, they also rejected everything else that was good, or at least not bad. "But thus far I do not find," writes the Lord of Zuilichem, Constantijn Huygens* <note>Constantijn Huygens (1596–1687) was a renowned Dutch poet, diplomat, and polymath</note> (*a prominent member of the body of the Reformed Church*) *“that anything, good or harmless in itself, should be judged as evil or harmful, simply because it is in use—or even in abuse—by those who are mired in other heavier or lighter errors.” And speaking of a certain custom of the English Church <note>The Anglican Church</note>, where in the mornings one finds church officials occupied with the reading of God’s word, the reciting of beautiful prayers, and the singing of hymns accompanied by the organ, he adds:* † *“Does it smell Roman? And is it better to remain empty: than our*

<meta>This page continues the author's critique of the religious climate in the Dutch Republic. The previous page ended with the observation that many people, in their rejection of the Roman Catholic Church, discarded not only its errors but also everything that was good.</meta>

...enemies imitated what is good? *Christians, un-blinded <note>original: 'ontblindthokte', implying being released from a coop or having blinders removed</note> Christians, dear members of the household of Faith, for the sake of the Lord in whom we believe, let us finally drive this childish spite from our hearts; I fear it keeps more good things out than it keeps bad things at bay.* This narrow-mindedness also displeased Charles I, King of Great Britain, a Prince of holy memory, who confronted a certain Scottish Teacher with the following: <margin>1 See *The Papers of the Conference at Neuchâtel* p. 18.</margin> *To say that an argument is bad because the Papists <note>A term used then for Roman Catholics</note> make use of it, or that a thing is good because it is in use by some Reformed churches, can have no weight with me at all, until the time you have proven to me either that the latter are infallible, or that the former advocate no truth at all.*

Some believe that they not only possess the truth, but that they alone possess it; indeed, that all others ought to bow to their opinion. When one is in <term>possession <note>original: 'posseffie', a legal term used here to describe the dominance of a particular religious group</note></term> of worldly honor, when one becomes the most numerous and the most powerful, one desires to rule over those who are lesser. <margin>2 Grotius, *Apology* [Verantwoordingh], Chapter V, p. 53.</margin> *But in matters of faith, possession has little power, and those who are fewer in number cannot be overpowered by the majority in this regard, except by force.* The greater part of the world had formerly become Arian <note>A reference to the 4th-century Arian controversy regarding the nature of Christ's divinity; at one point, Arianism was more widely accepted than the now-orthodox Nicene creed</note>: yet the other Christians paid no heed to numbers, which is often a sign of evil. Let us hear Nazianzenus <note>Gregory of Nazianzus, a 4th-century Archbishop and theologian</note> speak of this: <margin>3 Oration XXX, p. 440.</margin> *These, he said—namely the Arians—have the houses, we have the Householder; these have the temples, we have God; and this besides, that we are living temples of the living God, living offerings, reasonable burnt offerings, perfect sacrifices, [indeed as] Gods through the grace of the adored Trinity. These have the people, we have the Angels; these have audacity, we have faith; these use threats, we use prayers; these cast out, we endure; these have gold and silver, we have the purified doctrine.* How many now look to such outward appearances, to the great number, to the prominence of men; whereas in matters of religion one ought only to pay attention to the

<summary>The author argues against religious intolerance and the tendency to judge the truth of a doctrine based on who uses it or how many people follow it. He cites King Charles I and Gregory of Nazianzus to demonstrate that truth is not determined by worldly power, majority rule, or the rejection of everything associated with an opponent.</summary>

--- Page 12 ---
<meta>This page continues the author’s argument regarding religious tolerance. The previous page ended with a mention of the 4th-century Arian controversy, suggesting that the majority of the world had then followed Arianism rather than the teachings established by Christ.</meta>

...those things that the Lord Christ and his Apostles made known, commanded, and lived.

And how easily that which our understanding does not grasp, and which others hold for truth, is condemned as an error! Of oneself one says: we can err, yet we do not err; of others one shouts: they can err, and they do err. *But if it seems to us that they err,* wrote the tolerant Martin Bucer <note>Martin Bucer (1491–1551) was a prominent German Protestant reformer who famously sought to mediate between conflicting religious factions.</note> \*, *why do we not consider that we ourselves might possibly err where we think they fail? For no one errs intentionally; nor is anyone, however holy they may be, free from error. It is thus the case with human affairs that, as long as we are clothed in this flesh, even the lovers of truth allow themselves to imagine they see many things, even in the Holy Scriptures, which are nevertheless not found there at all. However, as long as that error persists, and the flesh takes such pleasure in its own inventions <note>original: 'gedichtſelen', referring to things made up or imagined by the human mind</note>, that which is false is often protected as true—even by very holy people—in such a way that, in order to maintain what is false, they even fiercely fight against the truth itself.* These [people], he desires that we should entrust to Christ their Lord, and yet honor as brothers, as long as one perceives from sincere and certain fruits that the Spirit of the Father has a place with them. *Indeed,* he says, *the more matters in which they err, the more it becomes you to treat them with more diligent and helpful love: so that they, feeling Christ’s spirit in you and being furthermore bound by your helpfulness, might more gladly hear what you say and sooner believe it, and you thus show yourself (as you are obliged) to be a fit instrument of the spirit of your Savior.*

But instead of listening to such lessons, one hates those who err even more than the error itself. Men commonly confirm their judgment with <term>anathemas <note>An 'anathema' is a formal curse by a church, excommunicating a person or denouncing a specific doctrine as damnable.</note></term> or curses, and give these as much force as they can. Thus one often separates, thus one tears apart; one burns, one denounces as heretics, one persecutes: each according to their power.

<meta>This page continues the author's preface, building on the previous page's discussion of Martin Bucer’s call for religious tolerance. These defects turn some churches into dungeons and torture racks for souls, which do violence to the conscience. This is the weed in the Lord's field, which often chokes the wheat <note>A reference to the Parable of the Wheat and the Tares from the Gospel of Matthew, often used in arguments for religious toleration to suggest that "heretics" (weeds) should be left until the final judgment rather than forcibly removed.</note>.

Yet this is no evil of today or yesterday alone: the seed of this chaff was sown long ago, even in the time of the Reformation; but that era also produced men who saw it, pointed it out, warned both clergy and laity, gave the best advice, and sought to keep them within the bounds of their duty. Thus Erasmus, Cassander, Franciscus Junius, Antonius Coranus <note>These were all famous "mediating" theologians who sought a middle ground between Catholicism and Protestantism, or between different Protestant factions.</note>, along with other godly theologians, stepped in to correct mistakes, moderate disputes, and seek peace. So that to all of them, in some measure, applies what was sung in particular of the great man from Rotterdam <note>Erasmus of Rotterdam (1466–1536), the most famous humanist of the Northern Renaissance.</note>:

> *All his prayer is for peace.*
> *Prudently he keeps to the middle,*
> *And fixes his gaze on the Apostolic stars,*
> *While here Charybdis and there Scylla burns.* <note>Scylla and Charybdis are monsters from Greek mythology representing a choice between two evils; Erasmus is depicted as navigating a dangerous middle path between religious extremes by looking toward the "stars" of the early Church.</note>

Regarding these and other events concerning the Reformation of church abuses, our contemporaries and countrymen should, in my opinion, have a bit more knowledge than is commonly found among them. For a true account of such histories can greatly serve a sound judgment, helping to weigh what partisanship—which seeks to maintain unnecessary schisms and to make the unnecessary appear necessary—brings forward to its advantage, and to distinguish appearance from truth. This is also so that one does not diminish the good, nor magnify the evil, but values everything according to its worth.

This objective recently led me to compile this *History of the Reformation in the Netherlands*, with some remarks serving that purpose.

But in doing so, one uncovers the sores of the churches.

It is true, yet they are old wounds; the more one covers, wraps, and disguises them, the deeper they fester, and the more schis- <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "scheur-", which likely completes as "scheuringen" (schisms) on the following page.</note>

--- Page 14 ---
<meta>The previous page discussed how religious intolerance and "weeds" in the church create a "torture rack for souls." This page continues that argument, emphasizing the necessity of historical honesty and admitting past errors to achieve true religious peace.</meta>

...cause the disease of schism <note>term: *scheurziekte* — a common 17th-century medical metaphor for religious divisions tearing the "body" of the church</note>. Discovery serves healing. Also, he who faithfully writes history is not bound—as **Onuphrius Panvinus** <note>Onuphrio Panvinio (1529–1568) was an Italian historian and Augustinian friar known for his commitment to historical accuracy over papal propaganda.</note> rightly said—*to describe the matter as it ought to have happened, but as it actually happened: for otherwise no actual events are written, but lies are forced upon us.* Let us then endure the truth, even if it goes against us. To err is human, after all; and it is a useful nobility of spirit to acknowledge one’s mistakes. Lesser minds, writes **Casaubon** <note>Isaac Casaubon (1559–1614) was a brilliant classical scholar who worked on the history of the early church.</note> in the dedication of his work on **Polybius** <note>Polybius was a Greek historian known for "pragmatic history," focusing on cause and effect and political reality.</note>, *do not allow anything to be taken from them, because they have nothing: but it is so far from the truth that excellent men, who have confidence in great matters, would take offense at the sincerity of faithful historians; on the contrary, they confess their own errors and failings with a noble heart.*

If we did this, how much would we learn that now remains hidden from our eyes! One would read and perceive past events, the defects, and the remedies, with such a heart as is proper. This History might perhaps be of use to many Christians who, like blind men led by blind guides, allow themselves to be led toward the ditch of partisanship <note>A reference to the biblical proverb "if the blind lead the blind, both shall fall into the ditch" (Matthew 15:14).</note>.

If those of the **Roman Catholic persuasion** <note>term: *Roomfchgefinden* — literally "those minded toward Rome," a neutral 17th-century term for Catholics.</note> here wished to hear and see, they could learn from their **Erasmus** (whom I also place among the Reformers, yet call "theirs" because he spent his days in their communion) that excessive superstition suppressed the truth; that human institutions gained the upper hand and turned Christianity into a Pharisaism <note>The author uses "Pharisaism" to describe a religion focused on strict outward rules and legalism rather than spiritual truth.</note>; that the raging of coercion of conscience was the work of executioners—but not of theologians. They could learn from their **Cassander** <note>George Cassander (1513–1566) was a Catholic theologian who sought a middle ground to reunite Christendom.</note> that the Papacy is in need of reformation, and that salvation may also be hoped for outside the Roman church. Thus they would become aware of the vanity of their fancied infallibility and look toward reform.

To the **Reformed** (by which I include all who set themselves against the Papacy), much could still come to light here through closer consideration of matters that was previously not unknown to them...

<meta>The previous page warned of the "ditch of partisanship" where the blind lead the blind. This page continues that warning, arguing that historical truth and religious tolerance are being forgotten in favor of narrow-mindedness and hypocrisy.</meta>

** 2

...which was previously known, but now seems to be forgotten by some.

Among other things, the truth of history would teach them: that some wrongly accuse the high authorities of their kindness toward the **Papists** <note>original: *Pausgeſinden* — literally "those minded toward the Pope."</note>, to whom some freedom of religion is still allowed in various places in this country by **connivance** <note>term: *oogluikinge* — literally "looking through the fingers." This refers to the Dutch policy where Catholic worship was officially illegal but tolerated in "hidden churches" as long as it was not public and taxes were paid.</note>; for that truth would remind them that in the times of our fathers, arms were taken up for the common liberty, even at the request and with the help of those of the Roman faith.

But they are idolaters, it is said; they fall down before men and lesser things. Yet are we entirely free from such or similar sins, when we, out of greed, serve **Mammon** <note>A biblical term for wealth or property, often personified as a false god that demands devotion.</note> or riches, and make the belly our God through excess? Those among some denominations who will not yield a single jot from everything their Teachers once understood and taught—whether it be true, untrue, or false—do they not in some way turn them into idols to whom they pay too much honor? <meta>This page continues the discussion of Franciscus Junius (1545–1602), a highly influential Huguenot theologian and professor at Leiden University. The previous page ended mid-sentence introducing his views on moderation and church unity. This section uses Junius’s own writings to argue that minor theological differences should not lead to the exclusion of others from the Christian community.</meta>

From him one would learn, *that one should not argue so much about certain persons, or the maintenance of their dignity, order, and authority, as if no church existed outside of this or that specific form of church. And truly, he says, that the churches are torn apart by them I do not find good at all: but neither do I find it good that those who, through their ignorance and weakness, tear themselves away, are so harshly cut off by your knowledge and authority—or rather your tyranny (whoever you may be). For if they do not recognize the church in which I live by God’s grace, it shall nonetheless be enough for me at this time if I see that some Church of Christ <term>kerke Christi: the universal body of believers across different denominations</term> is recognized by them. I shall not sweat much over whether they recognize me, or this or that specific church, as long as they merely recognize Christ; holding it for certain that if they are gradually strengthened in Christ, it will happen that, the eye of their understanding being more enlightened, they shall see that I and others live in Christ, and they shall unite further with the assembly of the godly. For if they defile that purest fountain of Scripture with the mud of their fictions and traditions, would we then think ourselves better defenders of that same truth than God Himself is?*

One would also learn from that same Junius †: *That diversity of opinion should not so easily break peace or unity. Even if we all, he writes, do not have one and the same opinion in all things, let it be far from us that we should therefore immediately conclude not to be one any longer, while we are at one in so many and in the foremost matters. Those who have one God the Father, from whom all things are; one Christ, in whom all things are; and one Holy Spirit, through whom all things are; one body in the unity of the Spirit; one faith in these foremost articles—even if they differ therein, so that one believes more here and the other less—shall we therefore deny who we are, and create schisms <term>scheuringen: formal splits or divisions within the church</term> among one another because we are not of one mind in everything? Why? Do we not see in one and the same person a will that struggles against itself, and that there is nonetheless but one will? The natural will shall desire that which the rational <note>original: *verstandige* (wise or intellectual)</note> will flees; the senses shall rouse a man’s will against his judgment.*

<meta>This page continues the excerpt from the Dutch theologian Franciscus Junius, focusing on his arguments for religious tolerance. <page-type>text</page-type>
<sig>** 3</sig>
<meta>catchword: 'T sal (It shall)</meta>

of his understanding: a sick person will, with the same will, desire his health and that which is contrary to health; toward the one, his senses will pull him, and toward the other, nature. Often a pious person will desire what the Lord does not will, and yet he will at the same time feel an inner burden for wanting what the Lord does not will—just as *Augustine* <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a central figure in Western Christianity whose writings on the "two wills" are referenced here</note> proved in former times by the parable of a son praying for his father's life to be lengthened, though God did not will it. Shall we therefore make two people out of one, or shall a man tear himself apart and break his own bonds? Do you wonder then that what happens in one man also happens in the great body of the church? And what you tolerate in a body that belongs to only one man, shall you not tolerate in *Christ's* body <note>original: *Christi*</note>, which has been brought together by God? Shall you not tolerate it in this time, now that the gathering of that body has only just begun, when you tolerate it in the fully grown body of a lowly man—that is, one who has reached his full height and stature? God grant us better. Let us rather all work together with one mind; so that, even if we are of a different opinion in specific matters, we may be one in general. Let us lift our eyes to behold the throne of His grace, set in heaven, where not only those who were of another understanding, but (what is far more) those who were at enmity with God, are reconciled with God through the blood of *Jesus Christ* <note>original: *Jesu Christi*</note>. If someone who holds a different opinion in human affairs wrongs me, I am commanded by the Lord's authority to forgive; yet if someone differs from me in the matter of faith, if he errs, he does not wrong me, but his Lord. Yet the Lord forgives him; and should I not forgive him? Furthermore, if he errs, the Lord has not yet revealed it to him; we must endure the erring one; we must wait upon the Lord, who may instruct the one who wanders. One must set one's hands to work, not to cast out the erring one, but rather to show him the way, if God should wish to use our service for his salvation and instruction.

<meta>This page continues the argument for religious tolerance by Franciscus Junius, specifically focusing on the importance of intellectual humility and mutual forbearance. It shall make us say, with Bucer <note>Martin Bucer (1491–1551), a Protestant reformer known for his efforts to find common ground between different Christian factions</note> and Sturm <note>Johannes Sturm (1507–1589), an influential German educator and diplomat associated with the Reformation in Strasbourg</note>: \*I CONDEMN NO ONE IN WHOM I FIND SOMETHING OF CHRIST <note>original Latin: *EGO NEMINEM DAMNO IN QUO ALIQUID CHRISTI REPERIO*</note>: *I condemn no one in whom I find anything Christian;* and with an older Church Father <note>St. Augustine of Hippo</note>: †*It shall not weary me, if I doubt in anything, to investigate; nor shall I be ashamed, if I err in anything, to learn. Therefore let everyone who reads this, where he is equally certain, proceed with me; where he is equally in doubt, investigate with me: where he notices his error, return to me; where he notices mine, call me back. Let us thus enter the way of love together, reaching out to him of whom it is said: seek his face always.*

That investigation shall make us think of means to help promote the harmony of Christians, each in his own way.

It shall suggest to us: That Christ alone is our Master, and that we are all brothers, and consequently ought never to separate or tear ourselves apart. It shall tell us: That no one among us should be wise beyond what one ought to be wise, but be wise unto moderation <note>A reference to the Apostle Paul’s advice in Romans 12:3 regarding humility and "sober judgment"</note>, not wise in himself, nor feel [or think] beyond what is written, but according to the measure of knowledge that God has shared with each: that one must bear with the weak and tender, so that they may gather in peace with us: that one ought to wait for those who, in some part of Religion, are of another understanding (if one cannot bring them to our opinion), until God deigns to reveal the hidden truth to them also: and meanwhile holding fast to what is known to everyone, the foundation of the faith, mutually tolerating each other in matters of lesser weight; until the time that we shall know everything perfectly, and no longer know only in part.

Such considerations tend toward ecclesiastical peace, which could well be found, if we were only what we ought to be, and if we were willing to give up our own for something better, or to bear with one another. In the Roman church, one can find more than three hundred questions that are disputed among the learned without schism <note>The author points out that even the Catholic Church, often viewed as monolithic by his peers, permits internal debate on many issues without those debates resulting in the group splitting apart</note>.

# PREFACE

### TO THE

# R E A D E R.

The writing of Histories, accounts, and the deeds of men has, from of old, had its difficulty and danger. Not only because of what was required regarding the Author and the writing itself, but also because truth—the eye, indeed the soul of History—is commonly hated and produces hatred. It is an old defect that people are much more inclined to do evil than they are to hear or read about what has been done wrongly. One also found, which is deplorable, that at all times the number of evil men, and consequently of evil deeds, far exceeded the number of good ones. So that, among so many human failings, there was much more to blame than to praise. This caused History to occupy itself mostly with evil, or to contain matters that were offensive to the wicked. 

Here, the historian <note>original: *Historie-schrijver*</note> could escape no hatred; for just as it was one of his primary duties that he spoke no falsehood, feared to write no truth, nor kept silent about virtues, so the truth required in particular that one must recount, alongside the mistakes <note>original: *misslagen*; can also be translated as "lapses" or "failures"</note> of friends, the virtues of enemies as well. The evil intentions, words, attempts, and deeds had to be recorded to deter others from evil by way of the reproach and dishonor of succeeding ages. Therefore, the Author had to rid himself of all favor and disfavor, love and hatred toward men, and [hold] the love of truth [above] all <note>The text ends mid-sentence; the catchword indicates the next page begins with "other" or "others."</note>

->* * *<-

They sought to forcibly silence the righteous judgment of truth regarding the reputation of the great and the small, which is pronounced in History.

# P R E F A C E.

...to correct what is evil or strive to improve it. I have no more concealed or excused the flaws of friends than the faults of enemies or opponents. I speak all the more boldly because one of the greatest Lights and oldest Teachers of the <term>Reformed Christians</term> <note>Members of the Dutch Reformed Church, the official state-supported church in the Dutch Republic.</note> in <term>Holland</term>, after reading the previous edition, deigned to declare to me in person that he found my History impartial and useful. 

Something occurred there which deserves to be mentioned here. He complained that concerning his grandfather—no minor instrument of the <term>Reformation</term> in the <term>Netherlands</term>—something was written in that work which portrayed him as very fierce and biased in his disposition; he also pointed out to me the man’s gentleness and modesty shown on other occasions. But when that upright man understood and considered the proof of my statement, he expressed himself with these remarkable words: *That proof is enough for me. Let it then, above my grandfather and above all else, remain there, because it is the truth.* Such was his love for the <term>truth</term>. 

Thus one submits oneself to the truth, and it sets us free from all partisanship. He who views the described matters with such eyes will not easily take offense at the account of his friends' faults, but will help lament and improve human failings. He will also find on various occasions material that will sow in his heart the seeds of modesty, moderation, reasonableness, and <term>flexibility</term> <note>The original Dutch uses "rekkelijkheit," a term famously associated with the "Rekkelijken" (the lenient or flexible) who favored religious tolerance, as opposed to the "Preciezen" (the precise or rigid).</note> concerning the handling of matters of faith: especially the seed of love, the mother of <term>harmony</term>, the nurse of all virtues, which—I say this in the words of <term>Casaubon</term> <note>Isaac Casaubon (1559–1614), a highly influential Huguenot scholar and classical philologist.</note>—is a conqueror and destroyer of all <term>heresies</term>; which extinguishes heresies as they arise and prevents their emergence. 

<margin>Casaubon in the Preface to the Epistle of Gregory of Nyssa to Eustathia, prefixed, p. A. 4.</margin>

From this arise narratives that obscure the truth.* This caused a man of great foresight to say: That the truth sometimes reaches our knowledge like money in the coffers of Kings—not without significant loss and great reduction. <note>The author uses a metaphor suggesting that just as taxes or tributes diminish as they pass through many hands toward the royal treasury, historical truth is often diluted or corrupted as it is passed from person to person.</note> *If it then does not show itself clearly enough amidst the variety of accounts, I shall apply all the more diligence in investigating and researching the true state of affairs. If I should nonetheless err in something, and be led away from the truth by some probability or misunderstanding, let it be forgiven me; as it happens not by design, but against my will, and after sufficient effort to strike the matter rightly.* 

But when the truth, deeply hidden under many wrappings, allows itself to be excavated only with difficulty, and matters are uncertain or obscure, then I shall describe the uncertain as uncertain, and the obscure as obscure. If one finds in the continuation of these histories matters recorded quite differently by other writers, these [my accounts] have appeared thus to me from credible and certain documents, which are almost always noted in the work or its <term>marginalia</term> <note>original: "kantschriften." # G. J. VOSSIUS. <note>Gerardus Johannes Vossius (1577–1649) was one of the most famous scholars of the Dutch Golden Age. His works on the "Art of History" defined how scholars of this period believed history should be researched and written.</note>

IT IS NOT ENOUGH THAT, IN THE WRITING OF HISTORY, WE DO NOT ERR THROUGH LOVE OR HATRED FOR THOSE NOW LIVING: BUT NEITHER SHOULD THE VIRTUE OR WICKEDNESS OF THOSE WHO CAN NO LONGER HELP OR HARM US BE THE OBJECT OF SUCH LOVE OR HATRED FOR US THAT WE DO NOT ALWAYS KEEP BEFORE OUR EYES WHAT LUCIAN SAYS: <note>Lucian of Samosata (c. 125 – after 180 AD) was a Syrian-Greek satirist. His essay *How to Write History* is a classic text that demands the historian be fearless, incorruptible, and a "citizen of the world."</note> ONE MUST SACRIFICE TO TRUTH ALONE, AND DISREGARD ALL OTHER THINGS. <note>original Greek: ΜΟΝΗ ΘΥΤΕΟΝ ΤΗ ΑΛΗΘΕΙΑ, ΤΩΝ Δ' ΑΛΛΩΝ ΑΠΑΝΤΩΝ ΑΜΕΛΗΤΕΟΝ.</note> ONE MUST SACRIFICE TO TRUTH ALONE; ALL OTHER MATTERS TRULY MUST BE SET ASIDE. <note>original Latin: SOLI IMMOLANDUM VERITATI, CÆTERA VERO OMNIA POSTPONENDA.</note>

->That is,<-

It is not enough that one does not overstep in the writing of Histories through love or hate for people who are living now: but even the virtue or the vice of those who can no longer further or hinder us may not be loved or hated to such a degree that one would ever forget what Lucian says: *One must stand in service to the truth alone, and set all other things aside.*

*Introduction.*
*Hugo Grotius, Annals, Book I, pages 8, 9.* <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645) was a Dutch jurist and scholar. Brandt begins his history by citing Grotius’s account of how early Christianity changed over time.</note>

The Christian Religion was, in times past, venerable for its simplicity alone; but when, shortly thereafter, the teachers of various Philosophies became Christians, they sought to adorn this religion with the rules of their own teachings. Furthermore, the Jews, Greeks, and others [added] their ancestral ceremonies, so that they might turn the dignity of those traditions—which had not been established in vain—to a better use. Yet these things, which for a long time had been left to each person’s freedom and were adopted only through the specific approval of certain individuals or churches, gradually increased through usage. Through the eloquence of the Teachers and the agreement of the Councils, they were transformed into law, made mandatory, and—following the crude ignorance of unlearned times—easily defended through the blind detours of disputations. Meanwhile, the Bishops of Rome, who had always possessed great authority, established a certain spiritual kingdom. Leaving aside the cities of Asia and Egypt, and also Constantinople (which vied for that same supremacy), they seized the highest authority for themselves. They appointed the Cardinals as assistants <margin>* Assistants or counselors.</margin> <note>original: *Asseſſores*. This refers to those who sit alongside a judge or leader to provide counsel.</note> or councilmen, and upon this established the long-lasting order of their power. At first, no one withdrew from that authority, because many European nations had received the Christian Religion through teachers sent from Rome. This caused the Latin or Roman ecclesiastical customs and language to be used everywhere in the church... <note>The text continues on the next page, as indicated by the catchword "fijn" (fine/pure).</note>

->H I S T O R Y<-

skillfully introduced. But these Bishops (now called Popes) went further; once they had seized authority over divine matters, they began to issue new decrees, interpret ancient ones as they saw fit, and keep the Holy Scriptures out of the hands of the common people. They argued that it was very dangerous if the "ignorant curiosity" of the public were allowed to judge such weighty matters as Religion. But Nicholas understood that the supreme judgment belonged to him, and summoned the Bishops who had allowed this to Rome. Therefore, Gunther 10 and Theutgaud 11, the Archbishops of Cologne and Trier, were sent there in the name of all. From a fearsome land, namely from the Roman Church, this harsh vision has been announced to me; from there comes the whirlwind like a tempest from the South. For the Bishop of Rome, the Father of all churches, sends letters against us to Robert, the Count of Flanders, which read as follows: *Paschal the Bishop, servant <note>original: "servant of the servants of God," a traditional papal title</note>.. Who is not filled with sadness over such letters?.. Not so much because of the dreadfulness of the danger, but because of the dreadful novelty of the matter, that such lamentable letters could be written by a mother against her daughters, even though they had sinned... In the judgment of Solomon (1 Kings 3), the true mother would rather see her son live with a foreign woman than that he should be divided in two by the sword of the judge... David once saw the striking Angel stretching out the sword over Jerusalem, and we, daughters of the Roman Church, see the Bishop of Rome, who is an Angel of the Lord, with the sword outstretched over the church. David prayed that the people would not be killed, and our Angel gives the sword to Robert, and prays that he kill us. From where has our Angel obtained this sword?.. There is a sword of the spirit, which is the word of God, .. and there is yet another sword of the Spirit, by which we kill the defects of our flesh... Since the Apostles had only two swords from the Lord <note>A reference to Luke 22:38, used in the Middle Ages to debate the "Two Swords" doctrine of spiritual and secular power</note>, from where then does the Apostolic man <note>The Pope</note> get this third sword, which he hands over to Robert, his squire, to use against us? Perhaps the Apostolic man ran to Ezekiel the Prophet to snatch the third sword out of his hand, to turn right and left, and to kill the good with the wicked?.. He sends his greeting as a Father to the beloved Son, and promises him the Apostolic blessing: but many also suspect that he commands him no works that can earn the salvation or the blessing of God... Who has ever persecuted God's people, who has ever persecuted God's church without punishment?.. And behold there the works of the "righteous war" which this Father commands to his Son, the Pope to the soldier of the Heavenly King, through which he can strive for the Heavenly Jerusalem: namely, by fighting against God's church. We thank you, he says, that you have carried out our command against the district of Cambrai <note>Robert of Flanders had recently ravaged the Diocese of Cambrai at the Pope's request because the city supported the Emperor.</note>. Who can recall without sadness how great the devastation and destruction of the church of Cambrai was? I, being a daughter of the Roman Church, grieved for the people of Cambrai out of a feeling of kinship; but now hearing that all this evil has happened by command of the Apostolic authority, I grieve now all the more, for I fear for my mother, that there might strike her that which God says through Isaiah: "Woe to those who make unjust laws.." <margin>1102.</margin>
*...that such great ruin of the church, such great oppression of the poor and widows, such great abomination of plundering and robbing, and what is even more, the murdering without distinction of good and evil—that all this, and even worse, was done by command of the Apostolic man <note>A title for the Pope</note>, unless he had betrayed himself through his own mouth? For whom is there more danger here: for him who commands it, or him who obeys it? To whom is this more harmful: the one who does it, or the one who suffers it? What shall be judged? We, as if struck on the head by such unheard-of things, investigate from where this new example comes to us: that the Preacher of peace, with his own mouth and by another's hand, makes war upon the church? Against the onslaught of Barbarians and enemies of God, the ecclesiastical Canons <term>Canons: the established laws and regulations of the Christian Church</term> also allow the clergy to take up arms for the defense of city and church. But that one should declare war upon the church by authority of the Canons is something we have read in no writings. I ask what I do not know, and I say what I know... Why are we called the Excommunicated? <margin>p. 519.</margin> Why was the sword placed above our heads? What have we done, worthy of death or excommunication, against the canonical rule of the church? We are all baptized into one body in one spirit. When was it ever reported to the church of Rome that there were quarrels among us? We are of one mind and speak with one voice in Christ. We do not say, "I am of Paul," or "I am of Cephas" <note>original: "Pauli... Cephæ"; refers to the biblical warning in 1 Corinthians against creating factions within the church</note>. And are we called "The Excommunicated" because of this harmony? They object against us—who keep God's law—that we transgress their new traditions. But to them the Lord says: Why do you transgress the commandment of God by your traditions? <margin>Matthew 15:3.</margin> Christ commands that one give to Caesar what is Caesar's, and to God what is God's. Thus also speaks Peter in his first letter (2:17, 18, 19), and Paul to the Romans (13:1, 2), and Colossians (3:22)... Because we then honor the King, and because we serve our lords not for appearance's sake <note>original: "naer de oogen", literally "according to the eyes"</note>, but in simplicity of heart, we are called the Excommunicated. But we have, it is said, entered our offices through Simony <term>Simony: the illegal practice of buying or selling church offices or positions</term>, or bribery. Those who have done such things, we avoid as much as is within our power; and those we cannot avoid, we endure, as the place and time require... These people, I say, we shun; but no less do we shun those who, covering the mark of greed with an honorable name, sell that which they boast of giving for free under the title of charity. Like the Montanists <term>Montanists: an early Christian sect known for its strictness, though here accused of financial manipulation</term> of old, who received gifts in a much more subtle manner under the guise of giving offerings. Someone will say that we are therefore held as Excommunicates,* <margin>p. 520.</margin>

...[the clergy argue that rulers] should therefore not be resisted with weapons, but with prayers poured out to God. In this way *Moses* prayed against *Pharaoh*, and *Paul* and *Jeremiah* prayed for *Nero* and *Nebuchadnezzar*. You claim that anyone who has been excommunicated <term>excommunicated: formally excluded from the sacraments and membership of the Church</term> and dies in that state is damned. Here, the authority of the Roman Church comes to our aid. For *Gregory the First* <note>Pope Gregory I, known as Gregory the Great (reigned 590–604 AD)</note> firmly established that the Bishop of Rome can absolve someone who has been unjustly excommunicated by another. Now, if the Roman Bishop can do that, who then will deny that God can also absolve a person, if the Bishop of Rome himself had excommunicated them unjustly? For no one can be harmed by another, unless he is first harmed by himself... In this way, the Church of Liège <note>A city-state in modern-day Belgium, then part of the Holy Roman Empire</note> resisted the Pope with the strength of reason; moreover, the Emperor resisted the Count of Flanders with the power of arms, invading his land with an army and laying everything to waste until the Count was forced to confess his crime and beg for peace <gloss>1</gloss>. But *Paschal* <note>Pope Paschal II</note>, tireless in his enmity, later sought to achieve through a close blood relative what he could not accomplish through strangers: a cursed method that *Urban the Second*, his predecessor, had already employed. He stirred up the son against the father and did not rest until the old Emperor—one of the most warlike princes of his age <gloss>2</gloss>, who during his life had fought sixty-two battles and had struggled against Papal ambition <term>ambition: the original Dutch 'heerschfucht' implies a lust for worldly power or dominance</term> for about twenty-six years, and had been excommunicated at least six times—was finally thrust from the throne in the year eleven hundred and six through hypocritical deceit and disguised violence by young *Henry*, his dearest son, whom he himself had intended as his successor. He did not long survive his misfortune; he died in that same year in Liège, where he was buried. But shortly thereafter, when that city was forced to bow before *Henry the Fifth*, the body was torn from the earth again (for *Paschal* would not release the people of Liège from the ban <term>ban: a formal ecclesiastical sentence of excommunication or interdiction</term> under any other condition), carried to Speyer, placed in an unconsecrated spot, and left unburied for another five years <gloss>3</gloss>, according to the Papal rule: *With whom the Church has no fellowship in life, she may also have no fellowship in death.* <note>original: "Met wien de Kerke in hun leven geen gemeenschap heeft, daer en mag sij ook doodt sijnde geen gemeenschap met hebben."</note> Several men of learning and virtue defended the Emperor’s cause with the pen; among others, *Sigebert* <gloss>4</gloss>, a monk at Gemblours in Walloon Brabant, wrote against *Gregory the Seventh* and *Paschal the Second*; but those writings have since been [removed] by the...

### OF THE REFORMATION. BOOK I.

...though he was called a layman, in Antwerp, and in nearby Flanders, but especially in Zeeland, against the Roman Church. He taught that the station and eminence of the Bishop was not instituted by God; that all those orders of clergy were not necessary; and that the Mass did not serve the salvation of men. His teaching achieved so much that in Antwerp, over a period of ten years, not a single consecrated host or wafer was to be found. He was also very eloquent, lived magnificently, and was hospitable; things which gained him a great following. His enemies say that the people listened to him as if he were an Angel of God; indeed, that people drank the water in which he washed his body. He always traveled accompanied by a bodyguard of three thousand armed men to ensure his safety against any violence from the clergy. He was also accused of lapsing into great unchastity with women and virgins; they say he maintained that the use of women should be held in common: yet others believe the envy of the monks had fabricated this about him. At last, while on a ship, he was murdered by a priest. But <margin>1115.</margin> his views—against which Norbert of Xanten <note>St. Norbert, the founder of the Premonstratensian Order, was sent to Antwerp specifically to combat the lingering influence of Tanchelm’s teachings</note> preached for many a day thereafter—did not perish with his death, but maintained a long-lasting life in the minds of the inhabitants. 

Meanwhile, the fleshly life of the clergy caused much offense here in this country. In the year eleven hundred and twenty-two, the Canons at Middelburg behaved so willfully that Godebald, the twenty-fourth Bishop of Utrecht, drove them out of their monastery and placed other religious from Antwerp in their stead <margin>1</margin>. Little had been heard of the killing of heretics in the Netherlands until the year eleven hundred and thirty-five; then, in Utrecht, some people were accused of heresy and burned alive by order of the Emperor Lotharius <margin>2</margin>. It is believed they held to the teachings of Berengarius <margin>3</margin> and did not believe that Christ's body and blood were actually handled, broken, and eaten in the Lord's Supper. It seemed a small number could be suppressed with fire and steel: but before long, several thousands dared to openly admit that they wanted no communion with the errors of the Roman Church. A citizen of Lyons, named Peter Waldo, began to openly speak against the Papacy around the year eleven hundred and fifty-nine and eleven hundred and sixty. The hearing...

# H I S T O R Y

<margin>They also flee to the Netherlands.</margin>
The hearing he <note>Peter Waldo, a 12th-century merchant from Lyon who gave away his wealth to preach a return to Apostolic simplicity.</note> found and the following he gathered became so great within a short time that the clergy branded him a heretic and incited a persecution. This scattered his fellow believers and filled various parts of Europe—including the Netherlands, where he himself fled—with exiles. They were named not only after Waldo as Waldensians <gloss>1</gloss>, or with a shift in letters, Vaudois; but also the Poor Men of Lyon, or Leonists; Albigensians; Agonists; Toulousians; Bulgarians; Picards; Weavers; Perfectists; Humiliates; Insabbatati; Cathari, or Gazaris; Chienards, or Caignars; Frerons; Dulans; Lollards; Turlupins; Paterines; Piphles, Popelicans, Publicans, Passagines; Petrobrusians; Henricians; Josephines; Arnaldists; and later also Bohemian Brothers and Hussites. These names were derived from a country or city where their teaching made particular progress, or from something they were accused of, or that occurred among them, or after someone who had propagated or defended their views before or after Waldo. For some hold it for certain that Waldo <gloss>2</gloss> first learned this doctrine himself from certain peoples living on the mountainous borders of France, but later considered it more closely, understood it better, explained it more clearly, and taught it in turn to friends and strangers. They believe that the errors and cunning inventions of the Papacy had never fully penetrated those peoples, because, enclosed in their valleys and amidst their mountains and separated from others, they lived mostly by themselves, and therefore had retained much of the old and simple purity of the Apostolic teaching. This antiquity <gloss>3</gloss> of the Waldensian doctrine was acknowledged even by their greatest enemies, in whose writings—amidst the slandering and name-calling—one still finds praiseworthy testimonies <gloss>4</gloss> of their modest lives, tireless diligence in searching for the truth, and fiery zeal to propagate it. In almost all respects, their doctrine agreed with the views of those who have opposed the Papacy since the times of Luther <gloss>5</gloss>. Some of them also rejected infant—

...those who had escaped from the defeats, to Flanders. Before that, the Pope had appointed two Commissioners to conduct an investigation into their faith and their fellow believers; with orders to banish them if they refused to be converted; also, if necessary, to compel them with the sword of the secular authority <gloss>1</gloss>. From this arose the office, or as it is called, the Office of the Inquisition: which was first commanded to the Spaniard <term>Dominicus</term> <note>Saint Dominic (1170–1221), founder of the Dominican Order.</note> <gloss>2</gloss>, and after him to the monks of his order, and thereafter also, alongside them, to the Minor Friars, or <term>Franciscans</term> <note>The religious order founded by St. Francis of Assisi, known for their vows of poverty.</note> <gloss>3</gloss> (for both those orders were established around this time); until finally the <term>Dominicans</term> <note>The "Order of Preachers," who became the primary agents of the Inquisition.</note> <gloss>4</gloss>, who because of their preaching against the <term>Waldensians</term> <note>A medieval movement emphasizing poverty and the authority of the Bible, labeled as heretics by the Church.</note>, also bore the name of Preaching Friars or Preacher Monks, through their zealous searching out, tracking, and persecuting of the named heretics, got the entire management of the Inquisition into their hands. These Inquisitors put the suspects under oath, and to draw them out, proposed many crafty questions <gloss>5</gloss> in which the simple-minded were easily entangled. Thus they introduced <term>ketterdooden</term> <note>Literally "heretic-killing"; the execution of people for their religious beliefs.</note>: but that heretic-killing became since then the greatest heresy, which murdered love—the very soul of Christianity. And though a few Waldensians succumbed under the cross <note>Meaning they gave in under the pressure of persecution.</note>, the majority nonetheless remained steadfast, and accepted death, which delivered them from many impending miseries, as a blessing <gloss>6</gloss>. Those who denied the charges laid against them were put to trials <gloss>7</gloss>, which, being borrowed from Heathendom and being unjust, were also unfit for finding the truth, and could as little be endured by the innocent as by the guilty. The suspect had to carry a glowing iron, over which some conjuration had been performed, in his bare hand for nine footsteps; thereafter the hand was bound, sealed, and after three days inspected; if it were scorched or injured, that was held as a proof of guilt, and upon that the sentence of death was pronounced. This trial was called <term>Ordal</term> <note>The Ordeal; a method of trial where divine intervention was sought through physical tests.</note>. Sometimes they made the accused stick their naked arm, up to the elbow, into a kettle of boiling hot water: a manner of proceeding indicated in the old Netherlandish, and especially Frisian laws, by the word <term>Ketelvang</term> <note>Literally "Kettle-catch"; a trial by boiling water.</note>. They also threw some, for proof of guilt or innocence, mother-naked into cold deep water, which was conjured not to receive the guilty, but to let them float. Sinking was then a sign of purifi-

Even more fiercely were the Waldensians in Flanders persecuted around the years twelve hundred and thirty-six, seven, and thirty-eight <gloss>2</gloss> by the monk Robert, who was also called Bugre <gloss>3</gloss> or Bulgarus <note>The term "Bugre" or "Bulgar" was a contemporary slur for heretics, originally referring to the Bogomils of Bulgaria but later applied to many groups across Europe.</note>, because he, before taking up the Dominican cowl, had been a Waldensian. Knowing, since he had lived among them, who they were and where they stayed, he found—having been made Inquisitor at that time by Pope Gregory IX—the opportunity to rage against his old friends. All those who refused to be converted to his way of thinking, he, being supported by the secular arm <note>The "secular arm" refers to civil authorities who carried out physical punishments, such as executions, that the Church itself was canonically forbidden from performing.</note>, had burned. So it was that in the space of two or three months, about fifty people, both men and women, were burned or buried alive. It did not stop there: in the end, he so far abused the power given to him that it displeased even the Pope himself; who therefore forbade him from his service, and thereafter, on account of certain crimes that later came to light and had been kept secret, sentenced him to perpetual imprisonment. Besides the painful death by fire, the cruelty of the persecutors found yet another punishment, which was much more painful due to its long duration, and was inflicted upon the Waldensians in Flanders. Their clothes being stripped down to the navel, and the skin flayed that far down, they were bound to poles; then whole baskets and swarms of hornets or bees were brought near, which stung the flayed victims in the fresh wounds of that raw flesh with their stingers, and tormented them on all sides, without ceasing, day and night; until at last, tortured to the end, they gave up the ghost <gloss>4</gloss>.

Clerical grandeur exceeded all measure. The Bishops of Utrecht behaved like petty Popes in their diocese. ...the least of them, seven witnesses 1. Through this, they believed they could silence anyone who had anything to say against them. The fact that in those crude times <note>meaning the "Dark Ages" or Middle Ages</note> so few among the Magistrates of the citizens and in the Courts of the Princes were found capable of wielding a pen, meant that the clergy were promoted almost everywhere to the positions of Secretaries. countries where the Papacy had any jurisdiction, [the Knights Templar] were completely rooted out; also in Holland and Zeeland. This occurred at Zierikzee <note>A prominent port city in the province of Zeeland</note>, and possibly elsewhere, in this manner: A sealed letter was delivered to the Magistrates, folded large, upon whose address it was written: that one should not open it, except on a certain night, named therein, at twelve o'clock, and in the presence of the full Council, gathered for that purpose; and at that same hour to carry out the contents, without any delay, upon pain of death. Being assembled at that hour, the opened letter commanded them to immediately attack and kill the Templars with armed force. That bloody command rang terribly in their ears. Good counsel was scarce <note>The Dutch "duur" implies advice was both expensive and hard to find</note>; but the fear for their own lives, which depended on the execution of the order, prevailed. A quick decision was made, and they immediately and quietly summoned those who were bound to the city through labor or other services, providing them with tools and weapons. Then the Magistrate, thus accompanied, went to the Templar house. The doors were broken open, and all were struck dead in cold blood, whomever was found by the bed or hidden elsewhere; except for two, who at that very moment were outside the house in a brothel. Elsewhere they were likewise put to death, mostly at the same time. This was the bloody end of the order of the Templars, which had lasted nearly two hundred years. Regarding the cause of this murder, much has since been spoken in various ways <gloss>1</gloss>. Some say they were accused and convicted of heresy, idolatry, renunciation of the faith, secret dealings with the infidels, sodomy, and other gruesome crimes; and that Pope Clement the Fifth had grounded the death sentence upon such matters at the Council of Vienne, held around this time. Others exonerate them, holding that this disaster was brewed for them by the Pope or the King of France, Philip the Fair, or by both, out of envy and greed, in order to seize their vast possessions. Some relate <gloss>2</gloss> that they boldly and openly spoke against the flaws and tricks of the Papacy, and thereby brought such hatred upon themselves. In that same Synod <note>The Council of Vienne, 1311–1312</note> <gloss>3</gloss> where the Templars were condemned, Guy of Hainaut, the forty-second Bishop of Utrecht, was chosen as Cardinal by the Pope; but he refused to accept the red hat and scarlet robe <note>Symbols of the high office of Cardinal</note>, for which other clerics generally yearned so greatly <gloss>3</gloss>.

<margin>
<gloss>2</gloss> *Vignier p. 525.*
Bishop Guy of Utrecht refuses the Cardinalship.
<gloss>3</gloss> *J. Beka p. 107. W. Heda p. 231. Buch. notes on Heda p. 237. §. I.*
</margin>

# OF THE REFORMATION. BOOK I.
<center>D 3</center>

...his cause, spent a great part of their days and nights at their own expense. In such a struggle with both arguments and weapons, he held the empire for nearly thirty-three years; whereas his predecessor Henry VII <margin>1 See Petrarch’s Works p. 589. Scriverius ibid. p. 328. [1313]</margin> (a Count of Luxembourg, and on his mother's side descended from Dutch blood) reigned for not even five full years; for he was poisoned by a Dominican monk with the wafer, or wine of the Sacrament <margin>2 Werner Rolewinck, Fasciculus temporum, fol. 83. b. 84. a. P. Langius, Chronicle of Zeitz, p. 826. H. Mutius, German Chronicle, book XXIII. p. 219. Chronological Compilation.</margin>. **1409.**
Around the year fourteen hundred and nine, the citizens of Hoorn suffered great harassment from the Dean of West Friesland. When he could not extort <note>original: "af kon perffen"</note> what he wanted from them by legal means, he seized their cows and cattle in the field; from others, he attached their land rents. The Magistrate complained about this to the Count who then reigned, namely, William VI. He commanded the Dean with a stern letter <margin>Count William VI seeks to curb the harassment and greed of the clergy.</margin> to leave the citizens in peace henceforth. That same year, the same Count also granted letters to the city of Delft, which had shown him the greed of the church and cloister-folk, by which it was established: that all those who henceforth wished to enter cloisters should use only the fruits <note>meaning the interest or income</note> of their property during their lifetime; that they should inherit nothing from their deceased kinsmen <term>maegen</term> <note>original: "maegen"; a term for relatives or kin</note>; and that their cloister should not inherit more than a third part of their assets. He likewise forbade the clergy in Amsterdam <margin>**1411.**</margin> from buying or inheriting any property, movable or immovable, within the jurisdiction of the city; the parish churches, and hospitals or almshouses <term>baijerden</term> <note>original: "baijerden"; specifically a place where travelers or the poor could stay for a few nights</note> that stood within the city walls were excepted.

This served somewhat to the disadvantage of the Papacy, but a few years later something else occurred <margin>Rise of the Hussites.</margin> that looked further. The Hussites in Bohemia, so named after Jan Hus (one of their most prominent teachers, burned at Constance in the year fourteen hundred and fifteen; although he had come there to the Synod with a safe-conduct from Emperor Sigismund, whose word and faith were broken by the Synod, for there they forged the rule that the church need not keep its word to heretics.)

Persecution at Douay.

M. Grabo, a Monk in Deventer, writes against the immoral life of the clergy.

...the Waldensians <note>A reformist movement often targeted as heretics for their rejection of certain Church hierarchies</note> began to raise their heads again. At Douay in Flanders, around the year fourteen hundred and twenty-one, a large assembly was discovered, broken up, and imprisoned. All those who remained steadfast—who were many in number—were sentenced to the fire <note>execution by burning at the stake</note>. The others escaped that suffering by renouncing their faith and conforming to the Papacy. In Overijssel around this time, or slightly earlier, there was a Dominican monk named Matthijs Grabo, who had written a certain book against the unbridled life of the clergy. When he was accused and interrogated on the matter, he not only confessed to it but declared, moreover, that he intended to continue with such writing. For this confession, he was condemned as a heretic by the ecclesiastical court at Utrecht; however, he appealed to the Pope. Consequently, Frederick van Blankenheim, the fifty-first Bishop of Utrecht, brought the case before the Council of Constance <note>A major 15th-century council of the Catholic Church held to resolve the Papal Schism and address heresy</note>. Here, the Bishop had the monk accused by two Priors and two Canons sent there for that purpose, seeking his execution. The complaint was heard, the book was read, and the author was cast into a dungeon, where the threat of the fire had such power that he finally confessed his guilt and recanted his writings. Meanwhile, the contents of his book had achieved so much that the authorities of various cities in Overijssel, especially in Deventer, maintained almost openly that the clergy were also subject to secular authority. The churchmen, on the other hand, pulled so hard on this rope <note>original: "trokken... aan desen stok," meaning they resisted stubbornly</note> that Bishop Frederick, who died in the year fourteen hundred and twenty-three, said on his deathbed: *“Among the clergy, everyone is eager to rule; no one wants to stand below others, and from this a terrible confusion shall arise.”* Immediately after Frederick's death, a terrible schism arose through the election of Rudolf van Diephout as Bishop of Utrecht. Pope Martin V refused to confirm him and gave the Utrecht mitre <note>the symbol of the Bishop's office</note> to the Bishop of Speyer, who, with the Pope's consent, transferred his right to Zweder van Kuilenburg. Rudolf entered Utrecht by force. Zweder established his seat at Dordrecht. Thus the factionalism came to spiritual and secular weapons. The Pope placed Rudolf and his followers under the ban <note>excommunication</note>, forbidding the clergy from performing any church services in places where Zweder was rejected. Fie! you poor despisers of the world! Who can satisfy your insatiable desire, and fulfill the greatness of your hearts? Never did I see monasteries flourish and increase in godliness that daily increased in means; but rather such in which poverty and patience dwelt together. To maintain ecclesiastical prestige, people spoke of heavenly dreams, spiritual visions, and holy revelations that some monks had dreamt, seen, or heard. These mostly concerned the state of the dead, which brought in the matter of Purgatory and the soul masses <note>Masses paid for by the living to shorten a deceased person's time in Purgatory.</note> attached to them. Henrik Mande, born of an honorable house in Dordrecht, formerly Secretary to Count William VI and the Countess Lady Margaret, and well-regarded at court, in time grew weary of courtly life. He allowed himself to believe that Christ himself had appeared to him, urging him toward the spiritual life. Consequently, he left the court and took up the monk’s cowl in the monastery at Windesheim near Zwolle. Here he developed the conceit of new visions: in his solitude, he communed with angels who brought him unknown matters. He gave out that he was like a second Paul—and the monks believed it—having been caught up to the third heaven. It was spread among the people that there, in a glorious procession, he had seen various monks who had died in the monastery.

<margin>Henrik Mande, a monk at Windesheim, leads the people by the ears <note>A Dutch idiom meaning to deceive or mislead someone.</note> by revealing strange visions. ibid. p. 261.</margin>

On his turn watching the monastery gate, he heard—so it was said—a knocking, and then let in a youth with a bright countenance who, when asked *who he was*, answered: *The Lamb*; adding further: *That this monastery was his Father’s house, and those who dwelt therein were his true brothers.* The report of these revelations being spread everywhere, everyone wanted to know what and whom he had seen in heaven. The monastery was daily overrun by seekers, and he was generously gifted in exchange for his answers. Thereafter, to give his visions even more weight, they let him travel about, primarily in Holland from city to city, and especially to Delft, where he found much credence and gathered much money. He usually said to the poor: "I have found the souls of your friends in heaven and left them there"; but to the rich, he said that he had heard their relatives mourning in a painful Purgatory... And then followed an exhortation to charity, especially for the monks of his monastery, so that through their intercession the tormented souls might be released as quickly as possible. But in time, his credibility diminished: the frequency, strangeness, and absurdity of the visions caused even the first ones to be regarded as fictions for the sake of the later ones. Also, another monk, Jan de Wit of Utrecht, rose up against him, who [exposed] the vanity of his thoughts...

<margin>He loses his credibility.</margin>

**1440.**
The invention of book printing causes harm to the Papacy and promotes the Reformation.
</margin>
Around the year fourteen hundred and forty or somewhat later, Laurens Janszoon Koster, a citizen of Haarlem, invented the art of typesetting and printing <gloss>1</gloss>; which soon filled the world with a multitude of books and sciences; and at the same time greatly disadvantaged the Papacy through the publishing and scattering of printed writings. Where previously only handwritten books were used, and for a Bible, written somewhat plainly on parchment, one used to pay four or five hundred crowns; one now bought it for sixty, and shortly, when the art became more common, for four or five crowns <gloss>2</gloss>. Thus a common citizen and craftsman, for whom the price of handwritten books was too high, in time gained the opportunity to read the Holy Scripture in print. The necessary truth, upon which salvation depended, was to be found here. Those who thereafter compared the teaching and conduct of most clergy against this single rule <term>rule of faith</term> <note>Original: "rechtfnoer des geloofs" — literally a "plumb line," referring to the Bible as the definitive standard for Christian belief and behavior.</note> of faith and life, saw all too much superstition and too little love. In contrast, self-love, which corrupts all morals, had sufficiently mastered the churches and cloisters. Many clergy also took up trading <gloss>3</gloss>; which was all the more disadvantageous to the common people, since they, being free from all taxes on all wares, sold much cheaper, and could sell so, than other shopkeepers,

### OF THE REFORMATION. BOOK I.

...[the greater sins] were as much priced and given for money as the minor ones. The price list, by which the Confessors <note>Priests authorized to hear confessions and assign penance.</note> had to govern themselves regarding the buying off of sins and matters that were not permitted—unless the Pope saw fit—was established by the Papal Court, which wrote no bulls <note>An official papal document, named after the "bulla" or lead seal attached to it.</note> for free <gloss>1</gloss>. In this document, which Wolfgang Musculus <note>A significant 16th-century Protestant reformer and theologian.</note> later made public through printing in one of his finer books <gloss>2</gloss>, one reads things that are worthy of wonder: That a Jew was permitted to have a synagogue in his own house was valued at thirty *tournoisen*, seven ducats, and six *carlijnen* <note>These represent various European currencies: the *tournois* (Tours pound) was a French silver coin, the *ducat* was a gold coin, and the *carlijn* (carlino) was a small Italian coin.</note>: to erect a new synagogue, sixty *tournoisen* and fifteen ducats. A female poisoner or sorceress, after she had sworn off her superstitions, had to pay six *tournoisen* and eleven ducats for each poisoning and conjuring. The absolution from heresy [which must be understood as referring to heretics who submitted themselves back to the Papacy] was set at thirty-six *tournoisen* and nine ducats; or at twelve *tournoisen*, three ducats, and six *carlijnen* for a layman <note>A "layman" is a member of the church who is not a member of the clergy.</note>. The absolution for all kinds of unchastity committed by a cleric, even with nuns, outside or inside the walls of the monastery, or with blood relatives or in-laws, or with his spiritual daughter, was set at thirty-six *tournoisen* and three ducats: unchastity against nature, at ninety *tournoisen*, twelve ducats, and six *carlijnen*. The keeping of a concubine, at twenty-one *tournoisen*, five ducats, and six *carlijnen*. The release from an oath to carry out one's affairs cost, for one person and in one agreement, seven *tournoisen*, eleven ducats, and three *carlijnen*. Murder of a father, mother, brother, sister, or wife: four *tournoisen*, one ducat, and eight *carlijnen*. On this basis, Jonkheer Henrik van Montfoort, around the year fourteen hundred and forty-eight, was forgiven a form of parricide. He had kept his father in prison until death; and for that evil, Rudolf, the Bishop of Utrecht, acquitted him in exchange for a monetary fine <gloss>3</gloss>. He was received here in this land as an envoy from the See of Rome with great reverence: secular and spiritual leaders welcomed him with banners, with crosses, and with the ringing of bells. They sang, *“You are welcome; you, whom we have now for so long expected in our darkness”* 2. Nevertheless, he did not fully bow his neck under the papal yoke; for in performing his duties here in this land, he opposed not only bad morals but also some abuses of doctrine that corrupted those morals. At Utrecht and elsewhere, he climbed into the pulpit and rebuked the disorder 7. He judged of **images** 8, that they were shown too much honor. They were nothing but signs of the pious life of the Saints: which, by viewing the images, was brought to mind so as to be followed more closely and constantly. He also released many from the promises of pilgrimages to certain images to which special powers were attributed 9. Of **indulgences** <term>indulgences: certificates sold by the church to reduce the temporal punishment for sins</term>, he was sometimes heard to say 10 that they did not make people better, but worse; for people did not weigh their sins heavily enough when they were so easily forgiven: that true repentance could well do without indulgences: that the **Jubilee year** <note>A special year of remission from sins and universal pardon, usually occurring every 25 or 50 years.</note> harmed both purses and souls: that the true letters of indulgence were to be found in the Holy Scriptures. Yet it seems he spoke thus only among trusted friends; for it is recounted of him that he himself distributed indulgences 11 and made the people believe that the money they gave for them would be used solely for the founding of monasteries and hospitals in their own land. It is further said of him that, in his indulgence-preaching, he made use of this reasoning 12: That the See of Rome could indeed forgive all sins for nothing, but not the punishments, which were necessarily [imposed] upon the sinners.
