<meta>This page continues the discussion on the state of the clergy and monastic life in the mid-15th century, shifting from Cardinal Cusa’s reforms to the conflict between secular law and the "right of sanctuary" in churchyards, ending with the 1459 persecution of the Waldensians under the guise of witchcraft.</meta>

### HISTORY

...had lost their minds, the other brothers immediately judged that they had fasted too strictly; and that since then, the following three questions were put to novices: *Whether they could eat well, sleep well, and obey their Superior?* That the clergy, through the places of refuge and retreat they provided for evildoers in their churchyards and monasteries, gained much prestige among the common people and obstructed the civil justice system, was offensive enough to the authorities. Some provision had been made against this in the year fourteen hundred and thirty-four, but the clergy held their ground as long as they could. In the city of Hoorn, in the year fourteen hundred and fifty-nine, it had gone so far that certain rioters, the city being divided against itself, stayed in the churchyard. From there, they ran through the streets at night with loaded and spanned bows, attacking the houses of their opponents. When they were resisted and pursued, or had completed their wicked intent, they retreated again to the churchyard, their fortress, where they were safe. But their wantonness was soon halted, and the **Bailiff** <term>Bailiff: (Schout) a local official responsible for law enforcement and prosecution</term> of Hoorn was written to on behalf of the Duke of Burgundy, as follows: *We authorize and command our Bailiff that he should seize and capture such persons as are staying and remaining in the churchyards and consecrated places within our city of Hoorn, and have gone, or do go, from the same churchyard and places to hinder our subjects in body or in property; and that he take them from the churchyards and consecrated places, and do so much that the power thereof shall be, and remains, his...*

In that same year, another bloody persecution arose in Flanders and **Artois** <note>original: "Atrecht"</note> against some innocent people, who were labeled **Waldensians** <term>Waldensians: a pre-Reformation Christian movement; they were often persecuted and, as this text explains, later falsely accused of witchcraft</term> or **Vaudois**. These people, compelled by pain, confessed to what was falsely attributed to them; among other things, that they served the Evil Enemy, worshipped him, copulated with him, and other unbelievable and unheard-of abominations. They appealed to the Parliament at Mechelen <note>The Great Council of Mechelen was the highest court in the Burgundian Netherlands</note>, or, if that were not allowed, to the Pope. To induce them to comply, the Brabantine clergy were brought to payment by *namptisatie* <term>namptisatie: a legal procedure involving the provisional seizure of assets or a mandatory advance payment pending a final court ruling</term>. The Zeelanders were likewise for the most part persuaded to yield. Those of Holland, having bound themselves to one another, had no ears for this. The clergy said they were not authorized to promise anything. Afterwards, they were summoned to Schoonhoven, where they again sent documents that plainly told those who summoned them that they would not give. Then they were called before the Parliament at Mechelen, where they likewise stayed away and sent their letters; asserting that they could not subject themselves to this burden without violating their oaths and conscience; that neither Emperor, nor King, nor any secular Lords could compel them to be taxed without the consent

from the Pope, to whom they further appealed. Because of this, Jan de Leeuw, a Councilor of the Parliament <note>The Great Council of Mechelen, the highest judicial body in the Burgundian Netherlands</note>, was sent to Holland. Consequently, several Priors and other clergy fled; three were taken into custody; six were summoned anew to Mechelen. *All the clergy from whom the last letter to the Parliament originated—so de Leeuw raged against them—had forfeited their lives and property; because by their appeal to the Court in Rome they had shown contempt for the Parliament, and at the beginning of their letter they had written "Greetings." Subjects were not allowed to use that word toward any Authority: to them, it was a sign of rebellion.* <note>In the formal hierarchy of the time, beginning a letter with a simple "Greeting" rather than a humble petition was considered an assertion of equality or a lack of due submission to the sovereign's court.</note> In Delft, he compelled the Mother Superior of the Saint Agatha’s Convent to hand over the records and financial status of the monastic properties. To strike even more fear into the rest, the three prisoners were secretly taken to Mechelen, where he summoned yet more clergy. Therefore, they requested and obtained some delay; and Bishop David of Utrecht meanwhile convinced them to drop their appeal to the See of Rome. But that this delay was no pardon was made clear to them later by the arrival of Jan van Boshuizen, the Duke's Chamberlain. This man, a soldier and Knight known as the White Falcon <note>original: "vitten Valk"; "vitte" is an archaic form of "witte" (white)</note>, had them gather in The Hague during Lent in the year fourteen hundred and seventy-six. There, he began to threaten and bluster with a voice and words that were terrifying to hear. "Let the clergy of Holland," he cried, "consider well what they wish to do in this matter that has been set before them for a long time now: for I now have the authority, courage, and will to seize the clergy unless they willingly pay the tax <term>schatting: a forced tax or assessment levied by the ruler</term>. And do not think that any of you shall be allowed to defend yourselves with any rights or laws against the Duke: there is no power or wisdom against him; for I shall not hesitate, by virtue of his authority and power, to torment you and do to you what has never been seen or heard before." At the same time, he boasted of the harassment he had inflicted on the clergy in many places at other times: "and no less," he continued, "shall I do to most of you as well." This caused those of Delfland and Hagambacht to grant the tax. The three imprisoned clerks were released. After this, the tax was also granted by several other clergy, provided that it would be paid in two installments: on Saint John’s Day in the summer, and at Christmas in the winter; but many around Leiden, Haarlem, Amsterdam, and in West Friesland held out for a while longer, some

The collectors waited until Epiphany <note>Literally "Thirteenth Day," the 12th day after Christmas.</note> $^1$; but before any new measures were taken against those who remained in default, the report spread through the land that the Duke had been defeated $^2$. Then the government lost its grip, and the collection of that hated tax ceased. The clergy called the collection "church-robbery" <note>sacrilege</note> and complained of force and violence. Others felt that their resistance in this matter smacked of stubbornness and rebellion; that one could not defend nor preserve the fatherland without war, nor wage war without pay, and that the pay must be found from the taxes, the taxes from the wealthy, and consequently from the clergy, who were now the richest and wrongly appealed to laws which had exempted them from burdens when they were still living in poverty. Now the times and the states of affairs had changed. This was also the view later held by the Court of Holland in the case of the five monasteries of the city of Hoorn: $^3$ *that as they were also protected by the common arms, they also ought to give their share in the burdens and taxes that arose therefrom.* That concerned church property, but what follows now concerns doctrine. In this same time lived Doctor Wessel Hermanszoon Gansfort, a native of Groningen, who, through his learning in the three principal languages <note>Latin, Greek, and Hebrew</note> and further knowledge of human and divine matters, so excelled in this ignorant age that he was called the Light of the World <note>original: "Lux mundi"</note>. Around this time, Jan van Goch, named Pupper—a priest and Superior of the cloistered virgins in Tabor at Mechelen—also made his voice heard against the doctrine of the Papacy. He lived, says Valerius Andreas <gloss>3</gloss>, a Roman-minded <note>Catholic</note> writer, at the same time as Wessel of Groningen, and was a man of the same understanding, as his writings testify. He dared to maintain <gloss>4</gloss> that the writings of Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note>, Albertus <gloss>5</gloss>, and other Scholastics <note>original: "Schoolleeraeren," referring to the medieval university theologians</note> obscured the truth more than they explained it; that one must follow Holy Scripture alone, and test all other writers against it, even the Decrees of the Popes and Councils. Vows involving things not required [by God] he rejected as useless for godliness and contrary to Christian liberty. He condemned feigned works of supererogation <note>original: "overtollige werken," referring to the Catholic doctrine of performing more good deeds than are strictly necessary for salvation</note>. He complained that Christianity had degenerated into Judaism and Pharisaism. He asserted that we were justified only through Christ’s merit and faith, and not through any merits of our own; but he added further that sin still truly remained within the godly, though it was not imputed to them, but forgiven for Christ’s sake. This, some thought, went too far if he spoke of sins in which one continued, and not of weaknesses against which one struggled. Only some of his writings <gloss>6</gloss> are printed, and those incompletely or mutilated. Nevertheless, they—as well as the books of Doctor Wessel—were later forbidden by the Council of Trent <gloss>7</gloss>.

In the year fourteen hundred eighty-six, in the name of Maximilian, King of the Romans, and Philip, Archduke of Austria, an Edict <term>Plakkaet: a formal public decree or law</term> was issued on the twenty-fourth of August at Bruges. These courts had no legal jurisdiction over worldly matters, yet for very wretched, small, and insignificant matters <gloss>*</gloss> <note>original: "Pour bien miserables, petites, & inutiles actions."</note>—such as ten or twelve groats <note>Small silver coins.</note> at once, or a little more or less—they proceeded against the defendants with excommunications and other censures for failing to appear. In such a way, they brought the aforementioned subjects to their utter ruin and poverty. Because of this, some were so overwhelmed, and others—in order to avoid the costs and effort of traveling or sending messages to those spiritual courts (located outside Flanders, some six, eight, ten, or more miles away)—were forced to enter into a disadvantageous settlement with their opponents. Some also, through an inability to pay, remained excommunicated and eventually died, to the great danger of their souls... In the year fourteen hundred ninety-six, Philip married Joanna of Aragon at Lier in Brabant. The new century, beginning with the year fifteen hundred, soon saw great changes regarding the matters of Religion. Charles, hereditary lord of these Netherlands, born on the twenty-fourth of February <note>original: "Sprokkelmaendt"</note> in that year—to whom the Netherlandish Abbots, on his christening day (when his father Philip and others gave him various gifts), presented the books of the Old and New Testaments with this inscription, *Search the scriptures*—lived to see the time in which the knowledge of the contents of those books reached many people.

<margin>
Bucholzer in *Chronological Index* <note>original Latin: "Indice Chron."</note> p. 449.
The Papacy suffers new attacks from various learned men.
</margin>
The Papacy, which was then mostly maintained by the monkhood, and the monkhood, which was sustained by the propagation of dull and deaf ignorance as well as by the force of tyranny, began around this time to suffer more attacks than before. This occurred through the writings of various learned minds, which this century, aided by the art of printing, produced in great numbers: for everything that came to light daily for the advancement of learning and godliness was sufficiently and directly opposed to monasticism, which hated all light of letters and sciences as if it were heresy or sorcery¹. In every part of Christendom, men of knowledge and judgment were now found who, with voice and pen, opposed the papal abuses and prepared the way for a greater Reformation. The principal figures who now set their hands to this work were: Giovanni Francesco Pico della Mirandola², and Baptista Mantuanus, Prior of the Carmelites³, in Italy; in Fran- <note>The text cuts off mid-word, continuing to "France" on the next page</note>

# OF THE REFORMATION. BOOK II.

...[found] the principal content of his teaching to be true; however, he required in him more gentleness <margin>1 Melanchthon in his *Life of Luther*.</margin>¹. Also, Erasmus complained that the zealous man <note>Martin Luther</note> was attacked more with insults and slander than with reason: that out of hatred for his person, people condemned what was true, twisted what was right, and damned things in his books as heretical that were read as orthodox and godly in the writings of Bernard <note>St. Bernard of Clairvaux, a 12th-century mystic and church leader</note> and Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo, the influential 4th-century theologian</note> <margin>2 Erasmus, *Letters*, p. 585.</margin>². One must not, he understood, openly condemn <margin>3 Ibid.</margin> that which one has not read, not weighed, and indeed not understood ³. He also sought, as much as was in his power, to prevent Luther <margin>4 Ibid., p. 584, 652. B, C.</margin> from being suppressed unheard by the faction of wicked men ⁴. *Noble minds*, he said, *desired to be instructed, and not forced. Instructing was the work of theologians; forcing, the work of tyrants alone* <margin>5 Ibid., p. 652. C.</margin>⁵. It pained him that such a mind had been so <margin>6 Ibid., p. 594. D.</margin> embittered ⁶ by the insane bellowing and shouting of the monks. <margin>7 Ibid., p. 1074. A.</margin> Through this, a great fire had arisen from a small spark ⁷. No matter how much Erasmus since then called him back, the more fiercely he <note>Luther</note> flared up ⁷. Therefore, the farsighted Dutchman <note>Erasmus of Rotterdam</note> predicted from then on <margin>8 Ibid., p. 1073. 2044. E.</margin>⁸ that this work would burst out into rebellion and turmoil, and would have a bloody end. However, he laid most of the blame on the clergy. *One must look*, he wrote <margin>9 Ibid., p. 585, 586.</margin>⁹, *at the origin of the evil. The world is burdened with human institutions, weighed down by scholastic opinions and teachings, and by the tyranny of the mendicant monks <note>Mendicant monks were members of religious orders, such as the Franciscans or Dominicans, who lived by begging and often held significant influence over local populations</note>... I do not condemn them all, but many are of such a nature that, in order to advance their profit and tyranny, they intentionally ensnare the consciences of men. They preach, now setting aside all shame and Christ himself, nothing but their novelties and often even shameless dogmas. Of the indulgences they speak in such a manner that even the laity could not endure it. Through these and many similar things, the power of the Gospel teaching gradually perished: and it is to be expected that, things always falling into worse states, finally that spark of Christian godliness, from which the extinguished love could be rekindled, will be completely put out. The greater part of religion was inclining toward ceremonies that were more than Jewish <note>Erasmus frequently criticized what he saw as "Jewish" legalism in the Church—an over-reliance on outward rituals and laws rather than inner faith</note>. Pious people groaned and wrote about these things; even theologians who are not monks, and some monks in their private conversations, confess this. These things, I believe, moved Luther's mind to first dare to set himself against the intolerable shamelessness of some. For what else should I think of him, who yet*

Erasmus <gloss>1</gloss>, Arasmus <gloss>2</gloss> <note>A pun on the Latin 'arare', to plow up or destroy</note>, Erasinus <gloss>3</gloss> <note>A pun on 'asinus', meaning a donkey</note>, Behemoth <gloss>4</gloss>, Devil <gloss>5</gloss>, Enemy of religion <gloss>6</gloss>, Blasphemer of God <gloss>7</gloss>, Slanderer of the Virgin Mary <gloss>8</gloss>, Schismatic <gloss>9</gloss>, Forger <gloss>10</gloss>, Forerunner of the Antichrist <gloss>11</gloss>, the Antichrist himself <gloss>12</gloss>, an Arch-heretic <gloss>13</gloss>, the origin and Head of the Lutheran Faction <gloss>14</gloss>, a worse heretic than Luther <gloss>15</gloss>. From his garden, it was said, Luther had gathered his deadly seed <gloss>16</gloss>. The egg was laid by Erasmus, and hatched by Luther <gloss>17</gloss>. But when certain monks—who had painted him in foul colors from the pulpit before the people—were asked what heresy they had actually found in his books, they gave as an answer: <gloss>18</gloss> That they had not read them, but that danger nonetheless lurked within them because of the difficult Latin. By such boasters was the Papal majesty defended and the church supported. On the other side, some were dissatisfied because he tolerated too much. He, who had opposed so many errors and abuses of the Roman Church, and had done so in public, ought (they felt) to separate from it entirely and join forces with Luther; indeed, he alone was blamed <gloss>19</gloss> for the fact that they had not entirely overthrown the Pope and the Papacy. Nevertheless, there were some who praised this neutral moderation to the skies. That he sought to hold the middle ground between two extremes they called prudence; but they were especially pleased that he distinguished between error, heresy, and sedition. It was for this reason that he rebuked the Church Father Hilary for his vehemence against the Arians <gloss>20</gloss> <note>Arians: followers of a 4th-century belief that Jesus was not fully divine/co-eternal with God</note>, whom Hilary had labeled as godless, devils, blasphemers, satans, plagues, and antichrists.

On the first day of the year fifteen hundred nineteen, the Canon Huldrych Zwingli <gloss>21</gloss>—who as early as the year fifteen hundred sixteen <gloss>22</gloss> had set himself against the Papacy at Glarus and elsewhere in Switzerland, when Luther's name was still unknown there—began to preach in Zurich. A certain Franciscan monk attempted here, shortly thereafter, to offer indulgences <term>indulgences: certificates sold by the Church intended to reduce temporal punishment for sins</term> for sale, but Zwingli resisted him courageously and exposed his deceit. Meanwhile, Emperor Maximilian had ended his days on the twelfth of January <note>original: "Loumaendt", an archaic Dutch name for the month of January</note> at Wels in Austria. He had been a Prince gifted with royal and Christian virtues <gloss>23</gloss>. The unjust dealings—

For, if one must forbid food in which there is a drop of poison because of the danger of infecting the body, so much more ought one to reject the teaching (however good it may be) which is mixed with, and under which hides, the poison of heresy.

<margin>1521.</margin>...or error, which corrupts (under the cover of charity) all that might be good, to the great peril of souls. Immediately, the authorities were commanded to faithfully and fully assist the Pope’s messengers or their authorized representatives, when requested, in the burning of those books. Furthermore, the edict forbade the making, printing, painting, selling, buying, or possessing of all writings and images full of ridicule, containing any dishonor, slander, or even any error against the Christian faith or the customs of the Roman Church; or tending to the belittling and defamation of the Pope, Prelates of the churches, secular Princes, Universities, or Schools... such writings and images were likewise to be burned. Finally, the Emperor commanded—which he willed and intended to obtain the force and power of an eternal, unbreakable law—that henceforth, upon the forfeiture of life and property, no bookseller, printer, or any other person, whoever they might be, should presume to print or cause to be printed any books or writings in which mention is made of the Holy Scriptures or the interpretation of the same, however small it may be, without first having permission from the <term>Ordinary: the local bishop or a church official with regular jurisdiction</term> of the place, or his deputies appointed for that purpose, with the advice and consent of the Faculty of Theology of the nearest University, approving (under the seal of the same University) the said books and writings... To print all other books, one first had to have the consent of the secular authorities, who would act upon the advice of the local Ordinary or his deputies in this matter. The violators would fall into the <term>crimen laesae Majestatis: the crime of lèse-majesté, or treason against the sovereign</term> and into all aforementioned penalties; namely, that those who appeared clearly rebellious, defiant, and disobedient to these ordinances would be seized with great diligence, in body and goods, in reality and with force, correcting them with the execution of the penalties ordained in secular and ecclesiastical laws. That the penalty of death was also included and intended here, the execution thereof has since taught. The issuance of this edict, signed on the eighth of <note>original: "Bloeimaendt" (Bloom-month), an old Dutch name for May</note> May, was an infringement against the country’s freedom; for whereas previously the old Counts of Holland made no laws of any weight except in the presence of the Nobles and the States <margin>\* *Grotius, On the Batavian Republic, chapter V, page 78. <margin>1522.</margin>

*...to take refuge in you as a benevolent father, and to present my most unfortunate accident with sighs and bitter tears; so that you, having mercy on me, might come to our aid with counsel and deed, and favor—as we entrust to your mercy and as your authority permits, being President of the council of this Court. It is such that I—as you perhaps have understood before, both from the accounts of others and from the petitions of my wife—was summoned to trial in the Emperor’s name, and immediately appeared in obedience, and appearing was heavily accused of the Lutheran <term>faction: a term used here to label the growing group of Protestant reformers as a divisive sect</term>. I had written a certain Preface for a certain small book by Jan Gocch <note>Jan Gocch, also known as Johann Pupper (c. 1400–1475), was a Dutch theologian who criticized the church long before Luther; his works were rediscovered by the Reformers.</note>, which bore the name of *The Freedom of the Christian Religion*. This was printed long before the Emperor’s <term>placard: an official public decree or law</term>. In the same, I—more out of imprudence than a combative spirit—rebuked those who burdened Christians with some servitude, and that at a time when saying and writing such things was not yet forbidden, and such writings were everywhere and by everyone praised with applause. I have a mind that is naturally very inclined to attempt everything. What I wrote somewhat imprudently was done more as an exercise of the mind than to give offense to anyone. Thus I learned poetry, music, the art of drawing or painting by myself. Thus I gained some taste for Latin and Greek. Thus I am very eager to learn the other languages that are useful for the knowledge of good sciences, as much as time and my ability permit. Therefore I have traveled through almost all of Italy, not without great labor, and sometimes in poverty. Therefore I have bravely despised my fortune, my means, and every opportunity to gather treasures, always satisfied with necessity and honest food. Whatever it was that was committed by me, it was the work-hungry mind that erred, not malice. If the human mind—tempted to evil by a desire for exercise in whatever way, yet not being evil, not perverse, not stubborn, but ready to be improved, disciplined, and subjected to a better judgment—should lead those endowed with it to destruction, then it would be better to be an unreasoning animal or a block of wood than a human; since by nature it cannot be otherwise than that a mind that is not ignoble must sometimes show its strength in something. If the mind—which was neither evil nor bitter, but always pleasant and lovable—threw Naso <note>Naso is the surname of the Roman poet Ovid, who was famously exiled by Emperor Augustus.</note>, that most sweet-flowing poet, into that anxious and eternal exile in Pontus <note>Pontus was a region on the Black Sea, where Ovid lived out his life in banishment.</note>; it would then have been better for him that he had never known of learning, or that he [had never written] the lovely, maligned loves,*

### OF THE REFORMATION. BOOK II.

<margin>1522.</margin>
...far from the sight and company of men, having fled to the wilderness, and, with that Athenian *Timon* <note>Timon of Athens was a legendary figure in ancient Greece known for his misanthropy and withdrawal from society; Grapheus is suggesting he would have been better off as a hermit than an intellectual.</note>, had led a desolate, wild, and man-hating life. If an intellect that is neither perverse nor stubborn, but ready to be corrected at the slightest warning, has entangled me in these difficulties that press upon me from all sides, it would have been more useful to me to have lacked my senses, or to have been an unkind slanderer, or a dishonorable fool, juggler, buffoon, stage-actor, or a rogue of such kind, than to be distinguished by my intellect (such as it is) or held in honor through learning. For that sort of people are admitted everywhere, and that openly, without punishment, to perform their fables, comedies, insults, tragedies—no matter how "salty" <note>In this context, "salty" refers to wit that is sharp, biting, or potentially offensive.</note> they taste, how sharp they are, how they bite, how filthy, how unchaste, how roguish they are—even with applause, as often as they desire, before the people. Truly, excellent minds, especially those who are not stubborn but obedient to good warnings, ought not to be immediately crushed, but rather stirred up for better use; not to be reviled, but to be enticed by the offering of reward, and helped forward in all sorts of ways; even though they might have erred through ignorance or imprudence, which is human frailty. 

But let us return to where we just deviated. After that preface I placed on the little book of *Gocch* <note>Jan Gocch, as mentioned previously, was a 15th-century theologian whose works Grapheus had edited.</note> had been picked apart point by point by <term>Commissioners: officials appointed to investigate and prosecute cases of heresy</term>, and after I know not how many conclusions, set down in articles, were extracted from it, I immediately—when I was better instructed—recognized my imprudence, felt regret, did not refuse to recant, loathed my stubbornness, and prayed for forgiveness for my recklessness. And see, immediately I am thrown into the dungeon like a <term>heretic: someone holding opinions at odds with established religious dogma</term>, where according to all laws, both divine and human, no one—even if he had fallen into some manifest error—may be held for a heretic, unless he, according to the command of the Gospel and of the Apostle Paul, were first privately and in a Christian manner admonished, and thereafter, having been rebuked in the presence of two or three witnesses, remained stubbornly clinging to his manifest error, or fell back of his own accord into his first heretical opinion—neither of which will be found to have been done by me. 

<margin>He showed remorse, and prayed for forgiveness. Was thrown into the dungeon as a heretic.</margin>

Therefore, nothing remains but that the husband be restored to his wife and the father to his children, or otherwise that we go begging from door to door, or that we lay hands upon ourselves: for it would be much better and more desirable for the wretched to die by whatever death, than to live with shame in the most extreme destitution. My distressed wife has petitioned time and again (which I believe is not unknown to your Reverence) for her husband’s restoration, namely that he, being at least restored to his former good name, might have the entire city of Antwerp as a prison instead of Brussels. We pray, we plead daily, without advancing at all, without obtaining anything, even though he, calling Christ to witness, so often promised that he would be merciful toward us. But where is the promised mercy, when he does not fulfill the little that we desire? Namely, the issuing of his advice. "But," he says, "it is not yet time." When shall it be time then? In this way, one could delay the answer until the seventh year. He says that new errors are sprouting up everywhere. What does that concern us? Surely I do not believe that anyone will think the Council over which you preside would have requested his advice if that same Council—circumspect as it is—had not known beforehand what power he held in this matter; anyone who believes otherwise does an injustice to the Council’s prudence and accuses them of ignorance. Yet perhaps he delays giving his advice to consider the matter with more mature counsel. But he has now fed the wretched ones with uncertain hope for nearly three whole months of deliberation. If he has not deliberated enough in three months, when will he finally decide? If he has been in labor for so long, when will he finally give birth and bring forth the fruit of his advice? Truly, this delay is no less heavy for me and my miserable wife than it is suspicious to us. For if his advice is to be fair and bearable for us, then we are wronged by delaying such a fair matter for so long; but if it is to be unfair, then it will be exceedingly hard for us to have awaited an unfair outcome with such great patience. For, to say nothing of the modesty of our honest and virtuous request, why (saving your judgment) does one need to expect advice from anyone else after the sentence has been passed, executed, and completed? Those who are conscious of some evil and are guilty of it seek mercy for the crime before the punishment is given. In such cases, one sometimes needs another's advice so that the judges might deliver the sentence with all the more discernment and peace of mind. But after I have been so punished that, stripped of all my means, nothing in the world remains to me except my diligence, knowledge, and intellect, no one should prevent me—without waiting for another’s advice on the matter—from being granted so much mercy through your highnesses' benevolence. I ask that I might at least honestly and freely enjoy and use my industry and intellect—first for the glory of Christ, then for the Emperor's honor, for the service and help of friends, and to deliver my wife and children from want and hunger. 

Nor shall you judge this to have been done for one who does not deserve it, if it becomes clear to you how great my inclination is, and always was, to serve the Emperor. One sees Jews or Pagans—those inclining themselves from Judaism or Paganism toward the Christian faith—who <margin>One ought not to treat Christians more harshly than Jews and Pagans.</margin> nevertheless, because they drank in the superstitions of paternal traditions from their youth, may perhaps never become sincere Christians, yet are cheered from all sides with praise and great proof of favor: why should the state of Christians, though they fell into error, be worse if they repent? Surely one ought to have compassion for their fall, and greet them upon their conversion (not revile them with harsh punishments), after the example of God’s Angels, who (as Christ himself testifies in the Gospel) rejoice more over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous ones.

But these, they say, must be sharply punished as an example <note>original: "spiegel", literally "mirror"</note> to others. Be it so. But as for me, I have served as a clear and public example to all. Therefore, if there is still a little Christian piety, if, according to the requirements of the Gospel, one owes some mercy to the penitent, then let me plead away further punishment, for the good of me and mine. Furthermore, most gentle father, deal with the humble supplicants in such a way that we may find you to be such a father as we take you for. It is a pious matter, not contrary to reason. Whatever you shall do in the case of these wretched ones, that you shall surely do to Christ himself, and not to us. That we wrote these things at greater length to your Reverence than was perhaps fitting, and that in haste, with an unrefined style, I pray your gentleness to take it in the best way; since the necessity of the wretched forced us to it. <margin>1524.</margin> ...**Canonries, Vicarages, and also Offices, and Sextonships** <note>These were various types of church appointments and their associated incomes.</note>, some of which are at our collation, presentation, and disposition <note>Legal terms for the right to nominate or appoint someone to a church position.</note>, and some at the collation of our Stadtholder <note>The provincial governor representing the sovereign.</note> of the said lands. Therefore, we, desiring to provide for this and to maintain and stand up for our Rights and Sovereignty, charge and command you to travel everywhere within the aforementioned lands, to the places where it shall be necessary and you deem fit, and there on our behalf to publicly announce and command in the churches that everyone who occupies or serves any benefices—be they **Churches, Canonries, Vicarages, or any Offices and Sextonships**—whether in his own name or in the name of others, must bring or send his **Titles** <note>Legal documents proving their right to the position.</note> or authentic copies thereof within one month after the publication of this notice. These must be delivered securely into the hands of our dear and faithful Master **Arnold Sandelyn**, Clerk of our Council Chamber in Holland, whom we have commissioned for this purpose, to be registered by him and sent to us. This is under the penalty and threat that whoever is in default and is found to occupy any Benefices, Offices, or Sextonships without having submitted his Titles in the manner prescribed, we shall, once the said time has passed, proceed to new collation or presentation of the same, to the profit of those whom we see fit, to the end that our Rights and Sovereignty be not diminished. To do this, we give you full power and special command. We therefore summon and command all our Officers, Justices, and subjects that they earnestly assist and obey you in doing this, without failing in any way, as they fear our wrath and what they might forfeit against it. Given under our **Seal of the Fiefs**, which we currently use in our aforementioned Land of Holland, printed here below in the space on the twelfth day of September <note>original: "Herfftmaendt"</note>, in the year **fifteen hundred twenty-four**.

# OF THE REFORMATION. BOOK II.

<margin>
**1524.**
</margin>

I return again to the affairs of the Reformation. Around this time, the Pastor of Mels—located two hours' walk from Antwerp—preached against the Papacy, often in the open fields because of the massive crowds. He once said, accusing himself and the other priests: *“We are worse than Judas; he sold and delivered the Lord: we sell Him to you, but we do not deliver Him.”* <note>The pastor is likely referring to the sale of indulgences or the performance of the Mass for money, contrasting it with Judas, who at least "delivered" Christ to the authorities.</note> This led to a new edict being issued against this Pastor and a certain Augustinian monk who taught in Antwerp. Their meetings were forbidden, and a bounty of thirty Charles guilders <term>Charles guilders: Also known as the Karolusgulden, a gold coin minted under Emperor Charles V.</term> was placed on their heads. 

Nevertheless, on a Sunday, a great many people gathered at some shipyards to hear the monk. But when no teacher appeared—no one knows what hindrance prevented it—a man from the crowd named Niklaes, who was well-versed in the Scriptures, felt that such a multitude of people, so hungry for the food of the Word, should not be allowed to depart without some spiritual nourishment. He then climbed onto a ship and instructed the assembly according to his knowledge. For this act, and for the sake of the reward placed on the preacher, he was seized by two butcher’s assistants, handed over to the authorities, sewn into a sack, and drowned near the city crane. <note>Drowning was a common method of execution for those considered heretics, intended to be less public and "bloody" than burning at the stake.</note> 

Henrik van Zutphen <note>1</note>, recently the Prior of the Augustinians at Antwerp, who had fled when his monks were persecuted, was martyred with a cruel death <note>2</note> at the end of this year in Dithmarschen <term>Dithmarschen: A coastal region in modern-day northern Germany.</term> by peasants who had been incited by the monks.

# HISTORY

<margin>

Even Martinus Dorpius of Naaldwijk, that learned Dutchman and theologian at Leuven, was believed by some not to be averse to Luther’s teachings at first, and alongside Erasmus, he ran the risk of losing his life in Leuven. Indeed, it is held that Philippus de Lens, the Emperor’s Secretary in the Court of Brabant, was secretly favorable to the cause of the Reformation. In Brabant, Wouter Deleen, a learned man who later taught the Greek language to others in Emden <margin>1 History of the Martyrs, page 310.</margin>¹, also joined that side. Petrus Nannius of Alkmaar, a man of great reputation among scholars and a priest, is also thought to have been devoted to this cause, along with a priest named Laurentius. In Naarden, Antonius Frederiks <margin>2 He was killed thereafter. See the preface by Hendrik Antonides, page B. 3.</margin>² began to set his hand to this work and gained many followers from among the most prominent citizens, along with the Pastor Herman Cocq and Nicolaus Quick, the Assistant Rector of the school. In Utrecht, the teachings of the Reformation were accepted by Johannes (others call him Henricus) Rhodius, the Head of the Hieronymian College <note>A school run by the Brethren of the Common Life, a pietist lay community.</note>, or Father of the Brotherhouse. But Luther spoke against it, while the others agreed with it. ->OF THE REFORMATION. BOOK II.<-

M 3

<margin>1525. See G. Gnapheus’s *History regarding the martyrdom of Jan de Bakker of Woerden* <note>Original Latin: "J. Pistorii à Worden." Jan de Bakker was the first person in the Northern Netherlands to be executed for his Protestant beliefs.</note>. *History of the Martyrs*, folio 86. *History of the Martyrs* from folio 55. b. to 69. a.</margin>
...brought him into this suffering. Master Nicolaus Copinus of Mons <note>Original: "Copinus à Montibus"</note>, Godschalk Rosemond, and Ruard Tapper of Enkhuizen were initially his primary examiners of faith <term>Geloofsonderfoekers: inquisitors appointed to investigate heresy</term>, accusers, and opponents from among the clergy. Master Joost Lovering, or Laurens, President of the Great Council of Mechelen, later presided over the conduct and conclusion of these proceedings on behalf of the high secular authority; he was also a prominent member of the Inquisition, whom Erasmus described in a letter to Willibald Pirckheimer <margin>† Letter, page 1931. d.</margin> † as hating learning more than death itself. They had many verbal disputes with him during his imprisonment; they insisted that all the institutions and traditions of the Roman Church had to be accepted as rules for faith and life; that heretics had to be forced or uprooted with the sword; and that priests were bound not to marry.

He testified that he wished to establish nothing other than what was expressed in the Holy Scripture, understood in the sense that the Holy Spirit—by whose inspiration it was written—intended it to be understood. He argued that for the interpretation of Scripture, it was not necessary to use any words other than those of the Scripture itself. He confessed that one should not lightly violate the institutions of the church, but rather maintain them insofar as they agreed with the Word of God. Furthermore, he asserted that Christians were not free to force anyone to the faith with outward violence. One had to "compel people to come in" <note>A reference to Luke 14:23, often used by the Church to justify forced conversions; Jan de Bakker argues for a spiritual interpretation.</note>, just as God compels and commands us to compel; not with prisons, with blows, or with fire, but with benevolence and the instilling of the divine word—a compulsion as gentle and lovely as it is powerful; a compelling through living well and teaching well.

He complained that fornication was daily practiced, confessed, and forgiven among the priests; that this evil—even though the clergy fell back into it time and again after being pardoned—was overlooked because of the vast number of wrongdoers. Yet in him, they would not tolerate a chaste and honorable marriage, which God had permitted. To abstain from women and resist the desires of the flesh, he had applied much labor; but the more he resisted the evil, the more the desire increased. When asked by what means he had opposed that evil, he gave this answer: Through those means by which that kind of demon is commonly driven out—through much fasting and constant prayer...

<meta>This page continues the trial and eventual execution of Jan de Bakker (also known as Jan van Woerden). He is defending his decision to marry as a priest, arguing that the Church's requirement for celibacy is not based on Scripture.</meta>

### HISTORY

<margin>1525.</margin>...and heavy labor. To this was added that for two years, while I thus tormented myself, I abstained from strong drink. His marriage had also not occurred except in secret and without witnesses. It was said that he had transgressed against Canon Law <term>Canon Law: the body of laws and regulations made by the Catholic Church</term>, which he had sworn to uphold when he became a priest. He, in turn, argued: "I swore that I would live according to the Canons as far as my ability and knowledge allowed. I have kept that oath." He understood that the Church indeed had the power to establish certain rules for the sake of order, but not to impose them as a necessary article of faith. This also applied to the unmarried state of priests, which was not confirmed by any truly canonical Scripture; therefore, not even angels from heaven could make a new article of faith out of it, much less the Church, which is governed by the Word of God and holds no dominion over that Word. What more was presented to him, and his defense, can be read in the *History* written by Wilhelmus Gnaphæus <note>Willem de Volder, a humanist scholar and fellow prisoner</note>, his fellow prisoner, regarding his suffering, as well as in the account translated from it in the *Dutch Book of Martyrs* <margin>* From folio 55 verso to 69.</margin>. When he had already been condemned, President Joost Laurens let slip words that I am ashamed to recount in full: "I wish," he cried among other things, "that you had been dealing with ten foul harlots when you first coupled with your wife, so much work and trouble you cause us." This wish, or rather curse, was heard with horror and contradicted with loathing. His old father, Jan Dirkzoon Koster <note>original: "Jan Dirkſoon Koſter." The name Koster indicates his office as a sexton.</note>, who had been dismissed from his office as sexton for his son's sake, strengthened the prisoner as soon as he was allowed to speak to him, with these or similar words:

<margin>1525.</margin>and heavy labor. Added to this is the fact that for two years, while I tormented myself so, I abstained from strong drink. His marriage had also taken place only in secret and without witnesses. It was said that he had transgressed against Canon Law <term>Canon Law: the body of laws and regulations governing the Catholic Church</term>, which he had sworn to uphold when he was ordained a priest. He, on the contrary, argued: "I swore that I would live according to the Canons to the best of my ability and knowledge. That oath I have kept." He understood that the Church indeed had the power to establish rules for the sake of order, but not to impose them as a necessary article of faith. This also applied to the unmarried state of priests, which was not confirmed by any Scripture that was truly canonical; therefore, not even angels from heaven could make a new article of faith of it, much less the Church, which is governed by the word of God and does not hold lordship over that word. What else was held against him, and his defense, can be read in the *History* that Wilhelmus Gnaphaeus, his fellow prisoner, wrote of his suffering, as well as in the account translated from it in the *Dutch Book of Martyrs* <margin>* From folio 55. b. to 69.</margin>. Of the monetary fine, one third would go to the benefit of the informant; the other third to the benefit of the local Officer; and the third to the benefit of the Emperor. Which penalties and fines, having been judged, would be executed, notwithstanding any oppositions or appeals. <margin>1527.</margin> In the year 1527, the fires in which their fellow believers were burned could still be seen smoking daily. Most of them punished the killing of heretics <term>ketterdooden: the execution of people for religious dissent</term> when it struck too close to home, endured it where they had to suffer it, and practiced it where they held the power. Thus they did to others what they did not wish to have happen to themselves. Some misused fire, others water. Those who knew better ought to have done better. Furthermore, they were not driven by a good spirit who wished to shove the strayed into the grave, drown the infected, and burn the blind, instead of <margin>* Hooft I. 32.</margin> leading them aright, washing, and enlightening them *. The first Anabaptists <margin>Anabaptist Martyrs Vol. II. p. 81. p. 91.</margin> who, as far as I can tell from their writings, were killed in Holland under the Papacy, were Jan Walen and two of his fellow brethren from Krommeniersdijk in Waterland <note>Krommeniersdijk is a small hamlet in the Waterland region of North Holland</note>. In the year fifteen hundred twenty-seven, these men were more roasted to death by a slow fire than burned in the Hague. In Brussels, in that same year, <margin>Hooft’s History I. 33.</margin> the Dean of Leuven, Inquisitor over Brabant, Holland, and the neighboring regions, sentenced some sixty persons, partly to death and partly received back through penance. At the same time, <margin>ibid. p. 32. 33.</margin> the Provost of the Canons Regular of Ypres was Inquisitor over Flanders and the surrounding districts; and the Provost of the Scholars at Bergen in Hainaut <note>original: "Henegouw"</note> held authority over that province and its surroundings. On the twenty-eighth of January <note>original: "Loumaendt," the 'chilled month'</note> of the year fifteen hundred <margin>1528.</margin> twenty-eight, another edict <term>plakkaet: an official public decree or poster</term> was published in Holland against forbidden books and runaway clergy. With another decree, issued in Brussels on the twentieth of February <note>original: "Sprokkelmaendt," the 'wood-gathering month'</note>, <margin>New edict against the greed of the clergy in Flanders. Edicts of Flanders p. 749. 750.</margin> the Emperor again forbade the subjects of Flanders from creating or transferring any real estate, inheritance, or rents to monasteries, churches, colleges, or hospitals; commanding that no ecclesiastical persons could appoint themselves as heirs in any estate, nor hold or accept any property under the title of inheritance. He also forbade them from engaging in trade for profit, or taking any lands in lease or rent, under penalty of paying the same taxes and duties as laypeople. In Tournai <note>original: "Doornijk"</note> at this time, an Augustinian monk named Henrik was imprisoned facing execution <margin>History of the Martyrs f. 95. b. History of the Martyrs f. 72. b. Wesenbeck p. 10.</margin> because he had cast off his cowl, married a woman, and preached against the Papacy. They offered him his life, provided he would confess that the woman he had married was his whore or concubine, but he refused to let his days be lengthened under such a condition, and chose rather to be burned alive. <header>OF THE REFORMATION. BOOK II.</header>

<margin>
1529.
New edict on the matter of Heresy.
Edicts of Flanders from p. 107, to 113. p. 109.
</margin>
...there came out again a new <term>plakkaet: an official public edict or decree</term> against the Lutherans, which was signed at Brussels on the fourteenth of October <note>original: "Wijnmaendt" — literally "Wine-month," the traditional name for October</note>. By this decree, those who did not deliver forbidden books to be burned within a certain time, or who transgressed any of the edicts issued on the matter of heresy, were sentenced to death, without mercy or delay. Specifically, those who had previously turned back from their error and had now relapsed were to be killed by fire. For others, the men were to be executed with the sword, and the women with the pit—that is, buried alive in the earth. This was accompanied by an offer to receive into mercy those who would convert, except for the "relapsed" (those who had fallen away a second time) and those who were already imprisoned. Furthermore, the harboring of any heretical persons was forbidden, upon pain of life and property. Those who had once fallen into heresy were henceforth forbidden from speaking or trading with one another regarding any matters prohibited by the church, likewise upon pain of life and property. No one who was in any way suspected of heresy was admitted to the service of any honorable offices. To better discover the heretics, the edict promised informers half of the forfeited property, provided it was not more than one hundred pounds groot <note>A unit of currency in the County of Flanders</note> in Flemish money; if it were more, they would receive, besides that half, the tenth penny of the remainder. The surplus was to be spent on works of piety and mercy. Finally, it was ordered that those authorized to put this edict into effect should proceed without long legal formalities, and as summarily as could be done in reasonableness and equity. They were further required to send every three months to the Emperor—or in his absence, to the Governess Margaret <note>Margaret of Austria, the regent of the Habsburg Netherlands</note>—a broad declaration of all the accusations and indications that had come before them, and of their proceedings against those who were accused, so that their diligence might be judged, upon pain of being dismissed from office if found lacking. This edict was proclaimed on the twenty-fifth of October. On the twentieth of the same month, one Willem van Zwol was burned at Mechelen for the sake of Lutheranism *. In the Hague, Teunis Teekspoon of Naarden, a youth of twenty-four years, was burned in the year fifteen hundred thirty because of his zeal against the Papacy. He had first been a student at Leuven, very dissolute in his lifestyle, until later at Naarden, during a certain walk, he was struck down as if from heaven and brought home for dead. He took the mules from his feet, the stockings from his legs, and distributed them to the poor. Meanwhile, the Reformation in Germany appeared so strange in the eyes of our Erasmus that, around this time, he admonished those of the Netherlands and East Friesland with a long letter; that they should not involve themselves with the riot by which Lutheranism, in his judgment, was being advanced in some places, but that they should stand firm upon the rock of Christ. "Keep yourselves," thus he addressed them, "within the ark, so that you do not perish by the deluge: remain in Christ's little ship, so that the waves do not swallow you up: persevere in the sheepfold of the church, so that you do not become a prey for the wolf, or for Satan, who always goes around seeking whom he might devour. Wait at least for the decision that shall be made by the Emperor, the Princes, and further in the <term>Council: a general meeting of church leaders to settle matters of doctrine</term>. For through them the Lord, as I hope, shall still this storm... From one sect, many others emerge daily. Let them first come to an agreement among themselves before you surrender yourself to this one or that..." In particular, he was also offended by the persecution that the <term>Zwinglians: followers of the Swiss reformer Huldrych Zwingli</term> introduced against the Anabaptists. For those of Zurich, around this time, issued a second <term>plakkaet: an official decree</term> † ordering that the Anabaptists should be tolerated nowhere, but should be captured to be punished with death. They push bravely for that, he wrote, "that one may not kill heretics, while they themselves punish the Anabaptists by the neck <note>original: "aen den hals straffen" — meaning execution, usually by beheading or hanging</note>, people who are condemned on far fewer articles, and of whom it is said that in their company are very many who have converted from the worst to the best life; and even if they wander foolishly in some opinions, nonetheless they have never seized churches or cities, nor strengthened themselves with alliances against the power of the Authorities, nor driven anyone from his territory or goods." He also relates how the <term>Evangelicals: a term then used for those following the new Protestant teachings</term> sought to force people to their views. "Is that not forcing," he says, "if you refuse to hear our lessons, then you shall receive nothing from the <term>prebends: church stipends or incomes</term>? That no one travel on such a day to such a feast, that..."

But in the Netherlands, such disorders as yet found little place. The <term>Papacy: the institutional Roman Catholic Church under the Pope</term> still held sway here; it stuck a gag in the mouths of those who spoke against it; it held them fast to a stake, and it intended to burn the disputes along with the people. Yet the substance of the ashes, which were scattered to the wind, gave daily new cause to shun or oppose such a murderous church. 

In <note>original: "Wintermaendt"</note> December, Lady Margaret of Austria died in Mechelen; she was the daughter of Emperor Maximilian and had governed the Netherlands for about eighteen years very capably as a woman. <margin>Lady Margaret dies and Lady Mary, the Widow of Hungary, becomes Regent of the Netherlands. 1531.</margin> In her place, in <note>original: "Wijnmaendt"</note> October of the year fifteen hundred thirty-one, the Emperor appointed Lady Mary, his sister, the widow of King Louis of Hungary; a wise woman, who also loved learning and was fond of Latin books; of whom Erasmus said, <margin>† In Letters, p. 846. g.</margin> † *The state of human affairs is changing; the monks know nothing of learning, and the women make much of books.*

However, it took another four years before these were published, and it was later found that this important work had many deficiencies. One of the first printers was sentenced to the sword and beheaded <note>1</note>. Someone later gathered the most comforting passages of Scripture and published them under the title *Fontein des levens* <note>Fountain of Life</note>. However, this little book, which contained nothing but the words of Scripture without any commentary and seemed intended to lead people away from superstitions toward God and Christ, was a great offense to the most vehement supporters of the <term>Papacy: the institutional Roman Catholic Church</term>; so much so that a certain Franciscan friar from Brabant undertook a journey to Amsterdam, where it was first printed, and bought up the entire printing, which he then burned <note>2</note>; but it was immediately reprinted in various places. The Emperor also commanded that the decree of the year fifteen hundred twenty-nine should be published again throughout all the Netherlands on the fifteenth of November <note>original: "Slachtmaendt", the "slaughter month"</note> next, and from that day forward every six months <note>4</note>. <margin>1531.</margin>...but only a reasonable sum of money or life annuities for necessary maintenance might be brought in. Likewise, no ordained persons were permitted to buy or acquire hereditary property or rents. Furthermore, no such property could come to the Convents or ordained persons through gifts, last wills, inheritances from fathers, mothers, friends, or relatives, or otherwise; whether by a pledge to return the same later, or by any other means. In the same way, no movable goods could come to the aforementioned ordained persons or Convents by inheritance, pledge, or other means—and all this upon the forfeiture of said goods, whether hereditary, movable, or immovable. This was despite the alleged customary practice of the clergy, or any charters and ordinances that they might have obtained through persistence, oversight, or any other way, from us—so the <term>decree: original "plakkaet," a public law or edict</term> speaks in the Emperor’s name—or our predecessors: *which we all together, if any such exist, for the preservation of the lands of Holland, Zeeland, and Friesland, and their inhabitants, and for our sovereignty, lordship, and service, have revoked, do revoke, and annul by these presents.* Against the <term>greed: original "baetsucht," an excessive desire for profit</term> of the clergy, measures had also been taken in Holland with decrees in the years fifteen hundred and fifteen <note>1</note> and fifteen hundred and twenty-four <note>2</note>.

In Holland, on the twelfth of February <note>original: "Sprokkelmaendt," an old Dutch name for the month when wood was gathered</note>, the sheltering of ministers who taught Anabaptism <note>original: "herdooperij," literally "re-baptizing"</note> was forbidden; and a reward of twelve guilders was set for every teacher who was taken into custody <gloss>4</gloss>. On the twenty-seventh, it was announced throughout all Holland by the higher authorities <gloss>5</gloss> that all who had been rebaptized and were repentant, and wished to confess as a sign of regret, and within twenty-four days of the announcement provided proof from their confessors, would—in such a case and for that time—be received in mercy; on pain that the stubborn would be dealt with according to written laws and the decree. On the last of March <note>original: "Lentemaendt," the month of Lent</note>, Lady Mary <note>Mary of Hungary, Governor of the Netherlands and sister to Emperor Charles V</note> wrote that she understood some weaponry for war had been found among some sectarians in Overijssel, which smacked of rebellion, and that the Court received such people, if they showed remorse, in mercy: but her opinion was that one should proceed against such guilty ones with such severity of the law that the error might be extinguished and the land remain at peace, yet taking care that the land was not too greatly depopoluated. Upon the report of the Court of Holland, that sometimes circumstances might require the stubborn heretics to be put to death in secret—which they believed would create more awe and serve as a greater example—Lady Mary wrote on the ninth of November <note>original: "Slachtmaendt," the month of slaughtering livestock</note> that she left the execution of the aforementioned persons to the discretion...

<margin>Origin of the fanatical Anabaptists</margin> Around this time, some Anabaptists began to show themselves in this country who were seized with fanaticism, or who persuaded themselves that they were led by the Spirit of God. They believed this could only be known through divine revelation. Yet the gift of prophecy, they boasted, was present in their assembly, through which they predicted future things and revealed hidden matters. They dreamed dreams, saw visions, and some of their women prophesied. Nicholas Storch <note>Niklaes Stork; a weaver from Zwickau and one of the "Zwickau Prophets" who influenced the early Reformation</note> pretended to be entirely unlearned—perhaps he truly was—and proclaimed that the knowledge leading to salvation was revealed to him from heaven. They held, among others, this rule: *That no one should make it his work to practice arts and learning; nor seek science and knowledge elsewhere than in the goodness of the eternal God, for which human aids were not necessary; for why would anyone want to serve and honor God otherwise, if He did not deign to show that same kindness with which the fathers and holy men were gifted in ancient times? Indeed, they understood that one must pray for the same fellowship and conversation with God, which was shared with those who persisted in asking for it.* Afterward, Storch took it upon himself to believe that the Angel Gabriel had promised him the highest place in a new kingdom that would soon arise. These were the beginnings of terrible disturbances that flew from one end of Germany to the other, even into the Netherlands; and many simple-hearted Anabaptists <term>Doopsgesinden; literally "Baptism-minded," referring here to the peaceful branch of the movement</term> allowed themselves to be entangled in great difficulties, joining too easily with these Sword-spirits <term>Swaerdtgeesten; radical, revolutionary Anabaptists who believed in using the sword to establish God's kingdom</term>: especially because they similarly urged the baptism of adults, foolishly thinking that it was also the Spirit of God that moved these people. Many Anabaptists were also viewed and punished by certain magistrates as being the same people, even though they did not join them. From this sect arose Thomas Müntzer <note>Thomas Muncer; a radical reformer and a key figure in the German Peasants' War</note>, who served as a leader to the Thuringian peasants in the year fifteen hundred twenty-five, leading them to their destruction †. This was the strange, dizzying spirit that also traveled through Holland at this time, though with fewer weapons, taking hold of many people and carrying them out of their senses. # HISTORY

->one hundred thirty-two.<- To prevent the gathering of the citizens and to make him depart, the Papal party <note>original: "Pausgefinden"; those loyal to the Catholic Church</note> gave him some money. He departed, but soon returned and preached as before. Indeed, some prominent citizens received him into the city and, when he was locked out of the churches, they placed a pulpit outside in the portal. But as the number of citizens and listeners increased, they demanded that the churches be opened to them, threatening otherwise to break them open by force. Thereafter, Rothmann <note>Bernhard Rothmann, the lead reformer in Münster who eventually turned to radical Anabaptism</note>, with the advice of his followers, summoned several learned men from Hesse to assist him. Then it was deliberated how the Papacy might best be abolished at the first opportunity, in order to propagate the Gospel with greater fruit. They drafted thirty articles, containing various Papal errors, which were delivered to the Magistrate with an offer to maintain that these were contrary to God's word. The Papal party was asked if they wished to assert the contrary. They answered: *That they (as Sleidanus <note>Johannes Sleidanus, a prominent 16th-century historian known for his chronicles of the Reformation</note>, a diligent and faithful historian, relates it) had nothing with which to defend their cause. And that their previous claims that their positions were virtuous and right had been made out of good intentions and ignorance.* Upon such a confession, the churches were taken from them by the Magistrate and assigned to Rothmann and his followers. Regarding this, they came to open violence against one another; the Papal party had to give way until, through the intervention of the Landgrave of Hesse <note>Philipp I of Hesse, a major political protector of the Reformation</note>, the matter was settled on this footing: That Rothmann and his followers should preach the Gospel in the six churches and reform what was evil, but in the Cathedral <term>domkerke; the main bishop's church</term> nothing should be changed. This treaty was even signed by the Bishop himself. In this state of affairs, when everything had been brought back to rest, the Anabaptists <term>Wederdoopers; literally 're-baptizers'</term> came to Münster and opposed Rothmann on the matter of baptism. At first, they held their meetings by night while others slept. The Magistrate ordered them to depart. They did so, but secretly returned to the city. Rothmann went over to them. The city was forbidden to them a second time; however, they came back inside and hid themselves secretly among their adherents. The Landgrave, at the request of the council, sent several Preachers to preach against them. They were offered a proper dispute <note>A formal theological debate</note>, under the condition *that one should act solely from the Holy Scriptures and take several learned, pious men as mediators...* This they refused—

<margin>1534.</margin> ...also melting down what those who had fled or been driven out had left behind; all books were burned, except for the Bible. Shortly thereafter, the city was besieged by the Bishop, and Jan Matthijszoon, the false Enoch <note>Matthijszoon claimed to be the prophet Enoch, signaling the end times.</note>, was killed during a military sortie. Jan van Leiden <note>Original: "Jan Bokelszoon"; he was a tailor from Leiden who became the "King" of Münster.</note>, acting as if driven by the spirit, then ran about naked and appointed twelve Judges to rule the New Israel. All virgins over the age of fourteen were also violated. After this, Jan van Leiden set himself up as King in Zion. # HISTORY

->116<-

<margin>1534. Amsterdam seeks to secure itself against the Anabaptists.</margin> It was made known from Friesland <note>original: "Vrieslandt"</note> that the Anabaptists <term>Wederdoopers<gloss>Literally "re-baptizers"; a radical Reformation sect that insisted on adult baptism and, in some branches, revolutionary social change.</gloss></term> were planning to seize the city by force. The militia <note>The "schutters" were civic guardsmen responsible for city defense.</note> were immediately gathered—those of the Our Lady and Cross Guilds—at the city hall. The Anabaptist plot was presented to them to determine what assistance the City Council <note>original: "Wethouders"</note> could expect from them in case of emergency. To this, they answered unanimously that they were ready to live and die for the common good. Consequently, it was forbidden to harbor Anabaptists under penalty of death. Foreign Anabaptists who were not citizens were ordered to leave the city by five o'clock that same evening, on pain of being punished by the neck <note>A euphemism for execution by hanging or beheading.</note>. In the evening, the guards gathered again in the market square. House searches were conducted everywhere, and twenty "Re-baptizers" <note>original: "Herdoopers"</note> were taken prisoner and brought to the *Boeijen*—the name given to the city prison <note>Literally "The Shackles."</note>.

On the second of May <note>original: "Bloeimaendt," the Month of Flowers.</note>, the Count of Hooghstraeten, Governor <term>Stadthouder<gloss>The provincial representative of the monarch, serving as the highest administrative and military official.</gloss></term> of Holland, arrived in the city with several Councilors of the Court. On the eighth day thereafter, two Anabaptists were beheaded. Those who had converted back to the traditional faith—eighteen in total—were required to walk in the procession on the tenth of the month, bareheaded and barefoot, dressed in linen, with wax candles in their hands. On the eleventh, four were beheaded and four were burned. On the twelfth, one was executed, and on the sixteenth, four more were beheaded.

In the meantime, Jan van Leyden, who was then still sitting on the throne of Münster <note>The Anabaptists had seized the city of Münster in Germany, establishing a radical "Kingdom of Zion."</note>, had been led to believe that God had granted him three mighty cities: Amsterdam, Deventer, and Wesel. He then sent Jacob van Kampen to Amsterdam to serve as Bishop there, with Jan Matthijssoon of Middelburg assigned as his assistant. Shortly before this, the Count of Hooghstraeten, in his capacity as Governor, visited the cities of Haarlem, Leiden, and Delft to establish order against the Anabaptists and the Sacramentarians <term>Sacramentariſſen<gloss>Reformers who denied the physical presence of Christ in the bread and wine of the Eucharist, viewing it as a symbolic memorial.</gloss></term>. He returned to Amsterdam on the first of October <note>original: "Wijnmaendt," the Wine Month.</note>, where he charged the City Council with being too negligent and lax in their punishments. It was from this leniency, he understood, that the rising evil continued to crawl further each day. # H I S T O R Y

<margin>1535.</margin>...[ran], stark naked through the city, with a terrifying cry: *Woe, woe, woe! the vengeance of God, the vengeance of God, the vengeance of God!* Upon hearing this midnight noise, the citizenry rushed to arms. The Naked Runners <note>A radical group of Anabaptists who believed that because they were "reborn," they were as innocent as Adam and Eve before the Fall, and thus should walk naked to represent the "naked truth."</note> were captured, except for one woman, who escaped. Brought to the city hall, they refused to put on the clothes offered to them. *We are*, they said, *the naked truth*. Meanwhile, the neighbors of the house where the runners had gathered noticed the stench of the clothes lying in the fire, but the door had been so firmly locked that the lock had to be shot open with a musket: just in time, for the bedstead had already been ignited by the fire, which was immediately extinguished.

<margin>Hortensius, p. 56.</margin>A house-to-house search was then conducted everywhere, the clock bells were struck, and the city gates were kept closed. On the twentieth of February <note>original: "Sprokkelmaendt," an old Dutch term for the month of "scattering" or wood-gathering.</note>, as many as a thousand Anabaptists from Hainaut arrived at Amsterdam near the New Dike: but it was wisely managed so that they turned back. On the twenty-

<margin>Seven Naked Runners and nine Anabaptists beheaded.</margin>fifth, the seven men who ran naked were beheaded. One cried: *Praise the Lord always*. The second: *Avenge the blood of your own*. Another: *Open your eyes*. The fourth: *Woe, woe!* On the sixth of March <note>original: "Lentemaendt," literally "Spring month."</note>, nine more Anabaptists were punished with the same death. Thus Lambertus Hortensius and Johannes Isacius Pontanus relate the naked running in Amsterdam, with the punishment that followed.

<margin>* The names of the Magistrates have stood in the Register behind the work since the year 1413 until 1548.</margin>But in the Registry * of the Ordinances <term>Willekeuren<gloss>Local laws or decrees issued by a city council or magistrate.</gloss></term>, kept at the Secretariat of that city, one reads that nearly fifty people ran naked through the streets; that they cried: *Woe Babylon!* and that twelve men and twelve women were captured. While in custody, they refused to eat or drink from any earthenware, smashed the clay pitchers to pieces, and danced on the shards. One of the men refused to eat unless someone chewed for him, saying, *I am a child*. When their Prophet, Dirk Snijder <note>Dirk the Tailor.</note>, was to be beheaded, he cried out three times: *Open your eyes, and behold!* He had prophesied that no instruments would be able to kill him, but he was a false prophet; the sword went right through him. Another cried out three times, *O fearless God, have mercy on the ignorant!* Another, *Father forgive them, for they know not what they do*. Another came dancing and jumping onto the scaffold, singing without ceasing, *Praise the Lord*, without wanting to kneel. When the Executioner threatened to bind him to a wheel, he finally began to kneel, and was beheaded while saying *Praise the Lord*.

They gathered in the village of Tzum near Franeker; from there they marched, about three hundred men strong, along with women and children, toward the Old Monastery <note>original: "Oudekloofter," specifically the Cistercian Bloemkamp Abbey</note> near Bolsward. They resolved to live and die together, opened fire, and repelled four assaults. But on the seventh of April <note>original: "Grasmaendt," literally "Grass month," an old Dutch name for April.</note>, the attack became too heavy for them, the monastery was overwhelmed, and everyone who resisted was put to death, except for sixty-two men and seventy women, with their children, who were sent to the court at Leeuwarden. On Schenk’s side, one hundred soldiers had fallen. Afterward, a gallows was erected at the west end of the monastery; twenty-four prisoners were hanged, fifteen beheaded, and many women and maidens were drowned near the blockhouse <note>A small fortification or defensive tower.</note> at Leeuwarden and in the Hempensermeer <note>A lake near the village of Hempens.</note>. Some, having been misled and deceived through simplicity, were set free.

<margin>1535. <note>original: MDXXXV.</note></margin> [believing that] judgment was at hand, [people came] from all sides, and that same night around three hundred persons allowed themselves to be re-baptized, persuading themselves that all who were not re-baptized would be damned. The unrest at Bolsward was stirred up by Jan van Geelen, whom the King of Münster <note>Jan van Leyden, the leader of the radical Anabaptist kingdom in Münster, Germany.</note> had sent with much money to Friesland and Holland to be the Commander of all the Anabaptist <term>Wederdooperſche; the Anabaptists believed in adult baptism and often sought to establish a "New Jerusalem" through social revolution.</term> hosts, whom he had been led to believe were gathering in those regions for his service. Having escaped from the defeat at the Old Monastery <note>Oudekloofter</note>, he went to Amsterdam, where he changed his name. But to more safely carry out his fanatical Anabaptist schemes, he later traveled to Brussels, pretended to renounce his errors, and obtained letters of pardon from Queen Mary <note>Mary of Hungary, the Governor of the Netherlands for Emperor Charles V.</note>, under the condition that he would do his best to deliver Münster into the Emperor's hands in one way or another. Since then, while still secretly keeping company with the Anabaptists, he moved openly among the citizens of Amsterdam: there, in a short time, he drew such a number of followers to his cause that he decided with them to seize the city by night—the city which they believed had been given to their King of Zion, Jan van Leyden. They designated the tenth of May <note>original: "Bloeimaendt," the Month of Flowers.</note> for this purpose, and set the ringing of the city hall bell as the signal to gather at the house of one Pieter Gael in the Arrow Alley <note>original: "Pijlsteeg," a narrow street near the Dam Square.</note>. However, on the very evening the attack was to take place at night, it was unexpectedly revealed to the Mayors. At first, they thought it was neither believable nor possible to conduct such a plot so secretly; but the informant gave so many reasons for his claim, and showed so much evidence of that intention, that they finally believed him. Then, it being already early in the night, they deliberated on how best to call the citizens to arms as quietly as possible and have them come to the city hall: but by taking too much time in consultation, without being able to understand one another, the time slipped away—time that required both counsel and action at once. <margin>1535. <note>original: MDXXXV.</note></margin> [The] magistrates escaped by the narrowest of margins; the guard was mostly killed or taken prisoner. A certain servant of the Sheriff, awakened by the first noise while he lay heavily intoxicated between chairs and benches where he slept (for the Archers of the Cross-Guild had been feasting with the Magistrates and the most honorable citizens, and the Anabaptists <term>Wederdoopers; radical reformers who practiced adult baptism and sought to establish a "New Jerusalem" by force</term> had taken advantage of that time), immediately climbed upstairs.
