The citizens were immediately stirred to occupy the entrances to the Dam <note>The central square of Amsterdam</note>; but all those who first went to the market to fight were shot through, many with poisoned bullets. Burgomaster Mr. Pieter Kolijn, a <margin>p. 63.</margin> learned and God-fearing man—who, because he had previously been somewhat lenient toward the Anabaptists <term>Doopsgezinden; another term for the Baptist-minded reformers</term>, had fallen under suspicion by many in matters of religion—now sought, in the sight of his citizens, to clear himself of that evil suspicion by leading them vigorously. Thus, he arrived at the market with more fervor than caution, where the Anabaptists rushed out. The citizenry was immediately driven back, and the Burgomaster was murdered. Afterward, <margin>p. 64.</margin> Burgomaster Gooswin Rekalf, an old soldier who had followed the wars, commanded that sails be stretched across the corners of the streets leading to the Dam, and that hop-sacks be rolled toward them to serve as breastworks for protection. Seeing that little could be accomplished with the citizens who had been seized by terror, he also immediately began to hire some volunteers on monthly pay for the service of the city and under the command of the Burgomasters, to lead the first attack. Meanwhile, the townspeople remained quiet, but the Anabaptists spent the rest of the night singing the Psalms of David. Jan van Geelen still believed that they would capture the city before ten o'clock the following morning, and that without bloodshed, with such a handful of people; for it is thought that the leaders of this plot were no more than forty strong. The next day, artillery was brought to the Dam, and the <margin>p. 65.</margin> door of the Hospital <note>The Sint-Elisabethsgasthuis</note>, at the side of the Town Hall, was shot down. The soldiers, followed closely by the citizens, broke in and drove the Anabaptists into the innermost parts of the Town Hall. On the fourteenth of May <note>original: Bloeimaendt, or "Flower Month"</note>, the hearts of several prisoners were cut from their chests on a butcher's block and thrown in their faces; their bodies were quartered, the pieces hung on the city gates, and the heads set on stakes. On the fifteenth, three more men were beheaded and two women drowned. On the twenty-first, two women were hung in their own doorways in the Pijlsteeg <note>Arrow Alley, a street near the Dam in Amsterdam</note> because they had known of the plot, sheltered the rioters, and poisoned the bullets. Before this, nine more women had been drowned. On the twenty-second, three more men were beheaded; three days later another, and on the first of July <note>original: Hooimaendt, or "Hay Month"</note> two more, because they had known of the treason and not revealed it. Also, a widow and her son were hung in her doorway because they had sheltered Bishop Jacob van Kampen and had not reported him. To capture this Bishop, a large bounty was placed on his head, and anyone who hid him and did not turn him in before sunset was threatened with being hung in their own doorway. He was not turned in, however, but was caught while hiding under some peat. He was thrown upon the rack <term>pijnbank; a torture device used to stretch the body to extract confessions</term>, but he would not confess to any treason, saying nothing other than: *I have forfeited my life; I have been rebaptized and have rebaptized [others]. I never wished to give permission for the treason of Amsterdam.* He had often written in his letters: *I, Jacob van Kampen, Bishop at Amsterdam, Lector at Münster.* His punishment, even before the pain of death, was increased with public shame. He was displayed on the scaffold for a full hour, wearing a two-horned miter <note>A mock bishop’s hat, used here to ridicule his religious claims</note> on his head for show. The tongue with which he had taught was cut out and thrown to the dogs, and the hand with which he had rebaptized was chopped off. Finally, they bound him to a butcher's block and beheaded him with a butcher's cleaver, burned his body in the market, and placed his head and hand upon the city gate. Jan Matthijszoon of Middelburg had escaped. On the same day, two more women, who served as messengers, were hung from the iron bars in front of the tribunal <term>vierschaar; the place where high justice was administered</term>. Among the supporters of Jan van Geelen were also many common folk from Benskoop, near IJsselstein, who

he <note>Likely referring to Bishop Jacob van Kampen</note> had summoned about three hundred men to Amsterdam around the tenth of May <note>original: Bloeimaendt, "Flower Month"</note>; but they arrived too late and, hearing of the defeat of their comrades, retreated again. He had also summoned more of his followers here; they too arrived only after the fight, when the harbor boom <term>boom; a heavy wooden beam or chain used to block access to a harbor</term> was still closed. These fled to England with two ships. Sleidanus, Book X, f. 162. See also Erasmus's Epistles, p. 1537, etc.</margin>. > That all those, men and women, who should be found infected with the rejected sect of the Anabaptists, or Rebaptizers <term>Wederdoopers; a radical wing of the Reformation that practiced adult baptism and sought total social upheaval</term>, of whatever state or condition they might be, their instigators, followers, and accomplices, should incur the forfeiture of life and property, and be brought to the ultimate punishment without any delay. Namely, those who remained stubborn, or those who had misled and rebaptized someone into the aforementioned sect, as well as those who had carried the name of Prophets, Apostles, or Bishops, [should be punished] by fire: and all other men (having been rebaptized, or who had secretly and with premeditated counsel sheltered someone else or any of the aforementioned Anabaptists, [but] who renounced their evil intent and views and had true sorrow and repentance for them) by the sword: and the women buried in a pit <term>in een put gedolven; a common execution method for women, often involving being buried alive or drowned in a pit</term>. Commanding all subjects to report these same Anabaptists, upon penalty of being punished as a favorer, follower, and accomplice of that sect, and promising the informant one-third of the resulting confiscation. Furthermore, forbidding anyone to promote mercy, forgiveness, or reconciliation for them, or for that reason to present any petitions or requests, upon penalty of being punished at the court's discretion.

# HISTORY OF THE REFORMATION. BOOK II.

<margin>1535</margin>
Considering that we neither wish nor intend, states the edict, *that these Anabaptists or Rebaptizers (on account of their evil intentions) shall be received into grace, but rather that punishment shall be carried out upon them as an example to others, without any concealment, favor, or delay.* To the creation of this edict, the madness in Munster, the running naked <note>A radical group of Anabaptists in Amsterdam ran naked through the streets in February 1535, claiming they represented the "naked truth."</note>, the seizure of the Old Monastery <note>Referring to the Bloemkamp Abbey or "Oudeklooster" in Friesland, which was briefly occupied by radical Anabaptists in March 1535.</note>, and the attack on Amsterdam had certainly given cause: yet, in the capture and sentencing, not enough care was taken to see if those brought to death were actually guilty of such outrages: instead, rage was vented against all Anabaptists, no matter how simple and defenseless they were, without making much distinction. Thus, the History of their Martyrs relates that in Amsterdam at this time, one Pieter, formerly a Sexton at Zaandam <note>original: "Sardam"</note>, was beheaded as if guilty of the riot, though he (being a Teacher among the more moderate Anabaptists) had opposed it with all earnestness. In the month of March <note>original: "Lentemaendt," the spring month</note>, five Anabaptists were captured at Hoorn: Sijbrandt Janssoon, Hendrik Gijsbertssoon of Kampen, Steven Benedictus, and the women Femme Egberts and Welmoedt Jans. They were left in prison at first, but at the urging of the Court, the Sheriff <term>Schout: a local official responsible for law enforcement and prosecution</term>, Master Antonis Sonk, was required to bring charges. At that time, the Pastor and other learned men worked hard to pull them back to the Roman Church, but they remained steadfast in their views, saying among other things to the Sheriff: *When the little sheep is fat, it must be slaughtered.* <note>A grim proverb suggesting that their "ripeness" in faith made them targets for the executioner.</note> For this reason, on the seventh of June <note>original: "Somermaendt," the summer month</note>, because they (so the sentence reads) *openly confessed to being rebaptized*, they were all sentenced to death. The three men were beheaded in the morning at the Bathland <note>original: "Baedlandt," a location in Hoorn</note>; and the two women were brought to the Head (as the pilings and pier of the harbor are called) and there, with a stone tied around their neck or body, were drowned in the sea. This did not happen without great pity from the citizens, and even from most of the Magistrates, to whom this business was so repulsive that they subsequently troubled their citizens so little over matters of faith as was feasibly possible. These were also the only people put to death in Hoorn for the sake of religion. In Amsterdam, on the twenty-fifth of July <note>original: "Hooimaendt," the hay month</note>, four more Anabaptists were beheaded, and among them Barent the baker of Zwolle, the King’s cook <gloss>*</gloss> <note>referring to the cook of Jan van Leiden, the "King" of Munster</note>. In Zierikzee, at this time, a certain simple countryman was put to death by fire <gloss>†</gloss> because he spoke against the bread of the Mass <note>original: "misbroodt," the Eucharistic wafer</note>.

The persecution, now spreading far and wide in the Netherlands, struck in the year fifteen hundred and thirty-six a stranger of good reputation and learning. William Tyndale, an Englishman, who had translated the New Testament into his mother tongue and distributed it throughout England, was captured for this reason in Antwerp, taken to Vilvoorde <note>A town in the Duchy of Brabant, near Brussels, which served as a primary location for the imprisonment and execution of heretics.</note>, and there finally strangled and burned *. While the murderousness of such a man-devouring church <note>A reference to the Roman Catholic Church of that era and the intensity of the Inquisition.</note> made the Papacy all the more hateful, and although some used the teachings of the Reformation for their own benefit, there nevertheless remained much to be rebuked in those who had separated themselves from the Papacy. The majority of the crowd led such an un-Christian life that Erasmus <note>Desiderius Erasmus of Rotterdam (1466–1536), the preeminent Dutch humanist and scholar who sought to reform the church from within through reason and education.</note> said of it: † *I am heartily concerned that Paganism shall follow upon Pharisaism.* <note>original: "Phariseefdom." Erasmus uses this term to describe a religion consisting only of outward ceremonies and legalism, fearing the Reformers' reaction would lead to a total lack of religious order.</note> The reasons he had presented some time before against the Reformers of this century—regarding their boastfulness, the paths they took to achieve their ends, and the fruits of their labors—should be briefly presented here, so that the reader may judge whether he had sufficient reason not to join them more closely. He addressed them in a certain writing, found in the ninth volume of his works and in the latest edition of his letters, with these words: *“But you boast that you are bringing back to light the Gospel truth <note>original: "Evangelische waerheit"</note>, which had lain buried for more than a thousand years. If you speak the truth, you are engaged in a heavier work than the Apostles undertook in times past: for the*

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s critique of the Reformers, contrasting the moral integrity of the early Apostles with the perceived lack of virtue in the new "Gospel" movement. It follows his warning that a lack of religious order might lead to a new form of paganism.</meta>

the *Jewish ceremonies* and the *superstition of the Pagans* could be much more easily undone and overthrown than such things which the *Leaders of the Church* have taught, honored, and held fast with such great consensus for so many centuries as oracles of God, and still hold fast today. To this he added that the absurdities of the *Pagan Religion* were so great that they were even noticed by the men of letters among them; and that it was foretold in the prophecies of the Prophets that the Pagans would acknowledge the true God; and that the *Jewish ceremonies* would *vanish as shadows* before the bright light of the Gospel. Add to this, he continued, that a perpetual consensus of doctrine, alongside the miracles, gave credit to the preaching of the Apostles; whereas you people <note>Erasmus is addressing the leaders and followers of the Reformation.</note> not only differ among yourselves, but while remaining the same, you constantly change both the ceremonies and the doctrines, and are entirely unprovided with that other gift <note>The "gift" refers to the performance of miracles, which Erasmus argues the Reformers lack as proof of their divine mission.</note>. I also believe that the miracles themselves did not have as great a power and impression to reform the world as did the morals of the Evangelists, which were entirely pure and blameless. I am not speaking now of fasting, or clothing, and similar institutions, which hypocrites also mimic: but a vigilant tranquility in persecutions, a gentleness in enduring injustice, a mind that was simple and mild, that wished no one ill, and sought to do good to everyone—a spirit that was elevated above all human matters and held life of little account—especially brought their teaching into high regard. They drew the people away from what they were accustomed to, but brought them to something much better. 

You people shout bravely against the excess of the Priests, against the ambition of the Bishops, against the tyranny of the Roman Pope, against the chatter of the Sophists <note>original: "Sophisten." Erasmus used this term to mock the Scholastic theologians of the universities, whom he felt used complex logic to obscure simple Christian truths.</note>, against the prayers, against the fasting, against the mass, and you do not want those things purified, but removed. Nothing of what was previously accepted pleases you at all. But you pull out the weeds with the wheat, or, to put it better, you pull out the wheat as if it were weeds. But meanwhile, what better things do you bring forth, things more worthy of the Gospel, to make us depart from our customs? Cast your eye over the "Gospel" people <note>original: "Euangelisch volk." This refers to the early Protestants who claimed to follow only the Gospel (*Sola Scriptura*).</note>, and notice whether they make less of excess, of pleasures, and of money than those whom we detest; bring forth one who, through that Gospel, has been made sober from a glutton; gentle from a cruel man; generous from a greedy one; a blesser from a curser; and a modest man from a shameless one. ...than they were before. The **Images** have been cast out of the churches, but what does it profit if the idols of vice are honored in the heart nonetheless? And I do not see what purpose some had in casting down the images with such passion, unless it were to serve as the watchword of a conspiracy. Meanwhile, the terrible sin of **idolatry** is used as a pretext: but who is now so foolish as to believe that understanding resides in stone or wood? And if such people should still exist, how little effort would it take to teach the people that images were invented solely for this purpose: to strengthen the memory of the unlearned <term>unlearned: literally 'the unskilled' (Dutch: *onbedrevenen*), referring to those who could not read and relied on visual aids for religious instruction</term>. The customary **Prayers** have been rejected, but now there are many who do not pray at all... The **Mass** has been abolished, but what comes in its place that is more sanctified? .. I have never been inside their churches, but once I saw them coming out from a sermon as if breathed upon by an evil spirit, displaying on all their faces a wrath and a strange wildness: and there was no one among them all who showed me—accompanied as I was by some honorable men—the respect that we show to everyone, except for one little old man. Thus, I think, do soldiers return from the address of a General when they have been incited to battle and martial bravery... **Confession** has been abolished, but meanwhile there are many who do not even confess to God. With **Fasting**, the distinction of food has been rejected: but meanwhile people lapse very heavily into excess; and while they have indeed fled from Judaism, they have done so in such a way that they have begun to become **Epicureans** <term>Epicureans: here used as a label for those who focus on material pleasure and the indulgence of the senses rather than spiritual discipline</term>.

The ceremonies have been trampled underfoot, but the spirit did not increase; indeed, as far as I can judge, it decreased greatly. **Paul** observed some Jewish ceremonies so that he would not alienate the Jews from the Gospel. One ought then, at the very least, to reject ceremonies in this manner <note>meaning with the same pastoral care and gradual approach as the Apostle Paul</note>. It is true that the **Apostles** knew of no set fast days; but they themselves fasted daily of their own accord, even though it was not commanded of them. They knew of no distinction of food, but they voluntarily used the poorest fare and were in all things extremely sober. No one was prescribed that he must eat peas and beans, but they were satisfied with them of their own accord, if the situation so required. No one was forbidden the use of wine: but **Timothy** voluntarily abstained from it to such an extent that Paul had to exhort him to use a little wine to strengthen the weakness of his body. .. ...cast down, but where are those who have bowed their necks under the gentle yoke of the Lord? And meanwhile, human institutions were changed into human institutions, indeed into such as are not very humane. The name alone is changed, for it is called the Word of God; for the rest, matters are so little softened that many good people have chosen a voluntary exile in preference to that so highly-praised liberty... Men have rejected the dominion of the Bishops, but in such a way that they did not even obey the secular Magistrates <term>Magistrates: civil authorities or government officials</term>. In former times, the Christians lived quietly under the Pagan Princes, cautiously taking care that they gave no occasion for sedition, giving honor to whom they owed honor, toll to whom they owed toll, and tribute to whom they owed tribute: the early Christians were exhorted to obey even the idolatrous Magistrates, and they prayed to God daily for their welfare: but these people, who are so Evangelical <term>Evangelical: a term used here for the early Protestants who claimed to return to the Gospel (Evangelium)</term>, are loathed even by the Turkish Emperor <note>original: "Turkschen Keiser," referring to the Sultan of the Ottoman Empire</note>, because, says he, they are born for sedition. In the beginning, they held Luther almost as a God; now he seems to them to be entirely doting <note>original: "suffen," implying he is senile or muddled</note>, because he does not accept the new teaching of the Lord's Supper <note>This refers to the "Sacramentarian" controversy, where more radical reformers like Zwingli disagreed with Luther over the physical presence of Christ in the Eucharist</note>... Luther everywhere preaches faith, and this, wherever it may be, cannot be idle; it works through love, and it works nothing but good... The love of riches, of pleasures, and the lust for damnation <note>This likely refers to a "damnable lust" or greed that leads to spiritual ruin</note> has crept into the Roman Popes and the other Bishops; you people want to rule immediately, you people want to become rich immediately... This is the misfortune of human affairs, that from the best beginnings they gradually degenerate into the worst. Indeed, one is ashamed to relate what the beginnings of your enterprise are like... <meta>This page continues the discussion of the Dutch humanist Desiderius Erasmus’s moderate approach to church reform. While the previous page critiqued the chaos of the radical reformers, this page outlines Erasmus’s specific suggestions for a "middle way" that avoids both stagnation and revolution.</meta>

->### OF THE REFORMATION. BOOK III<-
R
<meta>catchword: reasonableness</meta>

...reasonableness and trained judgment were notable. What these people decided upon had to be briefly summarized by a few individuals chosen for that purpose. The technical arguments of theologians were to remain within the walls of the schools. One should not hold every kind of opinion as an article of faith. Certain institutions should be abolished; others should be changed into simple exhortations. This ought to be the primary concern of Princes and cities: that such men be placed over the flock of the Lord who are well-versed in the Word of God and trained to teach, to exhort, to comfort, to reprove, and to refute... In a letter <gloss>1</gloss> that has come down to us only in fragments, it was indicated: what could be tolerated in the Roman Church, and what therein ought to be improved; what those who had abolished various things should have put in their place; as well as what points they could have agreed upon with one another. He also understood that one should not reform everything at once and in haste, but by degrees and gradually <gloss>2</gloss>. That one should not labor so much to dismantle the order of things as to ensure that every individual improved their own character within themselves <gloss>3</gloss>. That the Princes must take care to purify the entire state of the church, through whom such a task could be carried out without riot <gloss>4</gloss>. That the improvement of the church would not likely succeed unless it originated from the Authorities <gloss>5</gloss>. He required caution in those who sought to change everything, who sinned no less than the others who held fast with tooth and nail to whatever had once been accepted, whether it was right or not <gloss>6</gloss>. Instead of removing things because of their abuse, one should not take away the things themselves <gloss>7</gloss>: much less make things worse instead of better <gloss>8</gloss>: but rather overlook what one could not improve <gloss>9</gloss>. Above all, he rejected reforming through strife, violence, and riot; declaring that he had such an aversion to discord that the truth itself displeased him if it was seditious <gloss>10</gloss> <note>original: "dat hem de waerheit selve mishaegde als se oproerig was." This reflects Erasmus's famous preference for a "quiet" truth over a "noisy" or violent one.</note>. In particular, he recommended the remedy of mutual tolerance to both parties with these words: <gloss>11</gloss> It is to be wished that the business [of the Reformation], having been somewhat begun, might be brought to such moderation that those things harmful to piety might be healed with a fitting and cautious treatment: that we might be of one mind with a Christian heart in those things that are of piety: and in those things that are not very helpful nor harmful to piety...

...[to this] land I think of moving. But I shall do this with a more tranquil mind when I see the cause of Christ prevail. Luther has offered the world a hard and bitter remedy. I could wish that, such as it is, it might bring some good health to the body of the Christian people, which is corrupted on all sides by so much evil. Thus, in the judgment of some, Erasmus acted in his writings as a Reformer of the Reformers and the Reformation, who—like a Christian Gamaliel <note>A reference to the Pharisee doctor of the law in Acts 5:34-39, who advised the Jewish authorities to exercise moderation and caution toward the early Christians.</note> <margin>1 *Letter 2099. e. a. He also pretended to agree in all matters of Religion with the views of the Zwinglians <note>Followers of Huldrych Zwingli, the leader of the Reformation in Switzerland</note>, who were the dominant party in Basel; he diligently attended their sermons and the Lord’s Supper. He was obedient to the Magistrates, generous to the poor, comforting to the sick, and helpful to the needy. This meant that no one could easily suspect him of any evil, but rather he was held by many to be as honorable and great as he wished to appear, and as those close to him believed him to be. He was all the more respectable because of his grand physical stature, dignified presence, and honest appearance, as well as the great riches and costly jewels that he had partly brought with him and were partly sent to him daily from the Netherlands. His household was little less than princely, yet orderly. To hide himself more safely, he observed three rules.

<margin>Thuanus, ibid.</margin>
First, that no one from his household should utter the name of David Joriszoon (which was too well known in Holland and Friesland) in the streets; second, he forbade any mention of what his status, trade, or craft had been in his fatherland. Because of this, some thought he was descended from a noble line and wished to remain hidden for that reason; some believed he was a noble and wealthy merchant who conducted his trade through others by water and land. Above all, care was taken that no one in Basel or the Swiss Confederacy was enticed into his Sect; but meanwhile, he sowed and nurtured his doctrine in the Netherlands through letters, books, and messengers. Thus disguised, he lived peacefully in Basel for about eleven years, until Nicolaas Meynerts van Bleesdijk, his favorite pupil to whom he had given his daughter in marriage, began to doubt his teaching and rose up against him. Also, at that time, someone came from the Netherlands who described him and his entire household so clearly to the citizens that, through brooding over the danger he ran of being discovered, he fell into despair. Through that despair, he and his wife fell into a heavy illness, which first took her away, and shortly thereafter him.

<margin>He dies. * August 26, 1556. Grotius <note>Hugo de Groot, the famous Dutch jurist and historian</note>, *Annals*, Book 9.</margin>
Such was the end of the man whose opinions were testified to have insulted Christ, since he had presented himself as more divine, greater, and as immortal as Christ—so writes Thuanus. He was grandly buried with a great funeral procession—

# H I S T O R I E

...expected that the Princes would send ambassadors, or even come to him themselves, to offer themselves and all they possessed to him, according to the prophecy of Micah: *They shall devote their wealth to the Lord, and all their possessions to the Ruler of the whole earth.* <note>The author quotes a variation of Micah 4:13 to illustrate Joris's messianic expectations.</note> His death had greatly distressed his disciples, but there remained among them some hope that he would rise again within three years, and then accomplish what he had often promised. This occurred on the thirteenth of May <note>original: "Bloeimaendt," an archaic Dutch name for the "month of blooms," or May.</note> in the year fifteen hundred and fifty-nine. His views had previously been examined from printed and unprinted books and letters found at his house, and because of them, he was condemned to this disgrace as an arch-heretic. This is the History of David Joris, as left behind by the pens of distinguished and credible men. Yet his followers, and some of his friends, say: that these writers were misled in various matters by incorrect information; that the hatred of certain people had painted him in false colors; that some testimonies against him were squeezed out through torture; and that suspicion and slander led people to believe or invent things about him that he had never said or done, and had always detested—specifically regarding the having of many wives <note>This refers to accusations of polygamy, a common charge against radical Anabaptist leaders of the era.</note>; and that his writings, if properly understood, taught the opposite of what was attributed to him. How far this innocence can be seen in his dark, confused books and elsewhere, we leave to the judgment of the impartial.

...to separate from all others. Regarding the disputes that later arose among his fellow believers, he initially sought to take a middle path, believing that mutual peace and harmony should be maintained with discretion and moderation, without coercing troubled consciences. However, later, when strictness and severity gained the upper hand among the <term>fijnen; literally "the fine ones," referring to the more rigorous and conservative faction of the Mennonites who favored strict church discipline</term>, he allowed himself to be carried along with the majority toward their objective, which will be recounted at a more appropriate time. Yet he behaved even more vehemently against those who had departed from the <term>Papacy; the Roman Catholic Church</term> but were of a different mind than his own, particularly on the matters of Christ's incarnation, the swearing of oaths, infant baptism, and the office of the magistracy <note>government officials</note>. The Lutherans he called—in view of their disorderly lives—a "broad and free" sect; the Zwinglians, regarding their doctrine, he called a "horrible" sect. *Be warned in Christ Jesus,* he wrote \*, *believe it if you will, you are being miserably deceived in your poor souls by the doctrine of our opponents* (he had previously been speaking of <term>Martin Micron and Johannes a Lasco; two prominent Protestant reformers who disagreed with Menno on the nature of Christ's humanity</term>). *For it is a true vapor from the pit of the abyss <note>original: "put des afgrondts"</note>, which makes the noble, clear sun Christ Jesus and the light of His holy Word dark and obscure. It is the lie of the old serpent, indeed, a brood: if one eats of it, one must die, and if one treads upon it, an adder comes forth... In short, it is that hideous, abominable drink in the beautiful golden cup of that blood-drunk Babylonian woman, with which she has intoxicated all who dwell on earth.* On the twenty-sixth of <term>September; literally "Autumn-month"</term>, preaching outside of parish churches, the cloisters of the mendicant orders, and the hospitals of the large cities was forbidden in Holland by <term>plakkaet; an official government decree or edict</term>. <margin>1540.</margin>
When the Emperor <note>Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor and ruler of the Burgundian Netherlands</note> afterwards came through France into the Netherlands in the year fifteen hundred forty, to quiet the rebellion at Ghent <note>The Revolt of Ghent (1539–1540) was a local uprising against high taxes, which the Emperor suppressed harshly</note>, the entreaties of the Monks and Theologians had so much influence that a new edict <note>original: "plakkaet"</note> concerning the matter of heresy and heretical books was issued, which was signed on the twenty-second of the Harvest Month <note>September</note> at Brussels. It included not only the content of the previous edicts, but also turned them into a perpetual law, placing the Heretics and Anabaptists on the same level. Intending and declaring beyond what had been established before, that <margin>History of the Martyrs, p. 117. New Edict on the matter of heresy.</margin> from the day the aforementioned heretics had fallen into their errors, they would also be incapable of disposing of their goods: and that all transfers, gifts, cessions, sales, or assignments, wills, and last testaments made by them since the aforementioned day would be null and void. And to prevent the gatherings and <term>conventicles; secret or unauthorized religious meetings</term> of these people, it was promised that those who would discover or accuse any who had held the aforementioned conventicles—if they themselves had been part of the gathering—would be pardoned and released for that time, without being punished (for the reason of having been there)... Since some of the aforementioned Heretics or Anabaptists, having been accused and summoned, had fled abroad or hidden themselves, so that they could not be proceeded against for proper punishment, but only for banishment, and knowing that their accomplices and supporters were dead or executed, such that it would not be possible for the <term>Schout; a local official serving as a combination of sheriff and prosecutor</term> to prove against them that they were rebaptized or heretical: under this pretense and trust, they daily presumed to present petitions to obtain a <term>mandament of purge; a legal writ used to clear one's name of a crime through a formal declaration of innocence</term>, or other provisions of justice; which gave cause for contempt of justice, and boldness for the aforementioned heretics to return and spread their errors... Wishing to provide for this, the edict prohibited the <margin>Edicts of Flanders, from p. 122 to p. 129. p. 124. 125. p. 126. p. 127.</margin>

# HISTORY

<margin>1540.</margin>
The legal courts were forbidden to grant, seal, or provide any legal relief to the aforementioned suspects or those accused of the said heresy and Anabaptism <note>A radical wing of the Reformation that practiced adult baptism and was often viewed as politically subversive</note> who, having been summoned to court, had not appeared, but through defiance had allowed themselves to be banished. This was to prevent them from clearing their names or otherwise returning to the country. Instead, it was declared that such fleeing and banished persons should be held as convicted. To the books named and forbidden in the previous edicts, others were added; specifically the *Plays*, which were recently performed by the nineteen chambers <note>The "Chambers of Rhetoric," social guilds that staged dramatic competitions</note> in Ghent, and had even been printed with a license, on the theme: *What is the greatest comfort to a dying person.* Along with this, it was ordered that this edict be published every six months on St. John the Baptist’s Day and on Christmas Eve; under penalty that the officer who neglected this would forfeit ten gold Carolus guilders <note>Gold coins named after Emperor Charles (Carolus) V</note> for the first offense, twenty for the second, and his position or office for the third, without further declaration <gloss>1 Explanation</gloss>, which position would be obtainable <gloss>2 Available to be requested</gloss> as being vacant <gloss>3 Open</gloss>. Ordering that, whether the publication was made or not, the violators of this ordinance would nonetheless be punished without compromise, according to the penalties included therein, without being able to be excused <gloss>4 Pardoned</gloss> under the guise of ignorance <gloss>5 Lack of knowledge</gloss>. Finally, the edict commanded all the aforementioned points to be kept inviolably for all eternity, according to their form and content: proceeding and causing proceedings to be taken against violators by strict execution... without any grace... notwithstanding any opposition or appeal made, or to be made, nor any privileges, ordinances, statutes, customs, or usages to the contrary, which we, said the Emperor, do not wish, nor understand to have any place regarding this matter: but by our certain knowledge, authority, and full power, we have derogated and do derogate <note>A legal term meaning to partially repeal or overturn a law</note> from them by this document. Written below: *by the Emperor in his Council.* and signed: *Verreyken.* This edict was followed by heavy persecution. In Leuven, a house search was conducted one evening to find forbidden books, which caused great distress, shouting, crying, and fleeing. Twenty-eight persons were captured there, even two chaplains of St. Peter's Church, though one escaped from prison and the other recanted. Two men, being laymen, were burned, and two women were buried alive <note>original: "in d'aerde gedolven." Buried alive was a common execution method for women heretics at the time</note>. Some believe they were put to death in Ghent. How it ended for the other prisoners is not recounted. <margin>He is beheaded.</margin>
With joy he went on the ninth of August <note>Original: *Oegstmaendt*</note> to the marketplace to be beheaded, calling out to the bystanders: *“My dear and pious citizens, I pray you for God's sake, do not take it ill of me that I am somewhat joyful; for I cannot restrain myself, I must now be joyful in my God, since he is so favorable to me.”* Having arrived at the place of execution, he thanked God that he was considered worthy to suffer for His name, saying: *“O God, if it were possible that I might rise again immediately after this death, and then might die once more for this truth of God from heaven, you know, O my God, that my heart would desire such and do it with joy.”* Finally, he testified to his faith in God and in Jesus Christ, and that his foundation stood firm on the teaching of the Apostles and Prophets: he testified the same regarding David Joris, and wished to seal that testimony with his blood. When the Bailiff <term>Schout; a local official responsible for law enforcement and prosecution</term> said to this: *“David Joris is the most despicable heretic who ever was on earth,”* Joriaen cried out, *“The day of the Lord shall make known whether you or I have testified rightly.”* Then he knelt, commended his spirit to God, and received the stroke of death with an undaunted mind, in the thirty-third year of his life. This death brought many followers to David Joris. And it seemed that Ketel had learned nothing but good from that master. Some also believed that the virtue of this one disciple justified the master in everything; yet others understood it differently.

In Holland, on the twenty-sixth of January <note>Original: *Loumaendt*</note>, the harboring of fugitives on account of heresy and the management of their goods was newly forbidden by edict <term>Plakkaet; an official decree or proclamation issued by the government</term>. Those of Wesel had announced that they would establish a school on the upcoming Easter. This was done without having obtained permission from the Pope or the Emperor. Consequently, by an edict issued in Brussels on the seventh of March <note>Original: *Lentemaendt*</note>, the inhabitants of these lands were forbidden: *“that no one should presume to travel to or trade within the aforementioned city (where many Anabaptists <term>Herdopers; literally 're-baptizers,' a derogatory term for Anabaptists</term> and others infected with sects, says the edict, came and went), nor to send there their children, brothers, nephews, or others of their kin, friends, or others standing under their charge and management; on pain of being held as heretics and being punished everywhere as such, according to the contents of the edicts.”*

In that [year] of forty-one <gloss>1</gloss> <note>The text says "eenenveertig" (41), though the margin and historical records place Alard's death in 1544</note>, Alard of Amsterdam died in Leuven. He was held in high esteem by our Erasmus for his learning and eloquence, as well as by Petrus Nannius, Conradus Goclenius, and Ludovicus Vives. This man did not shrink, although he remained within the communion of the Roman Church, from pointing out certain things in the conduct of the clergy that deserved rebuke. In his *Admonitions concerning Alms*, where he was not very favorable toward Luther, he nevertheless pointed out that in former times the distribution of church treasures rested with the Deacons, who primarily cared for the poor; and there follows this wish: *Would to God that the church today had such Deacons, to whom that holy ministry was entrusted.* Indeed, he charged the Bishops and all the clergy with church-theft <term>Kerkdiefte; the misappropriation of church funds meant for the poor</term>, because they applied the goods of the church and the needy entirely to their own convenience and that of their kin, whereas they ought to draw no more than their bare necessities from them. He was by nature hard of hearing but smooth of tongue, regarding which Erasmus said that his tongue made good what was lacking in his ears. In his last will, he left his books to the poor orphans in Amsterdam and wrote this epitaph for himself:

But once, upon climbing the pulpit in Brussels to preach before Emperor Charles, he became so bewildered <note>Or struck with sudden stage fright/confusion</note> that no one could understand what he wanted to say, and the entire assembly fell into laughter. Having met with that disgrace, he returned again to Leuven; there, the shame of the disgrace and the reflection on what he had done against his conscience made him so anxious that he fell into despair. Often it escaped him in his lessons that he had fought against the truth. Petrus Brully, a preacher at Strasbourg, who at that time served on loan the congregations in the Walloon Netherlands <note>The French-speaking southern parts of the Low Countries</note> which had separated themselves from the Papacy, had a completely different end a few months later. He remained steadfast in the confession of the doctrine which he understood to be the truth, comforted his fellow prisoners and his wife through letters, looked upon the harshest death with composure, and, full of confidence, called upon his Creator and Savior in the midst of a slow fire until the very end. Around this time, there were several others who preached the doctrine of the Reformation in these lands with great danger: namely, Gerardus Gallinaceus, ... Galenus, Hermannus Modet, Petrus Gabriël, Christophorus Fabricius, Hermannus Johannes—who had formerly been monks—also Feito, Antonius Nicolaus, and Cornelis Cooltuin, who were previously priests; and from among the common citizens, Adriaen Hamstede, the first author of the Dutch *Book of Martyrs*, Aggæus Simons van Goor, Petrus Delenus, Petrus Carpenterius, Caspar Heidanus, Jan Arents, Ellard Gerrits, Everhardus Gerardus, Petrus Hasardus, Aegidius... <margin>Teachers under the cross <note>A term for Protestant ministers leading "clandestine" or persecuted illegal churches</note>. Henricus Antonides van der Linden in the preface to the System of Theology.</margin>
While Brully lay imprisoned at Tournai, some of his listeners were also burned. To sentence them—for the local magistrates were too weak for the zeal of the clergy—Councilor Karel Tisnacq was sent from Brussels to Tournai.

<margin>Further persecution.</margin>
A certain citizen named Bergiban, very well-versed in the knowledge of the Holy Scriptures and of a godly life, having been sought in his house in vain, decided thereafter—without being moved by the tears of his wife, nor the advice of his father, relatives, or friends—to surrender himself into the hands of the persecutors. He then settled his household affairs within three days, took his final leave, and gave himself up as a prisoner. At first, he also showed very great constancy; but when the Emperor’s commissioner had made him taste the hideousness of the sharpest imprisonment, and constantly threatened him with the cruelest death one could imagine, he eventually began to waver. At the persistence of the clergy, he recanted his first confession, and did so only to be killed by the sword instead of by fire.

<margin>Bergiban puts himself in danger without necessity and succumbs to it. History of the Martyrs, folio 161a. History of the Martyrs, folio 107.</margin>

He betrayed many of his followers to the authorities; some were found innocent and released, while others, being tied to the evil, were punished with the sword, and he finally, along with the Treasurer, was punished with the fire.

But she gave as answer, *“No, far be it from me that I should judge the children.”* "Do you then," said the others, "not seek your salvation in Baptism?" *“No,”* was her answer again, *“all the water of the sea cannot save me; but salvation is in Christ, who has commanded me to love God my Lord above all things, and my neighbor as myself.”* In <margin>at Amsterdam;</margin> the Autumn, a man and woman of that confession <margin>Ibid. p. 166.</margin> were also burned at Amsterdam. <margin>1549. <note>original: "MDXLIX"</note></margin>
Stijn Barbier, a native of Hainaut, had visited, comforted, and strengthened [the believers] with his gifts; for this, he was seized on the road four miles from Tournai and, along with his wife and the spouse of Augustijn (who escaped at that time), was led to Mons.
<margin>to Mons;</margin>
His wife allowed herself to be seduced by the promise of life into revealing the house where he had previously been sheltered. To examine his faith, the secular court made use of some <term>Friars Minor</term> <note>Also known as Franciscans, a mendicant Catholic religious order.</note>, whom he addressed with such reasoning that they were struck silent more than once, and finally cried out with one voice: *He has the devil in him; to the fire, to the fire with the Lutheran!* When death was announced to him, he thanked God, struck up a Psalm, cleaned his clothes of dust and straw, and said to the bystanders: *My friends, thus I cleanse myself because I am called to the wedding of the Lamb.* <note>A biblical reference to Revelation 19:9, often used by martyrs to describe their transition to heaven.</note> They forbade him from speaking to the people; nevertheless, as he went to his death, he cried out: *O Charles, Charles, how long shall your heart be hardened!* <note>A direct address to Emperor Charles V, who issued the strict "blood edicts" against heresy.</note> At that word, they struck him in the face. Then he turned to the onlookers with these words: *Alas, poor people, you are not worthy that the word of God should be presented to you.* When the Friars Minor still urged at the stake that he had the devil in him, he gave them the ninth verse of the sixth Psalm <note>original: "negenden vers van den sesten Psalm"</note> as an answer: *Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity; for the Lord has heard the voice of my weeping.* Thereupon they lit the fire, and he was still heard to cry out twice with his head held high: *O eternal Father, I commend myself into your hands.* With no less courage and trust in God's grace, Maria, the wife of Augustijn Barbier, allowed herself to be buried alive and trampled to death by the executioner. <note>Being buried alive was a specific form of execution reserved for women convicted of heresy to avoid the perceived "indecency" of public burning.</note> Afterward, Augustijn her husband was also captured at Beaumont and put to death. He conducted himself in the same way; although he was otherwise of a faint-hearted nature, he was very brave when necessity demanded it. What he understood to be the truth of the Gospel, he confessed freely. Someone who said to him: "Have pity on yourself, and if you will not save your life, at least save your soul," he gave this answer, thanking him for his kindness: *I have, as you can see, such great compassion for myself and for my soul that, in order to do nothing against my conscience, I would rather give up my body to be burned. In this, I consider myself fortunate: for I do not suffer for an evil life, but only for the word of Jesus Christ, for which all martyrs have shed their blood, as I also hope to do.*

# HISTORY
<column-break/>
<margin>
1549. <note>original: "MDXLIX"</note>
Prince Philip of Spain is inaugurated in the Netherlands.
*P. C. Hooft, book 3.*
*Beverw. Dordr. p. 246.*
</margin>
Amidst all this bloodshed, the Emperor <note>Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor and Lord of the Netherlands.</note> had his son Philip come from Spain to be inaugurated as the future Prince of the Netherlands and heir to his father. He was inaugurated at Dordrecht on the twenty-sixth of September <note>original: "Herffstmaendt" (Autumn month)</note> in the presence of Lady Mary of Austria, the Queen Dowager of Hungary; the Dukes of Savoy and Alva; the Princes of Orange and Ascoli; the Counts of Egmont, Hoorn, and Megen; the Marquises of Bergen, Astorga, and Pescara; and the Presidents Viglius and Everard Nicolai.

<margin>
*Sebastian Münster's Cosmography, book II, p. 130.*
</margin>
Prince Philip also traveled to Rotterdam in the same month, where he was received with great demonstrations of honor and joy. A life-sized statue of Erasmus had been erected at the place of his arrival, which offered the Prince a poem of welcome with an outstretched arm. Afterward, Philip, the Queen, and other nobles—moved by the memory of such a great man—visited the house and the room where he was born with great reverence. <note>Desiderius Erasmus (1466–1536) was a world-famous humanist scholar from Rotterdam whose works influenced the early Reformation, though he remained a Catholic.</note>

<margin>
The Emperor’s Declaration regarding the confiscation of the property of heretics.
*Plakkaat of Flanders, p. 153...*
</margin>
Shortly thereafter, the Emperor declared his position in a <term>plakkaat</term> <note>A formal public decree or edict issued by the government.</note> signed in Brussels on the twentieth of November <note>original: "Slachtmaendt" (Slaughter month)</note> regarding the disputes that sometimes arose over the <term>confiscation</term> <note>The legal seizure of property by the state as a penalty.</note> of fiefs, lands, and other goods belonging to heretics. This was because some Lords, from whom such heretics held property in <term>fief</term> <note>Land held by a tenant from a lord in return for service or loyalty.</note> and who held high jurisdiction in their own domains, claimed that these goods should revert to them. Against this, it was declared that such property, even fiefs, fell to the Emperor. However, the feudal lord (provided he was a subject) would retain his feudal rights; for if the Emperor sold or gave away such confiscated property, he would provide the lord with a new vassal.

<margin>
*p. 155.*
*Ibid.*
</margin>
When someone was condemned as a heretic by the sentence of the Inquisitor or a church judge and remained obstinate until the final punishment, their goods would be forfeited to the Emperor if they held them from him. But if they held them from a subject who had the right of confiscation, then the goods would be forfeited to that person. However, if someone was so condemned by secular judges, then the goods held as a fief from a subject would be divided half-and-half between the Emperor and the subject who held the right of confiscation.

For this had now become a tribunal or court of Dominican Monks, who not only prosecuted public or well-proven offenses with the most ignominious and painful death, along with the seizure of property; but sought out the most cunning wickedness to waylay people, to pry into minds, and to torture out of the prisoners the deepest secrets of their consciences, as much through horrific and unbearable threats as through the most agonizing methods of pain. Here there are two claimants: one, called the promoter of church law <note>A legal officer, often a clergyman, who brought the formal charges in an ecclesiastical court.</note>, being usually a clergyman, sues for a sentence of unbelief or heresy against the accused; the other, in the King’s name, for the forfeiture of property; and is always a layman. Whoever hears any incriminating words, even if it were from their own father, is obliged to betray him. Two testimonies, although regarding different matters, are enough to throw one into a foul dungeon; where food and drink are scarcely provided, and all comfort and visits—yes, even singing, as it is deemed too refreshing—are forbidden in his solitude, so that melancholy or despondency might wear him down. If it happens that he confesses what is charged and abjures his faith, promising to listen to instruction, then he does penance by wearing a garment they call *Sacco benito* <note>The "Sanbenito," a yellow penitential tunic worn by those condemned by the Inquisition.</note> (blessed sack), and with the loss of all his means. # HISTORY OF THE REFORMATION. BOOK III

<margin>
**1550**
<note>original: "M D L."</note>
*Paolo Sarpi, History of the Inquisition; and Marcus Antonius de Dominis, On the Ecclesiastical Commonwealth, Book VII, chapter VIII, section 26, page 122. Apology for Herodotus by Henri Estienne, Chapter XL, page 507. See also Nicolaus Burgundius, History, II, 124...*
</margin>
[...witnesses] for the fire <note>referring to execution by burning</note>; several for torture. The testimony alone, and even that only in a vague manner <note>literally "as if in a twilight"</note>, is reported to him, but in no way the names of the witnesses, as if revealing them would be dangerous for the witnesses and for the truth itself. However, if the accused suspects he has any enemies, he may guess at their names and, if he hits the mark, challenge them. But if there are others whom he does not guess, or if his challenge is rejected, their testimony remains valid. Torture is carried out with the rack, water, and fire, by torchlight in a dark cellar; the executioner is clothed from head to toe in black linen, with holes for the eyes. One finds those who sit there for twelve or thirteen years, and their only exit is death. There is no lack of examples of people who, being sincere Roman Catholics, confessed the opposite <note>i.e., confessed to heresy</note> just to free themselves through the appearance of penitence. Others (which is worse), being Christians in their hearts, were driven to that doctrine <note>Judaism</note> by a loathing of such madness, or by hearing arguments against Judaism which they thought were too weak.

<margin>
*Grotius, Annals, Book 10.*
</margin>
Secular judges were permitted to punish those who had been condemned solely by ecclesiastical verdict. Many of these judges, as if out of piety, competed to employ the most cruel punishments; but others—foreseeing that this style of justice would open a wide door not only for hatred but also for greed (since property was confiscated and there was profit to be made by informants)—did not allow the knowledge of the proceedings to be snatched away from them.

<margin>
*Annals, Book 10.*
</margin>
Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius, the famous Dutch jurist and historian</note> states that to be under suspicion was enough to send someone to the dungeon, and evidence of little weight was enough to bring someone to the <term>pijnbank</term> <note>the rack or torture bench</note>: even the Inquisitors could question anyone under oath, no matter what rank or power they held. And by this cunning means, they could penetrate not only the secrets of households but also of minds. For the more a person dreaded perjury, the more easily he betrayed himself. Otherwise, those who hesitated to kneel before the images of the saints and the consecrated bread of the mass in the church, or where it was carried openly in procession, could hardly hide themselves. Previously, this sort of Inquisition had been used once against the Jews and <term>Marranos</term> <note>Sephardic Jews who had been forced to convert to Christianity but were suspected of practicing Judaism in secret</note>; now it was put to work against everyone without distinction, with a wonderful cunning in its investigation; for attention was paid to speech, and even to silence.

# HISTORY

<margin>
**1550**
<note>original: "MDL."</note>
</margin>
...[accusa]tions, the friendships were deceptive, and one often had the accuser at one's side; so that it now appeared clearly enough that no one was so innocent that they could protect their life and honor against these people. That this is not exaggerated out of hatred, but recounted according to the truth, will not be denied by those who have ever heard what great disturbances regarding the Inquisition were stirred up in Spain,¹ and almost throughout all of Italy,² indeed even in the city of Rome,³ by people who adhered to the Roman Church. It was then no wonder that the people of Antwerp, then flourishing above all the cities of the Netherlands in trade and prosperity (blessings that usually accompany freedom of the mind), began to oppose this national oppression from this time forward. For the doctrine of the Reformation was preached here in secret around this time by several ministers, namely by Georgius Sylvanus and Caspar van der Heiden.⁴ They then raised objections to accepting and announcing the aforementioned edict <term>plakkaet</term> <note>A formal public decree or law posted in public places; in this context, it refers to the "Blood Edict" of 1550.</note>, which several cities, without paying enough attention to the content and consequences, had somewhat lightheartedly proclaimed. Even more so, because at the first rumor, by which it became known to the people that such an edict was at hand, they immediately saw the beginnings of the feared troubles rising before their eyes. For many merchants immediately prepared to depart; all trade stood still; people neither bought nor sold, neither sent nor ordered; the value of houses plummeted; the trades ceased; and the craftsmen lacked money. This moved the Magistrates <note>original: "Wethouders"</note> to conduct an inquiry through some of their own number, and to take note of all the damage the common good had already suffered through fear of the Inquisition, and what, according to all probability, was still further to be expected. A very large number of the most prominent citizens and merchants were heard on this matter under oath, and everything was put into writing and handed to Queen Mary <note>Mary of Hungary, sister of Emperor Charles V and Governor of the Netherlands.</note>; with a humble request that she would try to mediate the matter with the Emperor her brother, so that the most excellent merchant city of his lands would not be burdened or ruined by the Inquisition. From which burden, as well as from ecclesiastical jurisdiction, she [Antwerp] had always been free, and according to her privileges, ought also to remain free. The Council of Brabant also declared itself in favor of the country's freedom, against the edict and the Inquisition, supporting the people of Antwerp. Several other Brabantian cities did the same, who [withheld] the proclamation...

->### THIRD BOOK OF THE REFORMATION.<-

X

<margin>
**1550**
</margin>
...[proclai]ming the edict likewise. Lady Mary <note>Mary of Hungary, sister of Emperor Charles V and Governor of the Netherlands from 1531 to 1555.</note>, a Princess of a gentle nature and of such great discretion in matters of faith that Pope Paul III had informed the Emperor in the year fifteen hundred thirty-nine that she secretly favored the Lutherans <margin>* * * Paolo Sarpi, *History of the Council of Trent*, book 1, 78.</margin> and maintained an understanding with them, found herself highly distressed and finally compelled to travel in person to Augsburg, where the Emperor was then attending the Imperial Diet <term>rijksdagh</term> <note>A formal deliberative assembly of the Holy Roman Empire.</note>. <margin>Lady Mary travels herself to Augsburg to halt the Inquisition. Weesenbeeke p. 21. Grotius, *Annals* l. 12. Paolo Sarpi, *History of the Inquisition* p. 42. Same author, *History of the Council of Trent*, book III, p. 270. Bor, book 10. Thuanus, Vol. V, p. 300.</margin> Here she demonstrated to her brother what misery those things, which were called remedies, had caused; and that all the foreign merchants would depart, and trade—on which the entire state flourished—would suffer a Great collapse if one insisted on proceeding with the Inquisition. Through this representation, she brought about with much effort that the edict, issued by another at Augsburg on the twenty-fifth of September <note>original: "Herfstmaendt"</note>, was changed and softened in some articles concerning foreign traders; the words "Inquisitor" or "Inquisition" were also left out. However, it was stated therein: *that the ecclesiastical Judges (by whom some understood the Inquisitors), desiring as far as it concerned the ecclesiastical crime of heresy to proceed against anyone, might request from the Emperor’s sovereign Courts or provincial Councils that they be given someone from their college, or another associate <term>adjunct</term>, to oversee the information and procedures they wished to conduct against the suspects: Willing, commanding, and ordering all Officers, Judges, and Vassals, that they provide and give to the aforementioned [ecclesiastical] Judges and associate all help, favor, direction, and assistance, for the execution and fulfillment of their charge.* Furthermore, this edict was as strict and sharp as the previous one, with the conclusion that was so offensive, namely, *that one should proceed against the violators and the disobedient by execution of the prescribed penalties, notwithstanding opposition or appeal... nor any privileges... which were again derogated, as above.* <margin>Edict issued at Augsburg on the matter of heresy. *Edicts of Flanders* p. 191. and the entire edict from p. 186 to 200. Also in P. Bor book I. 5. a. 6, 7, 8.</margin> †. At the end, as also at the end of the edict <margin>† p. 142. 158.</margin> of the twenty-ninth of April <note>original: "Grasmaendt"</note>, was added a certain list of books newly condemned by the theologians at Leuven and forbidden by the Emperor, in much greater number than in the previous edicts. This list was signed on the twenty-sixth of March <note>original: "Lentemaendt"</note>. When this Augsburg edict was proclaimed everywhere in the Netherlandish cities by the ringing of bells, it was nevertheless not permitted by those of Antwerp, until <margin>*Edicts of Flanders* from p. 174 to 184.</margin>

In Antwerp, during the month of October <note>original: "Wijnmaendt," the traditional Dutch name for the month of wine-making.</note>, a certain Fleming named Jan van Oostende was likewise condemned to the fire for the sake of religion. Christ has had compassion on us, sending His truth among men to draw them to Himself thereby.*

...poor soul. Immediately a great silence fell upon the surrounding people, listening eagerly to these arguments, which vexed the <term>Bailiff</term> <note>original: "Leenman." A feudal official who, in this context, acted as a judicial officer.</note>, so that, half-ashamed and in a state of anger, he cried out to the prisoner: *What are you saying there, you brazen knave? You yourself know well that faith is a gift from God; that neither I, nor any man, may seize that blessed gift from God by force; that God gives His gifts to one early, and to another late, just as He called the laborers into the vineyard <note>A reference to the Parable of the Workers in the Vineyard from Matthew 20:1-16.</note>. Suppose now that I had not yet received that gift as you have; should you then kill me, who am so deprived? If you let me live, might God not still grant me that saving gift in a week, a month, or a year, just as He did for you? If you people prevent this by cutting off my time of grace, who else but you are the murderers of my soul?* These simple but upright arguments, spoken so earnestly with powerful truth by this simple old man, moved the hearts of the surrounding citizens so much that no small murmuring and commotion arose among them. This caused the Bailiff and the court officers to flee from the <term>tribunal</term> <note>original: "vierschaer," the traditional place where justice was administered.</note> into the city hall with the prisoner, as quickly as they did anxiously. There, having somewhat recovered from their fear, they and the others condemned this innocent old man to death, and had him beheaded that morning, to the great displeasure and bitterness of many citizens, who had to behold this murder while turning away with mournful pity.

He threw the remains at their feet, snapping at them: *You murderers, since you first ate his flesh, now eat his bones as well.* These were words too clever to have come from a fool, and too bold to have been spoken by a man of sound mind; yet perhaps the simpleton had heard them from others and repeated them, without noticing or fearing his own danger.

1 Peter 3:15.</margin>
*"That we should always be ready to give a reason to everyone who demands an account of the hope that is in us."* <note>The author quotes the New Testament to frame the schoolmaster's defense of his faith.</note> "I desire then, at this hour, an account of your faith" \*. At these words, the schoolmaster’s tongue was loosened: the previous constriction left his heart; his love for his wife and children gave way to the zeal that set his mind aflame, and to the powerful movement of his soul, which made him say to himself: *O my God, now is the time; stand by me, according to your promise.* Then, full of courage, he turned to the Inquisitor <note>original: "Kettermeester," literally "heresy-master"</note> with these words: "Ask now what you will; I shall answer you straightforwardly whatever God's spirit shall give me to speak, and hide nothing." And so, being questioned, he made a confession † that renounced the Papacy, exposed various errors, and refuted falsehoods. They sought to draw him away from his views with all kinds of cunning, and when words did not help, this was the heaviest trial: He was asked, *"Do you not love your wife and children?" "You know,"* he gave as his answer, *"that I love them from my heart, and that my love for them distresses me most of all. I tell you truly, if the entire world were pure gold and belonged to me, I would very willingly give it up just to have my wife and children with me, even with dry bread and cold water, in prison and shame."* "Abandon then," it was said to him, "your false views. You have but a word to speak, to recant and show regret, then you shall be allowed to go back to your wife and children, just as before." *"I would do that,"* the prisoner answered, *"if it did not conflict with God and my conscience. And therefore, not for wife, nor for children, nor for any creature in the world, shall I forsake my religion, which I know to be true, so long as God assists me with His grace."* He remained steadfast in his faith, and was finally declared a heretic by the Inquisitor, delivered to the secular authorities, strangled, and burned. Thomas Calberge, a tapestry maker at Tournai <note>original: "Doornik"</note>, had written down some spiritual songs in a certain small book, taken from a volume printed in Geneva. Then he set out—having commanded his wife and his brother to pray to God for him, that He might guide the plan he intended to carry out to a good end, without saying what it was—toward the Church of Our Lady, the main church of the city <note>This refers to the Cathedral of Our Lady in Antwerp</note>. See,”* he continued, and broke it into pieces between his hands, threw it to the ground, and trampled it with his right foot, *“this is for the honor of God, and to show that this has no power, and to expose it.”*

This deed, on such a day and high festival, brought such wonder and terror among the people that Bertrand could easily have hidden himself in the general commotion; but he did not move a foot and was seized on the spot. Being asked if he was not sorry for his crime, and also if he would do it again if it were yet to be done, he answered: *“That he would want to do it a hundred times more, were it in his power, and die a hundred times, had he so many lives, for the glory and honor of his Savior Jesus Christ.”* Three times he was very severely tortured to discover his accomplices, but he named no one. On the twenty-eighth of the month, a terrible sentence was passed upon him. The man was dragged to the market square on a hurdle <note>A wooden frame or sled used to drag prisoners to execution</note>, his mouth locked shut with an iron gag. Having preached for about six years at Garder, a small village on the Veluwe, a league and a half from Harderwijk, he was captured on the first of January <note>Original: *Loumaendt*</note> in the year fifteen hundred and fifty, taken to Arnhem, and forced by fear of death into a sinful recantation. His chief enemies were Franciscus Sonnius and Jan Gruwel. Two writings had been found with him: in one, his sermons were written; the other was of similar content to the *Guide* he was now bringing to light. In it, the Papal idolatry was contradicted, and God's noble truth, revealed through Luther and his helpers, was praised; along with a lament over the captured Elector of Saxony <note>Johann Friedrich I, who was taken prisoner after the Battle of Mühlberg</note>, the Landgrave Philip of Hesse, and the deposition of the Archbishop of Cologne <note>Hermann von Wied, who was removed for his Protestant leanings</note>. In particular, he lamented that the Emperor allowed himself to be so miserably deceived by the Pope. On the third of February <note>Original: *Sprokkelmaendt*</note>, having been condemned to perpetual imprisonment, he was taken to a high tower of the Castle at Hattem, where Sonnius and Gruwel nonetheless promised him that he might write for the Pope just as he had previously written against him. To this end, he was allowed a Bible and some of the ancient Doctors of the Church <note>The "Church Fathers," early Christian theologians</note>.

# OF THE HISTORY

<margin>1551.</margin>...and to use pen and ink. After having been imprisoned for about two years, he was released from the tower in December <note>Original: *Wintermaendt*, the "winter month"</note> of the year fifteen hundred and fifty-one, under heavy bail never to leave the house. Sonnius <note>Franciscus Sonnius (1506–1576), a prominent theologian and inquisitor who later became the first Bishop of Antwerp</note> kept him in this state for another year and a half, until Pentecost in the year fifteen hundred and fifty-three. At that time, he was permitted to leave Hattem <note>A fortified town in the province of Gelderland</note>, with strict orders to be in Leuven <note>Louvain, the intellectual center of Catholic orthodoxy in the Low Countries</note> within the next fourteen days, there to study Papal Theology for three years. 

He was expected to earn his food and clothing through celebrating Masses and singing in the choir, as he learned from opened letters given to him to carry to the Leuven theologians. These letters also stated that the theologians were to watch his life closely and report every opportunity to Sonnius. "Thus was I," he writes in the aforementioned Preface, "burdened with miserable necessity. I had to let my poor mother and other friends fall into great ruin, or let my soul remain in damnation. Although I intended in no way to participate in the idolatry of the Mass, I nevertheless traveled to Leuven, but departed from there on the third day without speaking to any of the theologians." 

He left for Strasbourg, where he wrote the *Layman’s Guide* <note>Original: *Leeken Weghwijfer*</note>. His conscience urged him to make amends for his denial of the faith with a public confession of his belief. He also humbly prayed to all who had been present at his "misfortune" (for so he calls his recantation), or who had heard of it, to forgive him for Jesus' sake and to view his work in a Christian spirit. *I hope*, he adds, *henceforth with God’s help to remain steadfast in the truth, and I pray the pastors that they think diligently on their service, and that they guard themselves against dangerous recanting.* The booklet itself discussed the articles of the Christian religion largely on the basis of the Augsburg Confession <note>The primary statement of faith for the Lutheran movement, 1530</note>, following the views of Melanchthon <note>Philipp Melanchthon, a key collaborator of Luther known for his more moderate stance on free will</note>; particularly regarding the matter of Free Will and Predestination. 

<margin>What he says concerning Free Will and Predestination.</margin>Having indicated what kind of Free Will God had implanted in man and graciously preserved in him despite sin—whereby one could either resist or cooperate with God’s drawing—he says afterward, *that my meaning is not that we earn the help of the Holy Spirit through the labor of Free Will: much less that we shall earn heaven by it. Therefore, this view has no fellowship with the Pelagians <note>Followers of Pelagius, an early Christian monk who was accused of denying the necessity of divine grace for salvation</note>, monks, or other sects, who [make] man’s small...*

<margin>p. 31.</margin>

<margin>1555. p. 32.</margin>
...[they] esteem human ability too highly and obscure the merits of Christ. *But the Predestinarians* <term>Predestinateuren: those who believe God has pre-determined the eternal fate of every soul regardless of their actions</term>, *he says, state that even a called person can in no way benefit or harm his own salvation; rather, if he is chosen, he must follow; if he is not chosen, he must remain in damnation. Likewise, that all sins and virtues happen entirely out of necessity. This opinion is (in my view) harmful to people, and not to be accepted. For if this were so, then God's secret Will would have to stand against His public forbidding and punishment, and He would even take pleasure in our sins and damnation.* By this, many good people will be hindered in their prayer, and always doubt whether they might be chosen. The wicked will become even bolder in all evil deeds, and always excuse themselves with predestination, as many rogues are now beginning to do. When Christ addresses the entire congregation through the Minister <note>Original: *Predikant*</note> with these words: *Amend your life, and believe the Gospel* <note>original: "Betert uw leven, ende gelooft den Evangelio"</note>, *Mark 1, and with the words in Matthew 11:28, 7:7, and Ezekiel 32.* Here Christ must grant salvation to all people equally, who are called with the same word of grace in one temple, or else He must mean something other than what He speaks. And a little thereafter: <margin>p. 33.</margin> *Early Christendom remained unanimous in such an opinion during the first four hundred years, as all the ancient Doctors* <term>Doctooren: the influential early theologians of the Church, such as Jerome or Chrysostom</term>, *Greek and Latin, testify. The earliest Christendom was the purest; therefore, its opinion is not to be lightly regarded, especially that consensus of the ancient Doctors in the first four hundred years.* Yet it must also be confessed that some have elevated human ability too high. It should also move us not a little that the Martyrs, who shed their blood for Jesus' word, held to this opinion... And that He has similarly decided to damn those others who are not obedient to their calling... To this sense all the verses that are thrown against us apply, such as Acts 13* <note>The OCR says "Act. <margin>1555.</margin> [God] has [ordained] that they shall be drawn into faith who allow themselves to be taught when they hear God’s Word; such obedient ones the Father has given to his Son, *John 17.* These He has chosen in Christ, *Eph. 1...* predestined according to His foreknowledge, *Rom. 7.* <note>Though the text cites Romans 7, the famous passage on predestination is Romans 8:29.</note> That "drawing," of which Christ speaks in *John 6,* signifies that our very small ability must be helped by God’s Word and the Holy Spirit. Through that preaching or reading, we are drawn and prompted to use our small <term>free will: the capacity to choose or lean toward God's grace</term>, and to pray for Divine help. <margin>On the killing of heretics, p. 327.</margin> **killing of heretics**. *Christ*, he says, *forbids his Apostles to burn the unbelievers, or to pray to God that such a thing should happen, or to advise men to do so. <margin>p. 28, 329.</margin> **true Christendom** persecutes no one. True Christians have always dealt mercifully with heretics, without tyranny or bloodshed. But the Papal Monks and Bishops are the most unmerciful of all... Oh, if only the ancient Christians could return to the earth, what would they say of such bloodthirsty tyranny? They are also beyond measure bitter toward the 
<margin>On the bitterness against the Anabaptists. p. 330.</margin> **poor Anabaptists**. <note>The Anabaptists (Wederdoopers) were a radical wing of the Reformation who practiced adult baptism and were widely persecuted by both Catholics and other Protestants.</note> Is it not against all scripture, reason, and propriety to kill someone for a past lack of understanding if they are of good life and prepared to follow better teaching? Even if one were allowed to kill all heretics, one should still spare such people, for they have never been heretics <note>Veluanus argues that being mistaken or uneducated is not the same as being a malicious heretic</note>. The Emperor’s sword <note>The power of the secular state to execute criminals</note> ought to punish such criminals as the situation requires—those who knowingly do violence and injustice to their neighbors. But those who are deceived in ignorance with good intentions, or who are still so bound in their conscience to a lack of understanding that they cannot so quickly accept better teaching, should in no way be killed... Some officers and judges catch and kill the Anabaptists merely to keep their lucrative offices, and some to become the heirs of the poor wretches... such judges would also [kill] Christ and his Apostles.
