### OF THE REFORMATION. BOOK III.
<margin>1555. p. 331.</margin>

...before they would lose their office. Where it is the custom to kill those <term>Anabaptists: a radical reform movement known for practicing adult baptism and often living in communal, pacifist societies</term> who lead a good and peaceful life, there is also the intent and desire to kill all true believers, whom they revile as Lutherans. They wish that all Lutherans had but one neck, which they might strike off at once, just as the Emperor Caligula wished for the Roman citizens. Here I call to witness the bitter consciences of the Monks, the <term>Inquisitors: ecclesiastical judges tasked with the detection and punishment of heresy</term> <note>original: "Kettermeesteren"</note>, and the Sophists of Louvain <note>A reference to the conservative Catholic theologians at the University of Louvain</note>. They are always ready to kill us, but few of us are ready to steadfastly confess Christ’s noble truth; both are to be lamented. What shall we answer before Christ’s judgment, that we do not live as blamelessly and die as steadfastly for our certain articles of faith, as some Anabaptists do for their various errors? That they have a gross lack of understanding regarding Christ’s incarnation and divinity, regarding secular authority, the church, and infant baptism, is much to be lamented; but that some live so blamelessly and die so courageously for all the points they believe to be divine, is in some ways to be praised. It ought to awaken us to remain even more steadfast in our certain articles, and to make us ashamed that many of us, under the name of the Gospel, live so impurely, fall away so easily, and forsake our faith to accept the <term>Interim: the Augsburg Interim of 1548, an imperial decree that forced Protestants to re-adopt many Catholic customs</term>...

If one were to kill heretics, then those Papists would deserve it most of all, who advise the Princes to protect all Papal heresy and let all dissenting Christians be miserably killed—as some Bishops, Monks, and other priests do, especially those who are Inquisitors and "blood-judges" over the poor Christians. Such followers of Baal <note>original: "Baâliten," referring to the priests of the pagan god Baal in the Old Testament</note> were killed by the Prophet Elijah and by King Jehu... I fear that the Monks and priests will continue to call for fire, water, and the sword, until God awakens a Jehu or a Josiah to treat them just as they have treated many thousands of Christians within a few short years.

In the midst of this bloody persecution, which most heavily afflicted the <term>Anabaptists: a branch of the Reformation that practiced adult baptism and often faced intense persecution from both Catholics and other Protestants</term> <note>original: "Doopsgezinden"</note>, they nevertheless increased greatly throughout the whole land; but at the same time, a certain self-conceit arose within their congregation, which in time led many of them to believe that the true Christian church existed among them alone, and that outside of their circle—as if it were the only <term>little ship of Peter: a traditional metaphor for the Church as the sole vessel of salvation</term> <note>original: "schipken Petri"</note>—there was no salvation. From this opinion sprang a rigidity that not only adopted certain human propositions as divine commands, introducing them among the simple folk and giving them the force of law, but also caused a certain Ban <note>The "Ban" refers to the practice of excommunication and social shunning used to maintain purity within the community.</note>, with which they excluded all those who were not of one mind with them. Because they did not remain in agreement for long, they shortly began to shut one another out of the congregations and, as far as was in their power, out of heaven itself. The misuse of this ecclesiastical ban, which is thought to have emerged long before the year fifteen hundred and fifty, became the cause of countless and great schisms for minor reasons; and it consisted, as some understood it, mostly in two things. First, that they wished to have exercised the ban for reasons other than those for which the Lord Jesus excludes and shuts men out of heaven; secondly, that in the exercise of the ban—whether for such unjustly intended reasons, or for righteous reasons declared as such by Christ himself—they wished to proceed so sharply that they thereby neglected, or even nullified and despised, other equally, if not more, necessary commands of the Gospel; just as if the exercise

...practicing the ban, which is after all nothing but a rule of order, was such an excellent and great commandment of Jesus Christ that all other commandments had to yield to it, even the commandments concerning morality. I. H. V. P. N., or Karel van Gent, if indeed he served as a scribe for the <term>Anabaptists: literally "Baptism-minded," a group practicing adult baptism</term> <note>original: "Doopsgezinden"</note> in the year fifteen hundred and seventy-eight during the Disputation at Emden (as he seems to indicate in his account of the *Beginning and Progress of the Disputes among the Anabaptists* <gloss>1</gloss>), testifies in that same writing <gloss>2</gloss>: that these people punished with the ban anyone who fell into public sins—those forbidden in the fifth chapter of the letter to the Ephesians and elsewhere—without any prior address or warning. This was the case even if the offender was highly repentant and wept over his transgression; all penance and reformation of the banned person could not take place among brothers or sisters, nor even in his own house if his spouse were in the congregation, but rather outside in a "worldly house," as they called it. Consequently, he was not allowed to attend any meeting, unless by special petition. During the ban, he had to be so strictly shunned by all brothers and sisters of the faith—even those bound to him by blood or the bond of marriage—that one could neither eat nor drink with him, nor engage in common trade <gloss>3</gloss>. Against this severity, some Anabaptists in Waterland and at Franeker stood up around the year fifteen hundred and fifty-four or fifty-five; they argued that the ban should not be practiced without three preceding warnings, according to the rule read in the eighteenth chapter of Matthew. However, they were later outvoted by the other drivers of the ban and shunning, punished with the ban, and cast out. Those thus banned and separated by the others gathered into a distinct people and congregation under the name of **Franekers** or **Waterlanders**: but Leenaert Bouwens, one of their most vehement opponents (who had become a Preacher from being a <term>Rhetorician: a member of a local chamber of poetry and drama</term> <note>original: "Reederijker"</note> <gloss>4</gloss>), gave them the shameful nickname of **Garbage Carts** <note>original: "Drekwaegens"</note>, because (in his judgment) they picked up and accepted all sorts of filth <gloss>5</gloss>. ...the **Waterlanders** <note>A more moderate branch of the Anabaptist movement, named after the Waterland region in North Holland, who opposed the strict application of the ban</note> at that time did not find as many foul customs and atrocious acts as among those who had rejected them $^1$. Menno Simons sought to prevent this separation; but the passion for schism had no ears for his warnings. In his letter $^2$, written on the thirteenth of **November** <note>original: "Slachtmaendt," the traditional Dutch name for the month when livestock were slaughtered</note> to the brothers in Franeker, he pointed out to both contending parties what displeased him in their conduct: on the one hand, that some did not wish to use the **ban** <note>Excommunication from the church community</note> except after previous warnings; which, he understood, should have no place in certain grave sins that immediately required and brought about the punishment of the Government. On the other hand, he disapproved that some wanted to ban all "workers of the flesh" without any prior warning, even the repentant, and that all penance had to occur outside the congregation; that they even held someone who had fallen out of weakness, and had openly confessed and wept for his guilt, to be a "worldly" person; and that one would be required to report to the congregation anyone who had confessed their hidden sins to us with regret and out of sadness of heart, upon penalty of otherwise being punished along with the offender... This was offensive to him. He advised them instead toward discretion and peace. In the conclusion of this letter, he spoke to them thus: *If you have gone at each other too harshly with any words, then cleanse your hearts, and reconcile with one another in Christ Jesus. Remember that you are the Lord's people, called in peace, placed under the cross, separated from the world, and hated unto death. If you are baptized in one spirit, then fulfill my joy, and be like-minded according to Christ Jesus: build and do not break: let one instruct the other in love: **DO NOT SPLIT NOR TEAR**, so that godly peace may exist among all children of God, and remain unbroken among us all, into eternal life.* At **Emden** <note>A city in Lower Saxony, Germany, which was a major center for the Reformation and Anabaptism</note> something also occurred at this time that furthered the schism regarding the ban and the **spousal shunning** <note>original: "echtmijding"; the practice of a husband or wife avoiding all contact, including intimacy and dining, with a banned spouse</note> that was tied to it, or as others believe, first caused it two years later. Swaentje Rutgers, an Anabaptist woman, refused to shun her husband (who had been banned for certain reasons) at the table and in bed $^4$. Henrik Naeldeman, Joriaen Heyns, and.. And therefore it is my soul's pain that I hear that Swaen Rutgers has been given such a time-limit, after which, if she does not leave her husband, she shall be handed over to the devil and banned. Oh chosen brothers, see what you are doing, what a wide mouth you shall make for the slanderers, and what an ugly reputation you shall lay upon the Lord's word and the congregation! How many people shall you separate from the truth, and similar dangers! Thus we have never dared to push it as a common doctrine, because we saw what might arise from it. Oh, if only they would still let it be at that, what a great joy that would make for us sorrowful men! My soul shall over such...*

Afterward, in the year 1558, Menno wrote his *Explanation of the Apostolic Ban*. Here he now pushed for marital shunning as something of the highest necessity; recounting, among other things, that in his time he had known no fewer than three hundred married persons who had not observed marital shunning toward one another and thus, he says, had fallen into apostasy and corruption with the other. He was fearful that this harm might have occurred, in part, through his own timid silence. He wished to speak now and prevent such ruin by pointing out the necessity of shunning. He also understood here that scandalous carnal sinners, such as fornicators, adulterers, and drunkards, should be removed or banned from the Lord’s congregation without any means of prior warning. Dirk Philips wrote that same year in his booklet on *Separation* <note>original: "d'Affonderinge"</note> that a truly repentant person would be satisfied with having their properly deserved punishment—which he calls the ban—imposed upon them by the Lord and His congregation. This caused much offense; especially since it was known that Menno, along with Dirk and the most prominent of the Elders of their congregations, being together in the land of Mecklenburg, had forgiven the crime of Gillis van Aken—that foul adulterer—when he confessed his sin before them, admitted his guilt, promised amendment, and desired forgiveness. Without cutting him off or banning him, they held him as their brother again. Gillis van Aken,

[Gillis van] Aken, mentioned just a moment ago, an Elder or Bishop among the Anabaptists <term>Doopsgesinden: literally "baptism-minded," the Dutch name for the Mennonite or Anabaptist movement</term>, was arrested in Antwerp at a time that is not specified in the memoirs from which I draw this account. Out of fear of the fire <note>referring to execution by burning at the stake</note>, he renounced his faith. He was even led so far by the promise of his life that he undertook to make some of his more steadfast fellow believers, who were imprisoned with him, fall away like himself. However, this plot was discovered and made known to his fellow prisoners. They refused to listen to him. Hans de Busscher—also known as "the Weaver," another Elder among those people—found a way to speak with Van Aken in the dungeon at the risk of his own life. He set Van Aken's sin so powerfully before his eyes that he understood it and showed remorse. Because of this, he was accepted back as a brother; nevertheless, he was beheaded as an apostate. Had he made his return to the faith known publicly, they would have burned him alive, as the brushwood hut <note>A small structure of sticks and straw used for burning heretics</note> already stood ready on the scaffold for that purpose. He was then seen coming onto the scaffold with a priest who served as his confessor, and it is said that before his death, or while under the sword, he said: *It would be too much to lose both body and soul at once.*

<margin>
Further misuse and consequences of the ban; I. H. V. P. N.
*In the same place, page 15.*
</margin>
The hard ban <term>ban: a form of excommunication that required the community to completely shun the individual</term> that we spoke of just now soon extended even further. It was applied not only to the open "works of the flesh" (though greed, self-seeking, partisanship, clever vanity, and wanton sensuality have mostly always remained outside the reach of the ban), or to false teachings that were obvious, or to heresies which they fundamentally did not understand; but also to various thoughtless, small, and secret transgressions. Indeed, they even banned one another over misunderstandings and differences of opinion, even in trivial matters. To put the marital shunning <margin>Regarding marital shunning; *In the same place, pages 16, 28.*</margin> against banned husbands into practice, wives were sometimes secretly hidden or spirited away without the knowledge or will of their husbands. As a result, some husbands could not discover where their spouses had gone for a long time—some for their entire lives. And through such marital shunning, which might better be called a divorce, many fell into greater evil: some into adultery; others into despair, who, seeing no other way out, laid hands upon themselves. They also placed under the ban and cast away from them, and out of <margin>*In the same place, page 474.* Regarding "Marrying Outside," *See also the Account of I. H. V. P. N. page 19.*</margin> heaven: all those who married outside their congregation—that is, those who entered into marriage with someone who was not of their persuasion, even if that person were not a Jew, a Heathen, or an idolater; but...

-># OF THE REFORMATION. BOOK IV.<-
->A a<-

<margin>1555.</margin>...but one who made a profession of the Christian Religion, yet in a different assembly than theirs; or at least not in theirs; which they called an <term>Outside-marriage: *Buitentrou*, the practice of marrying someone who was a Christian but not a member of their specific congregation</term>. They also refused to release such an "Outside-marrier" from the <term>ban: *de ban*, a form of excommunication and social exclusion</term>, nor readmit or accept them back, until he had moved his spouse to also become a member of their assembly, or until death had separated him from her, or her from him; even if he, or she, showed remorse for the outside-marriage they had committed.

<margin>Order to give force to the ban and marital shunning. *Ibid. p. 16. 17.*</margin>But also to give more force to the ban and <term>marital shunning: *echtmijding*, the mandatory practice where a spouse must socially and physically avoid their partner if that partner is placed under the church ban</term> between husband and wife, the following order was found good and brought into use: That no one among them desiring a wife might speak to or woo the one he had his eye on himself; but he must announce his intention to the <term>Ministers: *Dienaeren*, the leaders or "servants" of the Word</term>, seek advice from them, and let them make the request. If these [Ministers] wished to hinder the marriage, or suggest another suitor to the maiden, they could do so. If the marriage proceeded, then the Ministers gathered and questioned first the future bridegroom, then the bride, quite sharply on various points of their disposition, and especially regarding the ban and marital shunning: First, whether they were of one mind with the congregation in all those things? Secondly, should it happen, once they were married, that one of them was banned from the congregation, would the obedient person then faithfully shun his or her spouse along with the congregation? Here one had to say "yes," or the marriage would not proceed. That same confession and promise had to be made by that couple, upon a similar investigation and questioning, before the entire congregation on the day the joining or wedding took place.

<margin>*Ibid. p. 17, 18.*</margin>If, however, while these things were being enforced, some married one another without the knowledge of the Ministers, then that was held to be a heavy sin, and their cohabitation as open fornication, which was also punished with the ban for those so joined. However, this order later lost its force.

<margin>Disputes that occurred earlier. *See Succession of Anabaptists [Successio Anabaptistarum], chapter XIV. p. 75... 78...*</margin>Mention was also made of other disputes that occurred much earlier among the Anabaptist teachers: the first around the year fifteen hundred forty-seven between Menno [Simons] and Dirk Philips on one side, and Frans Kuiper and Adam Pastoor on the other. Two secret debates were held regarding this, called by Menno and his followers around that time, the first at Emden,

A Pastor turned to the views of the <term>Arians: <note>original: "Arrianen"</note> followers of a 4th-century heresy that denied the full divinity of Jesus Christ</term>, and was excommunicated by Dirk Philips; but Kuiper, who relapsed into <term>Popery: <note>original: "Pausdom"</note> the Roman Catholic Church</term>, was placed under the ban by Menno. Henrik van Vreen and Antony of Cologne separated themselves from the other Anabaptists around the year 1550: but I find little record of the causes and true circumstances of these differences. However, in the year fifteen hundred and fifty-three, the Dutch exiles—who had previously gathered into a spiritual community in London under Edward the Sixth and were scattered after his death by his sister Queen Mary—also found two types of Anabaptist gatherings at Wismar (during that sorrowful Northern journey, where they suffered so much at the hands of certain harsh Lutherans <gloss>1</gloss>). One group sided with Menno, who was staying there at the time; the other consisted of people who had been excommunicated or banned by him, solely because they listened to others from among the Lutherans preach, in addition to their own Teachers. They believed they were free to hear them and were unwilling to let that freedom be taken away <gloss>2</gloss>. At that time, Hermes Bakkereel, and later Martinus Micron, Teachers among the exiles, entered into discussion with Menno concerning the office of the Magistracy regarding the use of the sword, <term>marital shunning: *echtmijding*, the practice of avoiding a spouse who is under a church ban</term>, the incarnation of the Lord Jesus Christ, and especially regarding that presumptuous or thoughtless judging by Menno. They said that in his writings, he condemned without distinction and everywhere all those who did not agree with his understanding—especially Ministers—as worldly and fleshly men <gloss>3</gloss>. Thus, human frailty accompanied Menno’s good intentions. Nevertheless, one must admit that he labored greatly and did much toward the Reformation of doctrine and morals. In the fire of his zeal, one also saw bright rays of gentleness and <term>moderation: *rekkelijkheit*, a spirit of flexibility or tolerance in religious matters</term> occasionally shine through among his followers. But his harshness toward others, and his yielding to the recklessness and obstinacy of his most vehement brothers (whom he did not dare oppose enough due to his own inconsistency), obscured the brilliance of his virtues, in the opinion of some. That he had been too compliant toward Dirk Philips, Leonard Bouwens, and Gillis van Aken was something he himself felt and acknowledged before his death—as is believed by some of the most discreet Anabaptists. Indeed, some say that Volkaert Maertsz, a man of knowledge,

That house was held in suspicion because of a love that was considered too physical, and a religious fanaticism that was deemed too carnal. Hendrik Niklaes, a Westphalian born in Münster <gloss>3</gloss>, but who lived in Amsterdam for a long time and also for some time in Emden <gloss>4</gloss>, was the Father of this house. He, having risen around the year fifteen hundred and forty <gloss>5</gloss>, called himself the deified man; he boasted of high things and seemed to exalt himself above the human. He was, in his own opinion, more than Moses and Christ because, as he claimed, Moses had taught men hope, and Christ faith, but he taught love, which was greater than both the former things, and he was consequently greater than the Teachers of both: therefore, he wrote, Moses had been in the forecourt of the sanctuary <gloss>6</gloss>, Christ had held the ministry of faith in the Holy Place, and he, or his spirit of love, had his ministry of love in the Most Holy Place <gloss>7</gloss>. So it was that he did not point and lead away from himself toward Christ, as John the Baptist had done, but with Satan, he led away from Christ toward himself <gloss>8</gloss>. He spoke of his humanity and the essence of his Divinity... and also of the kingdom of Israel, saying it would be established or confirmed in that time under this (his) ministry. Some of his children or disciples held his writings to be better than the Holy Scriptures <gloss>9</gloss>: but people of a different understanding, who would accept no doctrine without first knowing it to be true, and who would recognize nothing as true without first testing it against the touchstone of God's word, understood <gloss>10</gloss> that they had read the writings of no one, among all the writers or sects of those times, in which there was less fault regarding modesty, less orderliness, less—

<margin>1555.</margin>
“Eighty years ago I was not yet born; how could I then be joyful, or know my own salvation?” *“I think that you are mocking me, Coornhert,”* the man replied. “No,” Coornhert then countered, *“I think you, a temporal man, mock me by falsely boasting that you are God: this is now evident from your own mouth, since God is eternal, blessed, and joyful, and you are not.”* About a month later, another person of the same sect, named M., came to speak with him and also claimed that he was God. Coornhert said, *“I recently had such a ‘God’ visit me, and I proved to him that he spoke wrongly.”* “If you said,” he continued, *“‘I am divine,’ that might be tolerated, but to say ‘I am God’ is as untruthful as it is crudely spoken.”* He answered, *“You allow for becoming divine; what is that other than becoming God?”* Coornhert said, *“There is a great difference. One certainly finds people who, having become partakers of the divine nature through grace, may rightly be called divine, but there is no more than one who is God of Himself. Here lies the same distinction that exists between being enlightened and becoming the light itself.”* Thereupon he led him out of his room into the light of the sun, saying: *“That you now, standing in the rays of the sun, are light, I see and know well; and you may therefore, through participation in the light of the sun, truly be called light. But if you wish to see that you yourself are not the light, then step out of the sunshine into the shadow or into this dark cellar, and see if your presence there will enlighten those shadows or the cellar. I’ll wager it shall fail you: yet that would have to happen, if you yourself were the light or the sun.”* At the same time Coornhert asked, *“Does God not know the thoughts of all men?”* The other agreed to this. *“Tell me then,”* said the questioner, *“my thoughts or the secrets of my heart.”* The answer was, *“I will not reveal such high matters to a scorner.”* *“And I,”* said Coornhert then, *“cannot believe such high-minded boasters.”*

To his son Philip, he handed over his Netherlands, along with the kingdoms of Spain, the Indies, and all that was subject to him. This abdication of the greatest dominion in Christendom had, some believe, been in the Emperor's mind for over thirty years <gloss>3</gloss>; though to others this is improbable <gloss>4</gloss>. Regarding the causes that moved him to this, judgments vary. Some believe that he was weary of the burden, as his health—which he blamed—or his usual luck failed him <gloss>5</gloss>; or that the gnawing of his conscience, regarding various things committed by him, had forced him to discharge himself from the world, and to reconcile with God in time; for there were things that pained his mind. Against this, the supporters of the Reformation claimed that these events, if viewed correctly, were indeed excusable <gloss>1</gloss>; but there was something else to be said about him: <gloss>2</gloss> so much war and stubbornness to bring France under his control; the upholding of the extreme insolence of mutiny and Spanish cruelty in Milan, in order to attach that Duchy to his house; King Francis [I] of France deceived regarding safe-conduct through his land to quell the Ghent uprising <gloss>3</gloss> <note>The Revolt of Ghent (1539–1540) occurred when the city refused to pay taxes for the Emperor's wars; Charles V famously marched through France to suppress it.</note>; the Landgrave <note>Philip I, Landgrave of Hesse, a key Protestant leader</note> caught in a net through false hope and duplicity <gloss>4</gloss>; and especially those streams of blood shed for the sake of faith; the making of edicts on the matter of heresy, which it was said were written more with blood than with ink, and had cost the lives of a mighty multitude of people, as many as fifty thousand <gloss>5</gloss> <note>The "Blood-Placards" were draconian laws intended to root out Protestantism in the Netherlands.</note>. These were, they understood, matters that might with more reason trouble his heart. Whatever the case may be, it was no light or small cause that brought about this change in the Emperor, but a very pious reason that came from heaven <gloss>6</gloss>. That he also sought to conclude his days with good deeds since then has become evident, as proof of the virtue of his purpose in abdicating his crowns. This, along with his providence, steadfastness, and composure in prosperity and adversity seen in other dealings, was, not without reason, highly praised: as was by many his piety, proven by the zeal and labor to settle the disputes in faith through a lawful Council <gloss>7</gloss> <note>Referring to the Council of Trent, which aimed to reform the Catholic Church and address the Protestant challenge.</note>. But nowhere, says Thuanus <note>Jacques Auguste de Thou (1553–1617), a renowned French historian and statesman.</note>, did he more display the greatness of his mind than in the end of his life; therein that great man, accustomed to conquering others, conquered himself; also this life, subject to so many misfortunes, he now contemplated a better one and renounced it before he died; and he who had lived for the common good began to live for himself and for God. The Prince was also often heard to repeat the memorable saying of his old military commander, who is better known by his virtue than his name; for when the latter requested his dismissal, intending to leave the war and the world with its offices, and being asked by the Emperor what the cause of such a new undertaking was, he then gave, it is said, this answer: *That between the business of life and the day of death, some interval of time ought to pass.* This wisdom the Emperor followed on a large scale. 1555.
A comparison between Emperor Charles V and Pope Paul IV.
<note>original: *Servit. Hist. Concil. Trid. V. 365.* — Paolo Sarpi, History of the Council of Trent, Book V, page 365.</note>
</margin>
People were now making a comparison between the actions of this Prince [Charles V], who from childhood had been raised and trained in the greatest and most difficult affairs of the world, and who, at not much older than fifty years, stepped down from his high station and left the world to dedicate himself entirely to the service of God, transforming from a very powerful Prince into a humble and devout religious man; and that of the other [Pope Paul IV], who had previously left the office of Bishop to enter a monastery, but having recently become Pope at the age of eighty, had surrendered himself entirely to all magnificence, pride, and greed for glory, while almost the whole of Europe was set ablaze by the war-related disturbances he had provoked.

<margin>
1556.
The Emperor sails to Spain.
<note>original: *F. Strad. l. 10, 11... Corput. ibid. p. 595.* — Famianus Strada, De Bello Belgico; and Abraham de Corput, The Divine Quality of the Reformation.</note>
</margin>
In August of the year fifteen hundred and fifty-six, the Emperor set sail for Spain with both his sisters, Eleanor and Mary; there he retired to the monastery of Saint Justus <note>The Monastery of San Jerónimo de Yuste in Extremadura, Spain.</note>, on the borders of Castile near Plasencia. At this time, King Philip, with an <term>edict — a "plakkaet" or official decree</term> signed on the twentieth of August, renewed, confirmed, and turned into an eternal command the previous edicts issued by his father on the matter of heresy, and specifically that of the twenty-fifth of September <note>Dutch: Herfstmaendt ("Harvest Month")</note> in the year fifteen hundred and fifty. This cunning was used to further introduce the Inquisition: due to the change of Sovereign, those who held any office or service were required, according to ancient custom, to bring their commissions to the Court and obtain new ones from the new Prince. The inquisitors did the same, but instead of renewing the secret commission they previously held—which was issued privately in their names—the officers and judges were now commanded by the open letters of the edict to assist and help the aforementioned inquisitors in the execution of their duties. However, while the edict was sent out in the hope that it would be proclaimed everywhere without much scrutiny—as usual commands are easily renewed during such times of transition—those in power found themselves deceived, and the very thing they sought to advance was set back. For the Magistrates of Antwerp (into whose hands this edict had been very strangely thrust), still mindful of what had occurred regarding this matter in the year fifteen hundred and fifty, did not proceed as lightheartedly as had been expected; instead, considering the consequences, they found such great difficulty in it that they [delayed] the proclamation

I have, therefore, preferred to be obedient to God in this than to a man.* 

One of the Magistrates asked, *What was done in your meetings?* Then Baldwin, the eldest son, took the floor, saying, *I shall, my Lords, if it please you, relate it in full.* Having permission to speak, he began thus: *When we are gathered there in the name of the Lord, to hear His holy Word, then we all likewise fall upon our knees on the earth, and confess in humility of heart our sins before the high majesty of God. Thereafter we pray all together that God’s word may indeed be rightly proclaimed and purely preached. We pray also for our Lord the Emperor, and for all his Council, so that the common good may be governed in peace and to the glory of God. And you, my lords, are not forgotten there either, as our Authorities, praying to the good God for you and for the entire city, to the end that He may maintain you in what is good. Does it seem to you that by gathering thus we committed such a great crime? Furthermore, I am prepared, should it please you to hear these prayers yourself, to recite them for you.* 

Some indicated with a gesture or sign that he should do so. Upon this, he knelt down before them and poured out his prayer with such heartfelt zeal, fervor of spirit, and deep emotion, that tears flowed from the eyes of some of the judges. *And these are*, he spoke, standing up then, *the things that took place in our meetings.* After this, the prisoners confessed their faith. # HISTORY OF THE REFORMATION. BOOK IV.
<page-num>195</page-num>
<header>OF THE REFORMATION. BOOK IV.</header>
<sig>Bb 2</sig>

<margin>1556. Robert and Baldwin Ogier sentenced to the fire.</margin>ings. Within four or five days, Robert and Baldwin were sentenced to the fire <note>Execution by burning at the stake was the standard punishment for persistent heresy during this period.</note>. Being about to go to their deaths, the father was urged by the monks to at least take a crucified image of Christ in his hand; saying further: "Lift up your heart to God; you know well that it is nothing but wood," and with that, they tied it into his hands. At this, Baldwin snatched it away, crying out: *“My father, what are you doing? Will you be an idolater in your final hour? May the people,”* he added, throwing the image away, *“not be offended by us because we desire no Christ of wood; for we carry Jesus Christ, the Son of the living God, in our hearts, and we feel His holy Word, written in the depths of our souls with golden letters.”* 

Having arrived upon the <term>scaffold — "schavot," the raised platform for public executions</term>, he requested to be allowed to make a confession of his faith in the hearing of the people. But the answer was: "See there your confessor; if you have anything to confess, confess it to him." With those words, they dragged him toward the <term>stake — "staek," the wooden post where the condemned were bound</term>. There he immediately began to sing the sixteenth Psalm <note>Psalm 16 was frequently sung by martyrs; it includes the line "I have set the Lord always before me."</note>, causing a <term>Friar Minor — "Minrebroeder," a member of the Franciscan order</term> to cry out: "Hear the wicked errors they sing to deceive the people!" *“Do you say,”* the other replied to him, *“that the Psalms of the Prophet David are errors? But it is your old habit to thus blaspheme the Holy Spirit.”* 

Turning toward his father, he cried out, *“Be of good courage, my father; it will soon be over.”* While being bound, the old man said to the executioner—for he was striking his feet with a hammer to bring them closer to the post—*“My friend, you hurt me. Why do you handle me so harshly?”* A monk, hearing this, burst out: "O, those villains! They want to bear the <margin>Horrible bitterness.</margin> name of martyrs, yet when one touches them a little <term>roughly — "onessen," likely an archaic variant of "oneffen" or "unevenly"</term>, they scream as if they were being murdered." *“Do you think,”* the son then let himself be heard, *“that we fear pain or death? Not at all. Had we <margin>Steady courage.</margin> feared them, we would never have surrendered our bodies to this savory death.”* <note>original: "smakelyke doodt." This is a striking metaphor where the martyr describes his death as something "tasty" or "desirable" because it leads to God.</note> Several times he repeated these words: *“O God, eternal Father, let the offering of our bodies be acceptable to You, in the name of Your well-beloved Son.”* 

"Wicked man, you lie," a certain Friar Minor burst out, "He is not your Father; you have the devil as a father." In this struggle, the youth lifted his eyes to heaven and turned to Robert, his father, with these words: *“See, my father, I see the heavens opened, and ten hundred- <margin>Joyful confidence.</margin> thousand times a thousand angels here around us, rejoicing over the confession of the truth which we have made before the world. Let us then—”*

*“Now the misfortune strikes me that I feared most. Arnout Dirkszoon, a Flemish countryman, was burned on the twenty-second of March in the year fifteen hundred fifty-seven, at Monnickendam, on account of his faith which ran contrary to the Papacy. Carolus Regius—or "the King"—formerly a Carmelite monk at Ghent, had left the Roman Church and lived for some time in England. There, he had translated into Dutch the commentary of John Bale on Revelation and the history of Francis Spira <note>Francis Spira was a famous 16th-century Italian jurist whose legalistic "recantation" of Protestantism led to a state of profound spiritual despair, often cited by Reformers as a warning.</note>. Having later fled to Emden due to the persecution under Queen Mary <note>Mary I of England, known as "Bloody Mary," who briefly restored Catholicism and persecuted Protestants.</note>, he was shortly thereafter captured in Bruges while visiting and strengthening his fellow believers in Brabant and Flanders. <margin>Karel de Koningk burned at Bruges. *History of the Martyrs, 404. b. He endured this death on the twenty-seventh of April with patience and courage. 

Sir Engel de Merle, or Merula—for the martyrdom of this elderly Dutchman has certain particulars that require a broader account, including matters that occurred earlier—was born in Brielle in the year fourteen hundred eighty-two into an honorable family. <margin>The martyrdom of Sir Engel Merula, Pastor of Heenvliet. *The Tragic History of Engel Merula, written by Paul Merula. In this service, which he took to heart, he began—through diligent study of the Holy Scriptures—to gradually notice more and more how many errors and stains the Roman Church was entangled and defiled with. <margin>Seeks to gradually improve the errors of the Papacy (October 1552); changes something in the Missal. *Angel Merula History, p. 3.*</margin> He also expressed this at times when the opportunity arose. However, not finding it advisable to change everything he understood to be contrary to God's word in his church all at once, he chose to proceed step by step. First, in the year fifteen hundred fifty-two, he made a beginning with the Missal <note>The book containing the prescribed prayers and instructions for the celebration of the Mass.</note>, changing something therein that concerned the merits and the mediation of all the Saints. <margin>Which the States of Holland prevented. History of Angelus p. 24, 25.</margin>
The States, having seen the request, ordered the Jailer not to hand over the prisoner; at the same time, they declared that they would consider the matter more closely in the next upcoming assembly and ordain what was right and fair. Meanwhile, Sonnius kept the matter dragging on, it is believed, to make the old man compliant through the misery of the dungeon. In opposition to this, the prisoner did his utmost through letters and messengers to further his case, or to be allowed to have the Hague as his prison under bail, all the more because winter was approaching, and he, besides his old age, was afflicted with many illnesses and ailments.

<margin>Lady Mary writes on behalf of Master Angelus. History of Angelus p. 49.</margin>
The Court refused to carry out this order because Master Angelus was the prisoner of the Lord of Kruningen. The matter having then been discussed with the Lord’s authorized representative, it was found good to move the prisoner, under bail, to a certain Convent, called the Priory of Middelburg, located in the West End of the Hague. However, that promise was never kept. They also frequently took it ill when the Lords took up some of the Pastor’s notes and explanations in their hands to read. He also complained that, given the short time allowed him to answer so many articles, he was overwhelmed, and could keep no copies of his assertions and defenses for himself; and when he sometimes requested to read and review his writings, previously delivered to them, to aid his memory, this was rudely refused him; to the end that he should not know what he had answered, and so that they might search out whether he faltered or changed his mind anywhere. When he complained to the Councilors that the Inquisitors were using force and violence against him, they gave as an answer: *We have been commissioned and appointed by the Queen only to be witnesses of what is to be done and has been done, not as Judges.* Thereafter, he was brought from the Provostry back to his old prison at the **Voorpoorte** <note>The "Gevangenpoort" or Gate House prison in The Hague.</note>, and after all the dispute of words followed the 
<margin>
Faint-heartedness of the Councilors.
*Ang. Hist. p. 53.*

The use of the feminine "Agna" (ewe-lamb) for Mary mimics the "Agnus Dei" (Lamb of God) traditionally reserved for Christ, a practice the author suggests was unscriptural.</note>: which is as much as if they said to her, *You Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world*. The people came rushing from all directions and from other cities toward The Hague, as it was thought that the sentence would be handed down. The entire assembly of the States of Holland was moved by the misfortune and the misery of that old man; in view of his good name, his outstanding learning, wonderful eloquence, uncommon piety, and inexhaustible charity toward the poor, who now cried out: *that they were being robbed of their father, protector, provider, only comfort, and helper in all their poverty and adversity.* He also—for he possessed great means (which it is thought first stirred the greedy Inquisitors against him)—had established several dwellings for the needy in the city of Brielle. There was a fear of rioting. Everyone cried out with one voice, especially the lawyers, that the Court in this matter was being subjected to force and violence by the Heresy-masters <note>original: "Kettermeesters," the Dutch term for Inquisitors</note>, who drew all the conduct of the law to themselves; that all order and style of justice was being broken. Nevertheless, others judged that no heretic had ever fallen into their hands who better deserved death: yet at the same time they had to admit that it was impossible for them to burn the man without putting themselves in great danger, so favorable to him was the common people, and also many of the great lords, though the latter let it be seen the least. To let him go was too much an affront to the honor of the clergy. To avoid the danger, and yet achieve their aim, the Heresy-masters sharpened their wits and their bitterness, and proceeded through a crooked detour of falsehood, which was too base to be devised by Hollanders, let alone Christians and theologians. They made use of the Bishop of Hebron, a man who was very well-spoken. This man, falling bareheaded and with folded hands at the feet of the prisoner (when on a certain day he expected to hear his sentence and had been brought from the outer gate to the council chamber), addressed him, and not without tears, with certain reasons which came down to this: *That they all well knew how they were not to be compared to him, who was a hundred times more learned than they, and...*

It was no Christian work to surrender fine parties <note>Meaning the judges and officials themselves.</note> to the madness and murderousness of the turbulent mob. 

"If you," said the Bishop, "are weary of life, why do you want to make us guilty of it? If you simply wish to die, you will surely find someone else—by whom you are not so well known nor so highly esteemed as by us—to soil his hands with you. Consider yourself then, and do not run to your destruction, which is unnecessary if you so wish. The people will hold you in high regard for a time, but afterward, cooling down and reflecting on the matter, they will admit that no one did you violence, but that you brought yourself to ruin: and were also the cause of more bloodshed. Preserve yourself for the sake of the many tears of the poor, who wish for your life; for the great favor of the congregation: for the great hope that all the Estates, specifically those present here, have for you. By preserving yourself, you shall also grant us this outstanding benefit: that we shall be regarded as Preservers of godly people, and not as oppressors, as people believe us to be. Give us the life that we have, which, though we did not receive it from you, we shall nonetheless admit to being indebted to you for as long as we live; for today it stands in your hand. Nor do we desire that you thank us, but only yourself, for your life. It is a small thing, by which you can mend all this evil; by which you can preserve our honor and yours; your life, ours, and that of many; namely: If you, setting aside the weighty articles of faith and..."

The entire assembly of the <term>States of Holland</term> <note>The governing body representing the various cities and nobility of the province of Holland.</note> was moved by the misfortune and misery of that old man; in view of his good name, his outstanding learning, wonderful eloquence, uncommon piety, and inexhaustible charity towards the poor, who now cried out: *that they were being robbed of their father, protector, provider, only comfort and helper in all their poverty and adversity*. He had also—for he possessed great means (which it is believed first provoked the greedy Inquisitors against him)—founded several dwellings for the needy in the city of Brielle. A riot was feared. Everyone cried out with one voice, especially the <term>jurists</term> <note>Legal experts and lawyers.</note>, that in this case, the Court was suffering force and violence from the Inquisitors, who had seized all legal management for themselves; they complained that all order and style of legal procedure was being broken. Nevertheless, others judged that no heretic had ever fallen into their hands who better deserved death: yet at the same time, they had to confess that it was impossible for them to burn the man without placing themselves in great danger, so favorable was the common people toward him, as well as many of the great lords, though the latter showed it the least. To release him would wound the honor of the clergy too deeply. To avoid the danger and yet achieve their goal, the Inquisitors sharpened their wits and malice, and proceeded via a sinister detour of falsehood, which was too wicked to be conceived of by Hollanders—and Christians and theologians at that. They made use of the Bishop of Hebron, a man of great eloquence. This man, falling at the feet of the prisoner (when on a certain day the latter expected to hear his sentence and had been brought from the front gate to the council chamber) bareheaded and with folded hands, addressed him, and not without tears, with several arguments that amounted to this: *That they all well knew how they were not to be compared to him, who was a hundred times more learned than they, and...*

He then allowed himself to be led. They brought him immediately onto the platform <note>original: "Rolle"—the public stage or tribunal where sentences were read</note>, where the people from all the cities of Holland and thereabouts were gathered together.

They did not read there the aforementioned indifferent points, but the main articles of his beliefs, and that so hastily, under their breath, that he could not understand it, partly due to his deafness, and partly because some, set up for this purpose by the Inquisitors, kept him in conversation during the reading. ...and had been improved. Shame fell upon the prisoner, and his friends were struck with embarrassment. Then followed the sentence, which doomed his books and all other writings tasting of heresy to the fire; deposed him from his Pastorate and all ecclesiastical offices; and commanded his abjuration and new confession to be proclaimed within fifteen days, on a Sunday or other feast day, from the pulpit in the church at Heenvliet. Furthermore, he was condemned to perpetual imprisonment, there to do penance with the bread and water of sorrow and to bewail his sins; moreover, he was to pay all the costs of the arrest, imprisonment, guarding, and the legal proceedings, according to the assessment and discretion of the Inquisitor Ruard <note>Ruard Tapper (1487–1559), a prominent theologian from the University of Louvain and a fierce hunter of heretics</note>. Up to this point, the old man still had no suspicion of any deceit; but when he was brought back to the Gatehouse <note>original: "Voorpoort"—the prison of the Court of Holland in The Hague</note> and heard from his nephew Willem Merula how he had been tricked, and that they were now boasting of his recantation, he saw the duplicity in their hearts, and what cause for offense had been given to the people by the appearance of his inconstancy. This, although it happened without his knowledge and against his will, grieved him exceedingly; his heart became heavy, and he poured himself out in this lament:

> *O my God, how deceitfully have those robed backbiters and slanderers dealt with me! ...had returned to Leuven and, as he claimed, it was now inconvenient for him to travel back to Holland to finalize the agreement with Heer Engel—an agreement that the Bishop of Hebron had orally promised. This agreement, it was pretended, would lead to a softening of the sentence. The prisoner, therefore, had to be moved to Leuven. A petition for this move was made to the Governess <note>Margaret of Parma, the Governor of the Netherlands</note>. Despite the great diligence shown by Willem Merula, his nephew, before the States of Holland to prevent this, the request was granted; however, the primary motive was to get him out of Holland and under the direct power of the church. Thus, in the year fifteen hundred and fifty-five, the old man was taken to Leuven by the Prosecutor General, in violation of the laws of Holland. Here, the Monastery of the *Sellebroeders* <note>The Alexian Brothers, also known as Cell-brothers, a religious order often tasked with caring for the sick and burying the dead</note> was assigned to him as a prison, and all access to his friends was denied. He was forbidden from the common table and from speaking with the monks; three times a week—Monday, Wednesday, and Friday—he was served only water and bread. Some say that he was locked in a dark hole alongside two insane men who lay in their own filth, and that he nearly suffocated from the stench. It is said that the *Sellebroeders* spoke with him in secret; they listened to him and took pity on him; and while begging at people's doors (for they were Mendicant Friars), they made it known among the citizens what they had heard from him—how he had been deceived—and spoke of his godliness and patience. This won him great public favor. He also now openly cried out that he intended to stand by everything he had ever preached, spoken, or written. To turn him from his convictions, another "battle of words" <note>a formal theological debate</note> followed at the beginning of the year fifteen hundred and fifty-six; but he held fast to the Holy Scriptures, refusing to yield despite the worsening conditions of his imprisonment and the most severe threats. *I do not fear my adversaries,* he said, *and for the truth which I taught and confirmed with my writings, I shall go into the fire as willingly as I would go into the dining hall to take food.* His books and writings were repeatedly taken from him, and his basic necessities withheld. They threatened to drown him in a sack at night <note>a method of execution used to avoid the public spectacle of an execution and the potential for a riot</note>; but even this could not shake his steadfastness. Some persons of high standing fought to quiet or soften Ruard's anger and severity through their intervention and intercession, but without success. so that the proceeding might not seem mixed with any deceit, injustice, or violence, it was spread among the people that this heretic had been captured in one of the nearest neighboring villages. Under this cover, Ruard sent some men to Bergen <note>Now Mons, in modern-day Belgium</note> who, acting as if he were a stranger, questioned him regarding his faith. Finally, they declared him to be a "relapsed" or fallen heretic, a status which carried with it the punishment of clerical degradation, sentencing to the fire, and delivery to the secular judge. This transport to Bergen was carried out very skillfully and secretly in order to do away with the man before the people of Holland could oppose the pressure of this Inquisition. For Ruard and his associates feared that the people would seek to uphold the rights of their native land according to the country's privileges, which were so significantly curtailed by this proceeding. <note>The "Jus de non evocando" was a legal privilege in the Netherlands stating that a citizen could only be tried in their own province.</note> This was the reason that Willem Merula learned of that last transport from Lissieux <note>Possibly referring to a specific prison or a transcription of a place-name like 'Lier' or 'Lille', though the text specifies Bergen/Mons as the final destination</note> very late, and could not hasten to Brussels quickly enough; he learned from the Inquisitor Ruard, who was there at the time, that the sentence had been passed, and further, that he would not find his uncle alive. He would indeed not have found him alive if something had not occurred on the day appointed for his death—namely, the twenty-fourth of July <note>Original: *Hooimaendt*, literally "Hay-month"</note>—which hindered the execution of the sentence. But hastening there in great haste day and night, and arriving in the city at ten o'clock in the morning on the twenty-sixth of July, the Pastor was drawn out of the prison to go to his death, leaning on a stick, and so wasted and undone that he was almost unrecognizable; for he had now lain for about six weeks in the dungeon of the Castle, tormented by hunger and thirst, by filth and vermin. Dragged from one place to another out of Holland, I have finally come here, being ready to offer myself entirely to Christ, my Savior, as a pure sacrifice. My soul longs for God—the soul which the opposing party recklessly said belonged to the Devil. Far be it from me, far be it! They judge wrongly and deceive the people; partly because of the teachings—which nevertheless agreed with God's word and which they were unable to refute—and partly regarding my body, which although wasted away, has nevertheless been handled so unworthily that everyone is revolted by it. For behold these filthinesses; if your eyes have an aversion to them, the stench itself shall reveal it. Thieves and murderers are treated more favorably. Go now and proclaim to friends, acquaintances, and others in the fatherland what you have seen and shall hear. You have faithfully stayed with me as long as they allowed it. To you, my heir, all my belongings were due; but bear the loss of your inheritance with as much courage as I bear the loss of my life. You do not lack understanding, nor the learning that you know I nurtured in you for as long as those people permitted me. You are coming into your years; take her as a helpmate <note>Merula is likely referring to a betrothed or a specific woman he had arranged for Willem to marry</note> whom I, while still free, assigned to you. I have performed a good work with my teaching in the households of the Heermans and Kerkwerven <note>These were prominent families in Brielle who supported the Reformation</note>. God shall give the growth. Trust in Him who shall bless the beginnings. Help, as much as you can, to promote the dwellings that I [established] for the poor...”*

# HISTORY

<meta>catchword: already.</meta>

<margin>1557.</margin>...foundations I established in Brielle <note>Original: "den Briel." A town in the west of the Netherlands where Merula had served as a priest and benefactor.</note>. I thank God, the most merciful Father, that I shall die in public, and that by this means my opponents are deprived of the opportunity to burden this my perseverance, inspired in me by God, with slanderous lies: which they would undoubtedly have done if they—as I always <margin>Apotheosis of Ruard Tapper, page 46. <note>Ruard Tapper was a leading Dutch theologian and Inquisitor who opposed Merula.</note></margin> feared—had done away with me by poison, or smothered or suffocated me in prison, or—as they attempted to do in the abbey of Lisieux—drowned me in a sack. My blood, however, shall not quench the fire that has risen against them: the same shall in a short time burst out into much greater flames, which neither they nor their descendants shall be able to smother. When his nephew thereupon comforted and exhorted him with these words, *“Believe firmly that you shall shortly see the salvation of the Lord in the land of the living. This was granted: But while fervently praying with bowed knees and uplifted hands in the entrance <margin>dies in prayer.</margin> of the hut, he finally sank down on his right side. The bystanders thought that he had fainted from fear of the upcoming pain, but rushing toward him, they found him without life, and at the end of his suffering. This was the passing of Master Angelus Merula, in which God’s merciful goodness was visibly displayed; for God seemed to take his soul to Himself at that very hour, so that he, who through many illnesses, and an age of seventy-five years, and the hardship of a nearly five-year imprisonment, was already...

# THE FOURTH BOOK OF THE REFORMATION.

<meta>catchword: by</meta>

<margin>1557.</margin>...was already broken and worn out by torture, and in his final moments felt no pain from the fire. The Executioner, startled by such a hasty and unusual death, refused to proceed, saying that justice had been satisfied. Therefore, some of the court officers set fire to the small hut; but the body, which lay outside and thus remained unhurt by those flames, was afterwards burned to ashes with another fire. This Angel, or Angelus <note>Angelus Merula (1482–1557) was a Dutch priest who turned toward Protestant teachings. His death is often cited by early historians as a peaceful passing before the flames could reach him.</note>, was the great-uncle of Paulus Merula, who later became Professor of History at Leiden and who also left the history of this martyrdom to posterity in Latin. In this same year, the fire of persecution also struck several Anabaptists <term>Anabaptists (Doopsgesinden)</term>: A wing of the Reformation that practiced adult baptism and often faced severe persecution from both Catholics and other Protestants. In Antwerp, ten men <gloss>1</gloss> and four women <gloss>2</gloss> were put to death for their confession of that faith. In Haarlem, a woman sat imprisoned who would have gone the same way, had she not remained in labor, being pregnant <gloss>3</gloss>: Joriaen Simons of Hallum from Friesland and Clement Dirks of Haarlem, both weavers, imprisoned alongside her, were sentenced to the fire: one had sold some forbidden books, and the other had read and studied them. The Judges declared all of Joriaen's goods entirely, and those of Clement up to the sum of sixty pounds—according to the privilege of the city of Haarlem <note>Haarlem held specific legal exemptions that limited how much of a citizen's property could be confiscated by the crown.</note>—to be forfeited for the benefit of the King. It was intended, once they had given up the ghost, to burn their books as well, but such a commotion arose among the bystanders that the court officials took flight, and the books were thrown among the people. Because of this, they were spread even more widely. The strict oversight of books caused some writers to seek the advancement of the Reformation through writings published anonymously or under unknown names, and printed abroad. Thus Johannes Sartorius of Amsterdam, in the year fifteen hundred fifty-eight, published his *Expansions on the Great and Small Prophets* in Basel, through the printer Jan Operijn <note>Also known as Johannes Oporinus, a famous Swiss printer of academic and Reformation texts.</note>, under the disguised name of Johannes Tossarrius, which expressed his own name through an anagram <note>original: "letterversetting"</note>. # H I S T O R Y

<margin>1558.</margin> ...distinguished by precious stones, purple, and silk, performing the sacrifice, where all other things are carried out individually in the manner of the Old Covenant; as that living, true, spiritual, and powerful church, which exists through the bare word of Christ. In this training school, we truly become Kings and Priests, but of Christ; for being anointed with an anointing that teaches all truth, we offer ourselves to the Lord as a living and holy sacrifice, saying with Paul: *I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me.* <margin>*Galatians 2:20*</margin> He had previously been in custody and narrowly escaped death without forsaking his faith <note>1</note>. ### HISTORY OF THE REFORMATION. BOOK IV.

<margin>1558.</margin> ...received the Lord's Supper, not through the mouth or throat, but through faith. Some of the <term>Schepenen</term> <note>Aldermen or municipal magistrates</note> said that they agreed with him on that point; nevertheless, he was finally condemned by them after nine months of imprisonment. A particular incident contributed greatly to this: news reached the Court at Brussels at this time that a certain <term>Anabaptist</term> <note>original: "Doopsgesind," referring to the radical reform movement that practiced adult baptism</note> prisoner in 's-Hertogenbosch, who was to be put to death despite having recanted his faith, had been forcibly broken out of the dungeon by night. This was taken so seriously by the King and Cardinal Caraffa <note>Giovanni Pietro Caraffa, later Pope Paul IV, known for his harsh stance against heresy</note>, who was then at Court, that the Margrave—out of a double fear of both men and wanting to avoid appearing as a "favorer of heretics"—immediately sought the death penalty for Du Champ and another Anabaptist. The Aldermen, moved by these same concerns, condemned the prisoners to death, which they suffered on the fifth of February <note>original: "Sprokkelmaendt," the old Dutch name for the month when wood was gathered</note>.

<margin>At 's-Hertogenbosch an Anabaptist was forcibly taken from the dungeon. *History of the Martyrs, ibid.*</margin>

<margin>Du Champ was strangled alongside an Anabaptist.</margin> While the Anabaptist was being strangled, the other [Du Champ] testified before all the people: *That he did not die for any errors of "re-baptism" or other heresies, but only for the teachings of the Prophets and Apostles.* He thanked God for the honor bestowed upon him in this suffering and prayed for his enemies. Gillis Verdikt of Hilverseel was later strangled and burned in Brussels for the same confession, where he had intended to preach. "Do you think, my Lords," he cried out to his judges when they announced his death, "to root out the Christians, whom you call heretics, with burning and murder? Ah, you are greatly mistaken. The ashes of my body shall blow across the city and cause the Christians to increase; for the blood of the martyrs is the seed of the church."

### HISTORY

1558. ...praise sat before the mast, in a throne; love at the helm: to symbolize that he had steered all his actions toward God's glory. For Emperor Charles, gradually wasting away, had passed away from a burning fever on the twenty-first of September <note>original: *Herfstmaent*, "Autumn-month"</note> in the monastery of Saint Justus <note>The Monastery of San Jerónimo de Yuste in Spain, where Charles V retired after his abdication</note>.

Thuan. ibid.</margin>He had spent the last two years of his life mostly in religious works and pious meditations: in great restraint and moderation; also in fasting and prayer. From his income, he spent only four thousand crowns ¹ annually; the other ninety-six thousand he used to provide dowries for poor daughters, to help widows, and to support orphans. He called himself nothing but Charles, and no longer Emperor ². All his company consisted of twelve persons, or, as others say, of four servants ³. He kept only one horse. He was, he said, of no use to himself or to God in this life... He often openly wept over his errors with sighs, saying that in all the years of his life he had never served God a single day as was fitting. Often he prayed to God for the peace of the church. *In your hands, Lord*, he said, *have I commended your church*. That he had long labored to settle the differences in religion by calling a general Council <note>The Council of Trent, intended to address the challenges of the Reformation</note> to settle the differences in religion, has been stated above. To this end, he sought to bring about that the Protestants should be given proper freedom to present and defend their cases; he also advised the Fathers of the Council that they should not immediately embitter those of the Augsburg Confession <note>The primary confession of faith of the Lutheran Church, presented in 1530</note> at the very start by condemning their books. In his last will, made ten years before his death at Augsburg, he complained about Pope Paul III, whom he seemed to believe had not acted in good faith in promoting such a Synod. This was the same Paul III who at a certain time threatened him with the ban <note>excommunication from the Catholic Church</note>, and whom he had his Ambassador tell: *If the Pope wants to thunder and lightning with his excommunication, I shall thunder and lightning with my cannons*. In the final solitude of his life, he comforted himself primarily by reading the Church Father Saint Bernard <note>Bernard of Clairvaux, a 12th-century mystic and doctor of the church</note>, with whose words † he, committing himself to God with all his heart, reasoned thus: *I am indeed unworthy to obtain the kingdom of heaven by my own merits, but Jesus Christ, my Lord and God, possessing it by double right—as much by the inheritance of his Father as by the merit of his suffering—is satisfied with one right for himself, and grants the other to me.*

<summary>This page records the death and private character of Emperor Charles V, highlighting his pious retirement at Yuste, his charitable works, and his complex relationship with the Papacy and the Protestant Reformation.</summary>

# HISTORY

<margin>1558.</margin>
...failed, or did wrong. It did not stop there; for because many simple people, both within and outside of Alkmaar, were led by his example to observation, inquiry, and the knowledge of matters, and rejected Popery, the hatred of the clergy—a fire that is seldom quenched—was so fiercely ignited that finally the Under-Inquisitor Nicolaus de Castro, upon some new and heavy complaints, came from Utrecht with his servants to Alkmaar. He intended to surprise him and take him by force, and to this end, he requested that the Bailiff <note>The *Schout*, a local official responsible for law enforcement and judicial matters.</note> lend him a hand. But Kooltuyn, having been warned by someone, left his house and fled to Emden. After his flight, they tried to persuade the people in Enkhuizen and Alkmaar that the doctrines he had preached there must be false because, some said, he did not go to defend them; or because, others said, he had not allowed himself to be killed for them—which they claimed he certainly would have done had he been sure of the truth of his teachings. To counter the offense that might be given to the simple-minded by such talk in a timely manner, he thought it advisable to quickly publish and send over a certain small book he had previously written, called the *Gospel of the Poor*. It contained, in various places, the principal teachings for which he had been branded a heretic, persecuted, and banished, so that the impartial and simple might judge their truth or falsehood. The Preface contained the letter to his friend Timothy, wherein, alongside the account of the persecutions by the Inquisitors from whom he had fled, he also answers the aforementioned objections. Among other things, he writes: *That I did not defend my teaching against the persecutors cannot prove it false; for it did not happen because I was uncertain of the truth of the teachings, or because I could not account for them and claim them as true: but because I would have to answer, not according to the Scripture, with which they agree and according to which they ought to be defended, but according to the new Roman Doctors <note>A term for Catholic theologians and authorities who prioritized Church tradition over the literal text of the Bible.</note>, whom they oppose and according to whom they ought not to be defended: from which I well knew that my teachings would not stand with the truth in their eyes.* He says further that the Romanists reject God's word and set up human teachings in its place; and so that they should not seem to do so, they persuade the simple-minded, he says, that the Scripture is difficult, beyond their understanding, and in many things contradicts itself, and that therefore the interpretation of Scripture...

### OF THE REFORMATION. BOOK IV.

[Scrip]ture belongs only to the Church and her **Catholic Doctors** <note>Theologians recognized as authorities by the Church.</note>, to whom Christ promised the spirit of truth. And so that they might have an appearance of truth in this matter, they dare to teach that the Church—which they boast of because of the Pope—is above the Scripture, and that for this reason one may not bring forward the Scripture against that church: but must interpret the same according to the church: from which it follows that everything brought forward from Scripture against their teaching is regarded as falsified Scripture, and that anyone who founds himself upon it must be a heretic. This is the reason why I did not appear before them: I knew well that, according to that format, I was already overcome by them through falsehood: for I would bring forth God's word, and they the Church.

Afterwards he asserts from the Holy Scripture and the books of the **ancient Church Fathers** <note>original: "Kerkenleeraeren". This refers to early Christian theologians whose writings were often cited by both sides during the Reformation.</note>, that the true Christian Church was not above God's word, but was born out of it, founded upon it, and governed by it: on the contrary, that those whose teachings did not agree with God’s word, but fought against it, did not have nor were they the right church; and that no one could justly be accused of falsehood because he had no testimony of truth from such people; for they were not judges, but oppressors of the truth. Saying among other things: <margin>Letter to Timothy, p. A. 5.</margin> 

*The Scripture teaches us that men shall not rule over our faith; that God does not wish to be served with human institutions; that one may not add to nor take away from God’s word: but all this happens when we do not believe the Gospel any further than men command us, or must interpret the same according to the will of men.* 

And a little thereafter: 

*Paul curses not only men, but also the Angels, who introduce another teaching than he had taught: clearly indicating that the Scripture may not be undone, and that therefore the Scripture shall not follow men, but that men shall follow the Scripture.* 

To prove that it had not been necessary for him to shed his blood for the confirmation of what he had taught, he makes use of these reasons: Christ, he says, did not command his Apostles that they should <margin>Whether he was bound to die for his teaching if he could escape the persecutors. Letter to Timothy, p. A. 8.</margin> recklessly await their enemies to be captured and killed: but that they should flee to another city when they were persecuted in one. Thus Christ himself has often done, and before him the Prophets, and after him the Apostles. This command, after all, also concerns me; these examples also serve me. If I had been betrayed, I ought not to have revoked my true teachings, but to have confirmed them with my death: but to throw myself into danger that I could escape, without an internal prompting of the

Thus, the persecution was strengthened by greed. But in carrying out the sentences, great difficulties appeared everywhere, because the steadfastness of the condemned in their suffering overflowed into the hearts of the bystanders, making them fearless in their compassion: to the extent that some were found who were not afraid to speak words of comfort and courage to the miserable ones going to their death. And even if these supporters, caught in the act, had to endure similar cruelty within a few days, it nevertheless caused so little terror in those who considered a sharp but soon-ending pain to be the certain and shortest path to eternal salvation, that they began, alongside the condemned, to sing the Psalms with a raised voice, in numbers greater than was safe to arrest. Finally, it went so far that whole congregations, losing patience, came to an unrestrained riot, and in several places, they snatched the condemned from the executioner, or attempted to snatch them away.

The great nobles, meanwhile, laughed in their sleeves and turned a blind eye, in the hope that when the clergy lost their following, everything would better settle into a moderate government. This was a form of edifying entertainment and song which, provided the authorities kept it in check, was of no small service in guiding the minds of the multitude... Furthermore, the Magistrate has no more powerful means than this to instill a peaceful submissiveness in the common folk and to maintain their own dignity against the authority of the clergy; for it seems destined that the clergy must work against all rulers who do not follow their exact whims. And let no one imagine that they can counter, through the scattering of pamphlets or printed booklets, the sharpness of a smooth tongue, which can move a great number of all kinds of people at once in a single hour, and knows well how to instill the passions of the speaker into them.* The freedom of speech of these people did not hesitate, where appropriate (and it was often appropriate), to touch the priests where it hurt; mocking blunt abuses and portraying the bitterness of persecution as something hateful. This was well-received by the people; and the more the church took offense, the more the common man suspected that the clergy knew themselves to be guilty. Meanwhile, the great lords laughed up their sleeves and turned a blind eye, hoping that when the clergy lost their following, everything would better settle into a moderate government. But the King had other views, and forbade—by a <term>decree—plakkaet</term> issued in Brussels on the twenty-sixth of <term>January—"Loumaent" in old Dutch</term> in the year fifteen hundred and fifty-nine—the divulging, singing, or playing, or the causing to be divulged, sung, or played in public, in company, or in secret, any <term>Chamber plays—plays performed by the Rhetoricians</term>,

# HISTORY OF THE REFORMATION. BOOK IV.

<margin>1559.</margin>
Between both the Kings, it was secretly discussed how best to exterminate all those suspected in the matter of religion in the Netherlands, in France, and throughout all of Christendom. They reached a sufficient agreement on this point. However, King Henry II <note>Henry II of France (r. 1547–1559)</note> unexpectedly let the basis of this plan slip to William, Prince of Orange <note>William the Silent, a key leader of the Dutch Revolt, who at this time was a hostage in the French court to ensure the treaty's terms</note>, one of the hostages, thinking that the secret had been entrusted to him. This later gave the Reformed in France and in this country cause to set themselves against it. Shortly before this, on the eleventh of the <term>Lent month—March</term>, Ruard Tapper of Enkhuizen, <term>Dean of Leuven—the head of the university's faculty</term> and <term>Grand Inquisitor—the chief official in charge of finding and punishing heretics</term> of these Netherlands, died in Brussels in the seventy-first year of his age. He was held in high esteem by the most fervent Catholics for his fierce zeal against those called heretics; but others loathed his bitterness. Besides what history testifies regarding his severity against the aged Engel Merula <note>An elderly priest executed for his beliefs in 1557</note> and others, it is also told of him that when, in the year 1543, much blood was shed in Leuven through his instigation, he undertook a wicked deed at that same time against Perseval of Bruges, a <term>Licentiate in Divinity—a degree allowing one to teach theology</term> at Leuven.

Because this man spoke his mind a bit too much against the Doctors of Leuven, Tapper summoned him to court. When most people took such pity on him that it was feared he might perhaps prove his innocence, Tapper smeared the prisoner—a blind, deformed man—with a rumor of <term>sodomy—at the time, a capital crime used to describe various "unnatural" acts</term>. Then no one dared speak for him, and Ruard found the opportunity, since the man would neither confess guilt nor show repentance, to shut him in a perpetual prison. But afterwards, hearing how the prisoner was perishing of hunger, and that the poor man's sold library was enough to feed him daily, he sought another counsel. To avoid suffering loss on account of the man's life, nor shame on account of his death, he gave him to a nobleman (who had prayed for him) so that the nobleman would keep him; but in such a way that he later made that nobleman a suspect for it, forced him to stand trial for it, and finally took all his goods. It is also attributed to him that, speaking of killing for the sake of religion, he used these words: *It is of little consequence whether those who die in this way perish guilty or innocent,*
