<header>HISTORY</header>

<margin>1560. <note>original: "MDLX."</note></margin>nations, who had torn themselves away from the Roman church, were rebellious against him, the Head of the church, and therefore stood in danger of falling from the faith, by cause of the deceit and the snares of the Sectaries, unless new and vigilant Watchers <note>Meaning the newly appointed Bishops</note> were set against them. It was also stated in the Bull <note>The Papal Bull *Super Universas* (1559), which authorized the creation of new bishoprics to better combat the Reformation</note> that each Bishop in his cathedral church might grant nine Prebends <note>Stipends or land-holdings attached to a cathedral</note>, whose Canons would be bound to assist him in the matter of the Inquisition, and to promote the same throughout his entire Diocese: indeed, two of those should themselves be Inquisitors. From this it was concluded that, since they could not openly introduce the so greatly feared and hated Inquisition, they now wished to usher it in through a detour with these Bishops. But when it became known how Antoine Perrenot de Granvelle had been endowed with the Archbishopric of Mechelen, and that the Pope had sent him the red hat <note>The symbol of a Cardinal</note>; people began to look even deeper into the purpose of the ecclesiastical and worldly secret, to discover it more clearly, and to spread it among the people. ***All this***, it was now cried out, ***was the doing of the Spaniards, directly against the liberties, and without the consent of the States of the land, in order to master the same, and to bring it into the same servitude as Naples and Milan: the source of it all being a lawless supremacy and the Inquisition of Spain, of which the Cardinal as head, and the other Bishops under him, each in his own district, would have the governance.*** To this was added, ***That, since certain Monasteries were assigned to the Bishops for their maintenance, it could be clearly perceived that not only Prelates and clergy would have to bow under this compulsion, but also nobles and commoners: seeing that from the Prelates, in many places, and namely in Brabant, the first estate of the States consisted.*** <note>The States of Brabant were the representative assembly, where high-ranking clergy formed the "First Estate."</note> For the Bishops, often foreigners, who were excluded from the government by the charters <note>Refers to the *Blijde Inkomst* or Joyous Entry, the constitutional document of Brabant that limited foreign influence</note>, and being always bound by oath to the Pope (a matter questionable for the King himself) had, as Prelates in respect of their monasteries, to appear at the assembly of the States. Presiding there, they would have the final word; they would suppress or stifle the liberty of the subjects; and everyone would look to the mouth of the Cardinal, as their Archbishop; who, by virtue of the Monastery of Affligem (since it was recognized as the most excellent in Brabant, and Brabant as the most stately of the provinces) would also be the first Prelate. And as the Cardinal was inclined to please the Spaniards and those of their Inquisition in everything, nothing else was to be expected than that they would get the entire conduct of Netherlands affairs into their power.

But later, as some of the Bishops began to force their way in and seize the ecclesiastical assets allocated to them, those who were being dispossessed rose up in protest—especially the Abbeys of Affligem, Saint Bernard, and Tongerloo in Brabant. They maintained that giving away their resources directly contravened their privileges, which had been sworn to by His Majesty, and went against the original intent of the founders of the Monasteries. To demonstrate the legal grounds of their position, they sought help from men of letters on all sides; they reportedly spent about thirty thousand guilders on consultations and legal opinions gathered from jurists in Italy, France, and Germany. Seeing little hope of comfort from other quarters, they requested to take the matter to court, but found that path closed to them. Finally, despairing of remaining entirely whole, they thought that if they could secure the rest of their property by surrendering a portion of their income, it would still be a bargain. They brought the matter so far that, by paying eight thousand guilders a year for the benefit of the Archbishops, they were released from the harassment. To this end, the King undertook to persuade the Pope, promising them that they could continue choosing new Abbots, as the old ones had died in the meantime. Nevertheless, because it was not only their own interests at stake, but also their duty as members of the States to prevent these innovations, they joined with the others to defend the ancient customs <note>original: "oud herkoomen"</note> and to tolerate no episcopal seats—or at least no more than one, and that one at Leuven.

About eighteen Anabaptists <term>Doopsgezinden: A "Baptist-minded" Protestant group that practiced adult baptism and was heavily persecuted</term> were put to death in this country this year on account of their religion. In this manner, in Antwerp, one Jan Buisson, a Merchant from Lille <note>original: "Rijssel"</note> who sought to leave the Papacy, was beheaded in the prison one night between one and two o’clock <gloss>4</gloss>. In Lille, people were now being arrested for some word spoken against the Roman Church long ago or spoken without thinking; they were sentenced to the fire for it, even though they still had little knowledge of the truth and were weak in faith <gloss>5</gloss>. Thus, at this time, or at the beginning of the year fifteen hundred and sixty-one, as some believe, four men were burned. There also Jacob van Loo was burned, on the fifteenth of February <note>original: "Sprokkelmaendt"</note> of that year. A few days before his death, he exhorted the members of the oppressed congregation with letters not to abandon their meetings because of the persecution; he also urged the Teacher Guido de Bres <note>A famous Reformed theologian and author of the Belgic Confession</note> to persevere in his duty, not to depart, and not to look to those who sought safe places to remain at their ease. All of his books had been found in the Minorite <note>Franciscan</note> Monastery to be examined, and the Bible, which was printed in Geneva, was sentenced to the fire. # HISTORY #

<margin>
1561.
*Strada, Book III, p. 127.*
Two ministers captured in Valenciennes.
*Strada, p. 128. See also Nicolaus Burgundius, History, Book 5.* <note>original: "Vid. & Nic. Burgund. Hist. l. 54."</note>
</margin>
...reconciled with the Roman church: giving their reasons for doing so in print, which were refuted by others. In Valenciennes, it turned out differently. Two ministers, Philip Maillard and Simon Faveau, were captured there; however, the Marquess of Bergen <note>Jean de Glymes (1528–1567), a high-ranking nobleman who was known for his moderate stance and personal dislike of the Inquisition’s methods</note> did not have them killed immediately, but departed to visit his brother, the Bishop of Liège. When the Governess <note>Margaret of Parma, the Regent of the Netherlands acting on behalf of King Philip II of Spain</note> rebuked him for this procrastination and commanded him to return there at once and perform his duty, he dared to excuse his absence by saying; *that the prosecution of heretics was neither in accordance with his office nor his nature.* Thus seven months passed before the magistrates dared to attempt anything against the two prisoners. For the common people supported them daily. Threatening letters were sent to the Aldermen <term>Wethouderen: local judicial and administrative officials</term>, warning of what awaited them if they took any severe action against them. Indeed, at night near the prison, people had been heard shouting to the prisoners, *that they should bear themselves like men, and that they would not lack help from the people, should an attempt be made to lead them to their deaths.* 

But the Governess, informed of what was happening, finally brought it about that the ministers were sentenced to the fire. The time for carrying out the punishment was set for a Monday; for they feared the common rabble, especially the wool-workers <note>Weavers and textile workers in cities like Valenciennes were often the most fervent supporters of the early Reformed movement</note>, who were accustomed to go out of town on Saturday evenings and not return to the city until Monday: partly to enjoy themselves in the neighboring villages; partly to escape the Mass on Sundays. 

On a Monday then, early in the morning before sunrise, the prisoners were brought to the market. However, this intention could not be so hidden or rushed that the place did not fill with a gathered multitude. Coming to the pyre or wood-pile, Faveau cried out with a loud voice, with all his might: *“O Eternal Father!”* At that cry, the people began to stir, to rage, to shout, to threaten, to press forward, and to throw stones. The place of execution was overwhelmed, the wood-pile broken apart, and the instruments of death overturned; therefore the judges had to lead the prisoners back to the dungeon under a hailstorm of stones. Then the violence of the people subsided. Following this, they began to walk up and down the city in an orderly fashion, in the manner of a procession, following a precentor <term>Voorſanger: a leader of congregational singing</term>, singing Psalms in unison: but having returned again to the market, the precentor was placed on an elevated spot to preach,

Meanwhile, the crowd grew to over two thousand men, who, either through the urging of the Precentor <note>The leader of the congregational singing, often a prominent figure in Protestant 'chanteries' or singing protests</note> or because of the growth of their own numbers, became active again.

First they wanted to head toward the Dominican Monastery, but soon changed their minds. *What benefit is it,* they said, *that we have put the city in turmoil, if meanwhile our brothers—from whose necks we have kept the death-noose on the market square—perhaps have to endure death in the dungeon?* They understood that they must go there to release them while they were still alive, or to avenge them if they were dead. Instead, he departed to visit his brother, the Bishop of Liège. When the Governess <note>Margaret of Parma, the Regent of the Netherlands</note> rebuked him for this sluggishness and commanded him to return there at once to perform his duty, he dared to excuse his absence by saying: *that the carrying out of the punishment of heretics was consistent neither with his office nor his nature.* Thus, seven months passed before the Magistrates <term>Magiſtraet: the city's governing body of aldermen and judges</term> dared to undertake anything against the two prisoners. For the common people sided with them daily. The Councilmen were found to be the target of many threats regarding what awaited them if they undertook anything severe against the men. Indeed, during the night near the prison, people had been heard shouting to the prisoners, *that they should behave like men, and that they would not lack help from the people if anyone should attempt to lead them to their deaths.* But the Governess, informed of what was happening, finally brought it about that the ministers were sentenced to the fire <note>sentenced to be burned at the stake</note>. The time for carrying out the punishment was set for a Monday; for they feared the "rabble," especially the wool-workers, who were accustomed to going out into the countryside on Saturday evenings and not returning to the city until Monday—partly to enjoy themselves in the neighboring villages, and partly to avoid the Mass on Sunday. On a Monday then, early in the morning before sunrise, the prisoners were brought to the market square. Yet this plan could not be so hidden or hurried that the place did not become filled by a gathering of a great multitude of people. Coming to the pyre or woodpile, Faveau cried out with a loud voice, with all his might: *O Eternal Father.* At that cry, the people began to stir, to rage, to shout, to threaten, to push, and to throw stones. The place of execution was overwhelmed, the woodpile broken apart, and the instruments of death overturned; because of this, the Judges had to lead the prisoners back to the dungeon under a hailstorm of stones. Then the violence of the people subsided. Thereupon they began to go up and down the city in an orderly fashion, in the manner of a procession, following a Precentor <note>a leader of congregational singing</note>, singing Psalms in unison. But having returned again to the market, the Precentor was placed on an elevated spot to preach,

### OF THE REFORMATION. BOOK V.

<margin>1563.</margin>
...to be held in regard. Also, all Pastors and Chaplains shall henceforth keep a book or register of all the children they shall baptize, recording the day, the year, and the names of the children and parents. Of this, the aforementioned Pastors shall grant access to the Officers at all times within the year, if requested. And furthermore, from year to year, they shall bring that register into the hands of the Magistrates <term>Wethouderen</term><note>Local municipal officials or aldermen responsible for administration and justice.</note> of their place of residence, who are charged with having the same registered and preserved. Also, all Officers shall keep good watch, and diligently inform themselves regarding all Anabaptists <term>Herdoopers</term><note>Literally "re-baptizers"; a radical wing of the Reformation that rejected infant baptism, and who were heavily persecuted by both Catholics and other Protestants.</note> and those who hold conventicles <term>Conventiculen</term><note>Secret or unauthorized religious meetings held outside the sanctioned Catholic Church.</note>, following the placards made by Emperor Charles the Fifth. Furthermore, it is forbidden on Sundays and other holy days—at least during the High Mass and the morning sermon—to go drinking in taverns, to play with the ball or bowls, or to shoot at the target, upon penalty of twenty stivers <note>A common coin in the Low Countries; twenty stivers made up one guilder.</note> for each offense, and for the Innkeepers where the same occurs, to forfeit double that amount. Charging parents to send their children to the schools and to the church to be instructed: the poor at least on Sundays and holy days, the others at least two or three times a week, with the penalty for failure to be recovered from the parents at the discretion of the judge. Commanding the Officers not only to visit the houses of booksellers, according to the placards, but also to watch diligently that no peddlers travel with or sell any books; also to investigate whether they have them in their packs or hidden among their wares. All those who have knowledge that any forbidden gatherings or conventicles are being held anywhere shall be duty-bound to make it known to the Officer of the place; and they shall be given, for every house where a conventicle is found to be held upon their report, twenty-five Carolus guilders <note>A gold or silver coin named after Emperor Charles (Carolus) V.</note>, which shall be credited to them in their accounts. On the same day, the Duchess <note>Margaret of Parma, acting as Regent for King Philip II.</note> wrote to the Council of Holland, stating that this placard should be proclaimed, and that the placards of the twenty-fifth of September <note>original: *Herfstmaendt*, "Harvest month."</note> of the year fifteen hundred fifty, and the twentieth of August <note>original: *Oegstmaendt*, "Month of the crop."</note> of the year fifteen hundred fifty-six, be renewed; also to make it known everywhere that everyone would be required to hear Mass on Sundays and other holy days according to the order of the Roman Church. Furthermore, that measures should be strictly provided against the Magistrates of Texel, who had been negligent in upholding the previous placards. In Flanders and Brabant, the Magistrates stood [for] the Papacy...

The Duchess <note>Margaret of Parma, the Regent of the Netherlands.</note> also charged the Court of Holland to assign him several Councilors and a Secretary for his legal proceedings—not those he desired, but those the Council saw fit; furthermore, they were required to offer him the "strong hand" <note>The "strong hand" or secular arm refers to the use of civil authorities and physical force to assist the Inquisition in its duties.</note> in all his investigations. <margin>
Placard for the continuation of the persecution and inquisition in Holland published.
*Repertory of Holland Placards p. 116, 117.*
*History of Martyrs f. 383, & 384.*
</margin>
> *No inhabitant of the Netherlands shall be received in any cities or villages of Holland to live there, unless he brings proof from the Parish Priest <term>Prochiaen</term>, the Officer, and the law of his previous residence, stating that he is considered a Catholic and not infected or infamous with any heresy. He who uses false proof shall be punished by the neck <note>This implies the death penalty, usually by hanging or beheading.</note>. And the Officers shall diligently question both those who from now on shall come to live within the cities and towns, as well as those who have come there from elsewhere within the last four years, as far as any notable suspicion falls or arises against them. The aforementioned persons shall likewise be required to bring proper proof that their children are baptized according to the custom of the Roman Church. No women shall be allowed to be Midwives in Holland unless they promise by oath not to receive any children [at birth] unless they take good care that they are christened; and if they find any difficulty therein, they shall be bound by their oath to report it to the Officer. Other women, though not Midwives, shall also be required to do this when they help any children into the world; under penalty that they shall be proceeded against as is proper. Women far gone with child and giving birth outside their residences shall, upon returning home, bring proper proof from the place where they lay in labor that their children are baptized according to the custom of the Roman Church, and this under penalty of being held suspicious...*

In the midst of this struggle, which felt more agonizing to him than death, he cried to God for help, until at last faith and the hope of a better life prevailed within him. He remained steadfast and exhorted his beloved wife—when she took her leave of him with many tears at the Steen, where he was likewise drowned—that she should walk in the path of truth and raise their child, that common pledge of love, in the fear of the Almighty. ### OF THE REFORMATION. BOOK V.
Kk 3
<meta>catchword: the military-</meta>

<margin>1564. And Georgius Cassander seeks to settle the religious dispute.</margin>
Georgius Cassander <note>A Flemish theologian known for his "Via Media" or middle-way approach to reconciling Catholics and Protestants.</note> could be employed in this same matter with great benefit. This Cassander was born in Flanders; such was the brilliance of his piety, moderation, and learning, that the Emperors Ferdinand and Maximilian earnestly sought his help to heal the grievous wounds of Christendom. Specifically, these men, viewing much of the old way as superstition and much of the new as presumption, and seeing schism sprouting from schism, wished to steer a middle course, marking the path of truth using fundamental principles alone.

<margin>Their objective. Hooft p. 46.</margin>
But amid the differences of belief, and the disputing and hair-splitting of every point, many tender or unstable minds became entirely lost in the matter, so that they fell into endless and wretched brooding, and even despair.

<margin>Difficulties arising from the disputing of articles of faith. Hooft I. 38.</margin>
Others, who were naturally more light-hearted, seeing so many arguments from various sides hanging in the balance, hastily judged that they differed little in weight and were worth very little in total. This gave birth to a disregard for piety and conscience, leading people to take up a reckless and lawless life.

<margin>The King insists on the eradication of the so-called heretics. Hooft I. 38. * Book IV. 170.</margin>
The King, meanwhile, commanded the Governess <note>Margaret of Parma, the Regent of the Netherlands.</note> by letter after letter to root out the heretics; he devoted his thoughts so heavily to this that he seemed to forget all other cares, and even the proper dignity of his royalty. The Jesuit Famianus Strada relates how the King, in writings by his own hand, instructed her on the manner of overtaking the so-called heretics; he essentially pointed out the trail to them and their nesting places, even preparing and sending lists on which they were described, including details of each person's neighborhood, status, age, and physical appearance.

<margin>Points out the means to track them down.</margin>
The Duchess was also personally zealous in this matter, and was well-followed at this time by most of the Governors <term>Stadtholders</term> <note>Provincial administrators who represented the King.</note> of the other provinces, who now felt obliged to every service following the dismissal of Granvelle <note>Cardinal Granvelle, whose heavy-handedness had previously caused great resentment among the Dutch nobility.</note>. Yet the punishment or persecution of heretics did not always have a predictable result.

<margin>A prisoner Priest sets fire to the Castle at Rupelmonde. Strada IV. 171. from the Governor's letters to the King.</margin>
At Rupelmonde, a Priest was imprisoned who had defected from the Papacy. Seeing no other way out, he decided to set fire to the adjacent room where the ancient charters and records of the land were kept, hoping to take flight in the confusion while the soldiers sought to extinguish the fire. Having discussed this plan with his fellow prisoners, nine in number, he lit the fire; the castle caught fire, but the flames were immediately [contained] by a sudden gathering and the diligence of—

The military quelled the disturbance, and the arsonists were captured in their flight and punished shortly thereafter; however, the priest was executed with the sword because he returned to Popery and renounced—even cursed—the Reformed view. But in Antwerp, there was more unrest surrounding the burning of Christopher Smit, or Fabricius, who proved more steadfast. He had been a Carmelite monk in Bruges, his city of birth, but had later left the monastery and the Papacy, married a lawful wife, and resided for some time in England. However, being called back to his fatherland by his fellow believers, he allowed himself to be employed in the ministry among the Reformed in Antwerp. In this service, he conducted himself very edifyingly for about six months, until a certain deceitful woman named Long Margaret, a bonnet-seller who pretended to desire further instruction in matters of religion, craftily betrayed him on the second of July <note>Original: "Hooimaendt," the traditional Dutch name for the "hay month."</note>; and with him Olivier de Bok of Aalst, a professor of the Latin language at Heidelberg, who had come here at this time to attend to his private affairs. The following day, he was thrown upon the rack and questioned regarding his office, his marriage, his fellow ministers, and the location and management of secret meetings. He refused to implicate anyone, but confessed his own faith and that which he had preached. Thereafter followed the struggle with the clergy, who fell upon him very harshly. They also sought to interrogate his fellow prisoner in the same manner, but he refused to answer them, always appealing to the Elector Palatine <note>The ruler of the Palatinate in Germany, a major supporter of the Reformation.</note> as his sovereign lord. The Elector, by sending a messenger with letters to the Court in Brussels, successfully brought about his release from prison on the first of September. But Fabricius found, and sought, no way out but death. Furthermore, having been sentenced to the fire, he bore the cross of his oppression with an unimaginable and incomprehensible courage, patience, gentleness, resignation, and serenity. He comforted, strengthened, and encouraged both friends and strangers toward the good through various letters written from prison shortly before his death; even writing to Long Margaret, who had betrayed him, forgiving her and exhorting her to repentance.

The people gather by night before the Steen and sing Psalms.
</margin>

They also spent the entire night there singing Psalms and spiritual songs...

<margin>1564.</margin>to sing, until the morning. The following day, the fourth of October <note>Original: "Wijnmaendt," the "wine month."</note>, as he was being led to his death, he saw that the people, rushing in from all sides, were greatly agitated. Fearing a riot, he addressed them with these words: *“My dear brothers, let no one step forward to rescue me. Some then called out: *“Fight bravely, dear brother, for this is the hour.”*

<margin>Fabricius seeks to prevent a riot.</margin>The Margrave <note>The "Markgraef" was the chief magistrate and military governor of the city.</note>, hearing this, cried out to his henchmen: *“Seize, strike, kill!”* and threatened to shoot. Having arrived at the market, Christopher knelt by the woodpile to pray to God in that final extremity; but he was immediately dragged to the faggots and pressed against the stake, where the executioner fastened him with an iron chain and also threw a noose around his neck to prevent both prayer and speech.

<margin>He is chained to the stake. Before he retreated, the Margrave was heard to cry: *“O Citizens, stand by us! Guards, stand by us! See what you do, this is the King’s justice!”* But no one moved a foot for him or stretched out a hand. The people were left to their own devices.

<margin>They seek to rescue the Preacher in vain.</margin>Some jumped into the enclosure to rescue the Preacher, cleared away the faggots, and pulled the chain loose, but it was too late. For the executioner, before he fled, had struck him in the head with an iron hammer and stabbed him from behind with a dagger. Thus they let the fire, which had already been lit, burn; and the man was seen (for it burned very slowly) even though he was so mortally wounded, to remain alive for a long time, moving his head, opening and closing his mouth, lips, and hands, until at last, falling into the fire, he gave up the ghost.

<margin>His painful end.</margin>Nevertheless, that martyred and terribly disfigured corpse remained lying there for eight hours after the fire was extinguished, a pitiful spectacle for friends and enemies alike. Then, at last, it was bound to a large stone and sunk into the Scheldt <note>The primary river flowing through Antwerp.</note>. Such was the end of Christopher Fabricius.

# HISTORY

<margin>1561. <note>original: "MDLXI." Master Marten Pieterssoon, Pastor of the Great Church—a very fitting man, also kind and peaceful toward people of other persuasions—had passed away on the first of February <note>original: "Sprokkelmaendt," an old Dutch name for February</note>; and now they sought to bring Clement Maertssoon, who also had a reputation for courtesy and moderation, into his place. Yet a greater and stronger impulse toward more moderation in matters of Religion came from a higher authority. Several lords of the Council of State <note>The main advisory body to the Spanish governor of the Netherlands</note>—among whom Orange, Egmond, and Hoorn were the most prominent—having gained more authority since the departure of Granvelle, sought on every occasion, great and small, to emphasize: *That it seemed impossible to them to root out, through sword and fire, so great a number of heretics as was seen growing there; rather, something else was required, namely the moral reform of the clergy and the good instruction of the congregation.*

*Velius, page 162.*
Several Lords of the Council of State lean toward moderation in the matter of Religion.
*Hooft, Book II, page 48.*

Stepping somewhat further after this, they confessed: *That, even if the people of the church devoted themselves to a more edifying life, and the people were drawn by more capable teaching, the edicts <note>The "plakkaeten" or "placards": harsh royal decrees that mandated the death penalty for heresy</note> should nonetheless be abolished, or softened and adjusted for the times, which could in no way endure such severity.* And gradually, opening themselves further, they let it be heard that if one allowed everyone freedom of conscience within their own home, without giving public offense; and if, in addition, one distributed both the wine and the bread in the Lord’s Supper, then the difficulties would be seen to vanish, and not otherwise. Indeed, in a certain meeting of the Council of State at the end of the year, called by the Duchess <note>Margaret of Parma, the Governor of the Netherlands</note> to deliberate over the country's troubles, the Prince of Orange spoke even more clearly, saying among other things (after it was deemed good to send the Count of Egmond to Spain to analyze the state of affairs for the King; and because President Viglius wanted to draft his instructions in general terms): that one must speak openly, without feigning any longer: *that because Religion, among all the neighbors of these lands, was in such great change and movement, it was entirely impossible here to maintain the religion in its old state through the means of the edicts, Inquisitors, and Bishops (the morals of the clergy being also so very corrupt). And that one must tell the King this clearly and plainly. Also, that the King greatly deceived himself if he thought to enforce the Decrees of the Council of Trent in these lands, so close to Germany...*

<meta>This page continues the report of the Council of State meetings in late 1564, specifically focusing on the Prince of Orange's influential speech regarding religious freedom and the subsequent physical collapse of the conservative President Viglius. ## HISTORY OF THE REFORMATION. BOOK V.

<margin>1564.</margin>
...situated, where all the Princes (not only the Protestants, but also the Catholics) rejected and spoke against those <note>The decrees of the Council of Trent</note> with many reasons. Therefore, the King would do better to turn a blind eye (as those Princes did) and remove the punishments of the <term>edicts<gloss>The "plakkaten": harsh royal decrees that mandated the death penalty for heresy</gloss></term>, or at least moderate them. And although he [the Prince], as he said, had intended to remain within the Catholic Religion, nonetheless he could not approve that Princes should want to command the spirits of men, and take from them the freedom of faith and Religion. The Prince spoke this with such power and passion of words that he extended his speech until seven o'clock in the evening, in such a manner that the Duchess <note>Margaret of Parma, the Regent</note>, wishing to go to dinner, postponed the matter until the following day.

<margin>Viglius is greatly upset.</margin>
But President Viglius, having returned to his house and being greatly upset by the speech of the Prince, slept almost not at all that entire night; without ceasing, he turned over in his mind what he should answer the next day. 1565.
The King consults with his theologians regarding the liberty sought by the Netherlanders.

...to depart, he summoned some of the most prominent Spanish theologians to advise him. He asked them what they felt regarding the freedom of religion, which several cities in the Netherlands so earnestly desired from him. However, most of them, seeing the condition of these provinces and holding that the King—in order to prevent a greater evil which was surely to be feared (namely, the rebellion of the cities and the injury to the Sovereign’s authority, to the detriment of the <term>Orthodox Church<gloss>The Roman Catholic Church, as seen from the perspective of the Spanish Crown</gloss></term>)—might permit the people some freedom of worship without sinning against God. But the King declared that he had not called them to him to learn from them whether he *might* permit it, but to know whether they understood that he *must* necessarily do so. And when they assured him that, in their opinion, there was no such necessity, he (as Strada writes from the mouth of one who was present) knelt upon the earth before a crucifix in their presence and was heard to say: *“But I, O God and King of all things, pray and beseech your divine Majesty, let me always keep this mind: that I never permit myself to be Lord, or to be called such, over those who have rejected you, Lord.”* Afterward, the Envoy of the Netherlands <note>The Count of Egmond</note> was sent away with a written answer to all that he had been charged to propose, without the King being willing to yield anything in the matter of Religion, even though Egmond had allowed himself to believe otherwise. During the Count's journey and stay in Spain, the <term>placards<gloss>plakkaeten: Royal edicts or decrees carrying the force of law, often prescribing the death penalty for heresy</gloss></term> regarding heresy were strictly enforced in Flanders. Joost de Creul was executed by the sword on the tenth of <term>February<gloss>Sprokkelmaendt: An archaic Dutch name for the month of February</gloss></term> at Ronse, on account of the Reformed Religion, which he had previously renounced out of fear of death during a prior imprisonment. Some say that the sermons of the Dean of Ronse, Petrus Titelman, had given him and others their first introduction to the teachings of the Reformation some years before; and now that same Dean was the strictest persecutor and <term>Inquisitor<gloss>A church official appointed to investigate and suppress heresy</gloss></term>, by whose inquisition people were condemned to death for a belief they had learned from him. On the twenty-first of the same month, Jan Disreneaux, a man of seventy years, gave his life for the sake of religion at <term>Lille<gloss>Rijffel: The Dutch name for the city of Lille in modern-day France</gloss></term> in the fire, or rather in the smoke, which some witnesses say stifled him before the fire was properly lit. Others write that this occurred in the following year. Jan de Graef

<margin>1565. Jan de Graef of Hulst: History of the Martyrs, folio 647 b. History of the Martyrs, folio 402.</margin>Jan de Graef of Ekkergem, formerly a miller at Heynsdijk in the District of Hulst, was strangled and burned at Hulst on the twenty-seventh <note>The month is not explicitly named here but is likely March (Lent-month), based on the surrounding context and the mention of extreme winter cold</note>, with the New Testament hung around his neck. In order to pull him away from the beliefs he had "sucked" from that book and bring him back to the Papacy, the clergy had gathered all manner of cunning tricks, heavy temptations, and other forms of force. During his imprisonment, which lasted over three months, he was tormented with hunger and thirst, being denied necessities; he was also tortured by being kept from the fire during an unendurable cold, for it was a very severe winter with hard frosts at that time <margin>* Bor, book 21, page b. D. Velius, Chronicle of Hoorn, page 159.</margin>*. Consequently, because the toes of his feet were almost entirely frozen off, he went to his death limping, yet not hesitating <note>The original Dutch contains a play on words: "hinkende" (limping) and "schoorvoetende" (shuffling or hesitating), emphasizing that despite his physical injury, he did not falter in spirit</note>, but went courageously. He exhorted the bystanders that, if the knowledge of the truth had come to them, they should remain steadfast in it and despise the world, which was not to be compared to the coming blessedness. Afterward, he called upon God in his distress, even praying for his persecutors. It is also recounted that it was very difficult to obtain wood and straw to burn him, for the citizens refused to sell materials for that purpose.

<margin>H. Destailleur and J. Pik at Tournai. History of the Martyrs, folio 627. History of the Martyrs, folio 408.</margin>In Tournai lived two young men, Hugo Destailleur and Jan Pik, who in their youth (the first was about twenty-two, the other eighteen or nineteen years old) had become great friends through a similarity of intellect, mind, character, and purpose, as well as in matters of religion; for they had both joined the secret congregation of the <term>Reformed<gloss>Protestants who followed the teachings of John Calvin, often meeting in secret to avoid persecution</gloss></term>. On the twentieth of August <note>original: "Oegstmaendt"</note> of the previous year, while they were outside the city contemplating a certain passage of Scripture, they were caught and imprisoned. Since then, bound even more closely by adversity, they bore the same chains with equal patience; until, on the twenty-second of March <note>original: "Lentemaendt"</note> of this year, having defended their confession with similar arguments, they were more perfectly united by a similar death, which they suffered with equal courage, being strangled together and burned in a single fire.

He cried out that a good method had now been found to discover the heretics. <margin>1565.</margin>
Around the twenty-fifth of May <note>Original: "Bloeimaendt," an old Dutch name for May</note>, six theologians <term>Godtgeleerden: experts in divinity and church law</term>, alongside the Presidents of Flanders and Utrecht and three councilors of the High Court of Mechelen, were summoned to Brussels. and although the Governess <note>Margaret of Parma, who ruled the Netherlands for Philip II</note>, together with the Prince of Orange and the Counts of Egmond and Hoorn, even leaned toward moderation, the Clergy were of another mind and said: *That His Majesty’s <note>King Philip II of Spain</note> writings gave no shadow of such doubts. Furthermore, he who thought to gain anything from the heretics through laxity or a change in punishment was greatly mistaken. Rather, the way to overcome them was to tackle the matter head-on with full force.* Further, the opinion of the summoned Theologians regarding the instruction of the congregation, the Reformation of the clergy, the education of the youth, and the change of the punishment for heretics, was set down in writing and signed by all those summoned on the seventh of July <note>Original: "Hooimaendt," an old Dutch name for July</note>, resulting in this: <margin>The proceedings of some theologians. *Hooft p. 52.*</margin> <margin>Their opinion on the matter of some Reformation in the church, and the changing of the punishment of heretics. *Hooft, p. 53.*</margin> *First, that regarding the instruction of the congregation, very good provision had been made by the Council of Trent <note>A major council of the Catholic Church held between 1545 and 1563 to address the challenges of the Protestant Reformation</note>. Concerning the moral reform of the people of the church; this too was well provided for by the decrees of the Council, where they spoke of the simplicity of ecclesiastical offices, not remaining away from their assigned places of calling, and similar matters; so that nothing was lacking there, except to follow through. The schools and the instruction of the youth were also so well regulated by the same Council that it only came down to compliance. Regarding the changing of the punishments, it was argued that the edicts <term>plakkaeten: official decrees or laws issued by the sovereign, often posted in public places</term>, made regarding the matter of faith and the rooting out of heresies—which had already been renewed twice over thirty-five years and steadily maintained—could suffer no change whatsoever. Nevertheless, to prevent offense and riot, and also to move reluctant Judges to execute the edicts, one might, by secret instruction, grant the Provincial Councils the freedom that, while punishing obstinate heretics with death, they might make a distinction between the sects as well as the persons, according to their status and age; in such a manner that, according to the evidence of the law, one would be handled more harshly and another more gently, and at times someone, instead of dying, would be sent to the galleys or perpetually banished from the land with forfeiture of goods. The penitent could be shown mercy with perpetual or temporary banishment, according to the circumstances of the case and the merit of the criminals: except for the Teachers, the relapsed, and the rebellious, who must not be spared from the punishment of the stubborn. Furthermore, those who, without being tainted by heresy, violated the edicts out of curiosity, negligence, or otherwise, had to atone with flogging, fines, banishment, and the like. Finally, it was necessary above all things, with pilgrimages*

Once this became known, it caused various speculations and emotional disturbances. Others foresaw that the Council—held in a place where the Lutherans and Reformed <note>The followers of Calvin</note> claimed they had no safe access—would be rejected by them as biased, since they had been condemned unheard, making them all the more averse to the Church. The general Inquisitors of Leuven, on the other hand, being offended that they were (as they believed) not yet held in enough respect, and that too little was done to please them, wrote to the <term>Governess: Margaret of Parma, the King's regent in the Netherlands</term> to be relieved of their office, as it no longer served any purpose. In this state of affairs came the King's answer to the advice offered by the council on the seventh of July <note>Original: 'Hooimaendt,' the traditional Dutch name for July</note>, and also regarding the anger of the Count of Egmond over the execution of the <term>Anabaptists: 'Doopsgezinden,' a radical Reformation group practicing adult baptism</term>. <margin>
1566.
Complaint of those of Flanders regarding the Inquisitor P. Titelman.
*Wesenb. p. 88... Bor f. 28. b...*
</margin>
...[he] had never shown his <note>original: "last", meaning his official commission or mandate</note> and daily presumed to act to the detriment of the country’s ancient liberties and customs, causing such persons as he saw fit to be arrested without a legal inquiry; even dragging them from their houses and conducting house searches without the knowledge of the <term>Magistrates: the "Wethouderen," local judicial and administrative officials</term>, taking only the <term>Bailiffs: "Baljuwen," administrative officials</term> and <term>Sheriffs: "Schouten," law enforcement officers</term> to his aid, who in various places dared not refuse him assistance for fear of being suspected or accused by him. They found this situation to be of such consequence that, if they allowed it to continue unremarked any longer without informing His Majesty, and permitted the Inquisitor to employ such absurd and intolerable innovations, it was feared that the common people might find cause to riot and also rise up against the court, whereby the land would be in danger of being lost.

<margin>
Their request.
</margin>
Therefore, they humbly prayed that the King, seeing what was written before—and especially the great and faithful services always willingly performed by those of Flanders—would be pleased to let them enjoy the aforementioned ancient liberties, and to strengthen and maintain them therein, just as he had sworn to do, both specifically and generally, upon his arrival and acceptance of the land, and as his noble ancestors had always kept inviolable: forbidding the Inquisitor and other ecclesiastical persons from using such innovations and unlawful means of inquiry any further.

<margin>
Answer of the Regent.

->HISTORY<-

<margin>1566.</margin> The King's command—concerning the implementation of the Council of Trent <note>A series of church councils that defined Catholic counter-reformation doctrine</note> and the Inquisition, as well as the appointment of such deputies from the Council without the consent of the <term>Estates: the "Staeten," the representative assembly of the provinces</term>—was not only a strike against the sovereignty of the Lord and the liberties of the land, but was also perceived as a way to turn that flourishing and populous region into a wilderness. Therefore, they requested that this disaster be averted by the revocation of the orders. They also stated and asserted that Brabant had never been tormented by the Inquisition, nor was it ever subject to it.

<margin>They say that Brabant is not subject to the Inquisition. Hooft, p. 69; Wesenbeeck, p. 69.</margin> Attempts were made to convince them that the King meant nothing but the best. They turned to the Governess <note>Margaret of Parma, the Regent of the Netherlands</note>. She saw fit to have herself further informed on the matter and to learn from the Inquisitors of Leuven themselves what truth there was to this claim of liberty.

<margin>The Council of Brabant and the Council of State also judge this. Hooft, p. 69.</margin> But the Council of Brabant, being pressed to reveal their understanding of the Inquisitors' opinion, finally stated plainly that the people of this province were not obliged to endure the Inquisition. This was also the judgment of the most prominent lords of the Council of State.

<margin>Trouble at 's-Hertogenbosch. Wesenbeeck, p. 50; Bor I. 26.</margin> At 's-Hertogenbosch, matters almost came to a riot because the <term>Sheriff: "Schout," a local judicial officer</term>, along with several others, wished to proclaim the aforementioned decree despite the opposition of the majority of the law and the community. However, everything here was still calmed with tact and good fortune, and the proclamation was left undone.

<margin>Wesenbeeck, p. 49.</margin> In various cities, the <term>Magistrates: "Wethouders"</term> had enough to do simply keeping the community from rioting, holding them off with encouraging words in the hope that the deputies of the four main cities would succeed in having the aforementioned letters withdrawn.

<margin>Hooft, p. 70.</margin> Elsewhere, the courage of the multitude now overflowed with impatience, driving some to such boldness that they used force to drag certain people, who had been imprisoned for their faith, out of custody.

<margin>Bor f. 29. b. Wesenbeeck, p. 53.</margin> Thus, in Antwerp on the twenty-sixth of <term>January: "Loumaendt," an old Dutch name for the month meaning "tanning month"</term> during the night, two young noble daughters, sisters, were helped to escape from the <term>Steen: a medieval fortress in Antwerp used as a prison</term> along with a watchmaker. Everywhere, people made increasingly great efforts to release the prisoners, since it was now known how people were being put to death in secret. Because they did not dare lead the condemned to death in public, this new kind of punishment had been devised: the wretched people were bound with their heads between their knees, submerged in a vat full of water, and gradually suffocated.

<margin>Thuanus XXXIX 488; Meteren l. 33. <margin>

</margin>
...all the household: to demand proof of residency for outsiders from the Pastor of their last places of dwelling: to demand a declaration and testimony from married couples from the Priest who married them, in order to know if they were married according to the customs of the Roman Church: to record the names and residences of those who come to them for confession, and of the children they shall baptize, as well as the names of their Father, Mother, Godfathers, and Godmothers; also of those whom they shall marry. Regarding the Schoolmasters, the Bishop of Bruges shall summon them before him and, after investigating the matter, either permit or forbid them from keeping school. The Pastors shall also be charged to conduct a diligent inquiry and <term>inquisition: here meaning a formal investigation or search</term> to determine if all those living on alms <note>Poor relief or charity provided by the church or city</note> are Catholic, attending confession and taking the sacrament at high festivals; and if they find any who do not do so, they shall then command the <term>poor-masters: "armmeesteren," officials in charge of distributing local charity</term> to provide such persons no further support; and these officials shall be bound to obey the Pastors. He desired that the <term>Law: "de Wet," referring to the local secular magistrates and city council</term> would assist him in carrying out these points. But when objections were raised, as they did not wish to subject secular citizens to the Bishop, the Inquisitor turned—both in his own name and that of the Bishop—to the Council of Flanders, complaining loudly against the Magistrates of Bruges and accusing them of various failings, requesting that they grant the following articles:

*First, That the Sheriff, the Burgomaster of the nations, the Lieutenant, the Beadles, and all other officials, immediately and without any delay when requested, shall be bound to provide assistance in making arrests—indeed, they must personally arrest those pointed out to them. Furthermore, that the imprisonment shall take place without the Law taking any information or stripping the citizenship of those they wish to catch <term>ontpoorteren: the legal process of revoking a person's rights as a "poorter" or citizen of the city</term>, as the arrest is often delayed and missed because of such procedures. That the prisoners shall be handed over immediately to the prisons of the ecclesiastical Court, or elsewhere as the Inquisitor desires, and leave him to deal with them there. That the aforementioned Lieutenant, other officials, and servants shall, in general, be charged once and for all to provide the aforementioned assistance everywhere, without needing to run to the Burgomaster or the Magistrates for permission and orders every time, by which many legal actions are missed, and the criminals* <note>The page ends mid-sentence; the word "criminals" likely continues as "criminals escape" or "criminals are warned."</note>

Bor ibid.</margin> to draw all their legal authority <margin>* Jurisdiction.</margin> to himself, just as he had recently caused a certain person in the land of Cadzand to be sought, breaking into his house with violence, notwithstanding that he had satisfied the sentence of the secular Judge, and having overtaken him, had him seized by his Sergeants and dragged through the streets. Which manner of proceeding, they said, could be held for nothing but extreme severity. Which, along with his other actions, made them fear that if matters remained in such a state, none of the inhabitants of the land, however pious a Catholic he might be...

### THE HISTORY OF THE REFORMATION, BOOK V. ###

->Nn 2<-

<margin>1566. <note>original: "MDLXVI"</note></margin>
...he was considered a Lutheran. Furthermore, it is written of thirty-two individuals who had recently been imprisoned for the sake of Religion; of whom twelve were burned, and twenty recanted their faith, though as soon as they were free and out of danger, they confessed it again.

<margin>Lieven de Bleker killed at Oudenaerde. *Hist. des Mart. f. 650... Hist der Mart f. 409...* <note>Citations from the "History of Martyrs," a common Protestant chronicle of the era.</note></margin>
Lieven de Bleker, a painter from Pamele, near Oudenaerde, having accepted the Reformed Religion and changed from a dissolute to a modest, temperate, and sober life, was betrayed by his own wife and mother-in-law. He was denounced as a heretic by the Dean of Ronse and delivered to the secular court, but was forcibly rescued from the magistrates by the common people. However, settling himself as best he could and crying out, *“Let the Magistrate deal with me,”* <note>Showing his submission to civil authority even unto death.</note> he was seized again, strangled, and burned.

<margin>(In January.)</margin>
This occurred not without great grumbling among the people, for when he was led across the market to his death, men and women called out loudly from doors and windows: *“Lieven, stay firm in your faith, fight bravely; for the truth is on your side.”* These were the fruits of the zeal of the Inquisitor Titelman, <note>Pieter Titelman was a notorious and energetic inquisitor in Flanders.</note> who caused so many complaints.

<margin>Those of Friesland complain about the Inquisitor W. Lindanus. *Bor I. 30.*</margin>
Regarding the Inquisitor Willem Lindanus <note>William Damasus Lindanus, later the first Bishop of Roermond.</note> and his actions against the country's liberties, heavy complaints were also made by the States of Friesland. They requested that someone else be appointed in his place, but in vain. Consequently, he became bolder and more indiscreet by the day; indeed, he forgot himself so far that once, when reprimanded in the full Council for his misconduct, he replied: *That he knew what his charge was and what he had to do, without being willing to show his warrant;* <note>Original: "zijn last" (his commission or mandate).</note> also saying *that those of the Court granted too much to the heretics and were far too weak in punishing them.* But this had happened earlier. At this time, however, to further stir up the aversion toward the Roman Church and the Inquisition, a multitude of lampoons and satirical writings appeared.

<margin>*P. Hooft II. 70. Bor. I. 30. b. Wesenb. p. 54.*</margin>
Books defending the Reformed view and inciting the people against the persecution flew through the entire land.

<margin>The Confession of the Reformed is printed again. *Hooft II. 70. Bor I. 30. b...*</margin>
Among others, the Confession of Faith, which the Reformed had published in the year fifteen hundred sixty-three, and which had now been revised by order of a Synod held in Antwerp at the beginning of May <note>Original: "Bloeimaendt" (the month of flowers/May).</note> (as mentioned above), was printed anew. It included a letter to the King of Spain <note>King Philip II of Spain.</note> containing: *A testimony before God and his Angels that they intended no rebellion, and desired nothing else but to live in obedience—*

### HISTORY ###

<margin>
1566. <note>original: "M D L X V I"</note>
Their letter to the King, in which they make known their objective and excuse themselves. See the confession printed at Leiden by Jan Paedts in the year 1609, p. 3.
</margin>

*...[submission] to the Authorities to live in purity of conscience, to serve God, and to reform themselves according to His Word and holy commandments. That none among them had ever refused the tax or toll imposed upon him: that they were never found bearing arms or plotting against their Sovereign Lord. The banishments, imprisonments, racks, exiles, tortures, and other countless oppressions prove well, they said, that our desire and disposition are not fleshly, since we could be much more comfortable according to the flesh without professing and maintaining this doctrine. But having the fear of God before our eyes, terrified by the threat of Jesus Christ, who says there that He will deny us before God His Father if we deny Him before men, we offer our backs to the blows, our tongues to the knives, our mouths to the gags* <note>original: "breidelstokken" — iron or wooden bits used to silence martyrs so they could not speak to the crowds at the execution pyre</note>*, and our entire body to the fire: knowing that whoever will follow Christ must take up his cross and deny himself. And never will a well-ordered mind, not blinded or deprived of senses, be able to think that those who labor to stir up everything are those who leave their country, their kin, and friends to live in peace and quiet; that those stand to take the crown from the King, or undertake anything deceitful against him, who die for the Gospel, in which they see written:* <margin>Matthew 22:21.</margin> *Render unto Caesar that which is Caesar’s, and unto God that which is God’s. Whereby, offering and surrendering their lives and property to the King,* <margin>Also requesting freedom of religion.</margin> *they humbly prayed His Majesty that they might be permitted to give to God what He demands. Further assuring him that it was not because of their small number that they did not rise up against him, but that there were more than a hundred thousand men in his Netherlands holding and following the Religion of which they now delivered the Confession to him. Yet, no preparation for rebellion was seen in any of them; indeed, not a word tending toward such was heard. That they told him of the great number of their brethren was not to frighten the least of his Officers and servants, but as much to refute the slanderous lies as to move him to mercy. Alas, they added, if you stretch out your arm to soak and wash it in the blood of so many people, O God, what destruction will you cause among your subjects? They also requested that he would judge them according to the Confession of Faith* <note>The "Belgic Confession" of 1561, a foundational document for the Dutch Reformed Church</note>*, which they offered him. Through this, they hoped, he would acknowledge that they were wrongly called schismatics and heretics; since they confessed not only the principal points of the Christian Faith, contained in the Creed* <note>original: "Symbolum" — referring to the Apostles' Creed</note>*, and common faith, but the entire doctrine—*

<margin>
Were fully 100,000 men strong.
</margin>

### OF THE REFORMATION. BOOK V. ###

->Nn 3<-

<meta>catchword: may</meta>

[who] may <note>The text continues from the previous page's thought on those who might "undertake anything deceitful."</note> be revealed through Jesus Christ for our life, righteousness, and salvation; proclaimed by the Evangelists and Apostles; sealed by the blood of so many Martyrs; and kept pure and whole in the early churches, until it was corrupted through the ignorance, greed, and ambition of the Preachers, and by human inventions and institutions. Finally, they showed that the person who carries the word of truth in his mouth is not rebellious simply because men set themselves against it. On the contrary, rebellion and scandal must be attributed to the irreconcilable Enemy of God and men, the Devil. In order not to lose his kingdom—which consists of idolatry, false religions, fornications, and other countless vices that are cut away by the Gospel—he stirs and raises himself up to hinder its course. They also noted the ingratitude of the world, which instead of receiving the word of its Master, Shepherd, and God with thanksgiving, sets itself against it, bringing forth no other reasons than the length of time <margin>† Prescription. <note>original: "Prescriptie" — a legal term meaning a right or custom established by very long-term use.</note></margin> that it has lived in its error. Thus, it wishes to resist, through the precedent of time, Him who made the world and the ages, and before whom all things are present. The conclusion contained these words: *It belongs to you, most gracious Lord, it belongs to you to have knowledge of these matters, in order to set yourself against the errors, however deeply rooted they may be through the length of time, and to protect the innocence of those who until now have been more oppressed than heard in court.* Behind the Confession was added a Remonstrance <note>original: "Vertoog" — a formal statement of grievances or a petition.</note> to the Authorities of the Netherlands, in which the petitioners said, among other things: *That they had prayed to the King to judge their cause, not according to the reports of the accusations of their adversaries, but according to their Confession. This they also desired from you, his Governors,* <note>original: "Stadthouderen"</note> *praying you to restrain a little your mindless, cruel zeal. O pious and highly esteemed Lords,* they said, *will you listen with such patience to those who say that light is darkness and darkness is light? How long will you deny the innocent sinner a hearing, and not set yourselves against the violence of his adversaries, who simultaneously accuse and condemn him, merely making you the executors and ministers of the censures, opinions, and views of the Monks, Priests, Beneficiaries, Scholastics, and Doctors, whom the primary distinction concerns in this same matter and the errors over which there is dispute. Shall it be for eternity that they shall regard you as secular and unordained or unholy people, so that you shall not*

<margin>
There were indeed 100,000 men strong.
</margin>
That they spoke to him of the great number of their brothers was not intended to frighten even the least of his officers and servants, but rather to refute slanderous lies and to move him to mercy. "Alas," they added, "if you stretch out your arm to soak and wash it in the blood of so many people, O God, what destruction will you cause among your subjects?" They also requested that he would judge them according to the Confession of Faith which they offered him. Through this, they hoped he would recognize that they were unjustly called schismatics and heretics; since they confessed not only the principal points of the Christian Faith, contained in the Creed <note>original: "Symbolum" — referring to the Apostles' Creed</note> and the common faith, but the whole teaching...

### OF THE REFORMATION. BOOK V. ###

[...revealed] through *Jesus Christ* <note>original: "Jesum Christum"</note> for our life, righteousness, and salvation; proclaimed by the Evangelists and Apostles; sealed by the blood of so many Martyrs; purely and entirely preserved in the early churches, until it was corrupted by the ignorance, greed, and ambition of the Ministers, through human inventions and institutions. Finally, they showed that those who carry the word of truth in their mouths are not rebellious simply because people oppose them; rather, the rebellion and the offense must be attributed to the irreconcilable Enemy of God and man, the Devil. In order not to lose his kingdom—which consists of idolatry, false religions, fornications, and other countless flaws that are cut away by the Gospel <note>original: "Euangelium"</note>—he stirs and rouses himself to hinder its course. They also blamed the ingratitude of the world, which instead of receiving the word of its Master, Shepherd, and God with thanksgiving, sets itself against it. The world brings forth no other reason for this than the long passage of time in which it has lived in its error: wishing to resist Him who made the world and the ages, and before whom all things are present, by claiming a "prescription" <gloss>† precedent</gloss> <note>The term "prescription" here refers to the legal concept of *praescriptio temporis*, where a custom is argued to be valid simply because it has existed for a long time.</note> of time. The conclusion contained these words: *It belongs to you, most gracious Lord, it belongs to you to have knowledge of these matters, in order to set yourself against the errors, however deeply rooted they may be through the passage of time: and to protect the innocence of those who until now have been more oppressed than heard in the court of justice.* Behind the Confession <note>The Belgic Confession of Faith</note> was added a Remonstrance <note>A formal statement of grievances and a petition for redress</note> to the Authorities of the Netherlands, in which the petitioners said, among other things: *That they had prayed to the King to judge their cause, not according to the reports of the accusations of their adversaries, but according to their Confession.* They desired this also from them, his Governors <note>original: "Stadthouderen"</note>, praying them to pause a little in their senseless, cruel zeal. *O pious and highly esteemed Lords,* they said, *will you listen with such patience to those who say that light is darkness and darkness is light? How long will you deny a hearing to the innocent sinner, and not set yourself against the violence of his adversaries, who simultaneously accuse and condemn him? They make you merely the Executors and ministers of the Censures, the esteem, and the opinions of the Monks, Priests <note>original: "Paepen," a derogatory term for Catholic clergy</note>, Beneficiaries, Scholastics <note>Theologians and teachers of the traditional church schools</note>, and Doctors, who are the primary parties in this same matter and the errors under dispute. Shall it be forever that they regard you as worldly and unconsecrated or unholy people, so that you shall not...*

# H I S T O R Y #
<meta>catchword: a</meta>

<margin>1566. <note>original: "MDLXVI."</note></margin>
<margin>What most of the ancient Teachers felt about the coercion of conscience.</margin>
[...are we permitted to] speak of the Scriptures, nor judge the doctrines and matters of Religion? *Most of the ancient Teachers have considered that the Government is not permitted to touch consciences, to violate and force them to believe, since the steel sword <note>The "steel sword" refers to the secular power of the state to punish physical crimes, as opposed to spiritual matters.</note> has been given into their hands to punish robbers, thieves, murderers, and others who disturb this human government. But concerning Religion, and that which belongs to the soul, only the spiritual sword of the word of God must and may diligently remedy this; separating the zeal and Religion that someone protects from the sedition and disturbance of the government.* But in this matter, we are content not to follow or believe these good Teachers. <margin>The Reformed are of a different mind.</margin> We confess that the Government must have knowledge of heresies (*which we admit are disturbances among the common people*) so far that under this cover innocence is not oppressed through the mere accusation of its enemies, without being heard and understood; but that the Government should think on what the Wise Man says: <margin>Prov. 17:15.</margin> *He who justifies the wicked, and he who condemns the just, both are an abomination to the Lord.* Whereby it is necessary that the Judge acknowledge within himself, and be assured of the unrighteousness and heresy, overcome by the word of God, before he stretches out his hand to attack the accused. Finally, they ended with these words: *We thank God that our enemies themselves are forced to give some testimony of our decency, piety, and patience: so that their common saying is: "He does not swear, he is a Lutheran <note>In this period, "Lutheran" was often used by the authorities as a general, derogatory label for any Protestant, including the Reformed/Calvinists.</note>: he does not fornicate, nor drink himself drunk; he is of the new Sect." And notwithstanding these testimonies of respectability, nonetheless no manner of punishment is forgotten to torture us. Begin then, O Lords, begin then to take our case into hands, and to investigate our innocence, which has been oppressed through the deceit, slanders, and violence of our opponents; so that the Lord, who considers the life of His servants precious and worthy, does not stretch out His wrath over you. And do not despise the weeping and sighing of so many innocents, so that God may hear you in your prayers, bless you in your offices and dominions, and make you prosperous in all that you shall do.* So be it. <note>original: "Dat moet geschieden."</note>

Thus Cornelius Gualterus honored the memory of Cassander, whose principal writings, even during his lifetime <gloss>1</gloss>, and many times thereafter, were forbidden and mutilated through the efforts of the most vehement Papists <note>original: "Pausgesinden," referring to those strictly loyal to the Pope</note> and book-expurgators <term>Book-expurgators|Official censors who physically crossed out or cut "heretical" passages from texts before they could be sold</term>. Yet fifty years after his death, someone in France—who was later found to be the learned Canon Johannes Cordesius <gloss>2</gloss> (a man of great modesty and a friend of Grotius and Vossius <note>Hugo Grotius and Gerardus Vossius were leading Dutch humanist scholars and friends of the peace-seeking "middle way" in religion</note>)—gathered his books together and, along with some unpublished writings, had them printed as a single volume in Paris. In this edition, one also reads his familiar letters, in which he spoke his heart among his friends, containing many instructive thoughts and concise lessons on peace <gloss>3</gloss>.

Around that same time, it began to be heard that several hundred of the most prominent Netherlands nobles—including many who were Roman Catholic—had entered into a sworn brotherhood after holding various secret meetings. They had bound themselves together to collectively prevent the introduction of the Inquisition, under whatever pretext it might be imposed. Some believe that this alliance, which was then called the *Compromise* \* among the common people, was first drafted at Breda at the home of the Lord of Saint-Aldegonde, Philip of Marnix <note>Philip of Marnix (1540–1598) was a key advisor to William of Orange and a primary author of the Dutch national anthem</note>. However, Franciscus Junius relates how he was called from Antwerp to Brussels on the very day the wedding of the Prince of Parma to Maria of Portugal was to be held. There, in the Culemborg house on the horse market <note>The Culemborg House was the Brussels residence of Floris van Pallandt, Count of Culemborg; it was later razed to the ground by the Duke of Alba as punishment for these meetings</note>, he preached and offered prayer before a small gathering of no more than twenty nobles. After the prayer, they entered into consultation; he stayed to listen in silence as it was resolved to enter into a league, both within and outside the country, against the Inquisition (which he called a violent and barbaric tyranny).

Among these Notes were several political exhortations, reinforced with human reasons and examples drawn from history, which he and **Jan van Blois van Treslong**, his tried and true friend, secretly sent to the Court; to make the principal Lords who were in the **Council of State** <note>The Council of State was one of the three "Collateral Councils" that advised the Governor-General of the Netherlands.</note> think of means tending toward the peace and tranquility of the state, by removing the prying into minds and consciences, by which the common safety was being completely overthrown. That kind of writing was highly praised by all, and they liked it: even the **Count of Egmond** <note>Lamoral, Count of Egmond, a high-ranking nobleman who was later executed by the Duke of Alba.</note> praised it, until he came to know that Junius was the author and a Frenchman. A hateful name, for the French were—on account of the war that had recently been waged with them—still held in such hot hatred that many, although he came to preach the Gospel to them, had taken him for a spy upon his first arrival. 

But because of the aforementioned writing, he was often sought by the **Magistrate** and often called in; it was even made known several times before the city hall, even within his own hearing, that anyone who knew the maker of a short Manuscript (it was written in his hand) and brought him to the Magistrates would enjoy a reward of three or four hundred guilders for that report. Finally, it was discovered by spies who were sent out that **Count Louis of Nassau** <note>The younger brother of William the Silent and a key leader of the Dutch revolt.</note>, at the end of the year sixty-five, had dealt secretly with the Reformed in Antwerp regarding a certain address written by **Franciscus Junius** to the King (for the advancement of common liberty and the abolition of the <term>inquisitorial edict</term> <note>These "plakkaten" were bloody decrees issued by Charles V and Philip II to suppress heresy through the Inquisition.</note>). ### OF THE REFORMATION. BOOK VI.

<margin>1566.</margin> [The description] of his person was handed to the Governess <note>Margaret of Parma, the regent of the Netherlands for King Philip II of Spain.</note> and the Council at Brussels; they, in turn, sent it to the Margrave of Antwerp to capture the man. The task was assigned to the Sheriff, who, to ensure success, summoned to his office the maidservant of the house where Junius lived, as she had recently served him. But he could learn nothing from her, neither through fair words, nor promises, nor even threats. Consequently, with the permission of the Burgomaster—as required by the <term>city privileges</term><note>The "Joyous Entry" and other charters protected citizens of Antwerp from arbitrary search and seizure without local judicial consent.</note>—he searched the citizen's house. But the Minister had departed for Breda just half an hour before his arrival to visit the congregation there. Furthermore, immediately after his departure, the master of the house was warned of everything by a certain friend, so that he was able to move his belongings out of harm's way, though not without great effort.

<margin>
His and Carolus Niëllius's courage.
* *Carolus Niëllius, formerly a Minister "under the cross" <note>The "Church under the Cross" refers to the clandestine, persecuted Protestant congregations.</note> at Cologne; thereafter the Walloon church at Utrecht; finally with the Remonstrants at Amsterdam.*

These were the beginnings of his hardships during this persecution; in which he bore himself so bravely that at one point, alongside Carolus Niëllius, his brother in the ministry (whose son * used to recount this), he preached at the very same hour that others were being executed in the market square for the sake of the Reformed doctrine. They stood in a place where, through the glass windows, they could see the flickering of the fires in which their fellow believers were being burned.

Meanwhile, in this state of affairs, the Duchess sought to consult with the Knights of the Golden Fleece and the <term>Stadtholders</term><note>Provincial governors who represented the sovereign.</note> of the various provinces regarding what reached her ears daily about the intentions of the confederated Nobles. She summoned them to Brussels and also sent several letters to the **Prince of Orange** and the **Count of Hoorn**, who had stayed away from the Court since the hope of obtaining any moderation in the matter of the <term>Placards</term><note>Edicts or decrees issued by the King, specifically the harsh laws against heresy.</note> had vanished, inviting them kindly for counsel. She found herself in great anxiety; for she had been informed that the joined Nobles had secretly arranged and held at the ready thirty-five thousand men, partly on foot and partly on horse. These were said to be ready to take the field immediately to rob and plunder (on which many had their eye, more so than on matters of faith) and invade the country, unless they were permitted to live in freedom of conscience. To this end, they had decided to arrive within eleven or twelve days—more or less—numbering about fifteen hundred...

...men-at-arms, to be dispatched from their number to her Highness <note>Margaret of Parma, the Governess of the Netherlands.</note>. The summoned Knights, Stadtholders, and other Councilors, being assembled, the matter was presented to them: and each was encouraged to bring forward, frankly and freely, whatever they thought might be beneficial—both for resolving the rising difficulties and regarding the matter of the <term>Inquisition</term> and the <term>Placcards</term> <note>The "Placcards" or *Plakkaten* were harsh legal edicts issued by Charles V and Philip II to suppress heresy, often carrying the death penalty for Protestant practices.</note>—for the honor of God, the service of his Royal Majesty, and the welfare of the land. Here it was remarked, *that the Inquisition was of two kinds: the ordinary, belonging to the Bishop, and the extraordinary, in the name of the Pope. Which latter, since the provinces were now provided with Bishops who performed this duty according to custom, might now be abolished, or at least suspended.* And, *although it seemed ill-advised for the service of God, the King, or the Country to revoke the Placcards entirely, the Emperor's <note>Emperor Charles V, father of King Philip II.</note> foresight had nevertheless, during the year fifteen hundred and fifty, conceded so much that they were partially moderated at the intercession of the Queen of Hungary <note>Mary of Hungary, sister of Charles V and former Governess of the Netherlands.</note>, his sister. That it might also not be unadvised to change their form and somewhat lighten the hand [of enforcement], in order to adapt to the present circumstances.*

The Prince of Orange <note>William the Silent, the leading figure of the Dutch Revolt.</note> allowed each to say his piece, and finally made himself heard thus: *“Oh, if only we had been granted the honor of being believed from the start! Then the last things would not have been done first, nor would the wandering spirits have been driven to despair by extreme threats. Who would not denounce a physician as insane who, without seeking healing through mild and purifying salves, immediately proceeds to amputation and eradication, and busies himself with cutting and burning; but who even now merely watches on? It has been properly observed today that the Inquisition is divided into two parts: namely, that which was brought onto the scene by the Pope against Luther; and that anciently practiced by the Bishops. The latter has become bearable through custom. One can also make do with it now, seeing as the land is currently more than well-provided with Bishops who, not slumbering as in former times, keep an eye on religion, as is proper for them and inherent in their very titles. The other [the Papal Inquisition] is the stumbling block; and should conveniently be cleared out of the way. For the Inquisitors have no mandate from the current Pope, and even that understanding which the old ones had expired with the death of the deceased. Concerning the Placcards: let one hear not me, but experience. What does experience say to this? Persecution incites superstition. The cruelty of the punishment is a temptation to sin. We have learned in the school of recent years how many have turned away from the Church simply by witnessing the steadfastness of those who received the sentence of death as an invitation to a feast, and with joy”*
