# OF THE REFORMATION. BOOK VI.

->Oo 3<-

<margin>1566.</margin>
...stepped into the fire. For to surrender life and limb, so dear by nature, to the most terrifying of pains without a very certain reason why, seems to them beyond all appearance of possibility. And with such a harsh and bitter medicinal tool, they have in France, in England, and finally here as well, treated the fire in the wound—and done nothing but multiply the heap of apostates. Well might, therefore, the ancient Christians say, that *the blood of the Martyrs was the seed of the church.* <note>A famous quote by the early Christian author Tertullian: "Sanguis martyrum semen christianorum."</note> Emperor Julian <note>Emperor Julian (reigned 361–363 AD), known as "the Apostate," who attempted to revive Roman paganism. He realized that making martyrs only strengthened the Christian faith.</note> understood this matter: he went more gently against those he held as such, and achieved more by it. Harassing, oppressing, and attacking had caused their zeal to awaken. Freedom, lack of worry, and idleness put it to sleep. Compulsion has no power over the conscience. Of this those mighty Kings became aware; who, no matter how they labored, failed to shift the stubbornness of the Jews. The Greek Empire <note>The Byzantine Empire.</note> suffered bravely from heresies; yet hardly a Heretic suffered anything beyond exile. Arius under Constantine, Aetius under Constantius, and Nestorius under Theodosius <note>Three major figures in early Christian theological disputes (Arianism and Nestorianism) who were banished rather than executed.</note> were spared with that. Bloody, certainly, to create a terror, were the <term>Placcards</term> <note>Official edicts or decrees issued by the sovereign; here referring to the "Blood Placcards" against heresy.</note> of the latter; but his sword was never used in this matter. The Arians, meanwhile, seem now to have vanished from the world, which then seemed almost too small for them. For lack of resistance, they ran themselves to an end. That is the nature of Heresy. *If it rests, it rusts.* He whets it who rubs it. The novelty must wear off, and with that it loses its taste. There is nothing safer than to follow the footsteps of such excellent Princes. Besides Emperor Charles <note>Charles V, father of the current King Philip II.</note> of exalted memory, and the softening of the Placcards in the year fifteen-fifty, we have also recently seen the Majesty of our present King <note>Philip II of Spain.</note> leaning toward the same. But his benevolence has been suspended by the counsel of the Bishops. They may see to it how they justify that. It cannot enter my mind that such massive misunderstandings could be uprooted all at once. Nor should anyone imagine that things will ever be entirely pure. For it was foretold by the Apostle <note>Likely a reference to 1 Corinthians 11:19: "For there must be also heresies among you."</note> that heresies shall always brood. Even if the Placcards appeared ever so just; the number of the defiled is too great. I see no way through it; but it is much more likely that despair will drive them to some madness. Thus it smoldered in France before the flame of war broke out. And it is already said that the **Confederates** <note>The *Bondtgenooten* or "Compromise of the Nobles," a league of Dutch noblemen who petitioned for religious tolerance.</note> hold an understanding with those from there. Therefore one must satisfy them to some extent, or place the peace of the land in danger. This counsel seems best to me; God bless that which you shall hold as such. Let no one wonder that so much knowledge of affairs and history appeared in this speech of the Prince. He had it,
<margin>Burgund. Hist. Belg. Lib. 11.</margin>
writes

### OF THE REFORMATION. BOOK VI.

<margin>1566.</margin>...aimed at the matter of faith, and perhaps once useful to the state, but now changed in nature and effect by the turning of the times, are henceforth likely to produce nothing but aversion, unrest, and rebellion, with all manner of misery and the ruin of the land. For, given the recent years in which—even without using the extreme severity—so much trouble has been encountered, it is easy to gauge what will come of it if, following the latest command of his Majesty, not only the harshness of the **placards** <term>placards: formal public edicts or laws issued by the King, specifically those detailing the death penalty for Protestant heresy.</term> but even the **Inquisition** is put to work. We find ourselves compelled to point out the rising storm now hanging over our heads, guided by the command of the supreme law: the welfare of the community. Furthermore, we are specifically forbidden from remaining silent any longer by necessity, which justifies all things. For if the common people <note>original: "het graeu," referring to the lower classes or the "mob."</note> are stirred to action, our houses, estates, and other properties, being located in the countryside, will suffer the first blow. Who also does not see that the Inquisition and placards, if they take hold, place our lives, property, and honor—and those of all inhabitants—into the hands and at the mercy of the first person who envies us, unless it pleases the Bailiff, out of favor or compassion, to turn a blind eye? Therefore, our humble request is that your Highness might,

<margin>Their request.</margin>as quickly as possible, dispatch some suitable person to present our humble prayer to his Majesty; to the end that everyone may be delivered from this anxiety, as not only extreme necessity, but even justice and reason demand. Not that we wish to dictate laws to the King. But let his Majesty be served by providing for this matter through safer, more fitting, and more timely means, by framing other ordinances with the presence and consent of a general assembly of the **States** <note>The States-General, a representative body of the various provinces of the Netherlands.</note>. We also humbly pray her Highness that she, while his Majesty considers our rightful request, will prevent the aforementioned dangers by a general standstill and suspension of both the Inquisition and the execution of the placards. We do this under the express declaration that, with this warning, we have fully acquitted ourselves of our duty as far as our interests are concerned, and we hold ourselves unburdened before God and men: so that we understand ourselves to be innocent of any neglect by which any trouble, commotion, riot, or bloodshed might be caused. Taking as witnesses thereof God the Lord, the King, your Highness, and the Lords of her Council, as well as our own consciences, that we have acted herein as belongs to good and faithful servants and upright subjects, without in the least exceeding the boundaries of our obligation. To this request 

<margin>Answer to the Request.</margin>of the Nobles, it was answered: That her Highness was well-disposed to send a mission to the King, trusting that his Majesty would strive...

They demand a suspension of these laws and a consultation with the States-General, disclaiming any responsibility for future violence if their warnings are ignored.</summary>

The Count of Berlaymont reportedly whispered this to Margaret of Parma to dismiss the petitioning nobles as insignificant.</note> Or according to other accounts: † *“Look there, a bunch of fine beggars.”* Whatever the truth of it, this name was thereafter not rejected by the Confederates; rather, it served at that time as a common symbol for those who sought to join hands for the freedom of the fatherland and faith. People greeted one another, in times and places of joy, with the cry of *Long live the Beggar* <note>Original French: "Vive le Geux."</note>. They wore medals, first of wax or wood, then of gold or silver, around their necks. On one side was the King’s face, and on the other a beggar’s pouch, held by two joined right hands, with these words around the edge: *Faithful to the King, even unto the beggar’s bag* <note>Original French: "fidelles au Roy jusques à la besage." This reflected the nobles' stance that they remained loyal subjects of Philip II, even if his policies reduced them to poverty.</note>. On some medals <term>penningen: Commemorative medals or tokens used as political symbols.</term> struck at that time, one side showed the King’s image, and the other showed two noblemen (with beggar’s bags at their sides, wearing hats like vagabonds) clasping hands, as if making an alliance or confirming their loyalty to the King. Some pinned a small wooden beggar’s bowl with silver bands to their chest or hat, with *Long live the Beggar* carved upon it; and they dressed themselves, so that everything would be consistent, in ash-gray cloth.

Little images of Our Lady, made after the statue of Halle <note>The Black Madonna of Halle, a famous pilgrimage site near Brussels, became a symbol of Catholic resistance against the Reformation.</note>, and struck upon silver medals, were attached to hatbands. Devout servants of the church did the same, as a sign that they remained bound to the Papal church and intended to oppose the Beggars <note>Original: "Geusen."</note>. Appearing in Brussels with this finery, they quickly gained many followers. This was so pleasing to the Governess <note>Margaret of Parma, the Regent of the Netherlands.</note> in the current state of affairs—for she sought to strengthen herself against the confederated Nobles—that she wrote of it to Pope Pius V. She brought it about that he, to provide fuel for this zeal, consecrated these medals according to the customs of the Roman church and granted various indulgences to those who would wear them. From this, the use of consecrated medals among those of the Roman faith took its origin, or at least became known throughout the whole Papacy.

Some of those who were accustomed to appear in such state assemblies were left out or excluded, even pushed out; and their places were filled with people known not to vote against the King. The representatives of the cities had also been forbidden from discussing the matter with their "broad" and "back" councils <note>Original: "breede en achterraeden." <meta>This page continues the discussion regarding the political and religious tensions in 1566. ### OF THE REFORMATION. BOOK VI.

<margin>
1566.
Contents of the draft.
Hooft p. 81.
Bor II. 45. b...
Wesenb. p. 104...
</margin>
...their opinion was never asked. The draft of moderation comprised fifty-three points, which amounted to this: *Teachers, Preachers, Deacons, and other officials of non-Roman religions; writers of books, songs, lampoons, and everything contrary to the old doctrine received in the church, tending to introduce the new Religion or Sect, or to incite rebellion; providers of places for forbidden gatherings, as well as those who cause great scandal in public, or make it their business to harbor heads of the new doctrine, should be strangled with a rope; their property forfeited where the charters permitted it. Those who recanted their faith would receive the sword <note>A more "merciful" death by beheading rather than burning or strangulation.</note>, and their heirs would receive their property. Mercy was granted to common and repentant heretics; the unrepentant were sentenced to banishment, while retaining the enjoyment of their goods, which they could not alienate by last will or other means, but must let pass to their heirs: these same goods would also be forfeited if they presumed to lead any countrymen astray.* But *Anabaptists*, remaining stubborn, forfeited their means where forfeiture was the law; <margin>The Anabaptists are more hated than relapsed heretics.</margin> where it was not, these fell immediately to their heirs. *Relapsed Heretics*, provided they showed new regret, might satisfy the law with banishment; however, the *Anabaptists* <note>Original: "Doopsgesinden."</note> could satisfy it only with their lives. On this point, the historian Pieter Hooft wonders at this ferocity and seeks the reason. <margin>Hooft p. 81. Cause of that hatred.</margin> "It seems strange," he says, "that they had such a more than common bitterness against these defenseless and worldly-unwise people; unless they wished to make no distinction between them (though they hold an unarmed life as a point of faith) and the attackers of Amsterdam or the occupiers of Münster, because they hold the same view regarding the matter of Baptism; or that the following of hypocrisy, along with the outwardly sought appearance of humility and innocence in clothing and countenance, as if reproaching all others for their godlessness and vanity, provoked the common hatred." But this moderation, which by the court—following its craving for Latin—was called *Moderatie*, immediately received the name of *Moorderatie* <note>A pun combining the Dutch "Moord" (murder) and "Moderatie" (moderation).</note>. It was clearly seen that little heed was paid to the resentment and aversion <margin>The moderation is called Murder-ation. *Hooft p. 81. Marten Baeyaert, G. du Flot, J. Dautricourt and N. Tournemine burned at Lille.</margin> that both great and small expressed and showed against the persecution; for the shedding of blood for matters of Religion did not cease. Shortly before the submission of the petition of the Confederates, when rumors were running everywhere that the Nobility was hurrying to Brussels to withstand the Inquisition and the placards <term>Placards: Royal edicts or decrees, specifically those carrying the death penalty for heresy.</term>, they had Marten Bayaert, Glaude du Flot, Jan Dautricourt, and Noël Tournemine at Lille <note>Original: "Rijffel," the old Dutch name for the city of Lille.</note> burned...

<summary>This page describes the "Moderation" proposal of 1566, which despite its name, still prescribed death by strangulation or beheading for various religious offenses. It highlights the particularly harsh treatment of Anabaptists and the public's cynical rebranding of the policy as "Murder-ation."</summary>

Some of those who were accustomed to appear in such state assemblies were left out, or excluded, or even cast out; and the places filled with people who were known to not vote against the King. They had also forbidden the deputies of the cities to discuss it with their broad councils and advisors, but commanded to keep everything hidden. their judgment was never requested. The draft of the moderation comprised fifty-three points, which amounted to this: *Teachers, Preachers, Deacons, and other officials of non-Roman religions; writers of books, songs, lampoons, and everything contrary to the ancient doctrine received in the church, tending to introduce the new Religion or Sect, or to stir up sedition; those who provide places for forbidden assemblies, as well as those who cause great public offense, or make it their work to harbor leaders of the new doctrine, should be strangled with a cord; their goods forfeited where the charters <term>charters: local laws or "handtvesten" that often protected citizens from property seizure</term> allowed it. Those who renounced their faith would be executed by the sword, and their heirs would receive their property. Mercy was granted to common and repentant heretics; the unrepentant were sentenced to exile, while retaining the use of their property, which they could neither alienate by last will nor by other means, but must let it pass to their heirs: likewise, the same would be forfeited if they presumed to lead any inhabitants astray.* But Anabaptists <term>Anabaptists: a radical reform movement ("Wederdoopers") that practiced adult baptism and was often persecuted by both Catholics and other Protestants</term>, if they remained stubborn, forfeited their means where forfeiture took place; where it did not, these fell immediately to their heirs. Relapsed heretics, provided they showed new regret, might satisfy the law with exile; however, the Anabaptists <note>original: "Doopsgesinden"</note> could only satisfy it with their necks. At this point, the historian Pieter Hooft wonders at this ferocity and seeks the reason for it. It seems strange, he says, *that they had loaded such an uncommon bitterness upon these defenseless and worldly-ignorant people; unless they wished to make no distinction between them (though they consider an unarmed life a point of faith) and the attackers of Amsterdam or the occupiers of Münster, because they hold the same view regarding the matter of Baptism; or that the suspicion of hypocrisy, along with their outwardly sought appearance of humility and innocence in clothing and countenance, as if reproaching all others for their godlessness and vanity, provoked common hatred.*

For this, he was accused before the Court in The Hague, but thanks to the good testimony given by the City Magistrates, he was released at that time. But afterward, having been accused and summoned before the Episcopal See at Utrecht, he traveled there and was held in custody for a time, until finally, in this year <note>1566</note>, he was sentenced to the sword. He was seen going to his death with good courage and cheer. It is also related as a memorable event how, upon the scaffold, he sang the Hymn of Praise *Te Deum laudamus* <note>original: "O God, we praise You"</note> ², and just as he reached the verse, *Laudant te omnes Martyres* <note>original: "All the Martyrs praise You"</note> ³, the sword passed through his neck. In Utrecht, not long after, the doctrine of the Reformation was greatly advanced through the writings of a certain Mr. Dirk van Abkoude, Vicar of St. Peter’s Church in that city; he lay in the ecclesiastical prison for a long time regarding matters of religion and was only released after a forced recantation, following the saying, *Lingua juravi, mentem injuratam gero*, that is, *I swore with my tongue, but my mind has not sworn*, or, *a forced oath is loathsome to God*. He nevertheless avoided the Mass, under the pretext of physical weakness, as much as he could. His writings, being very concise and generally bearing a fine motto before each illustration—*Sis sine felle pius*, or *Be godly without bitterness*—were secretly copied and read by some. People also secretly read certain sermons called those of the "Devout Friars Minor"; made, as it was held, by an Evangelical or Reformed Preacher; and the dialogue of *Pasquil and Marforius* <note>Pasquino and Marforio were "talking statues" in Rome used for posting anonymous political and religious satires</note> translated from the Latin: also *The Beehive of the Romish Church* by the Lord of Saint-Aldegonde, under the name of Isaac van Rabbotena <note>A famous satirical work by Philips of Marnix, Lord of Saint-Aldegonde, mocking Catholic rituals</note>. However, this last book appeared later. At this time, there lived in Oudewater in Holland a priest, Theodorus Æmilius, a dignified, learned, and godly man, who, having gained some taste for the doctrine of the Reformation, resolved within himself to perform the Mass no longer. For this reason, he frequently changed his place of residence, staying now in Paris, then in Leuven; then in Cologne, then in Utrecht. It was he who, noticing signs and proof of an excellent mind in Jacob Hermans (afterward known by the name of Arminius <note>Jacobus Arminius, whose theological views later led to the Remonstrant movement</note>) during his fatherless childhood, placed him in school and had him instructed in the foundations of languages and godliness, often admonishing him, *That he [should forsake] all views of earthly...*

Whether it was out of their own zeal, which burned more and more in many; whether it was that the congregation—accustomed to thrusting in their whole body where they get a finger—thus emboldened themselves out of recklessness, relying on the favor they thought they perceived from the Nobles; or whether the Nobles, learning of the lack of gratitude received for the Petition <note>original: "Request of smeekschrift." But the most internal cause seems to have been that *they wanted to extort freedom of religion from the King before the Moderation—by which the door would be forever closed to them—took effect.* 

That the Reformed hurried the public meetings and sermons to avoid the introduction of the draft of the Moderation <term>Moderatie: an attempt by the government to soften the harsh heresy laws (Edicts), though many reformers viewed it as a superficial change that still allowed for persecution.</term> is also to be inferred from what Franciscus Junius, who was then present in the most secret councils of the church leaders, relates. Around Whitsuntide <note>Pentecost</note>, he says, the Reformed throughout almost all of Brabant were still preaching in secret, to the heavy reproach of many who blamed them for sloth, envy of the common good, idle fear, and a distrust unbecoming of a Christian.

Whether it was out of their own zeal, which burned more and more in many; or whether the common people—accustomed to shoving their whole body in wherever they can get a finger—boldly grew reckless due to the favor they thought they perceived from the Nobles; or whether the Nobles (learning of the thanklessness received for the *Request* <note>The "Request" or Petition of Compromise was a formal protest presented by the lesser nobility to the Regent, Margaret of Parma, seeking the end of the Inquisition.</note> or petition, and seeing themselves in disgrace) had, out of desperation, incited the masses † and egged them on to make the Governess <note>Margaret of Parma, the Regent of the Netherlands.</note> fear that the ultimate necessity was approaching unless she secured their assistance and their safety. It is also possible that a great number of arquebuses <note>term: "handbussen" — early portable guns or muskets.</note> bought up by Spaniards, and some warships lying here and there at the entrances to the lands (which eventually sailed for Spain), caused skittish minds to bolt; or perhaps the renewed execution of some prisoners for their faith drove the fire into their heads. But the most internal cause seems to have been that *men wished to extort freedom of religion from the King before the "Moderation"—by which the door would be forever closed to them—took effect.* <note>The "Moderation" (Dutch: *Moderatie*) was a proposal to "soften" the harsh anti-heresy edicts, but the Protestants viewed it as a trap that would still lead to their eventual destruction, mockingly calling it "Murder-ation" (Moorderatie).</note> That the Reformed hastened the public assemblies and sermons to escape the introduction of the draft for the Moderation can also be gathered from what Franciscus Junius—who was then present in the most secret councils of the clergy—relates of it. Around Whitsuntide <note>Pentecost, 1566.</note>, he says, the Reformed throughout almost all of Brabant still preached in secret, to the heavy reproach of many who blamed them for sluggishness, envy of the common good, idle fear, and a distrust unbecoming of a Christian. There, to prevent greater inconveniences and difficulties for the churches, they deemed it necessary that they should assemble their churches in public and preach openly in Antwerp and elsewhere as opportunity arose, just as was now happening in Flanders. And thus the councils were...

# HISTORY OF THE REFORMATION. BOOK VI.

<header>HISTORY</header>

<margin>1566.</margin> ...ever closed by that <term>Moderation</term> <note>The "Moderation" was a proposal by the government to soften the death penalty for heresy to banishment or hanging, which the Protestants mockingly called the "Murderation" because it still criminalized their faith.</note> was overthrown by the breakthrough of public preaching, and the assemblies began to be carried forward to a degree of wonder. But although the lives and the entire ministry of all the other ministers, during the course of this zeal, seemed protected from the violence of the enemies, nonetheless Franciscus Junius remained in his former insecurity: because Lady Margaret, the Governess <note>Margaret of Parma, daughter of Charles V and Regent of the Netherlands.</note>, allowed herself to believe—though unjustly—that everything was being put into turmoil by the French church at Antwerp, and that this church was being set in motion by Junius. For even when she (aiming to dissolve the public assemblies through a new device) approached the churches with promises and threats to suspend the meetings for at least six weeks (until, having been moved to some leniency by the King, some good answer was brought from Spain), she found those of the <term>Walloon congregation</term> <note>The French-speaking Protestant community in Antwerp.</note> in Antwerp to be the primary obstacle, holding that whatever they did would be approved and accepted by the others without any resistance. It is also recounted that the Prince of Orange, and many other Lords, would have gladly had the preaching cease until the general meeting of the States <margin>* P. Scriverius in his Description of the Netherlandish Wars, p. 7.</margin>\*; but here there was no waiting. The freedom of preaching, having first broken through in West Flanders, then struck out from there into Brabant, and further into the other provinces. From the thickets they went into the fields, open places, villages, and suburbs, in great multitudes. The first assemblies occurred without weapons. But when they were threatened or disturbed, they went armed, with sticks and staffs to the sermon; first with rapiers, pistols, and carbines <note>original: "sinkroers"—a type of early firearm or wheel-lock gun.</note>, thereafter also with halberds, muskets, and other lethal weapons.

He, they say, was the first who had called the people to the public sermon, and that in his first sermon seven thousand people were present; though it is not believable that one could have known the exact number, due to the great multitude. <margin>1566.</margin> [The officer] at Gentbrugge was so bold that he aimed to disturb the sermon during that first rush of zeal. Seated on horseback, he charged in among them, holding a naked sword in one hand and a <term>hand-gun</term> <note>original: "handtroer"; an early portable firearm or pistol.</note> in the other. In this manner, he sought to seize the preacher. But the minister, knowing that he was the primary target, hid himself in the nearby woods at the first sound of the commotion. The people were almost without weapons, but their fury quickly found them some. They created a hailstorm of stones which flew at Kroesen <note>A local official or bailiff attempting to enforce the anti-heresy edicts.</note> from far and near. Wounded in several places on his head, his courage failed; he threw away his weapons, pleaded for mercy, and looked for a way to escape, narrowly evading death. The Reformed, encouraged by this, gathered again in great numbers on the twenty-third of <term>July</term> <note>original: "Hooimaendt" or "Hay-month."</note> in a large meadow not far from Ghent. Here they fashioned a <term>wagon-fort</term> <note>original: "wagenburg"; a defensive circle of wagons used for protection during outdoor assemblies.</note> in the manner of an army camp. They placed guards at all the entrances. Some had pikes, some axes, and many had guns. At the front stood booksellers, who distributed forbidden books for money to those entering. Along the roads, some were stationed to invite people they encountered—who knew nothing of the matter—to the sermon, pointing them toward the gathering. In great haste, a high chair made of planks was set upon a wagon like a platform, upon which Strijker <note>Johannes Strijker, a former monk turned influential Reformed preacher.</note> ascended to preach. After the sermon, all the people, men and women, sang a Psalm. Water was also poured into a basin, scooped from the nearby stream, and a certain child brought there was baptized. Preaching continued here for two days. Then the assembly was moved to Deinze, thereafter to Eeklo in the region of Bruges, and so forth through all of West Flanders. In those same days, Petrus Dathenus <note>A key figure in the Dutch Reformation, famous for his translation of the Psalms which remained the standard in Dutch churches for centuries.</note> preached at Poperinge and thereabouts in West Flanders. If they were only granted a place where they could meet under the protection of the Aldermen, without fear of being attacked, to practice their religion founded on the Prophetic and Apostolic teachings, then all unrest would end, trade would flourish better than ever, and they would be content to lay down their arms.* Therefore, they prayed once more that the Lords would consider this matter without passion, in fairness, and for the benefit of the city, and not refuse them the requested places. ...had stood two <term>Parish Priests</term> <note>orig: "Prochiaenen"; local Catholic clergy serving a specific parish.</note>, from whose lives it was gathered that they—without however cutting themselves off from the Roman communion—leaned toward the understanding of <term>Luther</term>; because of this, one had been imprisoned and the other banished. The Prince wrote of this state of the city to the <term>Duchess</term> <note>Margaret of Parma, the Governor of the Netherlands and half-sister to King Philip II of Spain.</note>; and advised that it would be most prudent to dissolve the distrust with civility, so as to persuade the Calvinists to lay down their weapons and place them in the hands of the authorities. With this goal in mind, he pointed out to those of Calvin's persuasion, and their ministers upon whom most depended, that it was unfitting to be found at sermons and in arms at the same time; therefore, they ought to yield to propriety and leave their weapons. They agreed to his reasoning and his decision; provided that they were secured against violence through his word, the promise of the <term>Magistrates</term> <note>orig: "Wethouderen"; the governing body of the city.</note>, or a letter from the Court. Furthermore, for the general satisfaction, in addition to the Magistrates, former <term>Aldermen</term>, Ward-masters, and Deacons of the guilds, the <term>Militias</term>, Brotherhoods, <term>Rhetoricians</term> <note>orig: "Rethorykers"; members of the "Chambers of Rhetoric," which were influential social and literary societies often involved in religious and political debate.</note>, and Merchants were also called to counsel. For this reason, two points were proposed. The first was to take twelve hundred citizens into pay and under military oath: the other was to suspend preaching. And the Prince declared that he and the Magistrates would most prefer to see this accomplished through mutual consent, until his Majesty, with the approval of the <term>States-General</term> <note>orig: "algemeine Staeten"; the assembly of representatives from the various provinces of the Netherlands.</note>, should unanimously establish order therein: whether that might be reached by securing those who had deviated from the Roman Church through a general pardon, or by some other means. Upon this proposal, they requested to hold a private consultation; which was granted. Having thereafter come together again, they brought forward: *That they found the raising of citizens as <term>hired soldiers</term> <note>orig: "waerdtgeldt"; mercenary guards hired by a city to maintain order, often controversial because they were not part of the regular civic militia.</note> in such a merchant city to be ill-advised, as it was likely to lead to discord and riot. For even if one took them from the citizenry, they would nonetheless be people of low means and hardly trustworthy. But they themselves offered abundantly to perform all the service for which one wished to use the hired men. Regarding the sermons, that these should be handled gently, and only through admonition and dissuasion; also that a general pardon would cause many to stay away; but that the assembly of the States-General would bear the most fruit.*

But everything was thrown into turmoil once more by the untimely zeal of one **Peter van Rithove**, a Doctor of Theology and Pastor of St. Peter’s in **Leuven**, who, disguised in worldly clothing, presumed to publicly rebuke the local preacher at **Kiel** <note>A district south of Antwerp's city walls</note> during his sermon. And though the preacher said he was prepared to discuss the matter with him outside the crowd, in some nearby house, the other nonetheless continued with his contradictions. The listeners, coming closer and hearing how the **Preacher** had silenced his opponent with scripture and reason, then raised a great jeer and outcry; indeed, some became so embittered that they would have killed the **Doctor**, had not several other citizens, at the risk of their own lives, protected his, forced him into a house, and hidden him in a cellar. But a great crowd remained outside that house, wanting him beaten to death, or at least that he be delivered into the hands of justice. Then the **Prince** sent the **Sheriff** there, who took him into custody: but shortly thereafter, having been questioned as to what had moved him to such presumption, he was secretly put on a ship and helped out of the city. The **Prince of Orange** had brought matters so far that the **Reformed** <note>The Calvinist faction</note> laid down their weapons for the most part; and it seemed all would have done so, had it not entered their minds that the **Bailiff of Brabant** <note>original: "Drossaard," a high-ranking judicial and military official</note> had reinforced himself with servants and horses. This, and his riding past the city, near where his residence stood, struck a fresh terror into them: such that they went to the preaching with even more weapons. Nevertheless, when the **Duchess**, at the request of the **Prince** and the **Magistrates**, forbade him from attempting anything to their detriment out of fear that they might move their meetings inside the walls, they grew somewhat quiet. If he should take this poorly, they would nevertheless rather endure his displeasure, however reluctantly, than hear the complaints of the people and live in fear of being suddenly attacked; which could easily happen with the help of the **Law** <note>original: "Wet," referring here to the city's Catholic magistracy</note>, and that without his knowledge. *Reael f. 11. a, b. 17. a.*

On the eighth of July <note>original: "Hooimaendt," the traditional Dutch name for the month when hay is harvested</note>, six of the most prominent citizens, together with Jan Arentszoon (Peter Gabriël having departed for another place), came together outside the St. Anthony’s gate, between the city and Houtewaal, on the side of the IJ river near the embankment, among the reeds. These men were Reinier Kant, Vrank de Wael, Cornelis Janszoon Koster, Albert Heyes, Willem Floriszoon, and Laurens Jacobszoon from "The Golden Real" on the Water.

<margin>
Six Amsterdam citizens decide with Jan Arentszoon to begin public preaching in Holland.
</margin>
In this small gathering, Jan Arentszoon offered a very solemn and fervent prayer, though in a soft voice, praying to God to send His Holy Spirit into their midst to help them decide what might most serve the honor of His High Majesty. After weighing all the difficulties, they set aside all danger and fear of death and collectively resolved that public preaching should also begin in Holland, just as it was being done in the other provinces of the Netherlands. However, they thought it best to meet once more after midday to determine the method they should follow in this matter. But while they were returning to the city one by one, the town hall bell began to ring.

<margin>
The edict of July 3rd is proclaimed in Amsterdam.
*Reael 17. b.*
This edict is found in its entirety in the History by *Bor, II. 51.*
</margin>
Consequently, two of the six men went to the Dam Square, where they heard the proclamation of the latest edict <note>term: "plakkaet" — an official public decree or law posted by the authorities</note> from the Court, which had been sent over by Lady Margaret <note>Margaret of Parma, the Governor of the Netherlands</note>. *It forbade anew, as had been partially indicated before, all conventicles <note>term: "conventiculen" — secret or unauthorized religious gatherings</note> and unlawful meetings, both secret and public, under penalty of the gallows for the Preachers or Teachers, and the forfeiture of all their goods for the benefit and profit of those who should capture them; who otherwise, in the absence of assets, would receive six hundred pounds (at forty Flemish groats to the pound) from the King’s funds. The same would be done to those who provided or permitted places for such sermons. Those who harbored or favored the Preachers would be punished with death, and those found in such gatherings would be punished at the judge's discretion; taking into account their status, and whether they were there out of curiosity or if they had come armed with sticks and staves <note>original: "gestokt en gestaeft," meaning prepared for a physical confrontation</note> to protect the aforementioned Preachers; such persons would be sentenced to the gallows...*

Around the same time, the Lord of Brederode <note>Hendrik van Brederode was a leader of the "Compromise of the Nobles," a petition against the Inquisition.</note> appeared at Hoorn * and in various other Dutch cities, in order to secretly gain followers for the confederated Nobles and to have the covenant approved by the most prominent inhabitants. Meanwhile, the rumor of the preaching at Hoorn ran through all of Holland. People cried out that Preachers were now found and available elsewhere as well. Many inhabitants of Amsterdam, citizens and foreigners, wished that they might also hear the Word thereabout. And hereupon those among the Amsterdam Reformed who had the management of affairs, or took it upon themselves, began to reveal themselves somewhat more freely, letting it be known: that if they were assured of obtaining a significant number of listeners, a Preacher would soon be at hand; who would put himself, and all those with him, in too great a danger if only a small number came to hear; for they knew that the <term>Magistrates [Magistraet]</term> would then do everything in their power to disturb the preaching. But so much desire and zeal was perceived to be present in such a gathering, that it was found advisable to meet on the twenty-first of <note>original: "Hooimaendt," the Hay-month or July</note> July, on a Sunday, outside Haarlem, at Overveen, located under the domain of the Lord of Brederode. ### H I S T O R Y

<margin>1566.</margin>...concerning Kant, that on the next day, at the same hour, he would preach on the Holy Way <note>original: "heiligen Weg," a road leading south-west out of Amsterdam</note>, at the Overtoom <note>A dam and portage point outside the city walls of Amsterdam</note>. But Kant, clearly perceiving what they were after, went at half past two, accompanied by Laurens Jacobszoon Reael, before the Burgomasters in the Little Tower <note>The "Toorentje" was a small tower on the city walls of Amsterdam used for administrative meetings</note>, and asked there whether they had spread such a rumor about him? They answered him: Yes, and that this had been reported to them by very trustworthy persons. He requested to know who these informants were, saying that they sought to bring him to his death through such false witnesses. But when they refused to name those people, he spoke plainly to them, **"That they themselves were the people who let such a rumor run,"** accusing them of doing him wrong; adding further: **"Although you people seek to hinder the preaching outside Haarlem by this means, (these were his own words) it is not possible; for that work of the Lord shall proceed, and all the Devils shall not prevent it, nor in any way hinder it through their lying instruments. There shall be preaching at Overveen, and we hope also to do so outside Amsterdam in a few days. For the people are fiery and understand the deceit of the Pope, and the doctrine of the Antichrist. And at this hour all the boats and wagons that were near the city are departed for Haarlem, full of people, to hear the Lord’s Word tomorrow, and we are also departing thither immediately."**

Meanwhile, the Haarlem <term>Magistrates [Wethouderen]</term> were informed by letters from the Burgomasters of Amsterdam that there was an intent to preach at Overveen, with an admonition to prevent it. Thereupon the <term>City Council [Vroedschap]</term> was summoned by the bell even that same evening at nine o'clock to deliberate on what they should do. The ringing of the bell so late in the evening brought Koster—who was staying with Peter Gabriël at the house of Ysbrant Staeszoon, a ship's carpenter—into great fear. They convinced themselves that the Preacher was being targeted, and kept him hidden that night, piled under wood shavings <note>original: "spaenders"</note>. In the morning the gates remained closed. At last, the Preacher also arrived. They struck two stakes into the earth and tied a cross-pole across them to serve as a support and railing for him. After the singing and prayer, he preached on the eighth, ninth, and tenth verses of the second chapter of the letter to the Ephesians <note>Ephesians 2:8–10, a foundational text for the Reformed doctrine of salvation by grace through faith</note>; and although he was very small and weak of person, he did so for about four hours in very hot sunshine. Finally, he prayed most fervently for all ranks of men, and specifically for the Government; so that few dry eyes were seen there. Some believe, with Bor <note>Pieter Bor (1559–1635), a prominent Dutch historian of the era</note>, that this assembly consisted of only three hundred persons, mostly women, and about fifty men with **firelocks** <note>original: "sinkroers," an early type of firearm</note>: but Laurens Jacobszoon Reael—who was present there along with Reinier Kant, Cornelis Willemszoon Hooft, his daughter Aegt Cornelis, Jan Janszoon Smit, and many others from Amsterdam—testifies that by estimation there were about five thousand people, both men and women, gathered together, without mentioning any weapons; also the Lord Binkhorst, who then lived at the House at Assen where he was the Castellan, was found at this meeting with his entire family. Upon departing, the assembly was informed that there were intentions to have another Preacher preach at the same place the following day at nine o'clock, near the Roman church dedicated to Mary Magdalene. Then Pieter Gabriël, along with three men, departed by wagon for Alkmaar to teach there the next day, which he did. But Laurens Reael was sent in haste to Amsterdam to learn how things stood there, and what had been decided regarding public preaching. ### H I S T O R Y

<margin>1566</margin> Egbert Roelofszoon, who also sided with the Reformed, reported that the **Town Council** <term>Vroedschap: The assembly of senior citizens who governed Dutch cities</term> had been in session not only on Saturday but also on that same Sunday. Furthermore, he learned through him, from Anthonis van Houf—one of the **thirty-six Councilors** <term>The "Council of Thirty-Six" was a specific advisory body in Amsterdam's government</term> (who was secretly somewhat favorable to the cause of the Reformed, though full of fear and suspicion)—that despite the repeated <margin>Reael f. 23. b.</margin> proposals of the **Burgomasters** <term>The chief magistrates or mayors of the city</term>, they had not yet been able to reach any other decision than this: that if the preaching were brought before the city walls, they would then act according to the circumstances of the situation. With this report, Reael returned to Overveen at eight o'clock in the morning to his fellow believers, who felt encouraged by it to persevere in their intention; for they noticed that the Magistrates, who were accustomed to acting harshly, were now proceeding step by step and sluggishly. This was not without reason, for they found themselves in great embarrassment, hearing that the preachings were being introduced in so many places at once, and not knowing what would come of this—especially because the **Nobility** <note>Refers to the "Compromise of the Nobles," a league of lesser nobles who petitioned for religious tolerance</note> were daily growing stronger in their demands for freedom. So, they proceeded <margin>Jan Arentsz, having preached outside Alkmaar on the 21st of July, teaches at Overveen on the 22nd. Memoirs of L. J. Reael f. 23. b. 24. b.</margin> with the sermon. Jan Arentszoon (who had also taught the previous day outside Alkmaar in a cornfield, with a great gathering from both the city and the surrounding villages) now preached this Monday at Overveen, on several words from the **hundred and eighteenth Psalm**, before a very large audience; for no gates were closed now. Many members of the clergy also appeared here among the listeners, marveling to the highest degree that this **Basket-maker** <note>Jan Arentsz was a professional basket-maker by trade, highlighting the "layman" nature of many early Reformed preachers</note>, a simple layman, explained the Holy Scriptures so skillfully, and maintained such good order in so long a sermon, lasting about four hours. After the preaching, once he had been brought under shelter, they and others were very eager to speak with him about the differences in doctrine, which he gladly allowed. When everyone had departed on their way, and many <margin>Reael f. 25. a.</margin> Amsterdammers returned home in the evening, they were asked what they had heard and seen; to which some gave the questioners this bold <margin>Bold answer of several Amsterdammers.</margin> answer: *“We have heard God's holy Word presented to the people clear and pure, which has been obscured with human teachings by the **Papists** <note>original: "Paepen" — a derogatory term for Catholic priests</note> and, until this time, has been contaminated.”* These were words that, shortly before, would have cost them their necks. Others dared to contradict the **Papacy** <note>original: "Pausdom"</note> even more clearly, and directed their criticism at all the—

That possibly, due to the malicious rumors of a segment of misguided and frivolous people (who misinterpreted their holy and godly conduct, which they now hoped to perform outside the city), the Law <note>The city government or judiciary</note> might believe it had the right to disturb them. This was because it was alleged that they undertook this preaching work out of a vain frivolity or stubbornness, in order to draw the common people—who are naturally inclined toward novelty—to themselves, and to elevate themselves to something great. It was claimed that this teaching led to deception, and this practice to contempt for the King’s edict <term>plakkaet: An official royal decree or law posted in public</term>, to defiance, and even to riot, even intending to bring trouble upon the Magistrates. Therefore, they (so that the Authorities might not act against them too soon to prevent, punish, or commit an injustice) had found it advisable to demonstrate their innocence through this imperfect Writing. They testified before God, the knower of hearts, that they—who stood as if on the slaughterhouse bench <note>original: "vleeschbank," a metaphor for being in constant peril of execution</note>, expecting every hour to be strangled or killed—were not driven by a frivolous spirit, but rather a heavy-hearted one, whose infirmity they had to overcome through God’s promises and the strengthening of the Holy Spirit. Anyone with any understanding could well judge that they did not seek to create a following, as in former

<margin>
* Acts 5:36.

times * Theudas <note>A Jewish rebel mentioned in the New Testament</note>, or in their own days Jan of Leiden <note>original: "Jan Bokelssoon," the leader of the radical Anabaptist kingdom in Münster</note>, David Joris <note>original: "David Jorissoon," a prominent Dutch Anabaptist mystic</note>, and others had done. They only aimed, following the example of Paul

<margin>

the Apostle, to bring Christ a pure bride. They were to be regarded as Servants of God and of Christ, whose honor alone they sought. He must increase and become great, and they must deny themselves. They did not boast in the flesh, but hoped to keep their glory in the cross of Christ for as long as they had breath in their bodies. Should it happen otherwise, woe to them. If their Teachers were people of simplicity and little learning <note>original: "letteren," referring to formal academic or classical education</note>, God had His reasons for that; it served as a beam of His glory that the "vain-wise" were put to shame in their own wisdom, and that the believers, without the foundation of human wisdom, leaned only upon the Crucified One. Yet they hoped that Teachers of greater knowledge would soon come forth. The promise of having the spirit of truth with them belonged to the congregation of God (outside of which there was no Holy Spirit). If they could now prove to the whole world that God’s truth was with them (as they did not doubt, by the pledge given to them by God), then it followed that they had the spirit of truth; and also, that their teaching did not lead to deception, but to the salvation of mankind. But what use were words? Experience itself must confirm this; therefore, their accusers were welcome to visit them; for they were always ready, according to the measure of their gifts, to give an account of their doctrine and their order.

<margin>1566.</margin>ning. That they turned away from the Pope and the un-Christian side-paths of the sects occurred so that they might escape the plagues destined for them. The reproach of rebelliousness was something they, like Paul <note>A reference to the Apostle Paul, who was often accused of inciting riots in the New Testament</note>, had to endure without turning away from their duty. If they could be convinced of error, they were prepared to publicly admit guilt and forsake their own views for a better one; if not, they requested that, while putting their party's doctrine to the test, they be granted safety to seek in a most Christian and loving manner who could win over the other.

# THE REFORMATION. BOOK VI.

<margin>1566. Pet. Gabriël preaches at the Hoornbrugge, and in The Hague: Reael f. 36. a.</margin>
allowed the first public sermon to be held by him <note>Referring to the preacher Peter Gabriël</note> at the Hoornbrugge <note>A bridge near Rijswijk, between Delft and The Hague</note>, with a great gathering of people from Delft, The Hague, and the neighboring villages. Shortly thereafter, at the insistence of the people of Delft, a day was appointed to preach in The Hague. At the designated time, many Delft civic guards <term>schutters</term> <note>Members of a local citizen militia</note> arrived in The Hague in full armor, or at least with some twenty wagons, which they had driven directly in front of the house of the President, Master Cornelis Suis. Here the wagons, upon which the guards remained seated, were arranged in a circle; the Preacher stood in the middle, and the other people, in great numbers, stood all around. Thus, there was singing and preaching, and that well within the hearing of the President, who had recently severely threatened the Preachers, and now being in his house, watched this proceeding, sometimes through a glass window—one can imagine his state of mind. Among the listeners were also some residents of Utrecht, who took Peter Gabriël with them and had him preach at Oostbroek, about an hour’s walk from the city. Several citizens of Utrecht had also traveled on the twenty-ninth of July <term>Hooimaendt</term> <note>Literally "Hay-month," the traditional Dutch name for July</note> to Kuilenburg for the sermon; and though the Sheriff <term>Schout</term> <note>The chief law enforcement and judicial official</note>, by order of the Magistrate, conducted an investigation to discover who had been there, he achieved little: some denied it; others said they were there on account of their trade, or to visit their friends.

Meanwhile, a shot was fired from the Castle with a carbine <term>roer</term> <note>An early type of handgun or light musket</note>, and a certain young girl was struck. After the sermon, Dirk Kater invited the Preacher into the city, to the house where he was staying; many listeners advised it. He then went there and was received; but that hospitality later cost the lady of the house her property and her life <note>The original Dutch "goed en bloedt" implies she was later executed and her assets confiscated</note>. ...by order of the Reformed at Amsterdam, to Cornelis Kooltuin of Alkmaar, then a Pastor at Emden, requesting that some Preachers be sent from there to Holland, specifically to Amsterdam; since God had provided such a favorable opportunity, the harvest was great, and the laborers were few. <note>A reference to Matthew 9:37, a common motif used by the Reformers to describe the urgent need for Protestant ministers to serve the growing crowds of converts.</note> Kooltuin, receiving these letters one after another, arranged for the following Preachers to be sent to Amsterdam at various times: Hermes Bakkereel, Pastor at Jemmingen in the Emden or Reiderland; Juriaen Epessoon, and Jan Davidssoon, Copinus... and Jellius, Pastor at Huite; (others write, joining the two names together, Kopping Jelles, Pastor at Bingum) Johannes Bilderbeek, Pastor at Zuiderhuisen, or Zuyrhuisen, Appius... and Reinerus, or (as one reads elsewhere) Appius Regneri, Pastor at Mansflacht, born in Gelderland. # HISTORY

<margin>1566.</margin>
Regarding the first point, it was agreed by all to request that Her Highness the Duchess, both in her own name and on the word of the Knights of the Order <note>The Knights of the Golden Fleece, the most prestigious and influential council of nobles in the Burgundian-Habsburg Netherlands.</note>, should give assurance that no harm would be done—neither to them nor to those seen to be their supporters—in any way on account of the Covenant <note>The "Compromise of the Nobles," an alliance formed to resist the Inquisition.</note> or the submitted petition.

<margin>Strada, p. 245.</margin>
Regarding the second point, they were not of one mind. Some argued that they should be satisfied once they obtained that for which the Covenant had been formed. But others were of the opinion that, if the first point turned out well, they should go further and demand: that no single religion be prescribed to the people, but that everyone should be left free to follow <margin>Ibid.</margin> whichever they wished. The Jesuit Famiano Strada calls this a "wicked sentiment," which so offended many confederates who remained in the Roman faith <note>The Roman Catholic Church.</note> that they gradually withdrew from the alliance.

<margin>Bentivoglio II. 101.</margin>
Cardinal Bentivoglio says that there were those who wanted to openly rise up against the King and obtain by force what they had not been able to acquire through the petition. Others wanted the States General <note>The representative assembly of the provinces; usually, only the King or Regent could convene them.</note> to assemble on their own authority, and by that means to overturn the placards <note>The *Plakkaten*: royal edicts that carried the death penalty for heresy.</note> and the Inquisition. Others suggested that, to better prepare their undertaking, they should first consult with their neighbors <margin>Hooft III. 98.</margin> and seek their favor. Hooft also indicates that proposals were made regarding military recruitment, the raising of funds, and foreign alliances.

<margin>Bor II. 69. a.</margin>
But when the Reformed in France, in the name of the Prince of Condé and the Admiral of Châtillon, sent a certain person to these confederates to advise them against any treaty (viewing it as deceptive) and offering four thousand noblemen at their own expense for their aid—who would be mounted <margin>French aid rejected by the Nobles. Bor f. 69.</margin> within a month after being requested—they thanked their neighbors for the favor of such an offer but politely declined it, being unwilling to incur the heavy hatred that was tied to bringing in the French.

<margin>The Reformed seek shelter with the Nobles. Hooft p. 98. Bor f. 56. a. * p. 17.</margin>
The Reformed, including those of the Augsburg Confession <note>Lutherans, who adhered to the 1530 confession of faith presented at Augsburg.</note>, sent delegates here to the nobles to seek protection for their religious freedom and to obtain a meeting of the States General. To that end, they placed a petition in their hands. Among the foremost Councilors, it was understood: *That to entirely suppress the <term>Inquisition</term> <note>The ecclesiastical tribunal established to find and punish heresy.</note> would be a diminishing of the authority of His Majesty, His Holiness, and the Church, which had established and introduced the same. Likewise, it should not be kept silent that every individual would come to be free in his religion, at least within the home, if one rejected this sole means which the Church had always used to make its care for doctrine and the consciences of men effective. Regarding the <term>Placards</term> <note>The "Bloedplakkaten" or Blood Edicts: harsh laws that made heresy a capital offense.</note>; if one instituted them according to the prescription of the submitted "moderation," then all sins of omission—such as not coming to church, not coming to the Sacrament, not keeping fast days, nor other ecclesiastical commands, and all negligence within the home—would remain unpunished; and only those would be guilty of punishment who happened to transgress in public, by gathering, preaching, reading of forbidden books, or by giving other offense to the true believers. The penalties themselves would also not outweigh the weight of the crimes; nor would they carry their title from the side of Religion; but would be put to work under the name of weaker emphasis, as in the matter of violating the peace and disturbance of the common rest. How could, if one took that track, the service of the Almighty, the duty of conscience, the dignity of the King, and the welfare of the land remain uninjured?*

Furthermore, all confederacies, assemblies, sermons, offenses, and the like, had to be removed.* But while the King thus proceeded on leaden feet, and before he deviated even this little from his usual severity, the entire country here rose up in turmoil and commotion through the <term>iconoclasm</term> <note>Literally "church plundering" (Dutch: *kerkplondering*); the violent destruction of Catholic statues and art by Protestant mobs in 1566.</note> which broke out at this time.

THE church plundering—that fearful riot, which was not unlike the disturbances that so often broke out among the Jews, or the storm of <term>iconoclasm</term> <note>The intentional destruction of religious icons and symbols.</note> that overcame Greece—took its beginning on the day ^1 before the day which the <term>Papacy</term> <note>The Roman Catholic Church.</note> dedicates to the memory of <term>Mary’s Assumption</term> <note>The feast day of August 15th, celebrating the Virgin Mary being taken into heaven.</note>, in West Flanders, between the <term>Leie</term> <note>A river in Flanders and Northern France.</note> and the sea. A few of the lowest rabble ^2, among whom several robbers, thieves, and prostitutes ^3 had mingled, were—one knows not by whom ^4—stirred up. Their weapons were sticks, axes, hammers, ladders, ropes, and other tools that were more suited for breaking than for fighting; a few were equipped with <term>firelocks</term> <note>Early portable firearms.</note> and swords ^5. First, they (having become bolder due to the absence of the Governor, the <term>Count of Egmond</term> <note>Lamoral, Count of Egmond, a high-ranking nobleman who was away at the royal court at the time.</note>, ^6 who had been called to Court by Lady Margaret) laid hands on the crosses and images that stood by the roads in the countryside. Then they moved to the villages; finally into the cities. Whatever they found closed—chapels, churches, and monasteries—was broken open: all images, paintings, <term>tabernacles</term> <note>The ornate containers used to house the consecrated bread of the Eucharist.</note>, altars, and other sacred ornaments were overturned, torn apart, and destroyed. Indeed, some did not refrain from desecrating libraries, epitaphs, graves, and dead bodies ^7. Suddenly, like a lightning strike, this evil came and flew forth, such that in three days more than four hundred churches were plundered ^8. In some places, the Magistrates, so that the people would not [learn] from this wantonness a

What began with boys soon escalated to men and the drawing of daggers against the sailor, who, being wounded, fled the church into the hands of the Scout <term>Schout: a local official responsible for law enforcement and prosecution, similar to a sheriff</term> and his officers; after being questioned, he was released. Nevertheless, although the noise was great, the people allowed themselves to be persuaded by the churchwardens to clear the church. It was then closed, and things remained quiet for that evening.

Negligence of the City Councilors.
Hooft, Bor, and Wesenbeeck.
</margin>
The City Councilors, who had the entire night available for deliberation, failed—whether they lacked courage or wisdom—to do anything to stifle the smoldering mutiny. They even neglected to test the militias and guilds to see if they were inclined to stop the wanton violence that threatened the common welfare. Yet they did not lack an understanding of the gravity of the situation, for they requested advice by letter from the Prince <note>William of Orange, who was the Stadtholder (governor) of Antwerp.</note>, their Governor. They also later claimed to know how Herman Modet <note>A prominent Calvinist preacher and leader during the Reformation.</note> and other ministers had, on that day, railed against idols, insisting:

That was the prelude to the evil. Some thought that if those of the Law <note>The city magistrates</note> themselves departed, they would draw the crowd after them and away from there. Therefore the Burgomasters <term>Burgermeefters: the chief executive officers of the city</term> stepped toward the town hall, to finally have the militiamen come in arms and to their quarters; and urged the crowd, which stood outside, to depart from there. The church was ordered to be shut, save for one door, to let the rest out. The Margrave <term>Markgraef: a high-ranking official representing the sovereign, responsible for military and judicial matters</term>, having worked outside with his henchmen to show everyone their way, returned inside, where he still found some Aldermen <term>Scheepenen: local judicial and administrative officers</term>; and set about, with them, to dispatch the remainder. Among these, as the most stubborn and therefore having lingered so long, were found those who refused with sullen faces and rebellious words. Meanwhile, a crowd of the rabble burst in again through this door: such that the Scout <term>Schout: a local official responsible for law enforcement and prosecution</term>, giving it up, left the church. No sooner was he gone than they began a singing of Psalms, with loud throats. The Treasurer and Governors of the church property, having brought the holy bones and jewels into the vestry, prepared to leave by the north door. The rabble from outside rushed upon it; forced the gate; and then struck all the others open. The Margrave and Magistrates, at this cry, turned back thither, but being frightened by the countless influx and the noise that resounded from the church, thought they would have enough to do in securing the town hall, which did not remain unthreatened.

> *To me, he writes, just as I would not trust a congregation of fresh and fiery zeal for godliness to descend into such loathsome roguery as to trample divine and worldly laws underfoot; so it seems not without appearance (since the dishonorable and the pious are found among all denominations) that the foulest individuals showed their true nature through these tricks; some feasting their eyes on the spectacle, seeing it as a plague they believed the clergy well-deserved for the bitterness of the persecution; others unconcerned, hoping that one madness, by exhausting the other, might give birth to a longing for moderate order among the parties. But the great bulk of the Non-Catholics certainly behaved with dignity, though they regretted that a necessary work <note>The removal of idols, which the Reformed believed was a religious duty</note> was carried out in such an improper manner.*

...were placed [to guard] the church. The following day, neither church nor monastery was opened, except for the Great Church <note>The Cathedral of Our Lady in Antwerp</note>. Meanwhile, many valuables that had been hidden during the iconoclasm <term>Beeldestorming: the "Image Storm," a wave of destruction of religious imagery by Protestant mobs</term> were voluntarily handed over to the Regents or owners; however, a great portion, and of greater value, remained missing. Therefore, on the same day, a decree was issued that all stolen goods must be returned within twenty-four hours and all further violence must cease, on pain of the gallows—which were immediately erected on the Great Market, which was occupied by armed guards. 

But to avoid causing a new disturbance with this proclamation, it was thought best to inform those of the Religion <note>the Protestants</note>—Walloons, Germans <note>original: "Duitschen," here referring to Dutch or Low German speakers</note>, and others—of it. The Pensionary <term>Pensionaris: a city's chief legal official and diplomat</term> Wesenbeek was sent to approach their Preachers with reason and promises. This was done so that they might, in their sermons, rebuke the people for the mischief and plundering committed, exhort them to surrender the stolen goods, to refrain from further violence, and to remain obedient—and, at the same time, make the new decree known. 

But while the Consistory <note>The governing body of the local Reformed church</note> was busy preparing a written response to this proposal, further violence occurred in the afternoon in the Great Church. People continued their looting there and even laid hands on the coats of arms of the King and the Knights of the Golden Fleece <term>Vliesridderen: an elite order of Catholic knighthood founded by the Dukes of Burgundy</term>, which were richly painted in the choir. Some, however, say they were broken by a falling crucifix that accidentally plummeted from a great height. With this, it seemed they were now attacking even the secular government, which the Magistrate <note>the city government</note> now took to heart. 

The Margrave <term>Markgraaf: the chief judicial and police official of the city</term>, several members of the Law <note>the city council</note>, with the beadles <note>original: "roeydragers," literally rod-bearers who carried symbols of office</note>, alongside some from the guilds and the militia, rushed there. The mob immediately took flight; ten or twelve were seized by the neck. Then it could be seen what had been neglected by not using such sternness at the start. 

Late that evening, a document was delivered by Taffin, Burgomaster Jacob van der Heyden, and the Pensionary Wesenbeek on behalf of the Preachers and Elders of the German and Walloon churches. It served as a response to what the Pensionary had presented to them that morning. First, they testified before God that what had occurred in the removal and breaking of the images had happened without their knowledge or consent. Furthermore, they loathed the robbery, theft, drunkenness, and other mischief that followed. For this reason, the Ministers would [exhort] their listeners in the congregation...

<meta>This page continues the description of the negotiations between the Antwerp city government and the Reformed (Protestant) leaders following the iconoclastic riots of 1566. The previous page ended with the city's legal official approaching the Protestant leaders to restore order.</meta>

# OF THE REFORMATION. BOOK VII.

<margin>
1566.
*Wesenb.* p. 156. 157.
*Bor* fol. 61. b.
*Meurs Gul. Aur.* 11. 14, 15.
*Hooft* p. 102.
</margin>
...gatherings <note>The Protestant assemblies</note> exhorted their followers to refrain from such things and to bring the stolen goods back into the hands of the Law. Furthermore, those of their church were ready to obey the Magistrates in all things, and to place themselves under their commands against all plundering, violence, and wantonness. They also acknowledged that their honors <note>the city officials</note> were placed in the office of magistrate by God, and bound themselves to obey them, not only out of fear, but also for the sake of conscience; consequently, they were willing to bear scot and lot <term>Scot and lot: a traditional form of municipal taxation and civic obligation</term>, tolls, taxes, and other burdens imposed upon them. For greater assurance, the Ministers and Overseers of the church were ready to swear the oath of loyalty to the Magistrate. However, they prayed that they might gather in some churches, suitable and large enough, under their authority and protection, to practice their religion; furthermore, that it might be held in good favor if they used some of them out of necessity until a further order was established. Meanwhile, they sought to force no one in their conscience, nor to bring anyone to their religion by force: keeping themselves content and thanking God that they had the means to serve Him according to their conscience, or to practice their religion with freer hearts. Finally, they humbly requested that it be forbidden to slander or embitter one another, by word or deed, regarding the matter of religious difference.

They also recognized their Lordships to be placed by God in the office of magistrate, and considered themselves bound to obey them, not only for fear, but also for the sake of conscience; consequently, they were willing to bear their share of taxes, tolls, duties, and other burdens placed upon them. Meanwhile, they sought to force no one in their conscience, nor to bring anyone to their religion by force: keeping themselves content and thanking God that they had the means to serve Him according to their conscience, or to experience their religion with freer hearts. <margin>

Franciscus Junius, intending to recount what had happened to him in Ghent at the time of the iconoclasm (for he had traveled there after his return from the assembly at Sint-Truiden at the request of the church of that city; he had also stayed there previously in <term>July</term><note>Original: "Hooimaendt" or "Hay Month."</note> at the desire of the brethren), says first: that the iconoclasts, who were unknown to him and his brethren, had—against their will—been egged on by thoughtless (as he believes) or even malicious people to attack all the churches and church images. <margin>He disapproves of them. Life of Fr. Junius p. 17.</margin>
> *“Truly,”* he says, *“such violent and disorderly counsels have never pleased me: never, I believe, has anyone been with me to whom I showed even the slightest sign that such actions found my favor. With this testimony, I wish to make publicly known my own loyalty, as well as that of my pious fellow brethren (for I do not count the unruly seekers of self-mastery).”*

But no sooner had news reached Ghent of what had occurred during the iconoclasm in Antwerp, than they sought to follow the same course here; the whole night through, the organ pipes that had been brought from Antwerp sounded through the streets.

Disturbance at Amsterdam.

...was imprudently ordered and carried out. The clergy ran through the streets with their treasures—with silverwork, chalices, <term>tabernacles</term><note>Original: "sacramenthuiſkens." This happened precisely at eleven o'clock in the morning, just as the craftsmen were leaving their work for their midday meal; so it was that everyone saw the precious items belonging to their own guild being dragged and carried through the streets by their <term>altar priest</term><note>Original: "autaerpaep." A common, often derogatory term for a priest who served at a guild's specific altar.</note>. Each person looked closely to see if the treasures were those that had come from their own guild. Some opposed this removal, snatched from the priests what they were carrying, and brought it back into the churches. Others went to the Old and New Churches, so that a great multitude of people gathered there. In the New Church, no mischief was committed; for the clergy did not sing Vespers that afternoon, and some citizens persuaded the common folk to leave with kind words, and then closed the doors. In the Old Church, the people initially kept quiet; but when they began to sing Vespers at two o'clock and brought many children for baptism, over whom the chaplains performed the <term>Exorcism</term><note>Original: "Exorciſmus," also called "d'Uitſweeringh" (the swearing out). You have deceived the world with your falsehood for too long. Baptize in the name of Jesus, as the Apostles did.”* Some women went home with their children unbaptized. Several children were blessed and baptized in the Dutch language, and Vespers was brought to an end, although the people grumbled continuously.

But between three and four o'clock, a grain-bearer named Jasper came into the northeast end of the church, near the tabernacle. <margin>\* The Tabernacle.</margin>
> Here lies enclosed in this Lock \*
> Jesus Christ, true man and God,
> Just as he was born of Mary:
> Whoever does not believe this, he is lost.

When he had finished reading (it might have been about twenty-five or thirty lines long), he cut it to pieces at his feet. The breaking of the glass that protected it made a loud noise throughout the whole church. Upon this, some boys began with...

<margin>Ordinance and Regulation for the stilling of the unrest created. Reael f. 44, 45. J. I. Pont. Hist. van Amst. p. 66. Hooft p. 104. Bor II. f. 71. b.</margin>
First, it was granted (*though all this, so the ordinance reads, was for that specific time, which was very dangerous, and until further orders from the Duchess and the Knights of the Golden Fleece*) that all images should be removed from both the large and small churches; and that the churches should remain closed until further notice.

<term>Preaching</term><note>Original: "Predikatie." Referring here to Protestant sermons, which were previously forbidden inside the city.</note> was to take place outside the city walls, without any hindrance being offered to the preachers or the listeners; and in case of foul weather, the Church of the Sick <note>Likely the chapel of the hospital or leper house.</note> might be used for that purpose.

Citizens were permitted, in times of illness, to be counseled by such persons—whether Priests or other Church ministers—as their own conscience found helpful.

When the Parish Priests walked through the streets with the <term>Sacrament</term><note>The consecrated bread of the Eucharist, often carried to the dying in a procession.</note>, they were not to ring any bells, in order to keep the peace.

Church desecration was henceforth forbidden on pain of corporal punishment, to be determined by the court according to the circumstances of the case.

No one was allowed to speak ill of or provoke another, in words or deeds, on account of their faith; rather, everyone was to leave the other in peace, on pain of being punished by the Court according to the severity of the matter.

In the event of a riot, every man was permitted to arm himself for self-protection, but he was not to step beyond the <term>stoop</term><note>The raised platform or steps in front of a house.</note> of his own dwelling; however, in the event of a fire, those ordered and required to fight the fire should run to the scene.

Furthermore, every neighborhood should have a <term>Captain</term><note>Original: "Hopman." A neighborhood leader responsible for local security.</note> and be obedient to him.

...the most prominent inhabitants, who were believed to be most involved with the affairs of the <term>Reformed</term><note>Protestant dissenters, largely Calvinist, seeking religious reform and the right to worship.</note>, were summoned to the town hall early in the morning. The <term>ordinance</term><note>Original: "keure." A local decree or set of regulations.</note> was read to them, and they were asked whether, if such terms were allowed, the common people could be kept in peace? They replied: *That they did not know, as they did not incite the people to any riot; and that the ministers preached nothing but peace, according to the nature of the Gospel. But they themselves well knew and had seen who were the cause of all the disturbances. You people, my Lords,* they continued, *provoke the rabble with many things. We cannot satisfy them; if you have the means to do so, it would please us. We seek nothing else but to preach Christ: for that purpose, the fields outside the city are suitable enough for us; therefore, there is no need to open the little Leper’s Chapel for us, nor to close the others. We have always been accused by you of rioting; but now you have been able to hear from the testimony of many credible men what is being preached: Or if you do not believe it, come then, we pray you, and hear with your own ears, so that you may judge from your own experience:* to which one of the <term>Burgomasters</term><note>The city's mayors or chief magistrates.</note> replied: *I would much rather stand in water up to my ears.*
