1566. ...searched the houses of God <note>In this context, "Godshuiſen" refers to charitable institutions like hospitals or almshouses managed by the church.</note> to see if any outsiders were hidden there. Afterward, some church-violators—or rather, female violators, for Strada <note>Famiano Strada (1572–1649), a Jesuit historian who wrote a famous account of the Dutch Revolt.</note> claims they were women—plundered the Monastery of the Friars Minor <note>The Franciscans.</note> and used the church for preaching. In Leiden, in Brielle, and in other cities of Holland, the images were likewise broken. In Dordrecht, Gouda, Rotterdam, Haarlem, and several other cities, some write that the <term>Magistracy</term><note>The city’s governing body of officials.</note> saw that they could not escape the <term>Iconoclasm</term><note>Original: "beeldeſtorm." The "Image Storm" or widespread destruction of religious icons by Protestant reformers.</note> and therefore found it advisable, in order to prevent a riot by the <term>rabble</term><note>Original: "graeu." A derogatory term for the common people or the mob.</note>, to do themselves what would otherwise have to be endured, and to remove the images in an orderly fashion. However, Mr. Pieter Hooft relates that in Dordrecht, all acts of violence were prevented with great effort by the Burgomaster and others; likewise in Gouda, mostly through the good foresight of the Castellan <note>The governor or caretaker of a castle.</note>, the son of the aforementioned Burgomaster, whose names had not occurred to him.

The city officials responsible for law and administration.</note>, and partly through the moderation of Clement Maertszoon and other leaders of the <term>Reformed</term><note>The Protestant faction, following the teachings of Calvin.</note>, who kept the reckless rabble in check with good admonitions.

<meta>This page continues the narrative of the Year of Wonders (1566), focusing on the tensions in Utrecht following the initial outbreaks of iconoclasm in other Dutch cities. It details the negotiations between the Reformed Protestant community and the Catholic city government over the use of church buildings.</meta>

# OF THE REFORMATION. BOOK VII. #

The news of armed men roaming through the countryside, doing the same <note>The "same" refers to the Iconoclasm, or the systematic destruction of religious images and statues.</note> everywhere in the year 1566, threw the entire city into great turmoil. It made the **Reformed** so bold that on the morning of the twenty-fourth of August, after holding their sermon, they demanded two churches from the **Magistrates**.

<margin>The Reformed demand two churches. Hooft III.105 i</margin>
Those of the Law <note>The city officials and magistrates.</note> replied that it was not within their power, but that they would convene the Council to discuss it. However, when a sermon was held that afternoon outside the **Tolsteeg Gate**, some of the "New Religion" went to the parish church of **Saint Gertrude** and began to break the images. The **Magistracy** immediately sent several city guards there. The plundering was then stopped, and it was later found, upon investigation, that a few young fellows, supported by others armed with muskets, had undertaken the act. The following day, the representatives of the Reformed renewed their previous request in the meeting of the **City Council** <note>Original: "Vroedtschap," the council of "wise men" who governed the city.</note>; they demanded the churches of the **Friars Minor** <note>The Franciscans.</note> and the **Preaching Friars** <note>The Dominicans.</note>; adding further, *that their congregation had resolved to remove the abomination of the images; without, however, wishing to harm anyone in person or property, nor to touch the treasures of the churches.*

<margin>Hooft p. 105.</margin>
The Council pretended that, due to the absence of some members, they found themselves "too weak" to reach a decision. Then one of the representatives urged them on, saying, *"Eat ham with mustard, then you will be strong."* This insolence was later paid for with his head <note>This refers to a later execution for sedition or insulting the authorities.</note>. After consultation with the Court, the Captain of **Vredenburg Castle**, several of the most distinguished nobles (among whom were some who had signed the **Covenant** <note>The "Verbond der Edelmannen" or Compromise of Nobles, a petition against the Inquisition.</note>), and the most prominent citizens, the Reformed were given this answer: That the city officials had no power to open any churches for them. Therefore, seeing the difficulties that were to be expected if they presumed to do so by force (as they boasted), the officials requested an eight-day delay to

<margin>Bor 64.</margin>
meanwhile learn the will of the **Duchess of Parma** <note>Margaret of Parma, the Regent of the Netherlands.</note> and the **Prince of Orange**. This proposal was made palatable to the representatives with many arguments and, at their request, was presented by several Lords of the city to the congregation, who stood in great numbers at the churchyard of **Saint Mary**, all armed and ready to carry out their design.

<margin>Agreement made with them.</margin>
They finally consented, on the condition that the clergy be forbidden from insulting the Reformed, and that the Friars Minor and Prea— <note>The text cuts off mid-word "Preekebroeders" (Dominicans).</note>

<meta>The catchword "Pree-" indicates the next page continues with the "Preekebroeders" (Preaching Friars/Dominicans).</meta>

<summary>This page describes the escalating tension in Utrecht during the 1566 Iconoclasm, where Reformed citizens demanded church buildings and began destroying images at St. Gertrude's. The city council, feeling pressured and threatened by armed groups, negotiated an eight-day delay to consult the Regent and the Prince of Orange.</summary>

Iconoclasm followed thereafter.

Then the armed people fell with great turbulence into the **Buurkerk**, into that of **Saint James**, and those of the **Friars Minor** <note>The Franciscans.</note> and the **Preaching Friars**: the images were stormed; all ecclesiastical finery was desecrated or plundered; the Missal <note>The liturgical book containing the instructions and texts necessary for the celebration of Mass.</note> and other books were cut and torn to pieces. The **Magistrate**, too weak to withstand them, did nothing more here than secure the city hall and, the following night, guard it with about one hundred and sixty of the most loyal members of the guilds.

<margin>
Negotiations are resumed with the Reformed.

The next day, the twenty-sixth of the month, new negotiations were entered into with the **Reformed**, who were gathered at the square of **Saint Mary** well five or six hundred strong in arms, ready to put their intentions further into action; at last, a four-day truce was brought about, so that in the meantime their demands could be made known to the **Duchess** <note>Margaret of Parma, the Regent of the Netherlands.</note> and the **Prince** <note>William of Orange.</note>.

<margin>
1566.
<note>Original: MDLXVI.</note>
The images at Leeuwarden broken and two Preachers brought to the pulpit. Bor 64. b. Hooft p. 105, 106.
<gloss>1</gloss> See: Ubbo Emmius's *Commentary on the Frisian Republic*, page 37. <note>Original Latin: "Vid. Ubbonis Emmii de Republ. Friſior. Comment."</note>

the moderation of the clergy and the patience of the persecuted. In Leeuwarden, nevertheless, on the sixth of September <note>Dutch: "Herfftmaendt," literally 'harvest month.'</note> all images, altars, and ornaments were cast out of the three parish churches. Yet this happened with the permission of the presiding Mayor, Tierk Walles, and the majority of the Council, some of whom even, along with the armed citizenry, brought the Teachers of the Reformed into one of the city's parish churches, called **Oldenhove** <gloss>1</gloss>. Arenberg <note>Jean de Ligne, Duke of Arenberg, the Stadtholder of the northern provinces.</note>, having been informed of this, made his way there; yet he demanded nothing more than the restoration of the churches and church services to their former state, along with the expulsion of the Preachers <gloss>3</gloss>. And when it was pointed out to him that this was not feasible due to the great number of the Reformed, he contented himself with securing the Castle with men and supplies against the threats of the rebels, who let it be known that they lacked no means to seize it.

<margin>
In Sneek the iconoclasm is prevented. Bor f. 64.
Also in Franeker. Bor f. 64. b.
</margin>
In Sneek, the breaking of images was prevented by the Law <note>The local magistracy.</note> and many citizens who opposed it; but the Mass and other church services had to be suspended. Likewise in Franeker, where the Reformed held several sermons without plundering the church.

<margin>
In Groningen the images are broken with the permission of the Magistrate. Hooft p. 106. Bor f. 65. a.
Church plundering in the Ommelanden. Bor f. 65. Hooft p. 106.

Groningen, where no person had ever been seen killed for their faith, was among the last to be overtaken by the unrest. But the example of Leeuwarden and others carried away the Reformed there; yet no further than that they took over the church of the **Friars Minor** <note>The Franciscans.</note>, leveling the images and altars with composure, by permission of the Magistrates, who ordered the city’s workmen to clear the floor of rubble and obstructions, making it fit for preaching. This, however, cost some of the workmen their lives in the year fifteen hundred and sixty-nine <note>Following the arrival of the Duke of Alba, many who participated in or assisted the iconoclasm were executed during the "Red Council" or Council of Troubles.</note>. In the villages of the **Ommelanden** <note>The rural districts surrounding the city of Groningen.</note>—at Winsum, Grashuisen, Westeremden, Ten Post, Middelstum, and elsewhere—the peasants were incited by the nobility, and many a church was plundered against the will of the Authorities, who judged that it would have been more just, in view of the freedom of conscience always enjoyed there, to spare the clergy this harassment.

Various towns in Overijssel endured the same wantonness <note>The author refers here to the "Beeldstorm" or Iconoclastic Fury described on previous pages.</note>, specifically Kampen and Zwol. But in Deventer—where Kasper Koolhaes <note>A prominent Dutch theologian who later became known for his moderate views during the Leiden conflicts.</note> preached from the fifth of September <note>Original: "Herfstmaendt" (Autumn-month).</note> until the sixth of May <note>Original: "Bloeimaendt" (Flower-month).</note> of the following year, with the knowledge and consent, and indeed at the invitation of the authorities—no one complained of mutiny or riot. No images were broken there. Those of the Papal faith were not hindered in the exercise of their religion, except only by public sermons (yet without bitterness or slander) and special admonitions from the Word of God. Through these gentle dealings, the two persuasions lived together in concord as good citizens, and many left Popery. In Luxembourg, in Artois, in a portion of Hainaut, in Namur, and thereabouts, there was neither preaching nor plundering †. How public sermons were introduced in the region of Limburg without damage to the churches shall be related in its proper place.

<margin>
Hooft p. 109...
* Nicolas Burgundius p. 321, 322.
</margin>

During the general riots, iconoclasm, and church plunderings, the Duchess of Parma <note>Margaret of Parma, the Governor-General of the Netherlands on behalf of King Philip II of Spain.</note> found herself in great distress: seeing also that all advice from Spain arrived only after the deed was done, and the evil was constantly growing, she decided—immediately upon the fresh cry of the disturbance at Antwerp, and the rumor that the same wantonness was intended for Brussels—to yield somewhat to the time and the necessity. She did this all the more because the Prince of Orange, and the Counts of Egmont, Horne, and Hoogstraten declared in the Council, *That the people, having risen to the number of two hundred thousand, were not to be disarmed without an assurance of being allowed to meet safely for preaching in the places where such was currently practiced; provided that they refrained from causing offense and lawlessness. And that otherwise the Nobles would not be satisfied, nor would the "Bands of Ordinance" <note>The elite heavy cavalry units of the Netherlands, often led by high nobility.</note> allow themselves to be employed; as they refused to serve against the Confederates <note>The "Verbond der Edelen" or League of Nobles.</note>, their brothers-in-arms, and refused to serve for the enforcement of the placards <term>placards: royal edicts that carried the force of law, specifically those related to the persecution of heresy.</term>.*

<margin>
Accord made with the bound Nobles.
Bor II. 67. b...
Hooft III. 109, 110.
Johannes Meursius, *William of Orange* book 2, 16, 17. <note>Original: J. Meurs, Gul. Aur. II. 16, 17.</note>

She was then pushed so far that, on the twenty-fourth of August <note>Original: "Oegstmaendt" (Harvest-month).</note>, she made an Accord with the bound Nobles, by which it was promised in the King’s name: to release the land from the Inquisition. Regarding the matter of religion, a new placard was to be made; though the King had not yet decided whether the States [General] were to be summoned for it; but she, the Governess, had done and would continue to do her utmost to persuade him to it. She granted letters of assurance to the Confederates in the form they felt best protected them, concerning all matters of the past.

The Nobles promised not to act against the King, his States, and subjects; but to lend a hand with all their might, and to do their utmost to still the unrest, to prevent <term>church-desecration</term> <note>Referring to the *Beeldstorm* or Iconoclastic Fury where religious art was destroyed.</note>, and to protect all clergy, other officials, and subjects of his Majesty from harassment. Furthermore, they would serve the King against foreign enemies and his rebels, according to their oath. Finally, they were to use all their influence with those who, for reasons of faith or otherwise, were currently dissatisfied, to bring it about that they should submit to whatever the King, for the advancement, peace, and unity of religion, should decide with the consent of the <term>States-General</term> <note>The representative assembly of the various provinces of the Netherlands.</note>.

One saw now, from day to day, the accepted freedom of **Religion** decrease again in many places; in some, it was narrowly restricted to certain places or times. Those who crossed these boundaries were sometimes severely punished. **Andries Bertelot**, of Hondschoote—who previously dared to accost the Priests and Monks in the streets and rebuke their teaching and life (wishing, when warned of the danger he placed himself in, to be allowed to suffer for Christ’s sake and become a witness to His truth)—now preached on the twenty-seventh of the Wine Month <note>Original: *Wijnmaendt*, referring to October.</note> near **Aalst**, against the prohibition of the **Magistrate**, in a different location than what had been designated to the Reformed for the practice of their Religion. But because of this, the gathering was disturbed, the Minister was captured, and sentenced to the gallows. Going to his death on the second of the Slaughter Month <note>Original: *Slachtmaendt*, referring to November.</note>, he sang a song of praise to God and prayed upon the ladder for his enemies.

<margin>
Disturbance at Axel.
Nic. Burgundius III. 371, 372.
</margin>
At **Axel**, there was still much trouble with the **iconoclasts** <note>Original: *beeldtstormers*, those who destroyed religious imagery during the "Beeldenstorm" of 1566.</note> at this time. Some were punished there. In order to release several who sat imprisoned there, a certain **Attorney** <term>Procureur</term> <note>A legal representative or official.</note> undertook a bold piece of work. Having stirred up about a thousand people to help them out, he climbed the ramparts with them; yet with so much noise and so little order that the citizenry became aware of them, ran to arms, and repelled the attack. Twenty remained dead on the spot, and one or two were captured. This was resistance by open violence.

<margin>
The ministers are expelled from Utrecht and taken outside the city.

</margin>
The **Duchess** <note>Margaret of Parma, the Regent of the Netherlands.</note> also opposed that which had been negotiated with some degree of order by certain Reformed groups. Thus, she commanded that what had been granted in **Utrecht** and **Amsterdam**—being in conflict with the <term>Accord</term> <note>The "Accord" of August 25, 1566, which supposedly granted limited rights to Protestant preaching.</note> entered into with the Nobles—be nullified. In Utrecht, the agreement of the twenty-seventh of the August Month <note>Original: *Oegstmaendt*.</note> was revoked by the public ringing of bells; and the Reformed were ordered to vacate **St. James’s Church**, and to preach not in the city, but outside of it. This command was obeyed; and five hundred men were taken into pay at the expense of the city and the clergy <note>These men were hired as a garrison or guard to maintain order and enforce the new restrictions.</note>.

In **Amsterdam**, matters were left as they stood; the Magistrate was fearful of opening a door to a riot. Yet there, the Reformed meanwhile provided themselves with Ministers and brought their church into better order. Their charge, and the call to his person, was made known to him. It was shown to him that *Jan Arentszoon*, their Preacher, had testified of him, how he, having full knowledge of the truth, had often deliberated with him to leave **Popery** <note>Original: *Pausdom*, a term used by reformers to describe the Roman Catholic Church</note>; but that his great burden of wife and children stood in his way and held him back. But now, it was added, *God provided the means to provide for him and his family, through the **Reformed** congregation of the city of Amsterdam*. Also, the time had now come to be of greater service. He ought not to extinguish the light that was kindled in him; but, in this time of freedom, to share it with the congregation; otherwise, he would have to give an account of that neglect to his Lord and God.

<margin>His answer. <margin>* See pages 322, 333.</margin> **Jan Arentsz**, though he understood nothing but his mother tongue <note>Dutch</note>; was on the other hand gifted with a bold intellect and sound judgment; because of this, he spoke with such order*, and was remarkably well-read in the Holy Scriptures, to the point of causing wonder. His zeal made him bold: with his eloquence, he knew how to move the hearts and kidneys <note>A biblical idiom meaning one's deepest emotions and thoughts; original: *herten en nieren*</note> of people in his preaching: he reasoned very sharply, and could powerfully withstand his opponents, not only the **Papists** <note>Adherents of the Roman Catholic Church</note>, but also **Arians**, **Anabaptists** of all kinds, and all sorts of **Libertines** <note>In this context, a term for those who held unconventional or radical spiritual views</note>. Many then brought their abundance of jewels and clothing to the Deacons; or turned them into money and placed it in their hands.

# H I S T O R Y

<margin>1566.</margin> ...as had been determined by the Aldermen <term>Wethouders; city officials responsible for administration and justice</term>, the Burgomasters <term>Burgermeefters; the chief magistrates of the city</term> sent forty guards into the church, with orders to let no one in except for the corpse.

<margin>*Memoirs of L. J. Reael folio 50. b... Hooft III. 112, 113.*</margin> When the funeral procession arrived before the church door, the friends of the deceased believed that the Sexton <term>Kofter; the officer in charge of the church building</term> would open it, just as he had been accustomed to doing since the twenty-sixth of the previous month; therefore they knocked. But as the guards intended to follow their orders, two men went to the Burgomasters, requesting that at least the immediate relatives be allowed into the church with the body. This was refused.

<margin>*Reael folio 51. a.*</margin> They then had to let the deceased be brought in and request the Sexton to receive the body. The outer door was opened, but the people—for while waiting there, a large crowd had gathered near the South door by the funeral train—presumed to force their way in at the same time. The guards sought to close the door, and indeed, one of the group leveled his musket <term>roer; an early type of firearm</term> and shot a certain man through the arm. But the commoners <term>’t graeu; a term for the lower-class masses</term>, hearing this, rushed in with such force that the guards, having no heart to face them, threw down their weapons and fled to the City Hall; where their gear was later carried to them without anyone being harmed. Then the dead man was buried. No further violence was committed there, as the commoners allowed themselves to be persuaded by some citizens to vacate the church, which was immediately locked.

<margin>*The commoners go to the Greyfriars’ monastery. Reael folio 51. b, a.*</margin> But it did not stop there: once the people were stirred up, they continued on their way and headed for the Greyfriars’ monastery <term>Minrebroêrs kloofter; a Franciscan friary</term>, shouting to one another that there must be something happening inside. This was because fifty armed men, stationed there about three weeks prior to protect the Monks, had not conducted themselves quietly. It was heard that a musket occasionally went off, and people convinced themselves that many men-at-arms or military supplies were hidden there. Having arrived before the monastery, nothing was done at first, but the crowd steadily grew.

<margin>*The most prominent Reformed citizens are requested to still the riot. Reael folio 51. b.*</margin> Some of the most prominent Reformed <note>The early Dutch Protestants following the teachings of John Calvin</note> citizens—such as Master Marten Koster, Clement, and Frans Volkertsz. Reael—who happened to be walking on the Dam <note>The central square of Amsterdam</note> at the time, were called by the Burgomasters to the Little Tower <note>Het Toorentje; a specific part of the Amsterdam City Hall used for council meetings</note>. They went there, except for Reael. They were entreated to go immediately to the monastery to calm the commoners; they were also authorized to promise on behalf of the Burgomasters that the Monks would depart from their monastery that very evening. <margin>1566. Second, regarding banishment.</margin>
...persecution could have prevented. Regarding banishment and the seizure of property, it may well be argued that subjects are not permitted to reject the laws of the Sovereign; but the common man will not accept this, for he would sooner lose his life than his livelihood and his fatherland. Therefore, look upon us as being once again in the necessity of starting a war, and of driving a multitude of people—primarily craftsmen—out of the country, and with them, all prosperity.

<margin>Third, regarding the granting of freedom of conscience without the exercise of religion.</margin>
The granting of simple freedom of conscience <note>The right to believe what one wishes in private, provided there is no public worship or assembly</note> would be more reasonable, yet it would be a means to nurture all manner of sects and heresies here, and leave the rest in a state of Atheism or God-forsakenness. From this, nothing but total disobedience without any respect for authority can arise. For the non-Romans <note>Protestants</note>, being on one hand wary of public Papal rites and on the other hand deprived of their own specific practice, would thus, in the course of time, concern themselves with neither God nor religion. They would die no differently than the senseless cattle, without caring for their souls; and so, instead of helping the evil, one would fall into the greatest evil of all. The King (it is well known) will sooner think it better to lose a great part of his land than to allow freedom of practice, or to do anything to the detriment of the old Religion.

<margin>Fourth, concerning the granting of free exercise of religion.</margin>
Various great Princes, and all his Council, both here and in Spain, will strengthen him in this: partly out of specific views of their own advantage, and partly out of ignorance of the country's situation. But how has such stubbornness in this matter fared for his neighbors? Those who—having seen their entire state collapse with irredeemable damage and terror—have learned to choose the lesser of two evils, and rather to yield somewhat to the times than to run their heads against a wall. For a conviction upon which a person believes his salvation depends takes deeper and deeper root, despite all violence.

But what if, sooner or later, we find ourselves at war again? Where would one find safety if exiles and refugees—driven by a longing for their fatherland and property, and provoked by a desire for revenge—were to use their knowledge of all the country's secrets to serve the foreigner? What if internal discontent, like a suppressed resentment constantly brewing, were to burst out all at once? What if one had the enemy at the chest, at the heels, and in one's own bosom? To avoid these difficulties, there appears no closer way than to set aside certain places for the free exercise of religion:

Likewise, the Emperor Constantine, who earned the title "the Great" because he, contrary to the rule of his predecessors, allowed places to be established for Christians to hold their assemblies, just as the Heathens had their temples. By doing so, he stilled countless complaints, prevented much bloodshed, pacified his empire, and through this harmony became prosperous and powerful. <margin>Franciscus Junius travels to the land of Limburg. *Franciscus Junius in his life [autobiography], p. 19.*</margin>
He therefore departed—for the congregation did not wish for him to leave the territory of the Netherlands, as was feared—on the fourteenth of October <note>Original: "Wijnmaendt" (Wine Month), the traditional Dutch name for October</note> for Limburg. He left all his household goods, including books and clothing, in the care of the Antwerp brothers with their consent; because of this, it later happened that he lost everything. On the following day, he arrived in the land of Limburg; where much hardship befell him thereafter.

<margin>Arrives at Herve; *Junius, ibid.*</margin>
No sooner had he set foot inside Herve (a village known throughout the Netherlands and Germany for the fame of its good cheese) than a riot broke out: but he kept himself out of that uproar and kept all those inside his house under control. The following day he was led to Limburg <note>The fortified capital of the Duchy of Limburg</note>. Here the Magistrates refused to allow his ministry to be exercised through their efforts. The good people taking this refusal poorly, he returned to a village named Summan.

<margin>Gives the first sermon to the people of Limburg, in great danger. *Junius, ibid.*</margin>
On Friday, the eighteenth of October, he delivered the first sermon to the people of Limburg in the open field, not far from Herve, along the road leading toward Liège, with a reasonable crowd in attendance. There stood a man directly behind him, armed with a hunting spear, who had previously sworn to kill him if he could only get close enough for his pike to reach. God "softened" that man, spear and all, so that he listened to the sermon with a calm mind and in peace. After the sermon, they went to Herve, about a hundred and thirty men strong, to eat the midday meal: however, an official sent from Limburg arrived at the same place with his servants to seize the Preacher, if it were possible. This official ordered the church bell to be rung to openly call the people to arms and summoned the inhabitants from the neighboring villages to come running. The Reformed <note>The Calvinist Protestants</note>, having barely sat down at the table, left their meal and came outside, still fasting. A great noise arose: men stood before the door in arms and fortified all the approaches to protect the Teacher and the house against all violence. However, since it was said that the people from the entire region would gather in very great numbers, as they indeed did, he did not wish to refuse his service—even though he had been warned of the approaching danger—nor did he want the stain of faint-hearted sluggishness to be cast upon him, which would reflect poorly on the ministry of the Gospel that had been entrusted to him. While they were preaching, all the people took flight twice, even though he earnestly called them back: twice they were brought back together by him. The first time they were moved by a loose rumor and news from a boy; the second time they were frightened by the sight of a good number of armed horsemen (for it is said there were about eighty of them) sent out by the Bishop of *Liège* to capture him, who were now descending into the low valley. This was no sooner requested than it was done. Then, taking heart in the open space, she answered the questioner that she had now been so tormented for over thirteen years: and how the talk of noisy neighbor-women was the cause of it, who had formerly accused her and assured her of her damnation because, having recently been deprived of her husband, she had been so hindered by the care of her nine children—all of whom were still small—that she could find no time to serve God—that is, she said, to attend the service of the Mass (as it is called). But the States, the Court, and the city rulers were so uncooperative that he took a written record of the matter, declaring that he would use it to excuse himself to the King and the Governess for any disaster that might result from their refusal.

Dispute at Franeker over the renunciation of the covenant.

The leaders of the congregation, hearing what had transpired at Harlingen, considered the renunciation of the covenant to be of no value and desired that the message be revoked upon the advice of the Ministers <term>Leeraers: literally 'Teachers,' the title for their ordained pastors</term>. Jeroen Tinnegieter and his fellow servants, on the other hand, maintained that the renunciation was right, scriptural, and Christian. Others also requested that the entire congregation be gathered for this purpose, and that the announcement be made to everyone in a timely and proper manner. However, these pleas fell on deaf ears. Consequently, the others

<margin>
The beginning of the schism between the Frisians and the Flemish.
p. B 7.
</margin>

(who were later called Frisians, because they were mostly natives of the land) gathered by themselves and chose four men to speak against Tinnegieter and his followers. These followers were later called Flemish, as they were mostly born in Flanders or thereabouts. The Frisian party demanded that those who had renounced the covenant prove to those who still held to it that the renunciation was scriptural. They informed them that, should they refuse, they would withdraw their support and brotherly admonition, declaring that while they were willing to regard them as brothers, they would no longer recognize them as Ministers. Thus, the Frisians created such a separation over a matter they had shortly before wished to submit to the council of Ministers, and they did so without now hearing the council's advice on the matter.

p. D 8. §. 25.
</margin>

Since that time, people began to behave differently regarding the Covenant, or the order of the four cities, than they had before. Judgment on both sides followed wherever favor or hatred drove them.

J. Outermans Declaration p. B 8. §. 28.
</margin>

The Frisians sometimes equated it to the word of God, declaring that whatever the Servants <term>Dienaers: deacons or lay ministers</term> and Ministers ordained and practiced must be held as Scripture or scriptural, and that offenders should be punished as rebels and troublemakers—yet they themselves did not hold to it, but rather to the dispute that had arisen from it. The Flemish, in their renunciation, had said or pretended that they wished to fulfill the content of the covenant while leaving the other congregations free to keep it or not. But afterward, as the dispute grew, so did their aversion; they compared it to idols <note>1</note> and to those human commandments of which Matthew speaks in the fifteenth chapter <note>original: "Mattheus, in 't vijfthiende capittel" — Matthew 15:9: 'In vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men'</note>, and those which are cursed in the first chapter of the letter to the Galatians <note>2</note> <note>Galatians 1:8-9 contains Paul's curse on anyone preaching a gospel contrary to what was first received</note>. Yet they also characterized it as an indifferent matter <note>3</note> <term>middelmatige ſaek: a translation of 'adiaphora,' meaning a matter not essential to salvation</term> whenever it suited their purpose. In this manner, some believed, the unity broke.

<margin>
1. S. P. Pointing out p. 6.
2 J. Outermans declaration p. C §. 29.
3 I. Outermans declaration p. C §. 29.
</margin>

That same night it was decided to expel Ebbe from the brotherhood and to remove Jacob Vreriks from his office. This plan was carried out. Job Janssoon was one of the six messengers who the following day renounced the brotherhood to Ebbe at his house, calling him a liar and a troublemaker; without being willing, at that time, to show him any reason for the sentence despite his request. He made his complaint to the congregation.

Ruyte Renix came again to Harlingen, desiring an account of what had been undertaken against Ebbe and Jacob: but just as he had refused to give the Harlingen Flemish a reason for his actions at Franeker, so they now refused to give him an account of theirs at Harlingen.

The Frisians ban some Flemish. *P. F. 4. §. 138. I H. V. P. N. p. 27.*

Then the Frisians began to <term>ban</term> <note>The "ban" (excommunication) was a severe social and spiritual punishment in Mennonite communities, often involving "shunning," where members were forbidden from eating with, speaking to, or doing business with the banned person.</note> the Flemish. First at Harlingen, although Nette Lips tried to stop them, and afterwards also at Franeker, and this mostly (it seemed) because of the condemnation of Ebbe, which some called retaliation. First, the six messengers of Ebbe’s ban were placed under the ban; then all those who had voted for his banishment; also those who associated or walked with them. Finally, it went further. The separation, the ban, was put into effect in a terrible manner, with slanderous words and accusations of heresy <note>original: "verketteringh"</note>, and pursued from house to house; even on the streets, on roads, at wagons and ships, over man and woman, over servant and maid. But before it came fully to that, a peace negotiation was brought about, which had a very unfortunate outcome and produced much more discord.

<margin>
The Brabant Teachers come a second time to Friesland. *I, Outermans Verkl. p. G 5, §. 188.*
</margin>
The Brabant <term>Teachers</term>, with several other men from their congregations, were sent a second time to Friesland to find a fair means of peace, demanding an account from both sides in each other's presence. To this the Frisians would not agree. The Brabantians had requested Jan Willemssoon and Lubbert Gerritssoon, North Holland Teachers at Hoorn, by letter to travel with them to Friesland, but the <term>Ministers</term> <note>Dienaers: Literally "servants," referring to the lay ministers of the congregation.</note> of the congregation in North Holland, having been asked about it, raised difficulties regarding the journey, unless a request was also made by Huyte’s side to have them there, just as had happened from the Flemish side. The congregations in North Holland did not desire that Jan Willems and Lubbert Gerritssoon should cease their service, nor travel to Emden, where they were summoned; but they requested that Dirk Philips, with his assistants, should come to Hoorn to handle the matter before the congregation there. Many criticized Dirk because, without the authorization of his own congregation which had sent him, he suspended other Teachers and Church servants from their ministry and renounced brotherhood; this was done without the knowledge and against the will of their own congregation, to whom the judgment of their misconduct actually belonged. But he was judged in almost the same way, and measured with the same measure.

A certain meeting of the Frisian side gathered at Hoorn. They consulted with various congregations about visiting Dirk Philips at Emden. He, in opposition, let them know that he stood by his previous demand: if the Frisians, Huyte with the strict party, <note>The "strict party" (Dutch: *fijnen*, literally "the subtle ones") refers to the faction that advocated for a more rigorous application of the "ban" or excommunication.</note> and the Dutch Judges would speak with their parties in his presence, accusing, defending, and explaining everything, then he would hear them; but if they refused that, then they were dismissed.

Dirk Philips, who the year before had published an earnest exhortation to Christian peace to the four cities, now brought to print in Emden a short account of the disputed dealings, directed straight against the Frisians. These men contended to hold a discussion with him regarding it <gloss>1</gloss>, which he refused; giving reasons for this refusal in a certain justification, which he called an *Apologia* <note>original: "Schutreden" - a formal defensive speech or writing</note>, and likewise brought to light. *The conversation that they now demanded, he pointed out, they had previously refused when he desired it. It was unjust that they wished to negotiate with him whom they themselves had already judged. To speak with apostates and to exhort them as brothers, who wished to be so exhorted, that was permitted to him: but to speak much with apostates who come there to maintain their injustice, to speak against the truth, to grieve the godly, and to pervert the listeners, was not only useless and in vain, but also openly against the word of God.* He would, therefore, hold no conversation with these people unless they first revoked the judgment they had given over him and others, and performed such penance as might stand before God and his congregation. Only then should both parties speak with one another, according to his previous demand: after which he was ready to justify himself. Meanwhile, his letters to Huyte Renix, Jan Willems, and Lubbert Gerritszoon, containing the renunciation of brotherhood, gained the force of law among the Flemish. From this there first arose a shunning <gloss>2</gloss> <note>The "mijding" or shunning was the practice of avoiding all social and business contact with excommunicated members</note> without a formal ban, so it was called, yet the ban was sufficiently included within it, and shortly thereafter it emerged in its full power. For at that time, they brought about this general ban and shunning—which some believe was decided only through the actions of four Flemish-leaning Teachers <gloss>3</gloss>—against all the Frisians. To go from house to house and announce the ban to the people, head by head, following the lead of the Frisians, was deemed too difficult <note>original: "had te veel voeten in d'aerde" - an idiom meaning it was too complicated or cumbersome</note>. It was then found advisable to cut off the entire group, with all its adherents, without distinction, without address, instruction, or exhortation, with a single word and judgment, wherever they might reside. Consequently, all congregations had to shun them, even though many had little or no knowledge of what was being charged against them. Those who refused to shun them were likewise to be shunned. <gloss>4</gloss> Then almost all the congregations in Brabant and Flanders, Groningen, the Ommelanden, and in East Friesland, as well as many in Holland, declared themselves for the Flemish: yet the congregation at Zierikzee, holding itself between the two without choosing a side,

Even Jan Willemssoon, one of the foremost Dutch arbitrators or judges over that unfortunate dispute—I recount this from the words of a pious descendant—was later heard to say boldly: That he would rather be torn apart by four horses on the Red Stone <note>original: "roode steen"; the main square in Hoorn where executions and punishments took place</note> (as the market in Hoorn is called) than to ever again, by word or deed, lend a hand to the making of any schism.

<margin>The Brabantian or Flemish Teachers separate themselves from the Frisians.</margin>
Since Dirk Philips had been given such a dismissal, the Brabantian or Flemish Teachers Hans Bosschaerdt, Hendrik van Arnhem, and Hendrik van Roseveldt also separated themselves from the Frisians, viewing them as apostates who had separated themselves from God's congregations.

Refuses to enter into discussion with them over it. *p. C. v. p. D. iij.*

Dirk Philips, who the year before had published an earnest exhortation toward Christian peace to the four cities, now brought to light in Emden a short account of the contentious dealings in print, directed straight against the Frisians. They requested to hold a discussion with him regarding this <sup>1</sup>, which he refused; giving reasons for his refusal in a certain Justification, which he called a *Schutreden* <note>original: "Schutreden"; a defensive speech or apology</note>, and likewise brought to the light of day. *The discussion they now demanded, he pointed out, they had previously refused when he himself had desired it. It was unjust that they wished to negotiate with him whom they themselves had already judged. To speak with apostates and to exhort them as brothers, who wished to be so exhorted, was permitted to him: but to speak much with apostates who come to assert their own wrong, to contradict the truth, to grieve the godly, and to pervert the listeners, was not only useless and in vain, but also openly against the word of God. He would therefore hold no discussion with these people unless they first revoked the judgment they had passed over him and others, and performed such penance as might stand before God and His congregation.* Only then were both parties to speak with one another, according to his previous demand: *after which he was prepared to answer for himself.*

It was then found advisable to cut off the entire crowd, with all its adherents, without distinction, without address, instruction, or exhortation, with a single word and judgment, wherever they might reside. Those who were offended, still not satisfied, spoke to him again—accompanied by one or two witnesses—acting, as it were, according to the **rule of Christ** <margin>† Matthew xviii. 15, 16, 17.</margin> <note>The biblical procedure for resolving grievances: first privately, then with witnesses, then before the church</note>. N. p. 34.</margin>, who placed the accused under the **ban** <term>ban: a formal act of excommunication where a person is cast out of the church and social community</term>, even though he confessed his guilt for a third time and begged for forgiveness. Furthermore, his wife was commanded to **shun** <note>original: *mijden*; the practice of avoiding all social and physical contact with an excommunicated person</note> her apostate, or rather, cast-out husband, in accordance with the congregation's rules. But the wife (her loyalty deserves that her name be known), **Doede, daughter of Dirk**, paid no heed to either the ban or the command to shun him. She remained with her husband just as before. Those who had imposed the ban found themselves in a difficult position and did not see fit to punish the woman. The man himself was even harassed by them, yet after the passing of nine months <margin>p. 35.</margin>, he was readmitted. 

Thus, at times, they allowed their high pretensions to fall away; and on some occasions, one saw the cord of **strictness** pulled so tight among these people that it snapped in their own hands. Yet at other times and places, hatred gained so much ground among certain stubborn people that, in order to give more force to the shunning of the separated—whether they were spouses, blood relatives, or strangers—they not only forbade the maintenance of Christian friendship, spiritual and other intimacy, or civil social interaction, but even the performing of all other duties of mutual service and help, even in the event of **danger by fire or water** 1. <margin>1 Against such hardness, Menno <note>Menno Simons, the leader from whom the Mennonites take their name</note>, who calls it a "pagan cruelty," had already spoken out around the year 1550. Someone allows himself to be killed for a faith, yet without love.</margin> Such a shunning had been experienced and witnessed by the author of the account of these schisms himself. He who wrote the life of the last King of the Anabaptists says he saw two **Anabaptists** <note>original: *Wederdoopers*</note> in Antwerp, both of whom had been sentenced to death. To follow [these events], I have stepped outside the scope of the time, where the story must now be resumed in 1567. On the same day that the Reformed in Amsterdam held the Lord’s Supper*, the Prince of Orange hurried there, arriving in the evening; he remained for about six weeks to bring the city into order. Two days after his arrival, an attempt was made through a ridiculous incident to provoke him against the Reformed. † At the corner of the Long Bridge stood a small house or little chapel containing a small statue of Mary, where the wife of a certain sand-carrier <note>Sand-carriers were laborers who transported sand for construction or floor-covering</note> kept her stall and sold the wax candles that people lit before the image. Her husband, while sitting at a drinking session with his companions, was mocked by them because of this. "You may well feast at our expense," they said, "for your wife is in partnership with Our Lady. They share the candle money together." He, being drunk, flew into a rage, ran home, attacked his wife with his fists, and knocked over her stall. She ran out the door, pulled it shut behind her, and locked him inside. Then, distressed and—due to the drink—without caution, he began to toll the small bell that hung there. As the neighbors and many people came running together, he was seized by an even greater fear. At last, he climbed out the window and ran toward the Reguliers Gate, where the watch detained him; however, through the intercession of others, they let him go again. 

This incident was reported to the Prince by the Burgomasters as if people were now daring to resume the **Iconoclasm** <term>Iconoclasm: the "Image-Breaking" (Beeldtstormerij), a wave of destruction of Catholic religious art that swept the Netherlands in 1566</term>, even in his presence. The Prince, noticing that the magistrates had become emboldened by the news of **Egmond’s** <note>Lamoral, Count of Egmond, a high nobleman who was at this time strictly suppressing religious dissent to prove his loyalty to the Spanish Crown</note> zeal against the iconoclasts and were unwilling to grant anything to the citizens, sought to ensure the peace of the city through a new agreement. He desired that the Magistrates propose some means for peace. They refused. He reminded them that they had already, without compulsion or necessity, drafted and completed the treaty of the last of **October** <note>original: *Herffstmaendt*</note> themselves. They, in contrast, tried to claim they had been forced into it. If they would not make a proposal, was his answer, he would carry out his commission regardless and command those of the [Reformed] religion to preach outside the city. This did not please the Magistrate, as they well thought that such a thing would not happen without a riot. Therefore, it was decided by the **Vroedschap** <term>Vroedschap: the council of "wise men" or elders who served as the city's governing body</term> to put some points on paper at the request of the Prince, but with a declaration that they had only drafted them to avoid falling into his disgrace. In Leiden, on the twenty-fifth of <term>January</term> <note>Original: "Loumaendt." An archaic Dutch name for January, literally the "tanning month."</note>, in the presence of the Prince of Orange, as Stadtholder of Holland, and Cornelis Suis, Lord of Rijswijk, President of the Court, a treaty was concluded for further order, and for as long as the preaching would be tolerated, of this content:

<margin>I.</margin>
*That, to avoid all further discord in Religion, and to better prevent all other rejected sects and heresies that might be sown under the cover of reformation, of which some beginnings had already been seen—namely <term>Mennonites</term> <note>A radical Protestant group that practiced adult baptism and pacifism, often viewed as a threat to social order by both Catholics and mainstream Protestants.</note> and <term>Adamites</term> <note>An extremist sect that sought to return to the innocence of Eden, sometimes through practicing nudity.</note>... those of the Reformed Religion should make a declaration of their so-called <margin>(* purported)</margin> Religion and doctrine, without performing any other preaching or teaching under that cover, whether they followed the Augsburg Confession, or the Religion of Calvin, or others that were then tolerated. (Upon this, those of the Religion declared, through the mouth of Juriaen Epessoon, their Preacher, that they wished to profess no other Religion than the sincere <term>Augsburg Confession</term> <note>The primary confession of faith for the Lutheran Church.</note>, just as it was professed by Melanchthon and explained in his letter to the <term>Count Palatine</term> <note>The Elector of the Palatinate, a high-ranking prince of the Holy Roman Empire.</note>.)*

<margin>II.</margin>
*That, accordingly, those of the Reformed Religion should help prevent and ward off all other sects and heresies, and give the Magistrate all assistance therein.*

<margin>III.</margin>
*That they should use no new ceremonies of singing or otherwise in the burial of their dead; however, they would not be forced to use the customary ecclesiastical ceremonies either.*

<margin>IV.</margin>
*That they should be allowed to hold no meetings, in secret or in public, inside or outside the city, except for their preaching: if any other meeting or consultation were necessary, they should inform the City Government of it and its cause, so that they might attend if they so pleased.*

<margin>1567. <note>original: "MDLXVII"</note></margin>...noticing and bringing in the pure truth; they had to mostly occupy themselves with resisting the frenzy of the Antichrist <note>A term commonly used by Protestant reformers to refer to the Pope or the Roman Catholic institutional power.</note>, refuting slanders, writing defenses, and disputing with **Monks and Papists** <note>original: "Monniken en Papen"; "Papen" (Papists) was a derogatory term for those loyal to the Pope.</note>. They had little opportunity to investigate the truth of Christian doctrine, as revealed in the word of God, in peace and through constant attention. This was the reason that their writings were filled with so many biting words, mocking and insulting names, and other unbecoming speech, which did not suit the **true Servants of God and proclaimers of the Gospel of peace**. Nevertheless, we tolerate such weaknesses, he said, out of respect for those unhappy times. But must we nowadays, now that God has sent us so many rays of his clarity, still remain hanging onto the light that came from the lightning bolts, which have already passed by? All this I say to prove how little reason

<margin>One must not make idols of the Teachers.</margin>we have on either side to make Gods, or (to speak better) Idols of our Teachers, and for their sake to always drive partisanship, strife, and conflict regarding the matter of our doctrine, to the offense of weak souls and the notable hindrance of the increase of the Christian congregation. If those of Corinth were rebuked because they created factions in the name of the holy **Paul**, **that chosen vessel of God**, **an Apostle of the Lord Jesus**, **a Teacher of the Gentiles**, a person endowed with most excellent gifts; how much more will God punish us then, if we, to maintain the opinions of some, strive against one another and wage war without ceasing; and, so to speak, snarl at each other like cats and dogs; and in doing so break the bond of love, which Christ has so dearly commanded us.

<margin>Christ gave his own love as a sign. She had never intended to allow the practice of non-Roman religion, but on the contrary, had promised the Nobles to prevent preaching where it had not occurred before that time. Never had it entered her mind to permit such disorder as to establish Consistories <margin>* Church Councils.</margin>, or to set up new Magistrates who would collect money—reaching several millions—to raise troops against their Lord, as people boasted; to seize the Sacraments for themselves; to throw the entire doctrine and church policy into confusion; to use unusual methods of confirming marriages, leading to the obscuring of the legality of inheritances; and a thousand other things to which they themselves saw no end. By granting such things, she would have far forgotten herself and her duty. Therefore, she had rightly written to the cities that the practice of this religion was not permitted. The agreement <note>The Accord of August 23, 1566.</note> spoke only of tolerating preaching, which she had allowed in some places out of necessity, provided it was without weapons or offense. The assurance was given not for the preaching itself, but to the Nobles on account of their covenant and petition. But they, in order to undermine the authority of the King, her own, and that of the Magistrates, had—against their own consciences—allowed so many cursed practices of heresy to be introduced, twisting the sincerity of her intentions and making her appear so loathsome to the common people... One passed over in silence what had been committed since and against the treaty by the foremost of these Nobles: statues and altars had been broken, churches and monasteries plundered; the preachings, which previously were only held in the open countryside, had been brought into the cities; the churches seized; the clergy driven out; foreign preachers called in; some sent out to stir up the lands where these novelties had not yet taken place; taking the rebels under their protection; and the royal artillery and weaponry seized;

# HISTORY OF THE REFORMATION. BOOK VIII.

### 1567 <note>original: "MDLXVII."</note>

...[confe]deration, <note>The word "deringe" on this page completes "confederatie" (confederation) or "vergaderinge" (assembly) from the previous page.</note> which might be made, whether under the guise of the **new Religion**, or other causes, not permitted nor authorized on behalf of his aforementioned Majesty: and that likewise I shall not be helpful, nor consent to sermons, whether in public or in secret, or other exercises of the **new Religion**; and furthermore I shall behave myself peacefully and modestly without proposing any novelty, awaiting that which shall be ordained by his Majesty, by the advice of the Lords of the Councils and the States, or otherwise.

Those who could not, or would not, take this oath, had to withdraw or suffer.

<margin>
Jan Bek refuses the oath.
From some notes of J. Wtenbogaert. <note>Johannes Wtenbogaert was a prominent Dutch Remonstrant leader and historian.</note>
</margin>
Jan Bek Michielszoon, a schoolmaster in Lier, refused the oath because no Christian, he understood, was permitted to swear to be obedient to the Authorities in everything, without any exception or contradiction, even if it were against his conscience: appealing to the example of the Apostles, who said to the leaders of the Jews: *Judge ye, whether it be right before God to hearken unto you more than unto God.* <note>Acts 4:19</note> Therefore, he said, I do not intend to swear to that point nor to keep it. Because of this answer, he was imprisoned on the twenty-fourth of April <note>original: "Graſmaendt" — literally "Grass-month," an archaic Dutch name for April.</note>, but how it ended for him is not told.

<margin>
Services of the Prince of Orange; Bor III. 103. b. Hooft IV. 129. His magnanimity.
</margin>
<margin>
Returns again to Antwerp, where they seek to stop the preaching. Bor III. 108... Hooft IV. 129.
</margin>
The **Prince of Orange**, having helped Holland, Zeeland, and Utrecht to peace, restricted the preaching mostly to the countryside. Having turned down a gift of fifty-five thousand guilders, which the States offered him for his troubles, he traveled back to Antwerp: there the Magistrates, at the prodding of the Regent, were advised to demand that the **Reformed** and **Lutherans** cease their preaching, in order to prevent the arrival of a foreign army, which would involve the certain loss of trade, prosperity, and freedom.

The delegates of the non-Catholics <note>original: "Onroomſchen" — literally "Non-Romans," referring to Protestants.</note>, having spoken with their people about this, declared, *that they could not yet do otherwise than abide by the agreements made, and would gladly know whether it was intended to keep them or not?* The Magistrate answered: that this question was untimely, but that they should heed their warning and request their dismissal.

<margin>
By the breaking out of a sudden fire in the Minrebroeders Monastery in Antwerp, the monks were caught.
</margin>
In this state of affairs, on the sixteenth of February <note>original: "Sprokkelmaendt" — literally "Fuel-gathering month," an archaic Dutch name for February.</note>, late in the evening, a heavy fire unexpectedly broke out at the <term>Minrebroeders</term> <note>Minorites, or Franciscan friars.</note>, near the bell of the monastery. A great multitude of people, noticing the fire from outside, ran there and found the Monks feasting, fattening themselves most luxuriously with boiled and roasted meats, to the great offense and scandal of many; for it was then precisely the [first...] <note>The text cuts off at the catchword "eersten," likely referring to the first days of Lent, making the monks' feast particularly scandalous.</note>

He explained the foundations of the Christian faith and drew many people back to the Roman church. Such was the effect that even the Catholics had to admit the change was due more to the diligence of the spiritual guardians than to the congregation itself. This roused the Calvinist Ministers to make up for the loss; along with more earnest preaching, they sought a following among the poor through generous distributions of alms. However, the Magistrates, who were not foolish, prevented this by forbidding the collection of money for such purposes. Near Antwerp, matters proceeded to actual violence. But the people answered with curses and slanders, threatening to shoot, as some indeed did; indeed, a certain <term>shearer</term> <note>A worker who trimmed the nap of woolen cloth</note> presumed to hold a loaded <term>arquebus</term> <note>An early type of portable long gun</note> to the Prince’s chest, crying out, *“You honorless and villainous traitor, you are the cause of this game, and that our brothers out there are being slaughtered and murdered.”* The artillery was fetched from the Eekhof, the city’s arsenal, and the muzzles were turned toward all the streets leading onto the Meir. A treaty was struck with their representatives, but it was rejected by the great multitude. They wanted to go to the market by force to drive the soldiers from there and seize the town hall. One had to deliver two barrels of powder and several bullets to them before they ran to fetch them themselves. Night fell; and several times a cry went up, *“Papists out, Papists out!”* It was pointed out to them that this went against the Accord of September <note>original: "Herfstmaendt." An agreement reached the previous year regarding religious exercise</note>. A part of them nevertheless wanted to push through; they flew to the monasteries, broke open the Steen, or city prison, and let the prisoners out. All the following day, people were busy attempting to frame a new agreement. But those of the Meir, listening to nothing, remained under arms through the following night, threatening to drive not only the clergy but also the Lutherans out of the city, unless they took their side. The Prince, almost at his wits’ end, thereupon sought help from those of the Augsburg Confession <note>The Lutherans</note>, bringing it about that they offered to join forces with the Catholics <note>original: "Pausgefinden," literally "Pope-aligned"</note> and the foreign merchants, if the ill-disposed—

->OF THE REFORMATION. BOOK VIII.<-

<margin>1567. <note>original: "MDLXVII."</note></margin>
...could be brought to no reason, nor to the laying down of their weapons. Therefore, on the fifteenth of the month, they took the Shore <note>The *Oever*, a district near the river Scheldt</note>; driving from there a great crowd of the Reformed <note>Calvinist Protestants</note>. In the Kipdorp <note>A district and gate in Antwerp</note> the Italians, Spaniards, and Portuguese were made to gather; the English were ordered to arm themselves within their houses. The Reformed, on the other hand, had the drums beaten to announce that the Lutherans had reached an agreement with them and were to gather on the Meir, so as to separate them from the Catholics <note>original: "Papiſten"</note>; but this ruse was immediately thwarted by the Magistrates through a different proclamation. At the same time, the Catholics, the Lutherans, and those of foreign tongues were told *that it was not about Religion here, but a plot to get at the money and goods of people of means.* Upon this, they declared themselves willing to risk life and limb for the King's service, the preservation of the city, and their wives and children. Here it was hardness against hardness, and it seemed destined to result in a bloody battle and mutual slaughter. The Catholics spread rumors of bringing boats filled with gunpowder under the Meir—which is a large, vaulted bridge—to blow up everything upon it. But the Reformed, seeing that they were beset on all sides and too weak against such a great multitude, lost their courage and then laid down their weapons and the uprising at once; settling for the treaty *that they had previously rejected.*

<margin>* Bor III. 111, b. 112. a. <note>Pieter Bor, a contemporary historian of the Dutch Revolt.</note></margin>
In this treaty, it was granted to them among other things: *That no garrison would be allowed in the city except with the consent of all the members of the city, with their full council, without making a distinction on account of Religion. All agreements made on the matter of Religion were to be held in force; and that which had occurred in these days was to be considered as done for the preservation of the city.*

<margin>Hooft III. 87. <note>P.C. Hooft, author of the 'Nederlandsche Historiën'.</note></margin>
Thus Antwerp owed its preservation on this day to the Lutherans, alongside the Catholics: a clear proof that many different persuasions are better to handle and lead than two types under one Government.

Meanwhile, one saw the affairs of the <term>Reformed: The Protestant movement following the teachings of John Calvin</term> in the Netherlands failing more and more. Valenciennes was forced by <term>Noircarmes: Philippe de Noircarmes, the Spanish-appointed governor of Hainaut</term> in March <note>original: "Lentemaendt," literally "Spring month," a common Dutch term for March</note> to accept a garrison, relying on the King’s mercy and verbal promises of fair treatment. But once he was master of the city, Michiel Herlin, the Governor of the city, his son, and several wealthy citizens, had to pay with their heads *. Old Herlin † had at one time, before the siege of the city, been warned by the Count of Hoorn that the King would not allow the New Religion, and was asked what he intended to do in such a case; for it was thought that the people of Valenciennes would admit the French. But he had answered him: *“In that case I shall depart for Germany, with all my property, if I can; or if not, at least with my person; but never shall I go to France, nor permit the French to set foot within Valenciennes. I would rather have all my guts pulled out upon the walls. For I wish to be faithful to my Prince.”* <note>The "Prince" here refers to King Philip II of Spain, the sovereign of the Netherlands at the time.</note> During his imprisonment, his brother-in-law, a lawyer, drafted a certain Petition to be submitted in his name at Brussels, in which it was stated that consideration should be given to his age, that he had lived according to the laws of the Roman mother-church, like his parents, and wished to persist therein to the end. But the prisoner spoke out against the Writer, who read these words to him: *“Write that in former times I lived according to the custom of the Roman church, but such...”* <note>The text ends mid-sentence; the catchword indicates the sentence continues with "henceforth" or "from now on."</note>

When the sentence of death was announced to them, they received the message like good news, and prepared themselves as cheerfully for death as if they were going to a wedding: exhorting, warning, stirring up, strengthening, and comforting everyone with the hope of a better life after this one. See to it well, Guido cried, among others, to his fellow prisoners, that you do nothing against your conscience, for I see clearly how the enemies of the Gospel will employ all violence and craftiness to make you waver; to mislead you and make you act against your better knowledge. Peregrin de la Grange testified on the ladder <note>The ladder leading to the gallows</note> with a loud voice: that he died for no other reason than that he had proclaimed and defended the pure truth of God to the people: for this, he took heaven and earth as witnesses. Guido de Bres intended to offer his prayer before climbing up, and knelt for that purpose on the scaffold: but they yanked him upright and onto the ladder, where, locking his feet between the rungs, he still exhorted the people to behave respectfully toward the <term>Magistrate: The local civil government and officials</term>: pointing out to them that some in this matter had not performed their duty as they ought. 

<margin>Guido’s last words.</margin>
Afterward, he prayed that they would remain steadfast in the teaching which he had proclaimed to them: furthermore, likewise testifying with high words that he had preached nothing but God's pure truth. But before he had finished, a signal was given to the executioner to throw him off. Then a great commotion arose among the soldiers guarding the market. They ran, without anyone knowing what drove them, through the city with great turbulence, shooting at both <term>Papists: A contemporary term for Roman Catholics</term> and others: many were wounded, some shot dead.

Before I depart from Limburg, I cannot refrain from relating something that happened nearby that is noteworthy and serves as a mirror for cruel Rulers: a history recorded and left behind from the testimony of a Roman Catholic court clerk. A certain Confessor <note>likely a Reformed minister</note>, condemned on account of Religion, was brought a short distance toward the stake to be burned. On the way, he sang Psalms and Hymns with a wonderful courage. The Bailiff <term>Amtman</term> <note>a high-ranking regional administrative and judicial official</note> of the place, annoyed because he perceived greater joy in the prisoner than in his opponents, commanded him to be silent. The other continued singing and confessed his hope with joy. Thereupon

<margin>
Cruelty of an Official punished.
</margin>

the Sheriff <term>Schout</term> <note>a local official responsible for carrying out arrests and executions</note>, in a fit of rage, had his tongue pulled out to its furthest extent and cut off close to the root. The martyr died in silence and peace. Not long afterward, a son was born to the Bailiff whose tongue hung out of his mouth down to his chin, like a deer that had been hunted for a long time, and he could never pull it back within his lips. This, even if it were caused in the mother by a powerful imagination and a loathing of the cruel deed, could also be a working of divine vengeance.

Shortly after the settling of the Antwerp disturbances, the Prince of Orange requested that the Governess <note>Margaret of Parma, the Regent of the Netherlands</note> entrust his governorships to someone else, claiming that necessity forced him to go to Germany to arrange his private affairs. In response, she urged him through Secretary Johan Berti to persevere in his service and to take the new oath. He remained firm in his refusal and gave, among others, these reasons: that having sworn to uphold the privileges of the Provinces under his authority, if he were commanded to do anything against them, he could not obey while keeping that oath; nor could he remain a rebel if he took the new oath, as by it he promised to do everything commanded of him in the King's name, against whomever it might be. Zoom, and excused that action by writing to the Marchioness <note>The wife of the Marquis of Bergen</note>, explaining how she had an inkling of some plot being brewed by the heretics there, who were disturbed by the decree¹ that she had caused to be proclaimed against them a few days prior. But she concealed the death of the Marquis <note>Jean de Glymes, Marquis of Bergen, who died while being held in Spain</note>, which became public knowledge shortly thereafter and greatly increased the general panic and the inclination to flee. Because of this, seeing how the <margin>The Duchess writes letters to prevent flight. ² Bor III. 121. b. 112 d. ³ Bor f. 122. a,b.</margin> land was threatened with ruin due to the departure of both great and small, and was likely to be left half-empty of people, she thought it urgently necessary to restrain the people, as much with the hope of mercy as with the fear of punishment. But the letters² which she wrote to all the cities for this purpose were countered by the Reformed with a printed document³, attempting to impress upon everyone that her words, being ambiguous <note>original: "op schroeven staende" — literally 'standing on screws,' meaning unstable or untrustworthy</note>, were as empty or deceptive in foundation as they were fair in appearance, serving only to lead to an even more bitter cruelty. Furthermore, they released at this <margin>A Defense published by the Reformed. Bor III, 123.</margin> time a *Defense* <note>original: "Verantwoording"</note>, written in French, in which they excused themselves at length against all the slanders of rebellion.

> They had, they said, always obeyed the King in civil matters and the payment of taxes, and had sought to advance his kingdom under the Kingdom of God, the supreme King, according to the dictates of their conscience. From the patient death and exile of so many thousands of people, one could sufficiently perceive that they were not rebels. They had been condemned without a hearing. They were unjustly held to be heretics without this being proven from the Scriptures; for the Word was powerful enough to overcome all heresy. Rioters and cruel people were punished without distinction. The Catholics <note>original: "Paepen" — a derogatory term for the clergy or followers of the Pope</note> had caused the iconoclasm <term>Beeldstorm; the "Image-Storm" or widespread destruction of religious art in 1566</term> to begin, in order to be able to accuse those of the [Reformed] religion as rebels. This had been evident within Antwerp, where four Catholics had dared to resume the riot in the church, and were punished with the rope <note>execution by hanging</note> the following day. The breaking of the images was indeed proper, but it should have been carried out by the order and authority of the Magistracy. Yet it seemed that God, through a hidden judgment and unusual execution, had wished to punish that gross and terrible idolatry of the images to shame the wisdom of men; having stirred up a portion of disregarded people, women and boys, without status or power, who could give no reason for their actions; and through them, in the space of eight days, smashed all the images of the Netherlands to pieces without resistance; for all the Magistrates were seized with consternation. Thus they prayed that he would follow in the footsteps of his father’s <note>Charles V, the previous Emperor.</note> benevolence; and likewise maintain the course that necessity and experience had taught the King of France <note>Refers to the recent French edicts of pacification during their own wars of religion.</note> to be the only and supreme means to quiet disturbances, remove common miseries, and prevent bloodshed.*

This was what befitted the power of Your Majesty; this was what befitted Spanish greatness. To drive away a burning fever, one cleared the veins and the bowels. That required the lancet and poison: or at the very least, bitter drugs.”*

Proceeding against the liberties of the land, the Council bypassed the usual Courts of Justice and the local Judges under whose jurisdiction the cases originally fell. It resulted, on every side, in a catching and imprisoning of people of all ranks, all sorts, and all ages—often without any prior information or evidence. Innocent people, who were not even of the new Religion but had perhaps been only once or twice to a sermon of the <term>Reformed</term> <note>Protestants belonging to the Calvinist tradition.</note>, were put to death $^6$. The gallows, as recorded in the History of Mr. <term>Hooft</term> $^7$, stood ready; the breaking-wheels, the stakes, and the trees along the roads were laden with corpses—strangled, beheaded, or burned. It was so dreadful that the very air, created for men to breathe, was turned into a common grave and a dwelling place for the dead.

# OF THE REFORMATION. BOOK IX.

Each day brought its own wretchedness, and the tolling of the execution bell <note>original: "bloedtklokke," a term for the bell that announced a death sentence.</note>, which, in <term>1567</term>, rang in the heart with the death of a close relative to one, a brother-in-law, or friend to another. Furthermore, Alva decided to dominate the principal cities of the country with Citadels <note>Heavy fortresses built within cities to intimidate the local population rather than defend against outside enemies.</note>, in order to keep the entire land in constraint, starting with Antwerp. But the Duchess <note>Margaret of Parma, the Governor of the Netherlands and half-sister to King Philip II.</note>, feeling herself hardly recognized and foreseeing heavy times due to the proposal of extreme severity, earnestly requested the King to be entirely relieved of her charge *. This was finally granted to her. After which she took her leave of the Estates <note>The representative assembly of the provinces.</note> by letters †—since the meeting of the same was forbidden—and returned to Italy. Yet before her departure, she warned the King of the danger which, in her opinion, hung over the head of the state. It was her fear that, just as the dread of punishment had driven many people into other regions upon the arrival of such a mighty army, surely to the great detriment of the country, now the rest—prevented from fleeing and enclosed within the Netherlands by force—would be driven with more violence toward factions and disturbances. Respect, she wrote, could not well be brought about among the Netherlanders through terror. Those who perhaps pushed forward on this path of severity would (though she wished to be mistaken in her opinion) cause the Spanish name much more envy than power: and would ruin these provinces with civil war, with foreign arms, and finally with devastation. Therefore, she begged the King most highly that, being mindful of Divine mercy and his own, and taking revenge on as few as possible, he would rather be satisfied with the penitent regret of his subjects than with their punishment. [...govern-]ment <note>Completing the sentence from the previous page: Alva, having been appointed to a government...</note> of a finer sort, but which had always been held by persons who were blood relatives of the Sovereigns, was chosen by the King, and he immediately proceeded with the shedding of blood; so that in a short time, over eighteen hundred prisoners died at the hands of the executioners. The refugees now considered themselves fortunate to have escaped with their lives; they bore their exile and poverty with greater patience and lived together, comforting and supporting one another under foreign roofs, like brothers and friends. A large number of these people, having moved to Wesel in the land of Cleves <note>A territory in the Holy Roman Empire, now part of modern-day Germany, which served as a refuge for Protestants</note>, found it difficult enough to remain there. For the Duke of Cleves, incited—it is believed—by Alva, began to oppose them. They declared, in response to certain points presented to them: *First, that they were satisfied with such preaching and church services as were practiced within Wesel, and wished to introduce or propose no innovations in matters of faith. Second, that they in no way acknowledged guilt regarding any rebellion or revolt against the King; and if accused of such, they were prepared to defend themselves before the Council of Wesel, under whose jurisdiction they now lived, and to await justice. Third, that during their stay in that land, they wished to show the Prince and the city all due obedience and, if necessary, to bind themselves to this by oath.* Nevertheless, they were informed on behalf of the Duke that they must depart within a month; but their humble pleas, the intercession of friends, and gifts finally obtained them permission to stay.
