Master Jacob van den Ende, Councilor and Advocate of Holland <note>The Advocate was a high-ranking legal official who represented the interests of the province of Holland.</note>, was invited as a guest and then taken prisoner on the same evening in late January <note>Original: "Loumaendt," an old Dutch name for January.</note> by the Count of Bossu (to whom the Stadtholdership of Holland had been entrusted since the departure of the Prince of Orange \*). Because of this, the delegates departed and returned home with their mission unaccomplished. On <margin>(12 March 1569.)</margin> March 12, 1569, Van den Ende died at Treurenburgh <note>A prison in Brussels; the name literally translates to "Mourning Castle."</note> from distress and hardship, after a confinement of one year and six weeks. [of his] life, when no reason whatsoever appeared to him to hope for the preservation of his life, much less to gain any favor, [he wrote] a certain **Allegorical Play of Love and Sorrow**, of Hope and Fear, and of a Christianly resigned heart. It was in rhyme, concise, full of instruction, composed without the help of books, yet not entirely without the teaching of the best but sternest schoolmistress: experiential visitation. Here he likewise composed the **Praise of Imprisonment** <gloss>1</gloss>, the **Compass of Rest** <gloss>2</gloss>, and other rhymes. He finally knew how to defend himself so skillfully that they granted him the Hague as a prison. But after being warned that there was a letter from Brussels with orders to place him back in confinement, he secretly took flight to Haarlem, and subsequently left the country. But wherever he went, he was—this was his constant complaint <gloss>3</gloss>—unkindly received by the leaders of those who followed the teachings of Calvin and Beza. This was because he (as it seemed to him) could by no means say "Amen" or "Yes" to all the opinions of the two aforementioned teachers. Others believed that he fell into hatred because of his restlessness and his contradicting of many, or all, religious groups <gloss>4</gloss>. But he understood that work was being done to confirm the Reformation with harmful errors, which everyone, he as well as any other, had to seek to prevent <gloss>5</gloss>. **Willem Dirkzoon Bardes**, former Bailiff <term>Bailiff: the 'Schout', a high-ranking judicial and law enforcement official</term> of Amsterdam, was accused based on doubtful testimonies and signs that he had stoked the disturbances. To that end, he was alleged to have maintained correspondence with the Prince of Orange, with the Lord of Brederode, and, in cipher, with Dirck Coornhert; and even to have harbored a Calvinist minister in the Hague. Having been taken into custody at court for this, he was—after long confinement—cruelly tortured at the discretion of the **Blood Council** <term>Blood Council: the Council of Troubles, an extraordinary court established by Alva to punish ringleaders of the recent political and religious unrest</term>. Furthermore, he was whipped with rods at the age of seventy years. And although he endured this with unconquered courage, such that the aforementioned Council judged him innocent of the disturbances, they nevertheless held him on a long rope <note>meaning: they kept him in a state of prolonged legal uncertainty</note> under the pretext of other fine side-issues, and withheld a large sum of money that the King owed him. Later, when the division of the country began, finding no safety among the Spanish party, he betook himself to the other side: a cause for which his greatest assets, lying around Amsterdam, were made useless to him. This [misery] took its toll not only on his body, but finally on his mind.

1567. For his life, at a time when there appeared to be no reason at all for him to hope for survival, much less to gain any comfort, he wrote a certain <term>Morality Play</term> <note>Dutch: *Sinnespel*; a traditional allegorical drama intended to convey a moral or religious lesson.</note> of *Love and Sorrow*, of *Hope and Fear*, and of a heart resigned to Christ. It was written in verse, concise and full of fine teachings, composed without the help of books—yet not entirely without instruction from that best but strictest schoolmistress: misfortune. Here he likewise composed the *Praise of Imprisonment* <gloss>1</gloss>, the *Compass of Rest* <gloss>2</gloss>, and other verses; but he eventually knew how to defend himself so skillfully that they granted him the city of The Hague as his prison <note>This likely refers to a form of house arrest or city-arrest rather than a dungeon.</note>. However, having later been warned that word had come from Brussels with orders to return him to close custody, he secretly took flight to Haarlem and subsequently left the country altogether. But wherever he went—and this was a notable part of his lament <gloss>3</gloss>—he was ungraciously received by the leaders of those who adhered to the teachings of Calvin and Beza. This was because (as he saw it) he could not say "yes" to every single opinion of the two aforementioned Teachers. Others believed that he fell into disfavor due to his own restlessness and his habit of contradicting many, or even all, learned authorities <gloss>4</gloss>. Yet he maintained that efforts were being made to bolster the Reformation with harmful errors, which everyone—himself as much as any other—was duty-bound to resist <gloss>5</gloss>. 

Willem Dirksoon Bardes, the former <term>Sheriff</term> <note>Dutch: *Schout*; the primary judicial and law enforcement official of a city.</note> of Amsterdam, was accused based on questionable testimony and signs that he had helped incite the unrest. To this end, it was alleged he had maintained communications with the Prince of Orange, the Lord of Brederode, and, in cipher, with Dirk Coornhert; he was even accused of harboring a Calvinist preacher in The Hague. Having been taken into custody at court for this, he was—after much stalling—cruelly tortured at the discretion of the <term>Council of Blood</term> <note>Dutch: *Bloedtraedt*; the popular name for the Council of Troubles established by the Duke of Alva to suppress the Dutch Revolt.</note> and, furthermore, flogged with rods at the age of seventy. And although he endured this with unconquered courage, such that the aforementioned Council saw him as innocent of the unrest, they nevertheless kept him "on a long rope" <note>A metaphor for keeping someone in a state of prolonged legal uncertainty or suspense.</note> under the pretext of other minor legal maneuvers, withholding a large sum of money that the King owed him. Later, when the division of the country began, finding no safety among the Spanish supporters, he went over to the other side. This was the cause of the loss of most of his means, as his properties, being located near Amsterdam, were rendered useless to him. This eventually broke not only his body but also his mind.

1567, to the astonishment of many, [they were treated] as a defeated enemy. Others who had fled were summoned to court and, when they did not appear, were banished. Their property was seized, and their houses were offered for rent at the town hall by the tolling of the bell; however, none of the inhabitants could find it in their hearts to bid money for them. The same happened with their movable goods; when no citizens could be found who were willing to buy them, the authorities were forced to have the items appraised for the benefit of the owners' <note>original: "bloedtvrienden," meaning close kin or blood relatives</note> for their own use. The Magistrates were immediately summoned there, and several, including the aforementioned Verduin, were sent. Their first task was the preparation of a magnificent feast and the invitation of the Lords before whom they were to be heard the following day; even their accuser, the Parish Priest, was not forgotten, much less passed over when the wine was poured. Then, when everyone was at their merriest, Mayor Verduin began a lamentation *over the sad times, the novelties, the sects, the breaking of the holy images and altars, the violation and desecration of the churches, not in one place, but throughout entire lands. From this reasoning, he finally turned to the city of Hoorn, recounting, in a boastful manner, how everything there was quiet and peaceful: how the citizens there were devout and zealous in the ancient Catholic faith; how no images had ever been stormed there, nor churches robbed; how no sects or novelties were ever heard of.* Speaking thus, he asked at every point, "Lord Dirk, is it not so?" To which the other, whose bitterness was somewhat softened by the wine, answered with nothing but "yes": so that, since the sitting Lords had heard his own counter-testimony, he could thereafter come to no accusation. Therefore he departed, and out of spite and shame did not return to Hoorn. Consequently, the Magistrate summoned him through posted notices to face the forfeiture of his office; and even accused him of being a hireling who, seeing the wolf coming, abandoned his sheep and took to flight.

This encounter struck such a chill into the hearts of the **Aldermen** that they judged themselves better suited to excuse their own actions than those of others. They did everything possible to make their innocence known to the **King** and the **Duke** through <margin>2 Bor. IV. 150. b. 151. 154. b...</margin> extensive writings. Furthermore, Alva sent several commissioners to various places to investigate what crimes had been committed regarding religion during the previous disturbances. <margin>3 Bor f. 153. b. Several Dutch lords (especially **Viglius** <note>Viglius van Aytta, a prominent Dutch statesman and jurist who often advocated for legal procedure over raw force</note>) did not fail to point out to the King how such great severity conflicted with his interests and those of the country. They even found the **Pope** inclined toward some moderation. **Philip** [the King] also pretended not to be averse to this, but refused to do anything without hearing the opinion of **Vargas** <note>Juan de Vargas, the notoriously cruel Spanish official who headed Alva's "Council of Troubles"</note> and his associates. Thus they proceeded with a sentence so gruesome that its like will not easily be found leveled against entire nations since the beginning of the world. By doing so, they unleashed murderers upon the land to vent the fury of their thirst for money and blood upon a people already downtrodden and defeated.

As this cruelty gained ground and left heaps of people destitute, it drove a portion of them to such despair that, abandoning house and home, wife and children, they chose the forests of West Flanders as their refuge. From there, driven wild by despair, the harshness of the wilderness, and the arrival of all manner of outlaws, they fell upon the **Priests and Monks**, choosing the darkest nights for revenge and robbery. They punished them not only by taking their property, but by desecrating their faces and cutting off their noses and ears.

Yet the lawlessness continued its course until he suppressed it with weapons.

The steadfastness of the condemned man is worthy of note, for he looked certain death in the eye with such unconcerned tranquility that he even felt inclined, two or three hours before his death, to compose a good number of Latin verses, which were dedicated to his fine friends, Petrus Forestus of Alkmaar and Cornelis Verheiden of Leiden. For this, he was understood to be a heretic; however, he had fled, and was banished from the city on pain of death <note>original: "gebannen op den hals," meaning execution if he returned</note> for the term of one hundred years and a day, with the forfeiture of all his goods. Klaes Krijnen and Jacob Claeszoon, who were also fugitives, were banished for a term of six years, under penalty of being strictly punished if they returned before that time; each was also fined twenty-five "Heeren" pounds. Pieter Floriszoon, who had also escaped, according to the verdict of the Aldermen <note>original: "Schepenvonnis"</note>, by his reading, had appeared to want to practice the office of Teacher of the new Religion or sect.

In Amsterdam, on the last day of June <note>original: "Somermaendt," literally "Summer Month"</note>, as many as one hundred and forty fugitives were publicly summoned and subsequently banished: among them were many of the most prominent citizens of the city, including six women, five of whom were widows. Jacob Simonszoon de Rijk, a grain merchant, had been accused by the Sheriff of offering a barrel of English beer to certain grain porters if they would break into the Friars Minor <term>Friars Minor|Members of the Franciscan religious order</term> church: this proved to be false. However, it was later testified that they had demanded the beer from him on those conditions; he had answered that the Friars Minor church did not stand in his way; and with that, he had withdrawn into his house. For concealing this experience from the authorities, he was banished, and all his property was seized. Master Marten Koster also had to take flight, and pay for his exile with his labor (which was now considered a capital offense), because of the service he had rendered to the Burgomasters in promoting the signing of the articles drafted in late September <note>original: "Herfstmaendt," literally "Autumn Month"</note> of the year 1566. All that the Magistrates had previously granted or allowed to the Reformed for the best of the city, or to the people out of necessity—which, as the times now went, could hardly be justified—they now sought to shift onto the backs of others. Having been willing to serve them could now become a grave crime; especially when one could not prove they had received a direct order.

In *Belle*, on the fourth of February <note>original: "Sprokkelmaent"</note>, they executed a countryman from *Merries* ⁷, <margin>6 *History of the Martyrs*, f. 441. 442, 443.</margin> and afterward † <margin>† (18 April.)</margin> four others were put to death by the sword. They had very zealously maintained the preaching and, based on a certain proposal, had raised some money to "buy" freedom of religion from the King, as they thought, at least for a few years. But those funds, it seems, were used otherwise. *Joost van Beusekom* was hanged for the sake of his faith on the seventh of May <note>original: "Bloeimaendt"</note> at *Oudenaarde* ⁸. <margin>⁸ *History of the Martyrs*, f. 444.</margin> The same death and ignominy were suffered there on the eleventh

H I S T O R Y  O F  T H E  R E F O R M A T I O N.  B O O K  I X.

<margin>
1568. <note>original: "MDLXVIII"</note>

The muzzling of the condemned with a tongue-screw. Hooft p. 173. See also the History of the Martyrs <note>original: "Hist. der Mart."</note> fol. 452. b. and of the Anabaptist Martyrs <note>original: "Doopsgesinde Mart."</note> p. 730.
</margin>
As the condemned approached the fire, they would often, at the very last moment, open their mouths to make a bold confession of their faith. Even the wooden balls that were commonly stuffed into their mouths to prevent this would sometimes come loose and fall out. To counter this, a hideous device was devised. This consisted of two small irons between which the tongue was screwed; the tip was then seared with a glowing iron so that, as it swelled, it remained fixed in place, unable to slip or be drawn inward. In this way, the shackled victims, in the agony of the fire, could only utter a hollow sound, much like the bellowing of those thrown into the glowing copper bull—that masterpiece of Perillus <note>Perillus was the inventor of the "Brazen Bull," a legendary Greek torture device that turned the screams of the victim inside into the sound of a bull's lowing.</note>—under the tyrant of Sicily. This was a supreme test of what a person will endure when they are earnest in their desire to serve God, and a demonstration of how cruelty only blunts its teeth against such hearts. Arnout van Erp, a man of irreproachable integrity, used to recount how, while watching the martyrdom of some who were thus muzzled, he heard one of two monks standing among the crowd say to the other:

<margin>
Inhuman bitterness. Hooft ibid. History of the Martyrs fol. 469.
</margin>
> Hear how they sing; would they also dance?

This inhumanity so incensed Van Erp—though at the time he had only just reached the end of his childhood—that he could barely restrain himself from committing an act of violence against the monk, which would have brought himself and all his kin to immediate ruin.

The Anabaptists again found their share in the general misery. In Flanders, fourteen men and three women were put to death for their faith <gloss>1</gloss>; in Antwerp, a father with his two sons <gloss>2</gloss>; in Rotterdam, a shipbuilder from Brielle <gloss>3</gloss>; in The Hague, Jan Tielemans, and alongside him Job Janssoon <gloss>4</gloss>, who was mentioned in the account of the Anabaptist disputes <gloss>5</gloss>. The latter wrote a certain letter from his prison to Jan Willemssoon and Lubbert Gerritssoon, complaining that his confession of guilt had been based on their understanding and not his own; he also wrote of the delay, the judgment that followed, and the cutting off <note>A term for excommunication or shunning within the Anabaptist community.</note> by Dirk Philips. He further exhorted them to confession and repentance, as they had laid hands on the godly. At Brouwershaven, the schoolmaster Valerius <gloss>6</gloss> was put to death; a certain edifying letter of his, printed since alongside his *Test of Faith*, is still extant.

But Emperor Maximilian, at the request of Orange, had his brother Archduke Charles resume the business of mediation with the King, and represent to him: 2 *that one had seldom seen violent counsels in matters of Religion turn out well; for which not only mercy, but even prudence, required moderation and a reduction of the severity being practiced.* He also noted how the violation of the charters <term>handtvesten: traditional Dutch constitutional documents and privileges</term>, especially in the appointment of foreigners to the government 3, was burdensome to both the imperial princes and the local inhabitants. To this, Philip replied, among other things: 4 *That regarding the matter of faith, he maintained a uniform policy in all his Kingdoms and Principalities with other orthodox Princes, and followed the path of the Roman Church, from which he would yield neither to the left nor to the right. Also, besides the salvation of souls, the peace of the people depended on this: a duty that even the Pagans caused to be watched over concerning their own false religions. Regarding the subjects who had deserved such heavy penalties, he himself felt pity. But for those who wished to maintain the necessary respect for authority, how could he pass over [their crimes]? The punishment had gone no further than the heads [of the leaders]; the sharpness of justice had been tempered with mercy. Furthermore, when the time was right, mercy would not be denied its turn. Neglecting to do justice was a heavy burden on the conscience; besides which, in his judgment, it would have caused incomparably greater difficulties than those they were presently troubled with. He had left the government in its old form, although no charters could obligate him to do so when the country's best interests advised him to make changes.*

Some Magistrates were willing to please the Spaniard in this, some out of fear, some out of blind

...first, the hundredth penny <note>A 1% one-time tax on total wealth</note> of everyone’s means, for one time: furthermore, at the seller’s expense, the twentieth penny <note>A 5% tax</note> on immovable property, and the tenth penny <note>A 10% tax</note> on movable goods, as often as they should be sold. When this was refused by the States <note>The "States" were the representative assemblies of the various provinces</note>—as it tended to make the inhabitants poor in short order and drive away all trade—some were forced to hear that through their negligence in the previous disturbances, they had forfeited all their liberties and all right to meddle in affairs of state; therefore, the King might burden them as he pleased. But to those of Hainaut and Artois and others, he promised to keep them free of that burden if they would only grant his desire, so as to introduce it to the majority. They did so, and the States of the inherited territories <note>The "inherited territories" refers to the core provinces of the Habsburg Netherlands</note> had to follow their lead; they also gave their word, but under the express condition of not being bound if any province remained in default. The States of Utrecht showed a more manly steadfastness and helped the other lands with a legal excuse through their persistence in refusing. Even the clergy declared that they could not subject their property to this burden without violating their oaths and consciences: especially * since by the bull read in <term>Cæna Domini</term> <note>Original Latin: *In Coena Domini* ("On the Lord's Supper"). This was a papal bull traditionally read every Maundy Thursday</note>, that is, on the Lord’s Supper, all those who granted or received such taxes without the consent of the Pope were placed under the ban of the church.

Upon the refusal of Utrecht, the other provinces also stepped back. After much bickering, this tax was postponed for two years through a buyout <note>A lump-sum payment made to avoid the implementation of the recurring tax</note>. Thus he threatened the oppressed with greater sorrow to make them bow under the yoke. Yet they endured it with unconquered courage and sought to defend themselves in court.

1569.
Orders regarding the matter of coercion of conscience.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial letter 'D' embellished with intricate floral and foliate scrollwork.</image-desc>
MEANWHILE, the Duke of Alba, in order to tighten the noose of religious coercion <note>original: "gewetensdwang," or coercion of conscience</note>, sent orders to the Governors of the provinces that when the Host <note>original: "misbroodt," literally Mass-bread</note> or the holy oil for the anointing of the sick was carried through the streets, they were to observe everyone's gestures, posture, words, and facial expressions. Those in whom any lack of reverence was detected were to be punished. The dead, to whom the clergy refused burial in consecrated ground, were to be carried to the gallows field; this was to be reported to Alba, and their property was to be inventoried. Midwives were to be bound by oath to report all newborn children to the priest of their parish within twenty-four hours, so that it might be known whether they were baptized in the Roman manner. This order was made known in Holland on the first of June <note>original: "Somermaendt," the month of summer</note>.

The Edict of Augsburg renewed.
*Bor p. 224.*
</margin>

This was once more made a perpetual command, revoking all other declarations and orders that conflicted with it, as having been issued contrary to his intent and will.

<margin>
Seven-stuiver people.
*Bor [Vol] V. 208.*

These were called "seven-stuiver people" <note>a "stuiver" was a common low-value coin</note> by the public, because they received the reward for their loathsome service in coins struck at that value. Thus, the cruelty continued its old course...

<meta>This page continues the account of religious persecution in the Netherlands during the late 1560s. ### HISTORY

<margin>
1569.
**Dirk Willemsz** saves his pursuer's life, and loses his own.
*History of the Anabaptist Martyrs, p. 470.*
</margin>

**Dirk Willemsz**, a citizen <note>original: "poorter," a person with formal citizenship rights in a town</note> of Asperen and of the same faith <note>Anabaptist</note>, was pursued by a court officer on a winter's day. He fled across the ice, which was still thin, and managed to cross with great difficulty. However, the officer following him broke through the ice. Seeing his pursuer in mortal danger, Dirk immediately turned back, reached out his hand, and saved his enemy’s life at the risk of his own. The rescued officer sought to spare his savior, but a certain Burgomaster, arriving on the scene, called out to him with stern words: *Fulfill your oath.* At this, self-interest—fearing that showing gratitude would cost him his own head—prevailed. He then arrested the man, who was subsequently sentenced to the fire on the fifteenth of May <note>original: "Bloeimaendt," the month of blossoms</note>. On that same day, as the sufferer stood at the stake outside Asperen on the side facing Leerdam, the wind blew very strongly from the east, driving the flames away from the upper parts of his body. This caused the most excruciating pain of a long-drawn-out death; so much so that in Leerdam, toward which the wind was blowing nearly half an hour's walk away, he was heard to cry out over seventy times: *O my Lord, my God!* The Bailiff <note>original: "Drossaert," a local judicial official</note>, moved by the man's suffering and not having the heart to watch what the other endured any longer, turned his horse around, turning his back to the place of execution, and said to the executioner: *Dispatch the man to a quick death.* Such was the price this good citizen paid for his simple-hearted loyalty. Prior to this, Adriaen Willemssoon had been beheaded at Vianen.

<margin>
*History of the Anabaptist Martyrs, p. 448, 449. p. 469.*
*p. 533.*
1 *See above p. 419.*
2 *Read his letter to Jan Will and Lubb. Gerritsz, July 10, 1567, printed in the year 1609.*
</margin>

In Brielle, on the twenty-fifth of June <note>original: "Somermaendt," the summer month</note>, a farmer from Maeslandt was killed with the sword, and a woman from Swartewael with fire. Thijs Juriaenssoon, from Raerop in Waterland, a Minister of the Word who had preached at Muiden, was strangled and burned there, along with one of his listeners. In the recent schism <note>referring to internal divisions within the Anabaptist movement</note>, he had sided with the Flemish faction and had earnestly opposed the dismissal that had been given to Dirk Philips <gloss>1</gloss> <gloss>2</gloss>. In Zeeland, four Anabaptist men were killed: three in Middelburg <gloss>3</gloss> and one in Zierikzee <gloss>4</gloss>. In 's-Hertogenbosch <gloss>5</gloss>, one or two of these people were put to death; in Antwerp <gloss>6</gloss>, fourteen men and two women; in Ghent <gloss>7</gloss>, six men and seven women; in Kortrijk <gloss>8</gloss>, six men and two women; in Armentières <gloss>9</gloss>, one man; and in Ypres <gloss>10</gloss>, two men.

### OF THE REFORMATION. BOOK IX.

<margin>
1569.
**Herman Timmerman** and others found put to death.
*History of the Anabaptist Martyrs, p. 493.*
</margin>

<margin>
His writing against **Menno** and **Dirk Philips** regarding the ban. p. A iii.
</margin>

Among the Anabaptists <note>original: "Doopsgezinden," literally "baptism-minded," the Dutch Mennonites</note> who suffered in Antwerp this year for the sake of Religion was **Herman Timmerman**. It is written that, at the urging of his fellow believers, he was ready to evade the persecution for a time, but he was betrayed by one of the Margrave’s servants who had either fallen away from the Anabaptists or had deceptively moved among them to spy. His moderation in matters of faith is highly praised. About nine years earlier, he had written a small printed book addressed to **Menno** <note>Menno Simons, the namesake of the Mennonites</note>, of whose death he was then unaware, and **Dirk Philips**, opposing the schismatic and excommunicating spirit <note>original: "ban-geest"</note> of the unyielding ones <note>original: "onrekkelijken," the strict faction of Anabaptists who favored a rigid application of shunning</note> with very earnest and scriptural words and reasons. In the Preface, he recounted how Menno and Dirk Philips had fallen away from their previous gentleness regarding the matter of reception <note>of members</note>, and he expressed his sorrow that he had to oppose them, whom he otherwise considered worthy of all honor and advocacy for their diligent faithfulness. *He was driven,* he said, *by the bitter necessity of his conscience to defend the honor of God and the eternal, saving truth, and with an aching heart to value the salvation of many people more highly than their own honor. Therefore, he prayed and warned the Christian Readers that they should never, throughout eternity, look upon any flesh <note>follow any human authority</note>, but rather seek their faith, conduct, and delight from God's word alone. Through this, they could never be deceived.* To this end, he desired that the Reader believe not him, but the Holy Scriptures. It is told of him that his thumbs were cut off or crushed to pieces in prison to prevent him from writing. Not long before Easter, he was burned alive.

Keersgieter was a wise, kind, and eloquent Teacher who, in one of his letters written in the dungeon, sought to discourage the Anabaptists from the misuse of the ban and from premature condemnation and schism. Vlekwijk is also described by the Anabaptists as a member of no small gifts. They were both, one by one, engaged in long conversations over various points of faith with the Franciscan Monk **Brother Cornelis Adriaens of Dordrecht**, who sought to convert them in his own fashion. Among other things, the Monk had told Vlekwijk that if he did not convert and have his unbaptized children baptized in the Catholic manner, he might well be burned alive at a stake. <meta>This page continues the account of Anabaptist persecutions in the year 1569. While the previous page discussed the trials of Herman Timmerman in Antwerp, this page focuses on the famous and tragic sacrifice of Dirk Willemsz in Asperen and provides a tally of other martyrs across the Low Countries.</meta>

HISTORY

<margin>
1569.
Dirk Willemsz saves his pursuer’s life, and loses his own.
*History of the Anabaptist Martyrs, p. 470.*
</margin>

...a citizen <note>original: "poorter," a person with formal citizenship rights in a town</note> of Asperen, belonging to the same faith, was pursued on a winter's day by an officer of justice. He took to the ice, which was still thin, and managed to cross with great difficulty. However, the officer following him fell through. Seeing his pursuer in mortal danger, Dirk immediately turned back, reached out his hand, and saved his enemy’s life at his own peril. The rescued officer sought to spare his savior, but a certain Burgomaster <note>The Mayor or chief magistrate</note>, arriving on the scene, called out to him with harsh words: "Fulfill your oath!" Driven by self-preservation—convinced that showing gratitude would cost him his own neck—the officer then seized the man. Dirk was subsequently sentenced to the fire on the sixteenth of May <note>original: "Bloeimaendt," the month of blooms</note>. On that same day, as the sufferer stood at the stake outside Asperen on the side facing Leerdam, the wind blew very strongly from the east, driving the flames away from the upper parts of his body. This caused the most exquisite agony of a lingering death; so much so that in Leerdam, toward which the wind blew, nearly half an hour's walk away, he was heard to cry out over seventy times:

> O my Lord, my God!

The Bailiff <note>original: "Drossaert," a local judicial official</note>, moved by the man’s suffering and not having the heart to look any longer upon what the other endured, turned his horse and his back to the place of execution, saying to the executioner: "Help the man to a quick death."

<margin>
*History of the Anabaptist Martyrs, p. 448, 449. p. 469.*
</margin>

So dearly did this good citizen pay for his simple faithfulness. Previously, Adriaen Willemszoon had been beheaded at Vianen. Within Den Briel, on the twenty-fifth of June <note>original: "Soomermaendt," the summer month</note>, a farmer from Maeslandt was killed with the sword, and a woman from Swartewael with fire. Thijs Juriaenszoon of Raerop in Waterland, a Minister of the Word <note>A preacher</note> who had preached at Muiden, was killed there along with one of his listeners by being strangled and scorched <note>A common execution method where the victim was strangled before or while the fire was lit</note>. This man had, during the recent schism, sided with the Flemish faction and had with great earnestness <gloss>1</gloss> opposed the decree of excommunication <note>original: "afscheidt," referring to the formal ban or shunning</note> issued by Dirk Philips <gloss>2</gloss>. In Zeeland, four Anabaptists <gloss>3</gloss> were killed: the men—three at Middelburg <gloss>3</gloss> and one at Zierikzee <gloss>4</gloss>. Within 's-Hertogenbosch <gloss>5</gloss>, one or two of these people were put to death; in Antwerp <gloss>6</gloss>, fourteen men and two women; in Ghent <gloss>7</gloss>, six men and seven women; in Kortrijk <gloss>8</gloss>, six men and two women; in Armentières <gloss>9</gloss>, one man; and in Ypres <gloss>10</gloss>, two men.

# OF THE REFORMATION. BOOK IX.

<margin>
1569.
Herman Timmerman killed along with other Anabaptists.
*History of the Anabaptist Martyrs,* p. 493.
</margin>

Among the Anabaptists who suffered in Antwerp this year for the sake of religion was Herman Timmerman. It is written that, at the urging of his fellow believers, he was ready to evade persecution for a time, but was betrayed by one of the Margrave’s <term>Margrave: a high-ranking judicial official or military governor</term> servants, who had either fallen away from the Anabaptists or had lived among them deceptively as a spy. His modesty in matters of faith is praised. About nine years earlier, he had—with a printed booklet addressed to Menno <note>Menno Simons, the influential Anabaptist leader</note> (whose death he was then unaware of) and Dirk Philips—opposed the schismatic and excommunicating spirit of the "unbending" <note>original: "onrekkelijken," the strict faction of Anabaptists who favored a rigorous use of the "ban"</note> with very earnest and scriptural words and reasons.

<margin>
His writing against Menno and Dirk Philips regarding the ban. p. 412.
</margin>

In the preface, he recounted how Menno and Dirk Philips had fallen away from their previous gentleness regarding the matter of admission <note>referring to the process of receiving members into the church</note>, and expressed his sadness that he had to oppose them, who were otherwise worthy of all honor and advocacy for their diligent faithfulness. *He was*, he said, *driven by the bitter necessity of his conscience to defend the honor of God and the eternal, saving truth, and with the pain of his heart to value the salvation of many people higher than their honor. Therefore he prayed and warned Christian readers that they should never look to any flesh <note>meaning: to rely on fallible human beings</note>, but seek only their faith, conduct, and joy in God’s word. Through this, they could never be deceived. Thus, he desired that the reader should believe not him, but the Holy Scripture.* It is told of him that in prison his thumbs were cut off or crushed to pieces to prevent him from writing. He was burned alive shortly before Easter.

<margin>
Jacob de Keersgieter and Herman van Vlekwijk condemned to the fire.
*History of the Anabaptist Martyrs,* p. 503, 526, 525.
Conversation between Brother Cornelis and Herman van Vlekwijk regarding the killing of heretics.
</margin>

Jacob de Roore, or Keersgieter <note>meaning: "Candle-maker"</note>, and Herman van Vlekwijk were sentenced to the fire in Bruges. Keersgieter was a sensible, friendly, and eloquent teacher, who in one of his letters written in the dungeon sought to discourage the Anabaptists from the misuse of the ban, and from hasty condemnation and schisms. Vlekwijk is also described by the Anabaptists as a member of no small gifts. Both were, face to face, in long conversation over various points of faith with the Franciscan monk, Brother Cornelis Adriaens of Dordrecht, who sought to convert them in his own way. The monk had let it be known to Vlekwijk, among other things, *that if he did not convert and have his unbaptized children baptized according to the Catholic rite, he might well be burned alive at a stake.* *You would*, was the reply, *likewise—*

<meta>This page continues the heated interrogation of Jan de Vleeschouwer (also known as Vlekwijk) by the Franciscan friar Brother Cornelis. The discussion has shifted from interpreting specific Bible verses to the authority of Church Councils and the controversial title of Mary as the "Mother of God."</meta>

# OF THE REFORMATION. BOOK X.

<margin>
1569.
\* Acts 2; John 19.
</margin>
**VLEKW.** Because you want to name all things differently than the Holy Scriptures, which call her the mother of Jesus \*; and nowhere the mother of God?

**BR. CORN.** Bah! Do you think we care so much for the naked, bare, meager Scripture? Bah, the worthy holy Council of Nicaea <note>The first ecumenical council (325 AD) which established key Christian doctrines.</note> has decreed that one should call her the mother of God.

**VLEKW.** Do you not hold your recent Council of Trent <note>The Catholic Council (1545–1563) held to counter the Protestant Reformation.</note> as worthy, true, and holy as that of Nicaea?

**BR. CORN.** Yes, we do; for the Holy Spirit has taught and spoken through the Fathers of the one just as well as through those of the other.

**VLEKW.** Now I judge all other Councils by the Council of Trent; since in my time I have heard and seen the admission and manner of proceedings of that of Trent: by which all the previous Councils are made a mockery and brought to shame.

At this saying, the monk cast out new insults against the prisoner. He was a slanderer of the Holy Spirit, a Beelzebubian Anabaptist <term>Anabaptist: a radical Reformation group that practiced adult baptism and often lived in separate communities</term>, a hellish Trinitarian <note>Though Vlekwijk is questioning the Trinity, Cornelis uses this term as a slur for those he believes are perverting the doctrine.</note>, an enemy of the mother of God.

<margin>p. 148.</margin>
**VLEKW.** You yourself have said that there are three persons in the Holy Trinity, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and that those three persons are but one true God. If Mary is then the mother of this true God, then she is as much the mother of the Father, and of the Holy Spirit, as of the Son.

**BR. CORN.** Bah, I have demonstrated to you from the Athanasian Creed <note>original: "Symbolum van Athanasius"—an early statement of Christian belief focused on the Trinity.</note> that the Father is God, and that the Son is God, and that the Holy Spirit is God, yet that there are not three Gods, but one true undivided God.

**VLEKW.** If the three are not each particular distinct Gods, but the three are only one true undivided God, and Mary is the mother of God, then she must be the mother of all three, or those three must each be particular Gods. Where do you stand now with your Council of Nicaea?

**BR. CORN.** Bah, may the hellish fire burn you, you wicked, evil, base, false, cunning Trinitarian. Bah, you would drive a hundred thousand Doctors of Divinity into a mad rage...

Thus did this monk rage against his heretic, who, on the tenth of the Summer Month <note>June</note>, along with Jeronymus Keersgieter, was burned.

# HISTORY

<margin>
1569 <note>Original Latin: MD LXIX.</note>
Description of Brother Cornelis.
From P. C. Hooft’s *History*, Book XIII, pages 568–569. <note>Pieter Corneliszoon Hooft (1581–1647) was one of the most prominent historians of the Dutch Golden Age.</note>
</margin>

It was also the same Brother Cornelis who (as he is described) was overflowing with bile, smooth of tongue, stiff of jaw, and most richly gifted with the spirit of impudence. A short time prior, he had taken the pulpit and, with a biting mouth and words of nauseating filth, thundered not only against the non-Catholics, but even against the authorities and his own party. Beyond these public outrages, hidden ones were brought to light: how he gratified himself by pretending to "gauge the hearts" of various women and young maidens. He knew how to manipulate them so foolishly that they confessed to him their internal thoughts of fleshly temptations and everything that the night and the bedroom keep covered. Indeed, they would even strip themselves "mother-naked" before him, supposedly so that he might purge <term>tuchtigen: to discipline or punish, often in a religious or corrective sense</term> that unchastity with rods. Because of this, he was eventually forced to leave his monastery and the city at the insistence of the provincial court, and he remained in Bruges for three years. Having returned without permission in the year 1570, he shamefully slandered the magistrates who had exiled him. He continued his old ways, scolding and ranting without interruption—first due to the wildness of the times, and now due to the bitterness of the times, when no one dared "bark at the staff" <note>An idiom meaning to challenge the authority of the clergy.</note> of the priesthood. In this manner, he lived through the governorship of Alva <note>Fernando Álvarez de Toledo, the Duke of Alva, was the harsh Spanish governor of the Netherlands.</note> until things took a turn. At that point, he took it upon himself to rail against the Duke's actions with equal loud-mouthedness. Since then, as the light of the country's enlightenment rose higher, he adjusted his "cap" <note>Meaning he changed his behavior or allegiance to suit the prevailing winds.</note> accordingly; for this reason, he was tolerated, and perhaps even the other side <note>The Protestants.</note> was pleased that the Roman Church made itself loathsome through such a disgraceful minister.

<margin>
The Prince issues naval commissions.
Bor, Book V, p. 208b; Hooft, Book V, pp. 197, 198. <note>Pieter Bor (1559–1635) was another primary chronicler of the Dutch Revolt.</note>
</margin>

While Alva sought to establish himself through continued persecution and the demand for new taxes, the Prince of Orange, seeking to resume at sea what had failed on land, issued naval commissions to various exiles. He gave express orders not to harm the subjects of the Roman Empire, England, Denmark, Sweden, France, or any others who were devoted to the Word of God and the Prince of Orange.

The Prince, who had recently realized how a lack of money held back his designs, also did his...

# OF THE REFORMATION. BOOK X.

<margin>
1569.
Bor, Vol. V, 224. b. Hooft, Vol. V, 199. Meurs, *William of Orange* <note>Original Latin: G. Aur.</note>, Vol. V, 62. Uitenbogaert, *Church History*, p. 169. *Description of Dordrecht*, p. 348.
</margin>

...exerted their best efforts to gather a "bosom of pennies" <note>A figurative expression for a secret fund or collection</note> through weekly and monthly collections among the refugees, and even from the local inhabitants, at great risk. The principal men employed for this were Lord Diedrik Sonoy, Johan Basius, Reinier Kant, and Adriaen Manmaker. Sonoy, on the eighth of February <note>Original: Sprokkelmaendt</note> in the year fifteen hundred and seventy, received written orders to promote this matter, even through others: it was to serve to drive out the foreign ruler, Alva, and to protect the Netherlands in their liberty and the sincere Christian Religion. To this end, he set several Preachers and others to work, namely Leenaert Panhuysen, Jan Klaeszoon, Jan Adriaenszoon, and Richard Klaeszoon <gloss>1</gloss>.

<margin>(1 See Bor, Vol. V, 233)</margin>

Several teachers of the Reformed <term>Gereformeerden: followers of the Protestant Reformation, specifically the Calvinist tradition</term> performed their duties with great fervor, knowing how to make the inhabitants feel a matter of conscience if they gave little or nothing: indeed, they brought it about that many, driven by fear of shame, felt they could not be good Christians if they did not help support this cause—which, as the Preachers said, served only for God’s glory and the freedom of Christians—according to their ability. Pieter Adriaenszoon van der Werve, of Leiden, and the Preacher Juriaen Epeszoon (likewise provided with orders from the Prince) were found in various Hollandish cities such as Dordrecht, Rotterdam, Delft, Leiden, the Hague, and elsewhere, stirring the well-willing to great generosity. But those who possessed the most were the slowest to part with it; the most was brought in by people of small and middling means.

<margin>
(In February.)
2 Bor, Vol. V, 190, 191. a. *Annotations on the Peace Negotiations at Cologne*, p. 339.
(11 April.)
</margin>

On the Spanish side, little was known of what was happening. They slept through it all, except for the advancement of Popery and persecution. Alva now had Cunerus Petri <gloss>2</gloss>, a cruel man, installed as Bishop of Leeuwarden, commanding him among other things to have the Council of Trent <note>A major Catholic council (1545–1563) that clarified doctrine and condemned the Reformation</note> proclaimed, and to see to it that the edicts <term>plakkaeten: official decrees or laws, often carrying severe penalties</term> regarding the matter of heretics were maintained by his clergy. In Pamele in Flanders, shortly thereafter, two men were burned on account of their faith <gloss>3</gloss>.

...stripped of their holy orders ¹. He shaved a bit of hair from each of their heads; with a silver knife, he gently scraped their tonsures and the tips of their fingers, with which they were accustomed to lift the consecrated bread <note>This ritual scraping was intended to symbolically remove the holy anointing oil applied during a priest's ordination</note>. ⁴ At once the Pastors said to them: that they all knew better than they were acting. But when the Bishop, with a steady countenance, placed his hand upon his breast and, with a solemn oath, calling upon God, testified *that he knew no better; and felt in his heart that the Roman religion <term>Roomsche Godtsdienst: Roman Catholicism</term> was the surest way to be saved*, Arent Dirkszoon, a man of seventy years who had known him best, gave him this answer: "You also once knew the truth: but have rejected it through your ill-will; for which you shall give an account on the day of judgment." At these words, the Bishop was seen to stand trembling, and it unsettled all the bystanders; for many knew this Pastor to be a learned, wise, and godly man. 

The Bishop, thereafter, handed them over to the Lords of the Council <term>Heeren van de Raede: members of the judicial council, likely the Council of Troubles</term> who were present, with the customary plea that they should be handled mercifully; at which the aged Pastor burst out, *How Pharisaical!* <note>Original Latin: *Quam Pharisaice!* – a reference to the biblical Pharisees whom Jesus accused of hypocrisy</note>. Thus they returned to the prison. On the twenty-ninth, a Monday, toward evening, they were informed that they were to die the next day. At this news, they lifted their hands with joy toward heaven, thanking God that the day of their release was at hand, and singing with a loud voice the sixteenth Psalm, *Preserve me, O Lord...* <note>Original Dutch: *Bewaer mij Heer...*</note>. That same evening they held the Lord's Supper <term>Avondtmael: the Protestant celebration of Communion</term> for mutual comfort in the dungeon. They also requested their fellow believers not to trouble them further with conversation during the remaining time, but to pray to God for them. The entire night was spent by them in prayer, the singing of Psalms, and the reading of Holy Scripture. On the thirtieth, after hearing their sentence at Court, they were seen [going] to their death...

as a spy. Around this time, the Dutch exiles and refugees brought their complaints, by the advice of the Prince of Orange, to the Diet at Speyer <note>An Imperial Diet was a general assembly of the estates of the Holy Roman Empire; the city of Speyer was a frequent host for these significant political meetings</note>; with a unanimous prayer that their innocence might be accepted and relief might be sought. They showed at length what the Spaniard had long sought with the edicts <note>Original: *plakkaten*</note> and the Inquisition, to make himself Lord of all; but especially to root out to the very ground those who would not submit themselves to the authority of the Pope, and who subjected their consciences only to the unique Word of God, contained in the books of the Old and New Testaments... How Alva had also robbed the land of its ancient freedoms, laws, and privileges; driven out the most pious; shed the blood of the innocent; reviled the most godly; violated both ecclesiastical and worldly rights; profaned all that was holy; separated lawful marriages; defiled the Sacrament of Baptism; overturned all love and friendship; and left nothing undone of unheard-of cruelty. But the Duke’s envoys argued to the contrary, that the punishment of rebellious subjects belonged to their King.

The States, specifically those of Holland, raised difficulties regarding the proclamation of the edict. It was nevertheless read out in Amsterdam and elsewhere with much hesitation $^5$; but when it came time to appoint collectors or gatherers, those chosen would not accept the burden, nor would the Magistrates compel them to do so. In Amsterdam, the Aldermen <note>term: "Scheepenen" — local judicial officials</note> shifted the responsibility onto the Burgomasters, and the Burgomasters back onto the Aldermen. Consequently, the city—or as others claim, one of the Burgomasters $^6$—was sentenced to a fine of twenty-five thousand guilders $^7$. This caused great bitterness among the citizens, who dared to denounce Alva as a tyrant. The Court of Holland ordered processions and days of prayer to be held in all cities, primarily in Amsterdam. The people were exhorted to repentance, and God was entreated to soften the Duke's hardened and stubborn heart, so that he might give way to reason and equity; for now, treading the country's privileges underfoot, he proceeded only with the utmost rigor and the King’s will. Even the Friars Minor <note>term: "Minrebroeders" — members of the Franciscan Order</note>, especially in Amsterdam, spoke out against Alva, calling him a tyrant and a violator of justice. Thus the state of the country took on an entirely different appearance. Many, including the most devout Catholics as well as other inhabitants, yearned for change. <margin>

Just as hearts had been estranged during the general looting of the churches and the riots in Antwerp, causing many to side with the Duchess <note>Margaret of Parma, the former Regent</note>; so now did the severity of these current encounters make the Roman Catholics look once more toward the support of their opposing party. They gasped for the air of freedom from that direction, fearing the oppression into which they had allowed the state to fall—a state of such servitude. Every man thought it a base indignity that, while "born slaves" cost their masters purchase money and upkeep, the Dutchman himself should be forced to pay for his own slavery and continually nourish it. Furthermore, those of Utrecht remained just as steadfast in refusing this taxation <note>The "Tenth Penny," a hated 10% value-added tax imposed by Alva</note>. Many had suffered for their first refusal ¹, and they were yet to suffer more ², through the excesses of the soldiery. Neither robbery nor murder was respected. From such dealings in various regions, such a sense of desperation arose that some people offered the Prince <note>William of Orange</note> to place fire-faggots ³ in their own houses, so that upon his arrival they might leave the cities unable to offer resistance.

<page-num>520</page-num>
<header>HISTORY</header>

<margin>
1571.
</margin>
...place, who there on the tenth of November <note>original: *Slachtmaendt*, the "slaughter month"</note>, after he had likewise been tortured in vain, was put to death by fire.
<margin>
A new and strict order regarding books.
</margin>
Besides the public violence of the persecution, something else was undertaken in secret to damage the so-called heresy and to strengthen the Roman Church, by establishing a new, strict, and subtle order regarding the matter of books which the Inquisition had objections against. At this juncture, it will not be unhelpful, even for the clarification of the matters recounted above, to trace the origin of the prohibition of books somewhat further back.

<margin>
A short account of the origin of the prohibition of books in Christendom.
</margin>
<margin>
From P. Servita <note>Paolo Sarpi</note>, *History of the Council of Trent*, Vol 5, page 427.
See also M. Ant. De Dominis, *On the Ecclesiastical Republic*, book 7, chapter 7, from section 12 to section 23.
</margin>
In the early Christian church, no ecclesiastical prohibition was known in this regard: but godly men considered the reading of evil books unlawful for reasons of religion, to avoid the contamination of evil; not to throw oneself into temptation without necessity and without hope of benefit; nor to spend time on vain things. There was also a greater aversion to the books of the Pagans than those of the heretics, which were first forbidden by the Emperors for reasons of state. It was enough for the Councils and Bishops to show what in some books was evil and unscriptural, without going further; but they left it free to everyone to avoid them or to read them with some good purpose. 

Yet after the year eight hundred, the Roman Popes, having drawn no small part of the civil dominion to themselves, not only forbade the reading of books whose authors they themselves had condemned, but also ordered them to be burned. Nevertheless, until the year fifteen hundred, few books were found that were forbidden in such a manner. Pope Martin V indeed denied spiritual communion to all sects of heretics, and especially the Wycliffites <note>Followers of John Wycliffe, the 14th-century English reformer</note> and Hussites <note>Followers of Jan Hus, the Czech reformer</note>: but he made no mention at all of those who read their books, although the same were then in many hands. 

But Leo X, having condemned Luther, also immediately forbade the reading of all his books on pain of excommunication. The Popes who followed him have, in the bulls <note>Official papal edicts</note> where they condemned heretics in general, simultaneously struck those who read their writings with the same bolt of excommunication <note>original: *banblixem*, literally "ban-lightning"</note>. From this arose great confusion; for because the names of the condemned heretics were least expressed, one had to obtain knowledge of the forbidden books much more through their content than through the names of the 
autheu- <meta>catchword: autheuren (authors)</meta>

Pope Paul IV goes much further on that path than his predecessors.

Following this progress, Pope Paul the Fourth ordered the Inquisitors in Rome to likewise create and publish a Register <note>This became known as the *Index Librorum Prohibitorum* or the Index of Forbidden Books.</note> of forbidden books. This was carried out in the year fifteen hundred fifty-nine. In this, they went many steps further than had been done in past times, and they laid the foundations to maintain, and indeed greatly expand, the authority of the Roman Court <note>The "Roman Court" refers to the Papal administration or the Vatican.</note>. By this means, they deprived the people of the knowledge that was most necessary for them to protect themselves against the unjust seizure of worldly power, with which the Popes were constantly occupied: For until this time, the prohibition of books had been confined within the boundaries of heretical books whose authors were condemned: but this Register was divided into three parts.

<margin>
Register of forbidden books.
Ibid.
</margin>
The first part included the names of those whose entire works, no matter what subject they dealt with—even matters that did not touch upon Religion—were entirely forbidden. And among these were placed not only those who had confessed a doctrine conflicting with the Roman Church; but also many who had lived and died in the communion of the Roman Church. The second part contained the names of books that were specifically condemned, without forbidding the other books written by the same authors. The third part contained certain writings by anonymous authors: besides which were also forbidden all books that had been printed since the year fifteen hundred nineteen without the name of the author; even authors and books that scholars had used for three hundred, two hundred, and one hundred years in the Roman Church, and that in the sight, and with the full knowledge of the

1571. the Roman Popes, who had not spoken against it for so long a time. Suddenly, books by modern authors were banned—even those printed in Italy itself, indeed even those printed in Rome with the consent of the Inquisition and the Pope himself. Among others, the annotations of Erasmus on the New Testament were banned, despite having been approved by Leo the Tenth—after he had read them—with a papal bull <note>A "bull" is a formal public decree or charter issued by a Pope.</note> issued on the tenth of September <note>original: "Herfſtmaendt," literally harvest-month.</note> fifteen hundred eighteen. The Inquisitors also created a list of sixty-two book printers, forbidding all the books they had ever printed, regardless of the author, the subject matter, or the language in which they were written. To this was added a further measure with far-reaching consequences: that all books printed by any other printers who had ever published a single heretical book were also banned.

<margin>
What the Council of Trent decided on this matter.
* This list is found at the back of the Canons and Decrees of the Council of Trent, printed in Lyons by G. Roville, 1572. Read further in the *Selected Letters of A. Masius to G. Cassander*, p. 265, 266. See also Cassander's letters in his *Works*, p. 1191, 1192.
</margin>

This was the state of affairs regarding books until the Council of Trent <note>A series of important meetings (1545–1563) where the Catholic Church defined its doctrines in response to the Protestant Reformation.</note>, where it was decided not only to create another list * of books that were to be entirely forbidden, but also that all other books, no matter what subject they treated, should be put to the test by trusted theologians. With the advice, approval, and authority of the Bishops or the heads of the Inquisition, these men would "purify" <note>The process of "purifying" or "expurgating" involved blotting out or removing specific passages deemed offensive while allowing the rest of the book to be read.</note> whatever was found to be harmful to the Roman Church.

<margin>
How that decision was put into effect in this country.
From the preface of B. Arias Montanus to the *Expurgatory Index*, p. 6, 7.
</margin>

To put this decree into effect, the following method was used in the Netherlands. In the King's name, the Duke of Alva <note>The Spanish governor of the Netherlands, known for his rigorous enforcement of King Philip II's policies.</note> wrote letters to all the Archbishops, Bishops, Universities, and other learned men, as well as to the City Councils. He commanded them to divide the task of reading and overseeing the suspect books among capable persons, and to send their opinions on each of them to him. He also desired that the highly learned Benedictus Arias Montanus <note>A famous Spanish orientalist and scholar who edited the Antwerp Polyglot Bible.</note> should oversee this on his behalf. Within a period of nine months, everyone completed their task, and the notes and observations of each were sent in. Then, he called together a Theological College of Censors in Antwerp, where a learned Bishop presided with ecclesiastical authority and guided the proceedings; the aforementioned Arias Montanus was also added to this group on the King's behalf. This assembly re-examined the notes, observations, and findings of the first inspectors or overseers; they compared the flagged passages with the books themselves, and after everything had been reviewed...

# OF THE REFORMATION. BOOK X.

<margin>1571.</margin>
<margin>* Index expurgatorius <note>The "Index of Purging." Unlike the "Index Librorum Prohibitorum," which banned books entirely, this list specified which parts of a book had to be blacked out or removed for it to be legally owned.</note>. Register of expurgation. From the King's Ordinance, printed before the Index Expurg.</margin>
<margin>How it is handled. Ibid <note>Latin: "In the same place."</note>.</margin>
...a judgment and censure was devised; furthermore, a Register of expurgation* was written, or a "purger" of those things one wanted weeded out or struck through in the books. The King had this Register printed at this time at his own expense by Christopher Plantin, his chief printer; not to be sold publicly or issued, but only to be distributed to the Visitors <note>Inspectors or censors.</note> of books, who had been or would be appointed to this work by the ecclesiastical Prelates. These were commanded to "improve" <note>The authorities used the word "improve" (verbeeteren) as a euphemism for censorship.</note> all the books that, by virtue of previous edicts, had been gathered and kept in custody or that would be brought to them; and to cross out and cleanse therein all the passages declared in the aforementioned Register. Such corrected books, signed with the visitor's own mark, would then be returned to the owners; and might then also be traded. But whoever kept or traded any of the aforementioned books without them being cleansed and signed would fall under the penalties contained in the edicts on the matter of Religion. Also, the aforementioned visitors might choose in each city where there were booksellers one or two diligent and faithful persons, who would keep the same Register secretly with them, without making it common to others or giving a copy thereof; these people might "improve" the aforementioned books and, having been improved, let them be signed by the Visitors.

The Ordinance by which all this was commanded was made on the last day of July <note>original: "Hooimaendt," literally "Hay month."</note> of this year, in Brussels, and signed by the King in his Council by D'Overloepe. According to the contents of this secret Register, many excellent books were mutilated and partly ruined in a short time by the scratching out of very notable matters.

<margin>It is brought to light by F. Junius. † See Franciscus Junius's *Life*, p. 68, and his epistle to John Casimir, Count Palatine, prefixed to the *Index Expurg.*</margin>
The Register also remained hidden for several years; and was first brought to light in the year fifteen hundred eighty-six † by Franciscus Junius (who had fled from Limburg to Germany and was at that time Professor of Theology at Heidelberg), who had received it from a reliable source. Plantin's printing was put on display in the Palatine library <note>The famous library of the Electors of the Palatinate in Heidelberg.</note> for the eternal memory of such a bold undertaking <note>The author uses "bold undertaking" (stout bestaan) to describe the audacity of the government's attempt to edit the world's literature.</note>.

# HISTORY

<margin>
1571.
From the Acts of this Synod printed at Delft by Jan Andriesz, 1612. See also Uitenhogaert’s Church History, p. 175.
</margin>
The Minister of Frankenthal <note>A city in Germany that served as a refuge for Dutch Protestants.</note> presided. Here, order was established for the holding of Consistories, Classes, and Synods, and for the further care of the congregations. The first article crafted here was of this content: *No church shall exercise dominion over another church, nor shall any Minister of the Word, Elder, or Deacon exercise dominion over another; but each shall guard themselves against all suspicion and temptation to rule.* This appeared to be directed against the Episcopacy <note>The system of church government by bishops.</note> which held place among the Roman Catholics and also, though in a different manner, in the Reformation of England and Germany. It was also deemed proper by the brethren to sign the Confession of Faith of the Netherlands churches <note>The Belgic Confession.</note> as proof of unity in doctrine; likewise also the confession of the churches in France, to testify thereby their bond and unity with them. The Teachers <note>Ministers.</note> who were then outside the assembly, as well as those who would henceforth be called to service, were to be exhorted to this subscription.

<margin>
Art. V.
</margin>
In one of the drafted articles, it was stated that in the French-speaking congregations, the form of the Genevan Catechism <note>The catechism written by John Calvin.</note> ought to be used, and in the Dutch-speaking congregations, the form of the Heidelberg Catechism; however, if any churches used another form of Catechism conformable to the Word of God, they should not be forced to change.

In the year fifteen hundred seventy-two, the coercion of land and faith continued for a while in its old course. In Brussels, the Blood Council <term>Bloedraad|The Council of Troubles, an extraordinary court established by the Duke of Alba to punish leaders of the political and religious troubles.</term> banished several citizens of Dordrecht, even some women, from all the King's lands upon the gallows, with the forfeiture of all their goods. Within Dordrecht at that same time sat imprisoned Jan van Kuik Wouters, a local glass-painter and artist, a man of irreproachable life and conduct (as Doctor Jan van Beverwijk writes he understood from those with whom Kuik had lived) but a Mennonite <term>Doopsgesindt|An Anabaptist or Mennonite; literally "baptism-minded," referring to their practice of adult believer's baptism.</term>. But the monks began to roar at this laxity, even daring to shout from the pulpit that the Bailiff only kept the heretic imprisoned so he could paint for him. Consequently, one had to serve the bitterness...

The prisoner <note>Jan van Kuik, a painter and stained-glass artist.</note> was mercilessly tortured on several occasions to discover who his master and associates were, and who had re-baptized <note>The term "verdoopt" refers to adult baptism, which was a capital offense under imperial edicts.</note> and married him. But he endured everything with an unyielding spirit without incriminating anyone; as is recounted in several of his elegant letters, which (aside from him speaking too vehemently against infant baptism) breathed almost nothing but signs of fiery love for God, pure truth, his dear wife, daughter, parents, and friends. These were written with words tasting of the earnestness of a well-assured soul, who, already embarked upon the pains of death and looking forward to a better life, calls out a final adieu to the world. On the twenty-eighth of March <note>Original: "Lentemaendt" (Spring month).</note>, he was led to the fire at the city's waterfront, where the "New Work" is currently located, along with a woman from Molenaersgraaf. Their mouths had been gagged; but van Kuik managed to get the wood or iron out of his mouth and prayed to God with a loud voice for help. This moved someone to push through the crowd toward him and cry out: *Fight bravely, dear brother! after this you shall suffer no more.* Upon hearing this, the painter loosened his doublet <note>A close-fitting buttoned jacket.</note> and showed the caller his bloody chest, which had been broken by scourging on the rack <note>Original: "paleij," a hoisting torture device like the strappado.</note>, and said, lifting his eyes to heaven: *I already bear the marks of the Lord Jesus in my body.* <note>A reference to Galatians 6:17.</note> A search was made for the man who first called out, but he hid himself among the people. The woman was strangled first.

<margin>1572.</margin>

It was politely pointed out to him that the management of such matters did not rest with the military authorities, but with the country's government. However, he imagined that Admiral de Rijk lacked the goodwill to grant it. ### OF THE REFORMATION. BOOK X.

Xxx 2

<margin>
1572.
The Tenth Penny, and not Religion, was the cause of the war.
Reyd. p. 9. <note>Everard van Reyd, a Dutch historian and contemporary of these events.</note>
Grot. Annal. ll. 34. <note>Hugo Grotius, *Annales et Historiae de Rebus Belgicis* (Annals and History of the Belgian Affairs).</note>
</margin>
...the Tenth Penny <note>A widely hated 10% tax on the sale of all goods imposed by the Duke of Alva in 1569.</note>, and not Religion, was the first cause that cities and provinces set themselves against Alva; for what had happened before was the work of the exiles. That people of the Netherlands who previously, almost without moving, had seen their citizens burned, their officials killed, and their laws, religion, and republic oppressed, finally resolved to avenge what was past and to ward off what was threatened. However, that this casting off of the Spanish yoke and the first foundation of Holland's freedom is touched upon so briefly within this account of our Reformation has its reason: for upon it was built, in time, the freedom of conscience and of religion that we now enjoy. To this end, the Prince’s <note>William the Silent, Prince of Orange</note> intention was to protect even the Catholics in the exercise of their religion alongside the others. He expressed this anew in the instructions given to Lord Diedrik Sonoy, his Stadtholder <note>A provincial governor or representative of the sovereign</note> in North Holland. He first charged him to do his utmost to deliver the cities of that region from Spanish slavery and to restore them to their ancient freedoms, rights, traditions, and privileges.

<margin>
Prince William also seeks to maintain the Roman Catholics in freedom of Religion.
Bor VI. 273. <note>Pieter Bor, a Dutch historian known for his monumental 'History of the Wars'.</note>
</margin>
*Furthermore, he was immediately to see to it that the word of God was proclaimed and preached there: also permitting the exercise of Religion conformable to the same word, if the inhabitants, or any among them, desired the same; without, however, tolerating that those of the Roman Church should be done any molestation, or that they should be hindered in the exercise of their Religion, until such time as the Prince should have ordered otherwise; or unless necessity and urgency might otherwise require, according to the discretion of the Commander and the council there: the aforementioned Sonoy meanwhile doing his best so that all the aforesaid inhabitants might live together in rest and peace, not allowing any secret meetings to take place, whether by day or by night. Furthermore, he should make the Magistrates and inhabitants swear, among other things, in no way to tolerate that anyone should be hindered, harmed, or disturbed in the preaching or the exercises of the true word of God, following the Gospel; nor investigated in his conscience, or on account thereof, be persecuted by Inquisition or Edicts <note>original: "plakkaeten" — formal decrees or laws, often used to enforce religious conformity.</note>.*

Yet, that this casting off of the Spanish yoke and the first foundation of Dutch freedom is touched upon so briefly within the account of our Reformation has its reason: for upon it was built, in time, that freedom of conscience and religion which we now enjoy. To this end, the Prince intended to protect even the Roman Catholics <note>original: "Pausgefinden" — literally "those of the Pope's party."</note> in the exercise of their religion, alongside the others. He expressed this again in the instructions given to Lord Diedrik Sonoy, his Lieutenant in North Holland.

First, he commanded him to do his best to deliver the cities of that region from Spanish slavery and to restore them to their old liberties, rights, traditions, and privileges. Furthermore, he was to see to it immediately that the word of God was proclaimed and preached there: also permitting the exercise of Religion conformable to the same word, if the inhabitants, or any among them, desired it; without, however, allowing any harassment to be done to those of the Roman Church, or any hindrance to occur in the exercise of their Religion, until such time as the Prince should have ordered otherwise: or unless necessity and urgency might otherwise require, according to the discretion of the Commander and the council there. Meanwhile, the aforementioned Sonoy was to do his best so that all the aforesaid inhabitants might live together in rest and peace, not permitting any secret meetings to take place, whether by day or by night.

<margin>
1572. Edict forbidding the offending of the clergy; with the proclamation of freedom of religion. Bor Volume 1, folio 291. Hooft page 259.
</margin>
In the said month <note>July 1572</note>, a certain <term>plakkaet<gloss>an official edict or decree issued by a governing authority</gloss></term> was issued, by which the soldiers were forbidden *to harm, damage, or curtail anyone, whether clerical or secular, in property or in blood, on pain of being punished in body as rebels and disturbers of the common peace and welfare.* It further ordained and willed *that freedom of Religion, both of the Roman and of the Evangelical, should be maintained, without anyone being hindered or injured therein, on pain as before.* Furthermore, it newly prohibited all desecration of churches and plundering of monasteries. Thereupon, the Prince <note>William of Orange</note> marched into Brabant, and then toward Hainaut. Along with Mechelen and other cities, Oudenaerde was captured along the way.

<margin>
1572.
</margin>

<margin>
Dirk Volkertszoon Coornhert, Secretary of the States of Holland, is ordered to investigate the abuses of Lumey's captains.

<margin>
* 1 Uitenbogaert in his Diary, from the words of Hugo Grotius.

The lawlessness and wickedness grew so great that [Lumey] fostered, through his own perverse conduct, soldiers who resembled their commander in shame and villainy. Dirk Volkertszoon Coornhert <note>A famous Dutch polymath, theologian, and artist known for his advocacy of religious tolerance</note>, having returned to the fatherland from his exile and having become Secretary of the States of Holland—who around this time had composed the well-known song, *William of Nassau* <note>The "Wilhelmus," which became the Dutch national anthem</note>—received orders at this time to summon the <term>Schouten<gloss>local officials responsible for law enforcement and judicial administration</gloss></term> and authorities of the villages in Kennemerland to Haarlem. He was to conduct an investigation into the extortions and robberies committed by certain captains, so that these [stolen amounts] would be deducted from the payment of their wages. This had been stipulated following their excessive demands in a certain agreement made between the States and the captains, in which Coornhert, along with two other deputies, had been employed by the States.

<margin>
Coornhert’s Works, Part III, folio 361, 156b, 157.
</margin>

But some of these military leaders, knowing what they had committed in the aforementioned villages—which was bound to come to light through this investigation—turned all their malice against the Secretary. They masked their private hatred with a cloak of the common cause.

<margin>
Lumey gives orders to have him shot.
</margin>

<margin>
(* Velius Chron. p 195. Hooft p. 273. Bor f. 302.)
</margin>

<margin>
He flees the country.
</margin>

Coornhert had suggested that it was only fair, and also beneficial for the maintenance of internal unity, that the promise made to the Catholics at Dordrecht should be kept, regarding the practice of their religion and other matters. This was enough to denounce him as a wicked Papist and to blacken his name so much to Lumey that the latter swore his death and gave orders to have him shot. Therefore, he had to yield to necessity and flee. For the roads in the fields, and even the streets within the cities, were not safe for him. Even the Prince <note>William of Orange</note>, who had then come to Holland at the request of the States, had no means—so much did Lumey still have the military under his hand—to protect Coornhert's innocence, even if Coornhert had turned to him for help. He then departed again for Xanten <note>original: "Santen"</note> in the land of Cleves. However, in Haarlem, he left behind the records he had made based on the reports from the villages concerning the grievances against the captains, with instructions to deliver them to the States. This was prevented by the siege of the city which followed immediately thereafter. Those documents have also since been lost. But besides this reason of saving his life, two other weighty matters urged him to leave his office: these (as he later made known) he did not wish to reveal except to the ears of the Lords States; yet he let it be sufficiently known that they concerned his conscience and honor. And he gave, in this same year, whether before or
