<margin>
1573.
Conversation of Adriaen van der Mijle with Elector Frederick III.
From a letter of Adriaen van der Mijle to Singilinus, dated Speyer, 25 Feb. 1573. See *Selected Letters* p. 572, 573, 574.
</margin>
...did not keep his word in these circumstances. Regarding this matter, Lord Adriaen van der Mijle <note>A Dutch statesman and diplomat (1538–1590) who served as a counselor to William the Silent.</note>—who has since been employed in the highest offices of legal and state affairs—entered into a conversation at Heidelberg on the eighteenth of February <note>original: "Sprokkelmaent," an old Dutch term for February.</note> of this year with the Elector Palatine <term>Frederick III</term> <note>Frederick III (1515–1576), called "the Pious," was a major proponent of the Reformed faith in Germany.</note>, later called "the Pious" for his zeal for religion. The Elector sought to persuade Van der Mijle, who had stayed outside the country for a long time, to return to his fatherland. He said he had understood from Count John of Nassau <note>The younger brother of William the Silent.</note> that the Prince of Orange was in great need of loyal people and good counselors, saying, *That the course of action is bare of good and pious counsel.* <note>original German: "Das der gank bloß sey vom guten und frommen rhaet."</note> The other replied *that the situation itself clearly showed this*, adding, while speaking at length about the affairs of the Netherlands, *that it was particularly due to a lack of good counsel that, with the enemy so near, they had given the Papists—who were just as much against Alva and his tyranny as the Evangelicals—cause for complaint by taking away the churches in some cities which had been left to them by virtue of alliance or agreement.* Now, they complained openly enough that if their promises were broken while the situation was still in doubt, they could easily imagine what they had to expect once the work was fully accomplished. Through this, he added, *such a great change of hearts had been caused that some of the first and most prominent men, who previously conducted themselves bravely against Alva together with counsel and deed, now remained sitting in doubt, within or outside the fatherland, with great anxiety over the uncertainty of the outcome of this matter.* 

The Elector pointed out to him that it was an excellent thing if nothing but the word of God were preached in a city, and the true religion alone practiced. Van der Mijle gave him the answer: *That such a thing was indeed a most excellent matter, but it was easily brought about by a Prince who held dominion in his own territory, or by one who had conquered his land by the sword. But it was otherwise situated where inhabitants of different religions, entering into an alliance, agreed with one another to combat a common enemy and tyrant, and where each freely stipulated for his own religion.* Upon that saying, the Elector let himself be heard with these words: *Yes, that is true. I am a poor Elector; but if I could come to an agreement with land and people, and make a settlement, I would [do so] with...*

Resolution by the States against the Roman Catholics.

...held as such. Nevertheless, shortly thereafter, in the year 1573, at a certain assembly held at Leiden, it was formally resolved by the States of Holland <note>The sovereign governing body of the province of Holland during the Dutch Revolt.</note> that the practice of the Roman religion should be suspended and forbidden. However, when this matter was first proposed or first began to be stirred, the Prince <note>William the Silent, Prince of Orange (1533–1584).</note> would have preferred that it had been left alone; and it was even more against his inclination when it was actually put into practice. He makes this known in his *Apology* <note>original: "Verantwoording," referring to the *Apologie de Guillaume de Nassau*, his 1580 formal defense against the ban issued by King Philip II.</note> published in the year fifteen hundred and eighty, but says at the same time in defense of the States:

<margin>
*Apology of the Prince of Orange* p. 78, 79.
</margin>

*“that they, who in the beginning had found it good and useful for the preservation of the land that both religions should be maintained, later—through the bold attempts, clever tricks, and treacheries of the enemies who were mingled among the inhabitants—discovered that their state stood in danger of an inevitable ruin, unless they caused the practice of the Roman Catholic worship to cease; because those who made confession of it, at least the Priests, had sworn allegiance to the Pope by oath (as they did everywhere), making more of that oath than of the other which they had sworn to the land.”*

<margin>
What moved them to this.
</margin>

<margin>
p. 79, 80.
</margin>

*“It is not reasonable that such people should enjoy a privilege by which means they sought to deliver the land into the enemy's hands. They sought to betray the lives and property of the subjects: not just one, or two, or three privileges; but all the freedoms which from ancient times, beyond all human memory, and from generation to generation, had been preserved and maintained by the ancestors and forefathers.”*

The Papists <note>A common 16th-century term for Roman Catholics, referring to their loyalty to the Pope.</note>, thus banished from the churches, nevertheless maintained their religious assemblies in private houses; there they were permitted to continue with their Mass and other Roman ceremonies and institutions for a long time. People of this persuasion were also not easily promoted or admitted to high offices; not by virtue of any law, but out of prudence and mistrust.

<margin>

# HISTORY

<page-num>550</page-num>

<margin>
1573.

But nevertheless, they loathed all laws and coercion in matters of religion under the name of the Inquisition.
<note>original: *Grot. Annal. II. 41.* refers to the *Annales et Historiae* of Hugo Grotius, a seminal history of the Dutch Revolt.</note>
</margin>

...to protect <note>This sentence continues from the previous page's discussion of a ruler's duty.</note>, but also that He should be served in common in such a manner as He Himself had commanded; and many who neglected their duty in this regard also brought upon themselves the punishment with which the godlessness of others should have been repaid. These people, on the contrary, judged not only that they would refuse any such assistance, but they loathed within themselves all laws or coercion in the matter of religion, as if it were the Inquisition; therefore they argued that no one strayed from the truth willingly, nor believed against his will, but that the true understanding of religious matters was instilled into the human intellect by God: that also no piety was pleasing to God, unless it proceeded from a willing heart. It had also been experienced that bad opinions were not suppressed by force and human power so much as they were by the passage of time. But under this cover, public religion was not only despised with impunity, but amidst the evil that liberty sometimes causes, one often noticed the growth of absurd and wicked arguments that corrupt good morals.

<margin>
And other denominations were also granted freedom of religion outside of the churches.
<note>References: Bor XXII. 90. Bor XIV. 170. Hooft XVI. 636. Grot. Defense in Chapter III, p. 31.</note>
</margin>

The other denominations, which sought to further the Reformation according to their own understanding—among others the followers of the **Augsburg Confession** <note>The primary confession of faith for the Lutheran Church, written in 1530.</note>, or the **Lutherans**, and all the **Anabaptists** <note>original: *Doopsgefinden*. A branch of the Reformation that practiced adult baptism and often advocated for the separation of church and state.</note>—also enjoyed freedom of religion in private gathering places. But within Woerden, the Lutherans were granted the use of the public church for their worship. Even among those who were called simply "Reformed" and preached in the churches, there was still some diversity.

<margin>
Jan Ysbrandtsz., Preacher at Rotterdam, opposes Calvin's predestination.
<note>original: *Uitenb. Kerk. Hist. p. 48.* refers to Johannes Wtenbogaert’s influential *Ecclesiastical History*.</note>

# OF THE REFORMATION. BOOK X.

<page-num>551</page-num>

<margin>
* 1573
* See Part II of the *Response to the Counter-Remonstrance*, p. 45...
† See Grotius, *Apology*, chapter 3, p. 31, 32. See also *The Piety of the States of Holland*, p. 42. <note>original: "Vid. & Ordinum Hollandiae Pietat."</note>
</margin>

...the majority of the ministers in these lands, through the instruction * of their teachers, have fallen on the side of Calvin regarding the point of predestination <note>The doctrine that God has eternally ordained the salvation or damnation of individuals.</note>: yet it is certain † that from the beginning of the war, some ministers, many of the authorities, and countless members held the other opinion. This could not have been otherwise, given the high regard held in these lands for the writings of Erasmus, as well as the popularity of the *House-book* <note>original: *huisboek*; a collection of sermons by Heinrich Bullinger that served as a staple for family worship.</note> of Bullinger, the writings of Melanchthon, and the *Layman’s Guide* of Anastasius Veluanus <note>The pseudonym of Jan Gerritsz Versteghe, whose 1554 work was a foundational text for early Dutch Protestants seeking a middle way.</note>.

<margin>
The kind of Reformation the Prince of Orange and the States of Holland sought and intended to maintain. Grotius, *Apology*, Chapter 3, p. 29.
</margin>
There was also a marked difference in the matter of the Reformation between the Prince of Orange and the States of Holland on one side, and the clergy on the other. The Prince and the States did not merely have an abhorrence of the Inquisition and the bloody placards <note>original: *plakkaeten*; the harsh anti-heresy edicts issued by the Spanish crown.</note>; rather, since for a hundred years or more, many pious and learned men, noticing the great abuses that had crept into Christendom, had called for a Reformation—that is, an improvement and restoration of matters to their original state—so too were they heartily inclined toward this, without, however, binding themselves strictly to any specific opinions upon which even the learned men who deemed the Reformation necessary could not agree. In contrast, the ministers, feeling a zeal and affection for the masters whose lessons or writings had instructed them, sought to give the opinions of those masters as much status and authority as possible. This difference in perspective was greatly fueled by the fact that many of the "Politiques" <note>original: *Politijken*; secular leaders who prioritized civil peace and state stability over rigid theological uniformity.</note> had gained their knowledge of the abuses through the books of Erasmus of Rotterdam, who was always highly inclined toward peace and moderation. The ministers, on the other hand, had mostly exercised themselves in the books of Calvin and some others, who were very strongly pushing their own specific opinions.

<margin>
The word "Reformation" taken in two ways. Grotius, *Apology*, p. 29.
</margin>
From this it also followed that the word REFORMATION, or REFORMED RELIGION, was taken in a different sense by the authorities than by the clergy: for many clergy understood by it a total agreement in all points with their teachers;

<margin>
What the States understood by it. Grotius, *Apology*, p. 29.
</margin>
the authorities understood a service to God, cleansed of gross abuses, and furthermore not too narrowly defined in matters of opinion regarding disputable points. To avoid this ambiguity, the authorities often preferred to say the "Christian" or "Evangelical" religion, or...

...[dy]ing, they asked, "Why then is Monceau put to death?" To which the Monk, having no ready answer to offer, could only respond with silence. De Sor, having been brought to Brussels, underwent severe trials and temptations. Then they pretended they wished to release him, and made him believe this; they also told him he should send for his wife to join him. She came, escorted by Robert du Four of Tournai. But they were all seized, and the man, the wife, and their friend were together put to death. 

In this same year, after some negotiation between certain Frisian and Flemish Anabaptists <note>original: "Doopsgesinden." These were followers of the radical Reformation who practiced adult baptism and were often divided by strict regional and doctrinal differences.</note>, inhabitants of a part of Groningen called Homsterland, a peace and union was made upon certain minor conditions, which has since been called the **Homster Peace**. This agreement was viewed favorably by most Frisians, who had grown weary of the schism, and they waited in silence to see how others would receive it. However, most of the Flemish Anabaptists disapproved and opposed it, so that it lasted barely four years. 

After the relief of Leiden, which occurred on the third of October <note>original: "Wijnmaendt" or Wine-month.</note>, the Minister Kaspar Koolhaes entered the city. He had been called to the church service by the City Magistrates some months earlier, but had been shut out by the siege. He was the same man who, nine years prior, had helped introduce the Reformation to Deventer with great moderation *; and since then had preached the Gospel at Essen, in the Palatinate, and at Gorcum. At the Synod recently held in Dordrecht, he had spoken against certain proposals which, in his opinion, savored too much of Popish strictness <note>meaning excessive ecclesiastical rigor or legalism</note>: yet he nevertheless conformed in Leiden to everything he felt he could concede to the opinions of his fellow brethren. 

Christmas Day fell on a Sunday this year, on which day there was preaching in Leiden; but on the second and third days of Christmas, the Ministers refused to preach, to the dissatisfaction of many, in order to abolish those feast days according to the decision of the Synod. In contrast, at Dordrecht, Rotterdam, Delft, and in The Hague, there was preaching on those days †. In Leiden, they also baptized children by sprinkling, to please the Synod; yet there was not a single church in Holland or Zeeland that followed them in this. A short time later, on the eighth of February <note>original: "Sprokkelmaendt" or Wood-gathering month.</note>, in the year fifteen hundred and seventy-five, the **University** <note>original: "hooge Schoole." Founded by William of Orange as a reward for the city's endurance during the Spanish siege.</note> was established there in recognition of the steadfastness of the people of Leiden, and the first lessons in Theology were given by the Minister Koolhaes.

# HISTORY

<margin>1575.
J. Meurs, *Athenae Batavae*, Vol. II, p. 250.
Uitenbogaert, *Church History*, p. 177.
From the preface of Feugueray's *Opuscula*. Uitenbogaert, *History*, p. 178.</margin>
...concluded, until Guillaume Feugueray, called to be a Professor, arrived from France. In the year fifteen hundred and seventy, he published a certain small book, which he dedicated to the Prince of Orange. In his praise of the Prince, he wrote, among other things: *That the Prince does not use all types of men or means in the spreading of Religion. He holds, he says, that Religion must be propagated, and he labors toward that end, but not through such a path that would ruin both Religion and the Fatherland: for he believes that Religion must be encouraged, not forced.*

<margin>Johannes Holmannus, Professor of Theology.
Grotius, *Apology*, ch. III, p. 33. P. Bertius, *Oration on the Death of Arminius*, p. V. Address to Fr. Gomarus, p. Cij. Second part of the *Answer to the Counter-Remonstrants*, pp. 18, 19, 83, 84.</margin>
Among the first Professors of Theology at Leiden was also Johannes Holmannus Secundus, who, regarding the matter of Predestination <term>the theological doctrine that God has foreordained the salvation or damnation of every soul</term>, held the views of Melanchthon <note>Philip Melanchthon was a collaborator of Luther known for a more moderate and humanistic approach than some later reformers.</note>. He had been recommended to the school by the famous Theodore Beza, who at that time judged that his theology—that is, the Melanchthonian view—was the most suitable and edifying for these lands. It is told of Holmannus that in a public debate against Donellus, who pushed for predestination according to the strict views of the Genevan church, he openly said: *You make God a tyrant and an executioner* <note>original Latin: "Vos facitis Deum tyrannum & carnificem"</note>.

<margin>J. Meurs, *Athenae Batavae*, book I, ch. XIII, p. 37.
Bor, Vol. VIII, 103. d.
Uitenbogaert, p. 181.

† See Velius, *Chronicle of Hoorn*, p. 244.</margin>
The aforementioned Holmannus, whom Meursius (in the book he left concerning the University of Leiden) called an outstanding man, lived until the year fifteen hundred and eighty. Upon departing this life, he bequeathed all his books to the University library to serve the needs of those eager to learn. On the eleventh of April <note>original: "Grasmaendt" (Grass month), the traditional Dutch name for April.</note>, a Synod of North Holland ministers was held at Alkmaar, where doctrine and church order were discussed, and several disputes between ministers were settled. At this gathering, Lord Dirk Sonoy was to have been present to direct the proceedings with his authority; however, being hindered by the expedition to Barndegat †, his place was filled by Philips Corneliszoon, Burgomaster <term>the chief magistrate or mayor</term> of the city of Alkmaar.

Among the first Professors of Theology at Leiden was also Johannes Holmannus Secundus, who, regarding the matter of predestination, held the view of Melanchthon <note>Philipp Melanchthon (1497–1560) was a collaborator of Luther who took a more moderate, synergistic view of salvation compared to the strict predestination of Calvin.</note>. He had been recommended to the school by the famous Theodore Beza <note>Calvin's successor in Geneva.</note>, who at that time judged that his—that is, the Melanchthonian—Theology was the most suitable and edifying for these lands. It is told of Holmannus that in a public dispute against Donellus <note>Hugo Donellus, a famous French jurist at Leiden.</note>, who pushed for the doctrine of predestination according to the view of the Genevan church, he openly said: *Vos facitis Deum tyrannum & carnificem:* <note>Latin: "You make God a tyrant and an executioner."</note> that is, *You make God into a tyrant and a hangman.* The aforementioned Holmannus, whom Meursius called an outstanding man in his history of the Leiden University, lived until the year fifteen hundred and eighty-six. Upon departing this life, he bequeathed all his books to the University library to serve the needs of those eager to learn.

This was, it is believed, the only reason why the Consistories fell into such disfavor with the States that they were very nearly abolished entirely by a state decree.

# HISTORY

<margin>1575. Account of the Preachers against Koolhaes <note>Caspar Coolhaes (1534–1615), a liberal minister in Leiden who favored state control over the church, sparking significant controversy.</note>, printed at Dordrecht by I. Kanin 1582. p. 3, 4.</margin>
Ministers alone had preached and administered the Sacraments, admitting anyone based on their own trial <note>That is, based on the individual's own conscience or self-examination.</note>, and that the Magistrates should appoint and dismiss Ministers, and further govern the church in the manner they found most useful and appropriate. They judged that this would serve to preserve the freedom of conscience. They also said that the Ministers' intentions were a **new system of monkery**, through which they would in time again become masters over the Authorities, just as had happened under Popery. There were also Ministers found who showed little respect for the high Authority, and in the beginning of the war, called the Lords of the States "stakes" <note>Likely implying they were as useful or as stiff as wooden posts.</note> in their sermons because the States did not sufficiently yield to their will.

<margin>Grotius, *Apology* IX. 95.</margin>
In this state of affairs, the Spaniards captured Buren, Oudewater, Schoonhoven, and Krimpen.

<margin>Massacre at Oudewater. Bor VIII, 121. Hooft X. 424. Bertius’s *Funeral Oration for Arminius* p. iv, vi.</margin>
At Oudewater, which was taken by storm, a great massacre was carried out, including among women and maidens. Among others, the mother, sister, two brothers, and other blood relatives of **Jacob Hermanszoon**—later known by the name **Arminius** <note>Jacobus Arminius (1560–1609) became the foundational theologian of the Remonstrant movement, which favored a more liberal interpretation of predestination.</note>—lost their lives here; at that time, he was at school in Marburg with Rudolph Snellius, his countryman from Oudewater.

<margin>*History of the Martyrs* f. 495.</margin>
The Minister **Johannes Gelasius**, after seeing his son killed before his eyes and his wife receive several wounds, was brought unknown into the camp and ransomed for five hundred guilders; but when a Beguine <note>A member of a lay religious community of women.</note> revealed his identity, he was hanged from the gallows. **Christiaen de la Cueillerie**, a Minister of the French-speaking congregation, gave himself the name Anthony and posed as a soldier, through which he was released for one hundred crowns.

<margin>Uitenbogaert, *Preface to his Life* p. b. iv.</margin>
At Schoonhoven, the Priest **Pieter Janszoon Uitenbogaert** <note>The father of Johannes Wtenbogaert, the influential leader of the Remonstrants.</note> escaped the hands of the Spaniards in a wondrous manner and was since called to Delft, where he served the church faithfully and laudably for several years until his passing.

<margin>Anabaptists killed. *History of the Anabaptist Martyrs* 747.</margin>
Within Antwerp and Brussels, two men, two women, and two maidens, all **Anabaptists** <note>original: *Doopsgefinden*—literally "Baptism-minded," referring to the Mennonites and other radical reformers who practiced adult baptism.</note>, were put to death this year.

<margin>Some Anabaptists flee to England.</margin>
Some of that persuasion fled from Flanders to England, thinking that under the reign of **Queen Elizabeth** they might live according to their conscience, but they soon found themselves forced to flee back from England to Holland and Zeeland.

<margin>Are treated harshly there.</margin>
A persecution arose against them there, which belongs here as an insertion. Their meeting was disturbed, several were imprisoned, and five of them—after much verbal strife and threats of the

### OF THE REFORMATION, BOOK XI.

...death, to move them to accept the Reformed Religion. <margin>1575. History of the Anabaptist Martyrs, Vol. II, p. 748.</margin> Nevertheless, they were put on display at St. Paul’s churchyard with bundles of firewood <note>In the 16th century, carrying a "faggot" (a bundle of wood) on one's shoulder was a public sign that a person had been convicted of heresy and had narrowly escaped being burned at the stake.</note> on their shoulders, as a sign that they had deserved the fire. Fourteen women were deported from the country by ship, and a youth was tied to a cart, lashed with whips, and, along with the women, banished on pain of death. Five men were still held captive in a deep, filthy dungeon, where one of them ended his days. The Ministers of the Dutch and French churches in London worked with great effort to draw the other four to their viewpoint. The Bishop of London <note>Edwin Sandys (1519–1588), who was then Bishop of London.</note> dealt with them very harshly, pressing for the signing of these four points: *First, that they should renounce their sect and confess that the* <margin>From a letter by Jacob de Somere.</margin> *Devil had led them to it; furthermore, they were to believe and confess with heart and mouth that Christ had taken his flesh and blood from the substance of the flesh and blood of Mary. Secondly, that young children ought to be baptized. Thirdly, that a Christian could serve in a government office. Fourthly, that a Christian might indeed take an oath.* They remained firm in their refusal and wrote down their views on the aforementioned points, along with a plea to the Queen to be released. However, the Queen had been so turned against them by certain fierce people that she refused to receive their writings, believing that they denied God and Christ, rejected the office of the Government as ungodly, and made the people rebellious.

<margin>History of the Anabaptist Martyrs, Vol. II, p. 762.</margin> The Bishop also (as Jacob de Somere, a member of the Reformed church and later the Pensionary <note>The chief legal advisor or magistrate of a city.</note> of the city of Ghent, wrote from London to his mother) issued several Articles on behalf of her Majesty, among which was this: *That a Christian Government might punish stubborn heretics with the sword*, commanding all foreigners to sign the same, or if not, to provide bail to appear when summoned for examination and, if found guilty, to be punished. Most foreigners signed this. Finally, on the twenty-second of <margin>Two Anabaptists burned in London.</margin> July <note>Original: "Hooimaendt," the traditional Dutch name for July, meaning "Hay-month."</note>, the two oldest of the prisoners, Jan Pieterssoon and Hendrik Terwoordt—though many of the most modest, godly, and learned English and Dutch people made many pleas to obtain mercy for them—were both tied to a single stake at Smithfield <note>A famous site in London used for public executions and cattle markets.</note>, where the Reformed used to be burned in former times. There, without any strangling or gunpowder <note>Gunpowder was sometimes hung around the neck of the condemned to hasten death; its absence meant a slower, more agonizing death by fire.</note>, they were burned alive to ashes.

1575. Ministers alone had preached and administered the Sacraments, admitting each person based on their own testing <note>Meaning individual examination of faith</note>, and held that the Magistrates should appoint and dismiss Ministers, and furthermore govern the church as they should find most useful and fitting. They judged that this would serve to preserve freedom of conscience. They also said that the Ministers' intention was a new "monkery," <note>A derogatory term comparing the Reformed clergy's desire for power to the Roman Catholic monastic orders</note> through which they would in time again become masters over the Authorities, just as had happened under the Papacy. There were also Ministers found who showed little respect for the high Authority, and called the Lords States "stakes" in their sermons at the start of the war, because they would not sufficiently yield to their will. In this state of affairs, the Spaniards won Buren, Oudewater, Schoonhoven, and Krimpen. At Oudewater, which was taken by storm, a great massacre was committed, including among women and maidens. Among others who lost their lives here were the mother, the sister, two brothers, and other blood relatives of Jacob Hermanssoon, later known by the name of Arminius <note>Jacobus Arminius (1560–1609), the theologian whose ideas led to the Remonstrant movement</note>, who was at that time at school in Marburg with Rudolphus Snellius, his countryman from Oudewater. The Minister Johannes Gelasius, after seeing his son killed before his eyes and his wife receive several wounds, was brought unrecognized into the camp and ransomed for five hundred guilders; but when a beguine <note>A member of a lay religious community</note> identified him, he was hanged from the gallows. Christiaen de la Cueillerie, Minister of the French, took the name of Anthony and posed as a soldier, by which means he was released for a hundred crowns. At Schoonhoven, the Pastor Pieter Janssoon Uitenbogaerdt escaped the hands of the Spaniards in a wondrous manner, and was since called to Delft, where he served the church faithfully and laudably for some years until his passing. Within Antwerp and Brussels, two men, two women, and two maidens, all Anabaptists <note>original: "Doopsgesinden"</note>, were put to death this year. Some of that persuasion fled from Flanders to England, thinking that under the reign of Queen Elizabeth they might live according to their conscience, but soon found themselves forced to flee again from England to Holland and Zeeland. There a persecution arose against them, which is about to be described here. Their meeting was disturbed, several were imprisoned, and five of them—after much dispute of words and threats—

Nevertheless, they were put on display in St. Paul’s churchyard, with faggots <note>bundles of sticks used as fuel for fires; carrying them was a public penance signifying that the person deserved to be burned</note> on their shoulders, as a sign that they had deserved the fire. Fourteen women were taken out of the country by ship; a youth was bound to a cart and whipped with lashes and, along with the women, was banished upon pain of death. Five men were still kept imprisoned in a deep, foul dungeon, where one of them ended his days. The Ministers of the Dutch and French churches in London fought with great labor to draw the other four to their viewpoint. The Bishop of London was very hard on them, pressing for the signing of these four points:
<margin>From a letter by Jacob de Somere.</margin>
*First, that they should renounce their sect, and confess that the* Devil *had led them to it: furthermore, they should believe and confess with heart and mouth that Christ had taken his flesh and blood from the essence of the flesh and blood of* Mary <note>The Anabaptists often held a "celestial flesh" doctrine, believing Christ's body was divine and merely passed through Mary like water through a pipe; this was considered a major heresy</note>. *Secondly, that young children ought to be baptized. Thirdly, that a* Christian *might serve in a Magistrate’s office. Fourthly, that a* Christian *might rightly take an oath.* They persisted in their refusal and wrote down their views on the aforementioned points, along with a plea to the Queen to be released. However, the Queen had been so stirred up against them by certain vehement men that she refused to receive their writings, believing that they denied God and Christ, rejected the office of the 
<margin>*History of the Anabaptist Martyrs* II. p. 762.</margin>

# HISTORY

<margin>
1575.
1 *History of the Anabaptist Martyrs*, p. 749; 752, 763. See the *Chronicle of England* by Edmond Howes, printed by Thomas Dawson 1615, p. 678.
2 Caspar Grevinckhoven, *On the Freedom of the Sects*. Printed at Dordrecht, 1611, p. 23.
3 Read A. van Kornput’s *Divine Tribunal*, Part I, p. 160...
4 See the letter of Jacob de Somere in the *History of the Anabaptist Martyrs*, p. 764.
</margin>
burned¹: dying with great terror, crying out and shouting. Of one of those burned, it is recounted that he cried: "I confess that you are Christ, God and man, born of Mary according to the flesh," or similar words: and had he not already been for the most part consumed by the fire, they would have preserved his life². The first, Jan Pieterssoon, was a poor man of fifty years, with nine children, whose first wife had previously been burned at Ghent for matters of Religion, and he was now remarried to a woman whose first husband had likewise been put to death by fire for the sake of faith. He had pointed this out sufficiently to the Bishop, requesting to be allowed to depart with his wife and little children. But in vain. This harshness—not the first³ that had been committed in England since the Reformation—seemed unbelievable and strange to many Reformed <note>The author refers to members of the Dutch Reformed Church</note> who were still living "under the cross" <note>A term used for the persecuted Protestant churches in the Spanish Netherlands</note> in Flanders and Brabant.⁴ They were grieved that those who had recently suffered persecution themselves were now persecuting others for their Religion, and doing violence to the consciences of others with fire and sword; whereas they had previously taught the truth: that it did not belong to men to rule over another's conscience; that faith was a gift of God, and was implanted in man not by any outward force, but by the word of God and the illumination of the Holy Spirit. They argued that heresy was not a carnal but a spiritual crime, which God alone should punish; and that one should overcome lies not with force, but with truth. They held that the nature of the children of God was not to kill others for their faith, but to be killed themselves for the testimony of the truth. Finally, they believed that bloodshed over matters of Religion was a certain sign of the Antichrist, who thereby places himself in the seat and judgment seat of God, and usurps the dominion over conscience, which belongs to God alone.

<margin>p. 750.</margin>
The two remaining prisoners were released after being imprisoned for some time. The other exiles, having fled to Holland and Zeeland, found there the refuge of exiles and the freedom to practice their Religion.

# OF THE REFORMATION. BOOK XI.

<margin>1575.</margin>
his son *Nanning* <note>Nanning Koppe, a victim of the notorious persecutions in North Holland</note> was stretched upon the rack <note>original: *paleij*, a pulley-driven torture device</note> twenty-two or twenty-three times with exquisite inventions of cruelty, and, despite the fact that he protested his innocence every time despite the pain, he finally had his heart cut from his body and was quartered. To prepare him for death and put him in a state to think of God and his soul as the time required, the Judges gave him sweet wine to drink in order to dull his mind and speech; which he, thirsty as a hunted deer, drank deeply. Yet this did not make his brain so loose that he forgot, upon coming to the scaffold, to raise his plea of innocence once more. But the Preacher, *Juriaen Epessoon*, under the guise of strengthening him with Holy Scripture, interrupted his speech and drowned it out by shouting: rebuking him for his denial and asserting that he had previously confessed to the crime. Thereupon the sufferer summoned him to appear before God’s judgment seat within three—others say four or five—days. The Preacher ran home despondently after *Nanning’s* death, constantly complaining about the summons issued to him; he immediately fell ill in bed and was a corpse within the appointed time. Likewise, one *Pieter Nanningssoon* was brought to the rack in the most savage manner some twenty-four or twenty-five times, and thereafter also *Jan Jeroenssoon* and *Pieter Ellertssoon*, Roman Catholic citizens of *Hoorn*, were imprisoned based on the extorted accusations of *Pieter Nanning*. They were brought to the house at *Schagen*, and the last was tortured four times in two days. But the *Prince of Orange*, understanding the circumstances of the case through the Magistrates of *Hoorn*—who made their complaint to him as the Land’s Stadtholder <note>The provincial governor and military commander</note>—stayed the hands of the Judges, who by now were known among the people by the name of
<margin>
Bor VIII, 116.
</margin>
the Blood Council <note>original: *Bloedtraedt*</note>; also, the *Court of Holland* some time later ordered the prison at *Schagen* to be opened, the remaining prisoners to be taken to *Delft*, and, upon providing a guarantee, released. This resulted in no small praise for the Prince. It was he, people cried,
<margin>Hooft p. 419.</margin>
who blunted *Sonoy’s* bitterness, put his Blood Council to shame, and embraced all pious people, of whatever persuasion they were, with fatherly sincerity and even-handed justice. Indeed, the affection of all inhabitants was now needed to the highest degree to stand against the Spanish violence, which grew heavier daily. Efforts were made to separate *Zeeland* and *Holland* from one another, and they <note>The Spanish forces</note> gained a foothold on the island of *Schouwen*. *Brouwershaven* and *Bommenee* were captured, and *Zierikzee* was besieged. ...the English, which threatened to break out into an open war, and brought the Prince to such distress that he proposed that men, women, and children who loved freedom, along with their best movable possessions, should be loaded onto ships; that all dikes and dams be breached, and mills set on fire; and the entire land be devastated with water: in order, as had been practiced by various nations of old, to take up some other corner of the world, and there live free from slavery of body and mind. <note>This "Great Exodus" plan was a scorched-earth strategy where the Dutch would have literally drowned their country to prevent its capture, migrating as a nation to find a new home.</note> But this necessity was suddenly averted by the mutiny of the Spanish soldiery on the island of Schouwen, which they abandoned: and joining with others, they committed such outrages in Brabant and Flanders that the Council of State declared them rebels against the King and enemies. Since he, and Holland, had taken up arms for legal and proper freedom.*

To those of Utrecht.
*Bor IX. 159. c.* (Aug. 3)

The call of Bartoldus to Hoorn.
*Ph. Marnix. epist. ad A. Myl. in Epist. select. Centur. II. p. 711, 712.*

At this time, the Magistrate of the city of Hoorn had accepted a certain Bartoldus into the church service, in defiance of the <term>Classis</term> <note>A Classis is a regional governing body in the Reformed Church, composed of ministers and elders</note> and the other Ministers. But the Lord of <insert>Marnix van</insert> Saint Aldegonde, being then at Delft, advised them against it. He wanted them first to proceed in a gentler way, by submitting a petition to the Magistrate, whom he believed they could bring to fairness and duty much better through reasons and sweet humility than through the dominance and authority of the Prince, against which they might perhaps resist out of a troubled mind. That advice seemed very necessary to him at that time; because, if through the opposition of those of Hoorn any dispute, however small it was, should arise, it would greatly tend

*Selected Letters, Century II, Page 753.*

> *From your writing, very dear brother, I understand that you are concerned about the case of Bartoldus. What I have done in it, and what Lord Tassin finds good, is well enough known. You only want the offense given to be removed by a public confession of guilt. Oh, if only you obtained it! But what will happen if he refuses it, and would rather refrain from the ministry? Then you will perhaps think that the church will be well off. But how will the Magistrate behave in the meantime? Or do you think that all offense will be removed as soon as he is removed from his service? Truly I am very afraid that a new fire will be ignited, by whose flame no small part of the church will be burned. I am certain that most Magistrates, and a large part of the States, are highly opposed to this discipline.* <note>The "discipline" refers to the right of the church to punish or excommunicate members without the interference of the civil government.</note> *These could be won over without great trouble, with a moderate tolerance, to the very great benefit of the church. I believe that one ought especially to labor towards that. For since the strict rule is not so evenly and distinctly prescribed in the Word of God, I cannot see why regarding the same, according to the circumstances of the church’s case and the prudent discretion of the Ministers, something could not sometimes be yielded: if it were otherwise yielded to tighten the bowstring* <note>original: "peeſe ſtijver te ſpannen"</note> *which until now has been used loosely. I know that Bartoldus has transgressed, and will openly prove it if he does not repent. But I see that you are pressing hard with great danger on that which you could forgive him without any disadvantage; especially now that he confesses, signs, and begs forgiveness for his guilt—and that also in writing—before the Magistrate and before the entire Church Council. I do not want my judgment to count here, however: follow the judgment of the church. I shall certainly take care that no obstacle is thrown in your way by me. What you request, that I should deal with Van der Mijle and other godly men, I have already done before this. And I see that the feeling of all the most prudent and reasonable people tends that way. If, however, something more can be obtained without hindrance to the church, I shall praise it. The sequel and the end of the dispute with that Bartoldus...*

Governor of Holland, Zeeland, Friesland, and of the Province of Utrecht, and we, the States of Holland and Zeeland, with our associates: Having taken nothing more to heart (as is right) than that in our cities and other places of our Jurisdiction, the Doctrine of the holy Gospel be presented in its purest form, and also that the churches themselves be governed in the best possible way, have seen fit to establish these Laws with mature counsel, which we also wish to have kept inviolable; and it has seemed expedient to us that we should frame them chiefly regarding the administration of Church Government, of which four types are principally found in the Holy Scriptures; Namely, Pastors, who are also called Bishops, Elders, and Ministers in the Holy Scripture, whose office consists primarily in teaching God’s word and administering the Sacraments: Of Doctors, in whose place are now the Professors of Theology: Of Elders, whose principal office in former times was to watch over morals and to bring transgressors back to the right path with kindly admonitions; and of Deacons, who have the care of the poor and the sick.*

<margin>
Regarding the Preachers, and first regarding their appointment.
</margin>

1. *The Magistrate of each head city, upon the nomination and with the advice of their Preachers, shall choose Preachers for their city and all the places within their jurisdiction.*

2. *In the cities occupied by us, and those coming to our side, Preachers shall be found from elsewhere until the Magistrates of the same (having taken the proper Oath) have accepted the protection of our reformed Religion.*

### OF THE REFORMATION. BOOK XI.

<margin>1576. Regarding the gatherings of the Ministers.</margin>
10. *The Ministers <note>original: "Predikanten." These were the Protestant clergy.</note> of each capital city, and of the places that are subordinate to them, shall meet every other week in the capital city to which they belong, in order to confer on doctrine, so that they may maintain it purely and in unity.*

11. *In the event that any do not appear (unless there were a lawful excuse), the same shall be a shame to them, and if they stubbornly persist in staying away, they shall also be appropriately compelled to attend.*

12. *And so that it may be known how diligent each person is in their studies, the Ministers in these same gatherings shall, by turns, explain some text of the Holy Scripture, upon which it shall be free for the others to argue <note>In this context, "argue" refers to the formal academic practice of disputation or scholarly debate.</note>, in the event that anything was poorly said or done.*

<margin>On settling the controversies of the Ministers.</margin>
13. *If any controversy regarding Doctrine arises, the Ministers shall settle it among themselves, and if the matter requires it, they shall call the Elders <note>original: "Ouderlingen," lay leaders responsible for church governance.</note> to assist; if even then an agreement cannot be reached, the matter shall be brought before the Government <note>original: "Overheit."</note>, who shall ensure that the same is properly settled.*

<margin>On punishing the transgressions of the Ministers.</margin>
14. *A Minister guilty of a disgraceful crime shall, after being stripped of his office, be punished according to the written laws.*

15. *The accuser, if he does not prove his case, shall suffer the punishment established for calumny <note>original: "calumnie," meaning malicious slander or false accusation.</note>.*

16. *Regarding those crimes of the Ministers for which no punishment is set by law, yet which nonetheless cause offense—namely, unusual or improper explanations of the Holy Scripture, curious searching into vain questions, the introduction of any novelty into the congregation, negligence in studies, weak rebuking of faults, roguish jests, lies, backbiting, wantonness of the tongue, lightheartedness, guile, greed, immoderate anger in disputations and rebukes, excessive bitterness; or lack of restraint in clothing, gestures, or manners and other things of common life, and more of the like—the Elders (having found the matter to be true) shall make it known to the Government, and at the same time state their opinion on it; though in all cases the supreme judgment of the punishment shall always remain with the Magistrate <note>original: "Magistraet." This emphasizes that the civil government, not the church alone, held final legal authority over clergy behavior.</note>.*

17. *In the case of lesser faults, which deserve nothing more than a simple warning, the manner prescribed by the Lord shall be maintained, so that as a last resort the matters shall be brought before the leaders of the church.*

18. *And so that all the Ministers, both of each capital city and the subordinate places, (as much as is possible) may monitor the faults of their gather-*

Lay leaders responsible for church governance.</note> from each capital city, and one or two of the Ministers, shall travel together every year through the territory belonging to that capital city, investigating how the Ministers in each place conduct themselves; and if they find anything unbecoming in anyone, they shall report the same to the Magistrate of the capital city, so that the Magistrate may provide a timely remedy according to the circumstances of the case.*

21. *The Magistrate <note>The local civil government or town council.</note> of each place shall, upon the advice of the Ministers, ordain when and how often sermons should be given, such that in any case, in populous places, preaching shall occur at least three times a week; and everywhere on Sunday afternoons, the Heidelberg Catechism <note>A Protestant instructional document written in 1563, used to teach the core tenets of the Reformed faith.</note> shall be explained.*

22. *Baptism shall be administered by the Ministers alone, according to the form set behind the Catechism, and after the sermon. As often as children are presented, Baptism shall be refused to no one.*

23. *If the fathers themselves present the children for Baptism, it is godly and praiseworthy; however, if this does not happen, the Baptism shall nonetheless proceed.*

24. *It shall not be necessary to have witnesses for the Baptism, and any person shall be admitted as a witness.*

25. *The names of those baptized, and those of their parents, shall be recorded in a public book.*

26. *If any who are weak in faith request to have their sick children baptized at home, their desires shall be granted, provided however that (if possible) several godly persons may be present at the Baptism.*

35. The Ministers shall not forget those who are held in prison; but shall go to them, though only with the permission of the Magistrates.

At the same time, some Reasons for the aforementioned Ecclesiastical Laws were also put to paper in the name of the States of Holland and Zeeland, which are very remarkable and are of this content:

> That the godly Authorities have always claimed for themselves the establishment of the Laws concerning Religion is beyond dispute, and God has established such Laws not through Aaron <note>The High Priest of Israel.</note> but through Moses <note>The civil leader of Israel, here used to argue that the State, not the Clergy, has primary legislative authority.</note>, which also thereafter always remained so among the people of Israel: namely, that the highest Authority and power of the same Laws should reside with the Judges, Kings, and finally with the Princes, of which things the books of the Old Testament are full of testimonies. But at the time when the books of the New Testament were written, the Authorities were for the most part not only estranged from the true Religion, but were also very bitter enemies of the same, so that the godly were forced to keep to themselves, and—if something was required in the state of Religion—to decree it themselves. This situation lasted several hundred years; but after the supreme Monarch of the world, Constantine <note>Constantine the Great (r. 306–337 AD), the first Roman Emperor to convert to Christianity.</note>, had accepted the Religion, he himself decreed what was needed for the expansion, enlightenment, and support thereof, which his successors after him also maintained for many hundreds of years. Therefore, in the first book of the *Code* <note>original: "Codicis," referring to the *Codex Justinianus*, a collection of laws compiled by Emperor Justinian I.</note> there are many long titles concerning Religion, and in Justinian’s *Novels* <note>original: "Novellis," the *Novellae Constitutiones*, which were new laws issued by Justinian after the main Code was completed.</note> not a few institutions as large as books; and the Philosopher Leo, Emperor of Constantinople (as appears in his *Novels*) maintains this manner; in which also the other Emperors

### OF THE REFORMATION. BOOK XI.

persisted in, as *Zonaras* <note>Johannes Zonaras (12th century), a Byzantine chronicler and theologian.</note> testifies in *Photius's Nomocanons* <note>original: "Photii Nomocanonicis." A collection of Byzantine ecclesiastical law. The States are using Eastern Orthodox precedents to argue against Roman papal authority.</note>. Meanwhile, in 1576, in the West the Roman Bishop [the Pope] has gradually drawn this authority—as well as the realm itself—to himself, and has at once become the opposite of what he was before, and ought to be; whereby the godly have again fallen into the same distress in which they were under the godless Emperors, so that they also had to hold secret meetings for matters of Religion, and even provide for what was found necessary for it. But since God has granted us the grace that we may withdraw from the slavery of godlessness, and dare to make a profession of the pure Religion, we have deemed it our bounden duty, according to the character of our people, to establish laws for the Governance <term>Governance</term> <note>original: "Regiment." ### OF THE REFORMATION. BOOK XI.

...time had grown outdated, they requested in the year fifteen hundred seventy <margin>1576.</margin> from the Magistrate that the same be reinstated, protesting that they did not seek any profit for themselves therein, but rather so that both they and their descendants might be held more strictly to their duties. This matter is also recounted in the Ecclesiastical laws of that same city: and that the Bishops who are to be appointed should first be presented to the people, and everyone should be free to accuse them <note>This refers to the "right of objection," where a congregation could voice concerns about a candidate's character before they were officially instated.</note>; even *Justinian* <note>original: "Justinianus." The 6th-century Byzantine Emperor whose legal codes formed the basis of many European legal systems.</note> thought this good, following the prescription of the *Canons* <note>original: "Canones." These are the ancient decrees of church councils.</note>.

It is ill-advised to accept any public offices except under oath; it is therefore reasonable that the *Ministerial Office* also be accepted in this way. And since no one provides the whole community so great a benefit as a Preacher, it is also fair that he take the oath in the hands of the *Magistrate*, which is said for the sake of the eighth chapter.

Why the old ceremonies in the installation of *Pastors* should be left behind is explained by an evident reason in the *twenty-fourth chapter* of the *Synod of Dordrecht* <note>The Synod of Dordrecht (Dort) was a gathering of the Reformed Church; the author is aligning local laws with these ecclesiastical rulings.</note>; this pertains to the *ninth Chapter*.

It is entirely fair and very necessary that the *Proclaimers* of such excellent Doctrine, as they shall communicate it and exercise themselves therein, come together as often as possible, which the *three following Chapters* maintain.

Why indeed should the *Authorities* not settle the disputes of the *Preachers* when necessity so requires? For even if they are not all devoted to the Religion <note>This suggests that even if a civil magistrate was not a member of the Reformed Church, they still held legal authority over its ministers.</note>, they are nevertheless bound to it by Oath; and if something is beyond their understanding, they can bring the matter to us, which is what the *thirteenth Chapter* consists of.

The censure of morals belongs primarily to the *Preachers*; therefore they must take earnest care that they themselves are pure. And seeing as the eye is cast upon them far more than all others, they also sin by example, for which reason they are to be punished more severely; therefore no one shall withdraw them from the authority of the Magistrate, in which the equity of the *five preceding Chapters* almost entirely consists.

The benefit of the *nineteenth and twentieth Chapters* is seen clearer than midday.

Every *Magistrate*, with the advice of their *Preachers*, shall best be able to set order for the delivery of sermons, as it is not unknown to them what the place and the people require; nevertheless, care should be taken that there be as little inequality with other places as possible, which belongs to the *twenty-first Chapter*.

*This is the condition of our Government: that even the Catholics, who wish to follow our side for the sake of the common cause, are loyal to us through solemn promises; so that we ought also to tolerate the public exercise of the Papal Religion, were it not that the priests and monks, sworn enemies, had attempted to abuse the same to incite rebellion. ### HISTORY

<margin>1576.</margin> This is the current situation of our Government: that even the Catholics <note>original: "Pausgesinden," those loyal to the Pope</note>, who for the sake of the common cause wish to follow our side, are loyal to us through solemn promises; so much so that we ought even to tolerate the public exercises of the Roman religion, were it not that the priests and monks—sworn enemies—had attempted to abuse the same to incite rebellion. We even tolerate the Anabaptists <note>original: "Wederdoopers," a radical Reformation sect often persecuted for their beliefs on adult baptism and separation of church and state</note>; for we consider that true Religion is a gift from God, and that men should not be forced into it through the fear of exile or punishment, but rather should be invited with friendly admonition from the Word of God. 

In this mixing of Religions, we have not been able to avoid establishing some things differently than they might be handled among a people of a uniform Religion. In this regard, it should be seen that we do not wish for anyone to be refused Baptism; rather, we shall be protected by what Christ commanded <margin>Luke 18.</margin> when he said that one should not keep the children from him. Since he showed no regard for the parents' status in this, we have rightly decreed that Baptism should not be hindered out of respect for the parents' [failings]. Rather, in this confusion, it is the office of the Shepherds <note>the pastors or ministers</note> that they, following the <margin>1 Corinthians 9.</margin> example of Paul, become all things to all men, so that they might win over a great many. 

It may seem comparable that we allow all sorts of witnesses at Baptism, but no less pressing a reason has prompted us to this than that which, around the year fifteen hundred and sixty, compelled those of Bern <note>a reference to the Reformation in Switzerland</note> to make the testimony of Baptism common between themselves and the Papists. What they did to maintain friendship among those who were divided, we shall certainly be free to do to maintain and increase harmony among those who are mixed together. Public enemies of the Religion might well have been excluded, but such people will not easily present themselves for Baptism. Furthermore, that we allow private baptism at home <margin>Romans 14. 1 Thessalonians 5.</margin> we attribute to "weakness" <note>likely referring to physical illness of the infant or the spiritual fragility of new converts</note>, which the Holy Scripture has so strongly recommended; let this be said regarding the Chapters on Baptism.

Easter and Pentecost are held in such reverence that unless the Lord's Supper <note>original: "Nachtmael"</note> is administered then, it would lead to great offense; the day of Christ's birth <note>Christmas</note> is held in similar reverence. However, if the Supper <note>original: "Avontmael"</note> is held on the Sunday following the Nativity, all occasion for great offense will be removed. We have, for the present time, deemed it sufficient that the Lord’s Supper be celebrated only four times a year.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of proposed ecclesiastical laws in 1576, focusing on the civil government's role in appointing church officials and managing poor relief, before transitioning to the military and political upheavals of the year, specifically the Pacification of Ghent and the Spanish Fury.</meta>

HISTORY

<margin>1576.</margin>
*Just as it belongs to the <term>Magistrate<gloss>the civil government or city council</gloss></term> to grant all other offices, so it is also their right to appoint the <term>Elders<gloss>lay officers in the Reformed church responsible for discipline and oversight</gloss></term>. That others should elect them could not happen without the appearance of two different kinds of sovereign power; and because of the Magistrate, they receive more abundant authority and are more respected, being chosen by the Magistrate itself. But the confusion of religions and the troubled state of our <term>Republic<gloss>the emerging Dutch state</gloss></term> do not allow us at this time to assign to their office any other duties than what we have generally included in our Laws. The authority they used to have over individuals regarding their morals shall be generally recommended to them by the Magistrate, so that they may, as much as possible, curb all licentiousness and restore an elegant appearance to the Republic everywhere.*

*The counsel of the wise is that when the administration of the Republic must be renewed or improved, the old form should be kept as closely as possible. If this is based on reason—as it truly is based on very clear reason—then certainly nothing should be changed that is so well established that it can hardly be improved. Since our ancestors left sufficient income for all kinds of poor, and also prescribed the proper distribution of the same, let us not change their good intentions in this matter without worthy punishment <note>meaning: let us not recklessly deviate from these established charitable traditions</note>. Furthermore, because the income is hindered by the war, and many are made poor by its calamity, we shall have to tolerate the collection that takes place in the churches until, peace being granted again, our affairs have returned to their former state. May God, in his immeasurable kindness, grant that this good may soon shine upon us. Amen.*

<margin>P. 770. 771.</margin>
> *I thought during the torture, "O Lord, how shall I be able to endure this, must it last much longer?" Then it came to my mind that the eternal, hellish pain would be heavier and last forever. Then I took courage again and cried to God, "Help me in this need; so that I never bring my neighbor into this same sorrow," and the Lord gave me such courage that I would rather die on the rack... And a little later: The Lord took away my pain each time: when it was such that I thought, "it is impossible to endure," my limbs became as if numb. Praise, thanks, honor, and glory be to the Lord... My mind stands unchangeable and immovable... I am not only ready to let myself be tortured, but also to let my flesh be burned.*

That undaunted heart stayed with him until the end. In another letter, he addressed his wife, after thanking her for her service and loving companionship, commending her and her son to God, with these words: <margin>P. 775.</margin> *I send this letter in the face of the approaching parting, but it is no "letter of divorce" <note>original: "scheidtbrief," a reference to the Mosaic law in Deuteronomy 24:1</note> such as Israel wrote because of the hardness of hearts, and to thus leave you, my love. For this leaving happens for the love of God. For God's sake, all must be forsaken. God joined us together; God separates us again. I hand you and your child over to that Lord, as to a faithful Father. Stay faithfully with Him; He shall care for you in soul and body.* So peacefully did these people used to leave the dearest things they had, for the sake of God. </margin>
...month, the peace between the States of Brabant, Flanders, Artois, Hainaut, and other lands, and those of Holland and Zeeland, along with their allies, was concluded at Ghent.

<margin>Art. 2.</margin>
By this treaty, all suffering, injustice, crimes, and damages caused by the <term>disturbances<gloss>the "beroerten," referring to the ongoing Dutch Revolt against Spanish rule</gloss></term> were to be forgiven and forgotten. Furthermore, the provinces bound themselves to jointly drive out the Spaniards and other foreign soldiers, and thereafter to facilitate the meeting of the States General,

<margin>Art. 3.</margin>
just as they were convened at the time of the abdication of Emperor Charles <note>Emperor Charles V abdicated in 1555, a moment seen as the end of a more stable era of governance</note>: to the end that they might establish order regarding the affairs of the country, both concerning the matter and practice of religion in Holland, Zeeland, Bommel, and the places attached to them, as well as regarding the return of fortresses, artillery, ships, and everything belonging to the King that had been seized by them during the disturbances, or otherwise: to whose judgment both parties submitted themselves in good faith.

<margin>Art. 4.</margin>
The inhabitants of both sides would be free to go, return, frequent, trade, and reside everywhere. However, the Hollanders, Zeelanders, or others, whoever they might be, outside the lands of Holland, Zeeland, and those allied with them, were not to attempt anything to the detriment of the peace, and especially not against the Roman Catholic religion and its practice, nor were they to wrong, provoke, or annoy anyone on that account by word or deed, on pain of being punished as disturbers of the public peace.

<margin>Art. 5.</margin>
Nevertheless, so that in the meantime no one would be easily caught or cunningly ensnared and endangered, the edicts <note>the "plakkaeten," strict imperial laws issued to suppress heresy</note> previously issued regarding the matter of heresy, as well as the ordinances concerning capital crimes made by the Duke of Alva, were to be suspended,

<margin>Art. 6.</margin>
until the States General provided otherwise. The Prince of Orange would remain Admiral of the Sea and <term>Stadtholder<gloss>a provincial governor; while originally a royal appointment, by this time William of Orange held the office as a leader of the rebellion</gloss></term> of Holland and Zeeland, Bommel, and the places joined with them, to command in all things as he then did, until the States General ordered otherwise after the departure of the Spaniards.

<margin>Art. 7.</margin>
But regarding the cities and places included under the commission from the King received by him and not now under his authority, this point would remain suspended until these cities and places, joining this union, were satisfied and compensated by him regarding the points where they felt aggrieved under his government; both in respect to the practice of religion and otherwise.

<margin>Art. 10.</margin>
The Prince and all exiles and their heirs were to be restored to their property, name, and reputation, and all judgments and pleadings since the beginning of the disturbances in the year fifteen hundred...

<margin>1576. Art. 20.</margin>
sixty-six <note>Original: "sesentseftig." Though literally sixty-six, this refers to the period of unrest starting in 1566/67 through to the peace of 1576.</note>, whether for matters of Religion or for the taking up of arms, should be annulled and struck from the records. All secular Prelates and other ecclesiastical persons, whose abbeys, foundations, and residences lay outside of Holland and Zeeland, yet who held property within those same lands, should return to the ownership of those same goods.

<margin>Art. 21.</margin>
But regarding the monastic folk and other clergy who, being consecrated and owning property within the two aforementioned and neighboring lands, had remained outside or had departed from them, they (considering they were for the most part alienated from their goods) should, alongside those who remained, be provided with reasonable maintenance from then on, or be allowed the use of their goods, at the discretion, however, of the States; and all this by way of provision, until their further claims should be otherwise ordered by the States General.

<margin>(* 8 Dec.)</margin>
After the proclamation of this peace, the exiles returned: yet in Holland it was resolved * : that upon their arrival and restoration they should swear:

<margin>Oath demanded of those entering. Bor IX. 192. Hooft XI. 471.</margin>
>*To be faithful to the King as Count, the Prince as Stadtholder, and to the States; to help maintain freedom; to help resist the Spaniards; and not to attempt, by word or deed, anything directed against the Reformed religion and the exercise thereof, nor to seek to introduce or practice any other Religion in the land of Holland than that which was then present and publicly permitted by the Authorities, until such time as, after the expulsion of the Spaniards, it should be otherwise ordered by the States General, lawfully assembled.*

The Prince of Orange was of the opinion that those returning should not be burdened with this oath beyond the promise to uphold the points of the peace. However, the resolution of the States was followed. Meanwhile, Don John of Austria, the King's bastard brother <note>Don John was the illegitimate son of Emperor Charles V and a famous military commander, sent by Philip II to act as Governor-General.</note>, arrived here to govern the Netherlands on behalf of the King. He found little to like in the Pacification of Ghent: but the States, guessing where his grievance lay, obtained a declaration from the Theologians at Leuven that they found the peace—after weighing all its points and the current state of affairs—to be useful for the Roman Catholic religion.

<margin>The Pacification of Ghent judged to be useful for the Roman Religion. Hooft XI, 480.</margin>
This was also the judgment of the Professors of Law; and nearly all the Prelates, Abbots, Deacons, and Pastors of the Netherlands. Not long before this, the Spaniards also vacated Oudewater. In order to draw Amsterdam toward accepting the Pacification of Ghent and to unite it with Holland, the States of Holland wrote a persuasive letter to the Burgomasters on the seventeenth of <term>December<gloss>Original: "Wintermaent," the traditional Dutch name for the month of December</gloss></term>.

**Pope Paul IV** likewise held him suspect and considered him a friend of **heretics** $^4$. When he was exhorted on behalf of **Pius IV** to persevere in the **Roman Catholic** faith, with the promise that doing so would lead to his advancement to the **Imperial throne**, he replied: *That he thanked the Pope very much for his favorable affection, but that the salvation of his soul was much dearer to him than all worldly affairs*. But this, said the servants of the Roman court, was the language of the **Lutherans**, which revealed his estrangement from the **Papal see**. Also, while he was **Emperor**, he was favorable toward the **Augsburg Confession** $^5$. <note>The primary confession of faith of the Lutheran Church.</note>

A remarkable letter from Emperor Maximilian II to Lazarus Schwend.
This letter is found among the works of H. Conringius, added after G. Wicelius’s *The Royal Way* <note>original: "Via Regia"</note> printed at Helmstad for Henning Muller, 1650, p. 278. ## 1576. Beloved Schwend,

I have received your letter and read it. Your Christian and faithful mourning, by which you testify that my illness goes to your heart, is extremely pleasing to me. May the eternal God, who holds all things in His hand, deal with me according to His fatherly will. For above all I give Him thanks, as He who knows best of all what is useful and salvific for me, as well as what might be harmful. I resign myself patiently and fully to His divine will. For such are the affairs of this world, that one can find little pleasure or rest in them. Instead, everything is everywhere filled with difficulties, treachery, and deceitful tricks. May the Lord have mercy on us and deign to turn this evil away from His Christendom. Truly, it would be no wonder if someone, in this state of affairs, were struck as if in the head and lost their senses. There is much to write about this. I am beginning, by God's grace, to recover slowly and to walk with the support of a staff. God be praised in all His works. 

As for that "fine piece of work" <note>Maximilian is writing with heavy sarcasm here regarding the St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre of 1572, where thousands of French Protestants (Huguenots) were killed.</note> which the French performed so tyrannically against the Admiral <note>Gaspard de Coligny, the leader of the Huguenots, who was among the first killed in the massacre.</note> and his allies, I cannot approve of it in the slightest; and with great sadness of heart I understood that my son-in-law <note>King Charles IX of France, who was married to Maximilian's daughter, Elisabeth of Austria.</note> allowed himself to be moved to such a foul murder. Although I know that others rule more than he does <note>A likely reference to the influence of the King's mother, Catherine de' Medici.</note>, that is still not enough to excuse the act, nor to gloss over the villainy. Oh, if only he had included me in his counsels; I would have given him faithful and fatherly advice. He would never have done such things with my advice. He has defiled himself by this deed with so great a stain that he will not easily wash or wipe it away. 

May God forgive those who are guilty of this. For I am very fearful that, in the course of time, they will yet feel what they have gained by this path. And it is truly as you prudently write: the matters of godliness will not be settled or handled by the sword. No one in whom any piety and virtue, or zeal for peace and quiet remains, will understand it otherwise. Christ and the Apostles taught us no differently. For their sword was the tongue, the teaching, the word of God, and a life worthy of Christ. Their conduct ought to invite and entice us to follow them, just as and as far as they followed Christ. I say nothing of the fact that this foolish generation of men ought by now, over so many years, to have seen and experienced—even by the logic of things and the outcome itself—that this matter cannot be set right by cruel punishments, nor by cutting, nor by burning. In short, their deeds please me—

And although they would not follow my advice, so that I have reason to abstain from giving counsel, nonetheless I shall not so abstain that I will not still faithfully do all I can. As for me, I shall, if it please God, act honorably, Christianly, faithfully, sincerely, and uprightly; surely trusting that God, with His blessing and grace, will help me; so that I may please God and men with my deeds and counsels. Doing that, I shall not care for this wicked and vile world... Herewith I commend you to God, who governs all things according to His pleasure, for the salvation of Christendom and of us all. In Vienna, the twenty-second of February <note>original: "Sprokkelmaendt"</note> in the year fifteen hundred seventy-four.*

Act granted by the Prince of Orange to the Anabaptists <note>Original: "Doopsgezinden." These were followers of the radical reformation, often Mennonites, who were frequently persecuted by both Catholics and other Protestants.</note>

Since a petition has been presented to His Excellency <note>Referring to William the Silent, Prince of Orange.</note> on behalf of certain inhabitants of this city of Middelburg, in which they complained that the Magistrate of said city recently caused their shops to be closed, and consequently forbade their trade, which is nonetheless their only means of supporting their families; this prohibition proceeding from the cause that they have not yet taken the customary oath as others have done: the aforementioned inhabitants further demonstrating how they have now, for a certain number of years, without ever having taken the aforementioned oath, willingly borne all civic burdens, contributions, and taxes alongside other citizens and residents of the same city, without ever being found in any fault, and therefore they ought even now to remain unmolested in this regard; seeing as they desire nothing else thereby than to live in freedom of their conscience; in respect of which this present war against the King of Spain was undertaken by his subjects, and all ceremonies resisted which conflict against it: in which matter it has now progressed so far, through God's help, that the aforementioned freedom of conscience has been preserved, and therefore it would be improper to take it away from the Petitioners, who have helped to win it by bearing taxes, contributions, and other burdens, not without great peril to their bodies and lives. Having followingly presented this Request to the aforementioned Magistrate, they had received as an apostille <note>A formal response written in the margin of a petition.</note> the report that they must regulate themselves according to the policy and ordinances of the aforementioned city: by which the aforementioned Magistrate seems to attempt, by means of the oath, to drive not only the Petitioners residing within Middelburg, but consequently countless others in Holland and Zeeland who have placed themselves under His Excellency's protection according to his edicts, out of the country with their wives and children, to their total ruin. Through which no one can obtain any profit, but only these lands would suffer great and significant damage; since thereby trade would everywhere come to be greatly diminished; requesting, and therefore humbly praying His Excellency, looking upon the matter with compassion, to make proper provision therein: and especially seeing as the aforementioned Petitioners offer to let their "yea" serve in place of taking an oath, and that the violators thereof be punished as oath-breakers: so it is, that His Excellency, having considered what is written above, and having caused the matter to be very ripely deliberated upon, has, through the previous advice of the Governor and Council of Zeeland, ordered and decreed, and orders and decrees by these presents, that the aforementioned Petitioners shall be permitted by the Magis-

<margin>
