† Society.
</margin>
...could reject from civil order those who broke the bond of all human society †, and at the same time added what a great danger threatened both the state and the churches from such a decision—which in itself was ungodly—he [the Prince] answered sharply enough that their "yea" should indeed serve as an oath for them. He insisted that we must not push this matter further, unless we wished to simultaneously admit that it was reasonable for the Papists <note>A derogatory term used by Reformers to refer to Roman Catholics, implying they followed the Pope rather than scripture.</note> to force us into a religion that went against our conscience; and that the people of North Holland would in no way allow or suffer this. In short, I see us accomplishing almost nothing in this matter. This certainly causes me all the more pain as I notice more and more that the minds of many pious people are so embittered—I would almost say wounded—by the objection of I know not what untimely offenses, that they are less inclined toward those who strive to advance the cause of the churches to the best of their ability. 

The Prince indeed scolded me, partly on his own behalf and partly on behalf of the Estates, as if we were intent on the clergy arrogating to themselves dominion over consciences, and as if they sought to subject all others to their laws and institutions. And he praised the saying of a monk who was here recently, who, in response to what was then objected against him, answered: *That our pot had not been on the fire as long as that of those we so greatly accused; and how he clearly saw it coming that before a couple of hundred years had passed, ecclesiastical dominion on both sides would stand on an equal footing.* <note>The monk is suggesting that the new Protestant clergy would eventually become just as powerful and authoritative as the Catholic hierarchy they were currently criticizing.</note> These things go down well with the common people, and they even daze clever men; and, unless they are provided for with great diligence, they will cause no small damage. 

For this reason, I have—for my part, both now and always before this—labored to remove that offense from the minds of men, by which they are kept away from us through misunderstanding, malice, or deceit, by those who wish to claim that we are seeking to forge a new "monkery" <note>Original: "Monnikerij." A term used to describe a system of rigid, man-made religious rules or clerical tyranny similar to what the Reformers rejected in monastic life.</note>. For I do my utmost to make it believed that we contest and condemn nothing except what the Lord’s law, prescribed in His word, condemns: and in the rest we use <term>Christian liberty</term> <note>The theological concept that Christians are free from the ceremonial laws of the Old Testament and man-made religious traditions, governed instead by grace and conscience.</note>. Which rule I hold to be of very great weight above all others in the building up of the church. For experience, the teacher of all things, has taught me this. I have also often seen for myself in Brussels how great an offense that perception of our stubbornness—entrenched in the hearts of the Papists—brought about daily. And what is more common in these (Dutch) churches, what are people more inclined toward, what is more ready at hand, than that the...

# HISTORY

<margin>1577</margin>...foremost men of the nobility and from the Estates, as well as countless among the common people, excuse themselves from our meetings, solely for the reason that they dread a new dominion and the yoke of <term>ecclesiastical jurisdiction</term> <note>The legal authority exercised by church courts, which many feared would become as oppressive as the Catholic Inquisition.</note>. The Prince himself, when I visited him some years ago, held up only this shield against all my arrows. Indeed, in Germany there are countless people who, only because they fear our uncomfortable stubbornness, deliberately side with those with erroneous views <note>original: "quaelijk gevoelenden"; a reference to those remaining Roman Catholic or holding non-Reformed views.</note>. This writing, which is an almost word-for-word translation from the Latin, can teach us how much importance the Prince of Orange and the Estates of Holland and Zeeland placed on freedom of belief at that time, and what many then disliked about our Reformation. —

In the other Netherlands, meanwhile, **Don John** <note>Don John of Austria, the illegitimate son of Emperor Charles V, sent to govern the Netherlands.</note> was accepted as the King’s Governor after making a treaty at **Marche-en-Famenne**, by which the **Pacification of Ghent** <note>A 1576 treaty where the Dutch provinces united to drive out Spanish troops and establish religious peace.</note> was upheld, including the departure of the Spanish soldiers.

<margin>Pieter Panis beheaded in Mechelen for his faith. Bor X, 247; Hooft XII, 507; History of the Martyrs f. 496.</margin>While he was in **Mechelen** during the month of June <note>original: "Somermaendt"; literally 'Summer month'.</note>, the magistrates there sat in judgment over the case of a certain tailor named **Pieter Panis**, of whose conduct and character they heard very honorable testimony. He confessed to having heard a sermon by the Reformed in the small village of **Bolheyn**, not far from the city. He remained steadfast, not only in his faith but also in his refusal to name others who had been present at the same meeting. This further embittered the judges. His neighbors pleaded extensively for him with the Sheriff, **Willem de Klerk**, Lord of **Boevekerk** <note>The author notes that this title, which can be read as "Rogue’s Church," seemed fitting given his character.</note>, a title that did not seem to have fallen on him by chance, given the flippant answer with which he dismissed them, saying: *“That there was no mercy for such an obstinate heretic who would not forsake his convictions to escape the noose or the fire; and I,”* he added, *“would not want to stick my finger into a burning candle for the sake of my faith.”* Through a very earnest and friendly letter, the **Prince of Orange** also requested that the prisoner be spared, and that the old scenes of tyranny, the fountains of blood, and so much frequent misery not be re-established. Nevertheless, Panis was sentenced to death and publicly beheaded, with the approval of Don John. This burdened Don John with heavy criticism, especially from the Reformed, who by this act measured the likely course of his future reign.

...the help of the Hollanders, and the person of the Prince of Orange to come into Brabant, who in September <note>original: "Herffstmaendt," literally harvest-month.</note> went to Brussels, under written promise, also on behalf of the Estates of Holland and Zeeland, not to allow anything to be done against the general peace and especially against the Roman Catholic Religion and its practice. Shortly thereafter, those of Utrecht returned, accepting the Peace of Ghent <note>A 1576 treaty intended to unite the provinces and drive out Spanish troops while maintaining religious peace.</note> under his <term>Stadtholdership</term> <note>The office of an appointed governor or provincial representative.</note>, under the express condition of keeping the Roman religion uncurtailed in all things: that no soldiers or any teachers would come there to practice the Reformed religion; that no ecclesiastical benefits would be given except to those of Roman Catholic persuasion, judged capable by the Archbishop; that freedoms would be maintained; and the jurisdiction <margin>* Jurisdiction.</margin> of the Archbishop would remain in force.

The Hollanders and Zeelanders confirmed this treaty with their seal. With matters standing thus, the Prince of Orange was chosen as <term>Ruaerdt</term> <note>A traditional title in the Netherlands for a guardian or governor appointed during a crisis.</note> of Brabant. Archduke Matthias, brother of the Emperor, was invited into the country by some Dutch nobles in order to oppose the Prince; and Don John <note>Don John of Austria, the Spanish-appointed Governor-General.</note> was declared an enemy by the Estates-General. The Queen of England, seeing the power of the Netherlands, began to show them greater favor and provide help to secure herself against the designs of Don John.

but now many Flemish Teachers gathered at Emden to deliberate whether that treaty should stand, or whether it ought to be broken. Most were in favor of breaking it. Pieter van Keulen and several others, all of the Flemish faction, argued the contrary: that this treaty should be improved and accepted by other congregations as a good beginning. During this war of words over a dying peace, they were offered a public discussion and dispute concerning their doctrine and opinions by the Preachers of Emden, who had heard that so many Anabaptist Teachers were gathered there. This was to take place in the presence of the Magistrates or their deputies. The Flemings, relying mostly on one of their Teachers, Hans de Wever (also known as Buschaert), accepted the offer;

but when the conversation began, this Weaver could hardly speak before he was cornered or defeated by the Preachers. And had they not—according to the account of I. H. V. P. N. This man, who was very sharp-witted, eloquent, and firm in his conclusions, gave the Preachers so much trouble—even though he understood no other languages besides High and Low German <note>In this period, "Low German" or "Nederduits" often referred to the Dutch language.</note>—that Helmerus Diurken, a Doctor of Laws who presided over this dispute on behalf of the Count of East Friesland, said to him: *I tell you, Pieter, had you the learning that we have, you would dispute us all out of the church.* Nevertheless, in this dispute, which lasted twelve weeks, the Flemings were bravely tormented and taken to task by the Preachers over the matter of the ban and avoidance, <note>The "ban" refers to excommunication, and "avoidance" or "shunning" (mijding) was the practice of refusing all social and commercial contact with the banned person.</note> especially between husband and wife. The Peace of Humsterland broken.

The Flemings, who had married Frisians during the period of peace, were forced by this breach of the treaty to do one of two things: either to separate from their spouses, or to bring them into the Flemish congregation to be rebaptized <term>rebaptized (wederdoop): the Anabaptist practice of baptizing adults who had been baptized as infants</term> into that fellowship. Some time later, one also saw the Flemings cast out and excommunicate <note>In Anabaptist tradition, "the Ban" was a severe form of social and religious shunning.</note> Pieter van Keulen—the very man who had done them such great service in the Dispute at Emden—simply because he contradicted them in certain matters regarding the application of the Ban.
<margin>
Pieter van Keulen excommunicated.
</margin>

<margin>
The Reconciled Frisians.
</margin>
Thereafter, he joined that faction of the Frisians who were for a long time referred to as the "Reconciled" <note>Originally "Bevredigden," meaning those who had accepted or sought the Peace (Vrede).</note>. His alertness and zeal in promoting peace and defending the common cause of the Anabaptists were highly praised. It is told of him that he always knew how to obtain copies of everything proposed or decided against the Anabaptists in the Synods and assemblies of the Reformed.
<margin>
I.H.V.P.N. p. 38.
</margin>
Following the collapse of the Peace of Humsterland, the most moderate members of both these groups did not entirely give up on the work of reconciliation in Friesland and Holland. However, the greatest efforts were made among the Frisians. These people, who had previously been the most rigorous in driving forward the Ban and the schism against the Flemings, were now the first to come to their senses and seek peace in earnest.

<margin>
Peace negotiations at Hoorn. I.H.V.P.N. p. 38.
</margin>
The most virtuous members finally arranged for a meeting to be held at Hoorn, in North Holland, to negotiate reconciliation and unity. It is believed that the Flemish Teachers, who were not truly inclined toward the negotiations, appeared there only to give some satisfaction to the peace-loving members of their own side.
<margin>
Proposal of the Frisian Anabaptists.
</margin>
The Frisians proposed, as the best means to peace, that all past mistreatments and offenses committed by both sides should be burned in the fire of love, and that they should mutually confess their guilt to one another; also, that they should ask forgiveness of each other and, above all, of God, with a confession of their sins. Jan van Ophooren, at that time a Flemish-leaning preacher in Emden, gave this report of his journey and the outcome of the business upon returning to East Friesland:

<margin>Jan van Ophooren’s stubbornness. p. 39, 40.</margin>
> "We have been to Hoorn," he said, with a flat expression, casting his eyes toward the ceiling, "and found clearly that our opponents were laying cunning, deceptive snares, traps, and nets to catch us in this way, wanting us to throw all past unjust dealings and deeds together into one pot and smother them. But the Lord has preserved us: so that we, noticing their craftiness, did not grant their wishes. Then I must relate to you," he continued, "a parable of God's congregation. There was a woman who had born and raised many beautiful and dear children; then came evil murderers, who murdered almost all those good children. The woman bore other children again and raised them. Afterwards, those same murderers came and wanted to make peace with those later children, and agree to settle for all those previous murders; the children, not knowing the murder of their brothers so exactly, might have easily consented out of simplicity; but the mother, and the remaining oldest children, still remembering the murder of their brothers very well, would in no way agree to such a peace."

<margin>He believes at last that he and his wife alone are the true congregation, and excommunicates others.</margin>
From these words, one can hear what kind of spirit it was that rejected the offer of peace. And this was the same Ophooren who, after helping to drive the ban <note>The "Ban" was the practice of excommunication and social shunning used by Anabaptists to maintain the purity of the church.</note> in the strictest manner to reinforce the schism between the Flemings and Frisians, finally entangled himself so deeply in his own precision and strayed so far that he judged all the Flemish preachers and congregations to have departed from the true foundation of truth. He believed that, like Elijah <note>A reference to 1 Kings 19:10, where the prophet Elijah cries out to God that he is the only faithful one left in Israel.</note>, only he and his wife remained standing in the right. He also pronounced the ban upon some of the other Flemish preachers who wandered from his views, in the presence of his wife as his only and true witness. But because of this, he was abandoned by the Flemish congregation; therefore, he settled in Norden and, for lack of a following, fell into such need and destitution that he still had need on earth of those former friends whom he had, as far as he was able, banned from heaven; there he, through their alms and hand-

It wearies me to investigate further; all the more because the causes of their divisions are for the most part of very little importance, or obscure and inscrutable. I shall only say, with an author of great reputation <note>original: "Schrijver van grooten naeme" - referring to Hugo Grotius, the influential jurist and theologian cited in the margin</note>, that the Anabaptists <term>Doopsgezinden|A branch of the Reformation known for practicing believer's baptism rather than infant baptism and for their emphasis on non-violence</term> now have so many sects among them that there is hardly anyone who could state the number or all their names. At that time, Dirck Volckertszoon Coornhert <note>A famous Dutch polymath, engraver, and theologian who was a fierce advocate for religious freedom</note>, having returned again to Holland, became involved in a dispute at Delft with the ministers Arnoldus Cornelius and Reinier Donteklok, regarding the marks of the true church. He had fallen into the company of someone who boasted greatly of having left the Romish [Catholic] Church and having joined the Reformed Church, bringing forth reasons from which it was noted that he had as little knowledge of the church he had adopted as the one he had abandoned. This caused Coornhert to say to that man: *It remains to be considered whether you have found something better than what you rejected.* That saying was reported somewhat more severely and gave cause for the dispute. Coornhert wanted to prove that the churches following and believing the teachings of Calvin and Beza <note>Theodore Beza, the successor to John Calvin in Geneva</note> were not true churches, based on three points: Predestination, Justification, and the Killing of Heretics <term>Ketterdooding|The practice of executing people for their religious beliefs, which Coornhert vehemently opposed</term>.

<margin>*Bor, Book XIII, 82. c, h. Uitenbogaert’s History, p. 200.* <note>Johannes Uitenbogaert was a prominent Remonstrant theologian and historian.</note></margin>

<margin>
1578 <note>original: "MDLXXVIII"</note>
Oath demanded of the Clergy.
Hooft XIII. 568. Bor, XII, 27. <note>References to the historians Pieter Corneliszoon Hooft and Pieter Bor.</note>
</margin>
[...that] all officials, magistrates, and clerical persons should swear to the **Pacification of Ghent** <note>A 1576 treaty where the provinces of the Netherlands united to drive out Spanish mutineers and promote religious peace.</note> and pledge enmity against **Don John** <note>Don John of Austria, the Spanish Governor-General and half-brother of King Philip II.</note>. The secular priests in Antwerp took the oath; but the **Jesuits** <note>A Catholic religious order known for their loyalty to the Pope.</note> refused flatly, saying they were bound by oath to the Pope, and by friendship to Don John. The **Minorites** <note>Also known as the Friars Minor or Franciscans.</note> also raised objections to swearing: yet twenty eventually reconsidered, while nineteen continued to refuse and were escorted out under safe guard on **Pentecost** <note>The seventh Sunday after Easter.</note>. The common people thought this was handled too gently. They went from murmuring to shouting: *That the whole lot ought to be kicked out of the city.* However, the corporal punishment of two zealots, who had marched toward the monastery with evil intent and weapons, stilled the riot. To escape this oath, all the Minorites also departed from Utrecht. It went in a similar fashion in more other cities.

# H I S T O R Y

<margin>1578 <note>original: "MDLXXVIII"</note></margin> [Cornelis van] **Nek**, certain **City Councilors**, and **Cornelis Floriszoon van Teilingen**—all three of whom became **Burgomasters** <term>Burgomaster: the chief magistrate or mayor of a Dutch city</term> shortly thereafter—said to the Bridegroom: "You are an old **Patriot** <note>A 'Patriot' referred to those loyal to the Dutch cause against Spanish rule</note>, who has also wandered outside the country for a long time; it would not be fitting for you to marry outside the church. We shall see to it that the wedding takes place after the evening prayer." However, as the wedding time approached, the **Ministers** were unwilling. The Bridegroom, along with some of the "pious" <note>original: "fijnen"—a term often used for the more devout or strict members of the Reformed faith</note>, had to appear before the **Consistory** <term>Consistory: a governing body of ministers and elders in the Reformed Church</term>, which consisted mostly of foreigners. There, after some words and counter-words, he was told *that they did not wish to bypass the resolution they had recently adopted for his sake*; declaring quite bluntly *that the Gentlemen who had made him such promises had no authority to command them in this matter*. The other [the bridegroom] gave an account of his experience to Mr. **Egbert Roelofs**, as he lived closest to the church. He then went immediately to the Consistory and, with much effort, brought it about that they fulfilled what the Gentlemen had promised. Yet none of the city’s **Ministers** wanted to perform the wedding; so a **Minister** from outside the city had to be employed for the task.

Shortly after the conquest of **Amsterdam**, on **Corpus Christi** <note>original: "Sacramentsdagh"—a Catholic feast day</note>, the people in **Haerlem** also rose up following that example and method, and it devolved into great wantonness. It was also soldiers who did it; a company of rougher conduct.

<margin>

Bor XIII. 118. d; Hooft XII. 572; T. Schrevelius’s *Harlem* p. 114. 115.
</margin>

### OF THE REFORMATION. BOOK XI.

<margin>
1578 <note>original: "MDLXXVIII"</note>
The Reformed in Brabant and Flanders form large assemblies. Hooft XIII. 572; Bor XII. 37. b.
</margin>

In Brabant and Flanders, the Reformed <term>Reformed: those belonging to the Protestant church following Calvinist doctrine</term> still refrained from violence, but they moved toward greater freedom from day to day. In Antwerp, by the fifteenth of March <note>original: "Lentemaendt"</note>, they had already preached in fifteen locations and administered the Lord's Supper in fourteen, essentially ignoring the prohibition issued in April <note>original: "Grasmaendt"</note>; although the States <term>States: the governing assembly of the provinces</term> had not expected such a thing. In Ghent, they held assemblies of four, five, or six hundred people in various places, with as little fear as if it had been openly permitted. As their numbers grew daily, they eventually became so pleased with their own multitude and resources that they grew bold enough to request the free exercise of their religion; this was done on the advice of those who did not care by what means they advanced their worship.

<margin>
Hooft XIII 573.
</margin>

However, it is to be believed that there were also people among them who, having an aversion to the scandal of violent actions—which seemed otherwise inevitable—preferred to follow this legal path.

<margin>
First National Synod at Dordrecht.
</margin>

The same course of action was approved by a National Synod of Reformed Dutch, German, and Walloon <term>Walloon: French-speaking people from the southern Netherlands</term> churches, which met in Dordrecht from the second to the eighteenth of June <note>original: "Somermaendt"</note> ¹.

> *The reason for their departure from the Roman church had been indicated through various printed books, as well as by the Confessions of Faith, confirmed by the perseverance of many martyrs <note>original: "bloedtgetuigen," literally "blood-witnesses"</note>. To remedy all this, and to help shake off the yoke of Spanish slavery, they had never begrudged the sacrifice of their lives and property <note>original: "hals en have," literally "neck and goods"</note>. The refusal of the free exercise of Religion was a cause of distrust, leading some to undertake many things that were not equally dear to all the Reformed. <meta>This page continues the discussion regarding the religious unrest in the Netherlands in 1578. Following the National Synod at Dordrecht mentioned on the previous page, the text now details the arguments presented for allowing the public exercise of the Reformed religion alongside Catholicism to prevent social collapse or godlessness.</meta>

# H I S T O R Y.

<margin>1578 <note>original: "MDLXXVIII"</note></margin> ...either [to remain] without religion, or that they should in deed establish the public exercise of their religion. *The first was so harmful to the common good that nothing more damaging could be imagined; for it brought with it contempt for God and all godliness, an Epicurean <term>Epicurean: in this context, a derogatory term used to describe a godless lifestyle focused only on worldly pleasures, seen as a consequence of atheism</term> godless existence, and from that, a transgression and rejection of all divine and human* laws. The other means <note>the open practice of the Reformed religion</note> might give cause for the separation and division of the lands, and the destruction of the current state. Yet, if the rules of the ancestors, held by wise and prudent men, were to count for anything more, then one could take no better counsel than from the enemy. *For since the matter of the inequality of religion was the enemy's best weapon, with which he sought to conquer the Netherlands, one had to provide against it in such a way that this inequality would not serve him as an open storming-place <note>original: "stormplaetse" — a breach or vulnerable point in a fortification</note>, to thereby make an inroad for his tyranny between the same.* And since the experience of the past years taught that, because of the greatness of sins, not everyone could be brought to one religion, it was necessary to consider how the one and the other religion might be maintained without harm or disadvantage to the other; yet in such a way that the concord and mutual obligations of the Netherlands suffered no encroachment. *One should,* they prayed, *not lend an ear to those who objected against this, [saying] that one must uphold the Pacification of Ghent <term>Pacification of Ghent: a 1576 treaty intended to unite the Dutch provinces and establish religious peace</term>; that no two religions could coexist in one land; and that if such were allowed, the clergy would sit on a shovel without security <note>original: "op een schup souden zitten" — an idiom meaning to be in a precarious position, easily cast aside or discarded</note>.* The Pacification of Ghent had been broken by the Spaniard <note>referring to the Spanish crown/administration</note> through perjury. One could meet their needs without breaking faith, since in that treaty and agreement the provinces were bound to one another, and what they had bound, they could mutually unbind, and therein lighten or weigh <note>adjust the terms</note> for the welfare of the fatherland and for the breaking of the enemy's secret ruses. Yet they did not wish to act against the Pacification of Ghent, praying that, according to the same, the General States <term>General States: the assembly of representatives from the Dutch provinces</term> would provide for the matter of the free public exercise of their religion. The objection that no two religions could coexist in one land had been refuted by the experience of all ages. The Heathen Emperors had fared better by tolerating, and indeed employing, Christians in military service, than by persecuting them. Under the Christian Emperors, public churches were permitted to those who held entirely different doctrines, as one could read in the histories of Constantine <note>original: "Konstantinus"</note>, his sons, Theodosius, and others. Emperor Charles the Fifth found no other means to save himself from the utmost necessity than the...

### OF THE REFORMATION. BOOK XI.

...granting of the exercise of the one and the other religion. <margin>1578 <note>original: "MDLXXVIII"</note></margin> Emperor *Ferdinand*, a Prince of singular understanding and wise counsel, grandfather of Archduke *Matthias*, had granted the Religious Peace <note>referring to the Peace of Augsburg (1555), which allowed for some coexistence between Catholics and Lutherans</note>, and thereby quelled all rebellion. For nowhere did the clergy enjoy their property, estates, and privileges with greater security. In many cities, both religions were practiced without disagreement or riot; indeed, in some cities, even within a single church. Emperor *Maximilian* II, father of Prince *Matthias*, had left that freedom in effect and extended it into his ancestral lands; and Emperor *Rudolph* (brother of *Matthias*) had granted the same only a few days prior to the knighthood of *Hungary*. *France* lay too close for one not to know that the streams of blood, which flowed there in abundance, could never be stopped except by the granting of freedom of religion. That freedom gave rest there, whereas the hindrance of the same immediately set that kingdom into a bright flame, in danger of consuming itself. One could also take an example from the *Turk* <note>The Ottoman Sultan</note>, who well knew what it was to rule, seeing that he tolerated both *Jews* and *Christians* in his empire without fear of rebellion or defection; although there were more *Christians* in his lands who never accepted the *Pope* than there were in *Europe* who do accept the *Pope*. The King of *Morocco* and *Fez* did likewise. The King of *Poland* allowed, besides the inequality of religion in his kingdom, many *Mahometists* <term>Mahometists: a historical European term for Muslims</term> in great numbers, who were subject to him without rebelliousness. Even the *Pope*, whom the *Catholics* <note>original: "Roomschgesinden" — those of the Romish mind</note> held as their head, and whose examples they held as infallible rules, allowed in *Rome* and in his other cities that the *Jews* had their public *synagogues*. Concerning the third objection, they could not immediately make known to all people the good desire they had to live with their fellow citizens peacefully and in silence. Meanwhile, they prayed His Highness, the Archduke, and the Council of State, to propose means of security, which they wished to obey to the best of their ability. Thus the request remained: that both religions might be equally permitted, until it should please God through a good, holy, and free universal—or at least national—Council <note>a "Concilie" or "Synod" intended to resolve theological disputes across the Low Countries</note>, to reconcile all the conflicting opinions seen in the matter of religion in these lands. And that all matters that had occurred previously on both sides might be buried by a holy law of forgiveness and forgetting <note>This refers to an "Act of Oblivion" or amnesty to prevent revenge for past religious violence</note>, and no one <margin>Second petition of the Reformed for the same purpose. *Bor XII. 40. c.* <note>Reference to the historian Pieter Bor’s "Oorsprongk, begin, en vervolgh der Nederlandsche oorlogen"</note></margin> be investigated or burdened because of it. After fourteen days of following up for an answer, they submitted a second Petition, promising to provide certain Princes as guarantors for their obedience, and requesting the same from the Catholics. They also proposed several points for the security...

With the offer that the Reformed should testify before God with solemn words that they had no intention to disturb the Prelates and other ecclesiastical persons who profess the Roman Religion, whether in their persons, property, or the exercise of their religion. They would take no action against them but would hinder all trouble to the best of their ability. To meet them halfway, a draft of a *Religious Peace* <term>Religions-vrede: a proposed legal framework for the mutual tolerance and legal coexistence of Catholicism and Protestantism</term>, as it was called, was put on paper in the name of the Archduke and the Council of State. This was intended, in their opinion, to cause no division between the provinces, since its acceptance or rejection was left to the pleasure of each. The principal points of this draft were these:

<margin>
Religious Peace drafted.
Hooft XIII. 574. <note>Refers to Pieter Corneliszoon Hooft’s *Nederlandsche Historiën*</note> Meteren VIII. 154. <note>Refers to Emanuel van Meteren’s history of the Netherlands</note>

*That all mistreatment committed for the sake of religion since the Peace of Ghent <note>A 1576 treaty where the Dutch provinces united to drive out Spanish troops and establish religious peace</note> shall be forgiven and forgotten. So that there might be no more discord regarding the diversity of religions (which should not be maintained, planted, or suppressed by force and weapons), everyone should remain free and unconstrained concerning the two aforementioned religions, and serve God according to the understanding given to him, and as he would wish to answer on the Last Day. Everywhere, both in Holland and Zeeland and other places where the Roman Religion had been driven out, it should be readmitted; provided that those who desired it in large cities or villages should number one hundred households, each having lived there for at least one full year: but in small places, the petitioners must constitute the majority. In like manner, the Reformed should be allowed to practice their religion throughout the whole Netherlands. Where only the exercise of one religion was publicly permitted, no one should nevertheless be investigated or questioned regarding what he might do within his house concerning the other religion. Anyone entering another's church was to avoid giving offense and conform to the local customs.*

The Reformed outside of Holland and Zeeland would be required to observe Sundays, Christmas, the Apostles' days, the Annunciation of Mary, the Ascension, Candlemas, and the Feast of the Sacrament <note>Corpus Christi</note>, by closing shops and ceasing manual labor and trade. For a better bond of unity, in the granting of offices, no regard should be paid to denomination, but only to the fitness of the persons.

<margin>Grotius, Annals, III. 57. <note>Refers to Hugo de Groot’s *Annales et Historiae de Rebus Belgicis*</note></margin>

Among such various movements concerning the work of the Reformation in the Netherlands around 1578 [MDLXXVIII], something began to manifest in Utrecht through which the matters of religion, in the eyes of some, were disposed toward greater moderation than elsewhere; but others understood that this diversity did more harm than good. Yet this subject, by its own weight, deserves to be traced from an earlier point, so that the reader may judge with more knowledge.

The Magistrates, then, knowing him to be of a very peaceful nature, and also knowing that he had a very moving manner of preaching and gave emphasis to that gift with his virtuous life, thought they had found the right man to diminish the multitude of the other Reformed and to weaken their <margin>Hooft XXIII, 146.</margin> rigor through division. For (so much harder is it for human senses to strain toward embracing a uniform Reformation or improvement than toward the destruction of a rejected form) many people, although the Roman abuses were repugnant to them, nevertheless grumbled at this time: *that in order to clean the church, one was not only sweeping out the filth, but also the floor at the same time*: thus Duifhuis seemed destined to gain a significant following. events occurring in the surrounding places, the authorities found themselves in very great concern for the peace of the city. For the **Reformed** <note>The "Gereformeerden" or early Protestants</note> were now preaching in various places within the gates, in the Donker Street and elsewhere, with such an increase in numbers that it was not considered advisable to disturb them by force. Therefore, the Deacons of the five collegiate churches, or Chapters, were asked for their consent to grant the Pastor <note>Hubert Duifhuis</note> his request, made previously, and to be allowed to negotiate with him regarding it. But the Chapters said "no" to this, feeling obligated to adhere entirely to the Roman religion. This refusal displeased the Magistrates, who also did not flatly refuse Duifhuis’s request; instead, they allowed him to preach by turning a blind eye <note>original: "bij oogluiking," a Dutch legal concept of tactical tolerance</note>. 

However, he, fearing that discord or strife might arise in the city on his account, and also in consideration of his physical frailty, requested his dismissal, submitting himself to the Authorities as a good citizen. They refused to discharge him but agreed that he could stay within Rotterdam with his friends, without losing his position, until they could summon him back to Utrecht at a more favorable opportunity. Before his departure, he publicly renounced the Papacy. 

The citizenry, upset by his sudden departure, were led to believe that he had been forced out by the command of the clergy; they subsequently rose up and demanded of the Sheriff and Burgomasters that the **Friars Minor** <note>The Franciscans</note> be made to depart immediately. The Council, having gathered on the twenty-seventh of June <note>original: "Somermaendt"</note>, decided that in order to satisfy the community, they would notify the Friars Minor that they should leave the city for a time. 

Meanwhile, the draft of the **Religious Peace** <note>A proposal intended to allow both Catholic and Protestant worship side-by-side</note> was rejected by the States of Utrecht in August <note>original: "Oegstmaendt"</note>, mostly through the actions of the Clergy, although some of the Knighthood <note>The nobility</note> were of the opinion that they ought to agree to it; provided that they could secretly obtain some teachers of the <term>Augsburg Confession</term> <note>The primary confession of faith for Lutherans, which the Catholic clergy viewed as a more moderate "lesser of two evils" compared to the Reformed Calvinists</note>, from whom less danger to the Clergy and a significant setback for the Reformed was to be expected. However, the Magistrates of the city of Utrecht, who had different views on the matter of religion than the Clergy of that province, finally recalled Master Hubert Duifhuis—who was in Rotterdam, where he had stayed for several weeks and had been called to the church service in the Hague, but had turned down both calls—back to Utrecht, to the service of his old Parish.

Therefore, he desired to concern himself with no other discipline¹, on the Genevan model <note>referring to the strict moral oversight practiced by John Calvin in Geneva</note>, nor with excommunication²; holding that to be a dominion over consciences and a remnant of the Papal yoke. He allowed no persecution for diversity of opinion, not even against those of the Papal persuasion, nor did he wish to take part in it, saying to the Lords of the city:

> Where you persecute for faith, your affairs cannot stand before God.

He taught no Catechism from the pulpit. He said the Holy Scripture was his Catechism. To draw in those who could not yet entirely abandon following the Roman custom in some measure, he met them by explaining the Gospels and Epistles on Sundays, as they were arranged in the lectionary <note>the traditional cycle of Bible readings used in the church year</note>. He delivered his sermons with great zeal and moving eloquence: he insisted mostly on love, a godly walk of life, and inner virtues; without touching upon subtle disputes or high mysteries; 

<margin>Hooft XXIII, 147.</margin>
which, in the judgment of all modest teachers, one could safely bypass, and could not investigate except with the danger of destructive errors. Because of this impartiality, many gave him the name of Libertine, or free-spirit <note>terms used at the time to describe those who prioritized spiritual liberty over strict dogma</note>.

<margin>3 See the letter of P. de Bert, Minister at Rotterdam, in Bor XXI, 107. c.</margin>
The matter of Predestination he did not understand as deeply or highly as other Reformed ministers maintained³. On that point, as well as on original sin and justification by imputation <term>justification by imputation: the theological doctrine that a believer is made righteous in God's eyes by having Christ’s righteousness credited to them</term>, he spoke little. Those who were lost, he said, were lost through their own fault and willful intent. He went to visit all kinds of sick people when called upon, of whatever persuasion they might be. With this manner of proceeding, he gained many listeners from among the citizenry and great favor with the Magistrate <note>the city's governing officials</note>; who some time later had the images removed from the church. He also then laid aside his surplice <note>original: "koorkleedt," a white liturgical vestment</note> and preached thereafter in the long gown <note>original: "tabbert," the academic dress typical of Reformed ministers</note>.

<margin>The Minorite church taken over by the Reformed in Utrecht. Bor XXI, 108. b; Hooft XXIII, 147.</margin>
The other Reformed believers in Utrecht did not yet have any public churches at this time, but preached through ministers borrowed from outside in a barn near St. Nicholas, with such a crowd that this preaching place proved too small for them; therefore, they undertook to take over the Minorite church <note>the church of the Franciscans</note>, which was not being used then, and to teach therein; until the Magistrates consented to it and granted them the church. Then the images were broken, and they sought to advance the Reformation in the manner of the Dutch churches <note>referring to the more orthodox Calvinist model established in Holland</note>.

This was taken very poorly and reported in writing to the nearby churches of Holland. He was also accused of allowing a child to be baptized in his church who was later baptized again in the Papist <note>Catholic</note> church, without him having lodged a complaint about it with the authorities.

Afterwards, they spoke of other matters, but being upset by that vehemence, he gave them little...

One should instill in the sheep Christ's command not to hear the voice of the stranger, and if this did not succeed, they should ask the Prince of Orange to come to the aid of the church.* This writing, addressed to those of the Consistory in Utrecht, occurred at the end of the year. **Count John** was accused of turning a blind eye to these proceedings: with a request that the **Reformed Religion** <note>The Protestant movement following the teachings of Calvin, which was gaining political and social momentum in the Netherlands.</note> be abolished in the aforementioned places, and the **Roman** <note>The Roman Catholic Church.</note> religion restored. # HISTORY

1578. of those who, blinded by self-love and self-conceit, soon brought the whole country and themselves into the utmost distress.

<margin>
Jacob Hessels and Jan Visch hanged in Ghent.
Bor XIII, 70.
Hooft XIV, 593 594.
Meter. VIII, 156.
</margin>
In Ghent, the bitterness became so great that, on the fourth of October <note>original: "Wijnmaendt," literally Wine-month</note>, Jacob Hessels and Jan Visch—who had been imprisoned during a riot some months earlier—were sentenced by the court-martial by order of the Lord of Ryhove, Jan van Imbise, and others. Without proper legal proceedings <note>original: "dingtael," the formal right to a legal defense</note>, and before a military court where they did not rightfully belong, they were both hanged from a single tree outside the city on the road to Kortrijk.

<margin>+ p. 494.</margin>
Both were very bitter Papists <note>A common, often derogatory term for Roman Catholics at the time</note>. Mention was made previously † of Hessels' reckless cruelty in the Council of Troubles <note>original: "bloedtraedt," the "Blood Council" established by the Duke of Alba to prosecute rebels</note>; the words *to the gallows, to the gallows*, and similar executioner’s talk, sat so readily upon his tongue that his wife once confronted him, saying: *You always have hanging in your mouth; God forbid that it should one day happen to you.* Jan Visch, formerly the Bailiff of Ingelmunster, is reported to have conceived a hatred for one Hendrik de Kreus of Godsfelde over a certain lawsuit. He had the man imprisoned in Ypres on charges of heresy and sedition. But later, hearing that this man—an extremely old and wealthy person—had received a pardon, Visch (as if to show his zeal for the Roman Religion) took it upon himself on a Sunday morning to enter the dungeon with a monk and an executioner. He informed the prisoner that he would die before the Bishop’s Mass had ended. The prisoner was at that hour eating breakfast with some friends who had come to visit him. Seeking to delay, as he knew his letter of grace <note>A formal pardon</note> was on its way (which indeed arrived the following day), he demanded to see the sentence. But he was forced onward and hung strangled in the market square just as the Bishop and Bailiff were coming out of the church. There was no other evidence of his guilt than the fact that he had provided housing for his son, who belonged to the Reformed Religion. He left behind a wife and six children, who mourned in poverty—husbandless, fatherless, and propertyless—until they regained what was theirs through the Peace of Ghent <note>original: "Gentschen pais," referring to the 1576 treaty intended to unite the provinces against Spain</note>. Yet, notwithstanding all the cruelty previously committed by Hessels and Visch, all people of judgment and reason judged that those who killed them strayed even further into wrongdoing. <margin>Hooft XIV, 594.</margin> For the crimes of those two fierce men had, in some sense, the laws and customs of that time on their side—laws that were indeed shameful and cursed, but nevertheless not so godless as the unrestrained raging according to each man's insolence, which destroys the very root of civil society.

# HISTORY

<margin>1578</margin>
both parties still had the common enemy within the country. The enemy also took the protection of the Catholic Religion as a cause for war. And the Walloons <note>French-speaking residents of the Southern Netherlands</note> would rather accept this cause than endure violence or forced changes in religion.

<margin>
New riot in Ghent.
*Bor XIII, 72. c. Hooft XIV, 597, 598.*
</margin>
But while negotiations were ongoing, the rabble flared up again. On the eighteenth of November <note>original: "Slachtmaendt," the 'slaughter month,' traditional Dutch name for November</note>, they drove the remaining clergy out through the gates all at once. Furthermore, they destroyed whatever images and furnishings remained intact in all the churches and cloisters. This mob seemed not like a group of citizens, but like a breakout of madmen. The drums beat the call to arms so loudly that sight and hearing were lost. No respect was shown to the Magistrate <note>the city's governing council</note> or anyone else. Whoever dared to speak a conciliatory word was in danger of his life. They had to be left to run their course. This occurred right before the eyes of the Envoys.

<margin>
The Prince of Orange brings about a Religious Peace in Ghent.
*Bor XIII, 73, 74. Hooft XIV, 598.*
</margin>
Not long after, at the insistence of the States, the Prince of Orange <note>William the Silent</note> arrived in person within Ghent, although some of the ringleaders would have liked to prevent it. With great effort and after enduring much obstruction, he brought matters so far:

> That the free exercise of both religions, Roman and Reformed, was granted. The clergy were allowed back into the city and were granted their property, except for the mendicant orders <note>religious orders whose members lived by begging, such as Franciscans or Dominicans</note>, both men and women; these were to remain outside to relieve and unburden the poor community. Those who found the cloister life distasteful were not to be forced into it and were to be provided with maintenance. The churches were divided between those of the Reformed Religion and the Roman Catholics, with the condition that the latter would perform no public processions, nor carry the Sacrament with any ceremony through the streets. Both the Ministers and Consistory members <note>the governing body of a local Reformed church</note>, as well as those of the Catholic Roman Religion, were required to conduct themselves with all modesty, quietness, loyalty, and submission in all political matters, without interfering in any way with the exercise of jurisdiction or matters touching the authority of the Magistrate... Prohibiting the aforementioned Ministers and likewise those of the Roman Religion from preaching in public or in secret, or using words tending toward riot or discord.

The other points followed the same intent as those of Antwerp. This, in the form of an ordinance decided by the Bailiff, Aldermen, and Dean, was proclaimed on the fifteenth of December <note>original: "Wintermaendt," the 'winter month,' traditional Dutch name for December</note>.

<margin>*Bor XIII, 74. d.*</margin>

# BOOK XII OF THE REFORMATION.

<margin>
1578.
</margin>

The Walloon Malcontents <note>A faction of Catholic nobles from the southern, French-speaking provinces who opposed the radical Protestants</note> were by no means satisfied with what had been accomplished at Ghent; rather, they wanted the Religious Peace <note>The *Religions-vrede*, a proposal for mutual tolerance between Catholics and Protestants</note> to be abolished, as it conflicted with the Peace of Ghent <note>The 1576 treaty that united the provinces against Spain while attempting to maintain the religious status quo</note>. During this year, Doctor Justus Velsius resided in Haarlem, Leiden, The Hague, and other places in Holland, presenting himself as one sent by God to reform the whole world.

<margin>
Justus Velsius wants to reform the world and attempts to perform miracles.
Bor XIII, 81, 82.
</margin>

To this end, he preached first secretly and later openly. He promised to confirm his teachings with miracles and also undertook—though in vain—to make a blind man see and a cripple walk; saying, when he failed, that it was due to their lack of faith. He had written a certain letter to the States of Holland on the eighth of November <note>original: "Slachtmaendt," the 'slaughter-month,' a traditional Dutch name for November</note> of the previous year, rebuking everyone therein for their neglect and arrogance. He also dared to denounce them as rebellious and irreligious men who made laws in matters of religion where they themselves had no religion; concluding his writing with these words: *I tell them in the truth of God, indeed not I, but the Holy Spirit of God himself, who is in me, that if they do not cease from such an intention and arrogance, they shall bring God's wrath upon their own necks...* In Leiden on a certain day, he stood on a bench in the church to preach and gained many listeners, for whom he set an hour for the following day to preach there again. The Magistrate <note>The city’s governing body</note>, hearing of this, ordered the church to be kept closed that day. As he went to the church at the appointed hour, he was told by some that it was closed. He answered: *For me it shall not be closed when I come*, and proceeded on his way, followed by many. Arriving near the church, a laborer came out of the door with a long ladder, against which he pushed his way in, as did a multitude of people who were with him. Therefore he preached on the same bench, and some simple folk considered this a miracle. He also said he would teach again at the same place and hour the following day. But the city officials, fearing discord among the citizenry, had him escorted out of the city before daybreak. Displeased by this, he wrote a very fierce letter to the Magistrate, calling them worse than Mamelukes <note>A term of abuse suggesting they were "infidels" or spiritually enslaved</note>, whom he delivered that day, along with their Satanic false teachers, to Satan, to be punished in hellfire. Under the letter was written: *Of the righteous Judge of the living and the dead, Jesus Christ, to whom all power is given in heaven and on earth, called Ser-* <note>The text breaks off mid-word; likely "Servant" or "Dienaer" in the original</note>

This Velsius is ranked among the learned men originating from The Hague by Lodovico Guicciardini <note>An Italian historian living in Antwerp, author of a famous description of the Low Countries</note>, as an excellent physician

On the fifth of February <note>original: "Sprokkelmaendt," a traditional Dutch name for the month when wood was gathered</note> in the year fifteen hundred seventy-nine, Master Willem Artus, Councilor to the Prince of Orange, made a certain declaration before the magistrates <term>Wethouders</term> <note>Administrative officials of the city</note> of the city of Mechelen, which he had also made twelve years earlier in the King's Great Council, and which was noteworthy. Furthermore, that regarding public policy, both in religion and secular administration, as a common person having and desiring no public office <note>Artus is emphasizing his status as a private citizen despite his legal expertise</note>, he had always conformed, and intended to conform in the future, to that which (all commands of wickedness excluded) was openly, or should be, received or permitted. And regarding the matter of his private conscience in particular, he wished to give account before God’s righteous judgment. Praying that they would hold him in no other esteem, and receive his declaration in good part, with the testimony that he wished to maintain the aforementioned Christian unity and civil obedience, requesting a certificate thereof under the seal of the city.* This was granted to him.

*A few weeks earlier, on the eighth day of January <note>original: "Loumaendt," a traditional Dutch name for the month of January, literally "Tanning Month"</note>, those of Artois, Hainaut, and Douai allied themselves to maintain the Union of Brussels, the Roman religion, obedience to the King, and the Peace of Ghent, and to help resist the Religious Peace <note>A proposed compromise meant to allow both Protestant and Catholic worship in the same territories</note>. <margin>

<margin>Art. I.</margin>
*This Union provided: That the Provinces bound themselves to remain together for all eternity as if they were but a single province: without prejudice, however, to the particular privileges, liberties, rights, and customs of each province, the cities, and the inhabitants thereof, in which they would not cause each other any hindrance or injury.*

<margin>Art. XIII.</margin>
*And concerning the matter of religion, those of Holland and Zeeland would behave as they saw fit, and the other provinces of this Union might adapt themselves according to the contents of the Religious Peace already drafted: or establish such order therein, in general or in particular, as they should find useful for the peace and welfare of the Provinces, cities, and particular members thereof, and for the preservation of everyone's spiritual and worldly property and justice: without any hindrance or obstacle being caused to them by any other Provinces; provided that every individual in particular might remain free in his religion, and that no one might be pursued or investigated for the sake of religion, according to the aforementioned Peace of Ghent. # H I S T O R Y

<meta>catchword: to</meta>

<margin>
1579.
</margin>
...to keep the Catholic Roman Religion, and where the number of inhabitants of the Reformed Religion was not so great that they might enjoy the practice of the Reformed Religion according to the aforementioned Religious Peace <note>A proposed compromise meant to allow both Protestant and Catholic worship in the same territories</note>, they did not wish to exclude them from the aforementioned Union and alliance: but that they would nonetheless be prepared to receive such cities and Provinces, which would only wish to keep to the aforementioned Roman Religion, into their Union, provided they would otherwise bind themselves to the other points of the aforementioned Union, and bear themselves as good lovers *of the Netherlands* <margin>* Patriots.</margin>. It was not the intention that one Province or city should interfere with the work of another in the matter of Religion, and this was to maintain greater peace and unity among the Provinces, and to avoid and take away the primary cause of strife. <margin>Bor XIII, 87, 88. Hooft XIV, 615.</margin> To this alliance, various cities and persons later added themselves.

<margin>
Insolence and theft in Utrecht. Bor XIII, 85. a.
</margin>
The day after the conclusion of the Union, the eleventh of January <note>original: "Loumaendt," a traditional Dutch name for the month of January</note>, a bold act took place in Utrecht. As the Priest was performing Mass in the Cathedral <note>The Dom of Utrecht</note> in the morning, and lifted the chalice, someone came from behind and snatched the chalice out of his hand with a jerk, and ran away with it; for no one dared to run after him out of the church, as it was still dark. <meta>This page continues the narrative of the religious and political restructuring of Antwerp following the riots of 1579. While the previous page described the expulsion of the Catholic clergy, this page details the specific legal terms of the new "Religious Peace" that allowed some to return under strict conditions of civil obedience and tolerance.</meta>

636 H I S T O R Y

<margin>
1579.
</margin>

<margin>
Religious Peace proclaimed there anew.
Bor XIII. 116.
<note>Reference to the historian Pieter Bor’s multi-volume history of the Netherlands.</note>
</margin>

...would be allowed to return to the city, specifically the secular priests and other clergy, with the exception of certain individuals who—for reasons noted in a specific document and for the greater tranquility of the city—were to remain outside. These clerical persons would have no jurisdiction over secular matters, nor would they interfere in political affairs; rather, in those regards, they were to be subject to the Magistrates. They would also be required to help bear the burden of excises, imposts, tithes, the "hundredth penny" <term>hondersten-penning: a 1% wealth tax common in the 16th-century Netherlands</term>, and other civic taxes. To prevent all riots, no ministers <note>original: "Predikanten"</note>, regardless of their religion, would be permitted to preach unless they were first reported to the Magistrates and accepted after prior deliberation. The Roman Catholics would not be permitted to hold public processions, and they were required to carry their Sacraments without pomp or sound, but in private. The mendicant orders <note>original: "biddende orden," religious orders like friars who lived by begging</note>, including the Bogards <note>A lay religious community often associated with the Franciscans</note>, were to remain excluded. Those of Saint Michael and Saint Peter were allowed to enter. The nunneries were to remain in their old possession and use. The clergy were to renounce all alliances with other provinces or foreigners, whether made individually or collectively, under whatever pretext, with a promise to make no more. On the same day, alongside the Union of Utrecht <note>The treaty that unified the northern provinces of the Netherlands in opposition to Spanish rule</note>, a further order of Religious Peace was read and made known here, in which certain points of the aforementioned charter were more clearly explained. This order also stated: "Since no religion can or should be maintained or impressed by force or weapons, but that the same must be expected as a special gift from Almighty God, and that it befits all Christian people, of whatever religion they may be, to live together harmoniously and peacefully, submitting themselves to the civil order of their authorities; so it has been found good that those of the Catholic Roman and Reformed religions, as well as those of the Confession of Augsburg <note>The primary confession of faith of the Lutheran Church</note>, shall each remain free and clear in their faith, as they will wish and intend to answer before God for the salvation of their souls according to each person's understanding on the Last Day. Furthermore, that on account of the diversity of the aforementioned religions, no one shall disturb, hinder, or harm another in their ceremonies, sermons, schools, or other exercises; but shall leave each person to his own in peace and quiet, and let them possess and use all their goods; at least for as long as, and until such time that, by the consensus of the States General, or at least by a National Council <note>A general assembly of the church to resolve matters of doctrine and discipline</note> (where everyone is freely heard), it is otherwise concluded and established regarding these matters: upon penalty of being punished in body and goods as disturbers of the common peace, as an example to others, without compromise."

A short time later, the Religious Peace previously granted in Mechelen was broken through the maneuverings of Brother Pieter Lupus, or Wolf. This monk—the Provincial, or regional superior, of the Carmelites <note>A Catholic mendicant order</note>, and full of hatred toward the Reformed—was so eloquent that he could lead the people wherever he wished with his fine sermons. He was so bold that he took the entire government upon himself, and finally caused the city to defect to the Spanish side, to its great ruin. There, they dared to seize the church’s valuables and, among other images, they melted down the silver-gilt casket of Saint Rombout <note>The patron saint of Mechelen; his relics were housed in this famous shrine</note>; something which the men of the Prince of Orange and those of Alva had previously refused to touch. This led the Lord of Fromont, a Roman Catholic nobleman, to remark: *It seems that if God himself could have been turned into gold, he would also have been put into the purse.* Just as some ailments are contagious, spreading quickly and departing slowly, so the sickness of disorder, riot, and wantonness, once it had taken hold among the Netherlanders, seemed to strike like a poison that listened to no remedies.

Riot at Utrecht.
Bor XIII. 116. d. Hooft XV. 639.
</margin>
On the tenth of June <note>original: "Sommermaendt," literally Summer-month</note>, the statues were cast out of the churches in Utrecht amidst a great riot. After this, on the fifteenth, a certain treaty was made between the five "Godshouses" <note>Collegiate churches or religious foundations</note> in the name of the general clergy on one side, and the Magistrates, Colonel, Civic Militia Captains, and commanders in the name of the general citizenry, along with those of the Reformed Religion, on the other side.

Treaty made there.
Bor XIII, 116, 117, 118.

All crimes and injuries that had occurred since the Pacification of Ghent <note>A 1576 treaty intended to unite the provinces against Spanish rule and establish religious tolerance</note> were to be mutually forgiven and forgotten. The Reformed were to practice their religion freely in the church of the Minorites <note>Franciscan friars</note>, and those of Saint James, Saint Nicholas, and the Neighborhood Church <note>original: "Buurkerke"</note>. They were to remain satisfied with these, without being allowed to take over any more churches or places for worship. Those of the Roman Religion were to keep the church of Saint Gertrude as their parish church, to which those of Saint Nicholas would also belong; but those who belonged to the parishes of the Neighborhood Church and Saint James would be allowed to adopt the church of the Preachers <note>Dominican friars</note> as their parish. To maintain greater peace and unity, people of both religions were forbidden from causing any harm or trouble to one another in the practice of their religions, services, or ceremonies; nor were they to desecrate, plunder, or damage any church or other sacred place, or break any altars or statues. <margin>Bor XIII, 129, 130. Hooft XV, 640. Unrest in Bruges. Bor XIII. 120. Hooft XV, 641.</margin>In Bruges, a heavy disturbance broke out at the beginning of July <note>original: "Hooimaendt," the month of haymaking</note>. The City Council sought to have the Union of Utrecht <note>A treaty unifying the northern provinces in defense of their rights and religious freedom</note> accepted there. The Roman Catholic clergy opposed this, arguing that in Utrecht, where the Union was made, the clergy’s word was not kept and they were instead driven out. The largest trades—such as the Carpenters, Smiths, Tanners, Fullers, and others—who attended the sermons of Brother Cornelis <note>Cornelis Adriaensz, a famous and fiery pro-Catholic preacher</note> and were incited against the Magistrate, lashed out with threats against their Deans because they had consented to the Union. The Clergy, strengthened by this, further egged on the people. A mob rushed to the Carmelite Monastery to kill Jan Haeren, the Walloon <note>original: "Walsch"</note> Reformed Preacher. Failing to find him, they vented their anger on his wife, hitting, punching, kicking, and dragging her across the floor. Everyone took up arms; even Canons and Priests took weapons in hand, occupied the Castle <note>original: "den Burg"</note>, and held the Governors as prisoners. Afterward, a certain treaty was struck. However, both parties had sent for help, and the first to arrive was for the Magistrate; thus the Reformed remained masters of the city. The Preacher Haeren took his opportunity for revenge, hung a buckler <note>original: "rondas"</note> around his neck, and led several Frenchmen who plundered the house of Jeroen de Mol, who had been forced upon the Roman Catholics as Colonel. A large portion of the Clergy fled the city, and their churches remained closed; although the Roman Catholics were not prevented from practicing their religion in private.

<margin>Trouble at Weesp. *Bor XIII, 128. Hooft XV, 644.*</margin>Several Roman Catholics were in arms on that day, the first of July 1579 <note>original: "MDLXXIX. Hooimaendt," the month of haymaking</note>; and they fell to shooting at one another, without it being possible to say truly who began first. Forty citizens remained dead, and one hundred and twenty were wounded. Then the Reformed <note>Protestants belonging to the Dutch Reformed Church</note> pressed again for a garrison; but the Magistrate managed to deflect it, which moved the others to leave the city. At Weesp, in the heart of Holland, some mutiny smoldered in July over the introduction of the Reformed religion according to the Religious Peace <term>Religious Peace: A 1578 treaty intended to allow both Catholic and Protestant worship in the same city</term>. Consequently, Master Willem Bardesius <note>original: "Bardeeſen"</note>, Burgomaster of Amsterdam, was sent there by the States of Holland. Seven persons were removed from the City Council <note>original: "Vroedtſchap"</note>, and three of them, along with the Secretary and the old Priest Roelof Gijsbrechts, were expelled from the city; with the assurance that this was done without infringing upon privileges, and declaring that those departing would retain their property and honor intact. Bardesius left the punishment of the instigators of the riot to the local judges.

<margin>Great disorder and wantonness at Ghent. *Hooft XV, 644. Bor XIII, 126.*</margin>In Ghent, meanwhile, the Roman clergy suffered much this summer. Jan van Hembyze <note>original: "Imbyſe"</note> and his kin acted as if they had outgrown all divine and human laws. Churches, monasteries, and abbeys were given over to their captains and soldiers for plunder. Several people who adhered to the Reformed religion, but who stood in his way, he had banished from Ghent through hasty legal proceedings; others were done away with by soldiers without any trial at all.

# THE TWELFTH BOOK OF THE REFORMATION.

<margin>1579 <note>original: "MDLXXIX"</note></margin>
...Reformed, for the sake of peace, would depart, yet take hostages with them for their security. The dispute regarding the Monks, where one party wished to expel them and the other to keep them, was left to the Stadtholder <term>Rennenberg</term> <note>George de Lalaing, Count of Rennenberg, the governor of the northern provinces. He was currently trying to mediate religious peace but would later defect to the Spanish side.</note>. In the end, the Monks were forced out of the city, which was later secured with two companies of soldiers. However, although some of the Reformed did not keep their word to the Catholics <note>original: "Papisten"</note> and their Clergy—who had stipulated the use of their churches, monasteries, and property—and though several Preachers incited their followers to this end, they were not all of one mind in this matter. Indeed, some of the most prominent theologians declared at this time, in response to a specific question put to them by Count John of Nassau <note>The brother of William of Orange and a staunch leader of the Protestant cause.</note>, <margin>Some Reformed theologians assert that promises made to Catholics must be kept.</margin> *that one was also obligated to keep the covenants made with Catholics.* This they asserted in a long and dignified letter, with clear examples and weighty reasons. To the objection *that by maintaining the peace and the covenant made with those loyal to the Pope, one would thereby strengthen their ungodly superstitions,* <margin>Selected Letters, Second Century, p. 853. <note>original: "Epist. select. Centur. II, 853."</note></margin> it was answered *that experience taught the contrary; that there was no more powerful means to bring them to similar fairness, and further to propagate the pure religion and Evangelical teaching, than that the peace sworn by both sides be kept inviolate. Conversely, nothing would so greatly corrupt, overthrow, and finally extinguish true godliness and doctrine as internal civil strife, which arose from the trampling of good faith and the breaking of covenants, eventually erupting into murder, defeats, and gruesome butchery.* <margin>p. 863.</margin> Thereafter they said they confessed *that idolatry could not be abolished by violence and riot, nor could the true Religion be introduced that way; for it was certain that those who were forced in such a manner would either reject all godliness or conceive a much more bitter hatred against the zealots of the true Religion, which they would carry out with bitter scorn against everyone—even the most pious and innocent—at the first available opportunity.* <margin>p. 865.</margin> *If we*, they continued, *desire that our faith be kept, and that the rule—that "no faith should be kept with heretics"—be abolished among the Catholics, then it is of the highest necessity that we ourselves also keep the promises made on our side sacredly. We must reject the rule of those who think that one can piously confirm Religion through perjury, or who deny that one may make peace or a covenant with the ungodly or with idolaters. ...en <note>Presumably the end of the word "strengthen" or "versterken" from the previous page.</note>, laughing in their sleeves <note>original: "lachende in den vuist," an idiom for laughing secretly or mockingly</note> at the scorn and injustice done to the church and monastery folk in many places, they knew how to skillfully turn what happened to their spite to their own advantage, and through their supporters, blow into this fire, to set fire to all corners with the scattered sparks. At this time, most countries and churches where Luther’s Reformation had been accepted, particularly in Germany, were in a bright blaze of dispute because of a so-called <term>Book of Concord</term> <note>A doctrinal document intended to unify the Lutheran faith, though it became a source of great conflict with other Protestants.</note> or writing of unity, forged by the harshest proponents of <term>Ubiquity</term> <note>original: "Alenthalventheit"; the Lutheran doctrine that Christ's physical body is present everywhere at once.</note>, to testify to their unity by the signing of the same, while condemning those who felt otherwise. Through this, all domestic and foreign churches that refused to sign that formulary were excluded from Christian communion; it not only made the schism between the Lutherans and the Reformed larger, but also gave cause for dispute and schism among the Lutherans themselves. Many who were more moderate refused to sign, and were forced or sought to be forced to do so with no small inquisition, tyranny, and persecution. To stop this evil, which (despite what the Reformed of all regions and some Lutherans did against it) pushed forward for several years, the Teachers of the Reformed churches in the Netherlands wrote—by the pen of Petrus Villers \*, court preacher to the Prince of Orange—a long letter † to the authors of that Book of Concord. In this letter they spoke with great earnestness, kindly and brotherly: declaring their aversion to church dispute, to the condemning of brothers, and to schism, while professing their love of peace. In several lines of their letter—for its length does not permit it to be read here in its entirety—they used this language:

>
> We do not believe, they said, dear brothers, after the account of the misery and persecution suffered by the Dutch Reformed at the hands of the Papists and Spaniards, that these things are unknown to you. Indeed, no one believes that you would not have understood what happened to our people among you, when many of ours, through the storm of the unfortu-

# THE TWELFTH BOOK OF THE REFORMATION.

<margin>p. 4 and 10.</margin>
...during the times of Queen Mary, <note>Mary I, often called 'Bloody Mary,' who attempted to restore Catholicism in England (1553–1558), forcing many Protestants to flee.</note> driven out of England in the winter of 1553, they arrived by ship at your shores; yet, in the most dangerous season of the year and with the wind against them, they were forced to depart by the advice and urging of certain reckless people.
<margin>p. 5 and 12.</margin>
We do not recount this as if a single scar of that wound still remains with us—far be that from us, who profess Christian love—but only to present to you more clearly, as if in a painting, the state in which our churches find themselves. We are, according to the flesh, most miserable, as we could find no dwelling place even among our brothers (for you are our own flesh)...
<margin>p. 6 and 14.</margin>
Thereafter, they complained that the Lutherans, with their <term>Book of Concord</term> <note>The 'Formula of Concord' (1577), a document intended to unify Lutherans but which also condemned certain Reformed/Calvinist views.</note>, took up the struggle against those whom they ought to regard as their most beloved brothers. They fought to carry out their condemnations against all justice. The ministers pointed them to the peace-loving nature and flexibility of <term>Cyprian</term> <note>An early Christian bishop and martyr (c. 210–258 AD) known for his emphasis on church unity.</note>, requesting that they not be condemned unheard, but that a Christian inquiry be established. They asked that, according to ancient custom, a lawful—and not a murderous—<term>Synod</term> <note>original: "moorders Synode," likely referring to the Latin term "synodus latrocinialis" or "Robber Synod," a gathering that uses force or intimidation rather than law.</note> be held; that from such a gathering, the word of Christ might judge the entire dispute concerning the Lord’s Supper once and for all, if it could be judged in any other way.
<margin>p. 8 9. and 19.</margin>
Or if, they said, our sins should prevent us from obtaining such a thing from the Heavenly Father, then—following in the footsteps of our holy forefathers <term>Luther</term>, <term>Zwingli</term>, <term>Capito</term>, <term>Bucer</term>, <term>Melanchthon</term>, <term>Bullinger</term>, and <term>Calvin</term> (who thought this manner of proceeding very just)—both sides should use peaceful and moderate counsel. In the meantime, pious and wise men should consider whether we could not bear with one another for a little time, until the Lord opens our eyes, so that the eternal truth might fully enlighten our hearts, and a firm and lasting peace and harmony might be established in our churches...
<margin>

This is well worth noting against those who dispute these same points with too much vehemence. D. Blondel in his *Authentic Acts* <note>original: "ses Actes authentiques"</note> p. 70.

We are accused and reported as if we differ from you in the principal articles of faith, yet we believe it is sufficiently evident through the writings of many people and through our own teaching, which has now become openly known, that even those who are our greatest enemies nevertheless hold for certain that all the difference remaining between us consists mostly in two points *, namely in that of the Lord’s Supper, and of Christ’s person and His two natures...

<margin>p. 40, and 94.</margin>

Secondly, that you meanwhile abstain from insults and slanderous words, which we do not think it good to recount. Finally, if discord should possibly arise, that the difference be presented to the Father, as is becoming among brothers. Yet we shall understand the will of the common Father from His Word. We must all obey Him. You have understood our mind and spirit—how foreign it is to schism, and how inclined toward peace. We wish that you might be of that same mind. If then we can obtain nothing from you through our prayers, we testify before God and Christ...
