Peace negotiations at Cologne.
See Bor XIII. 103. d... 138... 147... Hooft XV, 631, 633, 658, 667... Uitenbogaert's History p. 202. Grotius's Annals III. 61, 62.
</margin>
Meanwhile, peace was being negotiated in Cologne between the Spanish and the States of the Netherlands, in the presence of the Imperial Envoys <note>Representatives of the Holy Roman Emperor who acted as mediators.</note>. Some believe that those on the side of the States would have secured quite reasonable terms at this time, had not some individuals hindered the general peace with their own private interests. Others, however, maintain that the Spanish had only initiated this work to weaken the allies through division. It is also said that the Prince of Orange <note>William the Silent, leader of the Dutch Revolt.</note>, fearing that any peace with the King would turn to his disadvantage, had secretly brought it about that they should insist on the matter of Religion and other points which they did not believe the King would grant.

<margin>Acts of the Peace Negotiations p. 37.</margin>
Nevertheless, the Envoys of the States maintained that nothing had been proposed from their side that should not or could not be granted in that state of affairs, or that they could not clearly prove to belong to them by their privileges and rights.

<margin>
The request of the States on the matter of Religion.
See the Acts of the Peace Negotiations p. 27, 363, 364.
</margin>
Regarding Religion, their request and proposal was: That the King, at the humble desire of his subjects, and so that the domestic disputes should not grow greater to the further peril of the Roman Religion, should suffer and permit the exercise of the Reformed Religion, and of the Augsburg Confession <note>The primary confession of faith for the Lutheran Church.</note>, in the cities and places where they were then publicly maintained. Likewise, the States would, in all the aforementioned cities and places, immediately after the proclamation of peace, again re-establish the exercise of the Catholic Roman Religion, provided reasonable conditions were set and kept inviolable. The States would also ensure that in Holland and Zeeland the use of the Catholic Roman Religion would be accepted in some places; until such time as, through further assembly of the States, it could be more fully provided for.

<margin>Peace Negotiations p. 54.</margin>
To strengthen their request, the Envoys argued among other things: That the Christian Religion was a great mystery, for the advancement of which God used no godless soldiers, nor bow, nor sword; but His spirit, and Pastors, or Shepherds, [sent] by Him

Ecclesiastical strife in Leiden.
Bor XIV. 169; Hooft XVI, 687, 688; Uitert. Hist. 205.

finding part in the current state of affairs, the concern to keep the other allies bound together for the common defense fell most heavily on those who had the most power. This had already begun to be seen in the past year between Pieter Kornelissoon and Kasper Koolhaes, ministers in Leiden. The former charged the other *that it was impossible to serve with him, since in various matters he refused to submit to the judgment of the brethren and to follow the resolutions of the Church Councils.* Others, on the contrary, said the root of the estrangement was that Koolhaes held outward behavior to be somewhat less, and inward disposition to be somewhat more necessary for salvation than Pieter Kornelissoon did <gloss>1</gloss>. But in particular, strife arose regarding the election of the Elders and Deacons <gloss>2</gloss> <note>Elders and deacons are lay officers in the Reformed Church; elders oversee discipline and doctrine, while deacons manage charity and care for the poor.</note>. The one [Kornelissoon] wanted the Consistory <note>The local governing body of the church, consisting of the minister and elders.</note> to nominate them and present them to the congregation without the knowledge of the Magistrate; the other [Koolhaes] wanted those nominated to be first presented to the Magistrates for their consent before being presented to the congregation. This latter procedure was demanded by the Magistrate <gloss>3</gloss>, and Koolhaes understood that it was their right. Furthermore, the Magistrates—to maintain good harmony and remove mistrust and suspicion—saw fit and resolved that Willem Jan Reyerssoon van Heemskerk and Jan Kerstantssoon, their fellow brothers in the court and council (both professing the Reformed Religion), should be present at all meetings of the Church Council to sit there on behalf of the Authorities and have oversight, with an oath to keep secret that which did not concern their knowledge. From all this arose a dispute regarding the office and authority of a Christian Magistrate in ecclesiastical matters. The States of Holland, who took the common peace to heart, sought to settle the dispute through their Deputies. It was in vain. The ministers of the Classes <note>Regional governing bodies in the Reformed Church, composed of representatives from several local consistories.</note> of Leiden, Rijnland, Delfland, and others also involved themselves. Therefore, the States commanded the ministers to set down in writing from the word of God what commonality and difference existed between civil and ecclesiastical government. This document <gloss>4</gloss> was delivered to the States on the twenty-fourth of May <note>original: "Bloeimaendt," literally "Bloom-month," an old Dutch term for May.</note>. However, the Lords of Leiden did not agree with it in all points. It said, among other things, *“That it was the office of the Magistrate to compel the despisers and falsifiers of the Divine word to leave the church in external peace: and [to punish] the disturbers of the church’s peace with imprisonment, corporal punishment, or with”*

declared, and still declares, that their intention never was, nor is, to rule over the church, but only to ensure that all disputes in the church of God might be prevented, and to keep seditious spirits out of the consistory <note>The *Consistorie* or *Kerkenraedt* was the governing body of a local Reformed church, composed of the minister and elders.</note>: that they should appoint godly men therein, not those who merely had the appearance of it: that Christian discipline should affect the great as well as the small, which until now had been more desired than seen: That they should choose worthy Ministers of the Word, who were capable of sweetly comforting the broken in spirit with the Holy Scriptures, and sternly rebuking stubborn sinners; but not those who were cunning in drawing the rebellious to their partisan side with sweet persuasion. That they should let Jesus Christ alone remain the head of the churches, and in no way any Ministers or Consistory-members; so that the same should not again set themselves up as heads of the churches, to strive anew for dominion over consciences, and thereby bring these free churches under a new Popery <note>The term 'Popery' (Dutch: *Pausdom*) was used here as a pejorative to describe any religious authority—even Protestant—that claimed absolute power over the state or the individual conscience, likening it to the Roman Catholic system they had recently rejected.</note> and yoke.

Thereafter they recounted what experience had previously opened their eyes to the partiality of some in the Consistory; namely, that they had, through deceptive tricks, driven an honest Minister named Klaes Janszoon Verstroot (at the time of this writing a Minister of the Divine Word at Naaldwijk) out of his service, and that undeservedly, indeed against his great merits; as he had remained within Leiden during both subsequent sieges <note>The Sieges of Leiden (1573–1574) were pivotal events in the Dutch Revolt against Spain. Staying in the city during these times was a mark of extreme loyalty and courage.</note>, where he had been very pleasing and dear to the congregation through his willing and comforting services.

*if today or tomorrow some differences concerning the matter of Religion should occur, who then would judge the same? The Magistrate? Or some Commissioners, authorized by them for that purpose? Or the Classes <note>A regional assembly of ministers and elders.</note> and Synods?* To the first, the Consistory <note>The governing body of a local Reformed church, made up of the minister and elders.</note> answered, *that they had not separated themselves from other churches, but other churches had torn themselves away from them, and that they had never desired anything more heartily, nor did they yet desire anything more, than to have peace with all churches, indeed with all people, as far as was in them.* To the second point it was answered, *that they submitted themselves to the word of God and were prepared to let themselves be judged by the same.* Koolhaes referred to his answer to three questions previously proposed. First, *if he was prepared to reconcile with his opponents from the heart?* To which he had answered, *Yes, and that from the bottom of his heart.* Secondly, *if he also intended to introduce any other teaching in Leiden than that which had been and was being preached there and throughout all of Holland for so long?* To which his answer was, *that he knew of no other teaching than that of the Biblical Scripture, the teaching of the Old and New Testaments, and therefore had taught no other teaching nor desired to teach any.* Thirdly, *if he did not also desire to come to the Classes and Synods, and was prepared to submit himself to the judgment of the brethren?* To this question he had given this answer: *I do not refuse to come to Classes and Synods, being called, and am prepared to let myself be instructed and rebuked by the very least of the congregation, indeed by anyone, through God’s word: also, being convinced out of God’s word, to confess my guilt and to turn from unrighteousness. But if the Classes or Synods, according to their own pleasure, laws, and human institutions, wish to judge, then I do not think to submit myself to that judgment; for I, having once been a Monk, do not desire to put on the cowl again <note>Koolhaes had been a monk before converting to the Reformation; here he uses the "cowl" as a metaphor for ecclesiastical rules that bind the conscience similar to those of the Catholic Church he left.</note>, nor let myself be bound to human institutions.*

...having become powerful, now opposed [them]. The arms of the Prince of Parma, <margin>1580.</margin> the King’s Governor and Commander-in-Chief after Don Juan’s death, gained ground daily to the great disadvantage of the Reformed <note>The Calvinist Protestants</note>, who suffered much in the conquered cities. This caused the Prince of Orange from then on never, or very seldom, to rely upon the Roman Catholics, however loyal they might seem. He had so firmly trusted Rennenberg, the brother of his late friend, the Count of Hoogstraten, that his defection seemed like a dream to him. This breach of faith later served as a nail in the Count's coffin <note>original: "nagel aen ſijn' kiſt"; a Dutch expression meaning a source of great distress that hastens one's end</note>, and was paid for with a remorse that pierced his soul. It appears that the poor outcome of his plan galled him more than the crime itself; it is certain that during his illness over Groningen he often cried out, wishing he had never seen the city. He also, in his final days, forbade his sister Cornelia, who had misled him *, from coming into his sight. 

Furthermore, the news from Groningen, spreading immediately, caused bitter resentment everywhere among the Reformed <note>The Protestant Calvinists</note>, and heated their heads so much that they hatched many an uprising, trusting themselves nowhere where they were not the masters. In Deventer and Zwolle <note>original: "Swolle"</note>, the citizens took up arms against one another; some of the Romish faith were driven out, and the monasteries and images were destroyed. In Friesland, the Ommelanden, and Drenthe, the soldiers fell upon whatever they could in churches and monasteries, threw down the images, and drove out the Roman Catholics. The rumor of these actions also helped set a great number of people in Utrecht in motion. On the seventh of June <note>original: "Somermaendt"; literally Summer-month</note>, they broke into the churches where the Roman religion was still practiced, and smashed the images, paintings, and altars to pieces. This unbridled violation of the agreement made last June was loathed by people of honor; but no one dared to oppose such a violent fury. 

The disturbance increased, and the entire citizenry took up arms. Then the Magistrate <note>The city government</note> sent some officials to the Captains of the Civil Guard, desiring that they should quiet the people and cause them to disperse, with the promise that their desires would be modestly considered. But the noise and clamor prevented them from being heard. At last, they drafted twelve points to be granted before their gathering would disperse. Some were granted to them regarding the security of the city: furthermore, *”the bringing up of orphans in the Reformed Religion; the Reformation of the Great Schools; the sending of three or four scholars to some Reformed Academies; the right to appoint the church in the future upon nomination by the congregation; the expulsion of suspected Roman Catholics”*: They also demanded that one...

Around this time, some wicked men again had a "Kingdom of Münster"—following the precedent of Jan van Leiden—in their sights. One Jan Schoenlapper <note>literally "John the Shoemaker"</note>, who after the death of David Joris took up the rule over his companions, had been hanged in Brussels. He was followed by Cornelis Appelmans, who was punished with death at Utrecht †. Afterward, there arose among this band Jan Willem Stevens, a son, it is believed, of a priest, born at Roermond. This man sought, with his brother Jacob, to gather the remnants of the Kingdom of Münster. He said that God had revealed to him that the teaching of the <term>Anabaptists; "Dooperen," a radical Reformation group practicing adult baptism</term> was the purest of all: that he was appointed to proclaim and establish it: and that no government should be considered legitimate unless it accepted this teaching. Therefore, one should in no way spare the Papists <note>original: "Pausgeſinden," those leaning toward the Pope</note>, who oppressed those who held better views than they did. He assured his followers that, in a short time, the kingdom of the New Jerusalem being established, the people, enlightened by God, would take the lands possessed by the "evil-minded," just as the Israelites of old cast the Canaanites out of their possessions and goods. To establish his power, he first gave freedom to have many wives, in the manner of Muhammad. But in order to have the means to support himself and his followers, he authorized stealing and robbery: under the pretext that the goods of this earth belonged to Christ and his disciples. These had been unjustly divided by human laws. Therefore God willed that he, being sent by Him, should distribute them with more justice among his own; that he should take from the rich what they had in excess, and give it to the poor, and those who were worthy of it—that is, those who conspired with him. The freedom to steal and rob having been given, they lived—

### THE REFORMATION BOOK XII.

...these people spent some time in great wantonness, boasting <margin>1580.</margin> that they carried out divine justice in good conscience with the sword of God and Gideon <note>A biblical reference to Judges 7:20, often used by radical groups to justify holy war or divine vengeance</note>. Many castles of nobles and houses of the rich were plundered and destroyed at night by these highway robbers; some people were also murdered. That evil spirit plagued the people in the lands of Cleves, Jülich, and Guelders for five whole years, until Jan Willemsz, the founder of this supposed kingdom, who now had three hundred robbers at his command, was taken into custody at Dinslaken, in the land of Cleves. He remained here until the year seventy-nine <note>1579</note>, and lived nevertheless in great abundance and luxury, among a great multitude of women whom he kept with him constantly, having established the freedom to have many wives through a printed book distributed among his followers. His guards turned a blind eye to all of this, for there was no lack of money nor cunning to bribe them. He perhaps also let them share in his luxury. Finally, everything was discovered through a girl from Wesel, named Catherine. One of his wives, named Elsken—who, having reached her senior years, had surrendered her daughter Elizabeth to the imprisoned King’s will in her place—and Anna, an old woman of seventy who had escaped the Siege of Münster <note>The 1534-1535 radical Anabaptist rebellion that attempted to establish a "New Jerusalem" through communalism and polygamy</note>, along with one Simon Pieterszoon, were captured and, after confessing to the facts, punished with death. From these, it was learned that a common mingling of marital practices <note>This refers to the sect's practice of polygamy and "spiritual" marriage</note> took place among them; for they argued that man was born for procreation, and therefore one might have many wives and abandon the infertile ones; they also called each other by the names of brothers and sisters as a testimony of mutual love. The other women, or "Queens," were granted their lives by the judges of Cleves, either because they had been coerced or because of their sheer number. They were ordered to do penance and sent back to Friesland and Holland, from where they had come. Finally, the false King, Jan Willem Stevens, who stubbornly denied everything, was overcome by the confessions of the others and sentenced to the fire. This punishment he endured at Cleves, on the twelfth of March <note>original: "Lentemaendt," the spring month</note> of this year, tied to the stake with the same stubbornness, without any sign of remorse or sadness, suddenly throwing himself headfirst into the flames. Others say that in the fire he constantly cried out,

In that same year of 1580, the Lutherans in Woerden lost the use of their church due to causes that must be traced back further. In this city, which had been pledged to Duke Eric of Brunswick <note>Duke Eric II of Brunswick-Lüneburg was a Catholic ally of Spain, which explains why Lutheranism was initially tolerated there as a middle ground</note>, they had openly practiced their religion according to the Augsburg Confession <note>The primary confession of faith of the Lutheran Church</note> for seven years. But despite enjoying this favor, which ought to have been acknowledged with modesty, one of their ministers named Jan Saeliger took it upon himself to repeatedly denounce the "Calvinists" (as he called them) from the pulpit. He labeled them oath-breakers, covenant-violators, and restless spirits who kept treaties only until they gained the power to force others through their Consistories <note>Governing bodies of the Reformed/Calvinist church</note>; he claimed they even sought to master the Magistrate. He also daily reviled the Papists <note>Catholics</note> and Mennonites, as well as the Calvinists, as deceivers and "soul-murderers." All of this was initially overlooked through official indulgence. But it did not stop there. He fell into the very evil he accused others of, interfering so deeply in matters of government that he gave the Prince <note>William the Silent, Prince of Orange</note> a swipe from the pulpit. He claimed the Prince had violated the privileges of the city of Woerden during the appointment of the Magistrates in May <term>Bloeimaendt|Month of Blossoms</term> of the previous year by bringing "false Christians" (meaning the Reformed) into the government.

<margin>
[August 9th]
</margin>

This, he said, should not happen without significant reason, especially since there were so many followers of both Popery and Calvinism, both of which taught falsely. The deputies of the States, taking them at their word, forbade them from preaching in the church from then on. This prohibition, once known among the people, filled the city with unrest, for most of the citizenry adhered to the **Augsburg Confession** <note>The primary statement of faith for Lutherans</note>. Nevertheless, the citizens who were not fond of Saliger because of his habitual scolding, but who nonetheless openly held to the **Augsburg Confession**, found it advisable to request a certain **Master Niclaes Simonszoon** to serve the church in Woerden for a time on loan; hoping that he would be the man to achieve peace. This man, formerly the priest at Jaepswoude, had previously been imprisoned for several years at the Bishop’s court in Utrecht as a Lutheran and a heretic, but had been released since the Peace of Ghent and called back to his village of Jaepswoude by the Lord of Warmondt. However, while identifying as a Lutheran, he had come to an agreement with the churches of Rijnland <note>This implies he was more moderate and willing to cooperate with the Dutch Reformed (Calvinist) authorities than the strict Saliger.</note>.

People also bitingly mocked Master Niclaes, criticizing and misinterpreting his preaching and **reasonableness** <term>reklijkheit: a term used for religious moderates who were flexible in dogma to maintain social peace, later associated with the Remonstrants</term>. That, he said, is true freedom: to be allowed to leave what one holds as evil, and to be allowed to do what one holds as good.* This, he continued, had been his opinion for over twenty-five years; and he had accordingly in the year sixty-six <note>1566</note>, when the Reformed were allowed the free practice of their Religion and the building of churches, contributed as much as anyone to the building of their church outside the Wood Gate <note>original: "Houtpoorte"</note>, although not being of the Reformed Religion himself; which was done at the peril of his life, as clearly appeared thereafter. <margin>
Uprising of the Catholics in Brussels. 
Bor XVI, 22, 23; Hooft XVII, 765, 766; Meteren IX, 195.

In Brussels, the Catholics expressed themselves with greater turbulence, because they wanted to keep the rebellious Parish Priest of Saint Gudula <note>The Cathedral of St. Michael and St. Gudula is the primary church of Brussels</note>, Antonis Ruiskevelt, in the city through an uprising, in defiance of the Magistrate who sought to make him depart. However, the City Council maintained the upper hand through the soldiers and obedient citizens, and took note of various rebellious acts conducted under the pretext of religious gatherings. Ruiskevelt was forced out of the city gates on the evening of the twenty-second of April <note>original: "Grasmaendt" - Grass month</note>, along with many of his followers. Churches and monasteries were closed, the images removed from them, and the practice of the Roman Religion suspended; a general pardon was granted to everyone, with few exceptions; those of both religious persuasions were taken under the protection of the Magistrate by public proclamation.

<margin>Bor XVI, 23, c, d.</margin>
In the proclamation issued regarding this on the first of May <note>original: "Bloeimaendt" - Flower month</note>, it was declared how it had become evident to the City Council that what the Clergy presented under the name of the *Sacrament of Miracles* <note>A famous local devotion in Brussels concerning consecrated hosts that were allegedly stabbed by Jews and miraculously bled</note> as three blood-stained Communion wafers, consisted of cloths mixed with other material: that they had caused the bones of beasts to be honored as holy relics, and had deceived the simple folk in many ways out of greed. Old wooden measuring rods <note>original: "elssen latten"</note> had been offered for adoration in place of pieces of the Lord's cross. In the heads of some statues, holes had been found where oil was poured to make the images "sweat." In some statues, clockwork mechanisms <note>original: "draeÿtuigen"</note> had been placed to move certain limbs. In this same month, the thirteen trades and six sworn guilds in Antwerp, out of fear of new iconoclasm <note>The "Beeldenstorm" or "Image Storm" where Protestant mobs destroyed Catholic art</note>, removed their altarpieces—painted by great and world-renowned masters—from the great church with the permission of the Authorities and brought them into safekeeping.

*Bor XVI, 21. c, d.* <note>Reference to the history by Pieter Bor</note>

> *That he had unexpectedly come into the company of the citizens who had the Petition drafted, and having only heard the end of it read, had said: That their request for the free public exercise of their Religion seemed right and reasonable to him; for he understood according to his conscience before God, that every church, whichever it might be, ought to be publicly permitted such exercise of worship as it held to be good and upright before God: since it was not only coercion of conscience to force someone to accept a Religion which he held to be false and evil, but that it was equal coercion to force the cessation of the public exercise of a Religion which someone felt in his conscience before God to be true and upright. That, he said, is true freedom: to be allowed to leave what one holds to be evil, and to be allowed to do what one holds to be good. This, he continued, had been his opinion for over twenty-five years, and accordingly in the year sixty-six <note>1566, the "Year of Wonders" and the start of the Dutch Revolt</note>, when the Reformed were allowed the free exercise of their Religion and the building of churches, he had contributed as much as anyone to the construction of their church outside the Wood Gate <note>Houtpoorte</note>, even though he was not of the Reformed Religion; which was done at the risk of his life, as became clear afterward. In Brussels, the Roman Catholics expressed themselves with great turbulence, because they wished to keep the rebellious Parish Priest <note>original: "Prochiaen"</note> of Saint Gudula, Antonis Ruijskevelt, in the city by way of a riot, in defiance of the Magistrate, who sought to make him depart. Churches and monasteries were closed, the images removed from them, and the practice of the Roman Religion suspended; pardon was granted to everyone, with a few exceptions; those of both the one and the other persuasion <note>meaning both Catholics and Protestants</note> were taken under the protection of the Magistrate by public proclamation.

</margin>

Old wooden alder slats had been allowed to be worshipped in place of pieces of the Lord's cross. In the heads of some statues, holes had been found where oil was poured to make the statues appear to sweat. In some statues, clockwork mechanisms <note>original: "draeytuigen"</note> had been placed to move certain limbs.

The treaty that had been concluded with those of Amsterdam in the year seventy-eight, and shortly thereafter broken by some from the community, was now, on the twenty-sixth of December <note>original: "Wintermaendt"</note>, annulled by mutual consent of the States of the land and the current Magistrates of the city, and another agreement was reached in which the matter of Religion was not mentioned. From this, the Roman Catholics <note>original: "Roomsgesinden"</note> drew little hope of being restored to their negotiated advantages. Also on the same day, in the name of the Prince of Orange, to whom the high Authority had been entrusted, an edict <term>Plakkaet: a formal public decree</term> was issued, not only forbidding the printing and selling of all scandalous, offensive, and seditious booklets, news, and poems—likewise the printing of anything without the consent of the Magistrate and the name of the printer—but also the practice of the Papal Religion, and the holding of public and secret gatherings, upon a fine of one hundred guilders. However, the edict stated that they did not wish to burden or investigate anyone’s conscience. It also forbade the wearing of clerical garments and the keeping of schools without prior examination and permission. This was the first prohibition issued in the form of an edict in Holland against the Papists <note>original: "Pausgesinden"</note>, nearly ten years after the States of the land had taken up arms against the Spaniards for freedom, intending to maintain both the one and the other Religion. But matters and times had greatly changed. Most Papists <note>original: "Paepisten"</note> were now regarded as Spanish sympathizers and as enemies of the current government. Nevertheless, that edict, insofar as people wanted to apply it to books dealing with the matter of Religion, was not put into effect or carried out in any of the cities of Holland where it was proclaimed; indeed, those of Leiden refused to allow it to be read out in their city.

> *From the Papal bond we are now, by God’s grace, released; yet some earnest people have been stirred up again by their own unwise zeal—not, however, to drive anyone toward false doctrine, as the Pope had done, but to urge the Authorities, as those permitted to do so, to support the true Religion with their power. Noting this, and finding that through the strength of this sickness of opinions so many thousands and thousands of thousands have died, we prefer to leave to God, our protector, the honor that belongs to him, and to humble ourselves in our weakness before His high Majesty, rather than stubbornly holding to foreign opinions and grieving others in those matters wherein we gladly acknowledge we may be mistaken. For this knowledge we thank God, and have therefore quite maturely decided to accept no religious coercion, in small or in large part, nor any statutes or decrees tending toward it...*

Turning now to you, who come forward with Synodical Acts, we ask: by what power and authority do you wish to force these upon us? Does the power come from God, or the authority from the Government? We cannot believe that God would have appointed you as Ministers <note>Church officials</note> to rule over the Government. That the Government authorized you as a Synod has not been proven to us. It is presented as "National." But many, along with us, do not consider it as such. If it were to be National, it would have to be convoked, determined, and approved by the head of the nation. The head of the nation, over which this Synod would extend as "National," are the States General <note>The central assembly of representatives from the various Dutch provinces</note>, by which legal assembly we do not believe it was convoked. And it could not be convoked by the same States General because their Highnesses do not assemble entirely* <note>original: "aling"</note> together. The Synod should have waited for that, if they wanted the name "National" to carry weight... 

What the Provincial States <note>The governing bodies of individual provinces</note> have done regarding the convocation of this National Synod, each will know best in his own province. Of Holland, we may say that such a convocation occurred without any legal permission from this Province. We, as a member of these same States, have not, until now, given our permission. If you say that we are to be blamed for this, then we might ask if we are the only ones who did not consent to the aforementioned Synod? Would you dare say yes to that? We can truthfully assure you that it is not so. We also do not see a single city that finds the contents of those Acts feasible...

The edict against heretical books, decided according to the form of a certain named Synod, has indeed been read out in many cities, but everyone, without exception, shows that they are of another opinion. . . Now turning to you, who come forward with *Synodal Acts*, we ask, by what power and authority do you wish to force these upon us? Does the power come from God, the authority from the Government? We cannot believe that God would have appointed you as Ministers to govern the Government. That the Government has authorized you as a Synod has not become apparent to us. It is presented as National. But many with us do not hold it as such. Should it be National, then it must be convened, determined, and approved by the head of the nation. The head of the nation, over which this Synod, as national, would extend, are the States General <term>the assembly of representatives from all the United Provinces</term>, by which legal assembly we do not believe it was convened. And it could not be convened by the same States General because their Highnesses do not come together completely <note>original: "aling"</note>. The Synod should have waited for that, if they wanted the name of "national" to gain force. . . What the *Provincial States* <term>the regional governing bodies of the Dutch provinces</term> have done regarding the calling of this national Synod, each will best know in his own. Of Holland we may say that such a calling happened without any legal permission of this Province. We, as a member of the same States, have not yet given our permission until now. Do you say that we are to be blamed for that? If we then asked you whether we are the only ones who did not consent to the aforementioned Synod? Would you dare to say yes to that? We can assure with truth that it is not so. We also do not see a single city that finds the content of it feasible. . . *We believe that you mean nothing but well, to bring the head together with the whole body into one coop <note>or "fold," implying a forced or confined unity</note>. Yet often some things have happened out of good intention which one cannot praise as good.* . . Just as we have also seen it to be true that the riches of the churches, which were born out of good intentions for Religion,

# HISTORY

<margin>1581 <note>original: "MDLXXXI"</note></margin>
...would finally have devoured the mother. <note>This metaphor suggests that the church, which was nurtured by the state, might eventually consume the state's authority.</note> If we have cast away the blunt rod, let us see to it that we do not bring a sharper one upon ourselves. Should new Synods be held every three years, the number of Synodal Decrees to which we would be bound would become so great that one could hardly find the beginning or end of this bond; and our children, as if they did not have enough to learn, would again have to deal with <term>Canon Law</term> <note>Latin: "Jus Canonicum"; the body of laws and regulations made by ecclesiastical authority (the Church)</note>. . .
<margin>p. B iii</margin>
By accepting the proceedings of the Synod, we would soon be held as nothing other than vassals of the Synod. . . Just as we wish to compel no one in what is theirs, so we also desire, in that which we must promote by virtue of our office—whether in spiritual or other matters—to be masters of our own conscience. . .
<margin>p. B iv.</margin>
We can agree to no <term>religious compulsion</term> <note>Dutch: "Religions-dwang"; the forcing of individuals to follow a specific set of religious beliefs or practices</note>, however small it may be. In this, we hope by God's grace to persevere until death. . . We can tolerate the learned writing and speaking against errors; but we declare that we have not the slightest thought of proceeding against anyone as a heretic based on church censure or the judgment of the learned. . . And it sounds very strange in our ears that one proceeds to the banning of books, and wishes to allow this only by grace and privilege (as the <term>Inquisitors</term> <note>Dutch: "Kettermeesters," literally "heresy-masters"; a reference to the Catholic officials who formerly suppressed banned literature</note> used to do). . . Freedom has always primarily consisted in the fact that one might express one's opinion freely. It was the sole mark of tyranny when one could not freely express one's thoughts. Reason, which opposes all tyranny, teaches us that truth, like light, can hardly be forced. Truth, placed like light in the darkness alongside lies, shines all the more clearly. The lie will always disappear of its own accord and will not be able to attach itself to the truth. Therefore, it is indeed tyrannical to ban good books, as did the apostate <term>Julian</term> <note>Referring to the Roman Emperor Julian (r. 361–363), who attempted to suppress Christian teachings and promote Neoplatonic Hellenism</note>, in order to stifle the truth. . . Finally, we only desire that the civil jurisdiction, as it is political, may also remain entirely and undividedly with the political Authority: and that we do not open any doors or gates for the churchmen to a new jurisdiction and mastery over the Authority, subjects, wife, and children. Declaring and testifying before God, and to you my Lords, that we never intend to consent to that, just as little as we would accept the old <term>Papacy</term> <note>Dutch: "Pausdom"; refers here to the Roman Catholic system of church hierarchy and authority</note> again. We humbly pray and brotherly exhort Your Honors and Excellency to join us in ensuring that we bear with the congregation in their particular opinions (so long as they do not conflict with civil peace) in love, attract them to us with love, keep them in love, and—as fathers with their children—may have the power, with a willing people, to resist the common enemy. He was, along with another accomplice, strangled and <term>quartered</term> <note>A brutal form of execution where the body was divided into four pieces</note>, and the pieces were hung upon the city gates: from where the Jesuits later removed them, publicly honoring them as holy relics, and finally burying them.

<header>HISTORY OF THE REFORMATION, BOOK XIII.</header>

<margin>
1582.
Request of the Roman Catholics of Brussels.
</margin>
The Roman Catholics of Brussels petitioned the new Duke <note>Francis, Duke of Anjou, who had been invited by the States-General to be the sovereign of the Netherlands in place of Philip II.</note> for the free exercise of their religion. The Duke wrote to the Amman <note>A high-ranking judicial official in Brussels.</note> and the Magistrate of Brussels, stating that he had three types of reasons for wishing to grant the petitioners' request.

<margin>
The Duke of Anjou’s instructions. Bor XVII, 27. Hooft XIX, 812, 813.
* Profession.
</margin>
First, for the sake of his own conscience, which obligated him to set an example in the profession * of the religion to which he himself adhered. Secondly, because of the treaty and agreement with the States-General, which was irrevocable and bound both him and them to the maintenance of the <term>Religious Peace</term> <note>The 'Religions-vrede' was a 1578 proposal by William of Orange to allow both Protestant and Catholic worship wherever 100 families requested it, aimed at maintaining national unity.</note>. Finally, to give satisfaction to the Roman Catholics; for it was not reasonable that they should be left in a worse state than the others. Otherwise, they would live like beasts, and consequently without the observation of duty, obedience, or respect—matters which (like all other things serving the strengthening of a Republic) arose from virtue and the fear of God. He also said he knew for certain that most of the cities still siding with the Spaniards would immediately throw themselves into his arms if they saw that liberty was given to the Catholics there. Therefore, he requested and commanded the Magistrates to first grant them the church of Coudenberg within the Court for the exercise of the Roman religion; since they, as well as the others, had taken the oath to him and had renounced the Spaniard. Furthermore, both parties were to live with one another in such good agreement in all other things that their wisdom might serve as a mirror for all his other subjects. Also, they should not tolerate anyone harassing the Catholics regarding their request made to him, or yet to be made, as he had been told they were being threatened. This would be unreasonable and something he would not endure. Despite this letter, signed on the eighth of June, nothing was achieved. It was not found advisable to grant the Duke's wish in this matter.

<margin>
Oath extorted from the Roman Catholics of Antwerp, which Parma treats with leniency. Hooft XIX, 813.
</margin>
In Antwerp, the fine of two hundred guilders mentioned previously still could not force the Roman Catholics to renounce the King and swear loyalty to Anjou. Consequently, on the thirteenth of July, all inhabitants were commanded, each under his Captain, to take the oath on pain of exile. Regarding this, the Prince of Parma <note>Alessandro Farnese, the Spanish governor and military commander.</note>, so that no despair of mercy from the King would cause them to harden their hearts, made it known by proclamation that he would never blame them for the forced oath, nor would he have a poorer opinion of their loyalty because of it.

New style in the calculation of time. Hooft XIX, 827. Bor XVII, 34.

<header>HISTORY</header>

<margin>1582.</margin>
...any lapse of time, or to correct the confusion regarding feast days, [it was ordered to] subtract ten days from this current year, commanding that after the fourth of <term>Wine-month</term> <note>original: "Wijnmaendt." This is the traditional Dutch name for October, referring to the grape harvest.</note>, the day of Saint Francis, the fifteenth should be counted instead of the fifth. Furthermore, to prevent the future shifting of the feasts, he decreed that after the year sixteen hundred, the first three upcoming centennial years should not be leap years, but the year two thousand should be a leap year, and so forth. Several high authorities, Kings, Princes, and States who did not recognize the Papal See, believing that the Pope undertook this work not solely moved by spiritual insights, but also out of ambition and political desire to raise himself, as the head of Christendom, above them and even above the Imperial Majesty, rejected his reformation and remained with the former system. But the Roman Catholic powers accepted the new one. Also, the Duke of Anjou commanded, with a decree of the tenth of <term>Winter-month</term> <note>original: "Wintermaendt." This is the traditional Dutch name for December.</note>, that ten days be removed from the year. Gelderland, Zutphen, Utrecht, Overijssel, Friesland, Groningen, and others, held to the <term>Old Style</term> <note>The Julian calendar, which was ten days behind the new Gregorian calendar at this time.</note>: but Brabant, Flanders, Artois, Hainaut, Holland, and Zeeland, conformed to the new style. At this time, a notable incident of wicked bitterness was seen in 's-Hertogenbosch, followed quite basely by the Magistrates. An eighty-year-old woman, Neesken de Greef, who had been a member of the Reformed congregation for eighteen years, now became deathly ill. Gisbertus Masius, the <term>Pleban</term> <note>A Pleban was a parish priest of a cathedral or major church, in this case, St. John's Cathedral.</note> of Saint John's Church, who went to her unsummoned, urged her to receive the wafer of the Sacrament according to the custom of the Roman Church, saying to her:

> *You must firmly believe that this is your Lord and God, with flesh and blood, just as he hung upon the cross.*

The woman turned him away with these words:

> *Depart from me. I have a living God in heaven, who shall save me.*

Thus she passed away. But then the Pleban complained about her to the authorities, stating she had died in the heretical faith without the Sacrament, and he brought about so much that the <term>High Bailiff</term> <note>The "Hooghschout" was the chief judicial and law enforcement officer of the city.</note> came to her house with his servants, had the threshold of the house dug up, the corpse snatched from the bed and dragged through that opening <note>This was a ritualistic punishment; the body was pulled *under* the threshold rather than through the door to symbolize its unworthiness of a Christian exit.</note>, thrown onto a hurdle, dragged to the market, and there put into a pit at the gallows.

<header>HISTORY</header>

<meta>catchword: v</meta>

<margin>* drafted</margin>
<margin>† to present.</margin>
In 1581 <note>original: "MDLXXXI"</note>, a Church Ordinance was drafted, in which the brethren <note>Members of the church leadership or synod.</note> understood certain articles to be included that the ministers and elders found themselves deeply aggrieved by. It seemed to them that these articles tended toward the disruption of the good ecclesiastical peace and order by which the Lord has wonderfully protected these lands. They decided, by common deliberation and unanimous advice, to remonstrate † to the brethren of the South Holland Synod via letters, so that this matter might be presented to His Excellency <note>William the Silent, Prince of Orange.</note> in the name of all the churches of Holland. This was done so that His Excellency might be pleased to remedy the situation with proper advice. For this purpose, Martinus Lydius, minister at Amsterdam, and Henricus Antonides, minister at Enkhuizen, were appointed to write to the brethren of South Holland.

<margin>‡ Hooft, Book XX, 872.</margin>
<margin>Proposal made regarding the thirteenth article of the Union of Utrecht, concerning the matter of religion.</margin>
<margin>Resolution taken by those of Holland thereupon.</margin>
<margin>See Grotius, *Apology* <note>original: "Verantw."</note> chapter 11, p. 19. Uitenbogaert, *History* <note>original: "Hist."</note> p. 937, 938.</margin>
Afterward, according to a certain point of description in the month of June <note>original: "Somermaendt"</note>, a proposal was made by some Deputies of the Provinces in a certain meeting of some of the United Provinces (where those of Gelderland, Utrecht, and Overijssel were not present ‡). This meeting was held this year in Middelburg. The proposal asked whether it would not be advisable to change the thirteenth article of the Union of Utrecht <note>The 1579 treaty that unified the northern provinces; Article 13 originally allowed each province to regulate its own religious affairs.</note> by common vote. The change would mandate that all Provinces remain with the Evangelical Reformed Religion and be allowed to make no changes therein, except by the unanimous decision of all allies. This was proposed with the understanding, however, that the regions, members, or cities of different persuasions who wished to join the alliance hereafter would be received without their freedom in matters of faith being curtailed. Regarding this proposal, only the representatives of Holland took a certain resolution, though it did not entail accepting the proposal exactly as it lay. Rather, they resolved that the Evangelical Reformed Religion should be maintained and protected without allowing the public teaching or exercise of any other religion in the currently united provinces, while still allowing others into the alliance according to the article. However, the other provinces postponed their resolution on this matter from time to time, so that no decision was made by the Generality <note>The States General, the federal government of the United Provinces.</note>. This later gave some cause to argue that this declaration by the States of Holland did not legally bind them, as no formal bond or treaty had been finalized upon it.

<margin>See the *Short and True Account of the South Holland Synod* p. 27 and the *Counter-report* of H. Herb. published p. 8, 9, 10.</margin>

Herman Herberts, a minister there who was suspected of impurity in doctrine <note>Herberts was a precursor to the Remonstrant movement, often clashing with strict Calvinist orthodoxy.</note>, was accused by his fellow brethren of having sought to [disrupt] the Wonderba... <note>The text cuts off mid-word, likely "Wonderbaerlijk" (wonderful/miraculous).</note>

<meta>The text continues from the previous page's discussion regarding Dirk Volckertszoon Coornhert's critique of the Reformed Church's growing authority. The catchword "d" from the previous page likely refers to "dulden" (tolerate) or "de" (the), fitting the sentence structure here.</meta>

<margin>1583.</margin> [to no longer] tolerate criticism, and made the critics suffer the sword, the noose, and the flames, until their bloody tyranny overcame the people's patience. Then the disturbed dregs <note>The "disturbed dregs" refers to the common people or the populist uprisings, such as the Iconoclastic Fury, which Coornhert views as a reaction to Catholic persecution.</note> threw the bottom of the barrel aside... Regarding such horrific offense and punishments against the rebuking of known errors, the inhabitants of this land had often and loudly complained, holding it to be intolerable tyranny and an intolerable <term>compulsion of conscience</term> <note>original: "Conscientiedwang"; the forced adherence to a specific set of religious beliefs, a central issue during the Dutch Revolt.</note>. This compulsion had been masterfully depicted by the Lord of Plessis <note>Philippe de Mornay (1549–1623), Seigneur du Plessis-Marly, a prominent French Huguenot writer and diplomat.</note> in his writing on the church, where he compared the critic of church failings to one who, seeing a secret fire rising in some city or the enemy climbing the wall, shouts "Fire!" or "To arms!"... He, Koornhert, had waited in silence and observation since the year seventy-nine to see where the actions of the <term>Ministers</term> <note>original: "Predikanten"; the Reformed clergy.</note> would lead, and he saw that they now aimed to command everyone else in matters of faith alone, and to make themselves masters over every man’s belief. For they, by making their views known in public print, 
<margin>See Koornhert’s Works, Vol. III, p. 460</margin> showed how much they disliked that freedom where each might believe what he pleased. To this end, they also pushed for the introduction of their <term>Catechism</term> <note>Specifically the Heidelberg Catechism, which the Reformed Church sought to make the official standard of faith.</note> alone, while forbidding all others. He considered their intention—both in the compulsion of faith and in the poisoning of the minds of the youth—to be more harmful than an enemy invasion or a destructive fire in a good city. He believed it was now time, or else never, to cry "fire" and "to arms" against it, as a warning to the authorities and the subjects. This action of his, intended for the common good, he could not believe would be taken poorly; for in this, he used that freedom in matters of faith which is one of the most desirable fruits we acquired through the harmful and bloody war in the Netherlands <note>The Eighty Years' War against Spain, which was fought in part for religious freedom.</note>. Which freedom, among other things, consisted of the right to speak the truth in matters of faith, modestly and boldly, without fear of punishment, for the benefit of one’s neighbors. This he did with faithful earnestness, not only to all common citizens of the land, but even to his Noble, Powerful, and Provident Lords, the <term>States</term> <note>The States of Holland, the provincial governing body.</note>. He hoped that their godly wisdom might find it advisable not to proceed with judgment in these most weighty matters (much less with the execution of punishment before judgment) before a full hearing of the other party—whom he admitted to be himself—against the aforementioned Catechism and against all those who wished to defend it as upright. He was prepared, if his short writing [*The Proof*] <note>Coornhert's book, *Proeve van de Nederlandse Catechismus* (Proof of the Dutch Catechism).</note> did not suffice, to have the 
<margin>* Report, bringing forward.</margin> judgment postponed; and if they would grant him a hearing (not before some biased Commissioners, whose report <note>original: "rapport"</note> was little to be trusted, but before the ears of the States themselves, whom it all concerned), he would there...

<summary>Dirk Volckertszoon Coornhert argues against the "compulsion of conscience" imposed by the Reformed clergy, comparing their religious intolerance to the tyranny of the Spanish Inquisition. He petitions the States of Holland for a fair, public hearing of his critiques of the Heidelberg Catechism, citing religious freedom as a primary goal of the ongoing Dutch Revolt.</summary>

# BOOK XIII OF THE REFORMATION.

[...to] declare themselves against the supporters of this <term>Catechism</term> <note>Referring to the Heidelberg Catechism, the standard of doctrine for the Dutch Reformed Church.</note>. This was done so that in such 1583. a highly significant matter, a judgment would not be passed without hearing the opposing party and gaining true knowledge of the facts. Also, if the <term>Ministers</term> <note>original: "Kerkendienaeren"; literally "servants of the church," referring to the Reformed clergy.</note> could not cleanse their Catechism of many ugly stains and foul impurities, they—who could not even prove their calling was lawful—should no longer be believed to the point of suppressing all other religions. Instead, they should tolerate others alongside themselves until the Lord Himself provides a solution, with the certain rooting out of the <term>weeds</term> by His angels; so that men, attempting this prematurely, would not sin by rooting out the good wheat <note>A reference to the Parable of the Tares (Matthew 13:24-30), often used in the 16th century to argue for religious toleration.</note>. For it was not long ago that the unwise zeal of the authorities thought they were doing God a service by killing Christ's disciples. He wished that God would protect the <term>States</term> <note>The "States" refers to the States of Holland, the governing provincial assembly.</note> from such a path. After some deliberation, the States placed Koornhert’s booklet into the hands of a Professor of Theology at Leiden, to review it along with a Minister, and to gather from it everything that contradicted the Catechism, condensing it into brief propositions, so that these

<margin>Koornhert III, f. 432.</margin>
might be handed to Koornhert. This was to see whether he would defend them with the Holy Scriptures or, if they were not phrased according to his meaning, that he might correct them for the same purpose; so that the dispute might be tested against the true <term>touchstone</term> <note>A metaphor for the Bible as the ultimate standard of truth.</note>. He, on the other hand, understood that there was no need to look for any propositions from his side. For the Catechism itself set forth two propositions that

<margin>Koornhert III, f. 433.</margin>

# HISTORY

<margin>1583.</margin>[...propositions, so that it might be shown that the] accuser’s ugly stains and impurities were his own: that it was not the <term>Reformed Church</term>, but that attacker of the Apostolic doctrine who had strayed, or rather had never stood rightly within it, and that he was bringing back to light the old heresies of <term>Pelagius</term> and <term>Celestius</term> <note>Pelagius and Celestius were 5th-century theologians whose views on human free will and original sin were condemned as heretical by the early Church; the Reformed ministers used these names to label Coornhert a heretic.</note>, which had been condemned by the Church based on God’s word: that not their calling, but his rebuke was unlawful, improper, and ungodly. In short, that no more credit should be given to him than to them, lest it lead to the disturbance of the Church and the darkening of the truth. The <term>States</term> <note>The States of Holland, the governing body of the province.</note>, after various deliberations and reflections, resolved with the approval of the <term>Prince of Orange</term> <note>William the Silent.</note> to hear the Ministers and Koornhert against one another in The Hague, in the presence of fifteen authorized gentlemen: six from the High Council, one from the Court, and eight from the assembly of the States. Before these delegates, <term>Adrianus Saravia</term> <note>A prominent Flemish-born theologian and professor at Leiden University.</note>, Professor of Theology, would contest the dispute on one side, and Koornhert on the other. But everything was to be recorded by the pens of two Notaries, one for each party. This <term>Dispute</term> was

<margin>Dispute between A. Saravia and Dirk V. Koornhert commenced in The Hague. See D. V. Koornhert’s Works, Vol III, f. 436...</margin>commenced on the twenty-seventh of <term>October</term> <note>original: "Wijnmaendt"; literally 'Wine-month'.</note> and continued until the third of <term>November</term> <note>original: "Slachtmaendt"; literally 'Slaughter-month'.</note>, on which day Koornhert, with the permission of the delegates, traveled by post to Haarlem to see and comfort his wife, who had become deathly ill, at her request. Thereafter, the dispute was resumed on the twenty-eighth of November: but Saravia spoke for nearly four days, filling about twenty sheets of writing for the pen: so that the delegates saw fit for Koornhert to travel home and write his counter-reply there. This became even larger, and that of the Ministers, following upon it, was incomparably larger still. The States, understanding from their delegates that so much time had been spent on the first point out of more than fifty, judged the work to be endless and ordered it—to avoid

<margin>It is broken off. Koornhert’s Works, Part III, f. 429, 468, 469.</margin>falling into greater discord—to be laid to rest. Thus <term>Bor</term> <note>Pieter Christiaenszoon Bor (1559–1635), a Dutch historian famous for his multi-volume history of the Dutch wars.</note> tells it. But Koornhert relates that the Ministers on their side remained in default, left his last writing unanswered, and broke off the dispute; although he came to live in The Hague in <term>May</term> <note>original: "Bloeimaendt"; literally 'Bloom-month'.</note> of the following year, solely to promote the matter with greater zeal. Nevertheless, the parties did not cease from attacking one another with printed writings thereafter. Some sought to extend the <term>edict</term> <note>original: "plakkaet"; a formal decree or law.</note> of the year eighty-one <note>1581.</note> against scandalous, offensive, and seditious booklets to the booklet that Koornhert had written against the Catechism.

...nothing was left to them but to endure and pray. It was also much better for godliness itself to gain strength through frequent oppression than to grow slack through too much freedom. Under Emperor Charles <note>Charles V</note> and King Philip <note>Philip II of Spain</note>, many had indeed been killed by the hands of executioners, but how many more were now killed by the weapons of war? In Holland, matters were now settled and prepared, after various deliberations and negotiations with the Prince of Orange, to accept and honor him as the Count of Holland. This was to be done, among other conditions, upon the requirement that he maintain the true Reformed Christian Religion and ensure that a general church ordinance regarding its practice, and all that pertains to it, be established and observed shortly, by the discretion of the Councils and permission of the States. This ordinance could not be changed except with the consent of the States assembled for that purpose. Furthermore, he was to ensure that he would not burden or persecute anyone individually regarding matters of faith or conscience, nor compel anyone toward any specific denomination, nor allow anyone else to be so compelled.

<margin>
See Bor XIX. 34.
</margin>
But before this plan—which had been blocked for some time by the cities of Amsterdam and Gouda—could be put into action despite those cities, the Prince passed away. On the tenth of July <note>Dutch: *Hooimaendt*, the "hay month"</note>, in Delft, he was shot through by a dishonorable and godless murderer, the Burgundian Balthasar Geraerds, who had been bribed by the enemies of the land. As he fell, he said: *My God, have pity on me and on the poor people* † <note>original: "Mon Dieu ayez pitié de moy & du pauvre peuple"</note> that is, My God, be merciful to me and the poor people.

The murderer

<margin>
The murderer was strengthened in his purpose by a Jesuit and a Friar Minor.

Balthasar Geeraerds <note>Balthasar Gérard, the assassin of William the Silent</note> suffered his deserved punishment with unbelievable callousness, and let his right hand be burned off with glowing irons, his thickest flesh burned out and pinched off, without making any sound of pain. Indeed, he still shook the stump of his hand as if to make a sign of the cross and bless the people. He had previously revealed the intention of the murder to a certain Jesuit in Trier, who had made it known to three others of his order; and had promised him that, if he were to die in the act, he would be placed in the number of the Martyrs. He had also spoken of his plan in Tournai <note>original: "Doornik"</note> with one Gery, a Friar Minor <term>Friar Minor: A member of the Franciscan Order</term>, Doctor of Divinity, who strengthened him in his purpose and gave his blessing upon it. To gain access to the Prince, he called himself the son of a father who had formerly been killed for the Reformed Religion, and feigning a burning zeal for that same Religion, he allowed himself to be found diligently attending the preaching in Delft for a time, and always carried the Psalms, the Bible, or some other book in his hand. Not a month after the murder of the Prince of Orange, Lord Jan van Imbyze <note>Jan van Hembyze, a once-powerful radical leader in Ghent</note> was sentenced to death for various crimes and his secret understanding with the Spaniards to deliver Dendermonde and Ghent to them. He prayed to the Ministers and other Reformed members for favor and intercession, in view of what he had formerly done for them. But it was understood that he, and his punishment, must be set as a public mirror <note>an example to others</note>. Thus he was publicly beheaded in Ghent with a showing of repentance, in the seventieth year of his age. This was the end of Imbyze, that fierce opponent of all moderation and accommodation, who had introduced the Reformed Religion in Ghent by inciting the common people, and through whom—by the rejection of the Religious Peace and the embittering of the Walloons—the uprooting of that same Religion was caused, not only in that city, but also ultimately in all of Flanders and Brabant. Shortly thereafter, Dendermonde went by siege to Parma... <note>Alexander Farnese, Duke of Parma, the Spanish commander</note>

Yet others understand that by the killing of those people, even if they were excluded from the treaty, he held his honor in little regard.

<margin>
Ghent is surrendered.
Bor XIX 33, and XXIV. 73.
Hooft XXI. 83.
</margin>

Ghent was surrendered to the Spaniard by agreement on the seventeenth of September <note>original: "Herffstmaendt"</note>. In the negotiations that took place there, Richardot, Parma’s deputy, played a clever trick on the people of Ghent, giving some blow to their hope of freely maintaining the practice of the Reformed Religion, simply saying that it would be best to postpone this matter, as the weightiest, until the end. This being agreed to, they were met so far in the other points that, enticed by temporal advantage, they let religion slip, when he, upon their inquiry about it, flatly said that all the previous work would fall away if they stood firm on the point of Religion.

The Reformed were then only permitted *to remain living there for a period of two years, without being investigated; provided they avoided all disorder, offense, or scandal; to, meanwhile, consider and decide whether they wished to live in the practice of the Romish Religion; and, if not, to depart from the country unhindered.* In the Law <note>the city magistracy or governing body</note> Parma appointed only those of the Romish persuasion and exiles: who (after the manner of outcasts returning to power) raged bitterly against the Reformed and other non-Romish denominations. This moved some to take their refuge with the Governor <note>the Duke of Parma</note>, with whom they found more modesty and reasonableness than with their fellow citizens.

### THE HISTORY OF THE REFORMATION BOOK XIII.

<margin>1584</margin>
...twenty-eight. This served to prove, as much from the writings of the Apostle Paul as from the course of the early churches, <margin>P. C. iij.</margin> That the first five hundred years had also not been free from Antichristian <note>The term "Antichristian" here refers to perceived corruptions or departures from the purity of the early Gospel, which many reformers believed began shortly after the Apostles.</note> delusions, and therefore also had to be counted toward the kingdom of the Antichrist. From which he then further concluded, *That so long as one did not completely bypass and set aside the entire period of fifteen hundred years passed since the time of the Apostles, one would have no right and lasting Reformation, and that to obtain this it was necessary to align oneself entirely with the true Apostolic churches, both in doctrine and governance. That in doing so, those new words and manners of speaking, composed by the <term>Church Fathers</term> <note>The "Church Fathers" (Oudtvaders) are the influential Christian theologians and writers of the first few centuries after Christ.</note> and introduced into the churches, would be better forgotten, and more pleasure taken in the simplicity left to us by Christ and the Apostles to express Divine matters.* He also says: <margin>P. B. iij.</margin> *That no one from his pointing out the delusion of the Church Fathers should conclude as if he wanted all the Church Fathers with their books to be damned or rejected: for one had to confess, reading the writings of Cyprian, Augustine, and some others, that without illumination of the Holy Spirit, they would not have had the power to write so heartily of the Christian Religion. Wherefore they must also be held as pious, upright Christians, who sought and found God from the heart.* And in another place, <margin>P. D. ij.</margin> *That one would not do wrongly when one examined their writings with discretion and understanding, and noted the good that was in them, yet taking care that one did not rely on their authority, nor chose the bad for the good. That one should bind neither oneself, nor others, much less Christ’s congregation, to any writings or words of the <term>Councils</term> <note>Formal gatherings of church leaders to decide on matters of doctrine and practice.</note> and Fathers, as if everyone must speak and believe exactly so, and as if they were heretics who did not want to speak with the Church Fathers, but preferred to remain with the words and manners of speaking used by the Prophets, by Christ, and the Apostles. What can we,* he asks, *demand more of anyone, and if we demand more, by whose command do we do it? Therefore let everyone use their Christian freedom in this and not hinder others in their freedom.* Lastly, he concludes with these words: *Therefore if it is the case that someone must necessarily use new and strange words to explain his opinion and faith in God, such that the words of the Prophets and Apostles are not enough for him, it is certain and sure that not only are the words new, but also his doctrine and faith: otherwise it would be impossible that good and suitable words of the Holy Scripture should be lacking to him.* This writing was not...

<summary>This page records a radical Reformist argument that true religious reform requires discarding 1,500 years of church tradition and "strange" theological terminology in favor of the pure language of the Apostles. While acknowledging the personal piety of Church Fathers like Augustine, the author argues they should not hold authority over the individual's conscience or the literal words of Scripture.</summary>

### HISTORY

<margin>
1584.
Bor, Book 19, p. 49.
</margin>
...was not well received, but interpreted as if the writer intended thereby to call everything into question, to gather a following, and to throw the church in this country into turmoil. At once, it was decided to search for the booklet and its author. Yet, such orders were given, and such discretion used, that they sought him from city to city, always at the place where they knew he had stayed the night. This was done so that he was quietly prompted to flee and leave the country.

<margin>
1585.
The death of the Minister Johannes Florianus.
Hist. of the Mart. p. 762.
Hist. of the Mart. p. 500.
</margin>
The Spaniards dealt differently with *Johannes Florianus*, Minister of the Reformed in Brussels, who, after the surrender of that city in the Month of Lent <note>March</note> of the year fifteen hundred and eighty-five, fell into their hands near Lier and was taken to the Spanish camp at Beveren, near Antwerp. His release was requested through several trumpeters <note>Trumpeters often served as diplomatic messengers between opposing armies.</note>. The others sought to force him to renounce his faith by worsening his imprisonment and using threats. But he remained steadfast. Finally, they did away with him; they tied him in a sack and threw it into a foul pit where there was barely enough water to cover him. Here he struggled for a long time, until they pierced him through with a spear. Thus he lost his life in the sixty-third year of his age. His widow, who was left with eight children, was told by a drummer that he had died of the plague. However, she later learned the truth of the account from credible witnesses, as well as the bitterness of the Margrave of Rijsburg, who addressed the Teacher <note>Original: *Leeraer*; a common term for a minister or preacher.</note> with these words shortly before his death:
> *I rejoice to have lived so long that I may help condemn you, such a desperate heretic.*

<margin>
Hooft, Book 22, p. 93.
Hist. of the Anabaptist Martyrs, p. 809.
Jan de Greve and his wife banished.
Bor, Book 20, p. 57.
</margin>
But that false joy was short-lived and followed by true disaster: for on the same day that Florianus died in the water, the fourth of the Grass-month <note>April</note>, Rijsburg perished in the fire of Gianibelli's fire-ship <note>Federigo Gianibelli was an Italian engineer who designed "hellburners"—ships packed with explosives—which were used to destroy the bridge the Duke of Parma had built across the Scheldt during the Siege of Antwerp.</note>, which blew apart Parma's bridge over the Scheldt, killing more than five hundred soldiers. At this time, three Anabaptist <note>Original: *Doopsgefinde*, literally 'baptism-minded'.</note> women were burned at St. Vith, in the land of Luxembourg. Jan de Greve and his wife *Janne*, daughter of Hendrik de Droge, were banished by the Burgomasters and Magistrates of the city of Veurne, in Flanders, on the first day of the Summer-month <note>June</note>, for matters of Religion, for a term of ten years; they were to vacate the city by sunset and the county of Flanders within eight days, on pain of being scourged with a sharp rod until their blood flowed.

In Nijmegen <note>The source spells this "Nieuwegen," a common older variation for the city of Nijmegen in Gelderland.</note> in Gelderland, the Papists, noticing the success of the Spanish arms, had for some time boldly requested a church, according to the order of the <term>Peace of Religions</term> <note>A treaty from 1578 that attempted to allow both Catholic and Protestant worship in the same city, provided there was enough demand.</note>. Doesburg followed the same path.

<margin>Several Catholic citizens removed from the cities. Hooft, Book XXII, 82, 83.</margin>
In other cities of Gelderland and Overijssel, where people wished to take that same path, more soldiers were brought in, and security was ensured by the expulsion of the Papists who were most under suspicion. This took place in Kampen, Arnhem, and Deventer. In Amersfoort, twenty-six Roman Catholic citizens, who were mistrusted, were escorted out of the city. In the Hay-month <note>July</note> following this, Mechelen surrendered, and in the Harvest-month <note>August</note>, Antwerp surrendered to Parma by treaty.

<margin>Testimony given to the Lutherans by the Magistrates of Antwerp.</margin>
Three days after the conclusion of the agreement between the city and Parma, the Magistrates gave to the Ministers and other servants of the church of the <term>Augsburg Confession</term> <note>This refers to the Lutheran Church, which follows the confession of faith presented at the Diet of Augsburg in 1530.</note>, at their request, a very honorable testimony confirmed with the city’s seal in green wax. Finally, they requested that all to whom these letters of testimony might be shown would be pleased to treat the bearers and their households with all favor and assistance.* This testimony, of which I have seen a legal copy, was written in Latin and signed by Joachim Gillis <note>The city secretary of Antwerp.</note>.

Brabanters and Flemings <note>Refugees from the southern Netherlands fleeing Spanish Catholic rule.</note>, who left their fatherland for the sake of Religion, brought the splendor and costliness of clothing into the cities that sheltered them; enticing the native inhabitants to the same misuse of vanity: also to the excess of banquets and delicacies, previously unusual and unesteemed in this country. These people, generally regarded as restless, difficult, and ambitious by nature—also more hot-headed than the Hollanders, and allowing themselves to be driven by a religious zeal that made them distinguish little in the ways they advanced it—were shortly the most forward in setting themselves against the current government of the States during the ensuing Leicester troubles <note>The political turmoil surrounding Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester, who was sent by Queen Elizabeth I to lead the Dutch forces.</note>. The United Netherlands had now, through blow upon blow of manifold disaster and loss, become so despondent that they almost offered themselves for nothing to the crowned heads of their neighbors, as if powerless to stand on their own feet.

<margin>

First to the King of France, Henry III, among other conditions (to keep the matter of religion as much as possible for themselves), on the stipulation *that neither he nor his servants should be allowed to change anything in Religion, or to investigate anyone in their conscience.* But the King of France rejected the offered sovereignty; for Spanish schemes, through the Guisards <note>The Catholic League led by the House of Guise, which opposed the French King and was supported by Spain.</note>, created so much internal turmoil and rebellion that he found it entirely unadvisable to attach the Netherlands to his crown and enter into war with Spain. This, viewed then as a disaster and a sign of divine wrath against the Netherlands, is found at this time (so dim-sighted is human understanding, and so do its wishes wander) to have served most of all for their benefit: because they, who otherwise faced an eternal servitude of body and soul, happened to wrestle themselves free from slavery and finally fight their way to a secured freedom; so that they must confess that God, out of singular grace, left their prayer at that moment unanswered; or answered it by withholding their desire.

Here, until now, the church of St. James and the Reformation, introduced there at times by Master Hubrecht Duifhuis <note>Hubrecht Duifhuis was a moderate reformer in Utrecht who resisted the strict discipline of the Calvinist Consistory, favoring a more inclusive and state-supervised church.</note>, had flourished; so much so that of the seven Preachers who then served at Utrecht, three were of the church and persuasion of St. James. To halt this progress and suppress that manner of Reformation, the other Preachers brought it about through Leicester that two of the three aforementioned ministers—namely, Hermannus Elkonius and Cornelis Martenszoon Roijenburgh—allowed themselves to be persuaded (despite the opposition of their entire congregation and, it is said, against solemn promises they had made to the contrary) out of fear of being dismissed, to unite with those of the Consistory <term>Consistory: the governing body of the Reformed church, composed of ministers and elders, typically representing the stricter Calvinist orthodoxy.</term>. By this means, the discord was more concealed than extinguished, and the church of St. James was brought under the authority of the Consistory.

On the twenty-eighth of April <note>Dutch: Grasmaendt, literally "Grass-month"</note> he delivered his last sermon in the church of St. Mary on these words: *I will strike the shepherd and the sheep of the flock shall be scattered:* <note>Matthew 26:31</note> using in the explanation more than usual zeal, exhorting his listeners to steadfastness and to put into practice what they had heard and learned for many years; giving them clearly enough to understand that their public church gatherings would last no longer. He was later accused of holding a large gathering at his house, but upon arriving there, they found the man lying sick in bed from heartache <note>Dutch: "hartseer," a 17th-century term for physical illness brought on by extreme emotional distress or grief</note>, due to the many difficulties he had encountered, with his wife and children all weeping around him, along with one or two friends who had come to comfort him. Upon his departure, the Magistrate gave him a very honorable testimonial, for he was very godly and virtuous in life and conduct, and everyone felt compassion for him on account of his burdened household. That agreement, to which Tako could not submit, was also very much against the grain for the States and Magistrates of Utrecht,

Thus, it seemed they intended to force these ecclesiastical laws upon the land through the authority of the Commander-in-Chief: whose personal preference, however, made little progress in this matter;

Foreigners, who had so long enjoyed shelter and hospitality within Utrecht, now drove out the most distinguished inhabitants without a hearing, without form of law, and without stating any cause, and distributed their offices among themselves; especially on the day of election, the first of October <note>original: "Wijnmaendt"; literally 'wine month'</note>.
