<margin>1587.</margin>
In the year fifteen hundred eighty-seven, at the end of <term>January|Loumaendt; an archaic Dutch name for the month of January, literally "tanning month"</term>, the consequences of Leicester’s government began to be felt. William Stanley and Roland York, both <term>Papists|A contemporary term for Roman Catholics</term>, and the latter a double traitor, delivered the city of Deventer and the fort across from Zutphen—entrusted to them against the will of the States—to the Spaniards. The Council of State, to whom he had entrusted the high management of affairs during his absence with a public document, sought to prevent this evil, but found their hands tied by another document that revoked the power previously granted. This second document, initially kept secret, was shown to them when they sought to oppose the intentions of the traitors. This duplicity from him <note>Referring to the Earl of Leicester.</note> who always had religion on his lips, and the resulting treason, caused great suspicion among the States.

Those of Holland, to secure the State, resolved that Prince Maurice, as <term>Stadtholder|The chief executive and military commander of a province</term> and Commander-in-Chief of Holland, West-Friesland, and Zeeland, should use his authority according to his commission and instructions, and have command over all military leaders stationed in these provinces, at the discretion of the States.
<margin>Hooft XXV, 231.</margin>
For this reason, they were to receive their commissions from him and take a new oath to him and the States, or be dismissed upon refusal.

Thus, there was insurrection within the land. *Regarding what had been done for the liberation of Holland, and the consequences in the other Netherlands, a part of which had fallen back into the enemy's hands <note>The "enemy" refers to the Spanish Crown</note>, accompanied by the disruption of the churches there, caused by a lack of unity between the authorities and certain ministers. For that reason, there was a fear of similar effects and division here. Therefore, it was necessary to strive for unity and to show respect to the authorities. To the contrary, the States of the land were now held in little regard here and there, and their actions were being made suspect. For many were spreading rumors that the States did not uphold the Treaty with England and Leicester <note>Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester, who had been sent by Queen Elizabeth I to assist the Dutch</note>; that they sought to suppress the Religion, or at least to maintain it poorly; that they wished to enter into peace negotiations with the enemy. Others, conversely, accused them of refusing to agree to any peace. Furthermore, it was alleged that among the States and Magistrates there were some who made no profession of the Reformed Religion, nor attended the Lord’s Supper; also, that zeal for the Religion and the defense of the land was flagging, and finally, that too little was being allocated to the ministers for their maintenance. On all these points, the States sought to inform the ministers so that they might exhort the people to their duty. It was pointed out to them how much the States valued the Queen of England and Leicester. Instead of uprooting the Religion, they allowed no other to be practiced publicly except the Reformed; even though not one-tenth of the country's inhabitants belonged to that Religion. This was then to be considered a great blessing from God: that those who were fewest in number might hear God's word openly and without anxiety, and practice their Religion, while the vast majority had no public exercise of theirs. The States did not wish to enter into any peace negotiations, knowing that the enemy would never permit the Religion.*

One could not introduce a change in Religion there, which would also not sound well in *Germany*, where the Reformed would be treated in the same manner <note>The Dutch authorities feared that if they were too harsh on dissenters at home, Lutheran princes in Germany would retaliate against Reformed minorities there</note>. The States would buy up and destroy the booklet written against the *Catechism*. That some of the States members did not even attend the sermons must be tolerated, and one should be satisfied that they helped maintain the practice of the Religion. The words spoken by some individuals within the States should not be blamed on the entire assembly, just as the States did not blame the clergy in general for what was said or done by a few. It was also asked whether it was necessary, to remove all confusion and disorder, to establish rules for the large gatherings of young people which began with a prayer and ended with a thanksgiving, and in which some passage of the Holy Scripture was explained in the form of a sermon. Regarding this question, it was decided that such and similar gatherings should by no means be permitted where they had not been introduced; and where they were in use, the Church Council should seek to discourage them through appropriate means. Nonetheless, those slanderers had found such favor with Leicester that, upon the submission of a petition by certain Ministers—mostly foreigners and poorly informed of the current state of the country—he had permitted the calling of a General Synod. Indeed, the nation seemed destined for ruin due to a lack of unity between Regents of high and low status, and between the provinces; because of this, the alliance made with England also stood on the verge of collapsing. Since it was permitted—indeed, granted—to every pious inhabitant and good Christian, and much more so to the Ministers of the Divine Word <note>The Dutch Reformed clergy</note>, whom God had graced to be His messengers and governors in His house, to promote before the Authorities that which served the country's preservation, they prayed that the States, now assembled to deliberate on the response and satisfaction to be given to His Excellency *Leicester*, would look upon nothing else than God's honor and the preservation of the country and the churches. They certainly trusted that the Lords took this to heart; but since occasionally such means were undertaken for the common good that did not truly serve it, or because sometimes some private interest hindered the eye of sound judgment, they prayed to Almighty God to grant the States the grace that, stripped of such obstacles, they might hasten to a good resolution to prevent further evil, and to avoid further alienating Her Majesty <note>Queen Elizabeth I of England</note> and His Excellency. </margin>

...[Ministers of the] Divine Word <note>The Dutch Reformed clergy</note>, whose treachery and hypocrisy were all too evident, had remained with the enemy, forsaking the true Christian Religion; nevertheless, it was highly to be feared that many others, not so openly discovered in such dealings, had spread themselves like sparks of that fire of discord through Holland, Zeeland, and other united provinces. And, intruding into both ecclesiastical and secular government under that same cloak of religion, they would gladly bring these lands into the same state as their own Fatherland <note>This refers to the southern provinces like Flanders and Brabant, which had recently fallen back into Spanish hands due to internal divisions.</note> had been brought by them. 

But because they saw the States of Holland, Zeeland, and Friesland, along with the Lords of the House of Nassau and their adherents, standing in their way, they attempted by every means to make those of the aforementioned House, the Nobles, and the Magistrates of the cities of the said lands, as well as other persons of well-proven loyalty, appear black, hateful, and suspicious to the common people and the whole world. They sought to ruin the welfare and resources of the lands by advocating for strange and unusual ways of governing, and by sowing and nurturing misunderstandings and dissensions. To this end, the States understood that there was running, racing, writing, and sending, night and day; and that many simple people were shamefully misled, who (if they did not turn back from that path in time) would complain too late, when the situation could no longer be salvaged. 

Indeed, the examples of the other provinces and cities were still so fresh and evident that it was most astonishing that many people, and particularly some Ministers of the Divine Word, did not use them as a better mirror <note>A "mirror" in this historical context is a cautionary example or moral lesson from the past.</note>. The States firmly trusted that Her Majesty of England <note>Queen Elizabeth I</note> would not allow the laudable agreement made between her and the united Netherlands to come to nothing, nor separate herself from these lands because the States desired to maintain and defend that for which they had entered the war—the cause for which so many thousands of people had perished, so many lands and cities had been devastated and ruined, and for the preservation of which Her Majesty’s help had been requested and promised. 

And it was also, they said, greatly to be feared that those who spoke most highly of His Excellency’s <note>The Earl of Leicester, the English governor-general whose authority the States were now challenging.</note> authority sought to carry out a plan such as was seen accomplished in Flanders—creating a hatred for the Lord Prince of Orange <note>William the Silent, who had been assassinated three years earlier in 1584.</note>, of most praised memory, and for the States of Holland. Or, at the very least, they sought to advance their own authority, purse, and profit, and wished to have done through their own hands and at their own pleasure, through disorder, that which [ought to be done] with good mutual understanding by the General and provincial States, by the Governors of the Provinces, Commanders, and others...

Finally, they desired, and as a matter of duty enjoined upon the aforementioned and all other **Ministers of the Holy Word**, that they should direct all their actions toward harmony, edification, and the building up of the Christian church; they should take warning from the downfall of the churches in Flanders <note>A reference to the southern provinces where internal religious and political division had recently allowed the Spanish to reclaim territory</note>, and avoid the course that had been taken there; furthermore, they should pray to the Lord God for all high and low Authorities, that they might not be led into a similar course; but in good unity, each might carry out their assigned duty for the advancement of the welfare of the lands. <margin>Bor XXIII, 57. d; Hooft XXVII, 321.</margin> This decision, signed on the sixteenth of **October** <note>original: "Wijnmaendt", the traditional Dutch 'wine month'</note>, was published in print by the States, and sent to the Magistrates of all the cities of Holland and West-Friesland, with orders to summon the Ministers before them, hand it to them, and command them to exhort the congregation to silence and harmony, to concern themselves with teaching and preaching, and to leave the government to the States and Magistrates. However, this announcement caused bad blood among the clergy, who felt they had framed their **Remonstrance** <note>original: "Vertoog", a formal petition or statement of grievances</note> quite respectfully and that they were being treated too harshly.

<margin>Bor XXIII, 63; Hooft XXVII, 332; Reyd p. 190.</margin> At the same time, **Provink** <note>Gerard Prouninck, also known as Deventer, a staunch supporter of the Earl of Leicester</note> sought to incite the citizens of Dordrecht to riot in service of Leicester, drawing up a certain petition for them to sign and present to the English Lord. In this document, besides much slander against the States, they offered to assist His Highness Leicester with their lives and property <note>original: "goedt en bloedt", literally 'goods and blood'</note>, and to work with all their power to ensure his authority over the lands was upheld.

This writing was shown by a man from Brabant, in the presence of a painter, to the **Minister Korput** <note>Abraham van de Corput, a Reformed minister in Dordrecht</note>, who advised against presenting it to Leicester, at least for the time being. It later came into the hands of the Magistrates of Dordrecht, who—although a large part of them were favorable to the English—made it known at the meeting of the States in Haarlem.

Yet in no city of Holland did the Leicester faction sow more seeds of mutiny among the common people than in **Leiden**; for here were several thousand Brabantians and Flemings who, having fled for their religion, convinced themselves that the States, and particularly the Lords of Leiden, sought to diminish Leicester’s authority in order to remain masters of the game, and to keep even the church under the lash <note>Under strict civil control</note>, leading to the corruption of religion. Also, the **Consistory** <note>The governing body of the local Reformed church</note> was more restricted here than elsewhere. For this reason, a dislike was taken toward his...

<margin>1587. Plan to seize Leiden. See *Bor* XXIII, 64. b. *Reid* p. 209. Cosmo imprisoned. ² *Bor* XXIII, 48. b. ³ *Reid* p. 209.</margin>
It was then planned how they would seize the city using the soldiers of De Maulde, and also those of Heraugiere, who were to come from Delft for that purpose, with the help of the complicit inhabitants. They also intended to take into custody several of the Magistrates <term>Magistrates; the 'Wethouders' or city officials responsible for local government</term> and others who stood in their way. <margin>*Reid* p. 209. Meeting of the English-leaning faction at the house of Meetkerke. Planning of the plot.</margin>
The Earl commanded them to proceed and showed his dissatisfaction that they had wasted several days out of fear. On the ninth, a Friday, a meeting was held again at the house of Adolf van Meetkerke, and it was decided to put the plan into action on the eleventh, a Sunday. De Maulde would ask the Magistrates for permission the evening before to depart the city with his banner, according to the open letters <note>official public commissions or orders</note> sent to him by Leicester. On Sunday morning at six o'clock, he would march with his soldiers along the Broad Street <note>original: "breede straet", a major thoroughfare in Leiden</note> to the front of the town hall. There, fifty or sixty armed citizens would stop him, declaring that it was for the maintenance of Religion and the service of His Excellency Leicester. After seizing the town hall, they would immediately announce a document from the platform <term>platform; the 'puye', a raised stone stage in front of the town hall used for making official proclamations to the public</term> and elsewhere, with this content:

<margin>See the defense of *F. Volmaer* p. A. 3. *Bor* XXIII, 68. c. d. Also the Admonition and Warning published by the Magistrate of Leiden. *Bor* XXIII, 71. d.</margin>
> Notice is given to everyone that the good citizens have taken up arms in the service of the Queen of England, for the maintenance of the true Christian Religion, and to restore the Earl of Leicester as Governor-General of these United Netherlands to the authority granted to him by my Lords the States General upon his first arrival in these lands. Therefore, everyone is commanded to remain quiet and to do no harm or damage to anyone in life or property, upon penalty of death.

<margin>See the Admonition and Warning of the Magistrate in *Bor* XXIII, 71. d.</margin>
The battle cry was to have been: *Long live the Queen of England and His Excellency Leicester*. However, the plot did not proceed on the appointed day. When it came to the critical moment, the instigators stood still. They feared—as the Magistrate later stated in a certain document—that they could not get the citizens into arms, whom they had led on a string by falsely making them believe that most of the Court <note>the city's judicial and administrative body</note>, with the exception of two or three, were part of the plot and would even lead the way; and that the citizens, seeing none of the officials leading them, would remain behind...

<margin>Warning and admonition of the Leiden Magistrate to the citizens.</margin>
<margin>Bor XXIII, 71. See also XXIV, 8. d.</margin>

This was the outcome of that plot, which had to be recounted with more detail because it was driven partly with the intention of promoting Religion and the Reformation, and partly under that cover. Many, especially among the common people, held the punishment of the accomplices to be very harsh and cruel, specifically regarding Maulde, a young, handsome nobleman, for whom the judges themselves felt pity because of his politeness and other abilities, virtues, and also services rendered to the State, recently at Sluis and previously at Ostend, of which he still bore the scars: being moreover a son of the late Lord of Mansart, who had done great service to Prince William and the fatherland; also two of Maulde’s brothers had lost their lives in the country's service, and he had been, as was said, entangled and brought into the plot by others.

<margin>See the Sentence over Maulde in Bor XXIII, 66.</margin>

After new deliberation, it was not found advisable to change the person. It was judged that the States had no need for suspicion, since his instructions were strictly defined.

Having come to speak with Lord Walsingham, the Queen’s Principal Secretary, on the twelfth of July <note>original: "Hooimaendt" (Hay-month), the traditional Dutch name for July.</note>, he heard their instructions read and said *that he shared their opinion that an alliance with the enemies of God could not end well, but added: great Princes are not always so zealous in matters of Religion. # H I S T O R I E

<margin>
1588.
*Bor, Book XXIV,*
22. a. b.
</margin>
What they said regarding freedom of conscience is noteworthy. These are their words: they say *that one shall permit freedom of conscience, without public exercise, and provided that no scandal is given.* But that is mocking people. Conscience, if it is to be free, cannot do without public exercise. The children of God have learned *that with the*
<margin>*Romans 10:10*</margin>
*heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.* <note>The author argues that belief must be accompanied by outward expression.</note> They could not serve God with only half of themselves. We look at the intent of this "permission" and how it has been used: namely, *one shall be allowed to do nothing concerning our Religion, and omit nothing concerning theirs; for otherwise one would give scandal, and yet, it is said, the conscience shall be free.* One need only pass a statue or the bread-god <note>A derogatory term used by Reformers for the consecrated Host (Eucharist) in the Catholic Mass</note> in the middle of the street, or read from a Testament to someone, or sing a Psalm, or comfort a sick person with God's word and similar things, to be immediately judged as giving scandal, and at once—while confessing the truth—be forced to prepare oneself for the fire <note>Execution by burning at the stake</note>. A fine freedom indeed, which strips a person of the use of all outward senses and limbs for the things commanded by God, and compels the same toward things forbidden by God,
<margin>
*Bor, Book XXIV,*
22. b.
</margin>
leaving nothing free but thoughts—and only because they cannot reach those. Such a freedom is slavery itself and, to speak accurately, the greatest possible torture of the conscience that could be found among men. Their request was that, in any case, the free exercise of the pure Reformed Religion in the United Netherlands should in no way be diminished, damaged, or endangered (to the exclusion of all false worship), but should be preserved and remain in its entirety under sufficient guarantees. They also requested intercession for their fellow believers living in lands held by the enemy. On the twentieth of the month, the Queen gave them an audience at Richmond. She
<margin>
Conversation between Queen Elizabeth and the clerical envoys.
*Bor, Book XXIV,* 83. Uitenbogaert, *History, p. 264.*
</margin>
said, among other things: *I wish your churches did not doubt that I care for Religion in these negotiations. The Spanish are said to have proposed granting free exercise for at least three or four years, and then the States would settle the matter there.* Daniel de Dieu, who spoke on behalf of everyone while kneeling, said, *But the majority of the States are* Papists <note>Catholic</note>. *I mean,* the Queen then spoke, *the States General*, to which the other replied, *the majority of those are also* Papists. *She asked, by whom were you sent? From which Provinces?* The answer was: *We have come with the permission of* Count Maurice of Nassau. The Queen then asked, *And the States?* They answered, *We are here with their knowledge.*

To her question, *Are you sent only by the Holland and Zeeland churches, and not by the others?* Helmichius replied: *We both are from Utrecht.* "How," she then asked, "is that young man also a Minister?"—referring to Helmichius. They answered that he had been in service for more than fourteen years, and was not as young as he appeared. *“It was,”* she spoke, *“considered a scandal among us in the beginning if someone so young was admitted to the ministry. I do not think I have shown myself to be otherwise; I have done so much for Religion.”* She also said she had not yet read their document, although Leicester <note>Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester, who had served as Governor-General of the Netherlands</note> had told them earlier that she must have read it, as he was able to tell them its entire contents.

<margin>Written answer from the Queen.</margin>
<margin>Bor, Book XXIV, 85. d.</margin>
Furthermore, they requested a written reply. This was delivered to them, and in it was stated: *That she—always maintaining the same zeal and diligence for the advancement of God’s honor and the preservation of the Reformed churches of the Netherlands Provinces (which had driven her from the beginning to accept their righteous protection)—had, of her own accord and before she was petitioned by the Ministers' request, commanded her commissioners for the peace negotiations, and thereafter charged them again, to insist above all things in those dealings that the inhabitants of the aforementioned Netherlands be granted not only freedom of conscience, but also the free exercise of the Reformed Religion. Those who wished to make the sincerity of her intentions suspect or arouse distrust, she considered common enemies, who craftily sought to break the bond between her and the inhabitants of the said Netherlands in order to deliver them to the enemy.*

<margin>Bor, Book XXIV, 84. b.</margin>
This answer did not fully satisfy the Ministers, since no mention was made therein of the exclusion of the false exercises of Religion—namely that of the Papists <note>A term used by Reformers for Roman Catholics</note> or others—which had nevertheless been clearly included in their written request.

<margin>p. 84. d. e.</margin>
Therefore, they wrote once more in their letter of thanks to the Queen, stating that the true objective of this mission from the churches consisted in this: *That the free exercise of the only true Religion be preserved in its entirety, without allowing the restoration of the Papal or other religions.* With this, they took their leave and returned to their fatherland.

# HISTORY OF THE REFORMATION,
## AND OTHER CHURCH HISTORIES.
### FIFTEENTH BOOK.

<margin>
**1588.**
North Holland Synod at Haarlem.
*From the Synodical Acts.*
</margin>

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut drop cap 'N' featuring a seated figure (possibly a scholar or biblical figure) within a classical frame decorated with foliage and fruit.</image-desc>Even before the departure of the church deputies to England, the North Holland Synod convened at Haarlem in the Month of Blossoms <note>May</note>, where some matters occurred that should be briefly touched upon. They considered the great boldness which it was understood the Papists <note>A term used by the reformers for Roman Catholics</note> and Monks were exercising, with the public practice of their mass and other superstitions of baptism and marriage, and the presentation of their doctrine; as well as the keeping of public schools, where Jesuit and Roman superstitions were being instilled in the youth. All this was understood to lead to evil ends, and it was decided that it should be presented in writing to the Lords States <note>The States of Holland, the provincial governing body</note>, with a request that the most appropriate means be used to address it. They also spoke of two former Ministers—one having fallen away to Popery <note>returned to the Catholic Church</note>, the other having joined the Anabaptists <note>Dutch: *Doopsgezinden*, followers of the Mennonite tradition</note>—to excommunicate them, or cut them off with the ban.

<margin>
Dispute at Utrecht over excommunication.
*Life of Uitenbogaerdt, pp. 6, 7.*
</margin>

Regarding the matter of excommunication, there had been some dispute at Utrecht, which, though it occurred earlier, ought to be reported here. Several members of the Consistorial <note>referring to the Reformed congregation governed by the Consistory, or church council</note> congregation fell into certain opinions that were said to be those of Koornhert <note>Dirck Volckertszoon Coornhert, a Dutch humanist and critic of strict Calvinist orthodoxy</note>. In the Consistory, there was talk of using church discipline against them, and they were exhorted according to church order; but when there was talk of excommunicating them, Uitenbogaerdt <note>Johannes Wtenbogaert, a leading minister and future figurehead of the Remonstrant movement</note> showed that he was reluctant to agree to this, and that no one should be handed over to Satan for such opinions. One of those people, named Cornelis van Diest, hearing that they were proceeding to the extreme,

They represented to the Magistrates that they found this manner of proceeding strange and improper, but nevertheless held the matter in abeyance until the Magistrate was changed by the Leicesterians <note>Followers of the Earl of Leicester, who favored a more radical Calvinist approach</note>. But afterwards, when the Earl of Leicester was still in the country, the Utrecht Consistory made no difficulty about halting the excommunication of one man and two women who had joined the Mennonites <note>Anabaptist followers of Menno Simons</note>, at the command and for the sake of that Earl, despite their names having been publicly proposed three times and their remaining in their Mennonite views. The exact time of these occurrences is not recounted.

<margin>Edicts at Utrecht against fornication, the keeping of mistresses, and the practice of the Romish Religion proclaimed. *Bor XXIV, 113. 114.*</margin>
But on the eleventh of the Hay Month <note>July</note> of this year, when the practice of fornication and the keeping of mistresses (as sins that ought not to be tolerated in a city where the Reformed Religion is practiced) were forbidden at Utrecht with a strict ordinance, a new edict against the practice of the Romish <note>Roman Catholic</note> Religion was also proclaimed there. This stated *that no one among those called spiritual or ordained persons should practice or use the aforementioned Romish Religion, upon a fine for the first offense of forfeiting their prebend <note>A stipend or land-use right granted to a clergyman</note> or maintenance and fifty gold reals, or if unable to pay, being banished for five years: for the second offense, the violator would be perpetually banished upon penalty of death. Those found present there would forfeit twenty-five, and those who provided or opened their house or property for it, one hundred gold reals; or otherwise be punished at the discretion of the court. The soldiers were forbidden, on pain of death, from attempting anything to enforce the edict, unless they had first brought in the Sheriff <note>Dutch: *Schout*</note>, his Deputy, or a Citizen Captain: but in the meantime, they might indeed detain the Priest with his listeners.*

<margin>Restoration of the lawful government at Utrecht. *Uitenb. Hist. p. 265. Bor XXV, 24, 25. — 35.* Modet's change. *Uitenb. Hist. p. 268.*</margin>
In the Wine Month <note>October</note> thereafter, matters were so managed at Utrecht by order of the States General that Gerard Deventer, otherwise known as Provink, and other rulers who had previously intruded unlawfully, were deposed, taken into custody, and the old lawful government was restored according to the privileges. The excluded Lords returned to the city and to their offices. Dirk Volkertszoon Koornhert <note>A famous Dutch polymath, artist, and theologian known for his defense of religious tolerance</note> had moved to Delft around this time to stay at the home of his friend Cornelis Adriaenszoon Boomgaerdt. He found himself too preoccupied in Haarlem and now sought to spend a year in silence at Delft on a project which he understood would serve the benefit of many and the harm of none. This project involved various excerpts and notes that he had collected and recorded with great diligence over thirty years from the Bible into various books and papers. He sought to bring these notes into order under specific titles. However, while he was busy with this, on the third of the Wine-month <note>October</note>, a certain document was read to him by two rod-bearers <note>officers of the court or bailiff's assistants</note>, by which he was commanded to leave the city within twenty-four hours, under threat of certain punishment. He requested a copy of that prohibition. It was refused. He then immediately complained in writing to the Burgomasters, requesting to know the reasons or to be received in court, so that he might defend his good name with proper and lawful means. They answered only by word of mouth: that he was not a citizen, and that he had to comply with the order. Thereupon he departed for Gouda, where he had a small Defense printed, under the title of *Shield of the Name* <note>original: "Naemscherm"</note> against the misdeed shown to him at Delft. In this writing, he complained that he—a good Patriot and a proven, well-deserving inhabitant of the land—had been denied the right at Delft which was not even refused to evildoers: that he had been able to obtain neither a hearing, nor knowledge of the accusation, nor of any secret grievance. Therefore, he was forced to defend his good name not with the great effort and cost of legal pleadings—in which they would overwhelm him—but lawfully with this writing. He claimed they could never convict him of any misconduct against the common good. The Disputations he had held against the Ministers had occurred at the request of the Ministers themselves, and with the consent of the Prince of Orange and the States of Holland; thus he had offended neither the country nor the edicts of the States, but those of Delft had made him leave only for the sake of his conscience. He believed that this trouble had come upon him from—

...the same disposition in secret at the Castle. Whether it was because they feared the power of public confessions sealed with blood, or because they had other motives, is unknown. One of those men, Joost de Tollenaer, very earnestly exhorted his fellow believers to peace in a letter written from the dungeon. He lamented that those in Haarlem and elsewhere were gripped by such a spirit of discord. *Alas,* he wrote, *would that God granted that they might bear with one another in love, and that the leaders would humble themselves before God.* He argued that if they were to yield a little for the sake of peace, it would not give them a bad conscience. *If everyone were small in their own eyes, how well things would go, and how quickly all would be settled!* Thus, the Anabaptists <note>The Mennonites or "Doopsgezinden," known for their pacifism and adult baptism</note> lacked no warning voices from among their own who opposed these unsociable hostilities. Among the Reformed, the arrogance of some sowed seeds of discord once again. In Middelburg in Zeeland, this summer, one Adriaen Vasseur, a Brabantine and Secretary to Lord Russell, the English Commander at Flushing, had been detained because he sought to incite conflict between the country’s government and the English. In a certain letter written to a minister in Bergen op Zoom, he had accused the States <note>The States-General, the governing body of the United Provinces</note> of seeking to hand over the city of Flushing to the enemy, along with other grave slanders. Regarding this arrest, there was first trouble with Bourglas, Russell’s lieutenant, who seized <margin>* arrest.</margin> several citizens of Middelburg who were then in Flushing; and he threatened to burn the tenant farms of the Middelburgers located in the countryside if Vasseur were not immediately set free.

However, the States did not allow the jurisdiction over the prisoner to be taken from them. The Consistory supporters at Utrecht hold separate meetings.

No peace followed, but rather greater unrest in church matters, which lasted for several years. Most members of the church, who were called the <term>Consistorianten</term> <note>These were the strict Calvinists who believed the church Consistory, not the city government, should have the sole power to appoint ministers.</note>, refused to hear the new ministers; they claimed that their calling, coming only from the Magistrate, was not legitimate. Therefore, they formed separate secret meetings both inside and outside the city, or they traveled, even while armed, to IJsselstein to hear sermons. But all of this was forbidden by the States and the Magistrate—who called such gatherings <term>conventicles</term> <note>From the Latin "conventiculum," meaning a small, unauthorized religious meeting.</note> and understood them to lead to sedition—by an <term>edict</term> <note>original: "plakkaet" — a public decree or law posted by authorities.</note> on the twenty-ninth of May <note>original: "Bloeimaendt" — literally "Bloom-month."</note> in the year fifteen hundred and ninety, under penalty of a fine of twenty-five guilders.

<margin>
Which was forbidden by edicts. Bor <note>Pieter Bor (1559–1635), a prominent Dutch historian of the era.</note> XXI, 114, 117, 1590.
</margin>
Afterward, traveling to IJsselstein for sermons was forbidden again on the last day of July <note>original: "Hooimaendt" — literally "Hay-month."</note>, under penalty of a fine of twelve guilders for the first offense, twenty-four guilders for the second, and banishment for the third.

<margin>
W. Helmichius writes against the edicts. Bor XXI, 115.
</margin>
Wernerus Helmichius, one of the dismissed ministers, wrote very earnestly against the first edict in public print, though without stating his name, saying,

> *That such edicts tended toward lordship over consciences, either to force the believers to approve of that unlawful church ministry, or to deprive them of the practice of their faith against their consciences. That the new ministers, seeing how they lacked spiritual weapons, now, in his estimation, called upon the secular arm and the sword of the authorities: but since the experience of many years had taught that spiritual matters are not settled and defended with the sword of the Magistrate, but only with the sword of the spirit, which was God's word, they should justify all their actions not with edicts, but with the word of God.*

On this writing, it was noted that the new ministers—if what Helmichius charged them with was true—were deviating from the form of the <term>Reformation of St. James</term> <note>Referencing the more moderate religious reforms associated with the St. James's church in Utrecht, which favored civil oversight.</note>, which loathed all violence in matters of religion; and that the Magistrate, to follow the path of St. James, ought not to forbid traveling for sermons, but rather traveling to sermons while armed, as that tended toward riot. However, the authorities maintained that no coercion of faith was taking place here, since there was no dispute over the practice of faith, but only over the lawful or unlawful calling and entry of the ministers and the church ordinance.

Concerning Baptism,

to be maintained, agreeing for the most part with the old Reformation of St. James's Church <note>The "St. James's Church" model (Sint Jacobs kerk) refers to a moderate form of Protestantism in Utrecht that allowed for more civic oversight, as opposed to the strict Calvinism of the Consistory.</note>. <margin>The Lord's Supper.</margin>
The Holy Supper *shall be purely taught, administered, and distributed according to the form of God's Word, and the order of reading and singing customary in the churches.*

<margin>Examination,</margin>
The examination <note>The spiritual check of a member's fitness to receive communion.</note> shall occur according to the teaching of Paul, *let a man examine himself*, without any other investigation into a person’s soul; yet those who desire to be examined and recorded shall be accommodated in that wish.

<margin>
Discipline,
Matthew 18,
</margin>
Church discipline, or brotherly admonition, shall occur according to Christ’s teaching; namely, that the Consistory, through one of its members, shall admonish anyone who lives in a disorderly manner. If he does not listen to the admonisher, one or two others shall be taken along, and if they are still not heard, then one of the Ministers shall join them and admonish and rebuke the unrepentant for the third and last time. If he still will not listen, then they shall commend him to God, and he shall be barred from the Lord’s Supper, without further "cutting off" or ban <note>original: "ban" — formal excommunication from the community.</note>.

<margin>
Marriage,
and Sermons,
</margin>
The announcement and confirmation of marriages shall take place according to the ordinances of the States <note>The "States" refers to the provincial government of Utrecht.</note>. The Ministers shall preach from the Gospels and Epistles of those days for the service of the weak on Sundays, and on other days, whatever they find advisable according to the circumstances: all from the Word of the Lord, and nothing outside of it.

### OF THE REFORMATION. BOOK XV.

<margin>1590.</margin>
...by the Magistrate of the city or cities; and in the countryside by the States <note>The "States" refers to the provincial governing body.</note>, or their Deputies: or that anyone should be subjected to any trouble, injustice, or harassment on account of their faith (since faith was a gift from God).

<margin>His promise to those of Gelderland and Zutphen. *Bor in the Supplement behind the II part of the III Vol. p. 33.*</margin>
Not long thereafter, Prince Maurice was also offered the Stadtholdership <note>The "Stadtholder" was the chief magistrate and military commander of a province.</note> of Gelderland and Zutphen, yet under the condition that he would maintain the Reformed Religion—which the major and minor cities of the Duchy of Guelders and the County of Zutphen held through the special grace of God—and promote it everywhere, including in the manors of the countryside, so that it alone, and no other religion, would be practiced in these lands. Yet no one, except for ministers of the church, would be investigated or questioned because of their religion.

<margin>The calling of Taco Sybrandts to Medenblik, and the trouble arising from it. *Bor XXVI, 57. XXXII, 71; Uitenb. Hist. p. 301; Grot. Verantw. III, 33.*</margin>
Meanwhile, Taco Sybrandts—formerly a minister of St. James's in Utrecht who had settled in Alkmaar—was called by the Magistrate of the city of Medenblik to serve as their minister, based on the approval and recommendation of the Classis <note>A "Classis" is a regional governing body in the Dutch Reformed Church, composed of ministers and elders.</note> of Alkmaar. The Consistory <note>The local church council.</note> opposed this calling because it did not originate from them. A complaint was made to the Classis of Enkhuizen, which, siding with the church council and against the Magistrate, declared the calling to be unlawful and contrary to the common church order. Prince Maurice and several Deputies from the States, being in Enkhuizen shortly thereafter in October <note>original: "Wijnmaendt" — literally 'Wine month,' the traditional Dutch name for October.</note> regarding national affairs, heard the complaints of the churchmen. But the Burgomasters of Medenblik, defending their actions against these charges, eventually convinced the Prince and the other Lords—after various negotiations occurring at different times—to declare that the aforementioned calling was legal and well-executed, desiring that it should no longer be brought into dispute.

<margin>J. Lipsius writes his book on Politics, and speaks therein of the punishment of heretics. *Lips. de Polit. lib. IV. cap. II, III, IV.*</margin>
In the preceding year, Justus Lipsius, Professor of History at Leiden—who had made a great name for himself through his concise eloquence and his explanations of Roman antiquities—had published a certain book treating of *Politics* or the art of governance. It was written in a new style using the maxims and words of the ancients, mostly drawn from Histories, and for the most part very successfully and concisely joined and ordered with fine language. Speaking of religion in this work, he asserts that only one kind of religion should be maintained in a realm, and this according to ancient custom, protecting the institutions of the ancestors and the holy ceremonies. Against this religion, he says, *offenses are committed in two ways: publicly and in secret.*

### H I S T O R Y

<margin>1590.</margin>Publicly, when one thinks ill of God and the accepted Religion, and incites others to that opinion: In secret, when one only thinks ill within oneself. The former, he [Lipsius] wished to see punished, especially if they cause disturbance. Clemency, he says, has no place here. *Burn and cut; so that some limbs might perish rather than the whole* <margin>1 From Cicero's Philippics VIII. D. V. Coornhert opposes it. 2 Coornhert’s Works II. 50. 3 Coornhert III. 146. d. 147. 4 Coornhert II. 43.</margin> *body* 1 <note>original: "Brandt en snijdt; op dat liever eenige leden, dan 't geh-lichaem verderve." This is a medical metaphor used by Justus Lipsius to justify the execution of religious dissenters to save society.</note>. Dirck Volckertszoon Coornhert, that sworn enemy of the killing of heretics and all compulsion of conscience, set himself against this writing of Lipsius. First, several letters were exchanged between them on that matter 2, and also with others 3, until the publication of the book named *The Trial of Heretic-Killing and Compulsion of Conscience* 4 followed, with a dedication to the Magistrates of the city of Leiden. Coornhert also sent this book to the Regents of the other Hollandish cities, warning them against the views of Lipsius. The latter took this publication very poorly. The Magistrate of Leiden, in order to please Lipsius, issued a proclamation from the town house declaring *that they did not accept the aforementioned Dedication: that Coornhert had done them no honor, nor friendship, nor service thereby; without, however, banning the book:* further expressing the high esteem in which they held Lipsius. They would allow their citizens to read Coornhert's little book, but exhorted them in contrast to read the magnificent writing which Lipsius had published against it. That was his Latin booklet on the one and only Religion, *against the Dialogue-Partner* <note>original: "tegens den Tsamen-spreker." This refers to Lipsius's work *De Una Religione*, written against Coornhert.</note>. With this proclamation Lipsius was not satisfied, all the less because he understood that Coornhert, who had been sickly for a long time, was still busy writing against him.

<margin>See the Testimonies at the end of Coornhert’s Life p. 7. before the 1st part of his works.</margin>It is told how he [Lipsius], in the assembly of the States of Holland, through the help of some cities, had sought to obtain an order that no one should be allowed to contest his book on *Politics* <note>term: Politics <gloss>referring to Lipsius's influential work "Politicorum Libri Sex" (Six Books on Politics)</gloss></note> in writing. But the Lord Geeraerdt de Lange, Burgomaster of Gouda, stopped it with these words: *If Lipsius writes the truth, one shall be able to lean more firmly upon it because of the powerless attack. But* <margin>Lipsius leaves for Brabant and joins the Papacy. Bor XXVIII. 9; Life of Lipsius, Aubertus Miraeus as Author p. 25.</margin> *if anyone finds some deceit in it to the detriment of the country, which we do not see, what harm is there in correction?* Shortly thereafter, Lipsius departed (under the pretext of going for a short time to the baths of Spa for his health) by way of Germany to Brabant and joined the Roman church immediately—a church which he had previously openly opposed in Leiden, as his verses in honor of Guillaume Fargereau and others testify †. # THE HISTORY OF THE REFORMATION BOOK XV.

<margin>
1590.
Lipsius, Letters, Decade VI, letter 4.
Grotius, History, V, 266.
* Life of Lipsius by A. Miraeus; Grotius, History VII, 329.
† Bor, Book XXXII, p. 2.
‡ Bor, Book XXVIII, p. 9.
D. Coornhert dies.

The Jesuit Franciscus Bencius <note>Franciscus Bencius (1542–1594) was a prominent Italian Jesuit orator and scholar.</note> records: *I testify in truth and before God, that in my religious sentiments I never held with the wicked <note>original: "quaeden" – in this context, Lipsius refers to the Reformed Protestants as "the wicked" from his eventual Catholic perspective.</note>. I always knew the ancient religion to be good. Nevertheless, we acted differently in places where others acted differently.* This was understood by some as a confession that he had conformed and feigned his beliefs in religious matters according to the currents of the times. Some also believed that the difficulties arising from Coornhert’s writings, and the fear that the Hollanders might face setbacks in the war against the Spanish, moved him to switch sides. Afterward, having become a Professor at Leuven, he showed himself to be as zealous a Catholic \* <note>original: "Paeps" – literally "Papist," a term often used polemically at the time for those loyal to the Pope.</note> as he was a supporter of the Spanish cause †. After the departure of Lipsius, Coornhert, on his sickbed, completed the *Justification of his Trial against Heretic-Killing*. His heirs had this work translated into Latin ‡ and made public through printing after his death. He passed away at Gouda on the twenty-ninth of October <note>original: "Wijnmaendt" – the "wine month," an old Dutch name for October.</note>, after an illness of eight weeks, at the age of sixty-eight. Upon his grave in the Great Church <note>The Sint-Janskerk in Gouda, famous for its stained-glass windows.</note>, near the front of the choir, this epitaph (composed by Hendrick Laurenszoon Spiegel, a dear friend, that great builder of the Dutch language and author of the *Heart-Mirror*) was carved:

On his sickbed, he was very patient and composed, saying among other things: *I have received a soul from God; it belongs to Him. I have no complaints, for God is good: He does nothing but good, and therefore He shall not destroy His good creature.* Many different judgments were passed upon him and his writings after his death. # OF THE REFORMATION. BOOK XV.

<margin>1590.</margin>Corneliszoon Hooft <note>Cornelis Pieterszoon Hooft (1547–1626) was a prominent burgomaster of Amsterdam known for his moderate views and support of religious tolerance.</note> later decorated his <note>Referring to the portrait of Dirk Volckertszoon Coornhert, a Dutch scholar and critic of religious compulsion who died in 1590.</note> image with these verses:

> He sampled seven [professions] and held nearly every status,
> But remained, in knowledge and freedom, undaunted,

And with the following, in which the Poet has him speak thus:

> I was received at Amsterdam, I gave my spirit at Gouda,
> Whose struggle was for Morals, Scripture, and Freedom.

<margin>South Holland Synod held at Dordrecht.</margin>
<margin>Trigland, History, p. 709.</margin>
In this same year, a South Holland <term>Synod</term> <note>A formal gathering of church leaders (ministers and elders) to decide on matters of doctrine and administration.</note> was convened at Dordrecht by the clergy, contrary to the resolution of the States of Holland passed on that matter. The Lords <term>States</term> <note>The "States of Holland" was the sovereign assembly representing the cities and nobility of the province of Holland.</note> allowed the Synod to proceed but sent two authorized deputies to attend the proceedings on their behalf; just as two had also been present in their name at the Synod of the previous year at Gouda. Furthermore, the Synodical <term>Classis</term> <note>A regional governing body in the Reformed church structure, composed of representatives from several neighboring churches.</note> had requested in writing, in order to promote the Synod, that the States be pleased to authorize some of their own members to attend this Synod at Dordrecht.

<margin>Declaration and resolution of the States regarding the holding of the Synod.</margin>
<margin>Trigland, History, p. 707.</margin>
<margin>* Commission.</margin>
The States declared in their commission * given to the authorized deputies that they were not well pleased that the Synod had been convened again without their prior consent and against their Resolution. Nevertheless, they currently consented to the Synod proceeding, yet with the instruction that the Synod should not deal with any matters concerning <term>Policy</term> <note>original: "Politie" — in the 17th century, this referred to civil administration and the government's role in maintaining public order, rather than modern "police."</note> nor the general order of the churches, and that henceforth no Synod should be held without the prior consent of His Excellency <note>Referring to Maurice, Prince of Orange and Stadtholder of Holland.</note> and their Noble Mightinesses. This declaration of the States is read thus in the synodical proceedings, and furthermore, the following is recorded:

<margin>Answer and request of the Synod.</margin>
<margin>Trigland, p. 707.</margin>
<margin>Acts of the Synod, art. 3. Trigland, p. 708.</margin>
Whereupon the Synod has unanimously seen fit—for certain and weighty reasons, and to avoid inconveniences that might otherwise arise (of which a declaration can be made if necessary)—all the more since their Noble Mightinesses send Commissioners to the Synod, that their Noble Mightinesses be pleased to trust the churches with such ecclesiastical matters without conducting an inquiry into them. For the Synod does not know of ever having handled anything in its assembly other than church matters, in a church-like manner, and still desires to do nothing else, following the general church regulations; just as they used to refer matters concerning the general churches to the General Synod. ### HISTORY

<margin>1590.</margin>
...to call and hold synodal meetings; with a request that their Noble Lordships <note>Referring to the "States of Holland," the governing body of the province.</note> be pleased to leave the churches to their custom regarding this matter; and to interpret in the best light that this present Synod was called without seeking broader consent from His Excellency <note>Prince Maurice of Orange, the Stadtholder.</note> or their Noble Lordships; for reasons which the Deputies of the Synod were to demonstrate to the Lords States; also requesting that their Noble Lordships be pleased once and for all to grant consent that the church might remain in its aforementioned custom of holding such meetings. And as it was suspected that this prohibition—against calling a Synod without the permission of the Lords States—must have arisen from some suspicion that the States held against the Ministers and ecclesiastical assemblies, just as it had been noted in other matters that the Lords had something against the Ministers and their actions, the Synod was therefore greatly distressed. For this reason, the Ministers requested a disclosure of the reasons for that suspicion, and that the States would authorize some gentlemen to enter into discussion and negotiation with the Deputies of the churches regarding this, so that, all things being considered, such order might be established that all further suspicion might be averted.

<margin>Synod at Hoorn. From the Acts of the North Holland Synod.</margin>
In the North Holland Synod, held this same year at Hoorn in the Summer Month <note>June</note>, a matter arose concerning Andries Volkaertszoon, a Minister at Valkooge, regarding the subject of Predestination <note>The doctrine that God has eternally decreed the salvation or damnation of individual souls.</note>. There, at the proposal of the <term>Classis</term> <note>A regional assembly of ministers and elders.</note> of Alkmaar, it was asked: whether the Synod would take it upon itself to instruct him in those points where he differed from the Reformed churches—the matter of Predestination and its related points—or whether he should be tolerated in his understanding if he persisted in it, or whether they should proceed against him with ecclesiastical measures? In the Synodal Acts, it is recorded that he gave the Synod sufficient satisfaction on several points through scriptural answers, declaring that he adhered to the Dutch Confession of the thirty-seven Articles <note>The Belgic Confession, the standard of doctrine for the Dutch Reformed Church.</note>. It was also decided to admonish him to conduct himself prudently, both in the pulpit and in daily conversation, so that the uninformed, since he was under suspicion, would find no cause to slander him behind his back.

### OF THE REFORMATION. BOOK XV.

<margin>1590.</margin>
...remained by the sweet explanation of Henricus Bullingerus <note>A Swiss Reformer whose more moderate views were often cited to bridge theological gaps.</note>. Thus it seems that some difference here was tolerated for the sake of suitability <note>The Dutch "gevoeglijkheit" implies a pragmatic compromise for social harmony.</note>.

<margin>The Papists in Breda obtain the public practice of their Religion in one church. Bor XXVII. 24. c.</margin>
The States of the United Netherlands also exercised great leniency in the matter of religion at this time, even regarding the Roman Catholics. For after the Castle of Breda had been captured in March of last year by means of a peat ship <note>A famous military ruse where Dutch soldiers hid in a barge carrying peat to infiltrate and seize the Spanish-held city.</note>, and the city had surrendered by treaty—preserving its privileges and freedoms—it was first agreed that the inhabitants, concerning their request for the practice of the Papal Religion, should follow what would be granted to them by Prince Maurice, with the knowledge of the States. However, later, for various reasons, the Roman Catholics were permitted the public practice of their religion in one church. In the other churches, the Reformed Religion was practiced.

<margin>Adriaen vander Mijle deceased. Bor XXVII. 26.</margin>
Not long after, on the seventeenth of June, Lord Adriaen vander Mijle, President of the Court of Holland, passed away, after having rendered many services to the fatherland, both civil and ecclesiastical, with blameless loyalty, unblemished justice, provident judgment, shrewd management, and kind-hearted modesty. He was a gentleman of excellent learning, a favorable patron and much beloved by the scholars of his age.

<margin>* See Book XIII, p. 685. 1591. Church Order established by order of the States of Holland. † P. Bor XXVIII. 21., Uytenbogaert's History p. 277. Documents of the Justification of the Resolution of the States of Holland of August 4, 1617. p. 35, 73; Grotius's Justification II, 17; VII, 79.</margin>
The States of Holland—knowing that the churches within their territory were daily falling into various disputes for lack of a fixed Church Order <note>A "Kerkenorde" is a legal framework governing the administration and discipline of the church.</note>, and that the ecclesiastical regulations established by the clergy in their Synods (particularly in the year eighty-six <note>1586</note>, during the time of Leicester, without the knowledge or consent of the States) were offensive to many—acted on the advice of Lord Oldenbarnevelt, Advocate of Holland. They had the draft of the Church Order, devised in the year eighty-three <note>1583</note>*, reviewed and organized in February and March of the year fifteen hundred ninety-one by eight gentlemen commissioned from among the States and the Courts of Justice, and eight Ministers. From that draft, a Church Order† was established, which the States sent to the Courts to hear their opinion on it. The Courts declared that this work was godly and edifying: not only useful, but entirely necessary, both for the welfare of the lands and the churches. This Church Order was also to be presented to the Noble Lords and cities of Holland and West Friesland, following a formal summons...

2 From the Acts of the North Holland Synod held at Enkhuizen.

...[the regulations] would have been accepted, were it not that five cities—Delft, Gouda, Rotterdam, Hoorn, and Medenblik—claimed that they stripped too much authority from the Lords States <note>The 'Lords States' refers to the States of Holland, the governing assembly of the province.</note> and the City Magistrates, giving it instead to the clergy. They argued they could not approve this for the service of the lands and cities 1. Yet this very insistence on maintaining civil authority so strictly against the clergy later caused these cities to suffer the greatest damage through the resulting disorders in the very areas they most wished to protect. On the other side, the clergy in the South and North Holland Synods also raised objections to the adoption. They requested *that even if all the cities should accept them as good, they should nevertheless not be put into use before they had been deliberated upon with the provincial Synod and approved, and that the churches should be heard on the matter* 2. Indeed, some of these clergymen even suggested *that the Ministers who had supported that work and signed it ought to be censored, as they had granted and surrendered too much to the Authorities, and had even sold the rights of the churches* 3. In this church order, which can be read in the History of Pieter Bor 4 <note>Pieter Bor (1559–1635) was a prominent Dutch historian whose massive "Oorsprongk" chronicle is a primary source for the Dutch Revolt.</note>, the Authorities were attributed more power than in any previous ordinances established by the clergy; even including some jurisdiction regarding church censures and the pronouncement of excommunication, alongside other points that some found offensive.

<margin>
In what manner the election of the Ministers, Elders, and Deacons would occur according to that church order. Bor XXVIII. 22.
† See the 3rd Article, in Bor XXVIII. 23.

What was stated in that church ordinance regarding the election and appointment of Ministers, Elders, and Deacons, amounted to this: *Whenever a Minister of the Divine Word <term>Minister of the Divine Word</term> <note>A formal title for a Protestant preacher or pastor.</note> should be lacking in the cities, the Burgomasters and Regents <term>Regents</term> <note>The ruling elite of the Dutch cities.</note> would authorize four persons, and command the Ministers and Elders to also authorize four persons, who together—after prior prayers and examination to be conducted by them in this regard—would proceed to the election of such a person as they deemed fit for that service. They would then present their election to the aforementioned Burgomasters and Regents, and if the choice made was pleasing to them, then the chosen person would be examined* †, *and, if found fit, presented to the congregation, and thereafter, according to the custom of each church, confirmed in the service. But if the aforementioned Burgomasters and Regents declared that the stated choice did not please them, then the aforementioned Authorized persons would conduct a new election in the manner described above. At Emmerich in the land of Cleves, the preacher had been driven out at this time, and the <term>Jesuits</term> <note>A Catholic religious order, the Society of Jesus, often seen by Protestants as political agents of the Counter-Reformation.</note> introduced. Prince Maurice, who was then stationed at Sevender with the army of the United Netherlands and had recently achieved several victories against the Spanish—which earned him great respect—showed his displeasure regarding this, for preaching had been tolerated there for a full forty years.

The Magistrate laid this matter upon the Council, and the Council, having come to the camp, laid it upon the Prince <note>Duke William of Cleves.</note>, saying that the establishment of the Jesuits had already been planned by the old Prince and was now carried out by his son, hoping that Prince Maurice and the Netherlands would not set limits for him in this, as he was a Prince of the Empire who had the power to practice such religion as he saw fit in his land <note>Refers to the principle of "Cuius regio, eius religio," meaning "Whose realm, his religion."</note>, but would nevertheless maintain good neighborliness. The Jesuits were supposedly to be entrusted with nothing other than the school. Prince Maurice gave as an answer:

> That he did not desire to prescribe any rule to the Prince of Cleves in his government, nor his religion, but he could not tolerate the Jesuits as neighbors. He knew well that they were the King of Spain's spies, and therefore sought to place their seat as close as possible to these borders. That they had also murdered his father <note>William the Silent, Prince of Orange, who was assassinated in 1584.</note>, and therefore he wished to remain their enemy.

After the departure of the army, Gerrit de Jonge, Captain at s’Gravenweert (or Schenkenschans), deprived those of Emmerich of their cows: promising to return them after the departure of the Jesuits. Because of this, they were made to leave. But that the Council of Cleves, regarding the introduction of the Jesuits, appealed to both the Princes of Cleves, father and son, was absurd: for God had struck them both in the mind <note>Both Duke William "the Rich" and his son John William suffered from bouts of mental illness or total mental collapse.</note>. The son had never yet been employed in the government.

<term>Ignatius</term> (first named Innicus or Enecus †) <term>Loyola</term>, a Spanish nobleman born in Biscay, having become weary of war (where he gained nothing but crippled limbs), turned his brave and warlike mind to more peaceful pursuits. Those who took pleasure in this novelty and joined him made nothing more their business than two things: the authority of the Pope and the power of Spain. The affairs of the Pope, which were then falling, they supported with powerful remedies, hitherto neglected, consisting in the restoration of good morals and all kinds of learning. # THE FIFTEENTH BOOK OF THE REFORMATION.

...they obtained all the more name and honor through their travels to America and the Indies in **1592**, while they also expanded the domain of Spain among the wild peoples <note>The author refers to the indigenous populations of the Americas and Asia encountered during Spanish colonization.</note> by introducing the Christian Religion in their own way. There, great miracles—as if they had actually happened to them—were spread and highly praised, aided by the remoteness of the places, the boldness of the preachers, and the gullibility of the listeners. Other good qualities were found among them in abundance, whether in reality or in appearance. Yet in some, one might well have required more loyalty and modesty. They gained great authority over the common people through the reputation of holiness, and because they taught the youth languages and sciences <note>This refers to the Jesuit system of education, which became the standard for the Catholic elite.</note> without receiving any payment. They had their **Superiors** in every city and country, and one who commanded over all of them throughout the entire world, who was commonly a Spaniard. <note>The Superior General of the Society of Jesus, often called the "Black Pope."</note> They governed wisely and obeyed faithfully. Not all those who entered their order lived together in communities. They held that the growth of their brotherhood would be too great to be confined within walls. Therefore, they also took householders and married persons into their order. <note>This likely refers to Jesuit "affiliates" or lay members who supported the order's goals while living in the secular world.</note> And there was nothing they sought more to teach and instill than that one must uproot the fear of death and all human affections. But they especially sought to draw to themselves those who possessed something outstanding above others, whether it be intellect, nobility, or wealth. They made use of every man: for they knew how to distinguish and choose talents as wisely as they could. They soon saw from whom they might hope to make famous through eloquent preaching or through well-considered writings. Since some among them were of illustrious nobility, they involved themselves in the weightiest counsels through their dexterity in investigating matters, and because there was no more powerful means to discover secrets than through **Religion**. Through the handling of last wills and testaments, and gifts from the living, they obtained great treasures. Through these schemes, it was seen that they—the youngest of all religious orders—in a short time surpassed the previous sects of **Monks** in prestige and wealth. This made them hateful to the others, as if they contradicted the customs of the same by acting entirely differently. But rising above those who envied them, they found entry into the courts of **Princes** by a middle way that was praiseworthy; for they kept themselves between foul, slavish subservience and surly arrogance, without fleeing from the faults of men...

> *Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them,* <note>Matthew 18:20</note>

It is one thing to call upon the name of God in spirit and truth, and another to disguise all one's deeds and resolutions under the cover of calling upon the divine name; as if the outward form of prayers could by itself sanctify human institutions before God. If Melanchthon, Bullinger, and various others, without any injury to the faith or disturbance of Christ's church, differed boldly from some in the interpretation of this matter, I hope that the same freedom will not be held against me as a crime. Thereupon recounting how even Apostles and Apostolic churches were not exactly alike in everything, but had various differences in the house of the Lord, he concludes that it was then no wonder that in these latter times there was a diversity of opinion regarding the explanation of this or that passage.

<margin>Persecution at Valenciennes. History of Martyrs, p. 765. History of the Reformed Martyrs, p. 502 and 503.</margin>
Elsewhere, such severity found a greater audience. At Valenciennes, a man named Willem de Rijk was put to death for the sake of religion. Margriete Pironne, wife of Ambroos Marchant, had not attended Mass <note>The central act of worship in the Roman Catholic Church, which was mandatory in Spanish-controlled territories</note> for a long time and occupied herself at home with reading the Bible. Her maid-servant reported this to the Jesuits and the Magistrates. Once she was taken into custody, she was told she would be released provided she stood upon a scaffold, prayed to God and the court for forgiveness, and threw her Bible into the fire. She asked, *whether her Bible was not good?* They said yes, and she replied: *Why then shall I throw it into the fire?* They answered, *to satisfy the Jesuit fathers; also, you shall burn nothing but paper and thereby save your life, after which you may buy another Bible.* At this, she let it be known: *I would rather you burn me myself than that I should burn that book.* Then they threw her into a narrower dungeon on bread and water; but enduring this hardship and every temptation, they finally brought her to the scaffold on the twenty-second of January <note>original: "Loumaendt," an old Dutch name for January</note> in the year 

<margin>1593.</margin>
fifteen hundred and ninety-three. There the Bible was burned before her eyes, and she was strangled <note>literally "the throat pinched shut," a common method of execution before or during burning for those who did not recant</note>, crying out during the burning of the book: *You burn the word of the Lord, which you previously admitted to be good and holy.*

In this year—the exact day is not recorded—Peter de Loyseleur, Knight, Lord of Villiers and Westhoven, passed away at Westhoven on the island of Walcheren. He was formerly the Court Preacher and Advisor to the late Prince of Orange, and later also an Advisor to his son, Prince Maurice. He was mentioned with praise in the preceding book under the name Villers *. He was born in Lille <note>original: "Rijffel," the traditional Dutch name for the French city of Lille</note> and was first an Advocate <term>Advocate: a lawyer or barrister</term> before the Parliament of Paris. However, on account of the fierce persecution against the Reformed, he fled to Geneva where, upon the advice of Theodore Beza <note>A prominent French Protestant theologian and successor to John Calvin</note>, he applied himself for some time to the study of Theology. There he joined himself in holy matrimony with Johanna de Brichanteau, daughter of Charles de Brichanteau, Knight, Lord of Saint-Martin and Nigerets, who had likewise fled for the sake of religion. Having been called to the ministry in Rouen, he served that congregation for some time, until the great massacre in Paris <note>The St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre of 1572, a wave of targeted Catholic mob violence against Huguenots</note> began and spread to Rouen as well. He then departed with his wife and seven small children to a certain castle located two miles from the city, but he was suddenly set upon there. Yet he escaped miraculously; for the persecutor, a hatmaker from...

Of this, although written a short time prior, I shall here provide the sense of the principal matters. The writing, translated from Latin, was printed in Utrecht in the year fifteen hundred ninety-five, and bore this title: *Admonition of Franciscus Junius to the Church of God which is at Utrecht, to maintain the communion of the Saints in godliness, holiness, love, and peace, through the unity of the Spirit*. The introduction was a thanksgiving to God for the grace granted to them, with a prayer for progress in goodness. After that, he urged them himself that they should walk in a manner becoming of their calling, namely in peace and unity, according to the requirement of the Apostle: *That they must not break that which they were in agreement upon, for the sake of any matter upon which they did not agree.*

<margin>Romans 16.</margin>
He pointed them to the example of the Lord Jesus Christ, who on earth did not break the bruised reed and did not extinguish the smoking wick... who, having sat at the right hand of God the almighty Father after His ascension, with the greatest tolerance raises the falling, strengthens the weak, does good to the wicked, and loves all people steadfastly, just as He has always loved His own from the beginning... He pointed them to the experienced builders of the church, the Prophets and Apostles: namely to Paul, that great servant of God, who, being free from all, made himself a servant to all, that he might win more; who became as a Jew to the Jews, that he might win the Jews... indeed, who became all things to all men that he might by all means save some... One should only turn away from those who create discord and offense against Christian doctrine. One could not tear oneself away from one another, but must receive everyone whom the Lord receives, and commands to be received through His Apostle.

<margin>1593.</margin>
<margin>One should not separate from Utrecht over doctrine.</margin>
They, the *Utrecht brothers*, strove for godliness, yet that was [not] <note>original: "wa[...]" likely "waren niet," meaning "was not alone"</note> alone, but accompanied by other virtues, especially love—that love, the true daughter of godliness, which they had to maintain with one another, <note>original: "elkander[...]" reconstructed as "elkanderen onderhouden"</note> as much in truth and in deed as also through the communion of the holy Sacraments. Why then did some withhold themselves from the communion of the church and the Lord’s Supper <term>Avondtmaels</term>? It could not, they understood, be due to a lack in the teaching. For the Teachers at *Utrecht* agreed on the main points of divine doctrine and truth. In teaching, many things were spoken with truth, but some were said so unsuitably <note>original: "onbequae[m]"</note>, or understood by others so, that they seemed to be false. And if anything were said that was false, and such a thing escaped someone unthinkingly out of human weakness <note>original: "fw[akheid]"</note> (for to fail in nothing is proper to God alone), either the truth was partially departed from, or entirely in some doctrine which, nonetheless, was not of such great importance that one should break unity <note>original: "d’[eenigheid]"</note> because of it. What should they do then, since they certainly agreed in the truth <note>original: "waer[heit]"</note>? Nothing else but to be of one mind, and if they felt otherwise, to wait until God revealed <note>original: "openbaerd[e]"</note> the same to them. Some took offense at the understanding or opinion of individual members, which concerned neither the preaching of the Word nor the common care of the church.

<margin>I.</margin>
He wished that those would consider two things. The first, that those who were of a different mind in some matters, and yet acknowledged one body, one spirit, one hope of calling, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father, and who wished to tolerate those who used the Sacraments <note>original: "Sacramen[ten]"</note> rightfully, could not then rightfully separate themselves from the communion. For as the Apostle said, to every one of us is grace given according to the measure of the gift of Christ <note>original: "Chrifti"</note>. The second:

<margin>II.</margin>
that they should not be narrower of conscience <term>conscientie</term> than the Apostle, who exhorted the Roman Christians to turn away not from all kinds of people and those without office who erred in simplicity of heart, but only from such who caused division and offense against the doctrine <note>original: "leere"</note> which they had been taught by God. For the error of the former could not harm the truth, neither in itself nor in others; but the error of the latter should not be agreed with even by the slightest sign, and from them...

<margin>Nor because of the lives of some in the congregation.</margin>
one had to turn away from these and not from those. Or did they take issue with the life of some in the congregation? It were to be wished that neither in Teacher nor in member <term>ledemaet</term>, neither within nor without the church, anything unedifying were seen; but why did Christ teach us to pray, *Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors*, if not because we should [recognize] our own weaknesses?

OF THE REFORMATION. BOOK XV.

<margin>1593.</margin>

[...to] complain, and instead cover the faults of our brothers, just as we wish and pray that our own might be covered by God <note>This refers to the biblical concept of "love covering a multitude of sins" (1 Peter 4:8), meaning to forgive or overlook faults for the sake of unity.</note>; and in view of this common stain of the church and of the specific members within it, we might learn, as the Apostle also exhorted us, to watch over one another to kindle love and good works, and not to leave our mutual assembly, but to exhort one another—and all the more so because we saw the day of Christ approaching. That was necessary, and in that one had to labor, so that by seeing another’s weaknesses and being mindful of our own, one might run to them to exhort them, to sharpen them, and to kindle the good that was in them (which was being contested by the surrounding evil) through a holy breeze of love. 

Regarding the life of the Pastors in particular, he said he had a good opinion of them and trusted that their lives agreed with their teaching. Yet, one should not judge the teaching by the life, but rather judge the life of the Pastors by the teaching. As for the "sheep" <note>A common metaphor for the congregation or laypeople.</note>, one could just as little judge the whole church and its fellowship by some defects in individual members. For just as it would conflict with nature if one felt poorly about a person’s entire body because of the deformity or blemish of one specific limb, so too would such a judgment of the church be entirely alien to Christ’s grace, truth, and love. Therefore, testing oneself to see if one was in the faith, one should hold others as servants of that Lord who is merciful and who can and will lift up those who have fallen.
