# FIFTEENTH BOOK OF THE REFORMATION.

<margin>Conflict with Cornelis Wiggertszoon, Minister at Hoorn. See Bor XXXII, 47-70. Uitenbogaert’s History p. 293-300, 749. Chronicle of P. J. Twisck II, 1483.</margin>
...to those whom it concerned, in its own time, and in such a manner as was becoming. And in 1593 <note>original: "MDXCIII"</note> *the God of peace, the Lord of glory, would shortly crush Satan under their feet. Herewith he wished all brothers the grace and peace of God.* While they worked so hard for peace among those of Utrecht, the conflict in North Holland also broke out. The Synod at Alkmaar had dismissed *Cornelis Wiggertszoon*, Minister at Hoorn, from his preaching office until further notice, due to his opinions and teaching regarding the matters of original sin, restoration, election, calling, saving faith, free will, good works and perseverance, the providence of God, and the image of God, as being impure in doctrine. This suspension from his service was confirmed by the Synod at Haarlem, held in the following year, with a request to the <term>States; the provincial governing body</term> that he might be barred from service through their authority. After much negotiation, both in person and in writing, the Synod at Amsterdam, in the year ninety-five, was ordered not to proceed further against him, as the Lords States themselves were taking notice of his case and intended to provide for it in the best interest of the church.

<margin>From the Acts of the North Holland Synods. Bor XXXII, 55. Is brought to resign his office, but preaches inside a house.</margin>
Afterward, matters were brought so far that he resigned from public church service. Yet, he did not cease to teach in a private house among people of his own opinion. The North Holland Synod complained about this to the States, saying *that this would be the foundation of a new sect, requesting that their Honorable Mightinesses would use their authority to employ such means by which such new and harmful <term>Conventicles; private, unauthorized religious gatherings</term> might be prevented.*

<margin>Clement Maertenzoon and Cornelis Meynaertszoon Spruit, Ministers at Hoorn, publish a defense and confession. Bor XXXII, 67, 68. a. Answer to the Counter-Remonstrants. Counter-Vertoog 11, 6.</margin>
In the meantime, *Clement Maertenzoon* and *Cornelis Meynaertszoon Spruit*, Ministers at Hoorn, who were both also under suspicion, published a short defense and straightforward confession, in which they said *that, as far as <term>Predestination; the doctrine that God has foreordained the salvation of some</term> was concerned, they would stick with the sweet explanation of <note>Heinrich Bullinger (1504–1575), a Swiss Reformer known for his more moderate and pastoral approach compared to some stricter Calvinists.</note> Bullingerus, not desiring to fly higher or climb further into it, but that they held with the highly learned Albertus Hardenberg, formerly a Minister at Emden, who in a certain sermon on the ninth chapter to the Romans, concerning Esau, said:* I would rather stay at the root of the tree than climb high, so as not to fall dangerously from a branch above. *And it is,* they said, *surprising that we are pressed and squeezed so hard, since even the learned themselves do not all climb equally high in this matter, and yet do not condemn one another for it, but bear with each other in brotherly peace and friendship.*

Secondly, he argued that the form of the religious exercises for which he was now being accused was in accordance with the <term>freedom of conscience; the right to hold one's own religious beliefs without state interference</term> that had been firmly promised to him by the <term>Advocate of the Land; Johan van Oldenbarnevelt, the highest official in Holland</term> in the presence of the <term>States; the provincial governing body</term>. This freedom was granted to the inhabitants under the United Provinces in the Union of the Covenant <note>referring to the Union of Utrecht</note>, just as it had been allowed to the <term>Mennonite; followers of Menno Simons, known for their pacifism and adult baptism</term> denomination under the peaceful reign of Prince William <note>William the Silent</note>, and was not yet denied to anyone except regarding the use of the public churches. Furthermore, he argued that the Word of God was not bound to the church, and that he practiced his calling outside the church’s jurisdiction with no more offense than other denominations, until such time as his accusers could prove his teaching contradicted the truth of God and that theirs agreed with the truth of the Divine Word. To this end, he offered to engage in such a <term>Disputation; a formal public theological debate</term> as the <term>Reformed; the official Calvinist church</term> offered to the Catholic Church, on the condition that both sides would yield to the truth. Nevertheless, the Church officials persisted earnestly for some time in demanding he cease preaching in private houses, finally threatening him with <term>excommunication; formal expulsion from the church community</term>.

They might, he said, proceed with their excommunication and do as they saw fit, since he had already separated himself from that church. He hoped for nothing but good from the States, but if anything else should befall him, he was ready to suffer for the name of the Lord, who he hoped would give him strength. They declared themselves bound by oath and nature to defend him, not only because they knew well that he was as sound in doctrine as he was lawfully called and confirmed in his service, but also because they had long since found how his singular godliness, peacefulness, and good conduct had made him so dear and pleasant among the common citizenry: that they would rather endure and expect all hardship and dangers before he should be driven out of the city. But the negotiation was immediately rejected. The States gave as their answer that they had been and continued to be sufficiently warned—by previous deceit hidden under such negotiations and by various identified traitors—of what they could expect from the King of Spain and the Spaniards.

To make the Spanish peace proposal even more hateful, much was said regarding the opinion held by many Roman Catholics: that one need not keep one's word to heretics. But those who pushed this idea rightly suffered the consequences and punishment of their own rule; for by providing such grounds for mistrust, they deprived themselves of being believed and, with their litigiousness, broke off all human negotiations. For all who measure what is fair and honest only by the yardstick of their own advantage cannot mask their shame with any cover: and to ensure they do not long enjoy the fruits of their treachery, some serve them with their own rule by keeping no word with them. At this time, **Michiel Renichon**, a Priest and Pastor in the land of Namur, was captured disguised in soldiers' clothing. This man confessed that Archduke Ernst of Austria, who then ruled the Spanish Netherlands on behalf of Spain, had said to him: "Son, if you do that which you have promised me, and kill the Tyrant," meaning Prince Maurice, "you shall go straight to Paradise." Also, the Councillor Assonleville <note>Christophe d'Assonleville, a prominent diplomat and member of the Council of State in Brussels</note> had assured him that, by the power of a Mass that would be performed in his presence, he would be invisible during the fulfillment of his purpose. Wherefore they have frequently lashed out at me in their sermons and meetings, for no other reason than because I was King: this they held to be the greatest evil. But because they were ashamed to confess such a thing openly, they performed a narrower investigation of my deeds; the mote in my eye seemed to them a great beam <note>A reference to the biblical parable in Matthew 7:3 regarding hypocrisy.</note>: and if by chance any false gossip to my disadvantage came to their ears, giving them such fine material, they knew how to make use of it masterfully. ### THE FIFTEENTH BOOK OF THE REFORMATION.

<margin>1596.</margin>

Afterward, the King had great difficulty with the clergy, who gave clearer signs of their design. When the Earl of *Huntley*, who <margin>\* *Camden’s Annals, Vol. IV, 592.*</margin> had killed the Earl of *Mouray* <note>Also spelled Moray</note> \*, very strongly petitioned the King to be received into grace and reconciled with the church, the *Consistory* <note>The local church council or Presbytery</note>, especially at *Edinburgh*, set themselves strongly against this, raving and ranting against the King and his Council.

<margin>Turmoil and riot in Edinburgh. From the letters of the Agent A. Damman to the States [General] written on March 22 and July 17. In *Epistolae Ecclesiasticae* <note>Ecclesiastical Letters</note> p. 49, 54. Ludovicus Molinatus’s *Supplement to the Admonition to the Builders of a State within a State* <note>Original Latin: *Corollar. ad Parenesim ad Ædificatores imperii in imperio*</note>. London edition, 1657, by R. Daniel, p. 119, 125.</margin>

Master *David Black*, a Minister of *St. Andrews* at *Edinburgh*, cried out openly from the pulpit with great vehemence: "That the King had now revealed his evil intention, his wicked and treacherous heart (hitherto covered with hypocrisy), since he had allowed the *Popish* <note>A term used by reformers for Roman Catholics</note> Earls to return to the country and to their own people; that the King was flighty and an *Apostate* or one who had fallen from the faith; that the Kings, as many as there were, were children of the Devil; that the Devil had his seat in the Court and in the greatest courtiers; that he expected no good from the Scottish Queen and therefore could not pray for her; that Queen *Elizabeth* was an atheist <note>Original: *godverlaekster*—one who mocks or abandons God</note>." He also said that the Lords of the Court were unbelievers who allowed themselves to be bribed through greed. All this came to the King’s ears, even through the English ambassador, insofar as it concerned his Queen. Therefore, the Minister was summoned before the Council. He came, but said that he would answer neither the King nor his Council. If offense had been given or taken, it was the office of the church to investigate and judge the matter.

He was summoned a second time, with a specific <margin>\* See also Dr. Bramhall’s *Warning against the Scottish Discipline*, chapter IV, pages 18, 19.</margin> description of the crimes with which he was charged. The clergy appeared in *Black's* place, saying how it conflicted with the freedom of the church that such unfounded accusations were given credit. One ought to send *Black* to the *Consistory*. This matter did not belong to the King’s tribunal; indeed, they openly threatened and testified that, unless the King desisted, they would defend their rights by issuing a public writing which they called a *Declinatorium* <note>A legal plea declining the jurisdiction of a court</note>, intended to withdraw themselves from the civil court. By this, they would openly testify that violence was being done to *Christ*, and that the secular power was usurping *Christ's* kingdom and church. No sooner said than done. That document was drafted, and many copies were found throughout the *Consistories*, with earnest warnings to all Ministers to sign it and to commend this cause—not *Black's* but *God's*—to *God* with their private and public prayers. The King commanded the assembly of Ministers who were directing this work to disperse. However, they remained together and sent word to the King through some of their number that he had himself to blame,

->HISTORY OF THE REFORMATION BOOK XV.<-

<margin>1597.</margin>
<margin>The States of Holland grant their request under a certain condition.</margin>
<margin>* Revised, or reviewed.</margin>
<margin>See the Answer of the States of Holland to those of Zeeland, among the Documents of the Justification of the Resolution taken on August 4, 1617, p. 75; Grotius's *Apology* II 17; Uytenbogaert's *History* p. 305; *His Life* p. 37. Persisting in Holland toward this same end, their request was finally granted by the States on the twenty-third of December <note>Original: "Wintermaendt" (Winter-month), an old Dutch term for December.</note>, yet under the condition, *that in the national Synod one should re-examine* <note>The Dutch term "resumeren" implies a formal review or reconsideration of the text.</note> *the Belgic Confession in the fear of God*, and consider how the Dutch Reformed churches might best be established, maintained, and increased in good unity according to God’s Word, while also removing the difficulties that had arisen. For in various ecclesiastical disputes, one party had sometimes accused the other of opposing that confession. Some had asserted that it bound no one further than it agreed with the Word of God, and also that it contained ambiguities or contradictory things and could not serve as a fixed rule of doctrine. The States sought to eliminate this cause for strife through a proper revision. At that time, this decision was not opposed by any minister. However, because the other provinces—no matter how much the churchmen urged them—continued to refuse to call the Synod together, and the permission of Holland in this matter could extend no further than a single vote, the Synod was delayed for many years, specifically by the States of Utrecht.

<margin>Anna van den Hove imprisoned in Brussels and buried alive for the sake of Religion. Bor XXXIV, 31. Grotius *History* VI, 285, 286. *History of the Martyrs* p. 503 and 504.</margin>
On the side of the Spanish Netherlands, there occurred at this time another terrible instance of "heretic-killing," as it was called; this was also used by the States of the United Netherlands as a reason to resist foreign powers who sought to reconcile them with Spain; for it showed what was to be expected from the Spanish in matters of religion. Two sisters, named Rampaerts, lived in Brussels with Anna van den Hove, a forty-year-old maidservant who served the sisters. All three were cast into prison on suspicion that their feelings on matters of faith did not align with the Roman Church. When the two sisters—overcome by threats, the prayers of friends, and the attractions of life, which even manly spirits might succumb to—obtained mercy by confessing their ignorance, this maidservant was not moved in the least. Rather, she testified with modest words *that she, being a woman, by her nature and humble status, was beyond any suspicion of inciting rebellion, and also, she believed, her feelings were right, or if it were otherwise, it was a simple error, and it would be just for them to treat her with kindness:*

# HISTORY OF THE REFORMATION BOOK XV.

<margin>1597.</margin> ...but if someone, carried away by fear, were to lie against their conscience—even if they spoke with the truth—that great evil was for God to avenge, not man. When her case was considered in the Council, it is said that Archduke Albert of Austria (a son of the late Maximilian the Second, that mild-tempered Emperor), who ruled the Spanish Netherlands after the death of his brother, Archduke Ernest, had answered when asked for his opinion: *Follow the Edicts.* <note>original: "Plakkaeten." These were the "Placards" or bloody edicts issued by Charles V and Philip II that mandated the death penalty for heresy.</note> But one must wonder even more that such a cruel punishment, which was so hateful to the onlookers, pleased the judges. She was buried alive under the earth outside of Brussels, on the Varen Heijvelt <note>Literally "Fern Heath," a location near Brussels.</note>. Yet it is believed that the authors of this cruelty had expected her to show regret or apostasy. For once placed in the dug pit, they first threw earth on her feet, then on her body up to her neck, with the Jesuits asking her each time if she had changed her mind, enticing her with the offer of mercy: but she cried out with an undaunted spirit, *He who seeks to save his life here shall lose it hereafter.* <note>A reference to the words of Jesus in the Gospels, such as Matthew 16:25.</note> She also prayed to God for help until the executioner finally covered her face with earth. Then he jumped upon her body several times, and she could still be heard calling out most piteously from under the earth, to the great dismay of the bystanders. The steadfastness of this woman was proclaimed everywhere with great pity and praise. The novelty of the case caused people to speak of it more and for longer; whereas in former times, the killing of many thousands was passed over lightly after only a brief account. Afterward, the Archduke found it advisable in similar situations to restrain people with threats or, if the matter became pressing, with more secret punishments. So that since then, as far as I know, no one in the Spanish Netherlands has been seen put to death for matters of faith. Between the Reformed <term>Gereformeerden: The mainstream Calvinist church</term> and the Anabaptists <term>Doopsgesinden: "Baptism-minded" or Mennonite groups who practiced adult baptism</term>, a conflict then arose—as if there were not already enough difference between the two—over this deceased servant girl, each party claiming she had died in their confession; her name and end were even recorded in the martyr books of both groups.

<margin>*History of the Anabaptist Martyrs, pages 847, 848.*</margin> However, the Anabaptists brought forward several Roman Catholic writers who had nothing to lose in this dispute and testified in their favor.

It also notes the subsequent dispute between Reformed and Anabaptist Christians who both claimed her as a martyr for their respective traditions.</summary>

<image-desc>An ornate woodcut initial letter 'I' decorated with scrolling foliage and floral patterns.</image-desc> IN Holland, it was now increasingly observed that the <term>Regents</term> <note>The "Regenten" were the wealthy merchant-class families who held political power in Dutch cities.</note> intended to uphold the common liberty for other denominations as well as for the Reformed. This was seen particularly in Amsterdam regarding the <term>Mennonites</term> <note>original: "Doopsgezinden." A group of Anabaptists known for their pacifism and refusal to swear oaths.</note>, who were treated and even cherished with all manner of favor and protection, even though many among the clergy were unfavorably disposed toward them. For the Magistrates of that great merchant city also sought to advance the matter of commerce through this means; knowing that these were people of great industry, and that they brought much advantage to the city by propagating all kinds of trade and business. It happened in the past summer that a certain sum of money belonging to several Mennonites in Amsterdam, coming from Spain, had been seized by English warships and was being held in England under the pretext that the proofs of ownership, which the owners had sent to London, had not been confirmed with the customary oath <note>Mennonites followed the biblical command "let your yes be yes," and thus refused to swear formal oaths, which often caused legal difficulties in international trade.</note>. Therefore, they requested and obtained a letter of recommendation from the Magistrates of the city of Amsterdam to Lord <term>Noël de Caron</term>, Lord of Schoonewalle, Envoy of the United Netherlands at the court of England, of the following content:

<margin>Recommendation of the Magistrates of Amsterdam on behalf of the Mennonites.</margin>

I shall insert his own words here, because of the weight of the matters. He then spoke this language:

->My Lords,<-

<margin>Speech of Mr. Cornelis Pieterszoon Hooft, <term>Burgomaster</term> <note>The chief magistrate or mayor of a Dutch city.</note> of the City of Amsterdam, to the other Magistrates.</margin>
<margin>The goal of the arms was freedom.</margin>
*We would have considered ourselves fortunate before this, had we been able to bring it to this point: that the goal of taking up arms extended no further than to ward off violence and tyranny, not to rule over the conscience of others in matters of faith;* <margin>Seeking defenses for liberty, not the license to attack others. <note>original: "Libertati præsidia quærentes non licentia ad impugnandum alios."</note> Livy, book 3, chapter 53.</margin> *seeking—to speak with the words of another—a refuge for liberty, and not an unrestrained power to attack others. Also, neither we, nor Prince William <note>William the Silent, Prince of Orange (1533–1584), the leader of the Dutch Revolt.</note> of highly praised memory, while being out of the country, would have ever found the means to get any footing in the land, had not the inhabitants, and among them many Catholics who were repulsed by Spanish cruelty, opened the gates to us themselves,* <margin>All coercion of conscience is improper.</margin> *with the firm hope that no one would be burdened in his conscience. Therefore, I still cannot understand that one ought to apply any compulsion to anyone's mind, but I judge that one must let each person live in all freedom, as far as it may be done without endangering our liberty obtained through God’s grace: otherwise, one might rightfully object to us what Valerius and Horatius <note>Two Roman heroes who helped restore the Republic after the tyranny of the Decemviri.</note> objected to the people in Rome at the time of the change of the <term>Ten Men</term> <note>The Decemviri, a ten-man commission in ancient Rome that briefly held absolute power.</note>:* <margin>Livy, ibid.</margin> † *Through hatred of cruelty, you rush into cruelty, and almost before you are free yourselves, you already wish to lord it over your adversaries. Shall our city then never rest from the severity of the Magistrates against the people, or the people against the Magistrates? We have more need of a shield than a sword. He is humble enough and more who lives with equal right in the city, neither inflicting nor suffering injury.* <note>original: "† Crudelitatis odio in crudelitatem ruitis, & ante penè quam ipsi liberi sitis, dominari jam in adversarios vultis. Nunquamne quiescet civitas nostra à suppliciis, aut patrum in plebem Romanam, aut plebis in patres ? Scuto nobis magis quam gladio opus est. Satis superque humilis est, qui jure æquo in civitate vivit, nec in ferendo injuriam nec patiendo."</note> *And if one might understand that some government had a right over the conscience—which we could not grant to the King of Spain, despite his great power—then it would, above all, not be fitting for us;* <margin>Not fitting for us above all.</margin> *for we did not come into the land under such conditions, nor were we let in or received by those who were already here.* <margin>It is not strange that so many various persuasions have not yet joined the Reformed church. Means to bring them there.</margin> *Since these lands, notwithstanding the heavy persecution of <term>Popery</term> <note>A historical term for the Roman Catholic Church, often used by Protestant writers of this era.</note>, were subject to various other persuasions, which mostly consisted of people of pious conduct who, if necessary, were ready to lay down their lives for it, it is not to be wondered at that all of them, in a time of twenty or twenty-five years, could not be brought to one single understanding; especially that large number which held to the Papacy. To draw all of these together, as much as is feasible, to the Reformed church, [continues onto next page...]*

# HISTORY

<margin>1597.</margin>
...remark, it seems to me, subject to correction, that the *Church Ordinances* <note>The set of rules governing the organization and practices of the Reformed Church.</note> ought to be directed in such a way that those who wish to present themselves for the Lord's Supper are not questioned so sharply on many points. One should also not impose upon newcomers that they must attend the sermon usually given before the Lord's Supper, which serves to make a verbal confession of faith before the Minister: for although the vast majority are simple, plain folk, poorly provided with the knowledge to speak on the foundation of these matters; nevertheless, hearing that sermon might serve as a burden to someone more experienced, who might not be able or willing to agree with the aforementioned confession—whether on the point of *Predestination* <note>The theological doctrine that God has eternally ordained the salvation or damnation of souls, a major point of contention in the Dutch Reformed Church.</note> or any other point—which he would seem to do by being present in the gathering; unless he wished to contradict that which did not agree with his conscience, which would not be fitting in such a gathering. Furthermore, silence there might also weigh upon his conscience, appearing as a deception against his own conviction, which would be entirely contrary to the example of the pious old man *Eleazar* <note>A Jewish martyr mentioned in 2 Maccabees 6, who refused to even *pretend* to eat forbidden meat, choosing death rather than setting a bad example for the youth by appearing to violate his faith.</note>.

<margin>
Foreigners should not be allowed into the government of the church.
</margin>
Furthermore, it is provided by the charters and privileges of these lands and cities for weighty reasons that none but the native-born may be admitted to the civil government; experience teaching that the common people, in any form of government, can least tolerate people who have come in from outside. Just as it is well known how strictly the other provinces, especially those of *Brabant*, insisted that they would not tolerate any *Hollanders* in any states or offices, so should attention also be paid, in my opinion, to the church government. One should not allow persons there who were not eligible, according to the privileges, to be employed in the civil government; since it is considered laudable and necessary that a good unity and mutual understanding be maintained between the civil and church governments, which does not sit well with foreigners. Indeed, in *Holland*, foreigners should not be preferred over the native-born in government; for besides the fact that in all state administration it is a primary point to know the nature of the lands and people, it is also no small matter that the conduct of affairs should rest with persons of a serious, steady, and peaceful mind, which virtues, in my view, have more place among the native-born than among those who have come from other lands to live here. It seems, therefore, quite absurd that *Elders* <note>Lay leaders in the Reformed Church who, along with the Minister, govern the local congregation.</note> born elsewhere should be employed here in *Holland* in particular *Church Councils*, and in other *Classical* and *Synodal* <term>Classical and Synodal</term> <note>Referring to regional (Classis) and provincial/national (Synod) assemblies of the church.</note> meetings; and there not only take notice of the disputes that occur, but also make decisions and [judgments...]

### BOOK XVI OF THE REFORMATION.

...to make <note>This follows from the previous page: "to make [laws]..."</note> over a land and people of a different nature, with whom they took refuge, and who received and cherished them as kindly as native-born citizens. Added to this is that these are people of whom it is to be feared that most, when necessity presses, would easily abandon us, or possibly <term>turn their coats entirely</term> <note>original: "den rok geheel omkeeren" — to change sides or loyalties</note>, as has been found more than too often in other corners of the land. One already hears how some of the most prominent (merely because prosperity decreased for a while) let it be known that they must depart, leaving us stuck in difficulty and to deal with the enemy. Besides that experience recently taught how, in the time of <term>Leicester</term> <note>Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester, who led an unsuccessful English intervention in the Netherlands (1585–1587) and was supported by the more radical Calvinist factions.</note>, the principal heads, such as Elders and Deacons, and also some others, mostly Flemings, Brabanters, and Walloons, were not only very restless but also incited others, natives of the land and naturally peaceful people, to similar unrest, so that many of the ministers were infected with the same defect, to the great danger of the fatherland.

<margin>1597.</margin>
<margin>
* It is the duty of a stranger and a resident to do nothing but his own business, to inquire nothing about another's, and least of all to be curious about another's republic. <note>original Latin: "Peregrini atque incolæ officium est, nihil præter suum negotium gerere, nihil de alieno inquirere, minimeque de alienâ republicâ esse curiosum."</note> Cicero, *On Duties*, Book 1.
</margin>
Here the excellent saying of Cicero applies: *It is the duty of a stranger and a resident that he only perform his own work, not pry into another's, much less meddle with another's Republic*: as also that remarkable example of Moses, who, choosing rulers over each tribe, appointed those who were born from the same, not from others.

<margin>The management of the ecclesiastical ministry here consists mostly of foreigners.</margin>
It is, my Lords, partly known that most of the difficulty that appeared, and still appears, in some parts of the United Netherlands is and was caused by the foreigners who have come into government there. It is then high time to provide against this in the future, the more so because we see how the foreigners, immediately after the surrender of this city <note>Referring to the "Alteration" of Amsterdam in 1578, when the city joined the rebellion and became Protestant.</note>, came into the church council and subsequently, from time to time, bring into practice the habit of keeping those offices among themselves, excluding natives as much as possible. Through which these people also labor to bring in similar foreign Preachers.

<margin>What benefits they have enjoyed from the Magistrates.</margin>
And although the Magistrates looked upon all this with favor, and very kindly received and richly maintained the Preachers chosen by them; and that the poor of the congregation, though they are mostly foreigners who have lived here only a short time, are provided for by the <term>Almoners</term> <note>original: "Huisfittenmeesters" — officials responsible for the relief of the "settled" poor who were not members of a specific church.</note>, contrary to the old custom of this city, as well as the other poor citizens; and that all the <term>alms</term> <note>original: "aelmoeffen"</note> of the Deacons, which are bolstered annually by the city with large sums of money, are distributed to the Church-poor alone, and that throughout the entire year, whereas the other old citizens, when they fall into poverty, are only [provided for] for a few weeks in the winter, for lack of means, by the Regents of the

<margin>1597.</margin>

It is to be thought that those Magistrates would then pay little heed to how those Clergymen—who never received such deeds from them—might regard them. It is to be feared that the expansion of the Gospel is more hindered than promoted by such means. # THE HISTORY OF THE REFORMATION BOOK XVI.

<margin>1597.</margin>
...to seek, and not to adopt any religion lightly, as some other peoples do, *who commonly obey their Princes in that matter whenever they change their religion.* I cannot believe that my Lords of the <term>Law</term> <note>original: "Heeren van de Wet" — a term referring to the city magistrates and legal authorities</note> are of such an opinion that those who cannot conform to the church in all things should therefore be subjected to any slander or other difficulty; for otherwise, if one were to follow the opinion of the <term>Preachers</term> <note>original: "Predikanten" — the Dutch term for Reformed ministers</note>, or indeed of even one of them, then those who are now working hardest to keep the hostile Spaniards at arm's length would be the very first to be mistreated by those to whom they thought they had done a great service. Then tyranny in these lands would not cease, but only the tyrant would have changed. Those who were previously themselves persecuted and oppressed would now *(appropriating to themselves all the advantage that, through God's grace and at the expense and burden of the entire community, has been gained against the Spaniards)* persecute and oppress others. This intention, while the blood of the <term>Papal persecution</term> <note>original: "Pauſſelyke vervolging" — referring to the Catholic persecution of Protestants during the earlier stages of the Dutch Revolt</note> is still so fresh before our eyes, I cannot entrust to any reasonable native-born citizen, believing that if any of them might have been misled by some wrong advice, they will change their opinion upon looking closer at the matter and considering it well. Some will perhaps disregard my reasons or reject them entirely because my wife goes to hear the sermons of the <term>Mennonites</term> <note>a radical Reformation group known for pacifism and believer's baptism, often viewed with suspicion by the state church</note>. But what can be done? At my urging, she has indeed been to the [Reformed] church, but she declares that she is not as well edified there as by the others. This situation I have in common with many, including people of standing, and it is worthy of neither slander nor punishment.

<margin>To what extent the Reformed should be brought into the government.</margin>
*I do not wish to deny that those of the <term>Reformed Religion</term> <note>the official state church in the Dutch Republic</note> might be brought into the government ahead of others of equal ability; but I also believe that one would bring the state of the country into the greatest uncertainty if one were to set as a fixed rule that, mistrusting all others, one must trust only those who make profession of that Religion.* Since experience teaches, and examples show, that the most unpious make the least difficulty in adopting any Religion, if it only serves to gain credit and achieve their purpose. So that the Spaniard, knowing this, would surely find means to pick out certain persons and take advantage of it at an opportune time. Therefore it seems most certain to me,

<margin>See the Preface to the Peace Negotiations of Cologne, p. † † iii b.</margin>
*that one, staying within the bounds of the privileges, should work to get people at the helm who lead a consistently good, honest, civil life, and who are held as such, and as lovers of the fatherland, both outside and inside the congregation.* Accordingly, the <term>Church Ordinance</term> <note>original: "Kerkelijke Ordening" — the set of rules governing the organization and activities of the Reformed Church</note> should also be directed accordingly,

->H I S T O R Y<-

<margin>
1597.
The <term>Gospel net</term> <note>original: "Euangeliſch net" — a metaphor for the reach and inclusivity of the Protestant church</note> ought to be cast as wide as possible.
</margin>
...that the <term>Gospel net</term> might be cast out as far and wide as is at all feasible, without binding that <term>Church Order</term> <note>original: "Ordening" — the regulations governing church life and government</note> to the opinions of people who, having come from elsewhere, are not sufficiently familiar with the nature of this land and people; or those who imagine that the Church Order or government of <term>Geneva</term> <note>The city-state where John Calvin established his model of strict ecclesiastical discipline</note>, being nothing more than a single city, was formed to fit all nations and should be adopted by them. This is a misunderstanding; for one finds that many things can be done on a small scale that do not succeed on a large one. Even those of the <term>Papacy</term> <note>original: "Pauſdom" — the Roman Catholic Church</note>, however strict, have learned well enough that they must allow for differences in ceremonies between one country and another, so that they not only tolerated each other in various weighty matters but also held those of a different understanding to be pillars and prominent lights of the church. Furthermore, one hears daily that the <term>Preachers</term> <note>original: "Predikanten" — Reformed ministers</note>, to strengthen their doctrine, cite with great respect <term>Church Fathers</term> <note>original: "Oudtvaders" — the early Christian theologians of the first centuries</note> and writers from the Papacy, who otherwise differ far from them in many other, even grave, points. 

As for me, many inhabitants know that I was always more inclined to obey than to rule; that while I held no office, I showed the <term>Magistrates</term> <note>original: "Overheit" — the civil governing authorities</note> proper obedience, wishing to remain in that state; but it was not to be my lot. Being called to government, a task for which I felt unsuited, I have sought to make a virtue of necessity and put my small talent to use, setting aside my private affairs and the advancement of my own house, and forgoing means to gain great personal advantage. This was solely to better satisfy my conscience in serving the city’s affairs, partially consuming myself so that I might better devote myself to the <term>common cause</term> <note>original: "gemeene ſaeke" — the public good and the collective effort of the Dutch Revolt</note>; hoping in particular that, by so doing, I might also contribute something to fending off the <term>Spanish yoke</term> <note>original: "Spaenſ-jok" — the rule of the Spanish Habsburgs over the Netherlands</note>. 

The goal was to pursue the true end of <term>Dutch arms</term> <note>original: "Hollandtſche waepenen" — the military efforts of the Dutch provinces</note>: namely, that alongside the security of the followers of the <term>Reformed Religion</term> <note>The official Protestant faith of the Dutch Republic</note>, all others who cannot yet agree with it—and yet help to pay the burdens of the war as much as any others, behaving themselves civilly and peacefully—might be maintained in equal rest and peace. This ensures that no one is forced in their conscience, but is instead tolerated with <term>Christian forbearance</term> <note>original: "Chriſtelijke doogſaemheit" — the principle of religious toleration and patience toward those of different faiths</note>, patience, and support, until such time as they might be brought to a better footing through Christian teachings and good progress, without misbehaving against one another, much less against the Magistrates. Such unruly intensity has been passed over in silence by the <term>Consistory</term> <note>original: "Kerkenraedt" — the governing body of the local Reformed church</note> and even the Magistrates until now. And from this lack of discipline, one must expect even greater discourtesy. This unlawful conduct makes me...

# H I S T O R I E

<margin>1597.</margin>...to make [them] equal. On the contrary, they ought to behave themselves in their preaching with foresight and moderation, without thrusting themselves too deeply or too boldly into the office of the Government <note>The secular municipal authorities</note>, as has happened before: especially in the case of alleged witchcraft <note>Hooft was famously skeptical of witchcraft trials, often clashing with the more dogmatic clergy who pushed for prosecutions</note> against that balance-maker <note>A maker of weighing scales</note>, near the old bridge, on the <term>Water</term> <note>The Damrak, Amsterdam’s main harbor at the time</note>, who moved from here to <term>Middelburg</term>. In this matter, indeed, such a prejudice was instilled by the <term>Predikanten</term> <note>The Reformed ministers</note>, without proper knowledge of the facts and, as is common, based only on the testimony of one party, that they did not hesitate to trouble the <term>Heeren van de Wet</term> <note>Literally "Lords of the Law," referring to the city’s Aldermen and Judges</note> with many visits and to stir them up sufficiently. By this, the Gentlemen [of the Law] were even more worried and in great danger regarding that matter—which in itself was very difficult and full of peril. But I hope that the <term>Predikanten</term> will now, through these past events, have learned enough to moderate themselves properly in all things for the future, so that my Lords the Aldermen shall have less trouble in governing this good congregation in good peace and unity.
*To which may God give His blessing.*

HISTORY OF THE REFORMATION BOOK XVI.

<margin>1598</margin>
Having been accepted and having made his profession of faith, he was required to make a new confession of his faith; therefore, he joined the German congregation <note>original: *Duitsche gemeente*; in the 16th-century Netherlands, this usually referred to the Dutch-speaking Reformed Church to distinguish it from the French-speaking Walloon church</note>, where this was not the custom. After eating the bread of the Lord's Supper with them two or three times, he had abstained from them, saying to one of the brothers that he found himself restrained in conscience. Then some Ministers came to him on several occasions to instruct him. Unable to reach an agreement, they asked him finally whether he would come to them and remain with his previous first faith, or whether he would persevere in his newly begun change; desiring an answer to this. But he, fearing to be taken into custody, found it advisable, after a stay of three-quarters of a year, to depart secretly, and returned again here to this city. He had studied Latin in Utrecht for two years, had reached the sixth school <note>The "sixth school" refers to the grade levels in a Latin School; reaching the sixth class indicated a significant level of secondary education</note>, and had exercised himself so well that he understood that language reasonably well. Four years ago, he learned to read Greek from someone who also explained it to him, and a year and a half ago, he also did some work in Hebrew. He declared that no one had exhorted or brought him to the change of his first faith, but he had done so of his own accord; because he could not understand that Almighty God, according to His divine essence, was everywhere. This view he had maintained in London and here in this city. He confessed that the little book titled *The Light of Truth* <note>original: *Het Licht der Waerheit*</note> was his own work, and that he had allowed it to be published without anyone's advice, declaring the content to be his confession of faith, in which he persevered. In the manuscript from which he had the booklet printed, some words were crossed out by him because the printer was hesitant to print them. This is the primary information found recorded regarding his confession. Some Lords <note>Referring to the city magistrates or "Heeren"</note> leaned toward severity; efforts were also made to transport him to The Hague <note>The seat of the high court of Holland, where religious offenders often faced harsher sentences than in Amsterdam</note>. However, the Lord Burgomaster Hooft, who sought to stop this, concerned himself so much with this matter and its consequences that he addressed the Lords Sheriff, Burgomasters, and Aldermen, in the presence of the two Pensionaries <note>Legal advisors and secretaries who managed the city's legal and administrative affairs</note>, on the twenty-sixth of the same month, with these words:

Thus, I judge this matter to be of such great consequence and among the most weighty that could be discussed in this country; for this was the primary root cause through which we fell into this long, difficult, and heavy war <note>The Eighty Years' War against Spain, which was sparked in large part by the persecution of Protestants</note>. <margin>
Further disclosure concerning Vogelsang's person and opinions.
</margin>
prisoner, I have never, to my knowledge, known him personally; however, during his imprisonment, I have heard from credible people that he always conducted himself piously and honestly, despite his impoverished circumstances and the heavy burden of his wife and children, without bothering anyone, and that he was held to be one who strove for his own salvation. I understand that he was cut off <note>original: *afsnijden*; excommunicated</note> from the congregation a while ago because of the opinion he now holds. With this excommunication, the church, having done its part, ought to be satisfied without troubling the poor man further, since he, according to the teachings of Paul <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 5:12–13: "For what have I to do with judging those also who are outside?... But those who are outside God judges."</note>, is now outside her jurisdiction and no longer concerns her. It is also certain that someone recently visiting his house to see how things stood there found his young children and his wife on the Lord's Day, with bowed knees, lying upon the earth, calling upon the Lord before their meal. From this, it seems evident that he has raised them in the fear of God according to his own understanding. That this prisoner, and with him his innocent children, should have to suffer so much because he drew some strange and literal opinion from the Scriptures regarding the Divine Being seems to me, given the character and nature of these lands, an all too harsh procedure. Since he is a stranger without influence, there is no danger of an uprising to be feared from him. Moreover, it is common, not only here but in all of Europe, to see representations of the Holy Trinity, and especially of God the Father, depicted in human form. This is allowed to pass unnoticed in old churches and paintings. No one was ever prosecuted for that. I also leave it to the wise to judge whether this man's opinion regarding the form and stature of the Divine Being is any stranger than that of the Papists <note>A term used by Protestants for Roman Catholics</note> regarding their bread of the Mass, or that of the Lutherans regarding their <term>Ubiquity|The theological doctrine that Christ's physical body is present everywhere at once</term>. However strange these things may be, no one undertakes or even thinks of treating those people in such a way.

<margin>
The harmful consequence of persecution.
</margin>
I know well that the Preachers sometimes seek to stir up the authorities against such people. But if we were to act according to their advice, what would follow? Would not everything throughout all of Christendom...

### THE SIXTEENTH BOOK OF THE REFORMATION.

<margin>1598</margin>
...thrown into turmoil—we domestically against one another, and abroad against the Lutherans and Papists <note>original: *Papisten*; a contemporary, often derogatory term for Roman Catholics</note>, and they in turn against all others. In this way, one would labor toward a Babel-like confusion. Surely David, a man after God’s heart, who was so zealous to build the Lord a temple of stone, 
<margin>Religion must not be promoted by external force.</margin>
was forbidden from that, because of so many wars conducted and blood shed, although those could be better justified than our own; it is then, in my judgment, a great misunderstanding that people now wish to build up the living temples of the Lord through the force and compulsion of external weapons. It is quite true that blasphemy in the Old Covenant was punished with death; but also idolatry, the cursing of parents <note>original: *Ouderen*; can refer to parents or elders</note>, adultery, and other evils, upon which much lesser or small punishments now follow. And should one now punish people with death over matters that the Ministers <term>Predikanten</term> <note>The Protestant clergy of the public church</note> proclaim to be blasphemies, and which the Magistrates are not permitted to judge?
<margin>The word blasphemy is being stretched too far.</margin>
The word blasphemy is also being stretched so far that it encompasses the Roman Catholics, the Lutherans, the Mennonites, the Enthusiasts <term>Geestdrijvers</term> <note>Literally "spirit-drivers"; a term for radical sects or individuals claiming direct spiritual revelation</note>, and, so it seems, almost all who do not agree with the church in everything. 
<margin>Considerations against the incitement to persecution.</margin>
The Lord of Aldegonde <note>Filips van Marnix, Lord of Saint-Aldegonde, a prominent diplomat and theologian</note> seeks to incite the States to persecute the Enthusiasts. But let him know that the number of those whom Alva <note>The Duke of Alva, the Spanish governor notorious for his "Council of Blood" which executed thousands</note> had put to death for matters of faith—of whom he spoke in his Oration at the Diet of Worms in the year seventy-eight, to move the Estates to compassion—did not consist solely of the Reformed; for Alva was the common enemy of all persuasions, and for that reason the costs of the war were borne with wonderful and unbelievable goodwill by the common people of all sorts of persuasions. Those among us who now wish to persecute were, without doubt, of a different mind when they were fugitives and subject to persecution themselves. It will be said that the Spaniard persecuted unjustly, and that we would do it justly. But that same thing is also said by the Papists and Lutherans where they are masters. Each believes justice to be on their side, and no one will lack material to fall into similar cruelty. If one wishes to take that path, the ruin of the country is bound to it. Therefore, one ought to ward off the beginnings of that evil. Instead of external compulsion, one ought to use spiritual and edifying means, proceeding from the spirit of knowledge, discretion, and gentleness. In this way, the church is built. If one now wishes to handle this Vogelsang harshly for his literal understanding, and the Enthusiasts because they, in Aldegonde's opinion, drive some things too spiritually, then the persecution shall first begin on two sides, and possibly go much further in a short time; if one wishes to follow the discretion of certain Ministers. But it would be be...

<header>HISTORY</header>

<margin>
1598.
One ought to forbid that incitement and keep the clergy in order.
</margin>
...better, and for the security of the state, that one should prevent such incitement with authority, and inform the clergy that they must keep themselves within the bounds of their calling. On this point, Mr. Johan Huig <note>Johann Huyghe, a legal advisor and diplomat from Hamburg</note>, Counselor of the city of Hamburg, once advised the Amsterdam exiles to be careful <margin>† See p. 592, 593.</margin>†. If one pays no heed to this, it will be regretted. Experience teaches that these people, when given too much leeway, *can hardly restrain themselves*; and they seek not only to stir up persecution against other denominations, but also cause disturbances among their own, and rebellion against the authorities. Thus, in the time of Leicester <note>Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester, who acted as Governor-General of the United Provinces (1585–1588) and often sided with the strict Calvinist faction against local city regents</note>, some pointed out the best Magistrates in their sermons as if with their fingers, stirring up the congregation against them and putting them in danger of life and limb. Not because they had changed in matters of religion, but only because they did not manage the affairs of government according to the mind of certain churchmen. <margin>See p. 806.</margin> What also happened in Scotland less than a year ago will still be fresh in the minds of some of these gentlemen, when the congregation was brought to arms against the King <note>Referring to the tensions between King James VI of Scotland and the Presbyterian clergy</note>, and that action was attributed to the prompting and pressure of the Holy Spirit. I leave others to judge whether some ministers <margin>Some ministers behaved rudely toward the Burgomasters.</margin> here in this city have not also behaved unworthily toward the Honorable Burgomasters on several occasions, when they were ordered to marry some young people outside the usual time, after the evening sermon; and they, although that was an indifferent matter <term>middelmatige saeke</term> <note>Also known as 'adiaphora,' these are church practices not explicitly commanded or forbidden by the Bible, which the civil government claimed the right to regulate</note>, dared to say quite rudely that the Magistrates should not charge them in such matters; and at another time, if the Burgomasters wished to be served or obeyed in such matters, they should provide more ministers. Whether one acts with such justice and without passion in the choosing of ministers as is proper, those who are called to it know. However, I believe I know for certain that some ministers dared to demand certain sums of money from the alms to spend at their own discretion, without the knowledge of the deacons. I could relate more grievances, but I shall keep them silent so as not to offend anyone. Nor do I wish what has been said to serve as a reproach; but only to show that something could also be found against those of the church if it could serve the unity of the country; and secondly, to infer from it how dangerous it is to build so entirely upon men. I recall that the Honorable Aldermen <term>Schepenen</term> <note>The judicial body of the city, responsible for trials and sentencing</note>, sixteen years ago, desired the opinion and thoughts of the ministers, for certain reasons, on a specific case; then the servants of the church gave their written judgment, signed with their hands, which sufficiently implied that the person concerned would have to die. But the understanding of the judges differed...

<page-num>829</page-num>
<header>BOOK XVI OF THE REFORMATION.</header>

...many of those advisors, that they let that man go without scandal. 1598

<margin>In the matter of persecution, one must not rely on far-fetched reasons, nor on the judgment of others.</margin>
*To return to the matter at hand, if one compares the opinion of the Ministers, according to their own teaching, with the Holy Scripture to be certain, from what passage of the New Testament shall one then be able to prove with clear words that one must persecute someone over matters of faith? One must not seek to draw this from far-fetched syllogisms and forced consequences: and it seems to me far too dangerous in such a weighty matter, involving life, limb, and salvation, to trust in the hair-splitting subtlety of the learned. These men should not use their intellect to cause those who have fallen into misunderstanding to be persecuted, but rather reflect on how deeply even some of the oldest and most prominent Church Fathers were entangled in heavy errors. In particular, it seems strange that persecution or religious coercion should be urged by those who hold so firmly to Predestination <note>The theological doctrine that God has foreordained the salvation or damnation of every soul; Hooft argues that if God has already decided a person's fate, human punishment is redundant</note>; for if that stands firm, then surely everyone must come to that for which they are destined.*

<margin>Persecution does not suit those who hold firmly to Predestination.</margin>
*Regarding the passages brought forward from the Old Testament, the learned write for and against persecution. Let it suffice us here that among the Jews, in the matter of the Pharisees, Sadducees, and other sects, they did not persecute one another, and that it has always been the ungodly who have persecuted the pious.*

<margin>Capital cases are very burdensome.</margin>
*We know with how much concern capital cases <term>halssaeken: literally "neck-matters," referring to crimes punishable by death</term> are handled by my Lords of the court, and how difficult it was for some Gentlemen from the beginning of this government to decide to sentence thieves to death, even if they had seriously misbehaved, even though the laws of these lands, the punishments included therein, and the constant custom of executing them, were sufficiently known to the Judges and the criminals. But those Gentlemen felt burdened because in the Old Testament no capital punishment was established against theft, and the deliberations that took place regarding this later gave cause for the founding of the house of correction <term>tuchthuis: a reformatory focused on labor and discipline rather than execution, for which Amsterdam became famous</term> of this city. And should one now so easily make capital cases out of errors of faith?*

<margin>The general opinion regarding liberty in matters of Religion in this country, and what it is based upon.</margin>
*Is there not also a general opinion among the people here that no one in this country should be harmed for their faith? An opinion which is surely based on the objective of the war, waged for so many years at such great cost to all inhabitants, for the freedom of Religion; also on various public Declarations and Testimonies made by the Authorities and the Reformed on that point?*

<margin>The Magistrate of Amsterdam should not be more hasty in the matter of persecution than other Administrators.</margin>
*Therefore, speaking with respect, I cannot approve that the Administrators of this city should be the most hasty in the matter of persecution in the entire land: so that it may not be said of us that we walk in the footsteps of the previous Magistrate, who [surpassed] all the Popish <note>Catholic</note> Regents of the other Hollandish cities in the matter of persecution,*

<header>HISTORY</header>

<margin>1598</margin>
...went far beyond. It would be much more reasonable that we, with proper means, opposed it, just as those of Antwerp did in former times—though in vain—even when it was forbidden to speak on behalf of heretics. 

<margin>Whether Vogelsang is punishable because he seeks to propagate his opinion.</margin>
The argument is made that this man does not simply believe his error privately, but also spreads it among others, and is therefore punishable. However, if one considers this well, it does not count so heavily against him: for generally people are inclined to share their understanding of matters of faith with others. Look at the Ministers <note>The *Predikanten*, or Reformed clergy</note>, with what zeal they seek to propagate their doctrine; the same happens with all others of various persuasions, with equal fervor. It is also alleged that this matter has been deliberated with the Lords States <note>The States of Holland or the States General, the provincial and national governing bodies</note> of the land, and a decision made by them that one ought to take action, and specifically to send this man to the Hague to be held there in prison. 

<margin>Remarks on a certain decision of the States against Vogelsang and his booklet.</margin>
I do not wish to speak here against the authority of the States, but rather with proper respect. However, since prosperity is often envied, it seems that we do not find too much favor with some of our neighboring members of the States; a fact that many past incidents have taught us. Regarding the decision supposedly taken by the States concerning the writing and printing of Vogelsang’s booklet—based on the advice of certain theologians and ministers—one should consider whether the States believed that the entire government of this city was unanimously in favor of treating the prisoner harshly. We must ask if they have directed a decision toward us and decided something more severe regarding this city than they would ever wish to be subject to in their own cities. 

For looking closer at the equality of all cities, one does not find that such a course of action has been maintained in any of them. It is known without doubt that while Vogelsang’s entire print run consists of only a few small booklets, other much larger, complete books—perhaps even entire wagon-loads—have been printed elsewhere. These were made by writers who are perhaps held in no better regard by the Ministers than this imprisoned man is. It does not seem new that people sometimes want to help make laws that they themselves have no intention of following. This is seen daily in other matters of great weight; especially in the drafting and establishing of instructions, 

<margin>* Convoy fees. † License fees.</margin>
ordinances, and lists of convoy fees <note>Taxes on goods escorted by warships</note> and license fees <note>Taxes paid for permission to trade with the enemy</note>, as well as in the regulations for the policing of the sea. Those who most often fail to follow these rules themselves are the first to offer to bind the Admiralty Boards in other places to the complete observance of ordinances—ordinances which are shamefully transgressed by them and their own people. Thus, in my opinion, we have good reason to excuse ourselves from complying with the aforementioned decision.

# THE SIXTEENTH BOOK OF THE REFORMATION. 831

<margin>1598</margin>
...Above all, I cannot approve of taking that poor man to the Hague and locking him up there, to the total ruin of his five motherless children and his currently pregnant wife. I still remember how the Old Burgomaster, Doctor Marten Koster *, eleven years ago † <margin>* See concerning him, J. I. Pontanus, *History of Amsterdam*, Book II, chapter 28, page 244. <note>original: "J. I. Pont. Hist. Amst. II. B. 28 c. p. 244."</note> † 1587, February 15. ‡ See Reid. page 169.</margin>, in the Council, with great earnestness and emotion, reported that he had been reliably informed of the intention of the King of Denmark ‡ and other Great Lords to allow themselves to be used to settle the war between the King of Spain and these lands. They established as a fundamental rule from the outset that—just as they and other Princes required their subjects to maintain such a Religion as they saw fit—we likewise in this country should have to adopt such a Religion as pleased the King of Spain. Against this, the aforementioned Gentleman argued with many reasons <margin>No Authority has power over subjects in matters of faith.</margin> serving to prove that no Prince or Magistrate was entitled to any authority over subjects in matters of faith; and he exhorted the Council that they should not, for any reason, allow themselves to be drawn away from that opinion. This was consistent with what had been claimed and maintained at all times from the beginning of the war. If that opinion was then righteous and well-founded—when one was less secure against the King of Spain than we seem to be now—then it seems to me that, with the prosperity that God has graciously granted us under this form of government, it ought not to have changed to the contrary, that is, for the worse.

<margin>The aim of the Churchmen in Amsterdam.</margin>
From the writing of the Church Council <note>The *Kerkenraedt* or Consistory, the governing body of the local Reformed church</note>, submitted last May <note>original: "Bloeijmaendt," literally "Blossom-month," an old Dutch term for May</note>, it can be sufficiently inferred where their intention leads: namely, to establish such order in the matter of Religion that no one of a different Persuasion should be allowed to share his understanding with others—which is there called "sowing his error"—and making those of the Reformed Religion restless, or grieving them in their consciences. This would indeed have some appearance of reason if such people <margin>What should be considered here.</margin> understood themselves to be in error. But since there are many thousands dwelling in such errors who are so well assured of their salvation thereby that they, under Spanish rule, were as encouraged as those of the Reformed Religion to offer up their bodies for it through the most painful death, with what plausibility can one then think that such zealous people—as if they were convinced of error within themselves—could be restrained so far as to not share their understanding with anyone? Just like the Reformed, those of other persuasions also find themselves bound to make their views known to others. If one nevertheless wishes to prevent them from this, one must consider by what means. Without doubt, by the external power of the Magistrate, if one...

# HISTORY

<margin>1598</margin> ...could not be drawn away from their opinion by any verbal instruction. Whereupon it must then be considered whether one should use that power according to the laws of Scripture, or whether one should, alongside it, in the manner of the Papacy, make other laws and edicts. And whether one would execute those edicts, once made and published, with more severity, with more fierceness, and with more success than the King of Spain did. What did he achieve by it? Notwithstanding his great power, to which this <note>The power of the local Dutch magistrates</note> is not to be compared, notwithstanding all his inhuman murdering and burning, one saw the so-called heresies increase more and more, until, after twenty or twenty-five years of slaughter, the common people dared to oppose it, and the matter progressed so far that the country's inhabitants threw that terrible yoke from their necks—not with the intention of having a similar one laid upon them again by those who, alongside others, were delivered from the yoke with so much effort and danger. 

I confess that this man's concern greatly troubled me in the beginning, partly because of the rarity of his opinion, and partly because I saw that some of the Gentlemen <note>The city councilors</note> were so vehement in the matter. But afterwards, considering the unfriendly treatment by the Ministers <note>Predikanten: the official Reformed clergy</note> toward various denominations in particular, and in general toward all those who do not unite with the church; also the incitements of *Aldegonde* <note>Filips van Marnix, Lord of Saint-Aldegonde (1540–1598), a prominent diplomat and theologian</note>, previously mentioned, as well as the fact that recently some members of the Reformed Church who had come from elsewhere, without the knowledge and permission of the Burgomasters, presumed to enter the houses of the *Mennonites* <note>A group of Anabaptists known for their pacifism and refusal to swear oaths</note> against their will, in order to harass the people about their faith—notwithstanding that those zealots knew full well that the *Mennonite* meetings are tolerated throughout the whole land by the Lords *States* and *Magistrates*. 

Bringing these things together, I could conclude nothing else but that once persecution or punishment in matters of faith is permitted, <margin>Persecution, once allowed, will soon spread.</margin> grounds will soon be found to proceed on the same footing against all those who do not join the Reformed Church: whether under the pretext that they spread errors, grieve the consciences of the simple, make the community restless, falsely accuse or contradict the church's doctrine, or even if it were only because, by not entering the congregation, they thereby give a bad example <note>original: "quade erger-gave"; literally, a cause for scandal or falling into sin</note>. 

How far this might go, everyone may consider. I believe that I and those like me are as much concerned with resisting the Spaniards as the very best and most zealous of the *Religion* <note>In this period, "the Religion" (de Religie) specifically referred to the official Dutch Reformed faith</note>; and that such people who resemble me in that matter are found in unbelievable numbers among various denominations within this city. Should all those good people now be so narrowly shut...

Nnnnn

<margin>1598.</margin>
...if the clergymen seem to seek such dominion as would go far beyond my estimation, and I wish to declare that my commitment to the Beggars' cause <note>original: "Geuferij." A term originally used as a slur ("Gueux" or Beggars) for the Dutch rebels against Spain, which they eventually adopted as a badge of honor.</note> has never aimed for that, nor does it now. If the church members may enjoy and retain the free exercise of their Religion in the manner and with the security that they now possess, that is surely much more than they hoped for in the beginning.

<margin>The church ought to be content with its freedom.</margin>
At that time, there was no intention to set laws over anyone in matters of faith. If the understanding and opinion of Gamaliel, of Gallio, and of Claudius Lysias <note>These are three figures from the New Testament (Book of Acts) who refused to persecute early Christians, often cited by proponents of tolerance to show that civil authorities should stay out of religious disputes.</note> were, in our view, grounded in reason then, for what reason should we now feel differently and labor toward any persecution in matters of faith? Especially since the Magistrate is held to be so unskilled in divine or scriptural matters that they are not permitted to judge them. <note>Hooft is pointing out the hypocrisy of the clergy: they claim the government is too "worldly" to understand theology, yet they want the government to use its power to enforce the clergy's theological rules.</note> Furthermore, if the Magistrate were to judge the outward differences in daily life and conduct between the Reformed and other good people, I would not think—to speak freely—that anyone judging impartially and with knowledge would place the Reformed so much higher in terms of morals <note>original: "feden/zeden"</note> (whether in regard to France, England, or even these lands) that one should, for that reason, act with such severity against other honest people. It would therefore be much more reasonable, and more beneficial for the welfare of the country, that we—following the old footing of the government of this country and this city, in which, praise be to God, we fared well—without troubling anyone over matters of Religion, should be willing to bear with each other's faults in matters of faith: as these things are beyond our power and only burden the conscience of the individual who holds them.

<margin>It is best to maintain the old footing of government and tolerate the various denominations.</margin>
So that, by doing so, the common, the usual, the ancient and necessary unity in the state being maintained and nurtured, we may persevere with a common hand in resisting the common enemy. But should those people, who seem to crave new persecution, imagine their opinion to be as well-founded as I, and many thousands with me, hold the contrary to be certain, then I fear that the state of these lands, and of those who ever stood against the Papacy and Spain, will shortly be brought to an irreparable ruin. I fear that these reasons of mine will not initially taste well to some, but I pray that I may enjoy in this the usual right of the Areopagites <note>The Areopagus was the high court of ancient Athens; Hooft is asking the council to judge the merit of his words rather than his person.</note>, so that attention is paid not to my person, but to what is spoken: so that everything may be weighed in sincerity and without prejudice. Then God will, I hope, grant a gracious outcome, and the old proverb—that mutual defense is the safest *—will be found true.

<margin>* Mutual defense is the safest. <note>original Latin: "Mutua defenfio tutiffima."</note></margin>

The Son of God stripped himself of his great Majesty when he sought to further the salvation of men; and we set up I know not what kingdoms, to the ruin and with the ruin of men, and wish to be held for Christ—for that Christ whose deeds differ from ours in everything. If you investigate the cause of this hatred against us, I know not what else I shall say than the truth of the matter: regarding this hatred, I say, against us Greeks, that is, children of the Eastern churches who follow the doctrines, the traditions, the commands, and decrees of the Early Church Fathers. You shall find nothing else than this very thing: that we, maintaining the pure doctrines and traditions of the Fathers, do not allow ourselves to be drawn away by any novelties of any men, nor by deceitful teachings, from those decrees which all the seven general Councils <note>The first seven Ecumenical Councils (from Nicaea I in 325 to Nicaea II in 787) which the Eastern Orthodox Church considers the definitive standards of Christian orthodoxy.</note>—to say nothing of the provincial ones—established firmly. The Symbolum, or the Confession of Faith composed at the first Council of Nicaea and completed at the second Synod <note>Refers to the Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed.</note>, explaining the article of the Holy Spirit most precisely, we preserve uncorrupted. The Symbolum falsely attributed to Athanasius <note>The Athanasian Creed, which the Eastern Church rejected, particularly due to the later Western addition of the *Filioque* clause (stating the Holy Spirit proceeds from both the Father "and the Son").</note>, with that addition by the Roman Popes, we testify to be as clear as day a corruption. We recognize the Roman Pope as the Pope of Rome. None but Christ do we hold, with Paul, to be the universal Head of the universal church. We recognize the same, from his own words, to be that cornerstone of Zion upon which he himself said the church must be built. For, he says, upon this rock (and this rock, says Paul, was Christ) for not upon you, Peter, but upon myself, shall I build my church, as the very diligent Augustine very carefully notes. Since we then believe these things, I do not know why some (as Sanders <note>Nicholas Sanders (c. 1530–1581), an English Catholic polemicist who wrote "De Visibili Monarchia Ecclesiae," attacking the legitimacy of the Eastern and Protestant churches.</note> has godlessly done) dare to compare the Eastern church with the church of the Devil (O great wickedness!). Such is the state of those unchristian minds: whatever does not suit their taste...

...captured and taken into custody in Leiden, [he] recounted how, burdened with heavy debts and thrown from one prison to another by the severity of his creditors, he had for a long time sought some escape from his distress without finding any. But having come to Douai, to the Jesuits, to whom he was accustomed to supply provisions of butter, the Superior of that society had—with a lengthy speech devised for the purpose—held before him how great a benefit one would do for all Christendom by doing away with a single man who, to the ruin of many, acted as master <note>This refers to Prince Maurice of Orange, the military leader of the Dutch Republic</note>. This had stirred and inflamed his spirit, now dejected by torment, to murder Prince Maurice. He was also moved by the fact that they promised a reward for him and his son, and even promised him heaven should the attempt fail. Furthermore, he was egged on by his own wife who, restless from many worries and impatient in adversity, demanded that he carry out the deed manfully. Thus driven forward, and confirmed in his intention by the Superior of the Jesuits with the administration of the Sacrament and the remission of sins, he had—after receiving some travel money—come to Zeeland, and from there to Leiden. But as his conscience regarding the evil undertaking gradually surfaced, along with the terror of the danger, his mind was slowly drawn away from the evil and brought to better thoughts. Since he frequently repeated this story in bursts, convicted by his own testimony, he was finally sentenced to death by the verdict of the Magistrates <term>Schepenen; the local judicial and administrative officers of a city</term> of the city of Leiden, and with the approval of the Delegated Councillors of the States of Holland and the Courts of Justice. On the twenty-second of June <note>original: "Somermaendt," literally 'Summer-month'</note>, he was beheaded and quartered. This history made the spirit of the Jesuits all the more known.

At the beginning of the year fifteen hundred and ninety-nine, one saw in Deventer, in Overijssel, how far a mad zeal, stirred up by hatred and anger, can lead someone. A certain Roman Catholic citizen, Hendrik van Achtervelt, driven by those evil counselors, targeted one of the city's ministers, Franciscus Schurrichman. On a Sunday, the twenty-first of January <note>original: "Loumaendt"</note>, as the minister was walking home from the church between two citizens after finishing his sermon, Achtervelt followed him from behind, attacked him unexpectedly, and stabbed him in the neck with a double-edged knife so that it came out through his mouth, touching his tongue. From this, the minister fell to the ground and died shortly thereafter. The murderer immediately fled out of the church and the city but was pursued on horseback and captured by the officers of the court. They sought to discover his inciters and accomplices through torture; however, he said that he had undertaken the deed of his own accord, without anyone's knowledge, because the minister had spoken against the Pope, and he called it a meritorious work. He was thereafter punished with death as a murderer, serving as an example to others.

The sect of the Puritans or Brownists arrived from England.
</margin>
Around this time, and also earlier, a new denomination came over from England which, wishing to purify the Reformation, separated itself from the other Reformed believers. These people, driven out by Queen Elizabeth and called Puritans because of their alleged purity—or Brownists after Robert Browne, one of the first founders of this sect—settled mostly in Leiden and Amsterdam. The primary reasons for their separation can be seen from ten Articles which they presented to someone who had previously been an Elder of their congregation, but who was at that time the Sub-rector of the Latin School on the old side of the city and a member of the public church, seeking to draw him back to them.
