Thus this century drew to a close, and people found themselves in the churches of these lands still far from the objective they had proposed for themselves in the rejection of the Roman Papacy. They had to struggle not only with the remaining Papists <note>The term used is "Pausgesinden," referring to those loyal to the Pope, or Roman Catholics.</note> (who diligently employed all sorts of ruses to keep their old followers and attract new ones), but they also found themselves in mutual disagreement with so many other denominations. Each of these walked on a particular footing along separate paths, without meeting one another in any way. The wisest saw well where this was headed and fought to bring matters to a better footing with propriety; yet the current of vehemence was too strong for them. One had to wait for better times and better men. Meanwhile, there were those at this time who burst out in their letters with such complaints and wishes:

<margin>Ecclesiastical Letters, p. 111. <note>original: "Epistolae ecclesiasticae"</note></margin>
> *How could anyone rejoice who—besides the general godlessness that reigns over the entire earth—now perceives even in the church of Christ, in Christendom itself, that there is such a great diversity of opinion on the matter of Religion: that among all kinds of people, some dare to break out so wantonly and cast out everything they think against the truth: that many, who have authority among their own, dare to prescribe and impose whatever they please upon Christendom as necessary articles of faith with such boldness and vehemence. And certainly, while I contemplate these things, my soul melts within me, and is snatched away and tormented by such a great urge of various thoughts that, not knowing what to do in this clamor, it finds itself forced to cry out to its God: Give, Lord, peace to your Israel; peace be within her walls, prosperity within her palaces. <note>A paraphrase of Psalm 122:7</note> Heal the blows and wounds of Joseph; so that the brothers and kinsmen, bound together by a bond of sincere love and of truth—necessary for your honor and the salvation of men—may speak your praise in your house, from generation to generation.*

the two most prominent and greatest Apostles, Peter and Paul, to whom John—whom Jesus loved above the others—is added, had labored to establish, teach, instruct, and complete the same [church]. Through this, it became the Apostolic See, perhaps even the only one in the West, and consequently the mother and teacher of many churches. For this expansion and propagation of the Christian religion, the power and majesty of the Roman Empire, which had its seat in this city, was highly useful (Ibid § 2, 4, 5..) Because of this, the authority of its Bishops grew over time, not by any divine right, but by custom or concession, and human right—partly the ecclesiastical law of the Councils, and partly the secular law of the Emperors—regarding the particular but worldly power of the city of Rome. In the 9th Chapter of the same book, de Dominis <note>Marc'Antonio de Dominis (1560–1624), an Italian Archbishop who defected to Protestantism and wrote "De Republica Ecclesiastica."</note> describes by what privileges or rights the Bishop of Rome excels above other Bishops. Ant. de Dominis in the 8th chapter of his 4th Book, p. 643. Read also *Erasmus's* Letters p. 1611 c; p. 167 B. Posterity should know how, not even thirty years ago, one had to hide oneself so carefully to read a Bible translated into the common language, just as one hides to strike counterfeit coins or to commit some other crime, which is even greater. At that time, one applied to many Teachers of the church what Christ said in Matthew 23, verse 13: for they themselves would not read the Bible, nor would they allow others to read it. He also testifies that an old Doctor, one of the most esteemed, used to say openly: *I am surprised that these young people bring us the New Testament: I swear to you by God that I had become more than fifty years old and did not know what the New Testament meant.* He also tells of a Bible translated into French by the clergy according to their own liking, and augmented with the gloss, or interpretation, of Orleans—that is to say, one that corrupted the text. Indeed, they had not placed the gloss in the margin, but mixed it into the text itself. By this means, they made it agree with the abuses and errors of the Roman church. This hodgepodge that they inserted in between was called an "antidote" for the laity, so that they would not be poisoned by errors; but it might better have been called poison. But Guillaume de Saint-Amour and others who had opposed it were afterwards branded as heretics by the Pope and, at his insistence, banished.

That one should therefore give the first place in teaching to them (the Teachers); nonetheless I do not see, he added, why one should keep the *unlearned or laity* away from the *Holy Scriptures*, especially the *Gospels*, and the *secular people* away from the holy things, which scriptures are brought to light as much for the unlearned as for the learned, for *Greeks* as for *Scythians*, for *slaves* as for *free men*, for *women* as for *men*, and as much for the *common people* as for *Kings*. That which they teach concerns all equally; that which they promise concerns each just as much. Also, they were brought to light in such a way that they are much sooner understood

<column-break/>

by a *god-fearing, modest man*, than by a *conceited philosopher*. It is characteristic of the *Jews*, who turned toward shadows <note>Referring to the ceremonial laws of the Old Testament.</note>, that they hid their secrets from the people. The *Gospel* light may not suffer itself to be extinguished. <note>The Dutch text is cropped here; "verdre / de" likely completes as "verdonkerde" (darkened) or "verdreven" (driven away).</note> See also Erasmus's letters p. 106[...], 1070 A B, 1071: and the ninth volume of his works <note>original: "ix ftuk fijn [wer]ken"</note> p. 909. Read also Marc'Antonio de Dominis <note>original: "M. Ant. D."</note>, book VII of *The Ecclesiastical Republic* <note>original: "de Repub. This seems to me to be entirely intolerable. But the coarse people, being blind led by the blind, would not [heed] the *Papal* shameful *excommunication*, which they [ignorantly] and foolishly fear, if they read the *Scripture* in a common and for them understandable language. All the heretics have [mis]used it... should they therefore be rooted out, or kept so locked up and hidden in [secrecy] that they are open to no one? That would be a madness, and one far more dangerous than the [original] sickness. A hundred, a thousand, and ten [thousand] shall draw great [benefit] from this *Scripture*, instead of one [misusing] the same. For the simple shall easily [see] and notice things which are clear and [evident]; those which are more difficult, they shall leave to the learned, and those with a [humble spirit]...

...break? <note>This continues the thought from the previous page, quoting the early Christian author Tertullian.</note> Or would the Moors, and Marcomanni, even the Parthians, or whichever and however many nations they might be, nevertheless be a people of a single place and restricted to their own borders, greater than the vast population of the entire world? Only the temples have we left to you. For what war would we not have been capable and ready, even with unequal power—we, who allow ourselves to be killed so willingly? If according to this teaching it were no longer permitted to be killed rather than to kill? Indeed, we could have fought against you even unarmed and without being rebellious, simply by separating ourselves from you. For if we, such a great multitude of people, had torn ourselves away from you to some remote corner of the world, the loss of so many citizens, of whatever kind they were, would surely have struck your judgment, passed against us, with shame; indeed, it would even have punished you through that abandonment. Doubtless the loneliness, the silence of the accused, and a certain daze arising from it, would have made you shudder: you would have been forced to look for people to rule over in the remains of a death-like city. More enemies than citizens would have remained for you.

## NOTES.

...force may be resisted with force, and that through the right of war one may resist the persecution of heathens or heretics if one has the power to do so, De Dominis <note>Marc'Antonio de Dominis (1560–1624), an Archbishop who wrote extensively on church-state relations</note> says, among other noteworthy things: "That a believer may indeed provide for his safety through flight and avoid persecution is, in my view, beyond doubt; for I have fully learned that as much from the Holy Scriptures as from the actions and defense of Athanasius <note>St. Athanasius of Alexandria, a 4th-century bishop who frequently fled from Arian persecutors</note>. But that one may resist one's own legitimate Prince with force and weapons when he is a persecutor of the faith—this I have not learned until now. Above all, I have not yet been able to convince myself that clergy, as ministers of Christ, have the right by virtue of their office and authority to take up or stir up arms against the persecutors of the faith to offer such resistance. I know the saying of Nazianzenus <note>St. Gregory of Nazianzus, a 4th-century theologian</note>, who speaks thus of Julian the Apostate <note>The Roman Emperor who attempted to roll back Christianity and restore paganism</note>: 'He is nonetheless constrained by the grace of God and the tears of the Christians, which were then shed in great number and by many, since they had no other remedy against the persecutor...' (Nonetheless, almost his entire military force consisted of Christians. *) If tears and patience, he says thereafter, are the only remedy, then there are no weapons, no violence, no depositions <note>original: "afsettingen," referring to the removal of a monarch from their throne</note>, no withdrawal of obedience and loyalty." Truly, the argument of Bellarmine <note>Cardinal Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621), a leading figure of the Counter-Reformation who argued for the Pope's power to depose heretical kings</note> arms heretical subjects against Catholic Princes who trouble those same heretics with physical persecution just as much as it arms Catholic subjects against heretical Princes. And by this same reasoning, all rebellions in general, even the most unjust, are incited, nurtured, and defended... for evil

<column-break/>

people, having the power to resist justice with force, will likewise say that they are being unjustly persecuted. * Those who were listeners to the Apostles, wrote Andreas Duditius to Beza <note>Theodore Beza was the successor of John Calvin in Geneva; Duditius was a diplomat and humanist who advocated for religious tolerance</note>, brought forth for the most part fruits worthy of the Gospel and of conversion... Neither did they publicly arm the people, nor establish that the matter of Religion should be advanced with war and weapons. Shall we say that those who do this are teaching and doing that which is consistent with the teaching of Christ and the Apostles? ...I pray you, take good note, wrote A. Albada <note>Aggeus de Albada (c. 1525–1587), a Frisian jurist and advocate for religious peace</note> to Master Adriaen van der Mijle (in *Selected Letters* p. 631, 632), of the passage in Revelation XVI, chapter 13... By those spirits are undoubtedly meant the Teachers of the Sects, who are accustomed to teach that one must take up arms for Christ’s kingdom, or who seek the protection of the secular arm <note>The "secular arm" refers to the use of state military or legal force to enforce religious doctrine</note> within Christ’s kingdom. And somewhat further (p. 633 and 634): "I would also very much like to hear from you which is that little flock of Christ, and what its nature is—whether it consists of sheep or of wolves. Who also its Shepherd might be, and what weapons he would use, in what world and for what causes he would fight. One ought not to hoodwink oneself into taking entire provinces, factions, and I know not what kind of people for Christ’s flock without judgment. I say to you freely that I do not count any of the Teachers, nor the pupils who advise or take up arms for Religion, among the number of Christ’s flock. May the Lord have mercy on the ignorance of some. I remain silent on what is done politically for the civil welfare by the politicians. I speak only of that which is done by Christians for the sake of Christ...

Page 64, line 23. *AND these things are intolerable heresies.* ] In that same letter where Erasmus spoke thus, he further makes himself heard in this manner:
> (p. 588) For all sorts of minor reasons, people immediately have it on their tongues: IT IS HERESY. In ancient times, a person was considered a heretic who did not agree with the Gospels, the articles of faith, or those things which had attained equal authority with them. And now, if someone at any time differs from Thomas Aquinas <note>Thomas Aquinas was a highly influential 13th-century theologian whose works became central to Catholic doctrine</note>, or if someone deviates from the fabricated reasoning which many a young Sophist <note>In this context, a student or scholar who uses clever but fallacious arguments</note> has invented in the schools, he is called a heretic. Whatever does not please them, whatever they do not understand, is heresy; knowing Greek is heresy, speaking a polished language is heresy; whatever they do not do themselves is heresy. I admit the crime of breaching the faith is grave, but it is not fitting to drag everything into a dispute of faith. And those who handle matters of faith must be entirely removed from all types of political ambition, greed, hatred, and desire for revenge. But who is there who does not see what these people are plotting? If one ever gives free rein to their lusts, they will begin to rage everywhere, even against the lives of the very best men.

Page 92, line 38. **HAD** married his own wife.] Various teachers of early Christianity highly commended the unmarried state to the clergy as being fitting and useful for the performance of their office, yet they could never command it as a divine decree expressed in the Holy Scriptures. On the contrary, there are many weightier reasons to recommend marriage to the Bishops or Overseers of the churches: not only as something very useful, but also as highly necessary to avoid much evil, offense, and sin—indeed, it is sufficiently commanded in 1 Timothy 3:2, 4 and Titus 1:6. See *Marc'Antonio de Dominis, On the Ecclesiastical Republic, book 2, chapter 10.* <note>Marc'Antonio de Dominis was an archbishop who famously defected to the Anglican church before returning to Rome; his works were highly controversial.</note> Consequently, the entire Eastern Church has also left their ministers free in this matter: he who could receive it (*Matthew* 19:12) might receive it, yet such "receiving" was not commanded. But what was the consequence? That some voluntarily and honorably practiced abstinence; but many availed themselves of honorable marriage. In the West, by contrast, the Papacy prescribed laws of abstinence to the Clergy; yet these laws, although marriage had to be forsaken, were observed by few. So much so that someone, speaking of the ancients, says: **Brothels are placed above the marriage bed.**

<column-break/>

*M. A. de Dominis, page 292 D.* Also, Pope Pius II (previously known as Aeneas Sylvius) was heard to say *that for many reasons priests had been deprived of their married wives, but that there now seemed to be even more reasons to give them back.* (Platina, in the *Life of Pius II*). Since then, Emperor Maximilian II also did not shrink from asserting, in a concise writing sent to Pope Pius IV, that the marriage of the clergy ought to be tolerated with some indulgence. *See Jacques Auguste de Thou, History of His Own Time, book 36, at the end.* Read further *Martin Bucer, Commentary on the Gospel of Matthew, chapter 19, page 400; Georg Cassander, Works, page 989; Daniel Chamier, The Catholic Panstratia, book 16; Martin Chemnitz, Examination of the Council of Trent, page 454; Conrad Vorstius, Part 2 of the Fourteen Books Against Pistorius, chapter 13, page 440;* and *Simon Episcopius, True Antiquity, page 48.* But if we wish to know until what time the clergy in the West retained and practiced the freedom to marry, as well as when and how the law to remain unmarried (which was long struggled against) was gradually introduced and finally forced upon them, one should read *Nicolas Vignier’s Ecclesiastical History*, including pages 72, 73, 80; 94; 98; 111; 117; 130; 148; 156; 169; 178; 184; 220; 234; 241; 248, 249; 253; 277, 278, 279, 281, 282; 286; 292; 310; 313, 314, 315; 337, 338; 345; 347; 350, 351; 370; 393, 394; 425: and especially *M. A. de Dominis, book 2, chapter 10, section 42, page 306.*

Page 93, line 14 **NOT** wanting to establish anything other than what was expressed in Holy Scripture.] Grotius <note>Hugo de Groot, known as Grotius, a Dutch jurist and theologian famous for his work on international law</note> asks in his *Dialogue on Baptism*, at the end of the *Proof of the True Religion*, page 109:

Pope Clement VIII wrote, at one time, while he served the legation of the Roman See in Poland, a certain letter to the King, by which he begged him, *That he should give no offices or dignities to heretics, assuring him at once that this was, after God, the most powerful means to convert them.* Since then, the Pope told this to Cardinal d'Ossat, and added further that the King had followed his advice, found it effective, and thanked him many times, for a great number of grandees had converted. ...men, through exhortation, advice, and prayer, and openly—as much as the honor of God and the salvation of mankind requires, where it is necessary and appropriate—to testify which articles and points he cannot agree with in the church and which, in his judgment, require improvement, especially the most important ones. Meanwhile, he should above all improve in himself that which he judges as evil in others. This befits the nature of the Christian Religion, rather than using violence and introducing Reformation through riot or weapons, or seizing control of churches, driving out false worship, and forcing improvement through coercion. The public churches belong to the Magistrate <note>The civil authorities or local government</note>; they may give them to whom they will and take them from those who have forfeited them. But if things are done in, through, and on behalf of the public church with which one may have no communion, then one must withdraw. Or, if the pointing out of defects and the seeking of improvement—in such a gentle manner as just described—is not tolerated, and the one who points them out is cut off and cast out, then he must suffer it. Outside of the public temples, he must seek Christian assemblies or Christians who are more teachable, flexible, and pious, and practice external worship and maintain spiritual fellowship with them. Yet, before one departs from any congregation, whether from public or other churches, one must take care not to reject any church or assembly too lightly. Even if one is cut off or cast out, one should not too easily imagine that the bond of spiritual brotherhood is thereby entirely broken. "Let no one say," writes Optatus of Milevis <note>original: "Optatus Milevitanus". A common Roman shout during persecutions, demanding that Christians be thrown to lions or other wild animals in the arena.</note>. Page 172, line 11. **SNATCHED FROM him the consecrated bread.]** When one, during such bloody persecutions, was discovered through an inquisition, betrayed by spies, or caught in any prohibited—yet religious and necessary for the maintenance of outward Worship—gatherings, and came into suffering because of the performance of one’s duty or office, then one had to add virtue to necessity and be truly patient. One had to remain steadfast in the understanding they had chosen as best, without allowing themselves to be led astray by any worldly insights, neither by death nor life, into changing or feigning their Religion against their better knowledge. This was well in accord with the content and requirements of the Gospel, the nature of Christianity, and the zeal, sincerity, and perseverance of the first Christians. However, that some undertook matters under the very eyes of the persecutors, whereby they knowingly and willingly walked into certain death—not through the certain knowledge of some clear command of God or Christ, but driven by an impulse which, though accompanied by a quiet mind, was somewhat religious yet at the same time uncommanded, untimely, and imprudent—some cannot consider such actions as necessary or praiseworthy as that other patience of the steadfast Christians. Professor S. Episcopius <note>Simon Episcopius (1583–1643) was a prominent Dutch theologian and a leader of the Remonstrants.</note>, speaking in his sermon on Matthew 5, verse 10, page 169, regarding what is required to suffer well, says among other things: “There must be added a good conscience, which rests upon a good and well-grounded science, or

<column-break/>

knowledge <note>The author is playing on the etymology of the word "conscience" (from the Latin *conscientia*), which literally means "knowledge with" or "shared knowledge."</note>; that is, upon certain reasons that convince our mind that what we profess, and why we suffer, is righteousness—that is, it is good and pleases God. Peter also makes this known in his first letter in Chapter II, verse 19, and in Chapter III, verses 16 and 21. That is grace, when someone suffers for the sake of a conscience toward God, or a divine conscience; that is, to keep one’s conscience pure and not to act against it, since it is regulated according to God's will, and God knows that it is good, or because his mind knows with God that that for which he suffers is good. Where there is a conscience, there is *scientia*, or knowledge with another; where then there is a conscience of God, there is a science or knowledge with God, in such a manner that just as God knows why, we also know with God why it is that we suffer. Now, for this knowledge to be firm and certain, it must look to two things: 1. whether the cause is good, and 2. whether it is so worthy or weighty that one is obligated to suffer for it. Both must be present: the first, so that one does not suffer for that which is evil or forbidden, even if one thinks otherwise; the second, so that one does not suffer for a matter that is not commanded. For the first, one ought not to suffer; for the second, one need not suffer. As an example: had Peter come into suffering because he cut off the ear of Malchus <note>Refers to the scene in the Garden of Gethsemane where Peter strikes the servant of the High Priest; Jesus heals the ear and rebukes the use of the sword (John 18:10-11).</note>, he would not have suffered for righteousness. It is true, he certainly thought that he might and should defend his innocent, blameless master, whose cause he knew was good and righteous; but it was not only not commanded of the disciples, but rather forbidden, to defend their master with violence in such a way. When he later came into the peril of suffering, when he followed Christ his Lord into the courtyard of the High Priest, that was no unrighteousness.”

### D 3

Stanislaus Hosius, Bishop of Warmia in Prussia (who later, having become a Cardinal, was one of the Papal Presidents at the Council of Trent) [praises] the Anabaptists <note>original: "Wederdoopers"; a radical Reformation group that practiced adult baptism and was heavily persecuted by both Catholics and other Protestants.</note> above the Lutherans and Zwinglians. I do not use these names to insult anyone, but only out of necessity. The spirit of schism created the need to speak this way to be understood. But it has often pained me that people, baptized in Christ's name, are called anything other than Christians. Of the Anabaptists, then, Hosius testifies in his book on heresies (f. 33 a) *That they ran to all kinds of punishments, however cruel they might be, as if to a joyful feast.* He also says that Calvin has no reason to highly exalt himself and his followers, or to place them above the Lutherans, on the grounds that they were more prompt and willing to endure all kinds of punishments. For, he adds (f. 34 a), *if the truth of someone’s faith must be considered as tested and certain as they are ready to die for the faith of their sect, then no faith will be more certain or true than that of the Anabaptists; since there are none, nor have there been any for twelve hundred years past, from whom heavier punishment has been demanded, and who gave themselves up to it more courageously, steadfastly, and alertly—even to the most cruel death.* But he had said before (f. 33 b), in order to strip the Anabaptists of the honor of martyrdom: *Though I give my body to be burned, and have not charity, it profiteth me nothing* (1 Cor. XIII, 3.) <note>St. Paul’s famous passage on love/charity; Hosius argues that because they left the "unity" of the Church, they lack the necessary love for true martyrdom.</note> *Yet whoever breaks unity does not have charity.* This stain of sin—even if, as Cyprian <note>St. Cyprian of Carthage (c. 210–258 AD), an early Christian bishop and martyr.</note> says, such people were killed in the confession of Christ's name—is not even washed 

<column-break/>

away. *He who is not in the church cannot be a martyr; he cannot come to the kingdom who leaves her who shall reign.* <note>Referring to the Church as the Queen or Bride of Christ.</note> *The Lord himself was crucified with murderers, but while the suffering joined them, the cause [for which they suffered] separated them.* To this was also added the saying of Augustine, *That the cause, not the punishment, makes the martyr.* <note>original: "Martyrem non facit poena, sed causa"; a key theological argument that simply dying for a belief does not make one a saint unless the belief itself is the orthodox truth.</note> Thus far Hosius. 

However, on all this, it remains to be examined: 
I. Whether the Anabaptists, and other Reformed Christians, bear as much guilt for the schism as the Papacy <note>original: "Pauſdom"; a term referring to the Roman Catholic institutional system.</note>, which first departed from much truth and cast out those who wished to better the evil? See the Note on p. 60, l. 26. 
II. Whether the Catholic <note>Used here in the sense of the "Universal" or "Whole" Church, rather than specifically Roman Catholic.</note> Church does not extend further than the boundaries of the Roman congregation? See the Note on p. 150, l. 19. Read also J. Ussher’s <note>James Ussher (1581–1656), Archbishop of Armagh, known for his vast historical and theological knowledge.</note> Sermon on Eph. IV, 13, regarding the catholicity or universality of the church and the unity of faith. 
III. Whether the Anabaptists, who confessed and lived according to the most important articles of the Christian Religion—even if they also suffered for some errors—should for that reason not be considered martyrs, or, what goes further, may be damned. 

Certainly, says G. Cassander <note>George Cassander (1513–1566), a Flemish theologian known for his "irenic" or peace-seeking approach to reconciling Catholics and Protestants.</note>, in these people (he spoke of the Anabaptists) two things are often observed: one, a certain intense zeal, and fear of God, and very great reverence and observance of His word. *The other, a wandering from the true sense of Holy Scripture, to which they were brought by some apparent probability: this latter is pitiable, but the former is also worthy of praise and recommendation.* The separation from the common brotherhood of the church is indeed a grave matter, but one must also place that among the errors; and oh, if only we ourselves did not give them great occasion for it. In his Works p. 1146. See also p. 1202. I hold,

...wisdom were estranged, most clearly in his own writings. To heal the defects of the church, he spoke of five parts, which he brought down to two principal chapters, of which the first concerned public, and the second, private healing. Public healing, he wrote to *Johannes Molinæus* <note>Jean Moulin (1500–1563), a French theologian and legal scholar who corresponded with moderate reformers.</note> (in his *Works* p. 1099) comprised three parts or special chapters. The first: That the abuses and scandals in the morals of the Clergy and the people be taken away, and the doctrine of both states <note>The "two states" refers to the clergy and the laity.</note> be restored according to the Evangelical rule and the ancient Canons; and that especially those who teach others and surpass them in dignity, should themselves live out the innocence, justice, and godliness that they command. Finally, that all who are considered to be of the Christian confession should express through their own lives and morals the purity and holiness of the Christian Religion—which consists mostly of mutual love—and, as the church sings, reject such things that conflict with this, and pursue those things that are conducive to it. Regarding this chapter, which consists of the necessary Reformation of the Church concerning morals and discipline, very many have written, especially *Guiljelmus Durantes* <note>William Durand (c. 1230–1296), a medieval canon lawyer nicknamed "The Speculator."</note>, commonly called the *Speculator*, throughout his writing *On the Manner of Holding a General Council*; *Petrus de Alliaco* <note>Pierre d'Ailly (1350–1420), a French cardinal and influential theologian at the Council of Constance.</note>, in the booklet *On the Improvement of the Church*; *Mattheus of Kraków* <note>Mateusz z Krakowa (c. 1335–1410), a reformer and rector at the University of Prague.</note> *On the Blemishes and Filth of the Church*; *Jacobus de Paradiso* <note>Jacobus of Paradies (c. 1381–1465), also known as Jacob of Jüterbog, a Cistercian and later Carthusian known for his reformist writings.</note>, first Abbot of the Cistercians, then *Carthusian of St. Theodoricus*, *On the Seven States of the Church*, described in the *Revelation*, and *On the Authority of the Church and Her Reformation*, also *On the Errors and Morals of Christians*, which writings are preserved here among the Carthusians; *Petrus, Bishop of Orvieto* <note>Pietro del Monte (c. 1400–1457), a Venetian jurist and bishop.</note> throughout his short *Explanations of the Pontifical of Damascus*;

...as one sees fit, one should preach sharply and forcefully; but that toward the people themselves, who are subject to the errors, one should show a Christian and brotherly gentleness and love. But private healing has two main parts. *The 1st consists of a faithful instruction and brotherly admonition, namely, that one should instruct those found to be adhering to any public heresy with very great gentleness and brotherly love, not terrifying or compelling them with surliness and authority. The 2nd consists in such a restraint, which at once turns away the infection from others, and allows the erring time for improvement; which manner of proceeding in the handling of heretics,* Optatus of Milevis <note>A 4th-century Bishop known for his writings against the Donatist schism.</note> *followed against* Parmenianus *and the* Donatists, *and seems to have approved.* Elsewhere he compares heresy to a long-lasting and severe sickness, which is entirely rooted in the bowels, and just as it was gradually gathered, is very difficult to drive out, and requires a slow and careful healing. *Thus, he says, in the healing of this soul-sickness, persistence and time are necessary. Add to this, that in this matter (it was desired that he should dispute with some imprisoned* Anabaptists <note>original: *Doopsgeſinden*. A radical reform group often persecuted by both Catholics and other Protestants.</note>) *above all, the Holy Spirit, whose proper work it is to drive out errors and to plant the truth, must be allowed to do His office; to wish to prescribe certain boundaries to His working is godless and blasphemous.* See his *Works* p. 1145. He also disapproved of the killing of Servetus <note>Michael Servetus (1511–1553), a Spanish physician and theologian executed in Geneva for heresy, a flashpoint for debates on religious tolerance.</note>, and openly opposed the killing of heretics. Read his *Works* p 1087; 456, 457; 1146; 1089; 886; 672; 1152, 1153. When some zealous Papists <note>original: *Pauſgeſinden*, meaning those loyal to the Pope; Catholics.</note> accused him of "limping on both sides" <note>A biblical idiom from 1 Kings 18:21, meaning to waver between two opinions or stay on the fence.</note>, he wrote on September 16 of the year 1565, a few months before his death, (for he passed

away on February 3 of the following year) a certain letter, which is to be found in his *Works*, in which he expressed his mind and defended himself, judging both the Protestants and their doctrine with great discretion.

> It is, thus he spoke, (p. 1212.) far from the case that I should "limp on both sides," that is, hang in doubt in the middle between the Catholic faith and heretical or schismatic unbelief; since I frankly confess to acknowledge no other church than that instituted by Christ, established by the Apostles throughout the whole world, and continued down to us. But all assemblies that slander the same church in a hateful and hostile manner—even though she is not entirely deformed <note>The author uses *gedefformeert*, acknowledging that the Church had lost its original "form" but was still the true Church.</note> and corrupted from her first form—and avoid all her communion as antichristian, and presumptuously attribute the name of "church" to themselves alone, I loathe and reject. Although I also acknowledge this, that in that field of the Catholic church the wheat is mixed with tares <note>A reference to the Parable of the Weeds in Matthew 13:24-30.</note>, and that threshing floor of the Lord is not yet entirely cleansed of chaff: nonetheless I feel with Cyprian <note>St. Cyprian of Carthage (c. 210–258), an early Christian writer who emphasized church unity.</note> that even if there appear to be tares in the church, one must not for that reason depart from the church. And I hold with Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430), whose theology dominated Western Christianity.</note>, that one may not leave the threshing floor of the Lord because of the chaff. Likewise in the faith, that under the title of the Catholic faith, Pharisaic leaven <note>A biblical metaphor for hypocrisy or corrupting legalism.</note> can also hide, against which every godly person must be on guard; and he who guards himself against it, should not for that reason be said to depart from the purity of the Catholic church: it is also beyond doubt for me, that Religion, like all other virtues, is situated in the middle of two extremes, that is, between Pharisaic superstition...

In a certain letter to Cassander (*Select Letters, p. 175*), he agreed, ,, *That one should rather, by bringing back the old Canons or rules of faith, and correcting the corrupt morals and customs of the clergy, purify God's church from heresy and restore it to its former luster and integrity, rather than by the other way that has been followed almost until now. Select Letters, p. 175.* <note>original: *Epiſt. Select. p 175*</note> And ,, *alas*," he wrote in that same letter, ,, *if the matter could be brought so far that, on the one hand, the bad morals of the clergy were removed, and on the other hand, those hateful and far too stubborn and entirely unnecessary questions and disputes, the pious on both sides might then devote themselves entirely to those things in which our true salvation consists. And even if some oppose this moderation very vehemently, we must nonetheless not deviate from our duty, but rather proceed against them all the more boldly. For the entire victory lies in this: that one unites the opponents with us, not through violence or through fear, but through kindness and benevolence. This shall, I believe, with God’s help, easily happen if they understand that we are no less enemies of the bad morals of our own people than of the bad opinions of the opposing parties. When it is added to this that they begin to notice how true Religion consists not in the subtlety of disputes and of manifold questions, but only in piety toward God and Christ, and love toward men: then I trust that they will not resist much longer, but will let go of their idle and superfluous opinions and betake themselves to the true church, having been purified and restored.*"

THE ARIANS now seem to have vanished from the world, which then proved almost too small for them.** Erasmus <note>Desiderius Erasmus, the famous Dutch humanist and theologian.</note> says in the Preface to the third volume of the *Works of Jerome*: The heresy of the Arians <note>Arianism: A 4th-century Christian movement that argued Jesus Christ was a created being, subordinate to God the Father, rather than being "of one substance" with Him.</note>, strengthened by learning and, so it seemed, supported by very strong proofs from Holy Scripture—furthermore aided by the favor and riches of Emperors and nations—has shaken the Christian world with very dangerous disturbances: to the point that it remained long in doubt which way the simplicity of the church would turn, and whether it would be more a faction or schism than a heresy. > *If anyone should break idols and be killed for it, we do not think it right that they be received into the number of Martyrs, because [the breaking of images] is not written in the Gospel, nor is it found to have ever been done by the Apostles.* <note>original: "Indien iemant afgodtsbeelden quaeme te breken... wesen." <column-break/>

zeal in this regard is unpraiseworthy, and adds:

> *one ought to wait here for the command of the Magistrate, although one finds that in our times such has often happened through a sudden zeal and God’s powerful driving.*

That it often happened in our fathers’ times through a sudden zeal, no one can deny; but that it happened precisely through God’s powerful driving would be difficult to prove. It is very dangerous for one to attribute any deeds, especially those occurring in a disorderly fashion, to God’s driving—and what is more, to God’s *powerful* driving. Thomas Müntzer and Jan van Leiden <note>Leaders of the radical Anabaptist movement known for violent uprisings in the 1530s.</note> convinced themselves, or at least those who listened to and believed them, that they were bringing the people to their feet by God’s driving to overrun lands and cities. To go safely, one tests their impulses and passions against reason, but above all against the Holy Scriptures, which contain God’s will. Everything that goes against that can come neither from God nor from what is good; it is much rather an inspiration and driving from that evil, cunning spirit, the liar and murderer of men from the beginning; who, by the breaking of order and the sowing of sedition, seeks to tear apart the kingdom of the Prince of Peace—which exists through order and obedience—to make it rebellious, and, through itself, bring it to ruin.

Those who say this, and at the same time lament it, may no more be said to lean toward Popery <note>A historical, often derogatory term for Roman Catholicism.</note> than one can charge this to the entire English Church: whose reform, begun not by private unrest, but with public counsel and authority, kept such moderation that it took away what ought to be taken away, but left remaining what could be left without godlessness and superstition. De Dominis <note>Marcus Antonius de Dominis (1560–1624), an archbishop who famously defected to Protestantism and then returned to Catholicism, seeking a middle way.</note> also opposed those who, not so much out of zeal for the purity of faith as out of hatred and partisanship, daily busied themselves to depart more and more from the Roman Church, and called everything used therein "Antichristian." I confess, he says, (*Book VII of the Commonwealth of the Church, chapter VII, section VI, page 113*) <note>original: "Lib. VII. de Repub. Eccles. cap. VII. § VI. p. 113."</note> that in the Roman Church some things have crept in that are superfluous; some that are superstitious; also others that are Antichristian; but the Catholic <note>Here meaning the universal or historical Christian faith, rather than the specific Roman denomination.</note> faith is preserved among them uncorrupted; many customs are very old and established by the Apostles. Indifferent things <note>referring to "Adiaphora," or matters not essential to salvation.</note> can be improved, but ought not to be taken away, and meanwhile one must hold fast to the unity of Christendom. That which is deformed, let that be reformed, and that which is good, let it remain. Cassander <note>Georgius Cassander (1513–1566), a Flemish theologian who sought to reconcile Catholics and Protestants.</note> also sought to impress this opinion upon his reader with the words of Protestants; for in a certain

*...much more dangerous when it is less felt. Through that all-too-great sickness for strife, you do not notice that along with the truth, love is also lost. # ADDITIONS.

<margin>Namely Floris van Boeffelaer. From the documents and notes held by Mr. Cornelis Boot, Burgomaster of the city of Utrecht.</margin>
on behalf of the Leagued Nobles <note>The "Verbond der Edelen" was a coalition of Dutch nobles who organized in 1565 to resist the Spanish Inquisition</note> of Holland, had himself represented in the assembly at Sint-Truiden, where it was decided to take the Sectarians and Consistorians <note>Early Protestant organizational bodies</note> under their protection, and to that end to keep several thousand High German soldiers, both on foot and on horse, on retainer. It was further alleged that in his lordship of Langerak, in the land of Utrecht, he had introduced the forbidden sects and eradicated the old Roman Religion; and to that end had allowed several preachers, both Mennonites and Calvinists, to enter there; so much so that in a period of half a year no Mass had been performed, nor any other customary religious service practiced. Also, that he, together with his brothers at Asperen, had been present at the breaking of the images <note>The *Beeldenstorm* or Iconoclastic Fury of 1566</note> in the parish church and at the house of the Crutched Friars, that he had consented to it, and had even helped tear the books of that church.

<margin>Aleyd van Bronkhorst.</margin>
Aleyd van Bronkhorst and Batenburgh had, the sentence stated, favored the preachers, fed them in her house, harbored some, and frequently heard their sermons.

<margin>Jan van Renesse.</margin>
Her son Jan van Renesse, Lord of Wulp, had signed the aforementioned league and had been a leader of the image-breaking in Utrecht.

<margin>Philips van Renesse.</margin>
Philips van Renesse had greatly favored the Reformed <note>The name adopted by those following the Calvinist tradition</note> and, alongside their authorized representatives, had appeared before the States of Utrecht, requesting that they be granted a church, saying in the full assembly of the Magistrate, *that one must deal slowly with the matter of the unrest, without bloodshed*; and when the Magistrate denied him entry into their chamber, he had threatened them with the Lord of Brederode, and upon the refusal of the church, cried out with a loud voice: *“You have refused us a church; when we return you will be glad to grant it to us, and we shall see what we have to do with you, and in particular with you, Burgomaster Veckt.”*

<margin>Jan van Diest.</margin>
Jan van Diest, a Prosecutor, had refused the oath by which the maintenance of the Roman Religion had to be promised, saying, *that he wanted nothing to do with the Priests*, and thereby causing many of his neighbors to follow him in that refusal.

<margin>Jan Pijl.</margin>
Jan Pijl, formerly a Councilor of the city of Utrecht, had collected alms in the aforementioned sermons, had a child baptized in his house in the Calvinist manner, kept great company with the sectarians, and provided their preachers with an escort to the sermons.

<margin>Gillis Spaens.</margin>
Gillis Spaens, a knife-maker, had helped introduce the new preachers and helped break the images, and said to the Pastor of Saint Gertrude’s, *that he must preach the true Word of God*. Indeed, he did not shy away from saying to the assembly of the Magistrate, alongside others, *that they intended to proceed with the breaking of images begun the day before; that they would no longer tolerate the horrible idolatry used in the churches until now, and that the people had been misled long enough with the round God*—this is what he called the sacramental wafer <note>A derogatory term used by iconoclasts to mock the Catholic belief in the Real Presence of Christ in the Host</note>—followed by a further demand for a church and a brief answer.

<margin>Jan and Hendrik Gillis.</margin>
His sons, Jan and Hendrik Gillis, had started the breaking of the images. Herman Klaeszoon Brouwer had collected money in the aforementioned sermons, helped bring the preacher there, and furthermore sent a barrel of beer,
